20082-warrior-gap-a-story-of-the-sioux-o:
Warrior Gap tells a story of the Sioux outbreak of 1868, on the western frontier. A young lieutenant leads his column toward home after hard service. Barely two years an officer, he rides with a light heart. Each mile brings him closer to the home he longs for.

He had spent one hard year as a plebe at the military academy. At twenty-five, most of his years had seemed bright and glad. War on the plains will test that bright outlook soon enough. Readers get a frontier tale of troops, Sioux resistance, and a young man's trial.
4185-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-61-jan:
January 1667 to 1668 opens with Pepys in his chamber all morning, making up accounts against the new year. About noon he goes abroad with his wife, who is to dine with Hewer and Willet at Mrs. Pierce's, though he has no mind to join them.

He finds his wife troubled at his ways, and the volume follows a marriage under strain beside office work and inquiry. Accounts, dinners, and jealousies share the page. Readers get a new year that starts with sums and ends, as always with Pepys, in human complication.
4186-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-62-feb:
February 1667 to 1668 sends Pepys to the office pretty betimes, but the Board does not meet as soon as he wishes. Forced to Whitehall in expectation of a Tangier committee, he finds it put off and comes home to sit at the office till past two.

High words at the Board follow, in a month of delayed meetings and sharp talk. The volume follows inquiry winter, when committees slipped and tempers rose. Readers get Pepys waiting, walking, and arguing, in the diary's most procedural and human key. Put-off committees and high words mark an inquiry winter.
4187-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-63-mar:
March 1667 to 1668, a Lord's day, sends Pepys very betimes by coach to Sir William Coventry's, carrying all his notes and papers. There he runs over their whole defense in the business of tickets, in order to answer the House on Thursday next.

Pepys thinks the defense will hold unless the House judges without reason, a clerk's hope before a political storm. The volume follows the ticket inquiry, where sailors' pay became a parliamentary weapon. Readers see Pepys preparing, paper by paper, for a hearing that could end his career. Notes and papers, carried by coach, are his armor for Thursday.
4188-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-64-apr:
April 1668 finds Pepys dressing himself and calling, as he uses, Deb to brush and dress him, then working at his office till noon. Out to bespeak things against his wife's going into the country tomorrow, he comes home to dinner alone with her.

She is mighty busy getting her things ready, and the house hums with packing. The volume follows a household on the edge of a country trip, with office hours and domestic bustle side by side. Readers get a spring month of farewells, fittings, and a wife's departure.
4189-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-65-may:
May 1668 holds Pepys to office business all morning, then to Westminster Hall, where Sir William Pen labors to have his answer to impeachment read by the Commons. The Lords have sent it down, but the House is so busy on other matters that Pen cannot get a hearing.

The volume follows the Navy's men under parliamentary fire, with impeachments hanging over old officers. Pepys watches a colleague wait for a reading that never comes. Readers see Restoration politics as delay and procedure, where a man's name waits on a crowded agenda.
4190-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-66-jun:
June 1668 sends Pepys with Sir John Minnes to Westminster, where in the Hall he meets Harris and Rolt. He carries them to the Rhenish wine house, where he has not been in a morning, nor any tavern, these seven years and more.

There he gets the words of a song of Harris that he wanted, a small prize for a music-loving diarist. The volume mixes Hall business with tavern song, as Pepys returns to old haunts after years away. Readers will enjoy a summer month where a song matters as much as a committee.
4191-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-67-aug:
August 1668 fills Pepys's morning with office business, then after dinner to the King's house with his wife and Deb. Coming too late yesterday to hear the prologue, they like the play better now, finding true wit in it beyond the common sort.

The volume mixes office days with theater nights, as Pepys judges plays with the same care he gives accounts. His wife and Deb share the pit and the talk home. Readers get a summer of stage pleasure late in the diary, when Pepys still loved a good comedy.
4192-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-68-sep:
September 1668 keeps Pepys at the office all morning and again after dinner till about four, then abroad while his wife goes to Hales's about drawing her hand anew in her picture. He goes to see Betty Michell, but her husband is within, and there is no pleasure in the visit.

So to other company and home, in a month of work, portraits, and small disappointments. The volume follows late diary days, when office hours lengthen and pleasures narrow. Readers get Pepys near the end, still busy, still watching, still frank about a spoiled call.
4193-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-69-nov:
November 1668, a Lord's day, keeps Pepys with Hewer in his chamber all morning, going further into his great business for the Duke of York. At noon comes dinner, then Hewer writes fair what he had written, while Pepys's wife reads to him all afternoon.

Mr. Gibson joins them later, and the day closes in work and reading. The volume follows Pepys's late diary rhythm: dictation, fair copy, and a wife's voice reading aloud. Readers see the household as an office, with family labor carrying a Navy man's great business. Dictation, fair copy, and reading aloud fill the whole day.
4194-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-70-dec:
December 1668 keeps Pepys at the office all morning, at noon with his people to dinner, then at the office very busy till night. Home, he has his boy read to him Wilkins's Real Character, which pleases him mightily, and after supper he goes to bed with great pleasure and content.

The volume follows a working December lit by evening reading, as Pepys tests a scheme for a universal language. His content comes from work done and a book enjoyed, a quiet close to a hard year. Readers get Pepys the reader, ending days with ideas rather than accounts.
antony-and-cleopatra-pg2268: Enobarbus describes the barge in this edition: Cleopatra on the Cydnus, "the barge she sat in, like a burnished throne, burned on the water." The serpent of old Nile beguiles Antony to ruin. The richest love tragedy ever written.
arxiv-2412-00268:
Gengzhi He, Curtis Sparks, and Nicholas Gravish wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It builds a two-armed robot whose arms are tape springs that roll up tight for storage and unroll to grasp and roll objects on a flat field.

Stiff arms trade reach against packed size. A two-way tape spring packs small yet stands stiff when out, with far more buckle strength than a lone tape. In the rig, named GRIP-tape, the arms can shift and spin a load at once and ferry several loads in line. The springs are stiff yet soft to touch, so bumps are safe by build. Far fields such as space and deep sea are the aim.
arxiv-2412-01568:
H Dutra and a team report on Diomedes, a Jupiter Trojan asteroid, in a two thousand twenty-four paper. Trojans keep traits from the early solar system, and sizes trace the group that gave rise to the Kuiper Belt. In two thousand twenty, Diomedes passed in front of a star, catching three chords. The team fit a 3D shape model with no set size to those chords.

Its spin period is just under twenty-four and a half hours. The same-volume radius is fifty-nine point four kilometres, give or take zero point three. Pole angles are one hundred fifty-three point seven three degrees, give or take two point five, and twelve point six nine, give or take two point six. The surface bounces back three hundredths of the light hitting it, give or take four thousandths. A precise position was also found.
arxiv-2412-02368:
Leixin Zhang and eight co-authors test how well multimodal models draw scientific images from written prompts. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Image generators shine on everyday scenes, but science needs exact shapes, counts, and labels. Errors there can mislead students and researchers alike.

Their bench, ScImage, grades three skills: layout, number sense, and trait reading, plus mixes of them. Five models were tried, some answering with code and some with direct pictures. Prompts came in four languages, from English to Chinese. Eleven scientists scored the outputs for correctness, relevance, and scientific accuracy. The best model handled simple single-skill prompts passably. All models struggled as prompts combined skills. The bench exposes a real gap in today's generators.
arxiv-2412-04268:
Wenyang Li, Hanxiao Wang, and Jiongmin Yong prove that coupled forward backward Volterra integral equations are well posed. The drive comes from the optimality system of controlled forward Volterra equations. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The unknown pair takes two arguments, which sets these equations apart. By treating one argument as a fixed knob and the other as time, the system reads as differential equations with values in an endless space. A fresh non local monotonicity rule builds a bridge in that space. A continuation method, grown from classic work on differential equations, then yields existence and uniqueness, with a chain rule step at the core.
arxiv-2412-05368:
Michael Gnewuch, Klaus Ritter, and Robin Rüßmann pinned down error rates for averaging and fitting functions of very many variables in a 2024 paper. The function spaces use Gaussian kernels, a standard smooth setting, and algorithms may only sample function values. In the hardest case the number of variables is infinite, which arises in models with endless inputs.

For both averaging and least-squares fitting, they prove matching upper and lower bounds on how fast the best possible error shrinks as samples grow. For finitely many variables they improve known tractability results for averaging. A key bridge shows each Gaussian problem mirrors a Hermite-space problem with matched settings, letting results transfer. The bounds tell practitioners when high-dimensional sampling can succeed.
arxiv-2412-06668:
Rodi and seven co-authors reported in twenty twenty-four a short sky flash that may be a giant flare from a magnet star in a near galaxy. The flash lasted a fifth of a second and had a hard, high tone. Its spot on the sky was pinned by a coded mask tool on a space craft.

A near galaxy sits in the small error zone of that spot. At that far range the flash strength fits a giant flare from a magnet star well. Its time and tone traits match the few such flares seen past. A plain short burst is less apt, they argue.
arxiv-2412-06868:
Zhang, Cheng, Zhang, Liu, and Chen present a paper from twenty twenty-four on a theory for shrinking neural networks without losing skill. Compression usually trades size for accuracy in murky ways. Their framework defines a safe neighborhood where compression stays lossless. Differential math draws that boundary and higher-order limits around it. Quantization is recast as a grouped packing puzzle inside the safe zone. Decomposition gets automatic per-layer ranks from the same theory. Tests span many network types and datasets.

Lossless shrinkage is achieved without fancy tricks, they report. Efficiency rises alongside the size cuts. Code will be released in public. The authors frame the boundary idea as the missing systematic piece.
arxiv-2412-07768:
Hanxue Zhang and five co-authors present Test-time Correction, in a 2024 preprint, a system that fixes a self-driving car's 3D detector while it drives. Normal detectors are frozen after training, so their mistakes repeat. This system watches for risky objects and corrects errors on the spot, with no retraining. Help comes from side signals: clashes with 2D detections, road descriptions, or a user's click. An add-on module turns those signals into visual prompts, which are stored in a buffer for later frames.

The prompts steer the detector toward the objects it tends to miss. Across many tests, the system repaired errors far better than the frozen detectors it wrapped. Gains held with few labels, in unseen settings, and in bad weather. The authors hope the work starts a line of post-deployment repair tools. Cars, they argue, should keep learning from their own near misses.
arxiv-2412-08068:
Xin-Cheng Wen and five co-authors hunt silent security patches in software repositories in a 2024 paper. Vendors often fix vulnerabilities without announcements, so defenders must spot security patches among ordinary code changes. Older detectors look only at the patch itself, ignoring how the changed code connects across files and functions.

Their framework builds a graph of the whole repository, merging code from before and after the patch, then blends graph and sequence views of the changes. A staged learning scheme balances meaning and structure. On two standard datasets, expanded to tens of thousands of repository versions, the method beat six existing detectors and five graph learning models. The authors give the datasets and code a public release.
arxiv-2412-08568:
Akua Dickson and co-authors found a shortcut in 2024 for steering soft robots, whose floppy bodies make motion planning slow. A soft manipulator bends continuously, and computing control inputs for a desired path usually means solving nonlinear differential equations in a loop. The authors noticed that the standard piecewise constant curvature model of such robots can be differentially flat. A form in which every system factor is an algebra-based function of a few chosen outputs and their derivatives.

They prove flatness under stated conditions, with the segment curvatures as the flat outputs. Path generation then splits into two fast steps: inverse kinematics turns the wanted end-effector path into a curvature plan. And the flatness transformation converts that plan into control inputs respecting speed limits. In models along three paths, the planner ran more than twenty times faster than real time, fast enough to replan on the fly.
arxiv-2412-09068:
Shachar Shayovitz, Doron Ezri, and Yoav Levinbook worked on signal decoding in MIMO systems. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with systems that send many data streams at once in the same band. That trick boosts speed but the streams clash and noise builds up. Decoding them well is the hard part. This matters most for the uplink, from user to tower.

The team built a new decoding method that grows out of a known one. It models the messages passed in decoding with a mix of bell curves. That mix fits the true signal shape better when the old method fails. Readers get a way to decode dense, high order MIMO signals with more care.
arxiv-2412-10668:
Lee-Che Lin and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about entanglement between an electron and a qubit that moves past it. Their setup nests a quantum dot, a tiny trap for electrons, inside a larger structure. Exchange interaction, a quantum effect from overlapping spins, links the electron and the passing qubit.

The authors measure the link with mutual information. An electron lifted to a scattering state generally entangles more than one that stays bound. In the bound state, the final entanglement wavers with the qubit's speed and can be tuned by it. Long-range interaction gives strong entanglement regardless of direction, while short-range interaction depends on direction. Without the nested dot, the best possible link is fixed by the starting spin angle alone.
arxiv-2412-12268:
Manuel Goimil-Garcia, Shashank Shalgar, and Irene Tamborra ask a 2024 question about neutrinos in dense places such as dying stars. Neutrinos are ghostly particles that can swap flavor as they travel. In thick swarms, each neutrino's path is shaped by all the others, and studies usually treat that shared field as smooth, an approach called the mean-field approximation.

The authors test, in a rough exploratory way, whether a quantum rule called Pauli blocking changes the picture. That rule limits how neutrinos can pack into the same state when the swarm is degenerate. They find the corrections move the borders between stable and unstable flavor patterns. Some swarms that would flip flavor calm down, while some calm ones turn unstable. The work urges a closer look at the limits of the standard treatment.
arxiv-2412-16368:
Sergi Elizalde, Nadia Lafreniere, and colleagues count special set families in grid-shaped orders in a 2024 combinatorics study. An interval-closed set in a partially ordered set is one that traps everything between any two of its members. The authors study these sets in the product of two chains, a grid of points ranked by both coordinates.

A bijection to two-colored Motzkin paths, walks that never dip below the axis, yields a generating function for the count. For truncated rectangle orders, including a root poset from Lie theory, a bijection to walks in a quarter plane gives a functional equation instead. Bijection turns counting into walk enumeration.
arxiv-2501-00568:
Dimitris Bertsimas and Georgios Margaritis test if ChatGPT can do firm best fit work. That field deals with picks made when facts are not sure. With prompts made for the field, they walk the model through four steps. Step one frames a best fit task. Step two fits it to doubt named by the user. Step three works out the firm twin that can be solved. Step four makes code that solves it.

On plain tasks, ChatGPT did the steps with few flaws or none. The team also logs spots where steps went wrong, which keeps the read fair. Learn in the chat let the model fit a niche field. In that field its scores out of the box would be poor. The text is a probe of skill. It maps where a plain chat model can aid skilled staff now.
arxiv-2501-03068:
Junpeng Wang and five colleagues bring in SGLDBench, a benchmark for the design of stiff yet light three-dimensional structures, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Engineers want parts that use little material but flex just a bit under load. Many layout strategies claim that balance, yet no shared yardstick judges them.

The benchmark joins simulation and analysis in one frame, with six reference strategies so teams can compare work. A scalable multigrid elasticity solver runs the designs and checks how stiff they are. It backs a wide range of load cases and high-resolution designs. Visual tools link a design's shape to how stress spreads through it. Teams can now weigh material layout methods on mechanical performance in a fair way.
arxiv-2501-07968:
Comelli, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, builds a model of the cosmos in which the constant tied to dark energy shifts from place to place. The model forms a round bubble in space.

One fluid fills the model, with a dark energy part and a dark matter part. Comelli sets the spread rate of the cosmos to match the early value found by a space probe at young times, and the higher local value found near us. He works out near-solutions at the bubble's core and far out, where the cosmos looks smooth. He then draws rates of spread, red shift forms, and drifts over time for both cases.
arxiv-2501-08468:
Natarajan Balaji Shankar, Zilai Wang, Eray Eren, and Abeer Alwan merge speech models with care to sharpen child speech recognition, in work from twenty twenty-five. Big speech models shine on adult speech but falter on children's voices, since child data is scarce. Merging models trained on richer speech could fill the gap.

Their method, Selective Attention Merge, blends only the attention parts of task vectors from donor models. On a standard child speech database, word error rates fell by up to fourteen percent relative. The method beat older merging tricks and data augmentation alone. Combined with augmentation, it set a new best score for a small Whisper model on that database.
arxiv-2501-08968:
Gustavo C. Abade scrutinized simplified cloud models in 2025 and found a hidden flaw in how they spread out droplet sizes. Real clouds show broader droplet size distributions than simple condensation theory predicts. Some idealized models blame turbulence: droplets ride fluctuating updrafts, so each grows under different conditions. Abade analyzed two such schemes, an eddy-hopping model in adiabatic parcels and DNS-like variants, where growth variability comes from the turbulent vertical velocity.

He shows these models produce droplet statistics that vary with height, so the predicted distribution depends on the sampling depth used to measure it. That depth grows with time through the droplets' diffusive wandering. The dependence leads to spurious conclusions about how broad distributions become. Diagnosing the artifact matters because cloud droplet spectra drive rain formation and how clouds reflect sunlight, a major climate uncertainty.
arxiv-2501-13368:
Yuzhuo Li and colleagues argue that identifying an individual animal from camera trap photos should use more than the photo. Ecologists know identity correlates with context: temperature, time of day, season. Yet existing re-identification data sets ship pictures only. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team releases a multimodal data set pairing animal images with environmental metadata, built for modern vision-language models that can read text alongside images. On top of it they propose a small adapter module that plugs into existing re-identification systems and feeds the metadata in as extra features.

Across baseline models, adding the adapter and its context improved re-identification over vision alone, the authors report. The gain held consistently in their experiments. The data set and module are meant to push wildlife monitoring toward the multimodal habits that field biology already trusts.
arxiv-2501-13468:
Haomiao Xiong and six colleagues present StreamChat, a training-free framework for understanding streaming video and holding multi-round conversations about it. Existing video language models struggle with long sequences, multi-turn dialogue, and changing real-world scenes. StreamChat uses a hierarchical memory system to compress video features efficiently over extended streams.

A parallel scheduling strategy cuts processing latency for real-time interaction. The team also introduces StreamBench, a benchmark spanning diverse media types and interactive scenarios, including complex reasoning tasks. On StreamBench and other public benchmarks, StreamChat beat state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and response time. The authors release the code for the framework.
arxiv-2501-13668:
Marco Peruzzo, Tommaso Grigoletto, and Francesco Ticozzi ask, in a 2025 paper, whether the unknown state of a multipartite quantum system can be reconstructed from repeated measurements of local observables. For a static system, such local measurements may not determine the initial state uniquely. The authors examine the problem from a dynamical, system-theoretic viewpoint.

Using observability analysis, they show that the system's own dynamics can make reconstruction possible even when a static measurement cannot. As the system evolves, local measurements taken over time carry information about parts of the state that a single measurement would miss. The authors discuss how the choice of dynamical generators affects this, and how a finite number of measurement samples limits accuracy. An illustrative example demonstrates the approach.
arxiv-2501-13968:
Uesugi and co-authors make fake trios to train shot hunt tools with no hand work. Shot hunt by text pairs a base shot, a change text, and a goal shot. Hand tags for such trios eat time and hands in vast sums. Their way builds trios by what-if shot makes in code. What-if makes bend shot traits in a steered, set way. Those bends yield goal shots that match the change text.

Fake trios thus flow with no hand tags in the loop. More and rich trios can be made at scale by the way. Big sets should lift how well hunt tools learn their task. Tests in the work back that hope for the fake sets. The way frees crews from the tag grind for such tools.
arxiv-2501-14668:
Tian-Jun Li and Shengzhen Ning study symplectic four-manifolds whose divisor complements are ruled by punctured spheres, in the spirit of a classic algebraic theorem. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Log Kodaira dimension minus infinity marks the simplest open surfaces in algebraic geometry. The symplectic world lacked a matching structure story.

They define symplectic affine-ruledness for the complement of a normal-crossing divisor. Then they prove the analogue of the Fujita-Miyanishi-Sugie-Russell description. For rational manifolds the ruling curves are unicuspidal, with one cusp sitting on the divisor. Recent curve existence results and a cone theorem do the heavy lifting. Deformation questions are settled too: such pairs match Kähler pairs up to deformation. The dictionary between algebraic and symplectic surfaces grows by a chapter. Singular curves carry the translation.
arxiv-2501-15768:
Micah Reich presents a control method for quadrotor drones in two thousand twenty-five. The method aims at robust tracking of a planned path. It uses an error-state form of a linear quadratic regulator, a standard tool for optimal feedback control.

Orientation errors are written in exponential coordinates, which lets the system be linearized for real-time use. The design pairs the regulator, acting on the full state, with a cascaded body-rate controller for the motors. Reich gives detailed derivations of the error-state dynamics, the linearization, and the controller design. The stated aim is precise and stable flight in dynamic settings. The paper is a methods piece, focused on formulation and design rather than flight trials.
arxiv-2501-17568:
Ehsan Aminian, Rita Ribeiro, and Joao Gama wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with one surname in fuller form in its text. It predicts rare values in live data streams with histogram-based sampling, for regression tasks where most values cluster in a dull middle.

Batch tools have long fought skewed targets. Streams add drift, and past stream fixes assumed the rare values sit at the extremes. Histograms that grow as data flows in can spot rare zones wherever they lie. One method trims the common cases, the other clones the rare ones, both guided by those live histograms. On fake and real test streams the pair lift rare-case accuracy a lot. They also hold their own against the team's past Chebyshev-based tools.
arxiv-2502-00568:
Samiran Dey and five co-authors show that gene expression made from tumor images can stand in for real molecular tests, in a two thousand twenty-five medical paper. Joining pathology slides with transcriptomics improves cancer grading and survival prediction, but tests of gene activity are rarely ordered in public healthcare.

Their diffusion-based model, PathGen, builds gene expression profiles straight from tissue-slide images. Across four cohorts spanning glioma, renal, uterine, and breast cancers, adding made-up data greatly improved grading and risk estimates. Calls with synthetic features could not be told apart from those using real transcriptomics. The system also reports well-scaled uncertainty and attention maps that doctors and nurses can inspect.
arxiv-2502-00768:
Vargas-Montoya gives a p-adic test for when special power series must be algebraically linked. The series in question solve differential equations and include G-functions and certain E-functions. He works over a finite extension of the p-adic numbers with full ramification. Each operator must carry a strong Frobenius structure. Each must also meet a maximal order condition at zero.

Under those terms, the series are dependent exactly when some product of their powers lands back in the base field. That neat either-or gives a working tool. It can probe independence for wide classes of G- and E-functions. The paper is the first part of a larger study.
arxiv-2502-01068:
Dongwon Jo, Jiwon Song, Yulhwa Kim, and Jae-Joon Kim present FastKV, a method to speed up large language models on long contexts. Long inputs call for heavy prefill work and a large key-value cache. That burdens both the prefill and decoding stages. Past methods cut that cost but tie prefill savings to the cache budget. They also ignore how key context varies by layer, which hurts accuracy.

FastKV uses the fact that token importance settles in later layers. It works through the full context up to a chosen layer. Then it sends only the most useful tokens onward. From those tokens it picks, on its own, which key-value entries to cache. That split lets users trade speed against accuracy with ease. In tests, FastKV sped up both stages a lot.
arxiv-2502-01468:
Blake Hansen and co-authors built a Bayesian method in 2025 for reading the mutational signatures written into cancer genomes. Each mutagenic process, sunlight, tobacco smoke, faulty repair, leaves a characteristic pattern of mutations, and decomposing a tumor's catalog into those patterns reveals its history. Tumors from varied cancer types are more and more collected, but most numeric tools still study one study at a time.

Their multi-study non-negative grid factorization pools several cancer types in one principled model. A mixture form inside it enforces thinness in a smart way: each tumor is explained by a subset of signatures rather than a smear of all of them. And which subset is plausible depends on the patient's covariates. The Bayesian probit form quantifies doubt throughout. The authors argue the design sharpens identification of the signatures themselves while respecting how tumors differ.
arxiv-2502-01568:
Benjamin Spiegel, Lucas Gelfond, and George Konidaris ask how picture-based writing could first arise, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The earliest writing in some cultures used pictographs, signs that look like the thing they mean. No other animal uses such a code, so its birth is a puzzle.

The team built a game where software agents must signal actions to each other with pictures. Their agents use a form of visual theory of mind: they guess how a partner will read a sign. With that skill, stable pictograph systems can emerge in play. The work ties the rise of proto-writing to social inference, not just to drawing skill.
arxiv-2502-03568:
Emanuele La Malfa, Christoph Weinhuber, and colleagues test whether simulating code can stand in for harder reasoning tasks in a 2025 study. Many planning and problem-solving tasks are algorithmic in shape: follow each step correctly and the answer follows. Handcrafting natural test tasks takes great care, limiting how many can be made.

The authors pair natural tasks with synthetic ones built from common programming constructs, such as straight-line code and critical paths. In many cases the synthetic versions track model ability just as well. Synthetic tasks are far easier to generate at scale. That makes code simulation a cheap proxy for measuring broader reasoning skill.
arxiv-2502-04168:
Carla Ferradini, Victor Gitton, and Vilasini build a framework for causal models with loops, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Causal models link observed correlations to causes, drawn as directed graphs. Most tools assume no loops, where standard theorems apply, but feedback and exotic physics need cyclic models.

The authors propose a framework that covers all consistent quantum and classical cyclic models on finite systems. They give a robust probability rule and a new graph property, p-separation. They prove that property is sound and complete for these models. Their approach maps cyclic models to acyclic ones with post-selection, using a teleportation protocol. The work lays ground for causal discovery tools in loopy networks.
arxiv-2502-04568:
Piotr Wyrwiński and Krzysztof Krawiec teach the search steps of genetic programming to care about what a program does, not just how it is written. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In genetic programming, small edits can flip a program's behavior, so score alone is a rough guide. Blind edits waste much of the search.

Their operator uses a graph network that models how instructions and data interact. It paints a map of which spots in a program are worth changing. The search then favors programs that could become strong, not only those already scoring high. On symbolic regression tests, the method beat classic tree-based search. It also beat a stripped-down version of itself. The work argues that meaning, not syntax, should steer program evolution.
arxiv-2502-04968:
Saikat Biswas wrote a solo mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on Selmer groups attached to abelian varieties. An abelian variety is a higher-dimensional cousin of an elliptic curve, defined here over a number field. Selmer groups gather information about the variety's rational points and sit at the heart of modern number theory.

For an odd prime, Biswas studies two Selmer groups built from the prime-torsion points of the variety. He relates the sizes of those groups, and of the groups for the dual variety, to the sizes of component groups at various primes. Such duality results help turn local data into global arithmetic knowledge.
arxiv-2502-06068:
Sethi and four colleagues take spectra of eleven candidate giant radio galaxies with a Himalayan telescope in twenty twenty-five. Giant radio galaxies stretch jets across millions of light years. Firm distances are needed to prove the size. The two meter scope's spectrograph gave redshifts for all eleven hosts.

Every source proved a true giant, from under one to near three megaparsecs. Ten were galaxies and one a quasar. Two topped two megaparsecs, a rare class. One showed signs of a jet blown outflow of ionized gas. Line traits sorted the engines' states for follow up work.
arxiv-2502-06768:
Jaeyeon Kim, Kulin Shah, Vasilis Kontonis, Sham Kakade, and Sitan Chen dissect a bargain at the heart of masked diffusion language models: brutal training, flexible decoding. Unlike autoregressive models, masked diffusions must learn to fill blanks in any pattern, an exponential family of subproblems. At inference, though, they may reveal tokens in any order they like. The paper examines both sides of the trade.

Theory and experiments confirm the training subproblems are genuinely harder than the autoregressive counterpart's. Adaptive decoding order then turns the tables, steering around the hard subproblems at run time. On Sudoku, a pretrained model's accuracy leapt from under seven percent to about ninety with adaptive ordering. That beat autoregressive models seven times its size that were explicitly taught the right order. Train for the worst, the title advises, and plan for the best.
arxiv-2502-06968:
Three physicists wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on a rigorous theory for moire materials. Moire patterns arise when two atomic sheets stack with a slight twist, as in magic-angle graphene. These materials host striking effects, including superconductivity and strongly insulating states, that simple average-field theory cannot fully explain.

The authors build a many-body perturbation framework around the electron Green's function written in the band basis. For twisted bilayer graphene they recover known results at the simpler level, including symmetry-breaking states. Adding self-consistent higher corrections then fixes an overestimate of how much the material's compressibility fluctuates with filling.
arxiv-2502-07568:
Ignacio Ceresa Dussel, Julián Fernández Bonder, and Ariel Salort wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on an energy rule for functions living in a wide kind of space, an Orlicz space. The space is set by a growth rule that need not meet the tame growth condition. The energy counts how the far-apart points of a function differ, in a fractional way. As the fractional grade nears one, the energy should approach a whole-grade relative.

The team proves the key step with no tame condition in place: no sequence approaching the function can push its energy below the energy of the relative in the limit. From that step, the weak match of the two energies, their Gamma-convergence, follows. They then extend the proof to a case from the field of nonlocal force rules, peridynamics. The work frees a match from a condition it had worn.
arxiv-2502-09168:
Arianna Graciotti, Nicolas Lazzari, Valentina Presutti, and Rocco Tripodi build a benchmark for linking named people and works in old music texts to a knowledge base. Such linking is hard for past texts, whose names may be missing from standard bases. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The set holds hand marked lines from past music journals, rich in rare or absent names. Top models all found the set hard. The authors add a new unsupervised linker and a way to extend trained linkers with graph based logic rules. Guessing names absent from the base also helped. This mix beat plain methods on the past texts.
arxiv-2502-10168:
Shun Arai, John Peacock, Hironao Miyatake, and Atsushi Nishizawa developed a way to do CMB lensing tomography with better redshift data in two thousand twenty-five. The cosmic microwave background is bent by matter along its path, and slicing that lensing by distance needs the redshift spread of lens galaxies.

Their clustering method infers that spread from cross-correlations between lens mass and reference samples, within a linear bias frame. As a test, they correlated a Planck lensing map with radio galaxies and estimated their kernel from surveys with known distances. The resulting power spectrum gave a matter clumpiness value close to the Planck result. The authors present it as a proof of concept.
arxiv-2502-11368:
Zhengxiang Wang and co-authors published this study in 2025. It asks whether large language models can grade student writing across several criteria at once. The case study uses literature reviews by graduate students writing in a second language. Human experts graded each paper on nine points, with scores and comments. The team then had several popular models do the same job under varied prompts.

Judging the comments needed a new yardstick, which the authors built to be cheap, clear, and repeatable. Against it, the models produced decent, generally reliable assessments. Their scores and notes tracked the human pattern across the nine criteria. The authors release their corpus and code for others to check. The work suggests models could share the grading load in writing courses, with humans keeping the final say.
arxiv-2502-12168:
Yu-Tung Liu, Yu-Hao Cheng, Shao-Yu Wu, and Hung-Ming Chen wrote this computer science paper, published in 2025. It speeds up a key chip design check, estimating voltage drop across a chip's power grid, by teaching a neural network on both picture-like layout features and circuit-list features.

Voltage drop forecasts guard a chip's reliability and speed, but the classic simulation is slow. Image-only models miss wiring detail, and list-only models miss spatial patterns. The authors' network, CFIRSTNET, fuses both feature families in one frame. A custom convolutional network reads the power grid's features and predicts the drop map. On the open benchmark from a 2023 design contest, the method took the best quality score. The authors present fast, accurate drop estimation as a practical need as chips keep shrinking.
arxiv-2502-14668:
Qinglin Ma, Cheng Li, and Yanhan Guo study how small halos cluster around pairs of big dark matter halos. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses the Illustris-TNG simulation of the universe. They measure, for each small halo, its angle from the line that joins the pair.

Two patterns show up. The bulging pattern piles small halos along the pair's line, and the lopsided pattern piles them between the pair. Bulging grows when the pair is far apart and the main halo is light, while lopsidedness grows with the main halo's mass. A simple overlap effect, with alignment counted, can explain most of the signal. The team also checks how the view flattens in 2D and under survey-like selection.
arxiv-2502-15368:
Anand builds a class of electron-pair systems whose low states shun a plain form in this twenty twenty-five paper. The work feeds a big open ask on how hard it is to guess a system's rest energy. Weaker kin asks have seen slow gains, and this work adds a fresh brick.

Inside, the author crafts systems where states of the plain wave form can not dip below a set energy floor. That floor holds by a fixed gap, not one that shrinks as the system grows. The build bends a route first used for a kin claim to the pair-electron case. Such floors give one type of proof that hard rest-energy asks may stay hard at scale.
arxiv-2502-15468:
Fani Dosopoulou and Joseph Silk propose catching two signals from the same galactic core: gravity waves and gamma rays shaped by dark matter. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A giant black hole at a galaxy's heart can grow a dense spike of dark matter around it. A smaller black hole spiraling in would stir that spike.

Inside the spike, dark matter particles wipe each other out and glow in gamma rays. As the small hole plows through, it thins the spike and dims that glow. The dimming can range from a tenth to nearly all of the light. At the same time the pair sings in gravity waves that a planned space detector can hear. Watching both signals together could reveal dark matter where light alone cannot.
arxiv-2502-15568:
Ina Dormuth, Sven Franke, Marlies Hafer, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It audits the AI tools German voters might consult before the 2025 federal election, and finds the supposedly neutral helpers leaning and straying.

The team compared chatbot answers and voting advice apps against the parties' own answers to thirty-eight statements in the established Wahl-O-Mat tool. Large language models aligned over seventy-five percent with left-wing parties on average, around half with the center-right, and only about thirty percent with the right. One advice app deviated from party positions in a quarter of cases; another in over half. Simple prompt tricks made that app hallucinate, inventing a link between a party and right-wing extremists. The authors warn voters to treat AI election help with suspicion.
arxiv-2502-17868:
Changyo Han, Yousuke Nakagawa, and Takeshi Naemura designed small robots that climb from a table onto a wall in a 2025 study. Swarms of mobile robots can rearrange a room as an interface, but wheeled robots normally stay on one flat surface. Crossing from horizontal to vertical usually demands extra motors or grippers.

Each robot in their design carries a sloped structure shaped for the crossing. A partner robot pushes it toward the new surface, and the slope turns that push into a smooth rotation onto the wall. Only passive mechanical parts are used, with no added active electronics. The team studied which design settings make the handoff reliable.
arxiv-2502-20068:
Tianyang Qi, Shibo Chen, and Jun Zhang guide electric car drivers to cheap charging spots without sharing global data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Drivers face shifting traffic, moving power prices, and rivalry for chargers. Top learning methods need data on all cars at run time, which costs bandwidth and leaks privacy.

Their method keeps the policy on each car and adds a recommendation model built from a generative network. A second part squeezes global rivalry data into a compact form for training. A balancing method steadies training across two goals. Tests based on a real district in Xi'an, China beat local only methods. Loss versus global methods stayed under eight parts in a hundred.
arxiv-2502-20468:
Nancy Lynch looks back on her career building a theory of distributed systems, in a manuscript from 2025. Distributed systems are groups of computers that must work together without a single control point. Lynch began this work at Georgia Tech in the late 1970s and continued at MIT from 1981, with many students and partners.

The account stresses the early work and its effect on the field. It covers new methods for shared tasks, careful proofs, and errors found in earlier methods. It also covers limits that show what such systems can never do, no matter the design. Lynch explains the math tools she helped build for modelling these systems. Uses range from shared data stores and wireless networks to living systems.
arxiv-2503-03668:
Ankit Shrivastava, Kaushik Dayal, and Hae Young Noh simulate force chains in granular piles in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. When grains are squeezed, load travels along chains of stressed particles. What sparks those chains was not fully separated into its factors.

Their mixes pair two particle sizes under one-way compression, with packing measured so its effect can be isolated. Mixed sizes boosted chain formation in near-ordered packings. As size gaps grew, packing turned messy, giving fewer chains that carried bigger loads. Stickiness between grains always reduced chain counts, whatever the sizes or packing. The findings matter for silos, soils, and powders where load paths decide failure.
arxiv-2503-04668:
Riccardo Brumali, Guido Carnevale, and Giuseppe Notarstefano set out a shared tuning scheme where a set of agents learn their own costs from data as they go. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

In the frame they use, each agent's cost rests on its own choice and on a sum of all choices. No agent knows its cost's form. Each can probe it at one point per step, from a sensor or user. The scheme has three parts. A net learns which way the local cost falls. A tune step moves the choice that way. A track step rebuilds the shared sums from local facts. The team proves, for strong cases, that the group nears the best joint choice.
arxiv-2503-04768:
Yansong Ning and co-authors published a 2025 paper on a chat assistant built into a major ride-hailing app. Booking a ride by typing or speaking sounds simple, but the assistant must reason about places, times, and traffic in a busy city. The team built the assistant, called DiMA, on a large language model and deployed it inside the DiDi app.

One part of the system plans orders step by step, calling outside tools for exact facts about time and place. Another part handles the chat itself, mixing reply styles to balance quality, speed, and cost. The assistant keeps learning from real chats and from practice dialogues, so its choices match what people prefer. In live use, it planned orders with ninety-three percent accuracy. Its replies scored ninety-two percent. Lab tests showed large gains over three rival agent systems, with lower delay as well.
arxiv-2503-04868:
Viktoria Kraxberger leads a large team in setting up a study of slow antiprotons that stop in thin solid targets. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. The work runs at the ASACUSA plant, which now has a beam line that feeds antiprotons at very low energy.

When an antiproton stops, it bursts into prongs of particles. New chip sensors will count them and read their energy and spread over most of the sky. A three-dimensional tool rebuilds the burst point from tracks in flat sensors, tuned on simulated runs. The data will weigh how bursts shift with target mass and feed better models of the event.
arxiv-2503-05268:
Francesco Cazzaro and three co-authors set up a test for graph querying in twenty twenty-five. Plain speech interfaces would let anyone query a knowledge graph with ease and speed. Property graphs are the stored form firms favor most for rich, linked facts. Yet work on parsing speech into queries has mostly passed them by, so few tests exist to grade new tools.

Their test set, ZOGRASCOPE, aims at property graphs and Cypher, their query language. It holds queries tagged by hand, ranging from plain ones to hard ones. The set splits in three: fresh queries of the usual kind, and sets that probe compositional and length generalization. Tests probe several large language models under varied ways of learning. The result is a yardstick for a skill firms need: turning plain questions into correct queries over the graphs they use.
arxiv-2503-05968:
Suraj Poudel and a large team of co-authors map the gas blowing out of the most active star-forming region in a nearby galaxy. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The region, 30 Doradus, sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Its young stars drive the fastest, densest wind in that galaxy.

The team read the near-side outflow along eight lines of sight using ultraviolet spectra from a space telescope program. Radio data filled in the cold gas picture. Close to the center, the wind tops out at well over a hundred kilometers per second. Ion counts peak at the center and fade outward. The outflowing mass runs to hundreds of thousands of suns. Light, not heat alone, charges most of the gas. The work quantifies how starbursts vent their fuel into space.
arxiv-2503-06568:
Qiyuan He and Angela Yao present Conceptrol, a fix for image generators that personalize pictures from a reference photo. Their paper appeared in 2025. Add-on modules can insert a person's face or a pet into new scenes without retraining. Yet the output often copies the reference and ignores the text prompt. The authors trace this to weak mixing of the reference image with the prompt inside the module.

Conceptrol adds a mask drawn from the text, which steers where the module may look in the reference. The change adds no extra computing cost. On standard tests, scores rose by as much as 89 percent over the plain add-on. The method even beat approaches that fine-tune the model for each subject. Code is shared openly for other groups to use.
arxiv-2503-07768:
Antoine Legouhy and co-authors present a framework from two thousand twenty-five for aligning medical images with a light deep learning model. Alignment, called registration, warps one scan to match another. Most deep methods feed the whole image grid into heavy networks, even when clean outlines of organs are already available at low cost.

Their method, called NimbleReg, works from the boundary surfaces of several outlined regions instead of the full grid. A compact point-based network learns one smooth, invertible warp for the whole space by fusing the regional matches. A velocity field setup guarantees the warp can be undone cleanly, with no folds. The authors report alignment on par with state-of-the-art image-based methods while staying light on hardware.
arxiv-2503-09268:
Baruah, Hazarika, and Phukon present a paper from twenty twenty-five on holographic images of black holes with added physics. A wave source rings at the edge of an anti-de Sitter space. Its echo through the bulk is imaged as an optical view. String clouds and higher-derivative terms modify the black hole. Views range from crisp Einstein rings to smeared bright spots. From the north pole, a bright ring always marks the photon sphere. Stripes ring it concentrically in that view.

Ring placement matches geometric optics predictions closely. Correction terms shift the optical features measurably. The study ties wave optics to gravitational lensing. It tests how exotic physics would look.
arxiv-2503-09468:
Ce Jin, Yael Kirkpatrick, Virginia Vassilevska Williams, and Nicole Wein revisit a classic placement problem in networks. The task is to choose a small set of centers in a graph so every node sits close to some center. Fast methods have long been stuck at answers within twice the optimal distance. Beating that factor outright is known to be hard, and for fixed center counts it appears to need long running times. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors relax the goal: they allow a small fixed extra distance atop a factor below two.

With that trade, they give faster algorithms beating the factor of two for every center count. For large counts they reach a factor of one and a half with only a half unit of slack. The two-center case gets its own fast method using matrix multiplication. The results reopen a problem many had considered settled.
arxiv-2503-09568:
Barylli and six co-authors reviewed network models of layered cell data in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Single-cell tools now read genes and proteins from the same kinds of samples, but rarely at once. Linking the layers after the fact is the practical alternative. The review surveys methods that infer such networks and stitch them together.

Approaches range from probability models to graph algorithms. The authors stress how to check that a stitched model is trustworthy. They catalogue the tools now available for building these multi-layer networks. Challenges in combining unlike data types get direct treatment. The intended payoff is a fuller picture of how cells work.
arxiv-2503-10068:
Han Liu, Riqiang Gao, Eileen Krieg, and Sasa Grbic present PanDx, an AI aid for spotting pancreatic cancer early on CT scans. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a swift and deadly cancer. Early signs on scans are faint, so most cases surface late. Their frame works coarse to fine on contrast-enhanced scans.

Two tricks drive it. A distribution-aware ensemble pools models by lesion type to travel across cases. A peak-scaled step then pulls candidate lesions with sharper placement. In the PANORAMA challenge the system took first place on the held-out test set. Scores on ranking gauges were strong. A radiologist helped sort the failure cases afterward. The authors map where such aids still miss and what to build next. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2503-11168:
Wumei Sun, Hongwei Liu, and Xiaoyu Wang tackle multi-constraint graph partitioning in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Splitting a graph into balanced parts with few cut edges is a classic hard problem. Their version adds vertex weight limits and vertices fixed to set parts.

They model the task as a zero-one quadratic program. A recursive two-way splitting algorithm then solves it, powered by a fast gradient method. Constraints are folded into an unconstrained form using balance terms and elimination tricks. Starting partitions come from a rounding method, then local swaps refine them. Tests on knapsack-constrained problems and industrial cases showed the method works well.
arxiv-2503-11468:
Ning Jiang, Liu Liu, and Huimin Yu build a numerical scheme for tumor growth models whose parameters are uncertain. Their paper came out in 2025. The model treats the tumor as a porous material that expands, and randomness in growth rates or the starting shape makes predictions a distribution rather than a single curve.

Their scheme works inside a polynomial chaos framework, a standard way to carry uncertainty through equations. It is designed to stay accurate in the stiff limit where the model turns into a sharp moving-boundary problem. They prove the scheme has that preservation property and study the solution's smoothness in the random variables. Simulations reproduce finger-like growth patterns and the life cycle of tumor cells: dividing, resting, and dead. The scheme captures how uncertain inputs reshape the tumor's edge.
arxiv-2503-14568:
Iman Peivaste, Ahmed Makradi, and Salim Belouettar teach a neural operator to model how grains grow inside materials. Their 2025 paper addresses grain growth, the shifting of crystal regions that shapes a material's traits. Classic simulations capture this well but cost much computing time, above all at fine scales.

Their method uses an operator that works in frequency space, which lets it handle varied scales without retraining. They trained it on data from classic simulations, pairing states over time so it learns to predict the next state. The trained model cut computing cost while staying accurate across scales. Past learning methods often failed when the scale changed. A fast, scale-free model could speed the design of metals and other materials for electronics and optics.
arxiv-2503-14668:
Mykhaylo Khoma computes cross sections for collisions between a hydrogen atom and a hydrogen ion at low to ultra low energies, in work from twenty twenty-five. Two outcomes are tracked: elastic scattering, where the pair just deflects, and charge transfer, where the electron hops across. Both matter for cold gas and plasma physics.

Energies span a huge range, from far below one electron volt up to ten. Khoma runs both a full quantum method and a semi classical method on the same problem. He weighs how far the cheaper semi classical route can be trusted at the lowest energies. Results are set against prior data in the literature. The work gives a check point for cold collision theory.
arxiv-2503-14768:
Ryota Nakano and a large team of co-authors report a magnetic pattern in a Weyl semimetal in two thousand twenty-five. The material, GdAlSi, hosts topological electronic states shaped by magnetism. Clear examples of an undistorted helimagnetic state in such materials had been missing.

Using resonant X-ray scattering with polarization analysis, they found a clean harmonic spin cycloid in the material. The pattern fits an interaction set by the crystal's polar structure. Under a magnetic field, the cycloid changed into a new multi-Q state with a noncoplanar texture. A numerical spin model with that interaction and anisotropic exchange matched the new state. The authors offer the material as a model platform for modulated Weyl systems.
arxiv-2503-15468:
Bernanda Telalovic and Mauricio Bustamante search the high-energy neutrino sky for a crack in a core physics rule, in work from two thousand twenty-five. The rule says physics acts the same in all directions. If it broke, the three neutrino types might favor unlike sky paths at high energy.

The team used seven and a half years of data from a giant ice-based detector. They found no sign that one type favored any direction over the others. From that null result they set tight caps on hundreds of rule-break terms. Many of those caps are the first ever placed, and others beat old caps by far.
arxiv-2503-15768:
Alexandra DeLucia and Mark Dredze wrote a 2025 paper on when a summarization tool, trained on one kind of text, fails on another. The task is to summarize many documents at once, from news articles to transcripts of conversations. Training plans fall into four kinds: direct, chunk-first, extract-first, and a call to a large model. The team asks how and why a tool trained on one field fails when it summarizes another, with no fresh training.

They grade the tools on three fields and three marks: similarity to a reference summary, quality, and factual accuracy. A failure is defined as a drop in factual accuracy, a drift from the target, and a fall in quality. They also probe the standard grading tools themselves. A grading tool built for news can misgrade a summary of conversations, they warn. One size, the conclusion runs, does not fit all.
arxiv-2503-15868:
Debabrata Mandal, Soumitri Chattopadhyay, and colleagues build one restoration network that repairs many kinds of image damage in a 2025 computer vision study. Blur, noise, and haze usually each demand their own specialist model, yet real photos arrive with several faults stacked together. A unified system also needs controls, so a user can say which fault to fix and how hard.

Working in a latent diffusion framework, their network handles multiple degradations under one set of weights. Controllable, all-in-one restoration fits consumer photo tools and archives where the damage mix is never known in advance.
arxiv-2503-15968:
Raul Cristian Bag proposed a data platform design in 2025 for blockchain and digital asset work. Research centers in this field juggle huge, fast-moving records that must stay secure, shared, and easy to query. Silos and weak scaling slow that work down and hurt repeat studies.

His design pairs lakehouse storage, which mixes raw files with tidy tables, with small cloud services that each do one job. Parts can scale on their own, and access rules guard sensitive records. Trials fed near-live data to scientists for their studies. Bag argues the layout boosts speed and sharing, and it sets up later work on machine learning operations for asset data.
arxiv-2503-16168:
Archisman Panigrahi, Vladislav Poliakov, and Leonid Levitov propose a way to image the phase of the order parameter of a superconductor. Exotic phases whose symmetry differs from the crystal lattice are a focus of study. But to detect the symmetry and topology of the order parameter is hard. Scanning tunneling microscopy near impurities shows the nodes of the gap well. Yet its phase winding has stayed out of reach.

Their method, superconducting order parameter tomography, uses patterns from pairs of impurities. The pairs act as beam splitters, in the spirit of Young's double-slit test. To rotate the impurity setup in a controlled way changes the pattern. From its reply, the momentum-space structure of the gap function can be rebuilt. As a case, they treat strontium ruthenate, whose order is still debated.
arxiv-2503-17668:
Kumari and Rana improve how camera paths are tracked to build accurate three dimensional models in twenty twenty-five. Wide swings in view angle and drift in alignment make the task hard. Their tweak to a feature matching tool pulls more match points at lower cost. A two camera setup then fixes small errors in rotation.

A stereo camera model gauges how the camera shifts through space and corrects its motion. The full system matched the true camera path almost exactly in tests. It beat current path finding methods on accuracy. The authors pitch it for high fidelity three dimensional rebuilding in fields like mapping and film.
arxiv-2503-18468:
Clara Leitgeb and five colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on measurements that future particle colliders should make to help cosmic ray research. Telescopes that detect gamma rays from space must reject a background of cosmic ray air showers that look similar. Predictions of that background disagree strongly between simulation programs.

The authors identify the main source of the troublesome background: collisions in which a large share of the cosmic ray's energy passes into the electromagnetic part of the shower. They then define the region of particle production angles, called pseudorapidity, that collider experiments should measure to pin this process down. Such measurements would sharpen the background models on which gamma-ray astronomy depends.
arxiv-2503-21368:
Jiaxin Han and a large team present the Jiutian simulations for the CSST surveys in two thousand twenty-five. The China Space Survey Telescope needs mock skies to plan its work. Jiutian is a hybrid suite built for its extragalactic surveys. Four modules split the suite by purpose and cost.

Primary runs use top resolution under the standard cosmology. Emulator runs scan nearby parameter space to train a fast predictor. Reconstruction runs rebuild chunks of the real universe. Extension runs swap in warm dark matter, altered gravity, and more. Mock catalogs add spectra, lines, and lensing traits.
arxiv-2503-21468:
Tran and Snasel propose WiGCN in twenty twenty-five, a graph model for recommendation systems. User ratings on items can be drawn as a graph for learning. Graph neural networks then extract traits of users and items to suggest new items. Not all ratings should count equally for a given user, the authors argue.

They build an extra graph that shows the recommended weight of an item for a target user. User links are inferred from shared consumption patterns, since friendships were not recorded. The weighted input feeds a graph convolutional model. Experiments use well known benchmark data sets for recommendation. Results are compared with leading models such as LightGCN and NGCF. Source code for the model is included with the paper.
arxiv-2504-00168:
Alfonso Artigue studies how wild a typical surface transformation can be. A homeomorphism reshuffles a surface while keeping it whole. Some maps are expansive in a continuum sense: nearby blobs get pulled apart until their fate is readable. Artigue asks how common such maps are among all surface maps.

He proves the expansive ones sit densely: any surface map can be nudged into one. More strongly, a typical map is almost expansive in a precise sense. Near it stands an expansive map tied to it by a collapsing map. The collapse crushes only tiny, connected, non-splitting sets. So typical surface dynamics, he shows, hide an expansive skeleton under a fine blur. The result links the generic case to a well-understood class.
arxiv-2504-00268: Alvarez and Rodriguez Ricard apply the Krylov-Bogoliubov-Mitropolsky averaging method to polynomial dynamical systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A flat polynomial system is first turned into a second-order differential equation by a polynomial change of variables. The method is then used on it. The authors pin down conditions for that change which suffice to show that a limit cycle exists. So the choice made ties straight to periodic behavior that is sure to occur.
arxiv-2504-00568:
Kanat Abdukhalikov, Askar Dzhumadil'daev, and San Ling classify quasi-cyclic codes of index two over finite fields. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in coding theory, the math of error-proof messages. Quasi-cyclic codes shift in blocks, which makes them compact to describe. Index two means the block structure has a set small size. A full sorting of such codes is the main prize.

Dual codes are worked out under three pairings: Euclidean, symplectic, and Hermitian. Self-orthogonal and dual-containing codes get their own account. Lower bounds on minimum distance tell how many errors a code can shrug off. Two elements at most generate any such code. The authors give tests for when one element suffices, for the code or its dual. The census serves builders of codes with tidy structure.
arxiv-2504-01768:
Suman Saha refines the orbits and traits of five long-period planets that cross their stars. The paper from twenty twenty-five uses fresh public data from the TESS and CHEOPS space telescopes. Long gaps between crossings let old orbit tables drift. Drift then skews size and path estimates. Saha merges the new transits with all past ones for a fresh fit.

A noise-cleaning step, mixing wavelet tools with Gaussian process fits, guards the light curves. Period values land with a precision of a few seconds for most targets. One planet's period stays looser but still tight. Other traits shift too, some by clear margins: an impact value, an orbit size, a planet radius. No timing wobbles hint at hidden planets. The fresh tables aid future deep looks at these worlds.
arxiv-2504-02668:
On and co-authors build a 2025 tool that outlines both upper chambers of the heart in a special MRI scan. The scan, which uses a contrast dye, shows scar and stiff tissue in the atria. Those maps guide personal treatment for a common rhythm disorder. Drawing the outlines by hand is slow and varies between readers, so an automatic method is needed.

Their pipeline runs a well-known medical segmentation network in two stages, mixing flat and three-dimensional versions. They boost the contrast of the input scans and clean the output maps with shape rules. The tool must mark the left cavity, the right cavity, and the wall of both. Its overlap scores against hand-drawn maps were high for the cavities and lower for the thin wall, which is the hardest part to trace.
arxiv-2504-02968:
Pastor-Perez, Alonso-Garcia, and Mauch improve flow networks for multi-objective black-box optimization with a global ordering, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Order-preserving flow networks sample diverse near-optimal candidates efficiently online. They rank training samples locally by Pareto dominance, avoiding scalarization. The authors show local ranking creates conflicting training objectives.

Global-Order networks convert the local order into one consistent global order. That conversion removes the conflicts at their source. Benchmark evaluations confirm the fix improves optimization quality. Sampling stays diverse near the Pareto front as intended. The method keeps online training and needs no preference weights. It promises stronger tools for design tasks with rival goals.
arxiv-2504-03468:
Antoine Dumoulin and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, a model that animates 3D clothing on moving bodies while respecting cloth physics. Garment shape depends on body shape, motion, and the cloth's material traits. Physics-based learning can be more accurate on strain and curvature than models that ignore material. Past work handled pose-based garment shapes or dynamic cloth from data. Their model, D-Garment, trains on fresh data from a physics simulator. It learns deformations tied to material properties, which helps with loose cloth and motion-driven wrinkles.

The model can also be fitted to sensor data such as 3D point clouds. It uses a diffusion model in a latent space, a compact code for shape, built from a 2D map of the garment. That map is independent of mesh resolution, so it can condition global and local geometry.
arxiv-2504-09068:
Hettige and Ong present a method for shrinking complex data while it streams in, in a 2025 paper. High-dimensional data is costly to store and draw, and curved patterns defeat straight-line shortcuts. Their method builds on a multi-scale framework that maps data clusters at several levels of detail at once.

Instead of rebuilding the map for each new batch, the method updates the cluster map, the local axes, and the detail coefficients step by step. Tests show the live map stays close to one built from all data at once, even when it starts from a small sample. The multi-level structure survives the updates. The authors aim the tool at live displays and graphics tools that must react as data arrives.
arxiv-2504-11268:
Juan Garcia Giraldo, Nikolaos Dimitriadis, Ke Wang, and Pascal Frossard merge several single task vision models into one model that does many jobs on the same image. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. A scene tool has to find depth, edges, and object classes from one photo. Past merging work took for granted that each sample had just one task, which misses this setup.

Plain merging here hurt scores badly. The team traced the drop to a mismatch: the merged encoder made features that no longer lined up with the decoder for each task. Two light fixes line those features up again after the merge. On indoor and street tests, the merged model matched joint training. It used fewer samples and steps, since it reused ready task models. The work also hints at how to read task links from merges.
arxiv-2504-11968:
Raphaël Gastaldello, Gabriel Stoltz, and Urbain Vaes reduced statistical noise in molecular simulations in a 2025 paper. Transport coefficients, like how heat or momentum spreads in a fluid, are computed from fluctuation formulas applied to long simulated trajectories, and the estimates wobble a lot, forcing expensive runs. Their method biases the dynamics slightly, using a Girsanov reweighting identity to correct the bias in the final average.

One tuning knob sets the size of the added push, and the authors analyze long-time behavior fully to predict how much variance falls. Theory and numerics agree: variance does drop, though modestly in most situations. Honest accounting of a small win matters in a field where simulation hours are precious.
arxiv-2504-12368:
Babak Ghassemi and six co-authors present BRIDGE-LC, a deep learning frame that adds place context to land cover mapping from satellite data. Such maps guide land and resource care, but models often skip place data that could help. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The frame learns from fine place marks, the exact coordinates, and coarse marks, the broad bio region, at once. Its light network splits region bound traits from traits that hold across regions. At run time it needs only the fine marks, which keeps it fast. Tests on an open field data set pit it against common methods used for large scale mapping.
arxiv-2504-13368:
Haoran Xu and four co-authors introduce, in a 2025 paper, a method for offline reinforcement learning called Iterative Dual Reinforcement Learning, or IDRL. In offline learning, an agent must learn from a fixed dataset rather than from new experience. The method grew out of an experiment in which a discriminator trained on offline data plus expert data gave strong results when its scores weighted behavior cloning.

The authors argue that existing Dual-RL methods estimate the key visitation distribution ratio incorrectly, so their weights differ from the optimal discriminator weights. IDRL corrects this step by step. Each iteration removes transitions with zero weight, as judged by the previous ratio, and reruns Dual-RL on the remaining data. Across D4RL datasets and corrupted human demonstrations, IDRL outperformed strong Primal-RL and Dual-RL baselines in both performance and stability.
arxiv-2504-13768:
Sharma and five co-authors built this prediction network in twenty twenty-five for machines with many moving parts. Digital twins need fast models that forecast both motion and internal forces. Forces matter because they hint at wear and faults before motion degrades. Their network, Equi-Euler GraphNet, treats parts as nodes and contacts as edges.

Two design biases do the heavy lifting. Edge messages act like physical forces and respect rotations and shifts of the whole system. Node updates mimic Euler time stepping, letting distant effects arrive over time. The test rig was a cylindrical roller bearing, modeled in fine detail. The network beat rival graph models and ran about two hundred times faster than the full solver. Rollouts stayed stable over thousands of steps.
arxiv-2504-15968:
Souptik Chakraborty, Diksha Gupta, Shammi Malhotra, and Konijeti Sreenadh prove a compactness result in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is a Brézis-Nirenberg type problem with mixed operators. A Laplacian and a fractional Laplacian act together there. Palais-Smale sequences for the problem get a profile split.

The domain is smooth and bounded, with dimension at least three. The exponent sits at the critical Sobolev value. Their global compactness result decomposes the sequences fully. As a use case, they solve a Coron type problem next. A positive solution exists when the parameter is zero.
arxiv-2504-19068:
Osmin Ferrer, Kandy Ferrer, and Jaffeth Cure extend a branch of analysis, in a 2025 preprint, that measures how much a function can vary. Functions of bounded variation are a classic tool in math. Their theory was first carried into normed spaces by Chistyakov, then into spaces with two norms by other authors including two of this team. The present paper works in a broader setting still, called generalized two-normed spaces.

The authors take up an earlier definition of bounded 2-variation and work out its basic traits. Several theorems spell out the core properties of such functions in the new setting. One result shows that a function of bounded variation on a semi-normed space can generate one of bounded 2-variation in the generalized setting. The paper is a careful groundwork piece for specialists in functional analysis.
arxiv-2504-19668:
Satyaranjan Pradhan and Madan Mohan Soren study how well a special sampling series can reconstruct functions, in a 2025 paper. Sampling series rebuild a signal from spaced samples, and the Kantorovich variant also averages locally, which suits rough data. Their version samples exponentially and uses a max-product operation instead of plain sums.

The setting is weighted spaces of functions that are continuous in a logarithmic sense and bounded. The authors prove the series converges to the target function, then measure how fast, using a weighted modulus that gauges smoothness. A Voronovskaja-type theorem describes the precise asymptotic shape of the error. They close with kernel functions satisfying their assumptions, illustrated with graphs. Approximation theory of this kind underwrites signal processing where exponential sampling is natural.
arxiv-2504-21368:
Pramook Khungurn and three co-authors retrain diffusion autoencoders in twenty twenty-five. These models rebuild images through a noise-based process. Standard training spends many steps at high noise, which recovers large structures. Fine detail comes back at low noise, so reconstructions can end up blurry.

The authors argue the latent code should already hold the structure of an image. Training can then spend fewer steps on structure and more on detail. Their method splits training into two phases. In the first, the model trains as a plain autoencoder at the highest noise level. That forces the latent code to carry structural information. Later training can then focus on detail. Readers get a training recipe aimed squarely at sharper rebuilds.
arxiv-2504-21768:
Lucas Alland and Robert Viator analyzed Steklov eigenvalues of nearly circular domains in twenty twenty-five. Steklov eigenvalues govern problems where behavior inside a region is driven by its boundary; for a disk they are known exactly. Earlier work expanded them for slightly deformed disks whose boundaries kept mirror symmetry, keeping area fixed at one.

The authors drop the symmetry assumption and compute the first-order correction in general. They also recover the second-order expansion. That extra term settles an optimization question: beyond the first positive eigenvalue, the disk is not a local shape optimizer — small asymmetric wiggles can improve the higher eigenvalues. The results refine how eigenvalue sensitivity to boundary shape is understood in spectral geometry.
arxiv-2505-00968:
Thanh Tran and co-authors generalize a fast distance between distributions in a 2025 math paper. The Wasserstein distance measures the cost of reshaping one pile of mass into another, and it is a workhorse of modern learning. Sliced versions cut the cost by projecting the piles onto lines, or lately onto trees, and solving the easy one-way problems. Trees capture shape better than lines at little extra cost.

Their step swaps the straight projections for bent, nonlinear ones. The risk is breaking the math that makes the distance valid. They design the projections so the linked transform stays one-to-one and the result stays a true metric. They build working versions for flat space and for spheres. Experiments test whether the richer projections read distributions more faithfully.
arxiv-2505-02568:
A large collaboration wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on experiments at J-PARC in Japan that hunt for an extremely rare kaon decay. In this decay, a long-lived kaon turns into a neutral pion plus two neutrinos. The Standard Model predicts it happens only about three times in a hundred billion decays, with tiny uncertainty.

Because the prediction is so clean, any mismatch would point to new physics. The experiments, KOTO and its planned successor KOTO II, are built to catch such a faint signal. The paper describes the experimental program and its reach. It is part of a wider effort to test the Standard Model at its most sensitive points.
arxiv-2505-03668:
