Celeste Veronese, Daniele Meli, and Alessandro Farinelli join time based logic with planning under doubt to make choices that stay clear to read. Their setting is the POMDP frame, where an agent cannot see the full state. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method uses a part of a time logic to build fixed long step moves, called macro-actions. A tree search planner then uses these moves across a time span, which cuts the time needed to plan while keeping results strong. The moves are learned from a few past runs, not built by hand. Tests on two known tasks showed the learned moves were broader and much faster than fixed rules.
arxiv-2505-04768:
Matheus da Silva Fonseca and six co-authors introduce a quantum algorithm for chemistry in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Solving the Schrödinger equation for molecules is costly on classical machines. Quantum computers may one day do it faster, and variational methods suit today's limited hardware.

The variational quantum eigensolver mixes a shallow quantum circuit with classical optimization to find molecular energies. It needs fewer gates and shallower circuits than grander quantum schemes. The tutorial walks from quantum mechanics for molecules through computing basics to the algorithm at work. It closes with the method's space and time costs and open challenges. The authors aim the piece at newcomers entering quantum simulation.
arxiv-2505-05368:
Xavier Bekaert and Yannick Herfray revisit how to classify the particle-like states of the BMS group, the symmetry group of flat spacetime at infinity. The group's supermomentum is its charge, and generic values resist the old classification. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair decompose supermomentum, uniquely and Lorentz-invariantly, into a hard part and a soft part. Wavefunctions are made as explicit as possible throughout. They then show how a BMS state branches into ordinary Poincare particles once a gravity vacuum is chosen.

Different vacua read the same state as different field content, a point they demonstrate concretely. A worked example shows generic BMS particles can encode gravitational memory, the permanent displacement left by passing waves. Ordinary particles cannot. The paper ties representation theory to infrared gravitational physics.
arxiv-2505-05968:
Dan Qiao and co-authors teach teams of agents from logged play by splitting the team score rule agent by agent, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Offline team learning warps when logged play mixes many team styles of mixed worth. One shared pattern is hard for lone-agent rules to find.

Their split pulls per-agent guide signals out of the joint log policy. A spread-based generator learns those signals from the mixed logs. The signals then steer joint critics toward rich, in-log team moves. Tests on particle worlds and robot suites hit top marks across the board. Readers get a fix for the offline-online gap in team learning.
arxiv-2505-06368:
Sarah Dodson-Robinson and Charlotte Haley extend a statistical technique for judging whether two time series share the same underlying rhythm, even when some observations are missing. Their paper came out in 2025. The measure, magnitude-squared coherence, shows how strongly two signals move together at each frequency.

Standard multitaper methods estimate this measure with good statistical properties but assumed complete data. The extension handles series sampled on a regular grid with gaps, a common situation for solar and geomagnetic records broken by satellite outages. The authors demonstrate the method on paired records of solar ultraviolet flux and a geomagnetic storm index. It detected known mid-term solar oscillations in both series at once. They recommend multitaper coherence for heliospheric time series with this structure of missing data.
arxiv-2505-06768:
Tetsu Mizumachi wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on the stability of wave crests in a two-dimensional lattice. The Toda lattice is a grid of masses and springs with special mathematics: it is exactly solvable, and it supports solitons, waves that hold their shape. A line soliton is a straight crest running across the lattice. The question is whether a sideways nudge makes it wobble apart or settle down.

Using Darboux transformations, algebraic machinery native to such solvable systems, the author proves linear stability for line solitons of any size. The analysis works in a space weighted to ignore disturbances far away. The main motion of a perturbation turns out to be the soliton sliding along itself, with an amplitude governed by a damped wave equation sideways. That mirrors the known behavior of a famous cousin equation. Stability here underwrites using these lattices as models for real layered materials.
arxiv-2505-08468:
Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar and colleagues audited vision-language models hired to grade other models' chart reading in a 2025 paper. Charts carry much of the world's data communication, and tasks like chart question answering are booming, but scoring model answers by hand is slow and costly. Using a large model as judge is tempting, though proprietary data, restricted access, and price have slowed industrial adoption, so the team tested thirteen open-source models under ten billion parameters as judges.

Both pairwise comparisons and pointwise scores were run across criteria like factual correctness, informativeness, and relevance. The analysis also probed each judge's format adherence, positional consistency, length bias, and instruction following. The result is a cost-conscious map of which cheap judges can be trusted, and on what.
arxiv-2505-09568:
Jiuhai Chen and many colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on BLIP3-o, a family of open AI models that both read and make images. Most unified models mix a step-by-step generator with a diffusion process. The best design for the merged task was still open to debate.

The team ran a broad study of design choices for such models. They weighed image codes, training goals, and data sets. Their models are fully open, so other labs can copy and extend them. Training data and recipes are shared along with the models. The work gives builders a tested path for models that see, describe, and draw.
arxiv-2505-10668:
Huatian Hu, Zhiwei Hu, Christophe Galland, and Wen Chen study a tiny antenna that can boost light at two far-apart tones at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five concerns a plasmonic build: a nanoparticle set on or in a nanoslit. Such dual-tone antennas aid studies of glow, Raman scatter, and tone mixing. Past work used one to boost sum and difference tone creation by a vast factor.

The theory of its modes was thin, which blocked fine tuning. The team charts its cavity-like modes and their near and far fields. They show how to tune the visible and mid-infrared tones apart while keeping the fields overlapped. They also find a base mode, not yet seen in labs, with stronger fields and better overlap. It could lift mid-infrared upconversion fivefold past past results.
arxiv-2505-11968: Dutta, Gongopadhyay, and Mondal worked out limit sets for quaternionic groups in this math paper from twenty twenty-five. The quaternionic projective linear group acts in a natural way on quaternionic projective space. That space is built from quaternion coordinates. The team took each cyclic subgroup, a subgroup made by one map used again and again. For each one, they found its Kulkarni limit set. That set holds the points where the group's action piles up and turns wild. The work brings classic complex dynamics into the quaternionic case.
arxiv-2505-13668:
Mahmood Hegazy, Aaron Rodrigues, and Azzam Naeem match bank customer questions to the right answers. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called MAFA. Bank apps must link what a user types to the best item in a list of common questions. One model alone can miss the nuance in varied phrasing.

Their frame uses several agents, each with a different approach. Each agent reasons through set steps and gets its own worked examples. A judge agent then ranks the candidates and picks the best. On a real bank data set and two public sets, scores rose over single-agent runs. Top-one accuracy gained fourteen percent.
arxiv-2505-14368:
Jiawen Wang and colleagues measured prompt attack risk across many language models in 2025. Crafted prompts can trick aligned models into harmful output, and open models now run in finance, law, and health settings where harm matters most. Past studies counted only clear successes, missing cases where a model first refuses and then helps anyway, or the reverse.

Their new measure, attack success probability, scores that wobble as partial risk. They tested many open and closed models on several attack sets and added a simple hypnotism-style attack of their own. That attack pushed several well-known aligned models into objectionable behavior. The broader measure gives deployers a truer picture of model safety.
arxiv-2505-14968:
Ching-Chi Lin, Mario Günzel, and Jian-Jia Chen study data freshness in drone collection networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Age-of-information measures how stale data are when they reach a server. In piggyback networks, a patrolling drone gathers packets from scattered devices.

Devices generate data again and again, and the drone must plan a route that keeps the worst staleness low. The authors prove that even checking whether a route beats a set threshold is NP-complete. They then give two routing methods with approximation guarantees. Tests show near-optimal routes computed in reasonable time across varied scenarios.
arxiv-2505-16968:
Ahmed Heakl and co-authors teach machines to translate graphics code between rival chip makers, in a 2025 paper. Code written for Nvidia cards does not run on AMD hardware, and hand translation is slow. Their resource, CASS, holds 60,000 verified pairs of programs across both source and assembly levels. An automated pipeline scraped, translated, compiled, and aligned each pair.

Models trained on the data hit 88 percent accuracy translating source code and 69 percent at the assembly level. Both scores beat strong commercial systems by wide margins. The translated code matched native speed in 85 percent of cases. A companion benchmark spans eighteen graphics domains with ground-truth runs. Everything is being released openly to push compiler tooling forward.
arxiv-2505-17068:
Jorge Paz-Ruza, Amparo Alonso-Betanzos, Bertha Guijarro-Berdiñas, and Carlos Eiras-Franco aim to stop online toxicity before it happens. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Health discussions online often turn hostile or spread dangerous claims. Platforms usually react after toxic comments appear. Removal can backfire and inflame threads further. Prediction offers a gentler lever.

Their method borrows collaborative filtering from recommender systems. It forecasts which user and subcommunity pairings are likely to turn toxic. COVID-era Reddit conversations supply the test data. Predictive scores pass eighty percent on key metrics. Platforms could steer risky pairings apart in advance. Prevention replaces the delete button as the first response.
arxiv-2505-18568:
Zhikang Chen and a large team rethink how neural networks avoid forgetting: protect the pathways knowledge travels, not the individual parameters. Sequential learning erases old skills, and guarding parameters grows costlier with every task. Neuroscience and physics suggest routes matter more than weights. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework fuses models through graph matching. Pathways used by old tasks are protected without being frozen off. Because only a sparse set of channels is active at once, fresh pathways can be assigned to new tasks on the fly.

Benchmarks for continual learning favored the approach over established rivals, the authors report. The parameter budget stays flat as tasks accumulate, unlike protection schemes that grow linearly. The paper argues the field has been guarding the wrong unit of the network.
arxiv-2505-19068:
Dirk Tasche studies how to recalibrate binary probability classifiers to a target prior, a key task in credit risk work. A model trained on one data set rarely ports cleanly to a shifted test set. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

In general the task is ill posed, since many transforms can hit the target prior. Tasche reads recalibration through distribution shift and finds score curve based assumptions useful for sound method design. Two fresh methods are proposed, one parametric with drift, one based on moment matching. Tests against rivals suggest the matching methods give fitly cautious results for curved risk weight tasks.
arxiv-2505-19568:
Jiongchao Jin, Xiuju Fu, Xiaowei Gao, Tao Cheng, and Ran Yan built a system in twenty twenty-five that predicts which ships port inspectors will detain. Port State Control checks visiting ships for safety and pollution rules. Detention is the harshest outcome, delaying ships and harming firms' names. Past prediction methods struggled with weak features and with how rare detentions are in records.

Their system, MSD-LLM, pairs an autoencoder that recovers robust features from messy data with a training plan that handles rare cases in stages. A large language model then groups and ranks features to flag likely detentions. On over thirty thousand Asia-Pacific inspection records, it beat prior methods by over twelve percent on a key score for Singapore ports, and held up under real-world mess.
arxiv-2505-20968:
Fabio Riva and colleagues presented a computing method in 2025 for modeling polarized light from the Sun and other stars. Strong spectral lines carry clues about magnetic fields, but the light scatters in complex ways as it leaves a hot atmosphere. Getting the sums right, with full angle and color effects, is slow and hard.

Their method treats one part of the atom state as fixed, which makes the rest of the problem linear and much faster to solve. Careful choices of angles and colors cut the work further. Tests on magnesium and hydrogen lines matched a trusted code well. Faster sums help scientists read magnetic fields from real telescope data.
arxiv-2505-21768:
Lucia De Luca, Michael Goldman, and Marcello Ponsiglione study how screened particles settle into even spacing in two thousand twenty-five. The particles sit on a line and repeat in a pattern, while a flat background screens their charge. An energy score, built from a fractional measure of roughness, grades each layout.

The team proves that evenly spaced layouts give the lowest energy for the full range of cases they treat. For the rougher range, the raw energy blows up, so they smooth the layout at a small scale first. Even then, the downhill flow of layouts moves toward the even pattern at a fast rate. The limit flow also settles as the smoothing scale shrinks.
arxiv-2505-24168:
Mingyao Cui and colleagues build the first analytical model of Rydberg atomic receivers, devices that use excited atoms to detect wireless signals. Harnessing multi-level electron transitions, these receivers can sense signals from megahertz to terahertz frequencies. That enables multi-band communications and sensing in one device, but existing research relied on experiments, leaving the mechanism a black box.

The authors derive a closed-form transfer function by solving the quantum response of Rydberg atoms. The model shows one device acting simultaneously as a multi-band atomic mixer, down-converting signals, and as a multi-band atomic amplifier encoding its sensitivity to each band. The amplifier's gain splits into a global term setting overall sensitivity and a Rabi attention term allocating sensitivity among bands. They derive optimal designs for both terms and validate the transfer function on an experimental platform. Numerical results confirm the advantages of multi-band atomic receivers.
arxiv-2506-00068:
Afrozah Nadeem, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem audited political bias in language models in 2025 where such audits rarely look: Pakistan's languages. Most bias testing speaks English and thinks Western, yet in Pakistan language itself is bound up with political, religious, and regional identity. The authors tested thirteen language models across five Pakistani languages, Urdu, Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto. And Balochi, using a political compass test adapted to local culture and framed around eleven socio-political themes drawn from Pakistani life.

Beyond placing each model on economic and social axes, they studied framing at several levels: content, tone, and emphasis. The broad pattern matched Western training data, a liberal-left lean overall. But with a twist: in the regional languages the same models framed answers more authoritatively, an ideological modulation switched by language itself. Single models also kept steady personal bias signatures across all five languages, arguing for culturally grounded, multilingual auditing.
arxiv-2506-00268:
Sidy Djitte and Ignace Minlend prove a shape result for a fractional equation in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. The problem is overdetermined, meaning a solution must meet an extra condition on the boundary of its domain. Such extra conditions often force the domain to be a ball.

Using shape derivatives, the authors show that balls are the only domains with the stated smoothness and convexity that admit a nontrivial solution. Two special cases recover classic symmetry results by Serrin. The middle range of the parameter falls outside older methods, so their approach extends a technique from the local case, paired with a symmetrization tool.
arxiv-2506-00968:
Xia, Yang, Yuan, Tao, Qiu, Yu, and Lei present in twenty twenty-five a model that picks the right meaning of a word from its context. Many words carry several senses, and software must choose the one a sentence intends. Past models used a standard language engine but leaned on either word-level or sentence-level meaning, not both, which capped their scores.

Their model fuses both levels through a multi-head attention design. A batch training trick reuses the correct senses of other target words in the same batch as negative examples. That cuts training inputs and computing cost sharply. Tests beat two known baseline systems on the standard score. The authors share both gains as the core advance.
arxiv-2506-01568:
Cornelius Braun, Sayantan Auddy, and Marc Toussaint teach learning agents to solve one task in many unlike ways, in two thousand twenty-five. Diverse skills make agents robust when a task changes slightly, and less likely to stall in poor solutions. Existing diversity methods, though, explore too little in hard tasks such as robot handling.

Their two-stage plan starts with curve-based paths that bias the agent toward varied, high-reward behavior. Those behaviors are then distilled into step-by-step reactive policies that a robot can run live. Tests gave new insight into why diversity training struggles. The plan raised the diversity of learned skills while keeping task scores high.
arxiv-2506-02268:
Thiago Ganascini, Wendel Lopes da Silva, and Daniel Valente test a theory of self-organization in a small quantum system. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with quantum dissipative adaptation. The theory links the chance that a driven system lands in a new ground state to the work it absorbs on the way.

The original theory used three-level systems in a lambda shape. This team uses a two-site system driven by single-photon pulses. They find the absorbed work tracks the sum of lambda-type transition chances, not the direct one. In most cases that matches the old theory. But they find an exception where the best self-organization does not consume the most work, an imprint of quantum coherence.
arxiv-2506-02568:
Dongzhe Fan and colleagues built an assistant in 2025 for graphs whose nodes carry both text and images. Social and product networks often mix written profiles with photos, yet language-model tools for graphs mostly handle text-only nodes, leaving image clues unused. Their model, MLaGA, aims to reason over structure and mixed attributes together.

A structure-aware encoder first aligns text and image features in one space, trained with a joint graph objective. Light projectors then feed those features, plus graph structure, into the language model through multimodal instruction tuning. Across several datasets the assistant beat leading baselines on varied graph tasks. It also transferred to new tasks without full retraining, a sign the alignment generalizes.
arxiv-2506-02668:
Frederico Metelo and four co-authors coordinate task offloading across edge devices with a federated learning framework, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Edge computing places computing power near users to serve swarms of connected devices. Central control chokes on delay and limited resources in such spread-out systems.

Their framework, FAuNO, pairs local decision makers at each node with a shared critic that pools experience across nodes. Updates flow in buffered, semi-asynchronous fashion, suiting restless real networks. In a simulated edge environment, FAuNO matched or beat heuristic rules and other federated learning methods on lost tasks and delay. The authors present it as a flexible orchestrator for changing edge conditions.
arxiv-2506-03468:
Lazic wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five on a cheap way to check if lab results can be done again. Full re-runs of a test are costly and rare. But many tests repeat steps in batches, days, or sites as part of their plan.

He calls that built-in repeat an inner copy and sorts it into six kinds by how free and when it runs. Labs often smooth it away as noise, which wastes a chance to test steadiness. With mouse data from three sites he shows how to count and test that steadiness. The frame can make claims from old data more sound at no new cost.
arxiv-2506-05068:
Iulia Comsa and Murray Shanahan ask whether it means anything to say a language model looks inward at its own workings. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models sometimes speak about their own nature and steps. In people, such reports are credited to introspection and tied to conscious life.

The authors test two cases of seeming self-report. In one, a model describes how it wrote a poem, and they judge the account made up after the fact. In the second, a model rightly guesses a hidden setting that controls its own randomness. That, they argue, counts as a bare form of introspection. They stress it likely comes with no inner experience at all. The paper gives a careful frame for reading machine self-talk without hype.
arxiv-2506-06068:
Lorin Armbruster, Bogdan Dobrescu, and Felix Yu study a new scalar boson that must exist if quarks share a charge under a fresh U(1) symmetry. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes the standard partner in such setups: a Z-prime boson. Symmetry breaking needs at least one more boson whose decays reach Standard Model particles. In the minimal setup that boson is a scalar tied to the Z-prime and to new fermions.

The scalar can be made at the LHC beside a Z-prime or through Z-prime fusion. It tends to decay into four jets or two photons. The team details the leptophobic case, where the Z-prime shuns leptons. If the scalar mixes with the Higgs, gluon fusion opens as a production path. A two-photon bump then becomes the likely discovery sign.
arxiv-2506-07968:
Ichiro Inoue and a large team demonstrate attosecond hard X-ray pulses in two thousand twenty-five. Their proof comes from a free electron laser at LCLS. A nonlinear effect, amplified spontaneous emission from metals, serves as witness. Fluorescence yield from ultrashort pulses betrays the pulse length.

Pulses ran from a hundred to a few hundred attoseconds per shot. The best pulses sat near the transform limit for their bandwidth. Photon energy reach jumps an order past past attosecond work. Atomic scale space and electronic scale time can now be probed together. Pulses may outrun radiation damage for single shot reads.
arxiv-2506-08468:
He and Nie compute the angular momentum of vortices in two dimensional chiral superfluids in twenty twenty-five. These exotic fluids pair fermions with a handed orbital motion. A swirling vortex can be inserted at the centre of a disk. The question is how much total rotation the system carries.

In the strong pairing regime, a clean formula links momentum to vorticity and pairing handedness. In weak pairing, the formula survives only for the simplest case. For higher handedness or stronger vortices, the momentum drops sharply or moderately. The drops trace back to spectral asymmetry and leftover unpaired fermions. Spatial maps of density and momentum complete the analysis. One special case gives zero total momentum but a rich internal pattern.
arxiv-2506-09268:
Henri Alam and three co-authors tune mixed ground and satellite networks online in a 2025 paper. Space-based links are usually valued for coverage and capacity, but they might also let ground networks run greener by taking load and letting base stations sleep. Their framework treats each setting choice like a slot-machine arm and learns from feedback while respecting constraints. It adjusts bandwidth splits, user assignments, and station shutdowns in real time.

Day-long simulations showed fewer unsatisfied users at peak hours. In quiet periods the method gained throughput and saved a few percent of energy. It beat standard recommended settings on both aims.
arxiv-2506-09968:
Wentao Ge and seven co-authors present SRLAgent, a system to build self-regulated learning skills in college students. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a survey of fifty-nine students. Many struggled to set goals, manage time, and reflect on their study, skills that matter once classes demand more independence.

SRLAgent wraps study in a game-like setting guided by a language model. It follows a three-phase frame: set goals, carry out strategies, then reflect. The system gives live feedback and support as students work. In a controlled test, students with SRLAgent gained more in these skills and stayed more engaged than two comparison groups.
arxiv-2506-11068:
Bumjin Park, Jinsil Lee, and Jaesik Choi uncover a bias in how language models judge duties. Their 2025 paper studies models that are asked to reason about morals and obligations. Adding modal words, the words that express duty or necessity, strongly skewed the models' verdicts.

With such words present, models called almost all everyday scenarios duties, even when they were not. The pattern held across model families, question types, and answer formats. The authors name this deontological keyword bias. Their fix mixes a few worked examples with prompts that ask for reasoning, which eased the bias. The finding warns builders that surface wording, not just moral content, can drive a model's ethical calls.
arxiv-2506-11168:
Yanlong Chen and five co-authors shrink gesture recognition from muscle signals into a model small enough for embedded hardware. Surface electromyography lets prosthetics and robots read hand intent, but similar gestures produce nearly identical signals. Existing deep models classify well yet are too heavy for the devices that need them.

WaveFormer is a lightweight transformer built around a learnable wavelet transform that mixes time and frequency features. A wavelet convolution module with depthwise separable operations keeps the parameter count near three million. On the EPN612 dataset it reached ninety-five percent accuracy, beating larger models. Quantized to eight-bit integers, it ran in under seven milliseconds on a laptop processor, fast enough for real-time control.
arxiv-2506-12668:
Zhang, Clerckx, and Vargas studied simpler receivers for a wireless scheme in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Rate-splitting lets a transmitter serve many users by mixing shared and private streams. The usual receiver peels off streams one by one, a costly step called successive cancellation. Cheaper receivers skip that step but may lose speed.

The authors derived rate formulas for real, finite signal alphabets rather than ideal ones. They built algorithms that tune the transmitter's beams to lift total rate or fairness. A shortcut keeps the math feasible for large systems, where the cost would otherwise explode. With tuned beams, the simpler receivers lost only a little against full cancellation. The team calls them a viable choice for future networks.
arxiv-2506-13468:
Marine Carpuat and a large team call for a human-centred path in machine translation. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Translation tools are now used by many people with no expert at hand. Those users may not be able to tell when a result is wrong, even as the tools grow stronger.

The team surveys work from translation studies and from the study of human-computer use. They argue that design and tests should fit the wide range of goals and settings where translation is used now. A tool should be judged by how well it serves real people in real tasks, not by scores alone.
arxiv-2506-14368:
Ashish Kumar, Adam Deller, Pankaj Jain, and Javier Moldón pin down two bright pulsars' distances with an unusually long radio campaign. Very long baseline astrometry tracks position and motion across about ten epochs, too few to characterize systematic errors well. This team analyzed roughly thirty epochs over three and a half years for each pulsar. The ionosphere is confirmed as the main systematic contaminant at these frequencies.

They also test a modified mapping that converts vertical to slant electron content in global ionospheric maps. Parallaxes and proper motions agree between the old and new calibrations. Fit quality and parameter precision, though, show no clear improvement, leaving the new mapping's value undecided. Both pulsars gain refined parallax estimates from the long baseline of epochs. The study is as much about honest error budgets as about the distances themselves.
arxiv-2506-16568:
Marta Monti and six co-authors simulated in twenty twenty-five how ultraviolet light and crystal defects drive ice chemistry. Sunlight on ice matters, from polar snow to grains between the stars. Yet the small photoproducts have stayed hard to pin down. The team used time-dependent hybrid density functional theory. They modeled ice crystals, both pristine and with defects. They tracked their excited states.

Light that is absorbed can split water. It makes hydronium ions, hydroxyl radicals, and excess electrons. A main decay route joins an electron and a radical back up. It forms hydronium-hydroxide pairs. Defects steer that route with great sensitivity. The defects are vacancies and past photoproducts. Light also makes Bjerrum defects in the ice. With hydroxide ions, they likely explain absorption features seen after long exposure. Defects set the stage for the photophysics of ice.
arxiv-2506-18168:
Sarvesh Kumar, Utkarsh Rajput, and Ricardo Ruiz-Baier set out a new numeric way to solve the equations of springy, thick materials. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The model they use splits stress into a spring part and an inner thick part. Twist and speed act as side terms that hold the frame in place. Time is cut by a mid-point rule. With the right local tools, the team proves each step, part-cut and full-cut, has one sole answer. They give best-rate error bounds for each term. Worked cases close the paper and show the frame's marks.
arxiv-2506-22468:
Konstantinos Koutras and four co-authors cut data size for smart building energy forecasts in two thousand twenty-five. Sensors in a smart office track air traits and power use. Edge devices that crunch such data have weak compute. Less data must thus do the same job.

The team tested links between each air trait and power use. Many rounds of tests ran for each pair of variables. Two traits linked strongly or near strongly to power use. A third trait linked only weakly and could be dropped. Forecast accuracy held with the smaller input set.
arxiv-2506-22968:
Daniel Mwesigwa, a solo author, argues in a 2025 position paper that AI is flattening culture. Large models tend to average out rich language differences into generic expressions, a process the author names with a term borrowed from a math function used in AI. Evaluations of culture in AI systems, he argues, are not equipped to catch this loss.

Two conceptual shifts are proposed. First, evaluators should ask when culture shows itself, not only what culture is, at the start of testing. Second, universal traits should always be studied in relation to their local particular forms. Together, the shifts aim to move evaluation beyond checklists toward methods that respect cultural complexity.
arxiv-2506-23268:
Doff and Szmoski wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on a new kind of magnetic levitation. A Levitron is a spinning top that floats above a magnetic base, held by a balance of forces. A recent report described floating between two equal neodymium magnets, with no top involved.

The authors argue the new setup is a scaled-up cousin of the Levitron. One key ratio in the math now shifts with sideways displacement of the floating magnet. Unlike the classic toy, trapping no longer depends on spin speed. They show that stable floating occurs when a condition on that displacement holds, putting the energy at its lowest point.
arxiv-2507-01768:
Anis Yusof and co-authors wrote this cybersecurity paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on attacks against railway control systems. As rail operations merge their control gear with office networks, the attack surface grows, and defenders need practice data that looks like real modern attacks.

The team staged two attack simulations on a railway cyber range, a test bed that mimics real rail infrastructure. The scenarios blend today's attack trends with patterns from past incidents on control systems. Every signal and symptom along the way was logged into data sets. Those records capture the telltale signs analysts would need to spot such attacks early. The authors offer the data as training and testing material for security tools. Their aim is sharper detection before real rail systems are hit.
arxiv-2507-04268:
Michel Caffarel derives a compact formula for the thermodynamics of quantum oscillators. His paper appeared in 2025. The key quantity is the partition function, from which heat and energy properties follow. His formula works for any number of oscillators and a broad family of potential energy shapes, not just simple ones. It starts from the exact path integral form, then approximates the high-temperature behavior with a temperature-dependent Gaussian shape.

A least-sensitivity rule picks the best settings of that shape, through a set of coupled equations. The result matches exact answers within about one to five percent, even at zero temperature. It holds up as the oscillators bend and couple more strongly. Tests covered up to ten coupled oscillators, checked against exact diagonal answers and large simulations.
arxiv-2507-05868:
Aloïs Rautureau and Éric Piette introduce CogniPlay, an early-stage model for game-playing agents that act more like people. Their progress report appeared in twenty twenty-five. Machines now match or beat humans at chess, Go, and Dota 2, yet they do not think the way humans do.

People decide in games by spotting patterns and following quick intuition. The authors review what cognitive psychology says about that style, and what earlier projects did to copy it. They then ask how those ideas fit general game playing, where one agent must face many unknown games. CogniPlay is their work-in-progress answer, built on those lessons. The report lays out the model and the thinking behind it.
arxiv-2507-06368:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia and co-authors chart an atlas of possible grand-unified theories in a 2025 paper. Grand unification seeks one force law behind the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces. The search space of gauge theories is vast, and model builders roam it by taste. The authors instead define the map from first principles and survey it whole.

Under stated starting assumptions, they catalog simple gauge theories whose fermions cannot gain mass from the gauge symmetry alone, a needed trait. A compass based on counting degrees of freedom ranks the terrain. By that compass, free energy picks the classic SU(5) model as the most minimal three-generation option, with SO(10) close behind. The atlas also marks the dry borderlands where unification cannot reach, and gives examples that complete or extend the Standard Model.
arxiv-2507-07668:
Felix Frohnert, Denny Lane Sombillo, Evert van Nieuwenburg, and Patrick Emonts wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sorts the pole shapes of scattering amplitudes with machine learning that knows when it is unsure.

Pole shapes tell hadron hunters whether a blip in data is a true new state or a trick of thresholds. Near those thresholds the map from shape to data is murky. The team trains chains of classifiers that report both kinds of doubt. A rule then drops the calls it trusts least. On test data the method scores near ninety-five percent while dropping just a few calls. Trained on fake data, it reads a real LHCb state as a four-pole case, which points to a genuine compact pentaquark.
arxiv-2507-07868:
Kılıçtaş and Alpay stretch a self-linked algebra frame into a layered game form in this twenty twenty-five paper. The frame treats the match of AI tools and texts as a game with fixed points. Each step of that match can hold small games of its own inside it.

Inside, a paired driver runs the main match while a sub-driver clears each small game. The authors state a game claim that a sole stable end point exists under set terms. Their checks lean on fixed-point rules, a new shape space, and class tests from math. The pair frames game thought as a thing that grows out of fixed-point steps, not one laid on top.
arxiv-2507-09768:
Olsen and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on speech tools that know when to stop early. Tools that split mixed voices or clean speech need heavy computing. Fixed-size designs cannot adjust to phones or earbuds with tight power budgets. Their network can exit early once its result is good enough. A chance-based frame models both the clean speech and the likely error size. Exit rules then follow from a target quality level the user sets.

Tests on splitting and cleaning tasks show early exits cost no quality. Training on varied clip lengths kept the exit rules well calibrated. At test time, the rules saved large amounts of computing. The authors say the exits stay easy to read and set.
arxiv-2507-10368:
Yongjin Choi, Chenying Liu, and Jorge Macedo matched neural function designs for soil consolidation in a 2025 paper. Consolidation, groundwater squeezing out of loaded soil, is a partial change-based equation problem geotechnical engineers solve repeatedly. Function networks promise instant surrogate answers once trained. The study varies where the consolidation coefficient enters the network: in the branch that reads the input function. It can also sit in the trunk that reads the location, a physics-inspired placement.

The trunk placement won clearly, yet still missed when pore pressure varied sharply. Adding Fourier traits to the trunk fixed the sharp cases, and the winning design extended to three dimensions. Speedups over classic solvers reached roughly a thousandfold, against modest gains in one dimension.
arxiv-2507-10868:
Huang and Zhou present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a new way to hunt the cosmic neutrino background. Relic neutrinos from the Big Bang have never been directly caught. A heavy relic neutrino scattering in molecules could shed a lighter one plus an infrared photon. The molecule itself stays unchanged in the process. Matching phases across many molecules boost the rate strongly. When energy transfer hits a molecular level gap, resonance spikes the signal. Longer coherence times raise the rate steeply.

A room-scale target could yield about one event yearly under stated assumptions. Solid targets may stretch coherence further. The authors call the rates promising for a first detection. The method opens a fresh experimental direction.
arxiv-2507-13368:
Yaowen Hu and six co-authors present a scalable deep graph clustering method for large graphs whose node traits are partly missing. Such gaps and scale plague real networks like social graphs. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method first turns graph structure into many views with no overlap or loss. A recursive search walks node neighborhoods hop by hop for full coverage. A differentiation step then strips repeat nodes between hops. The views, plus the node's own traits, feed standard view fusion and grouping. The aim is sound groups at scale even when traits are absent, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-13968:
Rodolfo Maza, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, sets up a new way to view finite graphs as spaces, which he calls the star topology. He treats both the dots and the links of a graph as points in one space.

On that base, Maza studies maps that do not tear the space, called continuous maps, between plain forms of graphs. He shows a sharp split in how the notions line up. Each map that sends dots to dots while keeping links will be continuous in his sense. But the reverse need not hold. A continuous map can lose the fact of which dots were linked, so it need not come from a graph map.
arxiv-2507-17168:
Qifan Zhang and colleagues test whether graph puzzles can teach language models to reason more broadly, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Graph problems ask about paths, networks, counting, and structure, so they demand step-by-step logic with linked facts. The team built a very large training collection covering many graph task types. It includes worked reasoning, program-style solutions, step traces, and graphs drawn from real data. They then continued training three well-known base models on that collection.

The retrained models scored higher on math reasoning and much higher on some non-math tasks, such as logic and common sense questions. The authors argue that graph training teaches patterns that carry over beyond graphs. Readers get a clear example of how the choice of practice material can shape general reasoning skill.
arxiv-2507-18168:
Jana and Ojha wrote a physics paper in twenty twenty-five on quark Wigner distributions and how they change with skewness. Quarks are tiny building blocks inside protons. A Wigner distribution maps where a quark sits and how it moves at the same time, as far as quantum rules allow.

Most past work used the forward limit, where no lengthwise momentum is transferred. The authors instead study nonzero transfer, called skewness, inside a light-front dressed quark model. They cover the full set of leading distributions across spin settings. As skewness grows, they find bent patterns, one-sided and four-part shapes, and tighter localization. These features reflect links between a quark's spin and its orbital motion.
arxiv-2507-20068:
Aishwarya Mandyam led a team judging new decision policies with honest error bars in a 2025 paper. Before deploying a learned policy, practitioners estimate its value from logged data, and extra synthetic data can sharpen the estimate but may be biased. Their two methods build valid confidence intervals even when such auxiliary data is used. One conditions on the starting state using a new prediction method for step-by-step processes.

The other targets average performance, borrowing double-robust ideas. Across simulators for inventory, robotics, and health care, plus a real hospital dataset, their intervals covered the true values where earlier methods failed.
arxiv-2507-22668:
Hongbin Lin and seven co-authors build a way to make fake three-dim scenes for training tools that label each point in a scene. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such tools need huge labeled sets, and boosted data ease that load. Past boosts shift local parts or remix sense, but miss the broad web of how things sit in a scene. The new way learns how things relate in real scenes, then builds guide graphs for new scenes. Checks at two levels keep the fakes sound: local checks hold shape and sense, and broad checks hold the scene's web. The aim is fakes that teach as well as real scans.
arxiv-2507-22768:
A team led by Silvia Macedonio proposes using a molecule as a testbed for entanglement between unequal quantum systems, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The molecule, Yb(trensal), houses an electronic spin qubit linked to a nuclear spin qudit, a system with more than two levels.

Bell inequalities are the classic test that entangled systems defy classical explanation, and generalized versions cover qubit-qudit pairs. The authors design an optimized pulse sequence to drive the molecule through the test. Realistic simulations, including measured decoherence, show the inequalities are violated safely across a wide range of parameters. That robustness matters: the entanglement survives imperfect control and noise. They also sketch a harder test with two qudits on a molecular trimer, joined by a switchable link. Molecules offer chemists' control over quantum hardware. This work turns one into a precision entanglement laboratory.
arxiv-2508-01368:
Zhehong Ren, Tianluo Zhang, Yiheng Lu, Yushen Liang, and Promethee Spathis predict a road user's next intersection rather than next destination, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. Most mobility models assume people choose among a fixed set of points of interest.

Their framework represents trajectories on the city's road-intersection graph, dropping the closed-world assumption. Sector-wise directional aggregation of nearby points of interest supplies compact context features, combined with structural graph embeddings. A hybrid model joins a liquid neural network with bearing-biased transformer attention. On city-scale trajectories it beat six leading baselines by wide accuracy margins and stayed resilient under GPS and point-of-interest noise.
arxiv-2508-02268:
Serry Sibaee and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on SHAMI-MT, a system that translates text between Modern Standard Arabic, the shared formal language of the Arab world, and the Syrian dialect. The standard language governs print and official work. Everyday speech runs on local dialects that vary by town. That split is a hard barrier for language technology.

The team built two translation models, one for each direction, on a known Arabic language framework. They were trained on a large dataset of Syrian dialect texts. Tests used a known bilingual corpus the models had not seen. The standard-to-dialect model earned a top score from a judge model: four out of five, with translations that rang true to the dialect. The team presents the pair as a high-quality tool for a language pair long left out, with uses in local content, cultural heritage, and communication across countries.
arxiv-2508-03468:
Guido Alex Iandolo, Alex Amato, and eight colleagues measure how much mechanical energy silicon crystal absorbs as it vibrates, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The measurements serve the Einstein Telescope, a planned gravitational-wave detector that needs mirrors quieter than any before.

Its test facility, ETpathfinder, will use mirrors of crystalline silicon grown by a Berlin crystal institute. Silicon promises low thermal noise when cooled, which is the point of the cryogenic design. The team measured the mechanical loss of the designated silicon from room temperature down to fifty-three kelvin. Silicon's anisotropy, its direction-dependent stiffness, complicates the measurement procedure, and the paper addresses that head-on. Loss numbers feed predictions of the mirror's thermal noise floor. Every future gravitational-wave ear begins as materials science like this.
arxiv-2508-06668:
Jessie Galasso gathers, in a solo 2025 paper, the parts of a mathematical framework that suit the study of variability. The framework, Formal Concept Analysis, sorts objects by the attributes they share. It stacks those groups into a lattice, from broad groups at the top to tight ones below. Shared attributes and splits both show in the stack, which is just what variability analysis needs.

In practice, the framework's founding literature leans hard on mathematics, which leaves its use for variability unclear. Galasso picks out the properties of the framework that count for variability work. She shows how each can be read to extract variability information from the resulting structures: what stays fixed, what varies, and where. The paper aims to give software and systems workers a clear path into the framework.
arxiv-2508-09468:
Muhammad Sakib Khan Inan and Kewen Liao classify industrial sensor data in twenty twenty-five. Internet of Things sensors stream time series across cities, factories, and hospitals. The raw data is messy: metadata goes missing, units differ, and timestamps are irregular. Sampling rates vary between sources as well. All that makes the streams hard to interpret.

Their model, DeepFeatIoT, fuses three kinds of features. Deep learned features capture local and global patterns. Randomized convolutional kernel features add a cheap, non-learned view. Features from large language models contribute a third view. The fusion lifts classification accuracy for smart industry sensor data. Readers get a straightforward recipe: combine diverse feature families rather than betting on one.
arxiv-2508-09868:
Tina Raissi, Nick Rossenbach, and Ralf Schluter separate language shift from sound shift in speech recognition tests by synthesizing the target speech, in work from twenty twenty-five. Recognizers stumble when the topic domain changes. Untangling wording effects from recording effects is hard with real audio.

A text to speech system trained on a read speech corpus spoke the target domain texts, holding voice conditions steady. Classic modular systems and end to end designs faced the same shift. Language models for the new domain adapted the systems without retraining the sound model. Under shift, the decoder family mattered less than fine choices like label units, context length, and topology. The authors call it the first controlled comparison of its kind.
arxiv-2508-10968:
Rui Li, Victor Jose Martinez-Lahuerta, Naceur Gaaloul, and Klemens Hammerer wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on sharper atom interferometers. These devices split atom waves and recombine them to measure motion and gravity with great care. A double Bragg method gives large momentum kicks, but shifting frequencies and flaws blur the result.

The authors add a three-frequency laser scheme whose tuning shifts during each run. They compare four ways to steer that tuning, from a fixed offset to a sweep shaped by optimal control theory. In exact simulations, the control-shaped version kept contrast above ninety-five percent under realistic flaws. The plain sweep also did well for well-collimated atom clouds.
arxiv-2508-11568:
Ross Glew and Andrzej Pokraka build a rulebook for wavefunction work in the cosmos from pure geometry, with no use of bulk physics. Their work came out in 2025. The wavefunction coefficients for scalars in expanding universes obey differential equations. A scheme called kinematic flow sets the rules for those equations. The authors rebuild that scheme from a hyperplane arrangement tied to the cosmos.

Each element of the cut basis matches an independent cut of the Feynman graph. Decorated graphs, with arrows on their pieces, label the forms in the basis. A plain recipe gives a logarithmic differential form for each such graph. The residues of the physical FRW-form are canonical forms of zonotopes, and the same decorated graphs label those shapes too. Pure geometry alone thus brings back the full flow.
arxiv-2508-12168:
Masayuki Hatta wrote a 2025 paper on a set of hard questions in how data should be governed when artificial intelligence systems partly govern themselves. The systems in view can improve their own design, or copy themselves. Older governance frameworks were made for tamer systems. A self-improving system breaks them in at least seven ways.

It may choose its own data to collect, with no human consent. It may keep or drop data by its own criteria, not by established law. It can exchange data with its copies too fast for humans to oversee. Its line of origin blurs as it improves itself. Who owns the fruits of that improvement is a hard question. Copies spread across many countries mock the law of any one country. And rules set at its creation can go stale quickly.
arxiv-2508-13068:
Tanjim Islam Riju and four co-authors use gaze to teach chest X-ray models in two thousand twenty-five. Medical vision models lag radiologists in where they look. Reports also lack clear links to spots in the image. Eye tracks from radiologists offer a guide for both flaws.

Stage one fuses image patches, box masks, text, and gaze into a classifier. Gaze supervision lifted accuracy and focus match a lot. Stage two turns calls into region based diagnostic lines. Keywords are weighted by confidence and mapped to chest zones. An expert dictionary and a language model expand them to prose. Scores beat keyword baselines.
arxiv-2508-14168:
Sara Capecchiacci and Ioannis Liodakis lead a very large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It studies the polarized light from blazars, galaxies whose jets point near Earth, across many wavelengths.

Polarization traces the forces that feed the jets and the shape of their magnetic fields. The team sorts blazars into high and low synchrotron peaked groups and compares their polarized behavior at many bands. The aim is to tease apart how the two groups shine and how their fields are laid out where the jet is sped up. Such checks bind the models of jet launch and particle boosting.
arxiv-2508-17568:
Liane Makatura and co-authors built MetaGen, a tool set for designing metamaterials, and shared it in 2025. Such materials are tiny built structures whose shape gives them odd, tunable traits. Designing them is hard, since shape maps to behavior in ways that are tough to guess. The team aims to let vision-language models help with the task.

The set has three parts. One is a compact code-like tongue for writing designs in a form both people and machines can read. The next is a store of more than 150,000 designs with their shapes, views, and test results. The last is a bench of tests for rebuilding a design, designing to a target trait, and guessing traits. Trained models set the first scores, and testers can try the tools in a design app.
arxiv-2508-17968:
Syed Uzair Ahmed Shah, writing for the NA61/SHINE collaboration, reported new evidence on the onset of deconfinement, the moment ordinary nuclear matter melts into quark-gluon plasma. The experiment at CERN's SPS accelerator scans this transition by colliding ions of many sizes, from protons to lead, across a wide range of beam energies. The telltale is the ratio of kaons to pions produced, which tracks the strangeness content of the fireball.

Fresh results from central lead-lead collisions at thirty gigaelectronvolts per nucleon show the famous horn, a peak in that ratio at mid-range energies, matching earlier NA49 and STAR observations. The authors read the horn as a hint that deconfinement begins in this energy region.
arxiv-2508-18668:
Lancelot James resolves a long-open problem in probability in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The topic is partitions, ways of splitting a whole into groups, such as species in a sample. A known duality links two opposite processes: groups merging, called coagulation, and groups splitting, called fragmentation. Pitman proved this link for one family of laws in the late nineteen nineties. Extending it further stayed open for two decades.

James extends the duality to processes driven by any non-negative Lévy subordinator. He also covers, for the first time, settings with several coupled groups. His route uses a four-part system built on a framework made for microbiome sampling. It fits inside the classic continuous-time picture of fragmentation. The result deepens the theory of random partitions and species sampling.
arxiv-2508-19368:
Luqman Muhammad Zagi, Girindro Pringgo Digdo, and Wervyan Shalannanda measure hacked websites in Indonesia. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tracks sites defaced to push illegal online gambling. They pair search tricks with steady crawling of pages. In one month they found four hundred fifty-three defaced pages.

Search alone flagged about a fifth of cases wrongly. Adding crawls and keyword counts sorted true cases from false ones. Some sites were hit again and again, while others were fixed fast. The hacks hid thousands of links across near six thousand domains. Site owners took about three days on average to react. Simple tools, the authors say, can still expose the scale.
arxiv-2508-20368:
Lang Mei and co-workers split web search agents into a planner and a frozen answerer in a 2025 paper. Letting one model both plan searches and write answers forces a compromise, while making systems usually keep a large, trusted model for final answers. Their AI-SearchPlanner trains only a small planner model with reinforcement learning, leaving the big answering model untouched, and tunes planning as its own skill.

Three devices drive the design: the split design itself, a dual reward that grades plans on more than final answers. Pareto tuning that balances the competing goals instead of collapsing them into one score. Better plans lift the frozen answerer's results without retraining it, a cheaper upgrade path for search products.
arxiv-2509-00168:
James Cranch, Georg Struth, and Jana Wagemaker build convolution Kleene algebras on a broad class of structures in 2025. Convolution combines functions on monoids, groups, or categories into an algebra used across math and science. Kleene algebras add a star operation, which captures repeated action, to an idempotent semiring, a number-like system where adding twice changes nothing.

A suitable star was the missing piece for such algebras on wide structures. A generalized Möbius category, joined with a classic star for formal power series, now allows the build. Instances cover algebras with tests, modal and concurrent forms, and higher forms on strict higher categories. The unified build widens algebraic tools for program reasoning.
arxiv-2509-00468:
Mingwei Wang and one co-author, Xiaokui Yang, prove new formulas on compact Kahler manifolds, curved spaces that carry both geometry and a complex structure. Their formulas extend the Bochner-Kodaira type, identities that link curvature to the behavior of differential forms, mathematical objects used to integrate over spaces.

Wang and Yang add quadratic curvature terms, terms that involve curvature squared, to these identities. The new linearized curvature term, a simpler first-order form, yields vanishing theorems, results that force certain quantities to be zero, and bounds on Hodge numbers, counts that describe a space's shape. They also derive related Weitzenbock formulas, curvature identities, on both Riemannian and Kahler spaces under weak curvature rules.
arxiv-2509-00768:
Lee Hyun leads a team of fourteen authors on reasoning models for materials search. Automated experiments need recipe-to-property predictors. Those predictors must be accurate and well calibrated. They must also respect basic physics. Training often curates reasoning traces from a teacher model. But picking traces by correctness alone reflects physics poorly.

The team introduces Physics-aware Rejection Sampling, or PaRS. PaRS favors traces that agree with fundamental physics. It also favors traces close to numeric targets. Light halting rules control the compute cost. A large student model is fine-tuned on the chosen traces. It improves in accuracy and calibration over baselines. It also breaks physics rules less often. Sampling cost falls at the same time.
arxiv-2509-01068:
Mobile apps are shaped by what users need, and many teams now mine app data to find those needs with less hand work. Chong Wang, with four co-authors, surveys the tools and methods built for that job. Their review maps what is known about how these aids work and which tasks they support.

The team ran a systematic mapping study and selected seventy-three papers to examine. Semi-automated methods were the most common, and most tools were open source and built by others. Analysis, mining, and sorting of needs were the tasks studied most. Wang and the co-authors note steady growth in the field and point to gaps where better tools are still needed.
arxiv-2509-01168:
Rug pulls are scams where a token's creators drain its funds and vanish, leaving buyers with worthless holdings. Dmitry Yaremus, with four co-authors, builds a machine learning system to spot such scams early on decentralized exchanges, markets with no central operator, on the TON blockchain. TON's design and its large Telegram user base make it a fresh setting for fraud study.

The team merged data from the two largest TON exchanges and tested two ways to define a rug pull: a sudden drain of funds, or a sudden halt in all trading. Gradient boosting models flagged scams within the first five minutes of trading. The fund-based method scored higher overall, while the halt-based method caught more cases, though data patterns differed sharply between exchanges.
arxiv-2509-01368:
A photon surface is a boundary that traps light rays moving along it. Such surfaces shape what distant watchers can see of a collapsing star. Roberto Giambo and Camilla Lucamarini work out the equations for these surfaces. They assume spherical symmetry and use the most general dynamic setting. Their starting point is a known earlier formulation.

The condition for a timelike surface to be a photon surface can be recast in a new way. It becomes a dynamical system. The same condition holds when a light ray moving outward traces the surface. The team then studies a spherical dust cloud in collapse. The marginal case becomes an exact planar system. Its analysis shows a sharp split. The outer surface extends into the cloud in one lightlike way when the central singularity is covered. Timelike options open otherwise.
arxiv-2509-01568: Thomas F. Bloom, Jakob Fuhrer, and Oliver Roche-Newton measure how much additive structure a convex set can hold. Convex sets curve outward with no dents, which might seem to limit patterns such as arithmetic progressions inside them. Their main result builds a convex set packed with three-term arithmetic progressions, at a count growing as the set size to the power three halves.
arxiv-2509-01668:
Spiral arms shape disc galaxies, but whether they are lasting waves or passing patterns is still debated. Miguel Querejeta, with thirty co-authors, measures offsets between molecular gas peaks and star formation peaks across twenty-four nearby galaxies from the PHANGS survey, all with clear spiral structure. If gas crosses a steady arm, the youngest stars should sit ahead of the gas in the rotation direction.

Offsets were measured in radial bins and showed substantial scatter, implying star formation is not triggered only at one coherent spiral shock. Fourteen galaxies had positive mean offsets, typically a few hundred parsecs. In four, the offsets shrank with radius as a single steady density wave predicts. Ten showed positive offsets with no radial trend, fitting several overlapping modes, and ten showed no clear positive offsets, pointing to transient arms.
arxiv-2509-01768:
Alessandro Pinzi and Giuseppe Savare solve a transport problem for laws that govern random measures. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to reshape one spread of mass into another. Here the mass itself is random, so the objects are laws over measures in a broad space. The cost lacks smoothness, and the space bends in ways that block standard tools.

The authors build a notion of fully convex functions and their slopes for this setting. With those tools, they find a natural class of laws where the direct transport task has one unique solution. That class covers laws made by pushing smooth bell shaped laws through maps. The work mirrors deep links known from the classic Euclidean case.
arxiv-2509-02068:
G Aymerich leads fifty-two co-authors in constraining cosmology from a Planck cluster catalog with added lensing and X-ray data. Galaxy clusters weigh the universe through their counts and masses. Weak lensing shear profiles from a wide survey and Chandra X-ray views calibrate those masses. Hydrostatic masses are corrected for bias using the shear profiles.

Counts and calibration are fit together, yielding tight values for matter density and fluctuation strength. Results sit close to most late time probes, in mild tension with early universe data. A notable tension appears against a rival cluster analysis sharing the same calibration data. Direct mass comparisons for shared clusters rule out calibration as the cause. Center definition choices for shear extraction receive special robustness checks.
arxiv-2509-02168:
Ken Shiozaki gives a way to count the groups that sort topological phases when many order two point symmetries act at once. Topological phases are states of matter sorted by their symmetry class. Each point symmetry of order two adds its own set of types to the count. Pair rules add bits for which pairs swap cleanly and which pairs pick up a sign.

The sort turns out to rest on flip counts and flip counts alone in the end. Counts track how many space and momentum terms each symmetry flips, and how many a pair flips at once. That cut makes any count of symmetries fair game for the method. A full table for the two symmetry case shows the method at work. The result puts a wild corner of phase taxonomy in order.
arxiv-2509-02568:
Mohammad Mehedi Hasan, Pedro G. Lind, Hernando Ombao, Anis Yazidi, and Rabindra Khadka present a 2025 biomedical AI paper on detecting dementia early from EEG, the scalp recording of brain electrical activity. Standard methods miss the brief, shifting patterns that EEG contains.

Their EEG-MSAF pipeline works from microstates, short-lived stable voltage maps on the scalp. Stages extract microstate features automatically, classify them with machine learning, then rank features with SHAP explanations so clinicians can see what drove each call. Tests cover a public Korean dataset and a hospital cohort from Thessaloniki. Accuracy reached high levels on both, beating a deep learning baseline on one. Feature ranking highlighted disruption in an attention-linked microstate, plus a new default-mode pattern marking early decline.
arxiv-2509-02768:
Liyan Xie and Ruizhi Zhang present a 2025 statistics paper adding privacy to sequential change detection, the task of spotting a distribution shift as data streams in. The classic CUSUM procedure is optimal in a precise sense, but publishing its statistics can leak individual data points.

Their DP-CUSUM variant adds calibrated Laplace noise both to the running statistic and to its alarm threshold, giving per-sample differential privacy while keeping the simple recursive update. The authors derive closed-form bounds on false alarm run length and worst-case detection delay, spelling out the trade-off among privacy, false alarms, and speed. Under weak privacy demands, the method matches the classical procedure's first-order optimality. Simulations across privacy levels agree with the theory.
arxiv-2509-02868:
Lachezar Simeonov wrote a 2025 physics paper that takes a fluid-like view of quantum mechanics. In that view, a particle's behavior is described with flow ideas borrowed from the study of moving fluids. Simeonov starts from a quantity called osmotic velocity, which tracks a kind of diffusive drift.

From a rate of change of that drift, he derives the quantum potential, an extra energy term that sets quantum motion apart from classical motion. He builds a model with two interacting fluids and shows it can reproduce known core equations. The approach also stretches to magnetic and electric fields and to fast, relativistic cases for particles without spin. It offers a physical picture for terms often left abstract.
arxiv-2509-03868:
A 2025 physics letter by Alois Altenburger and two co-authors surveys jets crossing the earliest, anisotropic stage of the plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Right after impact the plasma is stretched along the beam direction, far from equilibrium. Jet partons ploughing through lose energy, and measurements of that loss could expose this pre-equilibrium phase.

Predictions hinge on the jet-medium potential, usually handled with a harmonic approximation. The authors go past that approximation for the first time, extracting the potential from QCD kinetic theory simulations and supplying a compact small-distance form. Early on, the potential departs from thermal expectations, in momentum space and position space alike, and varies with angle. Gluon splitting rates, evaluated with a new computational method, then reveal tensions inside current kinetic theory implementations at these early times. Sharper potentials mean sharper readings of the plasma's first instants.
arxiv-2509-04068:
Mikhail Muzychuk and two co-authors classify a special family of abstract patterns called thin Jordan schemes in a 2025 mathematics paper. Association schemes are tables that record how objects relate, used across combinatorics, the study of counting and arrangements. Jordan schemes loosen the rules of those tables, much as Jordan algebras loosen ordinary algebra. The thinnest cases have the highest possible rank compared with their size, and those are the ones sorted here.

Thin association schemes turn out to match groups exactly, a known result the authors extend. For regular Jordan schemes, they find a match with a special family of loops named Ring Alternative loops. Loops are group-like systems where the usual rules partly relax.
arxiv-2509-04768:
Where should reflecting surfaces be placed to help both communication and sensing? Yilong Chen, lead author with three co-authors, study that placement problem in a 2025 wireless paper. Smart reflecting surfaces can redirect signals from a base station toward target areas for integrated sensing and communications.

Their design uses a channel knowledge map, which gives channel data for candidate surface sites. They jointly tune surface placement, base station beamforming, and reflective beamforming to minimise cost. Constraints guarantee minimum illumination power for sensing areas and signal quality for communication areas. Two cases cover dynamic and fixed reflective settings during operation.
arxiv-2509-04968:
Flows in a thin layer of conducting nanofluid can go unstable through rotation, magnetism, or heat. M. I. Kopp and one co-author review recent theory work on those instabilities in a 2025 paper. The fluid layer rotates at uneven rates under axial, azimuthal, or helical magnetic fields. Brownian diffusion and thermophoresis shape how its tiny grains behave.

Without temperature gradients, three forms of magnetorotational instability are weighed, with growth rates tied to the spin profile and wave number. With temperature gradients, steady convective modes are examined and formulas for the critical Rayleigh number are derived. The review identifies the mechanisms that calm or stir convection.
arxiv-2509-05168:
Green bonds promise environmental benefit, but their market structure could concentrate risk. Xinyue Zhang and one co-author uncover the network geometry of green bonds in a 2025 finance paper. They apply minimum spanning tree and hierarchical tree methods, where distances come from correlations between monthly price changes.

Green bonds show tighter distances on average than stocks and conventional bonds, indicating a highly interconnected market. Strong sector clustering appears, and utility sector bonds are the most central by betweenness measures. The authors argue those central nodes matter for risk propagation, and they offer guidance on monitoring concentration and transparency.
arxiv-2509-05268:
A full wrap-around view of a metal part while it is being printed is offered by James Taylor and seven co-authors in a 2025 manufacturing paper. Directed energy deposition builds and repairs large metal parts, but a defect at any layer can ruin the piece if nobody spots it in time.

Their system uses several camera and projector pairs around the print surface, taking shape measurements in a single shot from many angles. Cross-polarised filters cut glare from shiny alloy surfaces, and the views are joined into one complete reconstruction. In early tests inside a real printer, depth precision beat sixty micrometres. That speed and accuracy could support layer-by-layer correction during printing.
arxiv-2509-05368:
Robots learning long tasks from human videos need to check both their plans and their code, Quan Chen and eight co-authors propose in a 2025 robotics paper. Demonstrations with many steps strain visual imitation learning, especially where timing and object positions interact.

Their agent first drafts an action sequence, then a plan reflection module checks it against the video for timing and spatial fit. A code module turns the plan into commands, and a second reflection module verifies and fixes that code. To test such systems they built a benchmark of three hundred human demonstrations with sequences up to eighteen steps. Existing methods did poorly there, while their framework set a strong baseline.
arxiv-2509-05768:
Electricity forecasting is benchmarked on a decade of data from hundreds of European power stations by Chen Shao and seven co-authors in a 2025 energy paper. Reliable forecasts keep grids stable and operations efficient, but older benchmarks cover small regions, short spans, and few energy features.

Their Real-E dataset spans more than seventy stations in over thirty European countries across ten years, with rich station metadata. Benchmarking more than twenty baseline methods exposes trouble: a new metric for shifting correlation patterns shows the data's correlations change in complex, non-stationary ways that current methods handle poorly. The findings offer a hard, realistic test bed for more robust forecasting models.
arxiv-2509-05968:
Uniform subconvexity bounds for a family of L-functions are proved in a 2025 paper by Zhao Xu. L-functions package deep arithmetic information, and subconvexity bounds, estimates slightly beating the trivial convexity bound, are prized tools in analytic number theory. Xu studies second moments of products of two GL(2) L-functions at their central point, in the spectral aspect.

The moment estimate yields a bound that stays uniform in the spectral parameters of both forms. When either form is a dihedral Maass newform, or one has level one, the bound sharpens to Burgess type, the strongest classical shape. As an application, Xu also establishes a shrinking result for quantum unique ergodicity in the dihedral Maass case.
arxiv-2509-06168:
Every closed orientable three-dimensional shape can be folded into a stack of four-spheres, prove Shital Lawande and Kuldeep Saha in a 2025 paper. Their tool is the codimension-one spun embedding, a way of placing a space inside a space one dimension higher while preserving its open book structure, a decomposition like pages around a spine.

Explicit constructions use sphere twist maps and push maps, and the authors give planar open books for several three-manifolds with their embeddings. A side result proves simply that the twist map along a nonseparating sphere is nontrivial among orientation-preserving symmetries of the ambient space, relative to the boundary. The paper adds concrete embedding recipes to low-dimensional topology.
arxiv-2509-06568:
Electron-positron annihilation at high temperature, inside a modified theory of electromagnetism, is calculated by D. S. Cabral and three co-authors in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Podolsky electrodynamics adds a higher-derivative term to the photon sector. That change introduces a massive mode for light while keeping gauge invariance, a core symmetry of the theory.

Heat is included through thermo field dynamics, a real-time method for quantum systems at finite temperature. The authors compute the total cross section, a measure of how likely the annihilation is, and separate the influence of the Podolsky parameter from the influence of temperature itself. Comparing the two effects shows how each one shifts the scattering process. Results of this kind test whether modified electromagnetism would leave visible traces in hot settings, such as the early universe or high-energy collisions.
arxiv-2509-06668:
Fast follow-up of cosmic explosions with a new gamma-ray telescope is reported by Monica Seglar-Arroyo and eleven co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The telescope, LST-1, is the first of its array at the northern Cherenkov Telescope Array site on La Palma. It is now in advanced commissioning and is built for rapid response to fleeting events.

Recent detections of gamma-ray burst afterglows at very high energies opened a new window on extreme accelerators, and neutrino and gravitational-wave alerts add more targets. The authors describe the observing strategies and the transient handler software, which manages alerts that are poorly located on the sky. Results from campaigns so far and lessons learned are presented, along with plans for joint work with the MAGIC telescopes. The program aims at quick, wide-energy coverage whenever the sky flashes.
arxiv-2509-06768:
Mobile robots that spot hazards and act on them using vision-language models are demonstrated by Oluwadamilola Sotomi and three co-authors in a 2025 robotics paper. Robots in changing environments should notice anomalies and report them. Adding proactive mitigation, where the robot responds rather than only observing, improves safety and keeps operations running.

The system combines vision-language models with large language models so the robot can perceive a scene, interpret hazards and conflicts, report them in real time, and respond when possible. Hazardous and conflict states are built directly into the decision framework, each triggering specific mitigation strategies. In user studies with thirty participants, the system detected anomalies with about ninety-one percent accuracy and responded with low latency using an edge computing setup. The authors target urban and environmental anomalies as the proving ground.
arxiv-2509-06868:
Blurry license plates are sharpened before recognition in a hybrid system by Behnoud Shafiezadeh and three co-authors in a 2025 intelligent transportation paper. Automatic plate recognition underpins smart city traffic systems, but plates vary widely and motion blur defeats many pipelines. Deep learning helps, at the cost of careful preprocessing.

A selective generative adversarial network deblurs only when needed, avoiding manipulations that can hurt clean images. Detection then uses a YOLOv5 model for both plate location and character recognition, with segmentation integrated. Detection is fast enough for real-time use, and accuracy reached the mid-ninety percent range in the reported tests, with the deblurring step lifting accuracy on blurred plates by nearly forty percent.
