Dimer graphs are networks of black and white nodes joined by edges, borrowed from statistical physics. The team constructs them for classical untwisted Lie algebras and for twisted types as well. Reflective boundaries on the chains get their own dimer treatment. The key result links the graphs to five-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theory. The Seiberg-Witten curve of the pure gauge theory turns out to be the spectral curve of the Toda chain for the dual group. That match gives physicists a concrete graph tool for computing curve data.
arxiv-2510-01868:
Areces, Cassano, Dutto, and Fervari give a data-aware logic a full proof system in this 2025 paper. Modal logics can express reachability through structured data, which suits query languages like XPath and GQL. The richest such logic here, a hybrid system, also handles value comparisons and key-based navigation. Earlier work studied what the logic can say, not how to prove things inside it.

The authors present a Gentzen-style sequent calculus tailored to that hybrid logic. They prove the calculus sound, so its proofs never produce falsehoods. They also prove it complete, so every truth of the logic has a proof. Every rule in the system turns out to be invertible, which eases automated proof search. The calculus enjoys cut elimination as well, keeping proofs analytically clean. The work lays proof-theoretic foundations for reasoning about semi-structured data queries.
arxiv-2510-01968:
Lanzendörfer, Fearne, Grötschla, and Wattenhofer watermark music after the fact, without training a dedicated embedder, in this 2025 paper. Provenance marks help listeners verify clips and credit creators as synthetic audio spreads. Older schemes often break under ordinary compression or editing. Learned embedder-detector pairs are robust, but they demand heavy training pipelines.

Their method, Timbru, optimizes each snippet directly at embedding time. Gradient steps add tiny perturbations inside a pretrained audio autoencoder's latent space. A combined message and perceptual loss keeps the sixteen-bit mark strong yet inaudible. A pretrained CLAP model then reads the watermark back out. On the MUSDB18-HQ benchmark, Timbru earned the best average bit error rates against filtering, noise, compression, resampling, cropping, and regeneration attacks. It did so while preserving perceptual quality. The dataset-free design makes strong watermarking available without any training run.
arxiv-2510-02168:
The CMS Collaboration presents a normalized autoencoder that hunts new physics in collision data in this 2025 paper. Autoencoders flag anomalies by reconstruction error, but they often reconstruct outliers too well, hiding the signal. Their Wasserstein normalized autoencoder treats reconstruction error as an energy in a Boltzmann distribution. Training minimizes the Wasserstein distance between that learned distribution and the data.

The target application is semivisible jets, sprays mixing visible particles with invisible dark matter states. Trained only on simulated standard model jets, the model learns the input distribution in an unsupervised way. New-physics jets then stand out as anomalies without any signal-specific tuning. Training proved stable across tests. It beat standard normalized autoencoders across a wide range of signals. The signal-agnostic design suits the LHC, where the next discovery's shape is unknown. The method directly attacks the outlier reconstruction failure mode.
arxiv-2510-02668:
Ma and co-authors build recommendation agents that explain themselves without any task training. Their 2025 paper presents a framework called AgenticRAG. Recommender systems usually hide their reasoning from users. Foundation models bring knowledge limits of their own. The framework fuses three ingredients into one agent. Retrieval-augmented generation pulls in outside knowledge. Tool calls let the agent act on that knowledge. Chain-of-thought reasoning exposes each decision step. The agent then recommends items in a zero-shot setting. Transparency comes from the visible reasoning trail.

Three real datasets tested the framework against strong baselines. Ranking quality improved on every dataset tried. Gains were largest on the Yelp data. Explainability rose while compute stayed near traditional methods. Users can audit why an item was suggested. Trustworthy recommenders need that audit trail built in. Tool using agents look like a viable path forward.
arxiv-2510-02768:
Agnihotri and co-authors test whether safety training survives a popular trick that strips refusals from open models. Their 2025 AI safety paper studies model abliteration. Anyone can edit open weights at inference time. Abliteration projects out the directions linked to refusing. The question is which safety ingredients resist that edit. The team tracked a granular ladder of safety pretraining checkpoints. Twenty systems, original and edited, faced one hundred prompts each. Harmful and harmless cases balanced the prompt set. Several automated judges labeled refusals, checked against human labels.

The study maps robustness checkpoint by checkpoint. Data centric safety parts differed in how well they endured. Judge choice measurably shifted the evaluation outcomes. Models also varied at spotting refusals in their own outputs. A practical testing protocol emerges from the work. Safety claims should include inference time edits by default. Checkpoint level detail shows where training actually helps.
arxiv-2510-02868:
Razumov and co-authors probe the noise of a light source used for precision work. The source is an electro-optic frequency comb. It emits many evenly spaced colors at once. Their weakness is a small number of lines, set by radio power limits. A nonlinear fiber stage can spread the comb wider. The open question was whether that spreading dirties the comb's phase noise.

The team measured the spread comb with coherent detection and digital tracking. One part comes from the seed laser, the other from the radio source. The broadened comb still fit that same model. The fiber added no new noise terms. It did not amplify the old ones either. Stretching the fiber from nine to forty meters changed nothing. In effect, broadening acts like far stronger radio drive. Designers can widen combs without paying a noise penalty.
arxiv-2510-02968:
Habel and co-authors improve hover control for tail-sitter drones. A tail-sitter takes off upright, then tilts into wing flight. In hover, sideways motion is hard to command cleanly. Twisting the craft tends to drag roll along with it. Their YawSitter adds a new force model to fix that. Uneven thrust makes the two propellers wash the body unevenly. That uneven wash pushes the craft sideways along its body axis.

Yaw can then steer sideways drift without roll coupling. A YXZ rotation scheme tracks the pose and gravity terms. It keeps yaw control direct and avoids key singularities. Tests ran in a Unity-based simulator. The craft followed square and circular paths in hover. Position errors stayed low across both paths. Yaw stayed within a few degrees of target throughout. The authors plan a quaternion version to dodge the last singularity risks.
arxiv-2510-03368:
Meimandi and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper on governing AI responsibly inside firms where power is spread across many units. Their case study joins a research university with a multinational company. The team assessed AI use across more than fifty business units and use cases. Many rule books for fair, open, and accountable AI exist, yet few show how such rules survive contact with messy, global organizations and local habits.

The study found four patterns that shape how rules land in practice. Central guidance gets reinterpreted locally, abstract principles resist translation into daily steps, and regions vary in style. Oversight duties also proved uneven across units. The authors answer with the ARGO framework, built in three layers: shared base standards, central advice resources, and local fitting to context. The design sets firm floors while respecting local freedom, a balance the team argues big firms need most.
arxiv-2510-03468:
Charette and Boudreault present a 2025 arXiv paper making A/B tests detect effects by fusing two statistical tricks. Metrics like revenue per user are zero heavy and right skewed, so t tests lose sensitivity and experiments must run long. The CUPED technique squeezes variance out by adjusting for pre experiment behavior. Yuen's test compares trimmed means, shrugging off outliers and skew. The authors integrate the two, trimming inside the variance reduced framework.

Simulations showed the combined test delivering higher statistical power than tests. It held false positive rates closer to their levels. The advantage grew when pre experiment and experiment data correlated. Detecting effects with smaller samples means product teams decide and expose fewer users to losing variants. Skewed metrics are the norm in consumer products, not the exception. A test that respects their shape should be the default, and this paper gives experimenters a recipe.
arxiv-2510-03568:
Ankomah and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on outlining brain tumors in scans from Sub-Saharan African patients. Most tumor segmentation models train on rich country data sets and lose accuracy where data look different. The team worked with the BraTS-Africa collection and grew it with augmentation that respects tumor boundaries. They also built an ensemble of three model designs, MedNeXt, SegMamba, and a residual encoder U-Net, so the strengths of each could cover the others.

Their best single model, MedNeXt, trained for a thousand rounds and reached the top scores on lesion wise overlap and surface distance in the study. The ensemble, trained for half as long, gave the most balanced outlines across tumor subregions. Balanced performance matters when treatment planning depends on every subregion at once. The work shows that careful data growth plus model teamwork can lift diagnostic tools for underrepresented patient groups.
arxiv-2510-03668:
Tossou presents a 2025 arXiv dissertation chapter measuring what happened when Benin cut firing costs and let firms renew short term contracts without limit in 2017. Eight in ten workers work informally, so reforms aimed at formal firms could ripple. Using household microdata and countries as a comparison group, the study tracks employment, tenure, contract types, and wages. 

Formal sector employment rose by two and a half percentage points after the reform, a gain of a quarter over its level. Informal employment fell by a similar amount. The chance of holding a permanent contract in the formal sector jumped by twenty three percentage points. Wages rose by thirty four dollars a month. Tenure shortened for short term workers while lengthening for long term ones, matching the model's prediction that firms keep matches and churn the rest. Flexibility bought formal jobs and pay, at cost to stability for workers.
arxiv-2510-03868:
Ali and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how mission-driven organizations adopt artificial intelligence. These groups include charities, aid agencies, and conservation bodies that work for social goals, not profit. Little was known about how such resource-strapped, values-led groups actually bring AI into daily work. The authors interviewed fifteen practitioners from environmental, humanitarian, and development groups worldwide.

Adoption turned out to be selective rather than sweeping. The groups used AI confidently for content creation and data analysis, but kept humans in charge of mission-critical choices. When efficiency gains clashed with organizational values, decisions stalled instead of trading values away. The authors name five barriers that trap projects at the pilot stage, including weak data and vendor dependence. Many groups preferred open tools and local hosting to protect their independence. The study argues adoption here is conditional, proceeding only where AI strengthens the mission.
arxiv-2510-04068:
Delporte and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper proposing a new way to define eigenvalues for tensors. Matrices reveal their eigenvalues as roots of a characteristic polynomial, but tensors have resisted a single clean analogue. Existing tensor eigenvalue notions can yield exponentially many values, which makes spectral analysis unwieldy. The authors build their polynomial from a partition function of Grassmann variables instead.

Their definition covers general tensors, including totally antisymmetric ones, though not totally symmetric ones. Crucially, the polynomial always has exactly as many roots as the tensor's dimension, like the matrix case. For random Gaussian tensors, they derive how the roots distribute statistically. The density follows a generalized Wigner semicircle law based on the Fuss-Catalan distribution. Random tensor spectra matter for quantum gravity models, data analysis, and optimization theory. A tractable characteristic polynomial gives those fields a new invariant to compute with.
arxiv-2510-04168:
Molaei, Heravi, and Ghabcheloo present this 2025 arXiv paper on teaching an excavator to pick up large rocks with reinforcement learning. Scooping a single irregular rock from granular soil is a skilled operator's task, full of complex contact physics. Model-based control is impractical because rock and soil behavior defies explicit modeling. Earlier autonomous excavation handled continuous soil or needed specialized grippers instead of a standard bucket.

The authors train a model-free policy in the AGX Dynamics simulator with proximal policy optimization. The policy commands boom, arm, and bucket joint velocities directly for a CAT 365 excavator model. Extensive domain randomization varied rock shape, density, mass, and starting configurations. The trained policy generalized to unseen rocks and soil conditions. Its success rate, about four in five attempts, matched human participants while keeping the machine stable. The study is the first reinforcement learning controller demonstrated for rock capturing.
arxiv-2510-04268:
Algayres and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper benchmarking how well small language models learn rare words, the way children do. The BabyLM challenge trains models on child-scale data, but its metrics concentrate on frequent words. Children, by contrast, pick up new words from a handful of exposures. The authors build LongTail-Swap, a test set of acceptable versus unacceptable sentence pairs isolating rare words' semantic and syntactic use.

Models are scored zero-shot by comparing log probabilities across each pair. Two test sets match the ten-million and hundred-million word BabyLM training corpora. Sixteen leaderboard models were evaluated, and all performed poorly on the rare-word tail. Performance differences between architectures proved far more pronounced in the tail than in the head of the distribution. The benchmark redirects data-efficient language research toward the vocabulary children actually struggle to teach machines.
arxiv-2510-04368:
Mangla and three co-authors wrote this 2025 paper to share NegotiationGym, a free toolkit for lab tests of talks between computer agents. The agents are large language models that play roles such as buyer and seller. Each agent gets a score rule that says what a good deal means for it. Before this toolkit, each lab built its own setup from scratch, so results were hard to compare or repeat.

Users set up a scene by picking roles, goals, private facts, and stop rules in a config file. Agents learn across rounds from feedback tied to their score, then change plans. A test harness reruns the same scene many times and tracks score shifts. In a sample sale, learning from feedback left agents with more value and fewer talks that ended with no deal. That helps teams study markets and safe AI design.
arxiv-2510-04468:
Asif Mohammed Samir and Mohammad Masudur Rahman wrote this 2025 paper on finding the code behind a bug report. Developers spend much of their time hunting the files that a bug report blames. Classic search methods match words in the report to words in the code, and they miss meaning. Big language models read meaning well, but they are heavy and costly to run. The team blended both lines into a tool named IQLoc.

IQLoc uses a transformer model to judge which code looks suspicious for a report. It then rewrites the search query with that insight and runs a classic retrieval search. The team rebuilt a standard benchmark and added about thirty percent more recent reports. The new set holds roughly seventy five hundred reports. Across three scoring metrics, IQLoc beat four rival techniques by wide margins. Gains were largest for reports that carry stack traces or code snippets.
arxiv-2510-04568:
Naman Gupta and eight coauthors at Microsoft wrote this 2025 paper on reasoning over very long documents. Long inputs strain language models, and the usual fixes each lose something. Retrieval can skip evidence, context windows blur focus, and agent chains pass summaries that drop detail. The team replaced those loose messages with a structured shared memory. They call the framework COSMIR.

A planner agent first turns the user question into sub questions that can be checked. Worker agents then read the document in chunks under a fixed three step cycle: extract, infer, and refine. Every update lands in the memory in a format, not in free prose. A manager agent writes the answer straight from that memory. On long context tests, the design lost less information during handoffs than a chain of agents baseline. Accuracy rose as a result, and every claim in the answer can be traced through the memory.
arxiv-2510-04668:
Habin Lim, Yeongseob Won, Juwon Seo, and Gyeong Moon Park wrote this 2025 paper on putting several personal subjects into one generated image. Tools can teach an image model a pet, a face, or a favorite object from a few photos. Ask for two such subjects together and they often blend into each other. Their framework, ConceptSplit, attacks that mixing at two stages. First, training adapts only the value side of cross attention inside the model.

The team found that touching the key side, the common habit, breaks attention routing and invites mixing. Their second tool works at generation time by tuning the starting noise pattern. That tuning separates the attention maps of rival concepts before the image forms. Tests in pictures and numbers showed cleaner multi subject images than rival methods. Each subject kept its own look while sharing the scene. The code is public for other groups to extend.
arxiv-2510-04768:
Charles Zhang and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on reading an electron beam birth state from later measurements. Beams from photocathodes power microscopes, X ray lasers, and colliders. Brightness depends on how positions and momenta spread at the moment of emission. The team shows how to rebuild that four dimensional source picture from downstream data. Their method needs no detailed map of the beamline in between. It assumes only that transport stays linear and follows the rules of Hamiltonian motion.

They applied it to electrons from a patterned alkali antimonide cathode. The reconstruction exposed links between where an electron left and how its momentum spread. Such links stay hidden in summary numbers like average energy spread. The authors worked out the resolution limits of the method. Cathode designers can now see emission structure directly instead of guessing it. Sharper source pictures point to brighter beams for imaging and light sources.
arxiv-2510-04968:
Allen Daniel Sunny studies why people do or do not trust AI decisions in this 2025 arXiv paper. His test case is an AI system that approves or denies loans. Such systems often explain themselves with technical details about the algorithm. Sunny asks whether those explanations actually build trust with users.

Through a qualitative study, he watched users interact with the system's explanations. Users struggled with confidence scores, uneven wording, and hard-to-reach information. Technical transparency alone did not make the system feel trustworthy. Explanations that added social and economic context worked far better. Sunny argues that explainable AI should be designed around people's real situations, not just the model's internals.
arxiv-2510-05168:
Eric Jahns, Davi Moreno, Milan Stojkov, and Michel A. Kinsy upgrade the neuron model inside spiking neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spiking networks promise brain-like energy efficiency. Their standard neuron, the leaky integrate-and-fire, decays linearly and limits expressiveness. The richer quadratic neuron behaves better but trains unstably.

The authors present the first discretization of the quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron built for deep spiking networks. They derive surrogate gradient windows analytically from the model's own parameters. That derivation minimizes gradient mismatch and keeps training stable. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and an event-based dataset, their neuron beat leading leaky-neuron methods. The richer dynamics came with minimal extra energy cost. The result makes quadratic neurons a practical default for deep spiking systems.
arxiv-2510-05368:
Nicolás A. Barnafi, Felipe Lepe, and Francisca A. Muñoz analyze a numerical method for neutron transport in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reactor physics reduces neutron behavior to a two-group model of fast and thermal energies. Its steady states form a non-symmetric eigenvalue problem. Reliable finite element approximations of those eigenvalues are still understudied.

The authors derive the eigenvalue problem carefully from the transport equations. Using piecewise polynomials and compact operator theory, they prove convergence and error estimates. Numerical tests in two and three dimensions confirm the theory. The method introduces no spurious eigenvalues, a classic failure mode in such problems. A fuel assembly simulation against the IAEA two-dimensional benchmark validates the approach on realistic reactor geometry.
arxiv-2510-05468:
Song and colleagues tackle the cost of training large language models across many machines. In split learning, a phone or small computer runs part of the model and a server runs the rest. The two sides must swap data constantly, which creates heavy network traffic. Their 2025 paper, AMAQ, shrinks that traffic without hurting the model much.

AMAQ stores shared values with mixed precision, giving more bits to the parts that matter most. Routine parts get only three or four bits, while key parts keep six to eight. The bit budget shifts across layers and features as training proceeds. In tests on LLaMA and Qwen models, the method beat fixed-precision training at the same budget. Generation accuracy rose by about 2.5 percent, and training stayed stable at very low precision. The authors present AMAQ as a practical fit for real multi-machine training setups.
arxiv-2510-05968:
Frees documents design patterns for large-dataset reporting with language models. Models translate natural language into database queries well. Context windows, however, cannot hold complete reporting datasets. His 2025 paper extends the Model Context Protocol's ResourceLink for scalable reporting architectures.

The core dual-response pattern returns samples plus resource links together. Samples let the model reason and refine queries iteratively. Links let the host application retrieve full results out of band. Query generation is thereby decoupled from data retrieval entirely. Analysis tasks and retrieval tasks use context budgets fundamentally differently. Multi-tenant security patterns isolate each tenant's data on shared servers. Rendering happens outside the model's context, preserving tokens for reasoning. Resource lifecycle management and progressive discovery complete the framework. Standardization through protocol proposals is the stated future direction. Enterprise reporting is the production setting the patterns target.
arxiv-2510-06168:
Cheng and six co-authors report a new electronic order in kagome superconductor CsCr3Sb5 in a 2025 condensed matter study. Kagome metals mix geometric frustration, strong correlations, and band topology. This compound adds hints of frustrated magnetism and quantum criticality, a rare test case for unconventional superconductivity.

With spectroscopic imaging scanning tunneling microscopy on bulk crystals, the team found a cascade of density wave transitions. One state stands out: a unidirectional density wave breaking every mirror symmetry yet keeping a mirror-glide symmetry. They call it a frieze charge-stripe order, after the frieze symmetry groups of decorative patterns. Imaging, Fourier analysis, and simulations show that sublattice degrees of freedom shape the phase. Its interior holds chiral textures of opposite handedness. Superconductivity here grows out of the new stripe state, opening a fresh route for studying electronic order.
arxiv-2510-06468:
Lerner and Futoransky present BATTLE for Bitcoin, a dispute layer for optimistic bridges to rollups and sidechains, in a 2025 cryptography paper. Optimistic bridges assume assertions honest unless challenged. Attackers can weaponize challenges, flooding defenders with denial-of-service disputes. Each defense round traditionally demands fresh honest capital.

The design adapts the BATTLE tournament protocol to Bitcoin's UTXO model. BitVM-style components and garbled circuits run contests, with bonds posted on demand. Disputes resolve in logarithmically many tournament rounds. Rewards recycle between rounds, keeping the honest asserter's initial capital constant. That holds against many simultaneous permissionless challengers. The system is fully contestable: challengers may answer with higher-work counter-proofs. Everything runs on standard timelocks and pre-signed transaction graphs, no new opcodes required. Overhead grows quadratically yet stays practical beyond a thousand operators, enabling decentralized bridge committees.
arxiv-2510-06568:
Yujun Shi and Haijiang Ren report a pattern in a classic physics model. Their 2025 paper studies a chain of masses linked by springs, known as an FPUT chain. The chain is driven by a periodic force and loses energy through damping. In the original FPUT puzzle, energy kept returning to a few modes instead of spreading evenly.

Using computer simulations, the pair finds similar recurrence in this driven, damped chain. The effect appears only in narrow ranges of driving strength and damping. Energy swaps among a few low-frequency modes for a long time. Unlike discrete time crystals, the return period is not a simple multiple of the driving period. The largest damping that still allows recurrence falls fast as the chain grows. That trend suggests the effect would vanish in a very long chain. The work points to ways of creating long-lived rhythmic states in the lab.
arxiv-2510-06768:
Di Zhang and five colleagues design error-correcting decoders for 6G wireless links. Their 2025 paper targets the strictest service class, which demands extreme reliability with low delay. Linear block codes protect the data, but decoding them fast and accurately is hard. The authors exploit a mathematical mirror of the code, its dual codewords.

Dual codewords with varied weights turn out to carry useful clues. They reveal where error bits sit and how large those errors are. Two decoding schemes build on that insight. One uses only this intrinsic information in an iterative loop. The other mixes in prior information from the radio channel. Both schemes need only vector multiplication and comparisons of real numbers. That simplicity makes them easy to build into hardware. Simulations show the intrinsic scheme edging past standard decoders on error reduction. The authors argue the approach meets the reliability that 6G services will require.
arxiv-2510-06868:
Didrik Bergström, Deniz Gündüz, and Onur Günlü improve image transmission across relay chains. Their 2025 paper uses deep joint source-channel coding, where a neural network compresses and protects an image in one step. Sending an image through several hops adds noise at every relay. Standard schemes lose quality as the hops pile up.

Their scheme adds a module that computes a hash capturing an image's meaning. Training pushes the rebuilt image to stay close to the original in both pixels and hash space. That semantic alignment keeps the reconstructed pictures looking right. Quality, measured by a learned perceptual score, improved in multi-hop settings. The benefit held up under relay styles they tested, decode-forward and quantize-forward. It survived the effects of quantization. The authors point to secure authentication as a use. A hash-consistent image is harder to tamper with unnoticed.
arxiv-2510-07368:
Deng and co-authors simulate a merger of two gas-rich dwarf galaxies to see what really drives a starburst. Their 2025 study uses the RIGEL model at very high resolution. Conventional wisdom credits both denser gas and faster star formation per cloud. The team tracked individual dense clouds across two hundred million years of snapshots. Two matched non-merging galaxies served as controls. The merger raised the total star formation rate about one hundred thirty-fold and multiplied dense gas mass many times over.

Cloud-level behavior, though, barely changed. Individual clouds used up their gas on the same timescale, around seven million years, at every merger stage. Their lifetimes and formation efficiency stayed set by local stellar feedback. Galaxy-wide depletion time collapsed because compression made far more dense gas, not because clouds worked faster. Angular momentum loss and tidal squeezing explain the dense gas surge.
arxiv-2510-07468:
Siemonsen systematically maps the ergoregion instability of spinning bosonic stars. The 2025 paper examines stars made of scalar or vector fields rather than ordinary matter. Rapidly spinning versions host ergoregions without horizons, the recipe for this instability. Three methods, approximate, spectral, and time-domain, cross-check the unstable modes. Universal patterns emerge across star types. A zero-frequency mode signals the instability's onset. Frequencies and growth rates obey a simple scaling in the slow limit, and at high frequencies the modes lock onto the orbital frequency of trapped light rays circling against the spin.

Each spinning pattern supports only finitely many growing overtones. The fastest growth doubles a mode in roughly ten thousand times the star's mass in time units, fast on cosmic scales. A near-universal relation ties frequencies to growth rates across bosonic stars and even black-hole-like objects.
arxiv-2510-07768:
Yue and eleven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on giving language models better tool libraries. Models reason when they can call helper programs. Many fields lack ready-made tools, so systems now mine tools from reasoning traces. Collections grow messy, with overlapping tools that are hard to search. The authors build ToolLibGen, a pipeline that turns a pile of mined tools into an organized library.

The pipeline first clusters tools into coherent topics. Inside each cluster, a code agent merges scattered functions and extracts their shared logic. A reviewing agent checks that each merged tool keeps the ability of the originals. The process shrinks question-specific tools into fewer ones without losing function. Experiments across domains and base models showed better tool retrieval and stronger reasoning. Accuracy improved over fragmented toolsets, and the edge grew as collections scaled. Organization, not just generation, makes tool use reliable.
arxiv-2510-08068:
Singhi wrote this 2025 paper, condensed from a master's thesis, presenting language-model agents that trade Bitcoin together. Crypto markets swing on sentiment and regulation, which static models handle badly. His system splits the work among specialist agents reading technical indicators and sentiment. A decision agent allocates the portfolio. A reflection agent reviews performance and writes daily and weekly critiques into future prompts.

The agents adapt their priorities from words alone, with no retraining. Backtests covered ten months of Bitcoin prices across bull, bear, and sideways regimes. The quantitative agent beat buy-and-hold in rising markets. The sentiment agent turned sideways markets from a small loss into more than a doubled stake. Weekly feedback improved total performance further and trimmed bearish losses. Singhi argues verbal feedback is a cheap, transparent tuning method.
arxiv-2510-08168:
Gao, Wei, and Zhou wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how solutions of an anisotropic curvature flow behave far away. Inverse mean curvature flow expands surfaces at a rate set by their curvature, and its anisotropic version weights directions through a norm. The authors first prove a local gradient estimate for anisotropic p-harmonic functions. Unusually, the estimate's constant stays bounded as the power tends to one.

Passing to that limit transfers the estimate to weak solutions of the flow itself. As an application, they show the weak flow is asymptotic to the expanding Wulff shape solution, the anisotropic analogue of a growing sphere. That extends a classical Huisken and Ilmanen theorem to the anisotropic setting. Asymptotic shape theorems tell us the flow eventually forgets its initial details and remembers only size and anisotropy. Such results feed into geometric inequalities.
arxiv-2510-08868:
Shen and a team of astronomers study black holes that change their appearance over time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These changing-look active galaxies show or hide their broad spectral lines across years, defying the tidy picture where viewing angle alone sets a type. The team gathered two snapshots of the spectra of two hundred three examples, taken up to roughly eight thousand days apart.

Fitting the spectra split the sample in two. About half varied only mildly, as active galaxies normally do, while ninety-three objects showed true type switches, turning their broad lines on or off. In that group, a key line ratio tracked both brightness and how fast the black hole feeds, relative to its limit. The pattern points to changing feeding rates as the trigger: when the inflow rises, the extra light reshapes the line-emitting region. The result refines the standard unification picture.
arxiv-2510-09268:
Gödecke and co-authors measure the faint directional preference inside two magnetic metals, in this 2025 arXiv paper. At the right recipe, it proves strong enough to hold a lattice of magnetic whirlpools at low temperature. The B20 compounds MnSi and iron-cobalt silicide host skyrmions, tiny swirling spin textures. Big interactions set the broad phase diagram, but weak cubic anisotropy, the crystal's slight preference for some directions, decides the order of phases. Until now, the only known low-temperature skyrmion pocket of this kind was in an insulator.

Using angle-resolved SQUID measurements on crystals, the team extracted anisotropy constants across cobalt concentrations. In the silicide, the anisotropy depended strongly on how much cobalt replaced iron. Near ten percent cobalt it grew strong enough to stabilize a low-temperature skyrmion lattice, matching theory. The authors propose this alloy as the first chiral metal with such a stabilized skyrmion phase.
arxiv-2510-09468:
Florine Hartwig, Josua Sassen, Juliane Braunsmann, Martin Rumpf, and Benedikt Wirth build geometry tools for autoencoders in a 2025 arXiv paper. An autoencoder compresses data into a compact latent space, and the valid codes form a curved surface called a latent manifold. The authors describe that surface implicitly, through an equation rather than a direct map.

On that basis they develop a discrete Riemannian calculus, a set of tools that mimic classic shape operators on the surface. The tools stay robust when the implicit description is slightly inaccurate, as often happens in practice. To obtain the description, they learn a near-exact map onto the manifold by training it to remove noise. The framework computes geodesic paths, the shortest routes between points on the surface, and geodesic shooting from a starting direction. They test it on several autoencoders trained on synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2510-09568:
Yongda Zhu and eight co-authors, among them George Becker, study how the early universe became transparent in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reionisation is the era when the first galaxies ionised the hydrogen fog between them. The authors used the James Webb Space Telescope to survey two of the clearest sightlines through that era, regions where Lyman-alpha light passes unusually freely.

Earlier work marked these regions as low-density in Lyman-alpha emitters. The new spectroscopy shows they are also sparse in oxygen-line emitters, below half the cosmic average density. Other clear regions sit in average environments, so several pathways can produce high transmission. For the first time, the team measures how transmission correlates with galaxy positions in two dimensions. It peaks at a sideways offset of about zero point eight mean free paths, suggesting ionising photons escape along large structures offset from the line of sight.
arxiv-2510-09768:
Khang Ngo and Siamak Ravanbakhsh measure how symmetry shapes scaling in neural force fields in a 2025 arXiv paper. Neural force fields learn interatomic potentials, the energy landscapes that govern how atoms push and pull each other. Equivariant architectures build the task's symmetry in by construction, so rotating a molecule rotates the prediction in step.

The study finds clean power-law scaling with data, parameters, and compute, with exponents that depend on the architecture. Equivariant models scale better than non-equivariant ones, and the advantage grows at larger scales rather than shrinking. Among equivariant designs, higher-order representations earn better scaling exponents. For compute-optimal training, data and model sizes should grow in tandem regardless of architecture. The authors argue against leaving symmetry for the model to discover: built-in biases change how hard the task inherently is, and its scaling laws, especially as systems grow.
arxiv-2510-10068:
Pîrvu and Marius Leordeanu build probabilistic hyper-graphs for multi-modal learning in this 2025 arXiv paper in computer vision. Vision systems improve when data arrives in many modalities, such as images, text, and depth. Self-supervised pretraining with masked autoencoders, which hide parts of the input and learn to rebuild them, is a leading way to use such data.

The authors use several randomly masked autoencoders together and link their outputs in a hyper-graph, a graph where one edge can join many nodes at once. The setup supports semi-supervised learning across several tasks and modalities at the same time. Probabilistic edges express uncertainty about which elements belong together, instead of forcing a hard yes or no.
arxiv-2510-10368:
Marcus Lin and co-authors watch charged drops split on lubricated surfaces in this 2025 arXiv paper in fluid physics. Charged water drops are more common than usually assumed: raindrops carry about a picocoulomb of charge, and routine pipetting makes drops with far more. On a slippery, lubricated surface, such a drop can undergo spontaneous Coulomb fission.

Fission means the drop's own charge repulsion tears it into smaller drops. The authors study when and how this happens on lubricated surfaces, where low friction lets the process run cleanly. Understanding charge-driven breakup matters for printing, spraying, and lab handling, where stray charge can quietly change drop behavior and spoil precision work.
arxiv-2510-11268:
Editing an image classifier, to forget a class or adapt to new conditions, usually means expensive retraining or narrow error patching. Jaeik Kim and Jaeyoung Do introduce Class Vectors in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper as a cheaper editing handle. Where task vectors capture whole-task changes in weight space, Class Vectors disentangle each class's adaptation in the latent space during fine-tuning, one per class.

The authors show these vectors capture each class's semantic shift. Editing works by steering latent features along a vector, or by mapping the vector into weight space to move decision boundaries. Because the vectors are linear and orthogonal, class arithmetic supports flexible concept editing. They validate the approach on unlearning, adaptation to new environments, adversarial defense, and adversarial trigger optimization. The results argue that classifier behavior can be adjusted after training, without returning to retraining runs.
arxiv-2510-11368:
A factory or retailer ordering one product over many periods, with limited capacity and a quantity discount that kicks in at a single breakpoint, faces a classic optimization puzzle. Kleitos Papadopoulos solves a monotonic version of that lot sizing problem in this 2025 arXiv algorithms paper. The setting assumes purchase prices never increase over the planning horizon, there are no setup costs, and the all-units discount has one breakpoint.

Papadopoulos establishes several structural properties of the optimal solution under these conditions. He then designs a hybrid dynamic programming algorithm that keeps only essential information about its states in a compact representation, using linear equations for intermediate values. The algorithm runs in time proportional to n log n in the number of periods. That improves on the previous state of the art, which needed time proportional to n squared, a speedup for long planning horizons.
arxiv-2510-11768:
Valery Asiryan proves a result about a polynomial tied to the famous perfect cuboid problem. A perfect cuboid would be a box with all edges and diagonals whole numbers; none has ever been found. The polynomial in question has degree eight and depends on two whole-number parameters with no common factor. Asiryan's 2025 arXiv paper shows that this polynomial can never be split into smaller polynomial factors over the integers.

The proof works in stages. Over a larger number field, the polynomial splits into two conjugate quartic factors. Any further split would force a rational point on a certain genus-one curve. Asiryan computes with the Magma software that the curve's elliptic Jacobian has rank zero and a small, fully known torsion group. Those facts leave only two parameter values, both contradicting the assumptions. Hence the original polynomial is irreducible over the rationals and integers alike.
arxiv-2510-11868:
Rita T. Sousa and Heiko Paulheim improve how knowledge graphs are embedded into numbers. Knowledge graphs store facts as triples and power search and recommendation tools. Embedding methods turn each entity and relation into a short list of numbers so machines can predict missing facts. Their 2025 paper, presented at the International Conference on Knowledge Capture, targets a blind spot in how these methods treat absent facts.

Most methods assume a missing triple is false. Real graphs follow an open world instead, where missing often means merely unknown. Sousa and Paulheim exploit explicitly stated negative facts, which say what is not true, yet are rarely recorded or used. Their design trains two models side by side, one on positives, one on negatives. Each model proposes hard negative examples for the other to learn from. Across general and domain-specific graphs, the approach beat leading models on link prediction and triple classification.
arxiv-2510-12168:
Yoshiaki Koma and Miho Koma compute the string that imprisons quarks, ends included. In the dual superconductor picture of the quantum chromodynamics vacuum, color-electric flux between a quark and antiquark is squeezed into a tube, making separation cost endless energy. Their 2025 arXiv paper works within dual Ginzburg-Landau theory, an effective theory of that vacuum, using a new numerical formulation.

Placing the theory on the dual lattice lets them solve its field equations for systems of finite-length flux tubes systematically. Studying the quark-antiquark tube in detail exposes significant terminal effects, end behaviors entirely absent from the idealized infinitely long solution. The authors then examine interactions in two-tube and multi-tube systems, where tubes attract, repel, or rearrange. These are the configurations real hadrons and multi-quark states actually contain.
arxiv-2510-12368:
Riva and co-authors test a deep learning architecture that reconstructs the full state of a nuclear research reactor from a few temperature sensors, in a 2025 arXiv paper. These networks map the time history of sparse measurements to complete fields such as temperature, velocity, and pressure, including quantities no sensor observes. The method ignores sensor placement and handles noisy data through an ensemble strategy, with short training times and no tuning.

The test system is the TRIGA Mark II research reactor, modeled by a fluid dynamics simulation. Sensors sit in specific low dynamics channels, a deliberately hard placement. They ask whether it can rebuild every characteristic field from simulated and real temperature data, and whether sparse measurements can correct the output when model and reality disagree. Reconstructions proved accurate in real time for both data sources. The authors argue this suits interpretable monitoring and control inside a reactor digital twin.
arxiv-2510-12468:
Ho and co-authors craft adversarial images that fool deepfake detectors while staying visually unchanged, in a 2025 arXiv computer security paper. Their attack, MS-GAGA, works in a black box setting, where the attacker cannot see the target model's internals. It runs in two stages designed to balance transferability, fooling unseen models, against imperceptibility.

In the first stage, a dual stream module generates candidate attacks: one stream uses enhanced gradient calculations tuned for small perturbation budgets, and the other concentrates perturbations on visually salient regions. Together they widen the search space. In the second stage, a metric aware selector scores candidates by both their success on black box models and their structural similarity to the original image. The joint optimization raised misclassification rates on unseen detectors by up to twenty seven percent over leading attacks. The work exposes how fragile current deepfake detectors remain against carefully selected, nearly invisible perturbations.
arxiv-2510-12568:
Söylemez and Ünver prove approximation theorems that work on infinite intervals and preserve exponential functions, using a generalized notion of convergence, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Korovkin type theorems give simple criteria for when positive linear operators approximate functions well: checking convergence on a few test functions is enough. Classical versions can fail exactly when the convergence itself is nonstandard.

The authors employ power series convergence, and a special case built on Borel type summability through integrals. This yields a framework that applies where classical convergence or plain Borel convergence fails. They compare the resulting theorems with each other and present examples where classical results break down but theirs still work. They also analyze the speed of convergence using the modulus of continuity, a measure of how fast a function can change. The work extends a classical corner of approximation theory to exponential test functions.
arxiv-2510-12668:
Tang and colleagues dissect a new way of feeding documents to language models: encoding them as parameters rather than text, in a 2025 arXiv paper on retrieval augmented generation. Parametric RAG converts each document into a small adapter module and injects those parameters into the model at inference time. This promises deeper interaction between model and document than placing text in the prompt, at lower cost.

Their systematic study finds that parameterized documents capture only part of a document's semantic information. Used alone, they perform worse than ordinary text level interaction. However, the parametric form encodes high level document information. That improves the model's understanding of the same document given as text. Combining parameterized and textual documents lets the model use relevant information more effectively and makes it more robust to noisy inputs, beating either source alone. The authors recommend using both together.
arxiv-2510-12768:
Guo and colleagues at Texas A&M University tackle a hard vision problem in this 2025 arXiv paper: rebuilding a moving 3D scene from a single camera view. Their method, called Gaussian splatting, represents a scene with many small soft blobs, but standard versions treat every blob the same even when some are barely seen. That weakness causes motion to drift when objects hide each other and harms image quality at new angles.

The team built USplat4D, which estimates how uncertain each blob is at each moment and links the blobs in a graph across space and time. Blobs seen again and again act as anchors that guide the motion of less reliable ones. Tests on real and synthetic datasets showed steadier shapes during occlusion and cleaner images from extreme viewpoints than earlier dynamic splatting models.
arxiv-2510-13068:
Barmpas and colleagues build a large brainwave model around a new EEG tokenizer in this 2025 arXiv paper. Electroencephalography signals mix activity across many time and frequency scales. Foundation models that learn by guessing masked signal tokens depend entirely on how signals are chopped into tokens. Existing tokenizers lose high-frequency dynamics, limiting how well signals can be rebuilt.

Their system, NeuroRVQ, extracts features at multiple scales covering the full neural spectrum. It encodes them with hierarchical residual vector quantization codebooks, which build up a signal in layers. A phase- and amplitude-aware loss trains the tokenizer efficiently. The result compresses EEG tightly while reconstructing all bands accurately. That supports generative masked modeling. In tests, NeuroRVQ had lower reconstruction error than existing large brainwave models and beat them across a variety of downstream tasks.
arxiv-2510-13268:
Fliedner, Golak, Gül, and Neumann optimize bin retrieval in compact storage systems in this 2025 arXiv operations research paper. Compact systems stack uniform bins directly on each other with no aisles, maximizing space in crowded urban warehouses. Retrieving a target bin means lifting every bin blocking it first, which costs substantial energy unless the retrieval order is planned smartly.

The authors model the retrieval problem mathematically and prove it strongly NP-complete, meaning no efficient exact algorithm is expected in general. Structural insights from that analysis feed two exact methods, a mixed-integer programming formulation and a dynamic programming algorithm, plus a simple greedy heuristic for practitioners. Numerical experiments showed dynamic programming beating state-of-the-art solver performance on small to medium instances, while the greedy method delivered good, near-instant solutions when exact methods became impractical.
arxiv-2510-13868:
Ye and Wong bound optimal stopping values from above with a deep martingale method that escapes the curse of dimensionality. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies when to stop a process for the best payoff, monitored at discrete times. Dual methods certify upper bounds, complementing simulation approaches that estimate from below. Classical dual bases explode in size as dimension grows.

DeepMartingale represents the needed martingale with neural networks instead of fixed bases. The resulting upper bound is tight for the primal value function. The authors prove the bound converges under very mild assumptions. More strikingly, they prove expressivity: networks of dimension-independent size reach any target accuracy. That guarantee means accuracy costs do not blow up with dimension. Numerical experiments confirm convergence, expressivity, and stability in practice. High-dimensional stopping problems, common in finance, become tractable with certificates.
arxiv-2510-13968:
Kyle Boone and co-authors compare statistical tools for extracting cosmology from gravitational lensing maps, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Lensing maps show how matter bends light from the cosmic microwave background and from distant galaxies, Forecasters summarize them with the power spectrum, a standard measure of pattern strength at each scale. Wavelet methods, which probe patterns at chosen positions and scales, might extract more.

The team also introduces learned binning, a method that compresses summary statistics into fewer numbers while keeping them interpretable, and chose bins using separate data to avoid fooling themselves. For microwave lensing alone, wavelet scattering matched the power spectrum's precision on the matter density and fluctuation strength. Crossed with galaxy lensing from the Euclid mission's second data release, wavelet phase harmonics beat cross-power spectra by factors above two. Learned binning improved the wavelet statistics but not the power spectra.
arxiv-2510-14068:
Moritz Grillo and Tobias Hofmann study what sparse maxout networks can and cannot compute, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In these neural networks, each neuron reads only a fixed count of inputs from the previous layer and applies a maxout activation, taking the maximum over several candidate values. The setup captures features of convolutional and graph neural networks, where connections are deliberately sparse.

The authors establish a duality, a two-way correspondence, between functions these networks compute and a class of objects called virtual polytopes, turning questions about network expressivity into geometry. They derive a tight bound on the dimension of the polytopes, which becomes their analytical tool. Building on it, they construct depth hierarchies: sequences of functions needing deeper networks. While sufficiently deep sparse maxout networks can compute anything, they prove that when the depth is not reached, adding width alone cannot compensate for the sparsity of connections.
arxiv-2510-14268:
Mohammad Afzal Shadab, Howard Stone, and Reed Maxwell model how meltwater aquifers form and spread inside cold firn, the compacted snow layer atop glaciers and ice sheets, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Where surface meltwater pools underground instead of running off, it changes how much melt reaches the ocean, but the process is poorly constrained in more than one dimension.

Their multidimensional, vertically integrated framework borrows the mathematics of terrestrial groundwater and adds phase change, meaning water freezing into the cold firn, plus residual trapping of liquid water. They derive semi-analytical solutions for finite-volume aquifers, check them against numerical simulations and higher-fidelity models, and show an aquifer expanding in three dimensions through varied firn. Both approaches agree that lateral propagation slows at lower initial firn temperatures, because freezing reduces porosity and drains liquid water. It shows how meltwater is stored in percolation zones.
arxiv-2510-14468:
Lucas Vicente García-Consuegra and Azadeh Maleknejad generalize the Schwinger effect, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The effect is the creation of particle-antiparticle pairs from empty space by a strong electric field. They extend it to fields that fluctuate randomly. Real fields in cosmology and high-energy astrophysics are transient, uneven, and stochastic, unlike the constant textbook field in which the effect is computed.

Using the action formalism, the authors compute the vacuum decay rate and the number density of produced charged particles for fluctuating gauge-field backgrounds. They obtain closed-form expressions for both scalar and fermionic cases. To isolate the physics, the analysis is done in flat spacetime at zero temperature, a controlled setting where curvature and thermal effects can be ignored. As proof of concept, they present examples from astrophysical plasmas and early-universe scenarios, where stochastic pair production could leave traces.
arxiv-2510-14568:
Castronuovo, Dennunzio, and Margara, in a 2025 arXiv paper, study group cellular automata, which are update rules on endless rows of group elements. Each step shifts and recombines the row in the same way everywhere. The authors focus on expansivity, a strong form of sensitivity where distinct starting rows eventually become distinguishable at the center, no matter how far apart they began.

They give a characterization of expansivity for automata built on abelian groups, where the group operation commutes, and the condition is easy to check. For general groups, including non-abelian ones, they prove that expansivity is decidable. That means an algorithm can always settle whether a given automaton has the property. They also place the expansive automata in a wider landscape. Every expansive example is a topologically transitive injective automaton, but some automata of that broader kind are not expansive, so the containment is strict.
arxiv-2510-14668:
Rahman and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new way to train compact medical imaging models by chaining them together. The usual method, knowledge distillation, trains one small student model from one large teacher. That setup often loses knowledge along the way and needs either a very strong teacher or lots of labeled data. Weak supervision makes the data problem worse.

Their network, WeCKD, lines models up in a chain. Each model learns from the one before it, refines what it received, and passes the improved knowledge forward. Each link trains on only a fraction of the dataset, so supervision stays minimal. The team evaluated the chain on six imaging datasets spanning ear examination images, microscopy, and magnetic resonance scans. The chained models beat existing methods, with cumulative accuracy gains of up to twenty-three percent over a single backbone trained on the same limited data.
arxiv-2510-15068:
Zhang and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a jailbreak against multimodal language models that works by telling them a story in pictures. Safety alignments refuse harmful requests asked outright, but the models' appetite for narrative coherence is a cross-modal weakness. The attack decomposes a malicious query into innocuous storytelling elements, using an auxiliary language model as the screenwriter.

Diffusion models render the elements as comic-style images. Presented with the comic, the target model follows the plot. Its reliance on narrative coherence pulls it into producing the output that text alone never extracted. Across harmful queries from safety benchmarks, the method reached an attack success rate of 83.5 percent in the experiments, beating the state of the art by a margin, and it worked across categories of harmful content. The authors analyze which vulnerability factors matter. They probe defenses and find gaps against narrative-driven attacks.
arxiv-2510-15168:
Marc Harary finds a shared geometric backbone beneath many hard yes-or-no optimization problems, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Problems as different as low-rank binary optimization and trimmed covariance share one trait. The gain from any single flip or swap can be written as a simple affine formula in a low-dimensional feature map. Harary calls this the affine-predicate condition and shows it covers all rank-structured objectives of this kind.

His meta-theorem then proves that every locally optimal solution must sit inside one chamber of a hyperplane arrangement. Listing them takes time that grows manageably when the rank stays small, giving exact algorithms whose cost tracks the rank. As a corollary he obtains the first unified exact algorithm of this type for rank-r binary quadratic problems, including versions that limit how many variables may be on.
arxiv-2510-15268:
Karthik Gajulapalli, Zeyong Li, and Ilya Volkovich revisit oblivious complexity classes, a twist on interactive proofs where the provers hear only the input's size, not the input itself. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how this weakened setting compares with its symmetric cousin and with ordinary polynomial time. Such classes test how much proof power survives when the provers are partly blinded.

The team constructs, for each size bound, an explicit problem in the oblivious class that no circuit of that size can compute, the first fixed-polynomial lower bound of its kind. They also prove a hierarchy theorem showing that slightly more time always buys strictly more power in this setting, even for a semantic class. New structural links connect the oblivious and symmetric classes, and they make progress on an open question about NP from 2015. Their tools include uniformly-sparse extensions, which they flag as independently useful.
arxiv-2510-15868:
Shr-Ruei Tsai, Wei-Cheng Chang, Jie-Ying Lee, Chih-Hai Su, and Yu-Lun Liu improve lens flare removal when the light causing the flare sits outside the frame. Flare degrades images and harms tasks such as object detection and driving vision. Single-image removal methods falter when off-frame sources are missing or incomplete, since the flare pattern depends on them.

Their framework, LightsOut, uses diffusion-based outpainting to rebuild the missing off-frame sources first. A multitask regression module plus a LoRA-tuned diffusion model keep the invented surroundings realistic and physically consistent. Across hard scenes, LightsOut lifts the results of existing removal methods without any retraining of those methods. The five authors present it as a plug-and-play preprocessing step that can sit before any flare remover.
arxiv-2510-16268:
Babu G V R, Ratna Babu D, and Alemayehu Negash prove fixed point theorems. These are results about spots that a map sends to themselves. Their setting pairs three maps on a space with distances, where one map shrinks pairs of points in a weak, relative way. The maps also commute at the very points they share, a mild match called weak compatibility.

Under those terms, the three maps share at least one common fixed point. Two classic step-by-step schemes, the Mann and Ishikawa iterations, also march toward that shared point in spaces with a norm. The authors then turn to invariant approximation. They ask when a best approximation to a point must itself be a fixed point. Such theorems back many methods that solve equations by steady refinement.
arxiv-2510-16368:
Ali Shirali, writing alone, asks what it costs users to steer an algorithm toward what they truly want. Platforms learn from clicks and watch time, but users are inconsistent: an impulsive side lingers on content the reflective side values little. That noise can train the algorithm toward the wrong tastes.

Shirali models the user as two systems, a rational planner and an impulsive browser, in a Stackelberg game with the algorithm. The planner commits to a strategy, and the algorithm best-responds to what it sees. He defines the burden of alignment as the shortest span over which users must plan ahead to win. A sharp threshold appears: plan far enough and alignment succeeds, fall short and the algorithm aligns you instead. One small, costly signal, like an extra click, can shrink that burden a lot.
arxiv-2510-16468:
A. A. Vyguzov and F. S. Stonyakin refine a classic solver in their 2025 paper. The Frank-Wolfe method solves smooth tasks by steps toward a corner point. Smoothness here means how fast the slope of a cost can change. Their new form suits costs whose smoothness blends two rates at once.

The new method provably meets its goal faster than the classic form. A second, adaptive form tunes its own smoothness rates as it runs. That tuning adds speed and keeps the steps stable. Number tests back the theory with clear wins over past forms. Faster solvers help in machine learning, where such tasks run at huge scale. The pair share full proofs for both new forms.
arxiv-2510-16668:
Gabriella Agazie and fifty-two co-authors report wideband timing of four millisecond pulsars, combining data from the CHIME telescope with the fifteen-year NANOGrav data set. Millisecond pulsars are fast-spinning neutron stars used as precise cosmic clocks. Wideband timing measures one arrival time and one dispersion measure across the full observing band at once.

CHIME has watched most NANOGrav pulsars almost daily since 2019, far more often than other telescopes in the project. The team studies one isolated pulsar and three in binary systems. They describe their wideband pipeline and give updated timing results. The work shows how frequent low-frequency data can sharpen pulsar timing for gravitational wave searches.
arxiv-2510-17268:
Anthony Frion and David S Greenberg add doubt bars to data assimilation in this 2025 paper. Data assimilation blends a motion model with sparse, noisy reads over time. Most blends give one best guess and hide how unsure it is. The authors let the guess be a spread, not a point.

Their method learns the spread with a form of variational inference, a way to fit spreads by tuning. Tests use a chaotic air-flow toy model with waves of cells. Guesses come out near fully matched to true spread. Longer blend windows then help more than in the fixed form. Code is shared for use in wider assimilation pipes.
arxiv-2510-17768:
Jennifer M. Laing and Christine D. Wilson compare gas in the centers of barred and unbarred galaxies. Barred galaxies carry a long straight band of stars across the center. Earlier surveys found denser, more stirred gas in barred centers. The pair test whether that gas also forms stars faster.

They used sharp published measurements from the PHANGS-ALMA survey. A new recipe converts the gas signal using local gas motion speeds. Barred centers used up their gas faster than unbarred centers. The gap stayed even after accounting for active galactic nuclei. Extra non-circular motion, likely gas flowing along the bar, may explain it.
arxiv-2510-17868:
Xinyue Zheng and five co-authors argue that coding tests for large language models often flatter the models. Fixed test problems leak into training data, and models can pass by memory rather than reason. Their UniCode system turns seed problems into harder changed versions and builds tests for them on its own.

Scores of top models fell sharply on the changed problems, mostly from weak planning and scaling, not from syntax slips. Models also slid back to memorized answers for the seed problems. Readers who judge coding models get a sterner test and a warning about how much reported skill is recall.
arxiv-2510-17968:
Aritra Kundu, with eight co-authors, argues that studies of the early universe leave out half the story when they count only surviving small galaxies. Nearby galaxy history is used to infer the faint galaxies that lit the young cosmos. Broken-up galaxies, now seen as streams and mixed debris, are often skipped in that count.

Using the FIRE-2 simulations, the team shows the disrupted systems held up to about half the early star mass. Adding them raises the inferred galaxy counts and steadies the results. The near-far method for probing the first billion years becomes much firmer on this fuller accounting.
arxiv-2510-18068:
Rudolf Beran, as sole author, builds statistics for data that live on a sphere using plain Cartesian coordinates. Directional data are unit vectors, and axial data are directions without a sign. Old work leaned on a few simple exponential models, since harder ones lack tidy formulas for their normalizing constants.

The paper instead works from the sample's own distribution in Cartesian form. Nonparametric estimates and bootstrap confidence sets cover means, spread, and the distribution itself. Extensions to wider spaces and to regression are sketched. Statisticians who measure winds, orientations, or crystal axes get tools that drop the old model limits.
arxiv-2510-18268:
Yucheng Song, with Chenxi Li and three co-authors, presents TreeFedDG in a 2025 paper on medical imaging. The task is segmenting medical scans, meaning outlining organs or lesions in each image. Hospitals cannot pool scans freely, so learning must stay federated, with data kept at each site.

Uneven data across hospitals causes global drift, where the shared model slowly veers off course. TreeFedDG arranges model merging in a tree shape to steady that direction. It also mixes styles between the most different sites and fuses models with personal touches kept. At test time it retrieves the most relevant model chain for each scan.
arxiv-2510-18468:
Antonio Romano and his four co-authors build two large Italian data sets for medical question answering. Online forums where patients ask doctors for advice hold vast knowledge, but the writing is informal and hard for automated systems, especially outside English. One data set gathers 782,644 patient-doctor conversations across seventy-seven medical categories, and a second holds 25,862 multiple-choice questions from medical specialty exams.

The team used large language models to clean the forum text for clarity and consistency while keeping its meaning and style. They then compared many model designs on both open questions and exam questions. Systems helped by search over the collection, or fine-tuned for medicine, beat larger general models, suggesting that domain knowledge and good retrieval matter more than raw size. Both data sets and the testing framework are released for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-18768:
Harry Amad and his five co-authors improve synthetic medical data for the specific job of causal inference, estimating what a treatment actually causes. Real patient data are hard to share, so artificial data sets stand in, yet ordinary generators are not built to preserve the machinery that causal analysis depends on. The authors spell out three things treatment data must keep: the patient mix, the rule by which treatments were assigned, and the process that produced outcomes.

From those requirements they derive evaluation metrics tailored to causal usefulness. Their generator, STEAM, then mimics the true data-generating process itself and optimizes for the stated requirements. In experiments, STEAM beat existing generative models on the new metrics and reached leading overall performance, with its advantage growing as the true process behind the data became more complex. The work aims to make shared synthetic data trustworthy for developing medical treatments.
arxiv-2510-18868:
Claudio Ranucci and his four co-authors test a proposed safety check in cosmology. The target is primordial gravitational waves. Their strength is summarized by the tensor-to-scalar ratio. The signal hides in the polarization of the cosmic microwave background. Leftover galactic foregrounds could fake or bias a detection. Shape statistics called Minkowski functionals might warn of such residue. In principle, they flag non-Gaussian traces in cleaned maps.

The team simulated a LiteBIRD-like satellite. Instruments and foregrounds were modeled realistically. Maps were cleaned, then compared with purely Gaussian maps of the same signal. The check mostly failed. In most cases, the functionals raised no significant warning. Even the most refined scenario flagged problems only about a quarter of the time. The authors conclude the test cannot be reliably adopted for this purpose.
arxiv-2510-19068:
Shifa Sulaiman and three co-authors design an adaptive neural controller for the wrist of a prosthetic hand. Controllers matter greatly for prosthetic hands, since poor control makes an otherwise good device clumsy, and a soft tendon-driven wrist is especially hard to steer because it bends continuously.

The wrist is modeled with beam theory, which links motor current to tendon tension and bending. A neural network then predicts the currents needed from the bending error, adapting as it works. Comparing the controller with similar ones shows whether learning-based control can make prosthetic wrists move more naturally.
arxiv-2510-19568:
Xiazhi Hao and S. Y. Lou examine how the infinite symmetry algebra of the AKNS system of nonlinear equations simplifies when only multi-soliton solutions are considered. The AKNS system carries two families of symmetries, called K-symmetries and tau-symmetries, each forming an endless hierarchy. On pure soliton backgrounds, that endless structure turns out to collapse.

The whole K-symmetry hierarchy reduces to a finite module spanned by simple center-translation generators, and every higher symmetry can be rebuilt from them. The tau-symmetries resist this reduction on soliton backgrounds but become finite once the solution space widens to general multi-wave solutions. The result gives an algorithmic route to exact multi-wave solutions of integrable systems.
arxiv-2510-19668:
Alejandro Pajón-Sanmartín and five co-authors compare two ways of getting computers to recognize emotions in open-ended text: fine-tuning a pretrained model, or prompting a large language model. Emotion detection in free text is tangled by context, varied wording, and complex expressions, so general-purpose models struggle. The study runs three comparisons covering prompt designs and emotion grouping strategies.

A fine-tuned pretrained model scored above seventy percent on the test metrics. The language models, by contrast, needed carefully structured prompts and grouped emotion categories before their performance became competitive. The findings offer practical guidance for sentiment analysis and human-computer interaction systems that judge users' feelings from their writing.
arxiv-2510-19968:
Vipin Rathi and eight co-authors lay out Q-RAN, a security framework that hardens open radio access networks against quantum computers. Open RAN splits the mobile network among multiple vendors, enlarging the attack surface just as future quantum machines threaten today's public-key cryptography. The harvest-now, decrypt-later strategy makes the danger immediate, since intercepted traffic can be stored and read later.

Q-RAN deploys the standardized post-quantum algorithms for key encapsulation and digital signatures across all open RAN interfaces, in quantum-safe versions of the standard secure protocols. Quantum random number generators supply cryptographic entropy, and a central post-quantum certificate authority anchors trust inside the network management framework. The paper offers operators a complete roadmap for quantum-resistant migration.
arxiv-2510-20168:
Tian Lan and eight co-authors introduce DeepWideSearch, a benchmark for search agents that must combine deep reasoning with wide information gathering at the same time. Real jobs like market analysis need multi-hop retrieval for each item and collection across many items, and current agents handle that mix poorly. The benchmark was built by converting established datasets into two hundred twenty questions across fifteen domains.

Even leading agents average only about two point four percent success on the benchmark, showing how hard the combined task remains. The authors sort failures into four modes: lack of reflection, overreliance on internal knowledge, insufficient retrieval, and context overflow. They release the benchmark openly to push work on stronger information-seeking agents.
arxiv-2510-20468:
Tomáš Souček and seven co-authors investigate watermark forging, an attack where a watermark is stolen from genuine content and applied to malicious content. Watermarking has grown with generative models and legal pressure, and removal attacks are well studied, but forging post-hoc image watermarks remains underexplored. Their attack needs only a single watermarked image and no knowledge of the watermarking model.

A preference model first judges whether an image looks watermarked, trained with a ranking loss on purely procedurally generated images with no real watermarks involved. Optimizing an input image by backpropagation through that model can then remove a watermark or forge one onto new content. Tests across a variety of post-hoc watermarking models show the forging works effectively in a black-box, one-shot setting.
arxiv-2510-20768:
Austin Jia, Avaneesh Ramesh, Zain Shamsi, Daniel Zhang, and Alex Liu defend language model pipelines for cyber threat work against poisoned source documents. Retrieval systems pull in outside reports before answering, so a planted false report can steer answers if the system trusts it blindly.

Threat news is often brand new and skilled attackers copy trusted formats well, which breaks many standard defenses. The team ranks sources by a PageRank style authority score so trusted documents rise and hostile ones sink before retrieval. Tests on a standard search data set plus a proof of concept on threat feeds show clear separation of scores. The plan adds a credibility layer without changing the core model.
arxiv-2510-21468:
Emre Sahinoglu, Youbang Sun, and Shahin Shahrampour give the first timed guarantees for a hard optimization problem. Minimizing a jagged, nonconvex cost with noisy information while the search point must stay on a curved surface, a Riemannian manifold. Such problems arise in robotics and data analysis, where the natural variables live on spheres or rotation spaces.

Because jagged costs lack clean gradients, they adopt a smoothed notion of near-stationarity suited to curved spaces. Their algorithm translates an online method into a nonconvex solver and reaches near-stationary points with a sample cost that matches the best known rate on flat space. A second version works with function values alone, no gradients at all, at the same cost. Computer tests back the theory and show the methods behave well in practice.
arxiv-2510-21868:
Somasekhara Goud Sontti and Arnab Atta model how droplets form inside a square microfluidic flow-focusing device, a chip where one liquid stream pinches another into drops. Drop size, shape, and formation rate decide whether such chips work for chemistry and medicine, and they shift with flow rates, liquid thickness, and surface tension.

The pair built a computational model and mapped how the forming regime changes as those physical settings vary, across several liquid pairings. From the simulations they draw flow maps and propose a scaling rule that predicts droplet length over a wide range of operating conditions. The results give designers practical guidance for building devices that produce drops on demand, with the size and rhythm a task requires.
arxiv-2510-22168:
Shouvik Sadhukhan and C. S. Narayanamurthy try to calm a laser beam that turbulence has roughed up. Their laboratory setup manufactures the turbulence on a bench, using a rotating pseudo-random phase plate that mimics the Kolmogorov statistics of real air. Passes a cleaned Gaussian beam through it before reshaping what survives.

The shaping tool is a vortex phase plate, which twists the disturbed beam into Laguerre-Gaussian modes carrying different amounts of orbital angular momentum. The team measures the scintillation index, the flicker in the beam's intensity pattern, recorded on a camera at five positions along the beam's path. Compares modes and positions to see which arrangements resist the turbulence best. The experiments speak to free-space optical links, where atmospheric shimmer is the standing enemy of a clean signal.
