arxiv-2510-22268:
Qiao Li leads a six-author team matching the same pedestrian between a drone's camera and a street camera, a job called aerial-ground person re-identification. The viewpoints could hardly differ more, straight down versus eye level, so poses warp, bodies occlude each other, and the two image worlds barely look like the same domain.

Their network, GSAlign, attacks the geometry and the meaning separately together. A learnable thin plate spline module bends the pedestrian features themselves, guided by learned keypoints, to undo the worst viewpoint distortion. A dynamic alignment module then handles the semantic gap, adjusting how features line up across the two views. The authors present the pair as a joint answer to spatial misalignment and pose variation, the two failures that have capped progress on this emerging surveillance and search task.
arxiv-2510-22368:
B Cooper Boniece and two co-authors study how to watch a stream of data and flag when its whole distribution changes. They build detectors from a class of degenerate U statistic processes, in plain terms scores that compare samples in pairs. Three monitoring designs are covered, including one that folds old observations into the baseline over time.

Under no change, they derive limit results for all three designs and support a Monte Carlo way to set cut off values. For two designs they also pin down detection delays for early and late changes. Tests and a metro train sensor example show the methods compete well.
arxiv-2510-23068:
Ella Dodor and Cristina V Lopes present Checkstyle Plus, a tool that joins classic linters with large language models to cut technical debt. Good style aids reading and teamwork, but rule-based linters like Checkstyle only catch surface faults. Some style rules need a deeper read of what code means, beyond fixed patterns.

The new system uses model judgment for those nuanced rules while keeping fast checks for the rest. The goal is feedback that flags real maintainability problems, not just formatting slips. Development teams could use the hybrid to keep code clean with less manual review of style.
arxiv-2510-23668:
Fujiang Yuan and five co-authors forecast traffic flow by splitting the problem into three simpler ones. Traffic series mix slow trends, daily and weekly rhythms, and noisy leftovers, and a single model often misses at least one of those layers. Their framework first applies STL decomposition, which separates the series into trend, seasonal, and residual parts.

Each part then goes to a specialist: an LSTM network for long-term trends, an ARIMA model for the seasonal rhythm, and XGBoost for the nonlinear residual wiggles. Multiplying the three forecasts rebuilds the final prediction. On 998 traffic records from a New York City intersection in late 2015, the hybrid beat each standalone model across standard error measures. The authors credit the split itself: isolating each pattern lets every model do the job it suits, which lifts accuracy and makes the system easier to interpret and trust.
arxiv-2510-23768:
Philipp Denzel and three co-authors test whether deep learning models can translate between maps of a simulated galaxy, predicting one physical property from another. Working with high-resolution simulation data, they compare conditional GANs and diffusion models under one shared pipeline. Seven domains are in play: dark matter, gas, neutral hydrogen, stellar mass, temperature, and magnetic field strength.

Beyond standard image scores, the authors add physics-aware metrics that judge structural realism. Difficulty tracked physical coupling: gas-to-dark-matter and gas-to-hydrogen maps came out nearly perfect, while weakly constrained jobs like gas-to-stellar-mass stayed hard. GANs matched the diffusion models' quality at a fraction of the training and inference cost. The authors frame the study as the first systematic multi-domain test of its kind, pointing toward cheap forward modeling for the Square Kilometre Array era.
arxiv-2510-24268:
Eliseo Luongo studies whether adding randomness can restore well posedness to a supercritical heat equation with a focusing power nonlinearity, working alone. Recent work showed this equation has non unique local solutions in high dimensions for a range of powers below the Joseph-Lundgren exponent. Luongo tests two kinds of randomization for a better solution theory.

First, he adds a forcing term that is white in time and colored in space, and proves it is not enough: non uniqueness persists for local mild solutions with additive noise. He then discusses other randomizations and their effects. The results map where noise helps and where it cannot fix the equation's bad behavior.
arxiv-2510-24868:
Marcela Ribeiro and Arturo Fernandez-Perez set new count tools for germs of leaf like forms in the plane of complex numbers. Such a form, a foliation, has a lone odd point at the start in their setup. They name a k-th form of two known counts, the Milnor and Tjurina counts, for this case.

The pair give plain forms for the new counts and tie them to known marks of such forms. One new count for a plain map germ stays fixed under shape change, while its twin does not. In two dimensions, they settle a guess on a sharp low bound for one count. They also give a case that breaks a past guess on the ratio of the two.
arxiv-2510-24968:
Mario Hernandez Vera, the sole author, built FSIM, a teach first code frame for the Hartree-Fock method in quantum chem work. That method and its core sums are a hub of how molecule math is done, yet big pro codes are hard for students to pick apart. FSIM is a small, clear take meant to be read as much as run.

Written in an object based style in C++, the code stresses neat parts and plain form. It covers the known McMurchie and Davidson scheme for the core sums. Shared and spread run modes are both laid out for large machines. Small class tasks point to ways to speed the code and test its growth.
arxiv-2510-25268:
Wang Zhi led five co-authors on SynHLMA. His co-authors are Yuyan Liu, Liu Liu, and Li Zhang. Ruixuan Lu and Dan Guo complete the team. Their 2025 paper synthesizes hand movements from language. The hands must grasp jointed objects with moving parts. Such work helps embodied AI and virtual reality.

SynHLMA starts from a full point cloud scan. It codes each hand and object contact frame. The code is discrete, meaning split into fixed symbols. A language model links codes with describing words. A joint-aware training loss keeps grasps realistic. It tracks how the object joints move over time. The team test generation, prediction, and interpolation tasks. They use their new HAOI-lang data set. Results beat prior state-of-the-art methods, they report. They also show a robot grasping objects by imitation.
arxiv-2510-25368:
Julien Martinelli argues that biology should challenge physics-informed learning. His 2025 position paper concerns machine learning with mechanistic knowledge. Physics-informed methods have succeeded where laws are known. Physical laws there are well established and exact. Biology has many dynamical systems worth modeling. Its constraints differ sharply from physics, though.

Biological knowledge is multifaceted and uncertain in practice. Data are heterogeneous, noisy, and partly unobserved. Networks are complex and high-dimensional there. Martinelli argues these traits should drive method evolution. He proposes Biology-Informed Machine Learning as an extension. It keeps structural grounding from physics-informed methods. It adapts to softer, probabilistic prior knowledge instead. Four pillars form his roadmap for transition. They cover uncertainty, context, latent structure, and scale. Foundation models and language models can enable progress. Concrete recommendations aim to build that ecosystem.
arxiv-2510-25568: Abdelkrim Moussaoui establishes three answers for a Gierer-Meinhardt type system with Neumann edge settings, in a 2025 math paper. Two answers have opposite constant sign, while the third is nodal, with parts that share signs in a synchronous way. The proof mixes the sub-supersolutions method with Leray-Schauder topological degree, using a perturbation argument. The paper is a compact existence study for readers who work on reaction-diffusion systems and nonlinear edge value problems.
arxiv-2510-25668:
Tianyu Yang led five co-authors introducing ALDEN. Terry Ruas, Yijun Tian, and Jan Philip Wahle helped. Daniel Kurzawe and Bela Gipp complete six authors. Their 2025 paper helps vision-language models read long documents. Such models interpret text-rich images well. Long documents challenge them greatly.

Existing approaches use fixed reasoning templates or pipelines. Models stay passive and generalization suffers there. ALDEN is a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework. It fine-tunes models as interactive navigating agents. A novel fetch action accesses pages by index. Classic search actions complement that fetching ability. Document structure is exploited better by fetching. A rule-based cross-level reward supervises training densely. Turn-level and token-level signals are both provided. Visual-semantic anchoring stabilizes training against instability. Visual tokens from long documents caused instability empirically. ALDEN achieved state-of-the-art on five benchmarks. Active navigation beats passive document reading here.
arxiv-2510-25768:
Kush Hari, Ziyang Chen, Hansoul Kim, and Ken Goldberg present STITCH 2.0. Their 2025 paper extends augmented robot suturing. Surgical suturing is high-precision and impacts patient healing. Skill varies widely between surgeons in practice. Robot assistance could reduce that variability. Previous STITCH struggled to fully close wounds.

Inaccurate needle tracking and poor thread management caused failures. Seven improvements elevate the augmented dexterity pipeline. Extended Kalman filter needle pose estimation is better. New thread untangling methods manage suture thread better. An automated 3D suture matching method is added. Tests ran over fifteen trials for testing. STITCH 2.0 reached about seventy-four percent wound closure. It placed more sutures per trial than rival. Sutures increased by sixty-six percent in trials. Time fell by thirty-eight percent compared with rival. With two human interventions allowed, closure reached completion. Six sutures on average reached full closure then.
arxiv-2510-26468:
Sudip Sinha, Subhasis Sinha, and Sushanta Dattagupta extend a classic model of quantum loss. The spin-boson model pairs a two-state system with a bath of vibrations, and it is the standard test case for how surroundings drain quantum effects. The trio add spin-orbit coupling, a link between a particle's motion and its spin, for a particle in one dimension with a sub-ohmic bath, where low tones weigh heavily.

Using a variational polaron approach, a trial-state method, they find a localization transition as the bath coupling grows: a double well in momentum flattens to a single point at zero. With motion conserved, a magnetisation change is smooth, while the ground state jumps. In a trapped version, like a quantum dot, entanglement entropy marks both changes, and a cat-like split state gives the most entropy below the shift.
arxiv-2510-27168:
Jing Chang, with Chang Liu and four other co-authors, tackles a slow chore in machine learning in this 2025 paper. Before a model can learn, raw data must be cleaned and reshaped by a chain of steps. Picking the right chain by hand is slow, and blind search tries too many chains. Their tool, ShapleyPipe, rates each step by its fair share of the gain.

The rating idea comes from game theory, where a Shapley value splits credit among players. ShapleyPipe first picks broad kinds of steps, then fine-tunes the exact steps. Two tricks keep the math cheap: a bandit method, which tests options and backs winners, and a score that notes step order. On eighteen data sets it nearly matched costly search while using far fewer tries.
arxiv-2510-27268:
Dimitri Loutchko, Keisuke Sugie, and Tetsuya J Kobayashi review five years of work linking two fields in this 2025 article. One field studies gradient flows, systems that slide downhill on an energy-like slope. The other is information geometry, which treats probability spreads as shapes with distance and angle. Their shared stage is the hypergraph, a net where one link can join many points at once.

The review recasts newer physics ideas inside that frame. Among them are bounds on speed, splits of entropy growth, and rules linking noise to response. A split-view picture, with paired families of states, sits at the core. New notions appear too, like spaces of flow types and a thermodynamic area tied to speed limits. The authors hope to draw both fields closer.
arxiv-2510-27468:
Yu Wang leads five co-authors in explaining dust and water features around the outbursting young star V883 Ori as relics of a retreating water snowline. Its disk shows a shoulder in radio intensity profiles once blamed on dust pile-up from pebble breakup at the snowline. New multi-wavelength data instead show smooth spectral behavior across that region and water emission extending farther out, pointing to a snowline that once sat farther from the star.

A two-dimensional disk model follows cooling and vapor recondensation as the outburst fades. The shoulder arises naturally from excess surface density where vapor recondenses at the moving front, while outer water vapor lingers because recondensation takes centuries to millennia in the disk atmosphere. The shoulder should migrate inward measurably over coming decades.
arxiv-2511-00168:
Jinling Zhou, Xin Liu, Jiawang Nie, and Xindong Tang study a hard step inside methods that solve smooth optimization problems. The step, called cubic-quartic regularization, asks for the global best point of a function with both cubic and quartic terms, terms that use third and fourth powers. Direct search can miss the true best point, so the authors seek a safer route.

They relax the problem into a semidefinite program, a structured problem that solvers handle well, using just three matrix variables. They prove exact conditions for when the relaxed answer equals the true one. Tests show the method is fast, exact in the proven cases, and finds all best points.
arxiv-2511-00468:
Panwang Pan and six co-authors present HumanCrafter, a system that rebuilds a person in 3D from a single image and labels the body parts at the same time. Generative models now reconstruct humans with high fidelity, but downstream tasks such as 3D segmentation still lack support, and labeled 3D human data is scarce. HumanCrafter joins the two tasks in one feed-forward pass.

Geometric priors guide the reconstruction stage, while self-supervised semantic priors drive the segmentation stage. An interactive annotation procedure creates high-quality data-label pairs to ease the scarcity. Pixel-aligned aggregation lets the tasks reinforce each other, and a multi-task objective balances texture fidelity against semantic consistency. Experiments show the system surpassing leading methods at both 3D human-part segmentation and single-image reconstruction.
arxiv-2511-01068:
Andrei Lebed predicts a second forbidden effect in quasi one dimensional conductors, following his related work on magnetoresistance oscillations. Here the claim concerns specific heat, the amount of energy needed to warm the material, which he argues must oscillate in some of these metals in a way standard theory forbids.

The oscillations arise from electron electron interactions when magnetic breakdown occurs, a tunneling between open electron orbits that interfere with each other. Lebed names two organic conductors where the effect should exist, the same pair treated in his companion work, and suggests experimentalists look for the oscillations there. As with the resistance effect, the phenomenon sits beyond the Fermi liquid picture of metals.
arxiv-2511-01168:
Sheng Fang, Ziyan Wang, Jurgen Kurths, and Jingfang Fan review tipping points in the Earth system. These are thresholds where a subsystem, such as the Atlantic overturning circulation or the Amazon rainforest, can shift abruptly. Their lens is nonlinear dynamics and complexity science.

The review sorts tipping mechanisms into three kinds, driven by bifurcation, noise, or the rate of change itself. It evaluates early warning signals based on critical slowing down, weighing their limits alongside newer, unconventional indicators. A major theme is cascading: interacting tipping elements, often modeled as networks, can raise the whole system's risk under global warming. The authors close with challenges in data and method robustness, and point to artificial intelligence and network science as promising tools.
arxiv-2511-01368:
Nicolas Boulanger and Davide Rovere construct conformal gravity theories in even dimensions that are extremized by Einstein metrics, meaning the usual solutions of general relativity also solve the conformal theory's equations. They begin by tidying the known six dimensional construction of Lu, Pang, and Pope.

They then prove that a unique eight dimensional conformal gravity action with the Einstein property exists, and they build it in full. The authors relate the construction to Branson's Q-curvature and the Fefferman-Graham obstruction tensor. They conclude that in every even dimension there is a unique conformally invariant gravity theory, up to boundary terms, with this property. Such results sharply limit how gravity can be changed while keeping Einstein metrics as solutions.
arxiv-2511-01468:
Hao Wang and colleagues present DAMBench, a benchmark for deep learning approaches to atmospheric data assimilation, the task of rebuilding the atmosphere's state by blending sparse, noisy observations with a prior forecast. Classical methods work but scale poorly to today's large observing systems of many kinds, and learned rivals have been hard to compare fairly.

Earlier learned studies relied on simplified scenarios with observations spoiled by hand, and no standard benchmark existed. DAMBench pairs high quality background states from leading forecast systems with real observations, from weather stations and satellite imagery, all resampled to a common grid and aligned in time. Unified protocols govern training, validation, and testing, and the authors benchmark typical approaches, including latent generative models and neural process schemes.
arxiv-2511-01968:
Samik Dutta, Ankur Chhabra, Aritra Banerjee, Sajal Mukherjee, and Subhendra Mohanty compute gravitational waves from a flyby. Two massive objects swing past each other on a parabolic path. That path is the knife-edge between elliptical and unbound hyperbolic encounters. Such flybys carry the gravitational wave memory effect. It is a permanent displacement left in detectors after the wave passes. It comes in a linear form tied to the source, and a nonlinear form sourced by the waves themselves.

The authors warn against a shortcut. Extrapolating memory formulas from eccentric or hyperbolic cases to the parabola gives wrong answers. So they treat the parabolic case intrinsically, with its parameterization. Within effective field theory, it derives the signals and their energy spectrum. New features appear in the zero-frequency limit, absent in the hyperbolic case. The study uses the parabola as a separatrix to expose the challenges of memory physics.
arxiv-2511-02268:
Jerin Thachil, Chirang Patel, U. Ashwin, and Ashok Kumar track how quantum correlations between paired beams of light spread as the beams travel. The beams, called bright twin beams, are produced by four-wave mixing in atomic vapour. Their spatial correlations live in an effectively infinite-dimensional space, which makes them attractive for quantum imaging and cryptography. The question is how the correlation pattern evolves from the near field to the far field.

The authors derive a formula for that evolution and test it by measuring the noise in the intensity difference between matching regions of the beams. There, squeezing below the usual level signals quantum correlation. A plain Gaussian pump beam gave correlations that stayed localised near the source and flipped to anti-correlations far away. A structured Laguerre-Gaussian pump produced correlations that delocalised with distance, a transition the authors link to future quantum sensing and imaging uses.
arxiv-2511-02568:
Łukasz Cholewa and Eran Igra ask how faithfully a one-dimensional caricature can capture one of chaos theory's icons, the Lorenz attractor. A Lorenz map is a piecewise continuous map of an interval, modelled on the attractor's dynamics: simple enough to analyse completely, but possibly too simple to matter. The question the authors settle is how much of the real attractor's behaviour, including its bifurcations, such a map can actually govern.

They prove that open regions of the Lorenz system's parameter space admit a canonical reduction to a symmetric Lorenz map of constant slope between one and two. That single map encodes many essential features of the full attractor and, strikingly, governs many of its bifurcations as parameters move. The results line up closely with decades of numerical studies of the Lorenz system, and the authors suggest the reduction explains bifurcation phenomena those simulations had observed without a theory.
arxiv-2511-02768:
Steven Silverman asks what happens when a black hole's Hawking radiation grows so strong that its own energy bends the space around it. In that regime, treating the radiation as a small effect on a fixed background no longer works. His 2025 paper builds a simple spherically symmetric semiclassical model to follow the change.

Strong outgoing energy, the model shows, can form a second, short-lived trapping surface outside the original horizon. Silverman derives when such nested horizons split apart or merge, using a smooth Vaidya-type mass profile. He further proposes that the gap between the horizons may follow a discrete rule, like the old Bohr-Sommerfeld condition for atoms. That hint of discreteness could offer a geometric path toward quantum gravity.
arxiv-2511-02868:
M. Z. Haider, M. U. Ghouri, Tayyaba Noreen, and M. Salman propose a blockchain agreement method modeled on spiking neurons, the brain-like units that fire in brief pulses. Blockchains still fight slow speeds, delays, and high energy use. Proof-of-Work burns power, while Proof-of-Stake can drift toward central control, as their 2025 paper notes.

Their protocol, Proof-of-Spiking-Neurons, encodes transactions as spike trains. Leaders emerge from competitive firing among the units, and blocks settle through neural synchronization, allowing parallel, event-driven agreement with low energy overhead. The design runs on neuromorphic hardware with simulators such as Nengo and PyNN. Reported tests showed gains in energy use, throughput, and convergence over two rival schemes. The authors pitch it for Internet of Things and edge networks.
arxiv-2511-03268:
Tonghui Wang, Guoqing Zhang, and Haocheng Wen study how blocking backward pressure waves affects a rotating detonation engine. In that engine, a blast wave races around a ring channel and should raise total pressure as gases leave. Pressure that leaks backward toward the inlet works against that gain and can upset feeding.

Using a simplified valve model and mostly one-way flow math, the team varies how strongly backflow is blocked and how wide the exit grows. Stronger blocking does curb backward pressure and lifts the gain a little. Gains stay modest, which points to other losses holding the engine back. The results guide where designers should focus if they want the pressure promise of detonation to pay off.
arxiv-2511-03368:
Hongrun Ren and co-authors design TripleWin, a pricing system where data sellers, model builders, and model buyers all trade in one linked market. Most current pricing splits data deals from model deals, or lets a broker favor one side. Here, dataset payments flow forward into model price quotes that buyers see.

Buyer prices then flow backward to datasets through a Shapley-style split that credits each data source for its contribution. The two flows form a closed loop that settles at a fixed-point balance. Four kinds of interaction are tracked, covering supply and demand in both directions plus buyer coupling. The authors aim for a market where no side wins by squeezing the others out of fair value.
arxiv-2511-03468:
Jan David Fischbach and colleagues show that tracking resonances at complex frequencies settles whether light and matter are strongly coupled. In strong coupling, light and matter excitations merge into hybrids, enabling new control over emission and chemistry. Usual spectra at real frequencies only hint at that merger indirectly.

Resonant states live naturally at complex frequencies, so the team follows their paths as a cavity's shape changes. At the onset of strong coupling, those paths change character instead of merely passing by. The switch gives an unambiguous marker where spectral reading stays fuzzy. Cavity designers gain a cleaner test for when a device truly enters the hybrid regime.
arxiv-2511-03668:
Oleg R Musin casts a famed shape puzzle in graph terms. The puzzle concerns point sets that use just two gap sizes. Borsuk's classic claim has a twin claim for such sets. That twin stays open for a wide band of space sizes.

Each graph can be drawn as such a point set in some space. Musin uses that bridge in this short note. Graph tools can then hunt for a case that breaks the claim. Pure shape work has stalled on those sizes for years. The note also extends the bridge to sets with more gap sizes. A small graph, checked by machine, might settle sizes that proofs alone have not.
arxiv-2511-03768:
Candace Ross and colleagues build Common-O, a benchmark that catches multimodal models hallucinating when they reason across scenes. Models name objects in single images impressively, yet real-world reasoning still trips them into inventing content. Common-O asks a deceptively simple question across fresh, never-web-published photos: what is in common?

More than ten thousand examples, modeled on human cognitive tests, force comparison rather than mere labeling. Leading models, including ones trained for step-by-step reasoning, stumble well below their saturated perception scores. The gap shows that spotting objects is not the same as reasoning about them jointly. A contamination-free set gives the field an honest ruler for scene reasoning progress.
arxiv-2511-04068:
Arif Ullah is the lead author among seven authors on TXL Fusion, a hybrid machine learning framework for finding topological materials such as topological insulators and semimetals. First-principles screening is costly and experiments are slow, so a cheap pre-screen that respects chemistry and physics is valuable.

Chemical heuristics join readable descriptors for symmetry, electron count, and orbitals with semantic embeddings drawn from a large language model. Sorting into trivial, semimetal, and insulator classes improved overall, with better spotting of the minority class than descriptor-only baselines. Strong candidates flagged by the model were checked further, showing the tool can rank an outside search space before costly checks begin.
arxiv-2511-04268:
Iker Martin-Alvarez, Jose I Aliaga, and Maribel Castillo propose a parallel spawning plan for MPI programs that need to grow or shrink their resources while running. Malleability cuts waiting times and improves sharing, but respawning whole programs is costly, while reuse schemes often fail to release nodes when shrinking.

All processes help in spawning under the new strategy. Expansions reuse existing processes, and shrinking truly ends unneeded ones so nodes return to the system. Tests ran on two systems with equal and unequal machines. Lower reset cost makes dynamic resource handling more realistic for production high-performance computing.
arxiv-2511-04368:
Josef Demmel and his co-author study the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with slip at the wall. These equations describe how a viscous fluid moves inside a smooth, bounded region. The boundary rule, named for Navier, lets the fluid slide with a set amount of friction.

The pair proves that the weak solution is in fact strong for any positive time. Their trick is a shifted vorticity that vanishes at the boundary, tied to an elliptic problem. They then show that vorticity converges strongly as viscosity shrinks toward zero. The result sharpens what is known about the inviscid limit, a core question in fluid theory.
arxiv-2511-04668:
Ellis Brown leads six authors with SIMS-V, a way to teach spatial video understanding from simulators. Multimodal models still reason poorly about space across time. Real video with precise spatial labels is scarce and hard to gather.

SIMS-V generates training videos inside three-dimensional simulators, where exact positions are known for free. The team varies question types, data mixes, and scale to find what transfers to real footage. A minimal set of three question types carries most of the gain. They cover metric measurement, perspective-dependent reasoning, and one further spatial skill, guiding cheaper data recipes.
arxiv-2511-04768:
Rubens Lacouture leads seven authors with FuseFlow, a compiler for sparse deep learning on dataflow hardware. Sparse models and streaming architectures promise efficiency, but software must fuse operations to win. FuseFlow turns PyTorch models into fused sparse dataflow graphs.

It is the first compiler to support general fusion across separate sparse expressions. Parallel work, dataflow ordering, and sparsity blocking are optimized alongside fusion. A cycle-accurate model lets the team study fusion strategies in detail. Four real applications guide a design-space search, showing when full fusion pays and how hardware should be shaped for sparse work.
arxiv-2511-04868:
Susana Marín-Aguilar and her co-author simulate ultra-low-crosslinked microgels under crowded conditions. These are among the softest colloidal particles that labs now make routinely. How they behave when packed tightly together was still unclear.

Monomer-resolved simulations track structure, mechanics, and motion across many packing levels. The dangling outer chains of each particle drive the surprises. Unlike regular microgels, these soft ones do not facet when squeezed. Instead, neighbors interpenetrate deeply at high density. The findings rewrite expectations for the softest gels used in coatings, sensing, and drug delivery research. Particle-level detail is what makes those contrasts visible at all.
arxiv-2511-04968:
Jingwei Lian and Yao-Bei Liu test whether one model can explain two odd hints in collider data. One hint is a heavy bump near 650 gigaelectronvolts. The other is a light bump near 95 in the same scale. The heavy signal showed a Higgs-like particle plus the lighter state.

They place both hints in a broad form of the next-to-minimal supersymmetric model. A light singlet-like scalar fits the lower mass, and a heavier doublet-like scalar fits the upper one. Their scan shows the model can match both hints while it still fits dark matter counts, direct searches, Higgs data, and B-physics bounds.
arxiv-2511-05068:
Bruno Dall'Agnol de Oliveira and co-authors map cold molecular gas flows in three nearby Seyfert galaxies. Using the ALMA telescope array, they trace carbon monoxide light in the inner few kiloparsecs of each galaxy at sharp detail.

By fitting each gas profile with several parts, they spot zones whose motion breaks from plain rotation. In NGC 6860, gas flows outward around the twin cones of ionized gas, out to about 560 parsecs from the core. The study links cold gas inflow and outflow with the ionized gas in these active galaxies.
arxiv-2511-05268:
Haoyang Zhang and co-authors find a damping time in black hole accretion light curves that does not depend on the black hole's mass. Scaling laws that tie damping time to mass have long hinted at shared structure across huge size gaps.

The team studied long-term hard X-ray light curves for 106 black hole and neutron star systems, from a 157-month Swift catalog. To their surprise, the damping time stayed fixed across mass. That break from the known mass law asks for a fresh look at what sets flicker rates in accretion disks.
arxiv-2511-05468:
The CMS Collaboration describes DeepTau version 2.5, its neural method to pick out true hadronic tau lepton decays at the CMS detector. Fake taus, from quark or gluon jets and from electrons or muons read wrong, swamp the real ones, so a sharp sorter is key.

The new version adds domain adaptation by backpropagation, which cuts the gap between real collision data and simulation in the purest tau zone. A refined training flow also lifts its sorting skill. Tau leptons are core probes of Higgs and new-physics searches, so a cleaner tau tag pays off across the CMS program.
arxiv-2511-05868:
Hongjun Wang and co-authors shrink super-resolution models for phones and GPUs without wrecking image quality. Post-training quantization cuts model precision after training, but most methods quantize weights and activations separately. The team shows the two play very different roles, using tests on a leading restoration model.

Weights carry the learned knowledge of textures and edges, so quantizing them hurts structure. Activations carry the input's brightness detail, so their quantization hurts pixel accuracy. Their framework, HarmoQ, calibrates weights to offset activation losses, balances both with closed-form scales, and keeps refining the balance during tuning. Under hard two-bit compression it beat prior methods on a standard test set, with large speed and memory gains.
arxiv-2511-05968:
Nagur Shareef Shaik and co-authors write radiology reports from medical images even when parts of the clinical picture are missing. Real records often lack a modality, like the patient's context notes. Models also tangle shared and modality-specific features, which yields fused reports with invented findings.

Their model, built on a vision-language variational autoencoder with a mixture of experts, separates shared features from modality-specific ones. A constrained objective keeps those features aligned yet orthogonal, blocking bad fusion. A compact decoder then writes the report from the separated features. On two chest X-ray data sets the scores were competitive with far heavier systems. The authors stress resilience to missing inputs as the design's main virtue.
arxiv-2511-06068:
Moreno Invitti works in model theory, studying Lie rings that can be defined inside finite-dimensional theories. Earlier results covered the finite Morley rank setting, and the goal here is to push those results further. Lie rings are algebraic structures that resemble Lie algebras but allow more general number systems underneath.

The paper classifies definable Lie rings of dimension up to four in the NIP or connected cases. In characteristic zero it confirms a version of the Cherlin-Zilber Conjecture. It also describes how abelian, nilpotent, and soluble Lie rings can act, shows that definable envelopes exist for them, and proves that the Fitting and radical ideals stay definable.
arxiv-2511-06568:
João Mattos, Debolina Halder Lina, and Arlei Silva argue that the standard fairness test for link prediction can hide the bias it claims to catch. Link prediction guesses which connections a network will form, feeding social recommendations and knowledge graph completion. The usual fairness rule balances predictions between within-group and across-group pairs, a dyadic view of demographic parity.

That framing can average away disparities hitting particular subgroups, and parity itself fits ranking tasks poorly. The authors formalize those limits and propose a richer evaluation framework. A light post-processing step with separate predictors for different link types then cuts bias while keeping accuracy, reaching leading fairness-utility trade-offs in their experiments.
arxiv-2511-06768:
Tara Kemp and James G Lefevre work on Latin cubes, the three-dimensional cousins of Latin squares and Sudoku-like arrays. A Latin cube can contain smaller disjoint subcubes, and given a list of subcube sizes that add up to the whole order, the question is whether such a cube exists. For Latin squares with subsquares of at most two sizes, existence is fully settled, but the cube version was only partially solved.

Restricting to subcubes of two orders, the authors determine existence in almost all cases. Their constructions and impossibility arguments close nearly the whole problem, leaving only a small residue of undecided parameter combinations. The result extends a classic line of combinatorial design theory from two dimensions to three, where the extra dimension changes which size combinations can be realized.
arxiv-2511-07068:
Nikolas Adaloglou and four co-authors remove a hidden dependency from out-of-distribution detection, the task of flagging images that do not belong to any known class. Leading methods built on vision-language models like CLIP need the names of the in-distribution classes in advance, yet those labels can be unavailable, unreliable, or outdated after deployment shifts. ClusterMine instead mines positive concepts from large text corpora that anyone can obtain.

The method combines two consistency checks: visual-only consistency, grouping image samples by clustering, and zero-shot image-text consistency against candidate concepts. It is the first approach to reach state-of-the-art detection performance with no access to positive labels at all. Tests across many CLIP models show it scales and stays robust when the in-distribution data itself shifts.
arxiv-2511-07168:
Giusy Giulia Tuccari and five co-authors tackle author name disambiguation, the problem of deciding which publications belong to which real person when names collide. Ambiguity corrupts bibliographic databases and research evaluation. Their system, LEAD, links career records from CercaUniversità, Italy's official registry of academics, to author profiles in Scopus, a cross-source matching task.

LEAD combines semantic features extracted by large language models with structural evidence from co-authorship and citation networks. On a gold standard of 606 ambiguous cases it beat four alternatives, including label spreading, bibliographic coupling. A standalone language model approach, reaching an F1 score of 96.7 percent at lower computational cost than full language model pipelines. Bibliographic coupling was the fastest strong single method, and the hybrid design is presented as scalable beyond Italy.
arxiv-2511-07268:
Jonathan Lehmkuhl and five co-authors run a systematic comparison of how design choices affect transformer models that compose piano music. Symbolic music creation has many proposed designs but little comprehensive evidence on what matters. The team varies data sets, designs, model sizes, and training plans. It also examines a range of quantitative quality metrics, checking how well each metric agrees with human listeners in dedicated listening studies.

Their best model, a transformer of about 950 million parameters trained on eighty thousand MIDI files spanning diverse genres, writes music that listeners in a Turing-style survey often rated as human-composed. Beyond the winning recipe, the study's value is comparative. It maps which choices of scale, data, and training move quality, and which popular metrics can be trusted to track human judgment.
arxiv-2511-07368:
Dake Bu and co-authors, in work cataloged under a title on exploration and consistency, model how post-training reshapes reasoning. Foundation models know much but reason unevenly on set tasks. Reinforcement methods and test-time scaling help, yet they seem to strengthen old paths rather than find new ones.

Viewing reasoning steps as Markov moves helps explain the puzzle. Easy steps are likely moves, hard insights are rare moves, and training reweights their odds. Exploration helps by raising the chance that rare good moves get sampled and kept. The analysis reframes debates about consistency versus search. It guides choices about sampling budgets during training.
arxiv-2511-07468:
Jonas Pleyer built crate2bib to make citing Rust software painless. Rust libraries, called crates, live on crates.io, but turning them into bibliography entries by hand is tedious. Proper credit matters as research software spreads.

The tool queries the crate registry, pulls metadata such as name, version, and authors, and checks the code repository for citation files. It then formats entries for each candidate source it finds. Access comes through a website, a Python package, a command line tool, or a Rust crate. Researchers can cite dependencies accurately in seconds instead of copying details manually.
arxiv-2511-07668:
Ran Azouri surveys how to compute motivic shadows of a singularity. When a family of varieties degenerates at a point, nearby cycles capture what the smooth fibers leave behind. Their monodromy records how cycles twist around the singular point.

For quasi-homogeneous singularities, both the quadratic Euler value of nearby cycles and the motivic monodromy can be computed. The results refine the classic Deligne-Milnor formula with quadratic data in characteristic zero. Picard-Lefschetz theory likewise lifts to Voevodsky motives with rational coefficients. Singularity theorists gain direct formulas where only abstract existence was known, useful for counting and number questions.
arxiv-2511-08068:
P Arrutia Sota, E Cortes Garcia, and V Sansipersico model radio frequency knock out slow extraction from synchrotrons. The technique eases charged particles out of a ring slowly, giving users a steady beam over time. Uneven spill structure, meaning bursts in the extraction rate, is a problem for experiments needing uniform delivery.

The authors derive explicit analytic formulas for how many particles leave over time. From those formulas they can build, semi analytically, an amplitude modulation curve for the radio frequency exciter. Applying that curve flattens the spill macrostructure, which should help facilities plan smoother beam delivery for their users.
arxiv-2511-08268:
Vladimir Nazarov and E Gross extend the exact factorization framework for electron nuclear dynamics to systems under an electromagnetic field. Exact factorization splits the full many body problem into electronic and nuclear parts without approximation, then guides practical approximations for their coupled motion. Adding an external field creates an interplay between the real magnetic field and the Berry curvature field felt by the nuclei.

A known Born Oppenheimer result says that, for a neutral atom in a uniform magnetic field, the two fields cancel in the nuclear equation. The authors prove rigorously that the same compensation holds inside exact factorization, so the atom travels straight as intuition demands.
arxiv-2511-08368:
Chase van de Geijn and co-authors ask whether rotary positional codings for vision models really need to be equivariant, the property usually credited for their success. Rotary codings first proved themselves on one dimensional language sequences, and generalizations to images and video are now spreading. The team shows rotary coding is among the most general equivariant embeddings in one dimension, and that mixed rotary coding plays the same role in higher dimensions when generators commute.

They then propose spherical rotary coding, which drops the commutativity demand and uses non commuting generators instead. In tests it learns as well as or better than its equivariant relatives. Relative position may matter less than commonly believed in vision, freeing faster, better generalizing designs.
arxiv-2511-08468:
Yongchao Lu derives exact rules for superconformal indices of pure super Yang Mills theories in four dimensions, for any simple gauge group. These indices count guarded states and are usually given by sums that resist closed scoring. The approach applies Macdonald links for untwisted affine Lie algebras directly to those integral rules, producing uniform closed forms expressed both as q series and as eta quotients.

Related techniques yield exact half Schur indices with Neumann boundary conditions and reveal a bilinear structure inside the full Schur index. Within holomorphic topological twists, the results connect to line operator categories, the K theoretic Coulomb branch, Schur quantization, and rules for the BPS spectrum, plus class S constructions.
arxiv-2511-08568:
Jie Ren and six co-authors address a memory problem in deep learning recommendation models, the systems behind ranked feeds and product suggestions. These models need terabytes of stored embedding vectors, and cheaper tiered memory helps only if the right vectors sit in the fast tier at the right time.

Their system, RecMG, uses machine learning to predict which vectors will be reused after long gaps or hardly at all, and it caches and prefetches accordingly. Separate models handle caching and prefetching, guided by a new loss function that narrows the search. In tests it cuts on-demand fetches well below temporal, spatial, and learned rivals, and trims total inference time by up to forty-three percent in industrial-scale runs.
arxiv-2511-08768:
M. Dévora-Pajares and four co-authors built WATSON-Net, a neural network that vets candidate exoplanet transits from space telescopes. As detections pile up, humans cannot inspect every signal, and automated tools must judge the same diagnostic plots that experts traditionally read by eye.

Trained on the full Kepler dataset with ten-fold cross-validation, the system produces ten calibrated models that share one standardized input pipeline. On Kepler targets it ranks second among compared tools, just behind ExoMiner, on a strict recall-at-precision measure. On TESS signals it is the best classifier that was not fine-tuned for that mission, with precision near ninety-three percent. The open-source package plugs into the SHERLOCK vetting pipeline and is designed to extend to future missions.
arxiv-2511-09468:
Izabela Skwira-Chalot and six co-authors measure how proton therapy beams create short-lived radioactive nuclei in tissue-like targets. At the highest therapy energies, about a quarter of protons trigger nuclear reactions, so the beam flux falls along its path. The radioactive products matter because their emissions can be imaged to check where the dose landed.

The team irradiated stacks of up to fifteen targets at the AIC-144 cyclotron in Kraków. Targets were carbon, boron nitride, and silica, hit with beams below 58 megaelectronvolts. They measured production cross sections for carbon-11, nitrogen-13, and oxygen-15, whose half-lives run from two to twenty minutes. The results follow earlier excitation functions with uncertainties of only a few percent.
arxiv-2511-09568:
Peining Zhang, Jinbo Bi, and Minghu Song generate 3D molecules with a diffusion process built to be both fast and true in shape. Flow-based models sample quickly but often distort molecular shapes, while the denoising route is precise yet slow. Their system, VEDA, tries to keep the accuracy and drop the wait.

VEDA combines variance-exploding diffusion with an annealing-like noise schedule inside a symmetry-respecting equivariant design. A new preconditioning scheme aligns coordinate prediction with the diffusion objective, and an arcsin scheduler focuses sampling where it matters. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUGS it matches flow models' speed with top valency stability in just one hundred steps, they report. Its structures barely relax under quantum-chemical checks, unlike its baseline's.
arxiv-2511-10168:
Ilai Zaidel and Sharon Gannot build a deep beamforming system that enhances a moving speaker's voice for listeners using both ears. Their network learns time-varying beamformer weights from noisy multichannel recordings, guided by a continuously tracked relative transfer function describing the target speaker. The study analyzes the network's spatial behavior on an eight-microphone line array in three guidance modes.

With true or tracked transfer functions as guidance, beampatterns stayed smooth and followed the speaker's direction, while the unguided model lost its spatial focus. The framework then extends to binaural output, trained on simulated moving sources with head-related acoustics. Measured interaural level and time differences showed spatial cues preserved well, supporting use in hearable devices.
arxiv-2511-10268:
Zhe Xu, Zhicai Wang, Junkang Wu, Jinda Lu, and Xiang Wang trace a cause of object hallucination in large vision-language models: spurious correlations. When objects co-occur often in training, a model may report one simply because its usual partner is visible. Existing benchmarks detect hallucination but do not formally measure this co-occurrence bias, so the authors build a structural causal model of the recognition scenario.

Within that causal language they define spurious correlation precisely and construct Causal-HalBench, a benchmark of counterfactual samples scored with causal metrics. A generation pipeline using proprietary vision-language and text-to-image models produces those counterfactuals. Mainstream models all showed susceptibility to spurious correlations, in differing degrees, which reframes hallucination as a measurable causal failure.
arxiv-2511-10468:
Lorenzo Calibbi and Jiangyi Yi examine the new bosons predicted by a U(2) flavor model, a theory proposed to explain why particle masses and mixings follow the patterns they do. One boson in the model acts like a standard QCD axion, but the three states tied to its SU(2) part had never been studied in detail.

The authors work through both possibilities: the symmetry could be global, giving light pseudo-Goldstone bosons, or gauged, giving a triplet of light gauge bosons. Either way, the new particles couple strongly to flavor-changing processes. Rare decays such as kaons turning into pions plus an invisible boson give the tightest limits, probing symmetry-breaking scales far beyond what astrophysical observations can reach.
arxiv-2511-10568: Nicolas Fayard, Marc Pirlot, and Alexis Tsoukiàs write on decision theory, proposing a new framework for judging capability sets, the sets of options truly open to a person. Building on the Capability Approach, their method weighs each person's preferences over how diverse the options are. A compromise procedure balances negative freedom, the absence of interference, against positive freedom, the real power to act. The evaluation thus captures both the intrinsic worth of having varied choices and their practical value.
arxiv-2511-10668:
Akbar Anbar Jafari, Cagri Ozcinar, and Gholamreza Anbarjafari build a mathematical framework for a question usually left to speculation. Could AI capability grow without bound in finite time, the so-called singularity, and how would anyone know? Their framework links capability growth to measurable resources such as compute, data, and energy.

Physical limits on power, bandwidth, and memory define a service envelope capping how fast improvement can happen at any moment. A growth model coupling capital to compute, data, and energy yields a critical boundary between runaway and subcritical regimes. It also gives decision rules that turn observable series, like facility power and training throughput, into certificates for either behavior. Case studies and practical controls, such as power caps and evaluation gates, round out the analysis.
arxiv-2511-10868:
Yashshi Pipalani and four co-authors introduce Go-UT-Bench, a dataset aimed at a training-data imbalance in code models. Most training corpora overflow with raw open-source code and starve broader engineering tasks, especially in lower-resource languages like Go, so models autocomplete well but stumble at chores like writing unit tests.

The benchmark pairs 5,264 code snippets with their unit tests, drawn from ten permissively licensed Go repositories across varied domains. The authors fine-tuned two families of models on it, mixture-of-experts and dense decoders alike. In both families, the fine-tuned models beat their base versions on more than three quarters of the benchmark tasks. The authors offer the dataset as a remedy for a neglected skill in an underserved language.
arxiv-2511-11068:
Pu-Zhao Kow, Janne Nurminen, and Jesse Railo study whether a Bayesian method can reliably recover an unknown trait from just one noisy measurement in a fractional Calderón problem. That problem asks what can be inferred about a material's inside from outside data, here in a fractional form that spreads influence widely. Priors must be chosen with care so the method does not fool itself.

Their main result shows that the posterior, the updated belief after data, piles up near the true value as readings grow. They also pin down tight rates for how fast the mean estimate's error shrinks. Sharp stability bounds for both directions of the problem drive the proof.
arxiv-2511-11168:
Hangyu Li, Bofeng Cao, and their colleagues release CATS-V2V, a real-world data set for cars that perceive the road together by sharing sensor data. Shared perception can help self-driving cars see around blocks, but harsh weather and lighting are exactly where help is needed most and where data are scarcest. Two time-synced cars collected the data across ten weather and lighting conditions at ten sites.

The set holds one hundred clips with lidar sweeps, multi-view camera images, and precise position records. Box labels mark objects in 3D in a time-consistent way, plus static scene labels for a bird's-eye build. A target-based alignment method keeps every object matched across sensors.
arxiv-2511-11268:
R G G Amorim, A F Santos, and their colleagues build a cosmology that drops relativity's speed limit and rests on Galilean symmetry instead. Their model lives on a five-dimensional Galilean space and carries a uniform, even metric much like the standard expanding-universe metric. Two solutions of its field equations anchor the study, one empty and one filled with dust-like matter.

When the model is reduced to normal spacetime, it naturally turns uneven in its expansion and density, in line with the near-flat space that Planck data suggest. In the flat case it reproduces Milne's Newtonian cosmology, since pressure vanishes there. The frame offers an independent nonrelativistic home for cosmic dynamics.
arxiv-2511-11568:
Nicolas Cerardi and eleven co-authors ask a big question in cosmology. How much can a future radio telescope teach us about the epoch of reionization? That was the era when the first stars lit up and ionized the gas between galaxies. Their probe is the 21-centimeter signal from neutral hydrogen.

Mock data for one hundred and one thousand hours of telescope time feed a learning based inference method. The method learns how likely each past neutral share is. Simple summaries, such as power spectra, are compared with richer ones. The richer set includes Betti numbers and the bispectrum. The comparison shows which summaries truly carry facts about the reionization past. That guides how real data from the array should be read.
arxiv-2511-11668:
Chase van de Geijn and three co-authors ask if traveling waves can encode position in a transformer. Attention itself ignores order. So positional encodings supply the sense of sequence. Some encodings mark absolute places. Others mark relative shifts between tokens.

Their method, RollPE, rolls the query and key tensors in a circle. This creates a traveling-wave phase shift. Attention then depends on gaps between positions, not fixed indices. Tests show RollPE clearly beats classic absolute sinusoidal embeddings. It also performs on par with rotary embeddings, the current favorite. A simple shift matching a complex standard is a useful result. Positional data may need less machinery than assumed.
arxiv-2511-11768:
Yu Zhang and Bing-Zhao Li design filter banks for signals on graphs that change in time. Sensor networks and video are the model cases. Each frame is a graph, and time links the frames. Classic graph filter banks must split the joint graph into bipartite pieces. That split loses edges from the graph.

An oversampled joint time-vertex Laplacian matrix fixes the split. It supports extensions that keep every time and space edge. Two-channel banks built on it give redundant, multi-scale forms. Graph coloring guides efficient versions of the method. Tests on graph signals and on image and video denoising show the payoff. Keeping the full joint structure intact is the point.
arxiv-2511-11868:
Dhiraj K. Singh demonstrates a way to read three-dimensional stress inside a transparent block from three directions at once. Photoelasticity turns stress into colored fringe patterns, but conventional setups mostly visualize flat, two-dimensional stress, leaving the full interior state out of reach.

A low-elasticity epoxy cube with no built-in prestress is imaged simultaneously along three orthogonal axes under one applied load, in both transmission and reflection. Fringe orders estimated from the three views lay the foundation for reconstructing the complete three-dimensional stress state. Sensitive low-stress measurement in three dimensions would serve biomechanics and dynamic force analysis, where loads are small, complex, and poorly served by flat methods.
arxiv-2511-11968:
Christopher J. McDevitt and Jonathan S. Arnaud compute how long energetic ions stay confined in a tokamak by solving the adjoint of the drift kinetic equation, a backward formulation that yields mean escape times directly. Fast ions heat the plasma, but orbit losses and collisions leak them, and their slow collisional clock sits far from their rapid transit clock, which defeats naive solvers.

A physics-informed neural network, carefully designed for that scale separation, learns the escape time across tokamak geometry, the first such use for this equation. Direct orbit loss and collisional transport both enter the predictions. Knowing where fast ions escape tells designers where walls will take the heat.
arxiv-2511-12368:
Yiqing Shen and Mathias Unberath present FastReasonSeg, a way to shrink reasoning segmentation models so they can run on edge devices. Reasoning segmentation cuts out objects named by implicit text queries, a core skill for autonomous agents. Existing methods need multimodal models with billions of parameters, far beyond typical edge hardware.

Standard distillation fails here because it copies outputs and features, not the multi-step reasoning the task requires. The authors instead distill through digital twin representations, which split perception from reasoning. Training first follows teacher examples built on those representations. The split makes the reasoning chain easier to transfer into a smaller, faster model.
arxiv-2511-12768:
Noah Hong and Tao Hong look for phase transitions inside a very small language model. In large models, new abilities seem to switch on abruptly past certain scales, and some researchers blame phase transitions for that emergence. The authors ask whether the same reorganizations happen in small models, whether they can be seen without log-scale plots, and whether they occur early in training. They train a small GPT-style transformer on character-level text and watch its vocabulary behavior evolve step by step.

Standard loss curves showed nothing special. Their probes, tracking word lengths, correct versus incorrect words, vocabulary diversity, and word-connection statistics, revealed a clear transition point early in training, as coherence emerged. They conclude that transition-like reorganizations are a general feature of language model training, not a privilege of scale. The interesting event was invisible to the field's default measurements.
arxiv-2511-13368:
Kajetan Dymkiewicz and 5 co-authors map how fine-tuning a language model on one task or language helps or hurts others. They run a controlled study with LoRA tuning across several open model families and sizes. Each model is tuned on a single source and then tested on every other task and language pair.

Transfer is sorted into cross-language, cross-task, and combined regimes. Overall gains were positive but strongly uneven: same-task transfer across languages worked best and most regularly, driven mainly by the target language. Some targets absorbed gains from many sources while others stayed isolated, forming a stable donor and recipient pattern that tuning plans should respect.
arxiv-2511-13468:
Jean Rodriguez and 7 co-authors unveil a microscopy method that images magnetic films buried under thick opaque metal. Standard magneto-optical Kerr imaging fails once light cannot reach the magnetic layer, as with films capped by electrodes. Their spin-accumulation approach triggers and reads the signal from the same open side.

Short-lived spin accumulations are created optically and travel through the covering metal, carrying magnetic contrast back to the detector. In copper the signal reached about sixty nanometers, far beyond the twelve-nanometer reach of light itself. Magnetic contrast stayed readable through caps hundreds of nanometers thick, opening buried-layer imaging for spintronics and related fields.
arxiv-2511-13868:
Pedro J. Miana connects two settings for Koopman semigroups, families of operators that track how functions evolve under a dynamical system. One setting uses functions on the positive real line, the other uses sequences. A Poisson transformation and its adjoint carry properties back and forth between the two worlds.

Miana presents two Koopman semigroups on the sequence side and links them to two standard semigroups on the function side, each shifting and damping its input in a set way. In the final section he introduces Cesàro-like averaging operators built from these semigroups. The paper is a piece of operator theory tying discrete and continuous descriptions of the same dynamics together.
arxiv-2511-14268:
Zhenchuan Ma, Qizhi Teng, Pengcheng Yan, and four co-authors rebuild the fine inner build of porous stuff with control over the stats. To guess how a stuff behaves, engineers need its micro build, but often have few samples to learn from. The team's frame sums up the build by how local patterns are spread. It then draws new spreads that meet set target traits.

A neural net maps the input spread to the target spread of local patterns. A sliced distance rule, named for Wasserstein, plus slope-based tuning keeps the new build true to the target. The method works with small sample sets and can make large three-dimensional builds for tests of how build links to traits.
arxiv-2511-14368:
Rishi Gupta, Mukilan Karuppasamy, Shyam Marjit, and two co-authors teach vision-language models to understand hand-drawn sketches. Big models handle photos well but stumble on sketches, the quick abstract drawings people use for ideas words capture badly. The authors blame a missing training resource: no large data set jointly linked sketches, realistic images, and language instructions.

They built such a triplet data set, adding a generated SketchVCL collection to existing sketch corpora, and trained their model O3SLM on it. Across localization, counting, sketch-based retrieval, and visual question answering, O3SLM set new state-of-the-art results and substantially outperformed existing large vision-language models on sketch comprehension and reasoning.
arxiv-2511-14568:
Dae San Kim and Taekyun Kim redefine probabilistic Stirling numbers linked to a random variable. Stirling numbers count partitions and permutations, and recent work added a probabilistic version based on moments. The earlier definitions failed to satisfy key orthogonality and inverse relations. Those relations are central to how the two kinds of numbers interact.

The authors define the first kind through the cumulant generating function in a corrected way. With that fix, both kinds satisfy the crucial relations again. They also study degenerate counterparts of both kinds. Explicit formulas are computed for the numbers. The paper restores a clean algebraic structure for later combinatorial use.
arxiv-2511-14668:
Neeti Gauniyal and Victor Turchin write down explicit counting formulas for invariants of knots in high dimensions. Classical knot invariants were famously expressed through Gauss diagrams, which record how a projected knot crosses itself. The authors carry that idea to smooth embeddings of odd-dimensional spheres into spaces of roughly triple the dimension.

They project the embedded spheres onto a flat hyperplane and study the double and singular points that appear. From those patterns they build formulas in the style of Goussarov, Polyak, and Viro. One formula captures the Haefliger invariant, which fully sorts a key family of high-dimensional knots up to deformation. A side result links braid spaces with spaces of long links.
arxiv-2511-14768:
Bhavika Jain, Robert Pitsko, and two co-authors propose a social media recommender that watches how users feel, not just what they click. Most feeds chase clicks, watch time, and scrolling, even though steady exposure to charged content can wear down well-being. Their framework, ESMR, tracks each user's emotional path over time.

A transformer model predicts the user's emotional state from recent activity. When the state stays stable, a fast gradient-boosted model picks content for engagement. When negative states persist, a reinforcement learning agent with causally informed rewards takes over. Tests over thirty days of interaction history check whether the switch can protect mood without killing engagement.
arxiv-2511-15168:
Nguyen-Khang Le and seven co-authors train language models to generate Selenium test scripts for web form interaction. Automated browser testing validates modern web applications, and form handling is a core part. Scripts must be syntactically correct, executable, and cover many input fields. No public benchmark existed for this language model task.

The team curate synthetic and human annotated data sets covering diverse real forms. Metrics track syntax correctness, executability, and field coverage. Their training method produces higher quality form test cases in the Selenium framework. Empirical results are reported across testing scenarios. The work opens a practical path to language model assisted quality assurance for web software.
arxiv-2511-15268:
Mohammad Mortezaei Nobahari shows that flashing circularly polarized light on a single layer of molybdenum disulfide can flip its topological phase. The monolayer, in its distorted 1T-prime form, normally sits in a quantum spin Hall state, conducting along its edges while the interior insulates. A fast oscillating light field, too rapid for the electrons to follow directly, reshapes the energy bands instead.

Using a low-energy model with a standard high-frequency expansion, the author maps how the drive shifts band inversion conditions and Berry curvature. As the light strength and field parameters vary, the layer steps through a sequence of phases, including spin-polarized quantum Hall and valley Hall states, each marked by clean gap closings. Light thus becomes a knob for topology in a sheet one atom thick.
arxiv-2511-15368:
B. Martínez-Haya, N. Morillo, and A. Cuetos predict what shapes emerge when disk-shaped particles stick together. Flat molecules and colloids clump in ways that set a material's internal order: they can stack face to face like coins or percolate edge to edge like a net. Which pattern wins depends on the directions their attractions favor.

Using a flexible coarse-grained model of pair interactions between disks, the authors run Monte Carlo and Brownian dynamics simulations across tuned settings. The disks spontaneously nucleate into clusters with globular, planar, or stacked forms, each with its own internal order. A general map from interaction tuning to aggregate shape helps designers aim soft materials at chosen structures.
arxiv-2511-15668:
Bartosz Bieganowski and Daniel Strzelecki study whether a nonlinear scalar field equation with a critical Hardy potential has solutions. The Hardy potential is a singular attraction toward one point, taken here at its strongest borderline strength. The field equation balances spreading, that singular pull, and a nonlinear self-response of general subcritical type, posed on all of space except the origin in three or more dimensions.

Because the natural energy is defined on a nonstandard function space, they use variational methods in that completed space. They find a nontrivial solution that respects a key scaling constraint and minimizes the energy there. When the nonlinearity is odd, symmetric under sign change, they also prove a solution that is not radial.
arxiv-2511-15868:
Julio Guillen-Garcia, Manuel Fernández, and Roberto Gallardo-Cava generalize the eigenvalue interlacing theorem to pseudo-similarity changes. The classic theorem says eigenvalues of a squeezed Hermitian matrix interlace those of the original when compression uses unitary columns. Their note replaces that product with one built from a general matrix and its Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. The generalized product behaves quite differently.

Unlike the classic case, the new product need not be Hermitian. It deflates the count of nonzero eigenvalues, but not necessarily the dimension. Interlacing still holds under this broader building. The result widens a foundational matrix theory tool used across signal processing and numerical analysis. It clarifies which parts of interlacing depend on unitarity and which survive without it.
arxiv-2511-16268:
Erwan Dereure and four co-authors build an automated pipeline for finding and sorting alpha-synuclein aggregates in microscope images of midbrain tissue. These clumps, which form Lewy bodies and neurites, are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease, but mapping them across whole slides by hand is slow and labels vary between staining runs.

The method pairs weakly supervised segmentation with a ResNet50 classifier, so it needs few hand labels and tolerates staining differences. On tissue from Parkinson's and incidental Lewy body cases it told Lewy bodies from neurites with a balanced accuracy of about 80 percent. The tool opens the way to large studies of where aggregates sit and how they relate to nearby cells.
arxiv-2511-16468:
Akshit Pramod Anchan, Ameiy Acharya, and Leki Chom Thungon use graph neural networks to optimize quantum key distribution networks. These networks share encryption keys through quantum links and must stay secure against future quantum computers. These networks are hard to run well: conditions change, several goals compete, and resources are scarce.

The framework represents the network as a dynamic graph carrying both topology and quantum-specific link features, and learns how to route and allocate resources from that structure. In experiments the optimized network raised the total key rate from about 27 to 470 kilobits per second and slightly lowered the quantum bit error rate. The gain came at a small cost in average transmission distance. Tests across networks from 10 to 250 nodes show the gains are strongest at medium sizes.
arxiv-2511-16668:
Yang Luo and nine co-authors introduce V-ReasonBench, a benchmark suite for measuring reasoning in video generation models, whose zero-shot reasoning feats have outrun the tools for checking them. The suite tests four dimensions: structured problem-solving, spatial cognition, pattern-based inference, and physical dynamics.

Tasks are built from synthetic and real image sets and are designed to be answer-verifiable, reproducible, scalable, and unambiguous. Six leading video models show clear dimension-by-dimension differences rather than a single pecking order. The authors also compare video models with strong image models, catalogue hallucination habits, and examine how clip duration affects chain-of-frames reasoning. The benchmark aims to push video models toward reasoning that is reliable and aligned with human judgment.
arxiv-2511-16868:
Aryan Tajmir Riahi and Khanh Dao Duc extend the Gromov-Wasserstein distance, a powerful way to compare shapes and distributions living in different metric spaces. They extend it from matching two objects to matching whole collections at once. Many real problems, from shape collections to molecular complexes, need multiple-to-one or multiple-to-multiple correspondences that the pairwise tool cannot express.

Their Joint Gromov-Wasserstein objective supplies a non-negative dissimilarity that detects partial isomorphism between collections of metric measure spaces, with convergence guarantees under point sampling. It can be computed by adapting standard optimal transport algorithms, including entropic regularization. Benchmarks against partial matching variants show better accuracy and speed, and experiments on synthetic and real data, from geometric shapes to biomolecular complexes, confirm the method's reach.
arxiv-2511-16968:
Joseph McDonald studies a logical operation called the Sasaki hook inside a family of structures known as quantum cylindric algebras. To do this, he defines a new kind of structure, the cylindric quasi-implication algebra, built around that operation. The note sits in quantum logic, where algebra is used to model reasoning about quantum systems.

McDonald shows the two kinds of structure match exactly: each quantum cylindric algebra can be turned into one of the new algebras, and each new algebra gives back a quantum cylindric algebra. He then builds a geometric frame from one of these algebras in two different ways, extending earlier work on completions. Readers gain a cleaner algebraic handle on this corner of quantum logic.
arxiv-2511-17168:
Hui Liu and Tinggui Zhang study quantum batteries, small quantum systems that store and release energy, focusing on how much charge they can hold while exposed to noise. Their test systems are three-part GHZ states and near relatives, prized entangled states in quantum information. The noise comes from standard Markovian channels, which model environments that steadily degrade quantum states without memory of the past.

Different channels damage capacity differently. Under depolarizing and bit-phase flip noise, capacity can die suddenly after holding briefly; under dephasing it fades to a frozen, constant level. For amplitude damping applied to one part, the GHZ state's capacity falls steadily. Repeating the noise speeds the freezing. The analysis maps which environments a practical quantum battery could tolerate.
arxiv-2511-17268:
L. Correia and 11 co-authors chart the glow of six very nearby galaxies across a poorly observed stretch of the spectrum, from far-infrared to cm wavelengths. In that range a galaxy's emission mixes thermal dust, free-free radiation, synchrotron radiation, and possibly anomalous microwave emission peaking near 1 cm. The team combined four all-sky surveys, matched to a common resolution, covering 18 bands.

Their sample holds the brightest nearby systems, including the Magellanic Clouds and the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies, with Milky Way foregrounds subtracted. A five-component model fits each galaxy's energy distribution well, though the components blur into one another. It was not clearly detected in any galaxy, with weak upper limits, suggesting the signal dilutes at whole-galaxy scales. The study also infers cosmic microwave background ripples behind most of the sample.
arxiv-2511-17368:
Eric L. Melin and four co-authors study self-admitted technical debt in scientific software: the comments where developers confess that code falls short. Scientific codes evolve fast and collaboratively, and hidden debt in them can undermine the accuracy and reproducibility of the research built on top. The team compared debt in 27 scientific and general-purpose open-source repositories, and fine-tuned ten transformer models on some 67,000 labeled code comments to detect such admissions automatically.

Scientific software carried about nine times more scientific debt, and roughly five times more admitted debt overall, than general-purpose software. The authors attribute the gap to complex computations, domain constraints, and shifting research needs. Their best model beat existing detectors at finding the admissions. The study argues that managing this debt is part of protecting scientific validity itself.
arxiv-2511-17768:
Nazir Khan, Rahul Jangid, Taras Stanislavchuk, and six co-authors demonstrate control over the twist of soft X-ray beams using a sequence of patterned optical elements. A beam can carry orbital angular momentum, a kind of rotation tied to its spiral phase, in addition to ordinary polarization spin.

Passing the beam through fork shaped gratings one after another adds their twists, and that twist stays separate from the spin part. Working in the X-ray range opens direct ways to measure such beams from large light sources. It also opens ways to use them in scattering studies, without relying on indirect phase methods.
arxiv-2511-18068:
Si-Hong Liu, Ying-Xin Lai, and Di Wang give a full topological analysis of non leptonic decays of doubly charmed baryons. These are heavy particles containing two charm quarks. Such a baryon was first observed by a collider experiment in a specific decay, and searches for its relatives continue, but no organized breakdown of their decays existed.

Working in a flavor symmetry limit, they present the tree and penguin topological diagrams for two families of decays. They also derive linear links between topological amplitudes and symmetry based irreducible amplitudes. They analyze the size pattern of the diagrams using rescattering dynamics and a large color expansion, and derive links that test a classic theorem in the isospin limit.
arxiv-2511-18168:
Chamini Pathiraja, Deniz Wong, Christian Schulz, and three co-authors measure the low energy electron structure of two vanadium halides. These layered materials interest researchers in two dimensional magnetism and spintronics, and their ground states were poorly known from tests. They use high resolution resonant inelastic X-ray scattering together with ligand field multiplet calculations.

The spectra reveal distinct signals that pin down crystal field splitting, trigonal distortion, and related settings. Bond sharing grows from the bromide to the iodide, and the trigonal distortion has opposite signs in the two compounds, matching elongation in one and compression in the other. The math gives a high spin ground state for the vanadium ion in both, with different orbital fillings.
arxiv-2511-18468:
Md Akil Raihan Iftee and seven co-authors adapt vision models to new domains as they stream in, with no source data kept. A field model meets a string of shifts — new light, new place, new weather — and must adjust on the fly. Past methods lean on source data or marks, and slow shifts let errors pile up before the fix lands.

SloMo-Fast pairs two teachers. A slow teacher forgets at a crawl and holds long term know how from past domains. A fast teacher adapts at once to the live domain. The pupil learns from both, so it stays robust yet quick. The source free design fits private and low resource use. Tests target long runs of shifts.
arxiv-2511-18568:
Charalampos Katsis, Imtiaz Karim, and Elisa Bertino survey zero trust security for open cellular networks.
