New generations open the radio access network to apps from many sources that steer traffic in real time. That open, software driven design breaks the old closed model where inside parts were trusted by default.

Zero trust drops that default: each request must prove itself, each time. The survey lays out the core principles, then the hard parts of fitting them to Open RAN — split vendors, fast control loops, and edge compute. Open research paths close the review. The piece maps how a strict verify always stance can guard networks that now run like cloud software.
arxiv-2511-18968:
Bhuvan Sachdeva and ten co-authors build a system to catch complications during cataract surgery as they happen. Cataract operations are among the most common in the world, yet events such as iris prolapse, rupture of the posterior capsule, and vitreous loss remain major causes of poor outcomes. Their framework, CataractCompDetect, combines awareness of the surgical phase, tracking based on a segmentation model, risk scores tuned per complication, and vision-language reasoning for the final call.

To test it, the team curated the first video data set annotated for such complications, covering fifty-three surgeries, of which twenty-three had clinical complications. The system scores unevenly by event type, strongest on iris prolapse. An automatic early warning of this kind could also give trainee surgeons objective feedback after the fact.
arxiv-2511-19268:
Dewei Zhou and seven co-authors improve conditional image generation, where a model must follow both a text prompt and a guiding image or layout. Conflicts arise when the guide clashes with the text, or when the model's own biases break alignment even when inputs agree. Standard fine-tuning handles such tangles poorly.

Their method, BideDPO, builds two separate preference pairs, one teaching respect for the condition and one for the text, so the training signals stop interfering. An adaptive rule balances the two losses. An automated pipeline creates conflict-aware training data from model outputs, and repeated rounds refine both the data and the model.
arxiv-2511-19568:
Sunder Ram Krishnan and five co-authors estimate wireless coverage in cellular networks far faster than plain simulation. Stochastic geometry models these networks well, but Monte Carlo runs converge slowly because interference from the endless far field keeps fluctuating. Their estimator removes part of that randomness analytically.

The field is split into a few dominant nearby interferers, sampled exactly, and an infinite tail handled through a conditional Laplace formula. The resulting Rao-Blackwellized estimator is unbiased at any cutoff, with bias shrinking at a proved rate. In a high-reliability test, variance falls by about ninetyfold, cutting the needed simulation runs by nearly ninety-nine percent.
arxiv-2511-19968:
V Galkin and O Pochinka study which four-dimensional spaces can carry a non-singular flow whose saddle orbits all share one Morse index. Regular flows on closed manifolds have finitely many rest points and periodic orbits, and they admit a Morse-Bott function that drops outside the recurrent set. Such links between a flow and its carrying space run through the whole study.

For non-singular flows, a formula of Poincaré and Hopf forces the Euler characteristic to vanish, which settles the question in most dimensions. In dimension four, a saddle orbit can only have index one or two. The authors prove that if all saddle orbits share the same index, the space must be a direct or twisted product of the three-sphere and the circle.
arxiv-2511-21168:
The Ginzburg-Landau equation, born in 1950s superconductivity theory, now models nonlinear optics and other wave systems, and solving it accurately is a numerical challenge. Xianxian Cao, Zhen Guan, and Junjun Wang propose in 2025 an implicit Crank-Nicolson scheme in the discontinuous Galerkin family for it, pairing time-centred steps with polynomial pieces. The paper's core is a proof technique: they pin down a bound on the numerical solution, then handle the cubic nonlinear term with careful estimates.

From that route they prove the scheme always has one solution and delivers unconditionally optimal error bounds, in both the plain error norm and the energy norm, for any step size. Two numerical examples back the theory and confirm the second-order accuracy in time. Earlier schemes earned such guarantees only after linearising; this one does not. The authors offer the boundedness-first technique as reusable for other nonlinear wave equations.
arxiv-2511-21468:
M. Alemany-Gotor, C. Viglione, P. Fosalba, and I. Tutusaus run a controlled experiment on cosmologists themselves, in 2025. Stage-IV galaxy surveys will test gravity across the universe, but analysts usually assume Einstein's general relativity when fitting data. If gravity follows a modified rule instead, that assumption could quietly corrupt every inferred parameter. The team built twin full-sky mock universes, one relativistic and one with Hu-Sawicki f(R) gravity.

Both mocks were populated with galaxies by a halo occupation method tuned to Sloan survey data. Alemany-Gotor and her coauthors then ran the standard 3x2pt analysis, combining galaxy clustering with two kinds of weak lensing, on the modified-gravity mock while pretending relativity held. Even with cautious scale cuts, the recovered cosmological parameters came out very significantly biased. The warning for real surveys is direct: test gravity inside the fit, not after it.
arxiv-2511-21568:
Minjoon Choi tests whether language models actually understand questions or merely recognize their wording, in 2025. Models often answer a question correctly yet fail its paraphrase, betraying reliance on surface patterns. Choi built RoParQ, a benchmark of closed-book multiple-choice questions rephrased by proprietary models, keeping only items that made a judge model's confidence wobble. A new metric, XParaCon, scores robustness as the spread of accuracies across a question's variants.

Choi also proposes a cure: reasoning-based, paraphrase-aware fine-tuning that teaches semantic invariance, answering from meaning rather than phrasing. The alignment worked broadly, and on Llama-3.1-8B the consistency score climbed from 2.186 to 2.629 with the treatment. Fine-tuned lightweight models reached consistency rivaling much larger pre-trained models, showing robustness can be taught rather than merely bought with scale. Code for the benchmark and method is released publicly, inviting the field to grade models on meaning.
arxiv-2511-21668:
Shruti Bothe and five Ericsson colleagues ask whether every training example deserves equal effort, through a telecom lens, in 2025. Telecom AI, from radio access networks to user experience management, trains on noisy, high-dimensional data that is costly to store, process, and label. Standard workflows assume all samples count equally, an assumption imported from cleaner domains and expensive in energy and compute.

The team analyzes sample-level gradients across training epochs to expose patterns of influence and redundancy, then builds a sample importance framework that prioritizes impactful data. On three real-world telecom datasets, selective training preserved model performance on far less data and compute. The authors present the study as the first of its kind for telecommunications, whose tabular, time-ordered data, seasonal rhythms, and sudden anomalies make blanket training especially wasteful. The model-agnostic strategy advances sustainable AI where it is operationally needed most.
arxiv-2511-21768:
I. Cherkaoui and three coauthors fuse category theory, post-quantum cryptography, and zero-trust design into one security framework for AI models, in 2025. Quantum computers threaten today's encryption, while AI services need access control that never trusts by default. It models cryptographic workflows as morphisms in category theory, and trust policies as functors, yielding formal security proofs.

The authors test the design on an ESP32 microcontroller using lattice-based post-quantum primitives. Memory stayed comfortable: after cryptographic operations the agent sat at 91.86 percent and the broker at 97.88 percent of free heap. The system rejected 100 percent of unauthorized access attempts while answering in under a millisecond on average. Lattice encryption took about 10.97 milliseconds, decryption 2.89 milliseconds, small next to network delays. Power draw held a 300-milliwatt baseline, peaking near 479 milliwatts, consistent with quantum-resistant zero trust running at the edge.
arxiv-2511-22068:
Dou, Zhou, and Chen, physicists, propose a way to create switchable dissipative coupling between magnons. The quantized spin waves of magnetic materials, as a building block for magnon-based Ising machines that solve hard combinatorial optimization problems. Ising machines need interactions that can be flipped between ferromagnetic-like and antiferromagnetic-like on demand. Here the coupling is engineered through a three-body interaction linking a photon, a phonon, and the magnons themselves.

Two collective dissipation channels, carried by open conducting wires, are modulated by a nonlinear mechanical pump. Simply tuning the pump's phase switches which channel is active and hence the sign of the effective Ising interaction. Numerical simulations with two coupled magnon modes confirm both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic dissipative couplings, show switching works mid-evolution. Demonstrate robustness even against a strong uncontrollable contribution to the dissipation, which stronger engineered dissipation can compensate.
arxiv-2511-22268:
Chekhlov, Danchev, and Keef, algebraists, classify abelian groups with a self-map rigidity property. A group is co-Hopfian if every injective endomorphism is surjective; the strongly co-Hopfian variants studied here strengthen that requirement uniformly. Generalizing results of Abdelalim, the authors prove any strongly co-Hopfian group splits as a direct sum of an sp-group and a divisible group. Both are strongly co-Hopfian themselves, giving the class a structural description rather than a definition.

Mixed groups resist simple reduction: a group whose torsion part and torsion-free quotient are both strongly co-Hopfian is again strongly co-Hopfian. The converse fails in general, and counterexamples show mixed examples are complicated. A group is uniformly strongly co-Hopfian exactly when its maximal torsion subgroup is. The paper also gives examples showing genuinely mixed groups need not inherit the property from their parts in the reverse direction.
arxiv-2511-22468:
Viterbo and Buck introduce Odisseo, a simulation code for the gravity of star systems that can also compute gradients. Stellar streams, thin trails of stars torn from small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, trace the galaxy's gravitational field and dark matter, but using them needs fast, flexible modelling. Established N-body codes are accurate yet cannot provide derivatives, while differentiable stream models approximate the dynamics. Odisseo does the full N-body calculation in JAX, gaining automatic differentiation plus GPU acceleration.

As a demonstration, the authors simulate a mock GD-1 stream. By gradient descent they recover four parameters: the parent's accretion time and mass, and the masses of the Milky Way's dark halo and disk. Recovered values and stream shape matched the true inputs, and the code scales almost linearly across several GPUs. The authors note the direct force calculation limits them to below about a million particles.
arxiv-2511-22568:
Pustyntsev, Ramasamy, and Vanderhaeghen propose hunting light particles with a polarised positron beam. The target is the beam normal spin asymmetry in Bhabha scattering, positrons scattering off electrons in a fixed target. The setting is Jefferson Lab's polarised positron program with an 11 gigaelectronvolt beam, as planned. The asymmetry is sensitive to hypothetical mediators, scalar, vector, or axial-vector, that might connect ordinary matter to a dark sector in the megaelectronvolt-to-gigaelectronvolt mass range.

The observable has a prized feature: the Standard Model contribution crosses zero at one scattering angle, creating a background-free point where any measured asymmetry would signal new physics. Projected bounds for the three mediator types show scalar and vector scenarios extending search reach beyond existing constraints. The help comes because mediators can flip lepton helicity, which quantum electrodynamics strongly suppresses. Polarisation observables thus offer a route alongside bump hunts and missing-energy searches.
arxiv-2511-23368:
O'Grady re-examines the star HV 11417, a candidate Thorne-Żytkow object, meaning a red supergiant whose core is a neutron star. Using the sharper proper motions of the Gaia DR3 catalog. Earlier DR2 data had left open whether the star truly belongs to the Small Magellanic Cloud or is a foreground interloper. Which would make it far too dim for the exotic interpretation, and the new data settle its membership.

The star is very likely a genuine Cloud member, and relative to its local environment it moves at a transverse velocity of about 52 kilometers per second. Give or take 15 in measurement uncertainty, above the 30 kilometer-per-second threshold for a runaway star. That speed shows the system suffered a disruptive kick sometime in its past. But O'Grady cautions it does not prove the Thorne-Żytkow nature, since runaways are common among massive evolved stars.
arxiv-2512-00068:
Turbulence is the chaotic swirling motion seen in fast-moving fluids, from air over a wing to water in a pipe. Marcial Sanchis-Agudo and Ricardo Vinuesa offer a geometric foundation for its universal laws in a 2025 study. They ask where the small dissipative structures of turbulence come from.

Their framework treats tiny fluid parcels as random tracers whose paths carry some uncertainty. From that picture, the viscous term of the Navier-Stokes equations appears as a natural smoothing operator tied to microscopic diffusion. If the approach holds, it links everyday fluid equations to deeper variational principles and may guide new models of turbulent flow.
arxiv-2512-00168:
Deep neural networks show crackling, avalanche-like activity whose origin has lacked a clear explanation. Arsham Ghavasieh develops a stochastic theory of information propagation in such networks in a 2025 study. The theory builds in fluctuations at the level of the central limit theorem.

Four effective couplings characterize the dynamics, leading to a Landau-style description of the static exponents. The activity cascades take a directed percolation structure, a pattern known from statistical physics. Ghavasieh argues this framing can tune universality in network behavior, linking machine learning to ideas long used for phase transitions in physical systems. Avalanche language comes from physics, where crackling systems share the same mathematics. The work speaks to two crowds at once. Folks who build these nets, and folks who study how crowds of small parts act when they link up.
arxiv-2512-00268:
Teams of autonomous agents often need to agree on a shared solution while talking only to neighbors. Hong Wang studies decentralized optimization with explicit consensus penalties in 2025. Classical decentralized gradient descent is appealing for its minimal state, yet it fails to reach exact agreement with fixed step sizes.

Usual fixes add trackers or dual variables, which complicate each agent. Wang explores penalty terms that enforce consensus directly while keeping the method lean. Exact agreement matters in sensor networks and robot swarms, where a nearly shared answer can still mean inconsistent actions across the team. Exactness matters most at the end of optimization, when small disagreements become visible errors.
arxiv-2512-00468:
Radio waves bounce off building walls in messy patterns that network planners must predict. Tongjia Zhang and co-authors measure diffuse scattering from three typical building surfaces in 2025, at three frequencies including two in the new FR3 range. They also analyze the mechanisms behind the scattering.

The team proposes a three-dimensional measurement procedure that captures the full spatial character of the scattering. Its accuracy gains were verified with measurements at the highest frequency studied. Better scattering models improve coverage predictions for next-generation wireless networks, where walls are part of the channel, not just obstacles. Millimeter-wave and mid-band frequencies scatter differently, so measuring all three anchors the model. For folks who plan the next wave of cell sites, the gain is fewer blind spots. They can say how walls bend the waves long past the line of sight.
arxiv-2512-00568:
Zero cycles are formal combinations of points on an algebraic variety, and their equivalence classes form the Chow group. Alejandro De Las Peñas Castaño studies zero cycles on products of two elliptic curves over local fields in 2025. The curves have good supersingular reduction.

For such a product over a p-adic field, the author produces infinitely many rational equivalences in the Chow group. The construction uses genus two covers of the two elliptic curves. Chow groups encode deep arithmetic information, and explicit infinite families are rare enough to be valuable in themselves. Supersingular reduction is the extreme case, where the elliptic curve's arithmetic is most rigid. Genus two covers provide the extra room the construction needs.
arxiv-2512-00668:
Two-sample tests ask whether two groups come from the same distribution, and permutation tests answer by shuffling labels. Jungwoo Ho studies a restricted block permutation scheme for such testing in 2025. Permutations are limited to single cross-swaps between block-selected representatives.

The analysis yields three main results, beginning with an exact validity construction that applies to any fixed restricted permutation set. Restricting permutations slashes computation, which matters for huge modern datasets. Proving validity anyway keeps the statistical guarantee intact, so speed does not come at the price of untrustworthy p-values. Blocks keep related observations together, respecting structure that naive shuffling would destroy. Exact validity means the test's error rates are what they claim to be.
arxiv-2512-00968:
Ziyang Zeng and a large team improve search ranking at Xiaohongshu in a 2025 paper. Search engines must rank items by relevance to a user query. Traditional relevance models output a single score or a direct label. That limits how much reasoning they can show and how complex signals they can use.

Their generative ranking approach produces richer outputs, and reinforcement learning optimizes the relevance it achieves. Generative models can weigh many signals and explain their picks in words. Reinforcement learning then tunes them toward rankings users judge relevant. Better ranking relevance means users find what they meant faster, a core gain for a large social search platform.
arxiv-2512-01268:
Jongwon Sohn, Juhyeon Moon, Hyunjoon Jung, and Jaewook Nam present ViscNet in a 2025 engineering paper. Viscosity, how thick a fluid is, must be measured for process monitoring and for autonomous laboratories. Conventional viscometers are invasive: they must touch the fluid and need controlled lab conditions unlike real process settings.

ViscNet is a vision-based viscometer that works in line, inside the process. It watches a fixed background pattern through the fluid's surface. Mixing deforms that surface, and refraction distorts the pattern in ways tied to viscosity. Reading thickness from a camera could let mixing processes self-monitor continuously without probes.
arxiv-2512-01368:
Klaus Thomsen gives a new proof of a classic result on sofic shifts. A sofic shift is a set of symbol strings made by a labeled graph. Its future cover is a canonical graph built from what can follow each past. Krieger showed that cover is canonical.

Thomsen proves that claim by a fresh path. He also shows how to make new canonical covers from a given one. The new covers link to the future cover but tend to differ from it. Extra covers give scholars more tools to sort and compare symbol systems.
arxiv-2512-01468:
Ya-Wen Pan, Ming-Zhu Liu, and Li-Sheng Geng probe three-body forces in hadron systems. Such forces act when three particles meet at once. They are widely used in nuclear work. Whether they are truly needed is still hotly debated.

The trio focus on three-hadron systems with set charge parity. For those systems, they argue the need for a three-body force is certain. Charge parity here acts as a strict filter. A firm case in one class of systems would settle part of the debate. It would guide how nuclear forces are built from now on.
arxiv-2512-01568:
Sandro Andric asks if language models act on the values they claim. He tests whether their gut links and stated views predict real altruistic acts. Two dozen frontier models faced three test types drawn from human psychology. One test gauged implicit links to altruism.

Other tests asked the models to report their own views. A third set watched what the models did in choice tasks. Gaps between talk and acts would warn users not to trust stated values alone. The work gives a template for checks of model character. The three-way gap test can be reused for other traits like honesty or care, giving labs a shared audit for model character claims.
arxiv-2512-01768:
Ruiqi Bao and co-authors propose hybrid skin-topological states in exciton polariton lattices. The non-Hermitian skin effect piles bulk states at edges. That piling breaks the usual bulk-boundary rules. Polaritons mix light and matter, which makes them a rich test bed.

Their honeycomb lattice adds sublattice-dependent gain and loss. That non-Hermiticity couples to built-in topological edge modes. Edge modes then relocate in new ways. Hybrid states could yield light tools whose edge flow is both protected and tunable by gain settings. Gain and loss are tunable in polariton systems by pump shape, so the hybrid states can be dialed in during an experiment, not just predicted.
arxiv-2512-01968:
Cubic fourfolds are shapes cut out by a cubic equation in higher-dimensional space, and sorting them into families is a subtle art. Simone Billi and Lucas Li Bassi study in 2025 when two such shapes count as the same under a relation called L-equivalence, a weakening of being truly identical.

They prove that for very general cubic fourfolds, L-equivalence forces the shapes to be isomorphic after all, genuinely the same. Yet special examples exist that are L-equivalent without being isomorphic, so the relation is not empty of surprises. In special families tied to Hassett divisors, L-equivalence also implies the shapes are Fourier-Mukai partners, a deep kinship between their geometries.
arxiv-2512-02068:
Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, oscillating between types in a rhythm set by quantum mechanics. Bipin Singh Koranga, Parnav Kumar, and Baktiar Wasir Farooq ask in 2025 whether faint corrections from quantum gravity would leave a fingerprint in the entanglement carried by two-flavor neutrino oscillations.

They track the entanglement with the von Neumann entropy, a standard measure of quantum correlation, across successive oscillation cycles. The gravity-inspired changes enter through the neutrinos' dispersion relation, suppressed by the Planck scale and therefore tiny. Even so, the study shows how entanglement measures could, in principle, register effects far beyond direct experimental reach.
arxiv-2512-02268:
Emulating the climate with generative models promises fast forecasts at many scales, but earlier methods crawl forward weather-step by weather-step, too slow for century horizons. Jeremy Irvin and a large Stanford team present in 2025 a spatiotemporal pyramid flow matching approach built for climate emulation.

Autoregression at weather scale is inherently slow over long horizons and has yet to stay stable when the forcing driving the climate keeps changing. Flow matching sidesteps stepwise generation by learning the whole evolution at once, across a pyramid of scales. Stable, fast emulation under shifting conditions would sharpen long-range climate projections used in planning.
arxiv-2512-02568:
Matteo Capoferri and Matthias Täufer study waves in materials made of stiff matter dotted with soft balls. The soft spherical inclusions have random sizes, scattered through the stiff matrix. Operators of this kind model composite materials with strong contrast between their parts.

The pair examines the spectrum of these operators, the set of allowed vibration patterns and energies. Random high contrast media also arise in stochastic homogenization, which replaces fine detail with average behavior. Understanding when waves stay trapped, called Anderson localization, helps predict how real composites carry sound, heat, or light. The same math can guide the design of foams and gels built to block sound or shake in a planned way.
arxiv-2512-03068:
Bias inside AI systems can lead to real harm. Nicoleta Tantalaki, Sophia Vei, and Athena Vakali wrote this 2025 study on that risk. AI tools now help make choices in key fields, yet bias can enter at many stages of their life cycle.

The authors note that past work often lists bias and harm apart. Their plan links each type of bias to the harm it may cause, using both human judgment and large language models. That link could help teams spot risks early. It also gives builders a clearer map for checks before a tool goes live. For policy teams, linked bias and harm maps could shape safer rules for AI use.
arxiv-2512-03168:
Galaxies near us drift in a shared flow. Richard Watkins and Hume Feldman ask where that bulk flow comes from in this 2025 work. They use the CosmicFlows-4 catalog, a large list of galaxy motions.

The authors split the flow into parts made inside a set volume and parts from structures beyond it. That split shows how much of the drift is local and how much is pulled by distant mass. The answer tests models of cosmic structure. It also helps map dark matter that cannot be seen directly. Peculiar motions are direct signs of gravity at work, so their sources matter greatly.
arxiv-2512-03268:
A note in pure math extends old results to a wider setting. J. Beckmann generalizes work by Magnar Dale in this 2025 paper. Dale studied secant varieties of curves and proved facts using Terracini's lemma.

Beckmann shows that nearly all of Dale's proofs carry over to embedded joins of varieties. Joins are a broader construction that includes secants as a special case. As an application, he computes the degree of a canonical map between joins. Such extensions let one proof serve many cases in algebraic geometry. Join results unify older theorems, showing they were shadows of one broader fact.
arxiv-2512-03568:
Usability walkthroughs are useful but costly to run with people. Ruican Zhong, David McDonald, and Gary Hsieh test whether language models can simulate them in this 2025 work. A cognitive walkthrough steps through an interface as a new user would.

The authors compared walkthroughs by GPT-4 and Gemini against human participants. They asked how closely model performance aligns with human behavior in the task. Synthetic walkthroughs could give design teams cheap early feedback. They would not replace human testing, but could triage issues sooner. Alignment with human walkthroughs is the test, since a synthetic user must stumble where people stumble, not where models find code paths.
arxiv-2512-04168:
Did the early universe pass through a violent electroweak transition, and could two very different instruments hear its echo? Sahabub Jahedi, Indrajit Saha, and Abhik Sarkar explore that question in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Their setting is the Standard Model effective field theory, where extra dimension-six operators can reshape the Higgs potential and drive a first-order transition.

Such a transition leaves two fingerprints. It would produce gravitational waves, and it would alter Higgs pair production at colliders. The authors count the relevant operators: three modify the Higgs potential at tree level, one more at loop level, and all feed double-Higgs production. Current LHC runs suppress that channel, so they target the high-luminosity and high-energy upgrades for better reach. Their correlation analysis stresses complementarity: gravitational wave observatories and collider searches probe the same physics, and each sharpens the other.
arxiv-2512-04768:
Molla Basir Aahmed and Partha Pratim Roy refine the Bohr-Rogosinski inequality for bounded analytic functions on the unit disk. The classical Bohr inequality says the tail of a power series stays controlled inside a small disk, a gem of complex analysis. Rogosinski's version compares partial sums against the whole function. Their 2025 arXiv paper improves that comparison for the class of analytic self-maps of the disk.

The refinement folds in the area of sub-disks inside the unit disk. Area terms, absent from the classical statements, sharpen the constants and widen the range where the bound holds. Such sharpened inequalities matter wherever power series are truncated, from signal filters to control theory. They also feed a long tradition of squeezing exact limits out of simple function classes, where each improved constant marks real progress.
arxiv-2512-04968:
Christian Baer and Remo Ziemke prove a formula in geometry that counts how the tones of a certain operator shift as it changes smoothly. The operator, named after Dirac, links the shape of a curved space to the behavior of waves on it, and the count of its shifting tones is called spectral flow. An earlier result by Getzler covered part of the ground; this work covers twisted versions of the operator in full.

The formula expresses the count through the space's curvature, a form built from the changing connections, and correction terms from the start and end operators. The proof leans on a landmark index theorem for spaces with an edge, which makes the argument surprisingly direct. As a payoff, the authors give a clean proof of a rigidity result about curved surfaces sitting in flat space, one that works the same in even and odd dimensions.
arxiv-2512-05068: Baptiste Louf studies very large random triangulations, surfaces tiled by triangles, as their genus, the number of handles, grows. His focus is the separating systole, the shortest loop that splits such a surface into two pieces. He proves its length grows only logarithmically with the size of the tiling, far slower than the surface itself. The same methods show a counting quantity called the genus ratio settles to a limit, extending an earlier result proved with Budzinski.
arxiv-2512-05768:
Austen Fourkas and ten co-authors use the ALMA telescope array to study how dust grains line up in a young binary star system, BHB07-11. Its disk is threaded with spiral arms. Polarized light can reveal grain alignment, but what aligns grains in a disk is unsettled. The team observed the disk's polarization at three wavelengths.

In every band, the polarization pattern matches emission from aligned grains, and it follows the shapes of the spiral arms seen in sharp maps. That lockstep with the arms points away from magnetic alignment. Instead, it best fits a newer idea: grains align with the relative flow between gas and dust inside the arms, pictured like a badminton shuttlecock settling into the wind. The result gives grain alignment studies a case where flow, not magnetism, does the organizing, which feeds into how planets begin to assemble.
arxiv-2512-05868:
Brian Ezinwoke and Oliver Rhodes forecast price spikes in high frequency trading with spiking neural networks, models whose neurons fire in discrete pulses like real nerve cells. Market data arrives at millisecond scale, a natural fit for pulse based computing. The team converts price data into spike trains and compares three networks: an unsupervised spike timing network, a new one with inhibitory competition, and a supervised baseline.

Bayesian optimization searches the settings, driven by a new objective, Penalized Spike Accuracy, which punishes drift from the true spike rate. In simulated trading, models tuned this way consistently beat counterparts tuned on plain accuracy. The extended spiking model with the new objective earned the highest cumulative return in simple backtesting, about seventy seven percent, far ahead of the supervised alternative at about forty three. The case: match the model to the data's form, and the objective to the events' rarity.
arxiv-2512-06368:
Weitao Xiong and five co authors present HuPrior3R, a method for rebuilding moving human scenes in three dimensions from a single camera video. One camera gives no depth, so past tools often warped limbs. They merged people into the objects near them. They also let body edges drift into the backdrop when images were shrunk to save memory. The team argues the missing piece is a prior sense of how a human body is shaped.

Their pipeline mixes a standard body model with depth guessed from the video. It first reads the full frame for the broad shape of the scene, then zooms into cropped views of each person to recover fine detail. A fusion step blends the body prior with the image detail so surfaces stay consistent and edges stay sharp. On two test sets of moving people, the method beat prior tools at rebuilding dynamic human scenes.
arxiv-2512-06468: Olga Katkova and Anna Vishnyakova study number sequences with a strong positivity trait: every minor of the endless Toeplitz table built from the sequence is nonnegative. They ask which second sequences preserve that trait when the two are multiplied term by term, a question tied to convolution operators that keep total positivity. Among their results, a scaled power weighting of any such sequence stays totally positive once the base passes a stated threshold. They close with open problems on these preserving operators.
arxiv-2512-06568:
Richard Feder and Martin White forecast how well a planned imaging survey could measure the size of the cosmic sound horizon. That horizon, stamped by sound waves in the young universe, is a standard ruler for cosmic distances. Spectroscopic surveys read it precisely in three dimensions, but the imaging surveys that pick their targets already carry an angular version of the signal.

The authors study the Intermediate Band Imaging Survey, using clustering results from a pilot survey of galaxies at high redshift. Their forecasts say a wide survey could pin the ruler's dilation to a few percent at its peak era, limited mostly by shot noise. They then look ahead to the survey plans for a next stage spectroscopic instrument and beyond. Early angular measures from imaging could sharpen the later, fuller spectroscopic work, and may stand as precise high redshift results in their own right.
arxiv-2512-06668:
Hao Fu builds a theory for how cold pools set the size of the seeds from which tropical cyclones grow. A cold pool is the chilled air that spreads under a rain shower. Such pools can help the next shower form, chaining storms together until a vortex embryo emerges. Rotation's effect on embryo size had a theory; the cold pool effect did not, until this cloud chain model.

In the model, how much rain evaporates in one storm event sets the wind and moisture at the cold pool's edge. Those in turn feed moisture into the next storm, which sets the next pool's strength. The analysis shows a pool's influence reaches as far as its own size, weighted by how strongly lifting and heating trigger new storms. Coupling the chain to a rotation model yields a formula for embryo size. Forecasters care because embryo size predicts whether a cyclone forms.
arxiv-2512-06968:
James Tian studies a back-and-forth cleaning process for operators, the mathematical objects that act on spaces of signals and states. The process alternates between two fixed projections, each time removing the slice of an operator that one projection can detect, with weights set by a square-root twist. The resulting map is neither linear nor based on minimizing anything, so the classical theory of alternating projections does not apply directly.

Even so, Tian proves the flow settles: it decreases steadily and converges to a positive limit on the kernel both projections share. That limit always sits below a classical benchmark, the shorted operator of Anderson, Duffin, and Trapp. The two agree exactly when the projections commute, and differ otherwise, hence the gap in the title. An energy identity tracks how much is shed at each step, and a factorized form locates the gap precisely.
arxiv-2512-07068:
Emma Markle, Javier Gutierrez Bach, and Shira Wein build a parser that turns English sentences into Uniform Meaning Representation graphs, diagrams that capture who did what to whom. The representation is new and designed to fit the world's languages, including ones with few digital resources, so it could aid language documentation. But its uses stay limited until software can produce the graphs automatically and accurately at scale.

The team tries two routes. One fine-tunes existing parsers built for a cousin representation, Abstract Meaning Representation. The other converts from Universal Dependencies, a widely available syntactic annotation, using earlier work as the baseline. Their best system, named SETUP, scores strongly on two standard measures of graph quality. Those scores mark a substantial step toward automatic parsing for this representation.
arxiv-2512-07168:
Georgios Ioannides and co-authors turn a prediction-based learning scheme into a tokenizer for speech, chopping audio into compact symbols a language model can read. Their framework has two stages. First, a joint-embedding predictive architecture learns the meaning of speech by forecasting hidden representations of masked stretches, never bothering to rebuild the raw waveform. A density-adaptive attention mechanism inside the encoder weighs time steps by how informative they are.

Those learned representations are then quantized with a finite scalar scheme and packed efficiently, producing a slow stream of tokens, tens per second rather than thousands. A vocoder network rebuilds high-fidelity sound from the tokens when needed, so the representation is reversible. The mixture-based gating lets the encoder pick out layered structure in speech at a low frame rate.
arxiv-2512-07268:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh explore how black holes could betray two of particle physics' most wanted fugitives: cosmic strings and axions. The axion is a hypothetical light particle proposed to fix a symmetry puzzle in the strong force, and it doubles as a leading dark matter candidate. When its parent symmetry broke in the early universe, it would have left behind strings, thin lines of trapped energy that decay by radiating axions and gravitational waves.

The authors study what happens when such a string wanders near a Schwarzschild black hole. Their estimates cover the energy a loop radiates and how long it survives. Even a featherweight primordial black hole can draw a radiated total that is astronomically large in particle terms. The headline effect is catalytic: the black hole's presence makes string loops decay far faster, cutting their lifetimes substantially.
arxiv-2512-07668:
Ronan John, Aditya Kesari, Vincenzo DiMatteo, and Kristin Dana wrote this 2025 computer vision paper. It studies where walking people actually look as they move outdoors. Predicting that gaze helps machines share space with pedestrians safely.

The team introduces EgoCampus, a dataset recorded on a university campus. It covers dozens of outdoor paths totaling several kilometres of walking. More than eighty pedestrians wore Meta's Project Aria glasses for the recordings. The glasses capture eye tracking, front video, motion sensors, and GPS together. Most older egocentric datasets stay indoors or skip gaze entirely. This one centers attention during real outdoor navigation instead. The authors also build EgoCampusNet, a model that predicts pedestrian gaze. It learns from the rich first-person signals in the dataset. Both resources aim to push gaze prediction for navigation forward. Code and data are promised for public release at a later date.
arxiv-2512-07768: Dihan Zou wrote this 2025 paper in mathematical economics on log-concave functions. A function is log-concave when the logarithm of its values bends downward everywhere. Zou summarizes a 2005 review of the topic by Bagnoli and Bergstrom. He makes several corrections to that review along the way. He also adds further results that help establish monotone hazard rates. An application to monopoly pricing closes the paper. There, log-concavity of the demand curve forces the revenue function to be strictly concave in quantity.
arxiv-2512-07868:
Pouya Ahadi, Reza Marzban, Ali Adibi, and Kamran Paynabar wrote this 2025 statistics paper on optimizing costly experiments. Bayesian optimization hunts the best input for a black-box process. Most versions assume the outcome is a single number per trial.

Many real responses are whole curves, varying over time or wavelength. Averaging error across a curve hides the worst deviations that matter most. Their framework, MM-FBO, minimizes the maximum error across the domain instead. Functional principal components compress each curve into a few scores. Gaussian process surrogates then model those scores for prediction. A new acquisition rule balances hunting the worst case with exploring broadly. Its uncertainty term is integrated across the whole functional domain. Two guarantees support the design from theory's side. A discretization bound caps the worst-case objective's error. A consistency result shows the rule converges to the true goal. Physics case studies confirm the edge.
arxiv-2512-08268:
Shalev Ben David and Eric Blais, theoretical computer scientists, posted a long paper on arXiv in December 2025 about randomized query complexity. A direct product theorem says that solving many copies of a problem at once costs about as much as solving them one by one, even if the success chance is small. Such theorems anchor hardness results across computing.

The authors prove two new versions for Boolean functions. The first covers every success level, unifying and extending earlier results that each handled only part of the range. The second is a list decoding version that captures many partial computation tasks at once, and yields new threshold variants as corollaries. Both rest on a fresh complexity measure they call discounted score. That measure multiplies together cleanly across copies, a tensorization property that suits direct product questions. The approach may give future hardness proofs a simpler engine to build on.
arxiv-2512-08368:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh, physicists in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about hunting cosmic strings with gravitational waves. Cosmic strings are hypothetical thread like defects from the early universe, never yet observed. Black holes ring after a merger with characteristic tones called quasinormal modes, and a nearby string should bend those tones in a recognizable way.

The authors model a cosmic string as a perturbation of a non rotating black hole spacetime and compute how the mode spectrum responds. Their simulations find a floor to the perturbation strength: below it, string effects hide inside the signal. By reading the splitting and shifting of the mode frequencies, they show string properties leave distinct, detectable marks. The method even runs backward, estimating a string energy or charge from a detected signal. They present quasinormal mode analysis as a fresh observational strategy for a long sought object.
arxiv-2512-08568:
C Abel, K Bodek, E Chanel, and a large international team posted a measurement paper on arXiv in December 2025. They report the first direct measurement of a nuclear quantity for mercury 199: its neutron incoherent scattering length. The value matters for precision experiments, including the neutron electric dipole moment search, whose apparatus hosted the work.

The team worked with stored ultracold neutrons in that Ramsey apparatus. Mercury atoms exert a pseudo magnetic effect on neutron spins through the strong force, shifting the frequency at which the spins precess. By measuring that shift across several mercury densities and polarization levels, they extracted the scattering length. The result agrees in size with earlier indirect determinations. Its new contribution is the sign of the quantity, which had never been measured before. Knowing both size and sign removes an ambiguity precision experiments had to carry.
arxiv-2512-08668:
Stephen Eckel and coauthors describe how atoms and simple molecules could serve as new standards for measuring radiation temperature. Atoms are all alike, and their behavior follows fixed quantum laws, which makes them attractive for primary sensors. The core idea is to measure how blackbody radiation excites or drives emission in a chosen atomic transition.

The authors sum up two recent experiments and the rate models needed to read them. One uses laser cooled rubidium atoms to probe radiation near a set microwave band, with uncertainty near the percent level. The other uses rubidium vapor and tracks fluorescence to read the spectrum at a much higher frequency, with sharp relative precision. Both paths point toward primary temperature standards that need no reference to a like measurement.
arxiv-2512-08768:
Thomas Bader and coauthors map the phase diagram of a triangular lattice antiferromagnet in a magnetic field. The model, with first and second neighbor couplings, has been studied for decades yet its field behavior remained unsettled. Frustration on the triangular lattice creates strong competition among possible magnetic orders.

The team combines three methods: self consistent spin wave theory, a matrix renormalization method, and variational Monte Carlo. Together they resolve which orders win and where magnetization plateaus appear across the classically frustrated range. Near a key coupling ratio, a gapless quantum spin liquid gains a finite density of monopoles when a field is applied. Raising the field further produces two clear plateaus at set fractions of full magnetization. The authors discuss how that pair of plateau transitions could serve, in experiments, as a signature of the underlying spin liquid phase.
arxiv-2512-08968:
Mustapha Hamdi introduces StructuredDNA, a sparse transformer routing framework inspired by how biological systems achieve structure at low energy cost. Scaling large models has driven energy and compute costs sharply upward. The framework replaces dense mixture of experts routing with a routing layer guided by a physical energy principle.

Inputs are grouped dynamically into semantic units the author calls codons. Routing then picks a single expert by minimizing a global energy function that combines cohesion, uncertainty, and compute cost. Tests cover a specialized biomedical question data set and a large open domain text benchmark. On the specialized test, energy use density falls dramatically while semantic stability stays near perfect. On the open benchmark, a scaling law is shown as expert granularity grows while energy efficiency stays very high. The author frames the work as a proof of concept and discusses limits and paths to larger models, data, and hardware.
arxiv-2512-09068:
Bin Guo and Duong Phong survey new inequalities and estimates of geometric type for the Monge Ampere equation in Kahler geometry, in a special issue for Yau. Most of the paper covers results obtained in recent years with several collaborators. Those results depend in an essential way on Yau solution of the Calabi conjecture, itself nearing fifty years old.

The survey also covers many current directions in complex geometry that Yau more recently pioneered. Readers get both a focused account of progress on a central nonlinear equation and a broader map of the field shaped by his work. The Monge Ampere equation governs key questions about Kahler metrics and canonical geometry, so estimates for it have wide reach. By tying new inequalities to the classic solution of the Calabi conjecture, the survey shows how a landmark result continues to generate tools for present day complex geometry.
arxiv-2512-09168:
N A Emelyanov and Vl V Kocharovsky study how the electromagnetic skin effect changes odd transport of charged particles in dense plasma threaded by a turbulent magnetic field at small scales. The work uses near linear kinetic equations and combines closed form and numerical methods. It focuses on isotropic plasma as the first case in a series.

Closed form expressions are found for the diffusion tensor in the Fokker Planck equation, with the skin effect included. That equation is then solved by computer for magnetostatic turbulence. The skin effect lengthens the mean free path of particles in the turbulent plasma, which lowers its odd resistance. It also makes particle spreading uneven, so the steady speed spread becomes uneven as screening grows. Rough formulas are obtained for effective particle movement and for electric current flow of the plasma. Results matter where turbulence and screening jointly set how charge and current move.
arxiv-2512-09568:
Zhi Zhao, Hang Xiao, and Wei Rang present PHWSOA, a scheduler for assigning tasks to machines in cloud computing. Scheduling decides how fast jobs finish and how much they cost, but most current methods optimize a single measure, or a few, and neglect the trade-off picture. It aims at three goals: completion time, load balance across machines, and cost.

The method mixes two nature-inspired optimizers, the Whale Optimization Algorithm and the Seagull Optimization Algorithm. It patches each one's weakness with the other's strength, and uses Pareto dominance to keep balanced solutions. Extra ingredients include a Halton sequence start for a more diverse starting group, and a Pareto-guided mutation to avoid premature convergence. Parallel processing adds speed, and a step redistributes load among machines during execution. In CloudSim simulations using workload traces, it cut completion time, improved load balancing, and reduced cost against baselines.
arxiv-2512-09968:
Paulo Firmino and Laurentiu Leustean extract hard numbers from a convergence proof in nonlinear analysis. The object of study is a generalized viscosity approximation method. It involves a countable family of nonexpansive mappings that meet certain resolvent like conditions. Such methods are used to find fixed points and solve equilibrium problems. Classical proofs show the method settles down over time, but they say nothing about how fast. The authors apply proof mining, a set of logical techniques that mine constructive information hidden inside ordinary proofs.

Their quantitative results come in two flavors. In W-hyperbolic spaces, a broad class of curved metric spaces, they obtain explicit information about asymptotic regularity, the rate at which successive steps stop changing. In CAT(0) spaces, an important subclass, they obtain rates of metastability. Metastability is a finite, checkable substitute for convergence when no computable rate exists.
arxiv-2512-10068:
Jocelyn Nembé adapts the TwinKernel scheme to estimating how often events occur over time or space. The target is the intensity function of a point process, the instantaneous rate behind counts of events. When the intensity has orbital regularity, structure repeated by a symmetry group acting on the domain, kernel smoothing wastes that structure. Nembé transports kernels along group orbits, building a hierarchy of smoothed estimators of Nelson-Aalen type, the standard estimator in survival analysis. 

The results include uniform consistency, optimal convergence rates in new smoothness classes, and adaptation to unknown smoothness by penalized model selection. Boundary bias is corrected automatically by local polynomial extensions in the transported coordinates. Minimax lower bounds certify the rates cannot be beaten in general. The showcase application is hazard rate estimation under random censoring, where periodicity arises from daily rhythms, seasons, or treatment schedules. Tests show several fold gains over classic kernel estimators.
arxiv-2512-10168:
Satoru Ohgata and Satoru Hayami find a route to a large Hall effect that needs no topological spin texture. Multi-Q magnets superpose several spin density waves, and certain mixes form skyrmions, whirlpool spin patterns whose chirality generates a topological Hall effect. The authors study the opposite case: a double-Q texture whose scalar spin chirality cancels, making it topologically trivial. Its Hall response is strong, with a distinctive nonmonotonic dependence on the uniform magnetization, unlike a ferromagnet or a single spiral. A multi orbital Kondo lattice model explains why.

The double-Q superstructure mixes the electronic orbitals, and that mixing sharpens the Berry curvature of the electron bands, the momentum space quantity behind the anomalous Hall effect. The mechanism accounts for the giant anomalous Hall effect observed in two gadolinium compounds.
arxiv-2512-10368:
Michio Seto studies families of de Branges-Rovnyak spaces, a class of function spaces used in complex analysis, as they evolve under the radial and chordal Löwner equations. Those equations describe shapes in the plane that grow over time. And each point in time gives a related function space to compare with the others.

Seto builds his approach on a classical but little-known technique from the de Branges school, recast here in the modern language of direct integrals and integral operators. As a payoff, he proves Fourier-type expansion theorems driven by the Löwner equations, expressing functions as sums of simpler pieces. The results also answer a question posed by Fricain, Hartmann, and Ross, tying the growing-shape picture to concrete formulas analysts can use.
arxiv-2512-11268:
Brett Shapiro designs vibration isolation suspensions for a proposed gravitational wave detector on the Moon. The Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna would listen for waves at frequencies below what Earth based detectors reach and above what planned space detectors cover. The Moon's seismic quiet helps, but residual shaking still threatens the measurement, and its exact level is uncertain.

An early version of the antenna needs no suspensions, letting the Moon's own ringing respond to passing waves. The full version, however, requires freely floating test masses and filtering of the remaining seismic background. Shapiro sets out baseline suspension designs under different assumptions about that background. The work gives the lunar project concrete starting points for isolating its optics whichever seismic conditions the Moon turns out to have.
arxiv-2512-11368:
Albert Dombret and fellow authors ask how a porous membrane's permeability changes when its pores themselves keep fluctuating. Filters and separation membranes are usually modelled as static, yet real matrices breathe, vibrate, and respond to forcing. The team couples fluid flow equations to a porosity that varies in space and time through a friction term drawn from Darcy's law of porous flow.

A perturbative calculation produces an equation for the flow swings, which they solve to express permeability through the spectrum of the matrix's own swings. Surprisingly, swings can modify permeability strongly, unlike a frozen matrix of the same average porosity. Applying the theory to breathing matrices, sound like vibrations, and actively forced materials shows how much each excitation matters. The results offer guidance for designing membranes whose transport can be tuned rather than merely endured.
arxiv-2512-11568:
Harry T J Bevins studies a faint radio signal from the dark ages of the universe. That era sits between the cosmic microwave background, formed near redshift 1100, and the first galaxies, near redshift 30. The signal could teach us about dark matter, dark energy, and how fast space grows.

Bevins takes limits on the standard cosmic model from Planck, WMAP, the Dark Energy Survey, and baryon sound wave data. He then works out what those limits imply for the radio signal. Within the model, its depth is pinned down to better than 1 millikelvin, and its center frequency to within 0.05 megahertz.
arxiv-2512-11768:
Felix St-Amour and co-authors built a cheap gadget that tracks glacier melt on its own. Crews now read melt stakes by hand, a few times a season. Their add on box listens to how the wind makes each stake hum.

A stake hum pitch depends on how much of it sticks out of the ice. As melt frees more stake, the pitch shifts, so the box can log melt day and night. Field tests at Color Lake on Axel Heiberg Island in Nunavut read exposed length to centimeter accuracy. The parts cost about 50 US dollars and clamp onto stakes already in use. That price opens dense, fine grained melt records for remote ice fields.
arxiv-2512-12168:
Zheng Huang and ten co-authors improve how diffusion language models write text in a 2025 paper. Such models start from masked text and fill it in step by step, in parallel. Choosing which spots to open and which words to lock in is a huge search problem, and simple rules often pick poor paths.

Their framework, MEDAL, uses Monte Carlo tree search at the start to test promising unmasking paths. That gives a strong starting point for later steps, with no extra training. More search time can lift quality further. Across benchmarks, MEDAL beat older inference methods by up to 22.0 percent, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-12468:
Tina Tian and six co-authors teach robots to unweave tangled cables in a 2025 paper. Cable work means pulling apart cords and removing tangles, but cables bend and cross in many knot patterns. Past work mostly untied knots in a single cable. Unweaving many cables at once, so each can be handled apart, is a distinct and harder subtask.

Their method uses camera feedback and treats each move as pick and place on a graph model of the cables, which stores both shape and crossing structure. A transition model predicts how cables straighten and bend after a move, guiding two action types. In tests on electric cables and shoelaces, the system averaged 84 percent success.
arxiv-2512-12668:
Long-Zhou Huang and four co-authors improve prediction of plastic events in glasses in a 2025 paper. Glasses are disordered solids that deform by sudden local rearrangements. Vortex like defects in vibration modes, with negative winding number, correlate with those plastic events. But many such vortices are fake signals from the plane wave structure of the modes, and their count grows with frequency.

The team adds a geometric filter based on the Nye dislocation density, a measure of lattice distortion. Applied to vibration modes of a two dimensional model glass, the filter removes spurious defects and reveals true plastic precursors. In simulations, the filtered method beat the plain vortex method, above all at small strains and for genuine stress drops.
arxiv-2512-12768:
Tianjiao Yu, Xinzhuo Li, Yifan Shen, Yuanzhe Liu, and Ismini Lourentzou present CoRe3D, a reasoning framework for 3D understanding and generation, in a 2025 paper. Large multimodal models reason well in language and 2D vision, yet reasoning methods have barely reached 3D tasks. CoRe3D aims to let high level intent from language guide low level 3D content formation directly.

Its key device is a spatially grounded reasoning representation that splits the 3D latent space into localized regions. The model then reasons over geometry piece by piece, in a procedural way. Semantic chain of thought inference couples tightly with that spatial reasoning. Outputs showed strong local consistency and faithful alignment with the language descriptions, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-13068:
Zexin Pan analyzes when certain infinite sums converge, sums that arise in the theory of quasi-Monte Carlo integration. The sums involve weights of product and order dependent type, called POD weights. Knowing exactly when they stay finite is key to error bounds for high-dimensional integrals.

Pan proves a sharp criterion: for a natural class of weights, the sum converges for all positive scales if and only if the underlying sequence itself is summable. He also finds the growth rate of such sums in a key parameter family. The work extends to a smoother SPOD class, though a full criterion there stays open. An application gives dimension-free convergence for lattice rules.
arxiv-2512-13168:
Haoyu Dong and co-authors introduce Finch, also called FinWorkBench, a benchmark for AI agents doing real finance and accounting work in spreadsheets. Real enterprise work mixes data entry, modeling, checks, web search, and reporting across many messy files. Existing tests rarely capture that mix.

Finch was mined from real workspaces, including Enron files, with over 700 hours of expert annotation. It holds 172 workflows with 384 tasks, using 1,710 spreadsheets with 27 million cells. Under human grading, the strongest system tried spent 16.8 minutes per workflow on average yet passed only 38.4 percent of them. The gap shows how hard real office work remains for agents.
arxiv-2512-13468:
Andry Rabenantoandro introduces the peripheral hyper-Wiener index, a new numeric descriptor of a graph's shape. Topological indices compress a network into a single number used to compare structures. The new index extends the peripheral Wiener index the way the hyper-Wiener index extends the classic Wiener index, focusing on peripheral vertices, the far-flung nodes of the graph.

The paper establishes basic properties of the index and computes it for Cartesian products of graphs and for trees. Hypercubes receive an explicit closed formula. Bounds in terms of the graph's order, size, diameter, and number of peripheral vertices are also proved, mirroring known results for the older indices.
arxiv-2512-13568:
Leonard Bereska and co-authors offer a way to measure superposition in neural networks. Superposition means a network stores many features as overlapping directions, instead of giving each feature its own neuron. That saves space but causes interference, and it makes networks hard to read.

Their measure uses Shannon entropy on sparse autoencoder activity to count effective features. That count tells how many virtual neurons the network acts as if it had. The metric tracks truth in toy models and shifts under dropout and grokking. It also tests whether superposition causes weak spots under attack. They find the link depends on task difficulty and network capacity, not on superposition alone.
arxiv-2512-13668:
Guoqing Liu and co-authors at Microsoft Research present QFANG, a reasoning language model that writes lab procedures for organic synthesis. Automated synthesis needs more than a route plan: each step needs a workable lab procedure. Bridging that gap is key for robot-assisted labs and faster drug discovery.

QFANG generates precise, structured lab steps from reaction equations, with explicit step-by-step reasoning. Training used a curated set of 905,990 reactions paired with action sequences drawn from patent texts. A chemistry-guided scheme built the reasoning data, followed by fine-tuning and learning from checked rewards. QFANG beat strong general models and search baselines on NLP metrics and a chemistry-aware judge, and adapted to new reaction classes.
arxiv-2512-14068:
Shuang Cheng and co-authors present SDAR-VL, a framework that makes block-wise discrete diffusion practical for vision-language understanding. Block-wise diffusion balances parallel generation with causal structure, a good backbone for vision-language models. High training cost, slow convergence, and shaky training had kept it behind autoregressive baselines.

Their training framework unifies three components: staggered block-wise noise scheduling, effective mask ratio scaling for unbiased loss scaling, and a growing beta noise schedule. Experiments span 21 single-image, multi-image, and video benchmarks. SDAR-VL improved training speed, convergence stability, and task scores over standard block diffusion. It set a new state of the art among diffusion-based vision-language models and, under matched settings, matched or beat strong autoregressive baselines such as LLaVA-OneVision.
arxiv-2512-14168:
Juan Diego Mazo Vasquez, Julius Gohsrich, Flore Kunst, and Lewis Hill present an algebraic method for Kerr resonators in a 2025 paper. These optical devices can show bistability, where one input gives two stable outputs, and spontaneous symmetry breaking between two paths.

Using polynomial resultants and Groebner bases, tools from nonlinear algebra, they derive compact formulas for all steady states in both intensity and amplitude form. Bifurcations, the points where states appear or change, follow directly from those formulas. The states can also be read as exceptional points of a related linear system. The unified frame should help control nonlinear optical devices and design new photonic chips.
arxiv-2512-14268:
Yifei He, Haoting Zhen, and Gyu Boong Jo review dipolar quantum gases from three dimensions down to low dimensions in a 2025 paper. These gases use atoms or molecules with large dipole moments, so their long range, direction dependent interactions differ from normal short range contact forces.

In three dimensions, strong dipole forces lead to anisotropic superfluidity, quantum droplets held up by Lee Huang Yang corrections, and supersolid states with density patterns. In two dimensions, the forces can drive angle dependent Berezinskii Kosterlitz Thouless transitions and possible supersolidity. Recent experiments with strongly dipolar gases in flat geometries support that picture. The review closes with open challenges and uses for simulating new physics.
arxiv-2512-14668:
A background of gravitational waves should reveal itself not only in pulsar timing but also in the apparent positions of stars and asteroids, which the waves shift slightly as they pass. Turning that idea into a precision tool needs a formalism that works from the Solar System out to cosmological distances.

A complete such formalism for gravitational wave astrometry is presented here, covering the full range of scales in one framework. The same background that delays pulses also displaces galactic objects, the author notes, so the two probes can cross-check each other. The work prepares the ground for using surveys of star positions to detect the gravitational wave background.
arxiv-2512-14868:
Guido Giachetti and a coauthor study a quantum model with many parts that all interact over long range. The model is the O(n) model taken at large n, where exact results become possible. In the strong long range regime, the system shows odd behavior on middle length time scales, around the log of the system size.

Nearly equal quantum modes start to resonate there, pushing the system away from the simple mean field picture. Using new proofs that the large n limit is integrable, the authors derive the exact resonance conditions and a phase diagram. They build the reduced Hamiltonian that runs the resonant modes and find the spectrum of the resulting motion. Many resonant modes together speed up the growth of entanglement in a logarithmic way and leave striped patterns in correlations.
arxiv-2512-15168:
Koustav N. Maity and four coauthors test whether gravitational wave echoes of black hole mergers can measure the universe. A small share of binary black hole signals will be strongly lensed by galaxies on the way, arriving as multiple copies at different times. The count of lensed events and their time delays encode cosmic parameters.

An earlier proposal targeted next generation detectors, expecting tens of thousands of lensed events. This study asks what the upgraded LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network can do, and it adds the detector selection effects the earlier work skipped. Dozens of lensed events should be detected, enough for modest constraints on cosmology at middle redshifts. Even with such small numbers, the authors show the method has real potential. For future detectors, their revised forecasts agree with the earlier ones.
arxiv-2512-15768:
Jamal Al-Karaki, Muhammad Al-Zafar Khan, and Rand Al Athamneh present PHANTOM, a framework for generating synthetic cyberattack data, in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Intrusion detection systems need attack data to train on, yet real attack records are scarce. Synthetic data could fill the gap if it keeps the true shape of attacks.

PHANTOM combines progressive training, a dual path variational autoencoder and GAN design, and domain specific feature matching to preserve attack semantics. On 100,000 network traffic samples, models trained on its synthetic data reach 98 percent weighted accuracy on real attacks. Statistical checks confirm the data keeps authentic distributions and diversity. Rare attack types remain hard under severe class imbalance.
arxiv-2512-15968:
S. Gwon and co authors measure the light yield of gadolinium compatible water based liquid scintillator in a 2025 paper. The material mixes scintillation and Cherenkov light in one detector medium, which improves event reconstruction over conventional neutrino detectors. Optimizing future detectors needs hard numbers for how much light each mix gives.

Using cosmic ray muons in the Brookhaven 1-ton testbed, the team measures light yield at scintillator concentrations from 0.35 percent to 1 percent by mass. Yield rises from 69.16 plus or minus 6.92 photons per mega electron volt at 0.35 percent to 87.32 plus or minus 8.73 at 1 percent. Those values set a quantitative basis for designing later detectors.
arxiv-2512-16068:
Eunkyu Seong and Seojeong Lee examine a central bank's forecasts in a economics paper shared on arXiv in 2025. The Bank of Korea publishes outlooks for growth, inflation, and jobs. The authors ask whether its inflation forecasts lean toward the bank's own inflation target, a bias that would make the forecasts less honest.

They extend a classic bias test so it depends on the state of the economy, split by whether actual inflation sits below target when the forecast is made. Under that lens, the forecasts do show bias. The authors then try correction methods based on simple time-series models, including state-dependent versions. The corrections generally improved accuracy, and one approach, an AR(1)-based fix, cut forecast error steadily across cases. The study offers a practical check on official forecasting.
arxiv-2512-16468:
Danial Safaei and six co-authors measure virtual test quality in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. Self-driving cars are vetted in simulators, but pretty synthetic images can still mislead the system under test. What matters is whether the car bases decisions on the same evidence in fake and real scenes.

Their metric, Decisive Feature Fidelity, uses explainable AI tools to find the features driving a system's outputs on matched real and synthetic image pairs, then compares those features across the pair. Counterfactual explanations supply the estimates, and a calibration scheme uses the metric to improve the simulator itself. On 2,126 matched pairs from KITTI and VirtualKITTI2, the metric exposed gaps that conventional output-based fidelity missed. Calibration guided by it improved feature-level and input-level fidelity without hurting output fidelity, across several systems under test.
arxiv-2512-16668:
Fabius Krämer and Tim Laux give a fast way to compute mean curvature flow with obstacles. In such flow a surface shrinks by its curvature, but cannot pass through blocked zones. Their method adds a simple point-by-point fix. The fix goes onto the classic Merriman-Bence-Osher scheme.

That small change keeps the cost of the base scheme. Yet it keeps two key traits of the true flow. One is a comparison rule for nested shapes. The other is a view as a sequence of energy drops. The energy view gives stability for free. From the comparison rule, the authors prove the scheme settles to the right viscosity solution. They prove the same for a grid version, before showing test runs.
arxiv-2512-16768:
Soon Hoe Lim studies hidden biases in flow matching samplers, a popular way to build generative models that carry a simple distribution into a complex target along smooth paths. The focus is on what changes when real, finite data replace the true target.

Lim lays out a ladder of such plug-in models, from the raw data measure to smoothed stand-ins. For affine flows he finds the exact best fit and a smoothed regime where the end law is a kernel mixture. Three biases stand out: the target itself shifts, the best fit may not be a gradient field, and one path can hide many particle motions. Tail bounds for kinetic energy hinge on the base distribution shape.
arxiv-2512-16868:
Jhinkyu Choi and coauthors probe heat versus charge flow in the kagome metal TbCr6Ge6, testing the Wiedemann-Franz law, which ties heat conduction to charge conduction in metals. In this ferrimagnetic rare-earth compound, the tie breaks badly.

Across the magnetic transition, both the plain and transverse Lorenz ratios swing far from the standard value. After a partial recovery near 5 to 7 kelvin, both ratios drop well below standard while charge flow stays metallic, and the transverse ratio flips sign. That split points to neutral carriers that move heat but not charge, steered by Berry curvature. The material offers a tunable test bed for such odd heat transport.
arxiv-2512-17068:
Primoz Moravec studies discrete torsion for the n-torus with a finite symmetry group, from the Dijkgraaf-Witten angle, where a cohomology class assigns a phase to each flat bundle. He asks which classes give trivial phases on all commuting tuples, the untwisted ones.

Those classes form a subgroup, written Br to the n of G, inside the full cohomology group. Moravec derives an exact sequence, using universal coefficients, that places the new invariant. In degree two it returns the Bogomolov multiplier, also known as the unramified Brauer group. Algorithms compute the subgroup and torus partition functions, with runs reported for families of finite subgroups of SU(4).
arxiv-2512-17268:
Matthias Bentert and six co-authors revisit a simple geometry question: how few straight lines does it take to pass through every point in a scattered set? That Line Cover problem is known to be hard in general, yet it becomes manageable when the number of lines stays small. The team asks what happens under natural twists on the question.

One twist, Line Clustering, lets points sit off the lines and charges for the squared distance. That version turns out far harder, with no fast method unless a major math guess fails. A flat-cover version in higher dimensions stays hard even with just two flats. For the unified Projective Clustering problem, their new algorithm matches the proven lower bound, so its running time cannot be much improved.
arxiv-2512-17368:
Byeongha Moon and a large team present 112 glowing gas clouds, called Lyman alpha blobs, found in a deep sky survey field. These blobs are huge clouds shining in the light of hydrogen, seen as they were when the universe was young. What powers them is still debated, and small past samples left their basic counts shaky.

The ODIN survey imaged a wide field in narrow color bands tuned to that hydrogen light. The team's new pipeline first models every ordinary galaxy and subtracts it, which exposes faint blobs the older cross-matching method missed: 23 extra finds. Near a young galaxy cluster in the field, blobs crowd in four times denser than average. Their brightness and crowding seem to depend on the neighborhood, a clue to their origin.
arxiv-2512-17568:
Kangchen Lv and coauthors teach robot arms to use the whole arm, not just the gripper, when they learn a task from demonstrations. Whole arm control matters when the arm must dodge obstacles with its elbow or push with its body. Yet most policies learn in joint space, which sits at a remove from the 3D world the task lives in.

Their framework describes the robot's state and its actions as a set of 3D points along the arm, the same form as the point cloud the robot sees. A diffusion policy then plans in that shared space, with the arm's kinematics built into the process so the planned motions stay feasible. An inverse kinematics solver then turns the plan into joint commands. In simulations and on a real arm the method reached higher success rates and adapted to new layouts better than prior approaches.
arxiv-2512-18068:
Juo-Tung Chen and five coauthors recover robot arm motion from plain surgical video. Robots learn surgery by copying expert runs, but the rich store of public operation videos lacks the joint angle records that training needs. SurgiPose fills that gap by fitting a 3D tool model until its rendered image matches the real frame.

The team tested the idea on two tasks, lifting tissue and picking up a needle, with a da Vinci research robot. Policies trained on the video derived motion scored about as well as policies trained on true measured motion. The result opens the door to learning from the large stock of surgical videos already online.
arxiv-2512-18268:
Si Wei Feng, Kartik Mohta, and Kangli Wang ask how few drone photos can cover a region at the finest detail. More photos cost time and money, so planners want the smallest set of equal square or round shots that still tiles the whole area. Their study treats the task as covering a flat polygon with a fixed count of shapes.

They prove the search is deeply hard: even getting near the smallest square size, within a factor of 1.165, is NP-hard, and the bound tightens to 1.25 when shot centers must stay inside the region. They also give a method that lands within a stated factor of the best. The same math guides where to place sensors or depots.
arxiv-2512-18368:
Yihang Zhu leads a five author team teaching robots small named skills that stack into long jobs. Copy based robot training falters when many tasks share one brain: clumsy demos, clashing habits, and skills that blur together. AtomSkill first cuts demo runs into atomic skills, short moves with clear meaning, and lines them up across tasks by a contrast based rule.

Each skill also learns to picture its own end pose, the keypose where it should land. At run time a sampler strings skills together, and the pictured end poses trigger smooth hand offs. In both simulated and real trials, AtomSkill beat top copy based and skill based rivals on multi task work.
arxiv-2512-18468:
Daniel Berend and Michael D. Boshernitzan turn the classic cops-and-robber game into a continuous chase. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, plays the game on a metric graph, where each edge has a real length and both players move along edges at bounded speeds. Unlike the classic version, the cop never learns where the robber is and must follow one fixed path that is guaranteed to cross the robber's route.
