The linked state lets the team gauge phase gaps in decays. Those gaps are key to maps of how charm bits change. Fine gauges feed tests of the base theory of matter. They also aid hunts for new effects in charm decays. The set holds twenty inverse femtobarns of data.
arxiv-2601-16868:
Anna Abbatiello, Miroslav Bulíček, and Petr Kaplický test the firmness of flow laws for thick fluids. Their fluid fills a 3D zone and bears heat as it flows. It is thick in a non-Newton way, like glue or blood. Wall heat is set, and the walls grip the flow. No push from the back acts on it. Their 2026 preprint asks if the flow's path stays firm under small shifts.

The stress law in view spans power-law and Ladyzhenskaya forms. For a span of powers, no one knew if paths stay unique. Nor was the energy count on firm ground. Firmness proofs would put such flow codes on safe feet. Thick heat flows sit in plants, food lines, and care gear.
arxiv-2601-17168:
Judy Zhu, Dhari Gandh, Himanshu Joshi, Ahmad Rezaie Mianroodi, Sedef Akinli Kocak, and Dhanesh Ramachandran argue that agent checks must rise a level. Chatbot agents now plan in steps and act in the world. A lone model's word for its acts won't do. Their 2026 preprint calls for system-level checks in place of model tales. The whole chain of steps, tools, and acts must face review.

Such checks trace who set each act in train. They show where blame sits when an act goes wrong. Firms that field agents need that trace for law. It also helps teams fix flaws at the right joint.
arxiv-2601-17268:
Jaideep Pathak and twelve co-authors work on very short-term storm forecasts. Good forecasts of clouds and rain save lives and time. They guide severe weather warnings. They help planes fly safe and solar farms plan output. At storm scale, though, the best tools have clear limits. Math weather models can be slow or coarse. Simple track-forward methods fade fast.

The team learns storm growth straight from observed data. That path aims for sharp forecasts at the scale of single storms. Better short-range skill means warnings can come with more lead time. It also means fewer false calls. For weather teams, a data-led method could sit beside classic models and lift both.
arxiv-2601-17368:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors review how privacy policies are shown to users. Policies are the base of informed consent online. Yet most users do not grasp them. Decades of design research have proposed charts, icons, and layered views. Few of those designs spread in real products. The team scopes that body of work from a human-computer interaction view.

They draw guidelines from what the record shows. Good display must fit law's needs and human limits at once. The gap between intent and use is the core problem. Their guidelines can help teams design policy views people read. That would make consent more than a click through a wall of text.
arxiv-2601-17468:
Chia-Ming Lee and five co-authors present ReflexSplit, a method to split reflections from photos. A shot through glass mixes two layers. One is the scene behind the glass. The other is the reflected scene. Past methods confuse the two, mostly in deep decoder layers. Weak fusion and poor scale coordination cause much of that mix-up.

ReflexSplit uses a dual-stream design with three key changes. The streams handle the two layers with more care. Clean splits help photo tools, drivers, and store cameras. Glass is common in all those settings. The work aims at hard mixes, not just faint glare. It gives vision systems a clearer view through real windows.
arxiv-2601-17568:
Amritha Premkumar and Christian Herglotz speed up encoding of 360-degree video. Immersive video must stream at many quality levels. Each level needs its own encode at set resolution and quality steps. For 8K panoramic content, that work is huge. The team works in OMAF streaming workflows, the standard for such media. They propose fast multirate encoding.

Shared work across versions can cut total encode time. Streaming firms pay for each version they compute. Faster prep means fresher live and on-demand content. It also cuts energy per stream. The work targets ultra-high-resolution content, where costs bite most. Gains there scale to the whole catalog.
arxiv-2601-17768:
Raja Gond, Aditya K Kamath, Ramachandran Ramjee, and Ashish Panwar of Microsoft Research study a quirk of large language models. The same prompt can give a different reply each time the model runs. Their 2026 preprint traces the cause to math inside the machine. Adding numbers in a changed order can change the final sum, and batch sizes shift that order.

One fix is to turn off dynamic batching, but that slows the system down a lot. The team instead works on a way to keep results stable while the speed stays high. Their title calls the method verified speculation. Steady output matters for tests, audits, and any use where the same input must give the same output.
arxiv-2601-17868:
Zhihao He and co-authors present VidLaDA, a video language model built on diffusion rather than step-by-step writing. Their 2026 preprint targets video understanding. Most video models read frames with a vision encoder, then let an autoregressive model talk about them. That style has two costs. One-way attention limits how well the model can pool events across time and space. Serial decoding also slows output down.

A bidirectional diffusion design attacks both costs at once. Each part of the reply can draw on the whole video context. Steps can also be refined in parallel rather than one token at a time. The aim is faster, more global video understanding. Such models serve search, summary, and monitoring tasks.
arxiv-2601-18368:
Caterina Fuster-Barceló and six colleagues built a tool that reads MRI scans of the inner ear with no help from a human hand. The scans show a fault where fluid in the ear swells past its right share. Doctors call that fault endolymphatic hydrops, and its size helps them judge ear disease.

Their tool, named OREHAS, runs in three steps. First it sorts the scan slices by type. Next it finds the inner ear in each slice. Last it marks the fluid zones and works out how much of the ear space they fill, ear by ear. Since the whole flow runs on its own, clinics could get the same clear count each time. There would be no slow hand work to slow the count down.
arxiv-2601-18468:
Daniel Hier and Tayo Obafemi-Ajayi ask why some facts stick in a language model and some do not. After first training, a model holds facts with quite unlike strength. Some facts sit in its weights but stay hid when it writes in its plain mode. Some facts are barely there at all.

The pair fine-tune a model on fact pairs from two big maps of body and gene terms. Those maps link each term to a code used in health work. The team then check if the strength of a fact before the tune-up tells how fast the model learns it in the tune-up. A firm link would help teams plan how to teach a model new facts. It would also show which facts need more drill to stick.
arxiv-2601-18568:
Sanu Kumar Gangwar and five colleagues chart the waves that can run through a cloud of cold atoms with a twist. The cloud is a rare state in which many atoms act as one. Its atoms can point in three ways, and a twist in the lab makes spin and path trade push. That trade can let the cloud form stripes that act both as a stiff solid and as a free fluid.

The team work out the full set of waves the cloud can hold, across a wide range of pull strengths. Their maths shows which waves stay calm and which ones grow wild. Wild waves mark where the cloud would break or shift phase. A firm chart helps labs pick set-ups that hold the rare state still. It also guides the hunt for new phases in such clouds.
arxiv-2601-18768:
Nizar El Idrissi and Hicham Zoubeir prove two new claims in the maths of gaps and lengths in spaces with a dot rule. One claim ties the four sides of a four-point form: the long side can't beat the sum set by the rest in a set way. Claims of that kind are old and prized, since they bind how far points can sit from each other. The next claim uses a table of dot scores for a set of points.

That table, called a Gram table, holds the cos-like scores of all pairs. From it, the pair draw fresh bounds on joint gaps. Such bounds feed work in shape maths, in codes, and in the tests that prove a set of points must act in a set way. Pure claims like these are tools that next work can lift whole.
arxiv-2601-19068:
Chaoliang Tang, Hehui Wu, and Junchi Zhang pin down a Turán type bound for sparse hypergraphs. A linear 3-graph links triples of points so that any two links share at most one point. The question: how many links can such a graph hold with no path of length five hiding inside?

The team proves the count stays under a fixed share of the point count, and they name the only graph that hits the bound exactly. It is built from copies of one small graph with eleven points. Sharp bounds with a named extremal case close a problem fully, a prized outcome in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-19168:
Brianna L. Wimer and seven co-authors help blind students grasp data structures through touch and sound, not pictures. Blind and visually impaired students face built in barriers when learning how data is organized. Most aids just turn diagrams into alt text, which tells how a picture looks, not how the structure works.

Richer aids often fail to scale in complexity or cost. The team builds nonvisual support aimed at the structure itself, so students can reason about links and order directly. Their work was shared at the CHI conference on human factors in computing systems.
arxiv-2601-19468:
N. M. Zubarev and E. A. Kochurin simulate what a charged liquid surface does when an electric field pushes it hard. A non conducting liquid with charge on its free surface, set in a field along the surface normal, grows unstable. The team follows the strongly nonlinear stages of that growth by direct simulation.

Two stages stand out: first, dimples form on the surface; then the pattern develops into sharper structures. Knowing the stages helps read real systems, from inks and sprays to liquid metal devices, where charged surfaces meet strong fields.
arxiv-2601-19568:
Ke Xu and eight colleagues work on a slow step in automated software development: finding the right code. Before an agent can fix or extend a program, it must locate the files and lines that matter. Running search tools one by one is slow. Running them in parallel could help, but agents often call the same tools again and again, wasting the gain.

The team reports that current agents repeat a large share of their tool calls. Their method, FuseSearch, plans parallel searches as a joint problem of quality and efficiency. Calls that add nothing are cut before they run. The goal is fast discovery with less waste. Better code localization speeds up every repair and feature task built on top of it.
arxiv-2601-19668:
Luis Amorim and four colleagues build fake time series that behave like real ones. Forecasting models, especially deep learning ones, need large training sets to generalise well. Real datasets are often small, so data augmentation creates extra examples. Many existing tricks transform the data in ways that break its key properties.

Their method, Grasynda, generates synthetic series using graphs. The graph view is meant to preserve the structure that matters for forecasting. Synthetic series that keep the right properties can train models without leaking real records. The approach targets settings where data is scarce but decisions depend on forecasts. Better augmentation could lift forecast quality in energy, retail, and beyond.
arxiv-2601-19768:
Shir Rozenfeld and five colleagues build a safety monitor for large language models. Activation monitoring watches a model's inner signals, not just its words, to catch harmful behaviour. Existing monitors are trained on broad misuse data. They often suffer from poor precision, little flexibility, and no clear explanation of their alarms.

Their system, GAVEL, moves toward rule-based safety through activation monitoring. Rules let operators define exactly which behaviours to flag. That promises clearer control and more interpretable alerts. A monitor that explains itself is easier to trust and to fix. The work addresses a growing need as language models take on sensitive roles.
arxiv-2601-19868:
Shrajal Bajpai and Lakshmi Kanta Patra work on estimating variances that are known to come in a fixed order. Their data model mixes two normal distributions at different scales. Component-wise estimation asks for each variance separately while respecting the order. Two loss functions frame the problem: squared error loss and entropy loss.

The authors derive general results on when one estimator improves on another. From those results they construct estimators that beat the standard best affine equivariant estimator. Ordered parameters arise wherever theory fixes a ranking in advance. Better estimators sharpen tests and intervals in such problems. The work is a careful piece of decision theory with practical statistical payoff.
arxiv-2601-19968: Youngwoong Cho asks what artificial general intelligence would mean for offensive security work. The essay splits the question in two. First, can every offensive security task be reduced to manipulating symbolic language, meaning representation plus reasoning? Second, are powerful language models enough to handle any such manipulation? The answers decide whether general AI would transform cyber offence. The paper is a position piece, mapping the debate rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2601-20068:
Samuel Blitz, Gabriel Herczeg, and David McNutt study the geometry of null hypersurfaces, surfaces swept by light rays. Space-like and time-like surfaces inherit a natural connection from the spacetime around them. Null surfaces, like black hole horizons and the edge of all we can see, do not. That gap makes the physics built on them harder, flat-space holography included.

The authors examine potential Carroll structures on such surfaces. Carrollian geometry, named for the other Carroll limit of relativity, is the natural geometry of null surfaces. They identify special Carrollian manifolds with extra good properties. Clarifying this geometry supports holographic descriptions of gravity in flat space. The work is basic mathematics with physical targets. These are the sheets that light sweeps out. They rim black holes and the far edge of space. Their shape is a deep, hard thing. Few tools fit them well.
arxiv-2601-20268:
Long Van Tran, Truyen Tran, and Phuoc Nguyen study how to estimate the parameters of stochastic differential equations when time information is missing or hidden. These equations model real processes in finance, health, and biology. Standard estimation needs a correctly ordered, accurately stamped sequence of observations.

When the order is corrupted, missing, or withheld for privacy, standard methods often fail. The authors aim for robust estimation that works despite the lost time stamps. Their work matters for fields like medicine, where privacy rules may strip timing from data that researchers still need to model.
arxiv-2601-20468:
Mathis Brossier and four colleagues explore how touch-enabled spherical displays can support climate conversations in museums and science centers. A globe you can touch invites direct, embodied interaction with complex climate data. Groups can gather around it and explore together, which suits public discussion of a shared problem.

Current spherical displays, though, offer limited interaction. The authors run an exploratory study to find chances for richer interaction and the technical means to build it. Better globe interfaces could turn climate data from a lecture into a conversation visitors steer themselves.
arxiv-2601-20568:
Efstratios Zaradoukas, Bardh Prenkaj, and Gjergji Kasneci present a method for making large language models forget chosen training content. During pretraining, models memorize sensitive or copyrighted data. Laws such as the GDPR and the EU AI Act can require that information to be removed from a deployed model, without retraining from scratch.

Their approach uses reinforcement unlearning driven by group relative policy optimization. Unlearning by reinforcement steers the model away from the unwanted content while sparing the rest. A dependable forgetting method would let providers meet legal duties at a fraction of full retraining cost.
arxiv-2601-20668:
Shuhao Liao and nine co-authors study how to train legged robots to walk and move their whole bodies. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a method they call Growing Policy Optimization, or GPO. The work uses reinforcement learning, where a robot learns by trial and error. The authors frame this as a hard training problem.

The paper explains why such training is so hard in practice. The robot must choose smooth actions across many joints at once. Real hardware also limits what the robot can safely try. And the robot gets few chances to test new moves. GPO is the team's answer to these limits. Readers get a clear view of one current path toward robots that walk well and use their full bodies with skill.
arxiv-2601-20768:
Sergey Meliakov and six co-authors report long-lived electron spins in a perovskite semiconductor. Their 2026 paper measures spin coherence times in the millisecond range. Spin coherence is how long an electron's spin keeps its quantum state. Long coherence is essential for quantum technologies built on semiconductors. The enemy is spin relaxation, which erases that state.

The team used a method called spin mode locking to reveal the long times. They note that spin dynamics hinge on three features of the material. These are the band structure, the crystal symmetry, and quantum confinement. Perovskites are a family of crystals much studied for solar cells. Showing that their spins stay coherent this long opens a path to quantum devices made from them.
arxiv-2601-20868:
Rongzheng Wang and a large team of co-authors rethink how language models design solvers. Their 2026 paper concerns combinatorial optimization, the search for the best arrangement under rules. Large language models have advanced this field through automated heuristic generation. Instead of hand design, an LLM-driven process proposes solvers. It then refines them in rounds to reach high performance.

The authors add dynamics-aware optimization to that loop. The name signals attention to how a solver behaves as it runs. A solver that looks good on paper may waste time in practice. Watching its dynamics can guide the search toward speed as well as quality. The goal is solvers that are both efficient and specialized to their problem. The work speaks to logistics and scheduling, where good heuristics save real money.
arxiv-2601-20968:
Yulie Arad, Stav Ashur, and Nancy Amato speed up how robots refresh their roadmaps when the world changes. Their 2026 paper tackles roadmap graphs in non-static environments. A roadmap is a network of safe paths a robot can follow. When obstacles move, some edges become invalid. Checking each edge with full collision tests is slow. The authors want fast, semi-lazy updates.

They introduce the Red-Green-Gray paradigm. It modifies the earlier SPITE method. Cheap heuristic checks classify each node and edge by validity status. Green edges are safe, red ones are blocked, and gray ones need a closer look. The robot can then repair only what matters. The method suits warehouses and homes where scenes shift often. It keeps planners responsive without full rebuilds.
arxiv-2601-21568:
Antonio Almudévar and Alfonso Ortega unify two ways of judging whether two model representations are alike. One view is functional: can parts be stitched together and still work? The other view is about the information the parts carry.

The authors tie stitching success to conditional mutual information, a classic measure of shared usable content. Their frame covers both views across three dimensions of comparison. A shared yardstick helps researchers decide when two models really compute alike. That judgment matters for merging models, reusing parts, and trusting that a smaller model mirrors a bigger one.
arxiv-2601-21668:
Philipp Krah, Zetao Lin, and five co-authors blend two flow-mapping methods to solve the Vlasov-Poisson equation. That equation governs plasmas and galaxies, where particles move under their own collective field. Semi-Lagrangian methods trace the flow backward to where each parcel began.

One parent method iterates the flow numerically, and the other composes flow maps directly. Each has strengths the other lacks. The hybrid aims for accuracy over long runs without the cost exploding. Long, accurate runs matter for fusion and space plasma work, where small errors compound into wrong predictions about stability.
arxiv-2601-21768:
Alon Rozental argues that large language models are held back by the way they chop text into fixed pieces. Tools such as Byte Pair Encoding split words before learning starts, and that split cannot adapt during training. His 2026 preprint presents Zonkey, a model built to remove that fixed step.

Zonkey is a hierarchical diffusion model with a fully trainable path from raw characters up to representations of whole documents. Its tokenization can be learned along with the rest of the model, and its attention works in terms of probabilities. The aim is a system that adapts better to noisy text and to special fields where standard token splits fit poorly.
arxiv-2601-22068:
Mehmet Ozgur Turkoglu and co-authors make foundation models less cocky. These large pretrained models perform remarkably across tasks, but their predictions are often overconfident and poorly calibrated. The standard cure, training an ensemble of independent models, costs far too much at foundation scale.

The team's 2026 preprint builds ensembles from singular value pieces of a single model, creating varied members without full retraining. Spread among those members gives an estimate of epistemic uncertainty, the model's own ignorance. Calibrated uncertainty matters wherever a model's confidence drives action, from medical triage to financial risk. Because a system that knows when it does not know can hand off to a human in time.
arxiv-2601-22368:
Junyoung Park proves that a class of moving surfaces can glide for all time and settle to a stable shape. The flow is mean curvature flow, which moves a surface by its bend at each point. His 2026 preprint starts from the graph of a rough, merely continuous function over a slab.

He then checks the stability of known translator shapes, which move without changing form. They include the grim reaper curve and flatland and cylinder-like forms. Stability tells us which shapes a real flow would keep. The work is pure math, on how shapes evolve. It firms up a classic theory.
arxiv-2601-23068:
Joao Fonseca and Julia Stoyanovich estimate feature importance without opening the model. Knowing which inputs drive a classifier's decisions is key to explaining it. Shapley values are a popular answer, but they need direct model access and can be too costly to compute exactly.

Their ExplainerPFN approach aims at model-free, zero-shot importance scores for tabular data. Foundation-model style design lets it answer for new datasets at once, without retraining. Cheap, access-free explanations help audit models that vendors keep closed. Zero-shot estimation matters because a fresh dataset should not need a fresh explanation model trained before anyone can use it.
arxiv-2601-23268:
Milton Gomez and a large team release TCBench, a benchmark for tropical cyclone forecasting worldwide. It evaluates short to medium-range forecasts of storm track and intensity, from one to five days ahead. The benchmark builds on the IBTrACS observational record of past storms.

Forecasting is framed as predicting how an existing storm evolves, given its starting position and strength. A model-agnostic setup allows fair comparison across very different systems. Shared global benchmarks help weather centers and AI teams improve warnings together. Conditioning on the storm's initial position and intensity keeps the benchmark focused on evolution, not on storm discovery.
arxiv-2602-00168: Ranjan Sapkota and Manoj Karkee present YOLOE-26, a unified framework for real time open vocabulary instance segmentation. It joins the deployment tuned YOLO26 architecture with the open vocabulary learning of YOLOE, keeping YOLO speed and determinism while moving past closed set recognition. A convolutional backbone with multi scale aggregation feeds end to end regression and segmentation heads. A key change swaps fixed class logits for an object embedding head, so classification becomes similarity matching against prompt embeddings from text, visual examples, or a built in vocabulary.
arxiv-2602-00268: Ariel Shaulov and colleagues propose TokenTrim, an inference time token pruning method for autoregressive long video generation. Autoregressive video generation builds long videos by conditioning each new batch on prior content. Errors then accumulate and amplify over long horizons as temporal drift. The authors blame drift less on model size than on reuse of damaged conditioning tokens at inference time. TokenTrim spots and drops unstable latent tokens before reuse, where unstable means far from the prior batch.
arxiv-2602-00368: Mannu Bardhan Paul and team investigate scatter reducing agents for reflectance mode near infrared imaging. They use food grade dye Tartrazine to enhance depth sensitivity and weak absorber detection in continuous wave reflectance readings. Signal rose on a chicken breast phantom with dye applied, yet fell when dye was uniformly dissolved in an intralipid phantom. That contrast shows the refractive index gradient from dye diffusing in the top layer boosts signal sensitivity. When scatter reduction is uniform throughout the phantom, as in that phantom, improved readings were not observed.
arxiv-2602-00468: Hongwei Yu and colleagues link two views of open quantum systems. In their giant-atom waveguide setup, closing of the Liouvillian gap in the reduced picture necessarily marks a bound state in the continuum in the full Hamiltonian picture. Tuning the giant-atom shape yields Rabi oscillations, fractional decay, or full exponential relaxation as the bound-state count moves from three to zero. When two such states share a frequency, the long-time state settles instead of oscillating, giving flexible control of open-system dynamics.
arxiv-2602-00568: Ke Xue and colleagues build DVPD, a lightweight diffusion model for speech enhancement that treats spectrograms as images and frequency signals. Score-based models that treat spectrograms as generic images waste structure and compute, so DVPD compresses spectra with an adaptive encoder that keeps low harmonics and prunes high redundancy. An image-based module adds a visual view with overhead, and a training-free boost refines output at inference without fine-tuning. Tests show state-of-the-art quality with 35% of the parameters and 40% of the compute of PGUSE.
arxiv-2602-00868: Nikhil Uday Shinde and colleagues present Safe Stochastic Explorer, a framework for safe, goal-driven exploration in stochastic settings. Robots in messy, high-risk settings, from planet rovers to warehouses and homes, must move and interact with little prior knowledge. Current safe-control methods assume known dynamics, while existing safe exploration often ignores the chance built into unknown real-world settings. Their approach balances safety with learning to reduce doubt about safety, learning the unknown safety function online from Gaussian Processes.
arxiv-2602-01068: Chaoqun Cui and co-authors train a subtitle translator that aims for vivid, lively lines, not just true ones. Broad translators lag in niche fields, and subtitle work needs flair on top of sense. The team first checks that big models can serve as fair judges and scorers for translation, then builds a multi-way subtitle pair set for training. Their ALPO trick tunes likes at fine grain, so the model learns small taste gaps. Multi-side tests rate the tuned model as top-notch for subtitle translation.
arxiv-2602-01168: Nina Gantert and co-authors stretch big-jump lore for heavy-tail sums into many dimensions. In one dimension, a rare big sum tends to ride on one big jump, but the multi-dimensional tale stayed thin. For sums of free random vectors, they prove big-deviation laws whose rate comes from at most k cost-map parts. A rare sum thus rides on at most k free vectors. Uses span powers of Gaussian vectors and high-dimensional ball casts, where light and heavy tails both show up.
arxiv-2602-01368: Patricia Marcella Evite and co-authors study explainability in finance AI as a tug with accuracy and compliance. Past lore frames the bind as accuracy versus explainability alone, too thin for finance, where rules, budgets, and latency press. Through talks with twenty finance hands, from chiefs and coders to regulators across regions, they rank explainability against accuracy, compliance, cost, and speed. Accuracy and compliance emerge as must-have hygiene factors, speed and cost as levers, and ease of grasp as the gateway to trust and use.
arxiv-2602-01568: Hamzah Khan and colleagues tackle robot teams where some robots plan around the plans of others while others move at the same time. They study forest shaped games in which each robot leads its own branch and separate branches settle into Nash play. A simpler quasi policy rule drops costly higher order terms, letting an inexact Newton solver handle the resulting conditions. Tests in simulation and on real hardware show the method converging in real time.
arxiv-2602-01968: Daniel Hernández-Hernández and colleagues solve optimal liquidation of a large portfolio of securities exposed to default risk. Default time follows a Brownian motion tracking firm value, with firm assets available to market investors. Selling many assets moves prices and portfolio value, so the control problem for the optimal liquidation strategy needs analysis. Under suitable model assumptions, the team gives an explicit value function solution and precisely describes the optimal strategy.
arxiv-2602-02068: Jemal Rogava and colleagues address the Cauchy problem for an abstract nonlinear coupled hyperbolic system. They propose a symmetric three-layer semi-discrete scheme with the term at the temporal midpoint, reducing the problem to a linear one at each step. Convergence is proved, with second-order accuracy. The scheme is applied to a one-dimensional Timoshenko beam system. By taking differences of Legendre polynomials, the resulting linear system is sparse and decoupled, and numerical experiments validate the approach.
arxiv-2602-02368:
S. Tchuiaga and 1 co-author examine the shape-changing maps of a geometry that loosens the rules of symplectic geometry, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is locally conformally symplectic, where the defining structure may be stretched by a varying factor. The authors study the flux map, a tool that measures how far such a map is from being Hamiltonian, meaning generated by an energy function.

Their results build exact sequences that pin down the Hamiltonian subgroup and give conditions for it to split neatly. They also prove versions of classic symplectic theorems, including a neighborhood theorem and a rigidity result for homotopies. A key role goes to the Lee form and its split into exact and harmonic parts. In the exact case they obtain energy-capacity bounds, a distance measure, and a twisted Calabi invariant for the general case.
arxiv-2602-02468:
Aiden Yiliu Li and 3 co-authors build a web agent that imitates human experience to finish long tasks on live websites, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous web agents still stumble on accurate element grounding, missing site-specific know-how, and shaky long-term tracking, especially over complex page structures.

Their agent, Avenir-Web, combines three ingredients. A mixture of grounding experts locates page elements more reliably. Experience-imitation planning injects procedural priors, the remembered steps humans use on familiar sites. A task-tracking checklist with adaptive memory keeps long jobs on course. On the Online-Mind2Web benchmark of live, user-centered tasks, Avenir-Web set a new open-source best. It significantly surpassed earlier open agents and matched top proprietary models. The result narrows the reliability gap for agents working on the real web.
arxiv-2602-02768:
Ronald Ogden and 2 co-authors compress video optically, before any electronics touch it, in a 2026 paper. Remote vision sensors must stream high-volume data over constrained channels in real time, and fast control systems destabilize without high sampling rates. Their sensing paradigm has an event camera observe the optically generated cosine transform of a scene, borrowing the transform trick modern video codecs use.

Computation-free compression happens in the optics themselves. Simulations compare this optically passive scheme against a standalone event camera under rate-distortion analysis, the standard trade-off between bits sent and reconstruction quality. The optical scheme wins across the board. Its advantage grows as the event camera's spatial resolution increases, the regime future sensors are heading toward. The work argues part of the compression pipeline can migrate from processors into lenses.
arxiv-2602-02968:
Extreme bursts of light in a semiconductor laser are brought under control by T. Wang and 8 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Such rogue events are rare, intense, and hard to predict in many physical systems. Optical setups offer a controlled place to study them, but triggering them deterministically has been difficult.

The team adds polarization-controlled optical feedback to a vertical-cavity laser. A waveplate inside a selective external cavity regulates how two light modes interact. That triggers heavy-tailed intensity fluctuations in one mode, with clear extreme-event signatures. The events arise from deterministic energy exchange between modes. Rotating the waveplate tunes their rate, intensity, and clustering. The setup offers a platform for studying extreme events in dissipative systems.
arxiv-2602-03068:
Collective creativity is given a cognitive foundation by Mirza Nayeem Ahmed and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. Simulation studies link social form to group results well. Creativity is harder, because novel ideas arise from cognitive mechanisms inside individuals, not only from how people are connected in a network or team form studied previously.

Their multi-level system gives agents a shared meaning vocabulary but other meaning network layouts. One generative setting tunes meaning modularity, producing individual differences in ideational breadth. When agents exchange traces of their ideation, two classic social-creativity patterns emerge without being imposed. Lower overlap before interaction predicts larger stimulation gains. Shared inspiration sources create network-level redundancy. The system supports mechanistic theory-building about cognition and social form together.
arxiv-2602-03268:
Toxic meaning that hides across image and text jointly is measured by Guanzong Wu, leading 3 other authors, with a graph-based system. Harmful content often looks benign in each modality alone, emerging only when meaning links combine. Their Toxicity Association Graphs model links between innocuous entities and latent toxic implications, turning that hidden form into something a detector can inspect and explain to moderators.

From those graphs comes a covertness metric, the first quantifiable measure of how concealed multimodal toxicity is. A new benchmark dataset captures high-covertness instances with nuanced cross-modal associations. Tests across low and high covertness regimes beat earlier methods. Results stay interpretable and auditable, which the authors frame as a base for context-aware explainable toxicity detection.
arxiv-2602-03368:
Best practices for retrieval-augmented generation in medicine are sought systematically by Liz Li, with 1 co-author. Retrieval-augmented generation has been adopted swiftly in industry. It pairs language models with external document search. No consensus exists, though, on which parts a system needs, how to organize them, or how to implement each one. That gap matters most for medical applications, where score and speed trade-offs carry clinical weight.

The authors analyze each part of a retrieval system and propose practical alternatives for each. Systematic reviews across three types of tasks follow. Those reviews reveal which choices improve the system and how language-model-based retrieval systems trade results against speed. The work aims at industrial practitioners building medical systems rather than at a single new model architecture.
arxiv-2602-03568:
Shubhabrata Das and Partha Sarathi Ghosh prove a stability result about the Haagerup property in group theory. Their 2026 paper concerns graph products, a construction that blends free and direct products by letting some subgroups commute according to a graph. The Haagerup property, also called Gromov's a-T-menability, says a group admits a well-behaved action on a Hilbert space.

The theorem states that a graph product of finitely many groups, each having the Haagerup property, again has the Haagerup property. Such permanence results matter because they let mathematicians build large new examples of Haagerup groups from smaller known ones. The graph product family includes free products and direct products as special cases, so the single proof covers both at once.
arxiv-2602-03668:
Robots can pretrain on human videos if the videos yield labels for the actions they show. Jung Min Lee and 7 co-authors improve those pseudo-labels in a 2026 paper with MVP-LAM, a latent action model trained across viewpoints. A latent action only supervises well if it stays informative about the true action, which single-view learning often fails to ensure.

MVP-LAM trains with a cross-viewpoint reconstruction objective: a latent action from one camera view has to predict what another view will show. That pressure strips out viewpoint-specific cues. On the Bridge V2 dataset, the learned actions share more mutual information with the true actions and predict actions better, even out of distribution. Pretraining robot policies on them improves downstream manipulation benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-03868:
Farm advisory services in India are going digital, but speech recognition stumbles on local languages and crop terminology. Chandrashekar M S and 2 co-authors benchmark automatic speech recognition for that setting in a 2026 paper, across Hindi, Telugu, and Odia. They evaluate nearly eleven thousand field recordings, each transcribed by up to ten different models.

Alongside ordinary error rates, the authors introduce an agriculture-weighted error rate and a domain utility score that penalize mistakes in the words that matter. Hindi performs best; Odia is hardest, reaching its best error rate only with speaker diarization. Choosing the best speaker after diarization cuts errors sharply on multi-speaker recordings. The paper catalogs recurring terminology errors and gives practical recommendations for low-resource agricultural speech systems.
arxiv-2602-04068:
Learned indexes promise fast distance answers on road networks. Gautam Choudhary and 3 co-authors ran the first broad empirical comparison in a 2026 survey paper. Exact algorithms like Dijkstra's are too slow for real-time, planet-scale queries, so indexes precompute or learn shortcuts.

Ten representative machine-learning techniques were benchmarked on thirteen real road networks. The study measured training time, query latency, storage, and accuracy, using both trajectory-derived and synthetic workloads. No prior survey had compared these methods head to head under one protocol. The results give system builders practical guidance on which learned index fits which deployment constraints.
arxiv-2602-04768:
Maya Bechler-Speicher and 7 co-authors present a recipe for billion-scale graph foundation models in a 2026 paper. Graphs underpin many applications, but foundation models that pretrain once and adapt cheaply, as in language and vision, have lagged for real-world graph data.

Their framework, GraphBFF, centers on a flexible transformer architecture built for heterogeneous graphs, where nodes and edges come in many types. The paper gives methods for batching, pretraining, and fine-tuning at that scale, plus neural scaling laws for such graphs. A billion-parameter model trained by the recipe was tested on ten real downstream tasks involving unseen graphs. It beat baselines consistently, sometimes by large margins, including in few-shot settings with very little task data.
arxiv-2602-04868:
Yannick Denker and Alexander Gepperth release a benchmark suite for continual reinforcement learning with simulated robots in a 2026 paper. Continual learning agents must master a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier policies, a challenge standard benchmarks rarely test under realistic physics.

Their suite, CRoSS, runs in the Gazebo simulator on two platforms. A wheeled robot with lidar, camera, and bumper sensors handles line-following and object-pushing tasks with many variations. A seven-joint arm performs goal-reaching under high-level and low-level control. Faster kinematics-only variants of the arm tasks run far more quickly when sensors are unneeded. The suite is extensible and ships in a container for reproducibility. Baseline results for standard algorithms are reported.
arxiv-2602-05168:
AU Mic b is a young hot Neptune whose dayside heat can be read from the dip in light when it passes behind its star. Kevin I Collins and 13 co-authors report that measurement in this 2026 exoplanet paper, submitted to the AAS journals, using the Spitzer Space Telescope in the infrared. A transit observed by the same telescope pinned down the system's geometry first.

The eclipse they tentatively detect is deeper than expected, implying a dayside brightness temperature around 1,031 kelvin, far above the roughly 606 kelvin equilibrium value. The team works through candidate explanations, from poor heat redistribution and gravitational contraction to stellar pulsations, instrument systematics, and the choice of prior, and finds none of them likely. Handling correlated noise in the data proved delicate, requiring the systematics to be split into slow and fast parts. Confirmation will need the James Webb Space Telescope.
arxiv-2602-05468:
A robot hand that touches itself can confuse its own contact with contact from an object, which risks damage during fine tasks. Pranav Ponnivalavan, Satoshi Funabashi, and 3 co-authors build on sensory attenuation, the brain process that dims expected self-touch so new stimuli stand out. Their framework, called TaSA, learns in two phases how a robot's own motions create touch signals.

In the first phase, the system models self-touch on its own, apart from object contact. In the second phase, that model joins motion learning, so signals from real object contact get more weight. The team tested TaSA on delicate insertion jobs: placing a pencil lead in a pencil, sliding coins into a slot, and clipping a paper clip onto a sheet. Across varied sizes, positions, and angles, TaSA-trained policies beat baseline methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2602-05868:
Judging whether AI generated code is secure usually falls to static analysis tools, and Ehsan Firouzi and Mohammad Ghafari test whether those tools deserve that trust. They reviewed more than a thousand language model generated code samples, built a human validated ground truth, and compared two widely used tools, CodeQL and Semgrep, against it.

About three fifths of the samples were genuinely secure, and the tools aggregate rates looked close. Per sample analysis told a different story: only about two thirds of each tool reports matched the ground truth. The authors argue that static analyzers alone are unreliable evaluators of code security, and that expert feedback is essential. They propose a framework that stores human feedback persistently in a retrieval augmented pipeline, so models can reuse past corrections for secure generation and vulnerability detection. The paper targets teams that benchmark code models.
arxiv-2602-06068:
Two classic families of fractions, harmonic numbers and central binomial coefficients, meet in new summation formulas from Micheal Bataille and Robert Frontczak. Harmonic numbers are the running totals of one over each whole number. Central binomial coefficients count ways to choose half of a set.

The pair study sums that mix inverse binomial coefficients with harmonic numbers in two new classes. They also give step-by-step recursive answers for two power sums built from these parts. One sum weights each term by a power of its index. The other adds a harmonic number factor as well. Such formulas help check identities that appear across combinatorics.
arxiv-2602-06668:
Keita Ishizuka studies vectorial functions over finite fields, the many-input, many-output maps that sit inside block ciphers and other cryptographic tools. Two such functions can look different yet be the same up to reshuffling by affine maps, and the symmetry group of a function measures how much hidden sameness it carries. The paper asks how common such symmetries are among all possible functions.

Ishizuka proves that almost all of these functions, as the field grows, have no nontrivial symmetries of this extended-affine kind at all. As a result, the number of truly distinct functions matches the naive counting estimate, and the chance that two randomly picked functions are secretly equivalent is smaller than any exponential. The result supports picking cipher components at random, since symmetric cases turn out to be vanishingly rare.
arxiv-2602-06868:
Xudong Sun, Armand Jordana, Massimo Fornasier, Jalal Etesami, and Majid Khadiv bring a global optimization method into robotics. Zero-order methods, which plan trajectories and policies without gradients, have recently gained attention, but the popular ones tend to settle into local optima because they estimate gradients locally. Consensus-based optimization instead drives a population of candidates toward agreement, and is guaranteed to reach the global optimum under mild assumptions.

The paper explains the theory and the intuition that separates this method from the local ones. It then tests the approach on three hard trajectory problems: a long-horizon task, a balancing task for a highly underactuated system, and a high-dimensional task with only a final cost. In all three, consensus-based optimization reached lower costs than existing methods, opening a new framework for global trajectory planning.
arxiv-2602-06968:
Xubo Luo and four co-authors solve positioning for autonomous lunar landing, where real-time six-degree-of-freedom location is mission-critical. Visual odometry drifts without bound, while map-based location fails on texture-poor or dark ground. Their framework, KANLoc, tightly couples odometry with a light absolute pose regressor to get the best of both.

At its core sits a Kolmogorov-Arnold network that learns the map from image features to map coordinates, yielding sparse but highly trusted global pose anchors. Those anchors feed a bundle adjustment setup, canceling drift while keeping local motion sharp. On synthetic and real lunar landing data, KANLoc cut translation error by 32 percent and rotation error by 45 percent on average, running at 15 frames per second or better.
arxiv-2602-07268:
Regular black holes avoid singularities, but how much energy do their vibrations carry?  S.  C.  Ulhoa and two co-authors study axial perturbations of regular black holes, reviewing their stability and quasinormal modes, then computing the gravitational energy those perturbations hold.

Using the teleparallel equivalent of general relativity, which supplies a well-defined energy expression, they evaluate the energy to second order in the perturbation and express it through the quasinormal mode functions.  The result ties the dynamical ringing of a regular black hole to the energy its perturbations carry.  Relativists get a concrete energy accounting for spacetimes whose singularity-free nature makes such questions subtle.
arxiv-2602-07768:
Teaching a small vision model to tell similar bird species or car models apart is hard when the teacher is a huge vision-language model. Qiuming Luo and three co-authors propose PAND, a two-stage distillation method that first calibrates meaning with adaptive prompt-aware anchors, then transfers local decision structure between neighboring examples.

Splitting those jobs beats fixed prompts and global matching: their ResNet-18 student reaches 76.09 percent accuracy on the CUB-200 bird benchmark, beating a strong baseline by 3.4 points, and leads on three other fine-grained benchmarks. The paper gives practitioners a practical recipe for squeezing large-model knowledge into lightweight classifiers.
arxiv-2602-07968:
Stochastic systems with heavy-tailed noise can jump suddenly, and truncating those jumps, as in some tuning algorithms, changes when the system first escapes a region. Xingyu Wang and Chang-Han Rhee analyze first-exit times for a stochastic gap equation and its truncated variant, where each step is capped at a threshold.

By connecting large-deviation theory with metastability, they characterize the joint distribution of exit times and exit locations precisely. As the truncation threshold varies, a discrete hierarchy of phase shifts in exit times appears, illustrating the catastrophe principle in which rare large jumps dominate. Probabilists and machine-learning theorists studying heavy-tailed stochastic gradient descent gain exact asymptotics for a practically motivated model.
arxiv-2602-08368:
Turning an idea into a video usually means many hidden reruns and tangled choices. Zhuoyun Zheng and eight co-authors present T2VTree, a visual tool that shows thought-to-video authoring as a tree. Their arXiv paper targets creators who want to compare, branch, and reuse their exploration instead of starting over.

Each tree node bundles an editable plan, covering intent, inputs, workflow, prompts, and settings, together with the video it produced. Collaborating agents turn step-level intent into a visible, editable plan before anything runs. In-place preview and stitching let users assemble multi-scene videos without leaving the workspace. Case studies and a user study show steadier refinement and practical reuse. Readers get a calmer way to direct generative video.
arxiv-2602-08968:
World-model research suffers from scattered, one-off code that is hard to reuse or compare. Lucas Maes and six co-authors introduce stable-worldmodel, a modular, tested, and documented toolkit for learning compact predictive models of how environments change. It bundles data-collection tools, standard test worlds, planning methods, and baselines in one place, with tunable visual and physical traits in each world.

Those controls support robustness and continual-learning studies that one-off code makes awkward. As a demo, the team uses the toolkit to study zero-shot robustness in DINO-WM, a world model built on self-supervised vision features. The project aims to cut bugs and make world-model results genuinely comparable.
arxiv-2602-09268:
Spread transformers usually feed text into making through focus layers plus a tuning setup driven by a pooled text vector, yet recent models drop tuning fully. Nikita Starodubcev and eight co-authors ask whether tuning is truly needed, and whether it can help. Their study finds the pooled vector, used in the usual way, adds little, hinting focus alone usually carries prompt facts truly.

Used another way, however, the pooled vector pays off: as guidance, it allows steerable shifts toward more wanted traits. The trick needs no training, is plain to run, and costs tiny run time, applying across spread models. It brings gains to text-to-image and text-to-video making and to image editing, saving a dropped guiding path.
arxiv-2602-09368:
Wei-Chen Li and Glen Chou tackle robot manipulation where contact makes gradients break down. Gradient-based simulation can tune controllers well, but hybrid contact dynamics often yield broken or vanishing gradients. Smoothing the dynamics to restore them creates a model gap that can fail on real hardware. Their 2026 paper plans with smoothed dynamics while explicitly measuring and compensating for the smoothing error, aiming for formal guarantees under the true nonsmooth dynamics.

The method smooths both contact dynamics and contact geometry inside a convex-optimization-based simulator, then treats the deviation as a set-valued mismatch. That mismatch enters the design of time-varying affine feedback policies through analytical reachable sets, enforcing constraints robustly while using only the smoothed model's gradients. Tests on planar pushing, object rotation, and in-hand tasks show proven constraint keeping with fewer safety violations and smaller goal errors than baselines.
arxiv-2602-09468:
Mojtaba Asadollahi and Mohammad Hossein Zarei ask what truly powers the quantum edge in quantum illumination: entanglement, discord, or their interplay? Their 2026 paper studies probe states whose marginals are maximally mixed, with a fully mixed environment, a setting where the quantum edge equals the discord spent on illumination. A conditional extremal analysis then maps what edge values are reachable for given entanglement and discord.

At fixed discord, high entanglement confines the edge to high values, making it sufficient for a strong edge. At fixed entanglement, low discord caps the edge at low values, making high discord necessary for a strong edge. The pattern holds across distinct correlation measures, from relative entropy to Bures entanglement and geometric discord, suggesting a robust feature rather than a quirk of one measure. In high noise, the edge grows linearly with starting discord, marking discord as the key shield against noise.
arxiv-2602-09568:
Ping Li and two co-authors systematically revisit critical orbits of test particles around black holes in their 2026 paper. Four backgrounds are covered: Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, Kerr, and Kerr-Newman spacetimes. Critical orbits are identified directly from the root structure of the radial equation, rather than through indirect arguments.

The paper gives explicit expressions linking energy, angular momentum, and charge-to-mass ratio to the critical radius, plus explicit formulas for the critical orbits in each case. Special attention goes to relationships among photon spheres, black hole shadows, and critical null geodesics, three faces of light and matter circling at the edge of capture. Extensive numerical results support the analysis across all four backgrounds.
arxiv-2602-09668:
Eric Sillekens and Ronit Sohanpal study carbon dioxide absorption in hollow-core fibre transmission in their 2026 paper. Gas lines from carbon dioxide degrade the transmitted signal, and the authors address that absorption with spectral pre-equalisation, digitally post-compensating the gas-line effect.

In reported tests, the technique cuts the quality-factor penalty by five and a half decibels, beating a long conventional equaliser by over a decibel. Spectral pre-equalisation thus offers a compact digital fix for gas absorption in hollow-core fibre, preserving signal quality without heavier equalisation hardware.
arxiv-2602-10068:
Leptons can bind into three-particle and four-particle systems, and their energy levels test quantum electrodynamics in a few-body setting. A 2026 paper led by A. V. Eskin, with three co-authors, calculates the ground-state energy levels of such bound states. The calculation uses the variational method with Gaussian basis functions.

Hyperfine structure enters through pairwise spin-spin interactions between particles. Though brief, the paper delivers the ground-state levels for both the three-particle and four-particle cases, giving a compact reference for few-particle lepton systems in quantum electrodynamics.
arxiv-2602-10168:
Cell-focused foundation models usually see single cells and are judged on tech metrics far from drug work. A 2026 paper from the Scienta Team, with eleven named authors, offers EVA, the first foundation model of immunology and inflammation spanning species and data types. EVA unifies transcriptomics data across species, platforms, and scales, and folds in histology data to produce rich, unified patient profiles.

Scaling laws hold clearly: larger models and more compute improve both training and downstream scores. A suite of thirty-nine tasks spans the drug pipeline, from zero-shot target and gene prediction to cross-species shifts, patient grouping, and treatment response. EVA leads state-of-the-art baselines in every task category, and insight work reveals linked features across species and tools.
arxiv-2602-10368:
Promise constraint satisfaction asks how many weaker constraints can be met when nearly all stronger ones hold. Robust versions of the problem have resisted clean answers. A 2026 paper led by Joshua Brakensiek, with four co-authors, continues earlier work with Guruswami and Sandeep. For one-in-three satisfiability versus not-all-equal satisfiability with negations, the authors prove hardness under the Unique Games conjecture. It shows the exponential loss of the earlier BGS algorithm is unavoidable for alternating-threshold polymorphisms, unlike the polynomial loss for majority ones.

For any Boolean promise problem admitting majority polymorphisms, they give an algorithm meeting nearly all weaker constraints when nearly all stronger ones are satisfiable. It generalizes the Charikar-Makarychev-Makarychev method for two-satisfiability and matches the best trade-off possible under the conjecture. The method extends to larger domains at an extra logarithmic cost, and robust satisfiability survives adding equality constraints.
arxiv-2602-10568:
Lev McKinney and six co-authors offer a simpler route to making language models forget in a 2026 paper. Standard training can leave models producing outputs their trainers deem unacceptable, and unlearning a forget set often damages conduct on data meant to be retained. The trade-off between forgetting and retention is the central hardness.

The paper shows that a few uphill Gauss-Newton steps computed from the forget set alone give a conceptually simple, state-of-the-art unlearning method. Computing such steps for large models is nontrivial, so the approach leans on Kronecker-factored bend approximations. The combined method, K-FADE, is presented as a useful balance: strong forgetting with limited collateral damage to retained capabilities.
arxiv-2602-10668:
Dong-Dong Dong and four co-authors sharpen monogamy inequalities for multiqubit entanglement in a 2026 paper. Monogamy limits how entanglement can be shared among parties, and the broad Coffman-Kundu-Wootters rule bounds that sharing. Stronger versions promise tighter constraints on many-part states.

The paper proves two new rules. A weighted strong monogamy rule modulates shares with weights rather than powers. A maximum rest version builds from only the largest many-part entanglement. The rest of the latter cleanly tells apart split states. Cases with four-qubit mixed and five-qubit pure states show the trade-offs among entanglement parts, giving theorists sharper tools for mapping many-part entanglement.
arxiv-2602-10768:
Dmitriy Kudryavcev and two co-authors construct exact dynamical regular black holes in a 2026 paper. Starting from a Vaidya-type shape with a radially dependent mass function, they regularize Kiselev answers through a physically motivated modification of the energy density profile. The result is a class of fully analytic answers for black holes formed by gravitational collapse.

The spacetimes are nonsingular, with a de Sitter core and finite bend invariants at the center. Their matter content follows a broad polytropic equation of state whose index is fixed by the regularization scheme. Within the system, the authors obtain exact dynamical generalizations of several well-known regular black hole answers. Those give theorists analytic models of collapse that avoid singularities without sacrificing motion.
arxiv-2602-11068:
Strong lenses bend light, but their surroundings may bend the models too. William J. Gottemoller and thirteen co-authors measure eighty-nine confirmed lenses from the AGEL survey, pairing each deflector's Einstein mass with its halo setting from galaxy density maps. Nearly half sit in cluster settings, while only a small share have cluster-scale Einstein masses.

Einstein mass and density correlate only weakly, which the authors link to selection bias toward galaxy-scale lenses and to faint arcs that hide large radii. AGEL deflectors also sit in denser fields than control fields. The study offers a way to flag setting effects in lens models and publishes lens settings and sky maps for all eighty-nine systems.
arxiv-2602-11468:
Robot task planners usually assume every needed object is already known. Raihan Islam Arnob and five co-authors build a planning frame for missing objects using learning-informed object search actions. Each such action is a policy to find and retrieve one object, informed by model-based expected costs.

High-level planning treats those actions as fixed, interleaving search and execution into plans that are effective, sound, and complete despite doubt. The design stays compatible with current full-knowledge solvers. Tests in simulated homes and in the real world beat non-learned and learned rivals on recall and meal preparation tasks. The work lets planners ask what is needed and when to look for it.
arxiv-2602-11968:
Tracking how word meanings shift over time needs corpora spread across years and languages, yet multilingual resources beyond a dozen major languages remain scarce. Mariia Fedorova and two co-authors present DHPLT, an open collection of diachronic corpora in 41 diverse languages, built from web-crawled datasets with crawl timestamps as approximate creation dates. The collection covers three periods, 2011 to 2015, 2020 to 2021, and 2024 to the present, with 1 million documents per period for each language.

Alongside the texts, the authors provide pre-computed word and token embeddings plus lexical substitutions for chosen target words, while leaving other researchers free to pick their own targets from the same data. DHPLT aims to fill the gap in multilingual diachronic resources and open new experimental setups for semantic change research. All resources are publicly available, sorted by language.
arxiv-2602-12268:
AI agents now handle real tasks through long chats and tool calls, but training them by reinforcement learning is awkward when goals lack checkable rewards. Zhen Zhang led this work with 13 co-authors, presenting CM2, a frame that swaps outcome rewards for checklist rewards. Each turn's intended behaviour is split into fine binary criteria with evidence grounding and structured notes, turning open judging into steadier classification.

Rewards stay sparse while evaluation criteria stay dense, balancing stability and signal. Training runs in a scalable language-model-simulated tool world, avoiding costly real tool engineering. From an 8-billion-parameter base on 8,000 examples, CM2 beats supervised fine-tuning by 8 points on tau-Bench, 10 on BFCL-V4, and 12 on ToolSandbox, matching or beating similar open baselines.
arxiv-2602-12468:
Diffusion language models generate text globally rather than word by word, but their continuous latent dynamics make discrete rules hard to enforce. Jinwoo Kim led this work with two co-authors, asking how to guarantee outputs such as a JSON file matching a given schema. Their training-free guidance method steers continuous diffusion models to satisfy formal syntactic constraints expressed as regular expressions.

The method builds an analytic score estimating the chance that a latent state decodes to a valid string accepted by a given regular expression. It then uses its gradient to guide sampling, with no auxiliary classifiers to train. Denoising targets the base model conditioned on syntactic validity. Implemented as Diffinity on the PLAID model and tested on 180 regular-expression constraints, it reaches 68 to 96 percent satisfaction. It incurs only a small perplexity cost, beating autoregressive constrained decoding on both satisfaction and quality.
arxiv-2602-12668:
Computing a sparse subgraph of a directed graph that proves connectivity is central to streaming and distributed graph methods. Ho-Lin Chen led this work with three co-authors, studying space cost of that job in terms of independence number. A k-node strong connectivity certificate is a subgraph H. For every pair of distinct nodes s and t, the count of pairwise internally node-disjoint paths from s to t in H is at least k. Otherwise it matches the count in the original graph.

Prior work focused on narrow graph classes, since directed connectivity problems are hard in general. This paper gives space bounds for certificates in graphs of bounded independence number, in both streaming and distributed models, with matching upper and lower bounds in key regimes. Results show independence number is a useful gauge for taming directed connectivity certification.
arxiv-2602-12868:
Spencer's six standard deviations theorem says signs can be chosen to keep many sums small, and a complex analogue has been conjectured. Tomasz Kobos and Marin Varivoda state the conjecture precisely. For vectors in complex n-space with entries bounded by one, a sign vector with unit-modulus entries should keep every inner product within the square root of n. That bound is sharp, as Hadamard matrices show.

Should the conjecture prove true in dimension n, it would also fix the Banach-Mazur distance between complex l1 and l-infinity spaces at the square root of n. The authors prove the conjecture for dimensions two and three, settling those distances, and verify a related conjecture about distances between complex lp spaces in dimension two. The result completes the picture for all such distances in two dimensions.
arxiv-2602-12968:
Chatbots that recommend without being asked must guess intent from behaviour and context, a zero-query task where semantic gaps hurt. Junhua Liu and five co-authors propose RGAlign-Rec, a closed-loop framework pairing a language-model semantic reasoner with a query-enhanced ranking model. The gap between discrete user features and knowledge-base intents, and the mismatch between generic model outputs and ranking goals, are tackled together.

Ranking-guided alignment, a multi-stage training paradigm, feeds downstream ranking signals back to refine the model's latent reasoning. On a large Shopee industrial dataset, the framework gains 0.12% in GAUC, cutting error rate by 3.52% relatively and lifting Recall@3 by 0.56%. Live A/B tests add up: the ranking model alone lifts click-through rate by 0.98%, with alignment adding 0.13% more, validating the closed-loop design in production.
arxiv-2602-13068:
Hot plasmas at kinetic scales, where small-angle Coulomb collisions rule, are modelled by the Vlasov-Poisson-Landau system. Daniel Finn and three co-authors present a structure-preserving number system combining particle-in-cell discretisation with discrete gradient time integrators. The scheme conserves mass, momentum, and energy by construction, plus monotonic mess production, in both continuous and discrete forms.

The conservative integrator serves both the Hamiltonian Vlasov-Poisson part and the dissipative Landau part, implemented with the PETSc library to show the preserved traits. For plasma mock run, structure preservation is not cosmetic: schemes that leak mass or energy, or reverse mess, can produce plausible-looking but unphysical results. This system aims to keep long kinetic mock runs honest by construction.
arxiv-2602-13268:
AI systems that decide for people need more than accuracy; they need a sense of what is right, and that sense is still poorly measured. This paper compares ways to build ethical skill into decision models, then adds a new yardstick called Expected Moral Shortfall. The yardstick models the risk of loss in the least moral cases, and the model is steered to shrink that shortfall while keeping its performance up.

The measure is tested on two data sets against rival methods, and the paper closes by weighing performance, complexity, and the scale of ethical skill against real social impact. Trade-offs are the point: a model can look strong on paper while still failing the cases where morals matter most. Aisha Aijaz leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13368:
Beauty judgments often favor average faces, a finding shown for women's faces in earlier work. This study tests whether the same holds for men's faces. It uses faces from the Chicago Face Database, morphed into average faces for low, medium, and high width-ratio groups, each built from 96 or 97 photos. Each average face was then shifted in width ratio across levels in both directions, yielding 21 faces for comparison.

In forced-choice trials, participants picked the more beautiful face in each pair, and a Bayesian analysis inferred which width ratio was judged most beautiful. Results support averageness as attractive in male faces too, with care taken to control image artifacts and to note ethnicity as a possible moderating factor. Theresa Tennstedt leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13568:
Language models increasingly meet social information: other agents' answers, tool outputs, or human recommendations. Humans weigh such inputs by source credibility and consensus strength, and this paper asks whether models do the same, and whether they favor human feedback over feedback from other models. Four instruction-tuned models faced three binary decision tasks, reading comprehension, multi-step reasoning, and moral judgment, with prior responses attributed to friends, human experts, or other models.

Across tasks, models conformed far more to responses labeled as human experts, even when those signals were wrong, and revised answers toward experts more readily than toward other models. Expert framing thus acts as a strong prior for current models, a credibility-sensitive social influence spanning decision domains. Anooshka Bajaj leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13768:
Relativistic spin-momentum locking was proven in materials with broken time order and zero net pull in the slow limit, such as altermagnets and tilted magnets. Using density functional theory, this paper shows the effect in ferromagnets, covering a broad class of magnetic matter with magnetic sites linked by rotation sameness and set beside fcc nickel. In strontium ruthenate, lopsided exchange yields spin canting at right angles to the easy axis. In all other cases spin canting is forbidden, yet relativistic locking still adds sizably in momentum space.

Sample ferromagnets including strontium ruthenate, chromium telluride and chromium arsenide, half-Heusler manganese platinum antimonide, and fcc nickel show strong effects. Minor parts of these ferromagnets host locking similar to altermagnets, while lopsided manganese platinum antimonide hosts relativistic p-wave patterns. Ferromagnets' larger bandwidths promise an even-wave platform. Xujia Gong leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13868:
Udhaya Srinivasan and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv paper on an AI helper for next-generation radio networks. AI-native radio access networks are hard for engineers to run in real time, and small firms often lack local expertise. Prior tools helped plan radio and core parts, but not joint control of radio and edge AI.

Their assistant handles turn-based chats about layered AI-RAN problems, with a user dashboard, an intelligence layer, and a knowledge layer. In validation it scored 78% on service design, 89% on operating AI-RAN tools, and 67% on tuning performance, with a mean reply time of 13 seconds. The authors note hallucination risks, but see lower running costs for small enterprise users.
arxiv-2602-13968:
Ngoc Cuong Nguyen, writing alone, offers a 2026 arXiv paper on the fine local behavior of functions in complex Sobolev spaces. The setting is a bounded open set in complex n-space, and the main tool is a functional capacity inspired by a global version due to Vigny in 2007.

The author proves a sharp inequality linking this capacity to the Bedford-Taylor capacity for plurisubharmonic functions, shows the new capacity is a Choquet capacity, and proves an Alexander-Taylor type inequality. Those steps strengthen results of Dinh, Marinescu, and Vu, and of Vigny and Vu. A Moser-Trudinger type inequality in the space is then characterized by a volume-capacity inequality.
arxiv-2602-14168:
Guilherme S. L. Fabris and four co-authors study a 2026 arXiv carbon material called hydrogen-substituted graphdiyne. This porous three-dimensional framework has drawn interest for tunable properties, yet how its stacking order shapes behavior was largely unexplored. The paper runs first-principles calculations across stacking sequences.

The AA and ABC stackings prove most favorable in energy, with AA as the global minimum, matching recent experiments. The material is an indirect semiconductor with a band gap of 0.89 eV, governed by interlayer coupling and van der Waals forces. Its optical absorption spans visible to ultraviolet light, pointing to uses in optoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2602-14468:
Chang Liu and five co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv reinforcement learning method that controls response length. Reward-driven training has strengthened language models, but it can also produce excessively long responses, inflating latency and compute costs. Older length controls lean on set heuristic reward shaping, which can clash with task goals and need fragile tuning.

LACONIC enforces a target token budget during training through an augmented objective combining task reward with a length-based cost. The cost scale adapts throughout training to balance brevity against task performance, with a theoretical guarantee supporting the method. Across math reasoning models and datasets, LACONIC preserved or improved pass@1 while cutting output length by over 50%, and held out-of-domain performance with 44% fewer tokens.
arxiv-2602-14968:
Wang and colleagues address a gap in automatic 3D scene building for robot training. Most methods place objects but ignore ties such as contact, support, balance, and containment. Their system, PhyScensis, pairs a language-model agent with a solver run by a physics engine. The agent puts forward assets with spatial and physical tags. The solver builds them, and solver feedback drives more rounds.

Chance-based code keeps scenes steady, while a second rule weighs steadiness against spatial ties. The system stays easy to steer through text and numbers such as relative spots. In tests it beats prior methods on scene richness, visual quality, and true-to-life accuracy, giving one pipeline for dense, lifelike scenes for robot hand work like shelves and packed boxes.
arxiv-2602-15768:
Reymondet and colleagues quantify how fine-scale sea surface temperature shifts drive latent heat flux shifts over the Southern Ocean. Latent heat flux is a main path for ocean-air exchange of heat and moisture. Yet the role of shifts at scales of 100 kilometres or less remains poorly known. The team uses a year-long, global, fully coupled ocean-air run at kilometre-scale resolution.

Year-mean flux in eddy-rich regions hits about 215 watts per square metre. That is roughly three times the eddy-poor value. Ocean mesoscale and submesoscale shifts account for up to about 80 percent of total flux variance in eddy-rich sectors. In eddy-poor ones, the share falls to 10 percent. Strong submesoscale fronts force a local secondary circulation reaching into the mid-troposphere. ERA5 reanalysis largely misses those fine ocean scales, muting the air response.
arxiv-2602-15868:
Boman models language model failure with a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine. Each tape stands for one stage of the pipeline. The stages are input text, tokens, word lists, model weights, activations, chance scores, and output text. This frame lets each fault be traced to the stage where it starts.

Token splits can hide letter patterns that counting needs. That shows one plain cause of a slip on a trivial task. Chain of thought helps by moving work out onto the output tape. But that move has hard limits too. Boman offers the model as a testable rival to shape metaphors. It adds principled error study to plain scaling laws.
arxiv-2602-16068:
Yanni Bills and J. S. Wettlaufer connect a stripped-down chaotic model to real wind reversals in lab convection. The Lorenz equations are a severe truncation of the equations for Rayleigh-Benard convection. The authors study a stochastic form of those equations. It models how warm boundary layers interact with the core flow in the lab setup. Long runs, out of reach for the full equations, yield a spread of times between lobe switches with a skewed, multifractal shape.

In the Gaussian frequency range, the runs mirror lab measures, and classic checks show Brownian second-moment stats. Closer looks reveal a nonlinear moment-exponent function, hence multifractality. A simple two-scale Cantor-cascade check reproduces these traits. The authors conclude that multiplicative intermittency, a hallmark of turbulence, strongly shapes the stats. That makes the stochastic Lorenz system a faithful low-dimensional stand-in for mean-wind reversals.
arxiv-2602-16168:
Supravat Sarkar proves a conjecture of Miyanishi about endomorphisms of varieties. The setting is a quasi-projective variety over a field, with a birational endomorphism that is injective outside a closed subset of codimension at least two. Sarkar shows such a map must be an automorphism, a result that generalizes an old theorem of Ax and settles Miyanishi conjecture. The statement is short, but its force lies in how little it assumes.

A key step is a finiteness result on class groups, interesting in its own right. For readers in algebraic geometry, the proof turns a local injectivity condition, failing only on a small subset, into a global conclusion that the map is invertible everywhere. The paper thus closes a long-standing question with a clean theorem, while supplying a finiteness tool that may serve other problems about varieties and their endomorphisms.
arxiv-2602-16468:
Jung Min Choi, Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi, and Lars Schmidt-Thieme propose HPMixer, a layered patching mixer for time series work. In long-term forecasting, capturing both repeat patterns and rest dynamics matters. HPMixer models cycles and rest in a split yet complementary way.

The cycle part uses a learned cycle module enhanced with a nonlinear channel-wise multilayer perceptron for greater expressiveness. The rest part passes through a learned stationary wavelet transform to extract stable, shift-invariant frequency-domain representations. A channel-mixing encoder then models explicit inter-channel dependencies, while a two-level non-overlapping patching mechanism captures coarse- and fine-scale rest variations.
