By combining split cycle modelling with structured, multi-scale rest learning, HPMixer offers an effective framework. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show it achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance against recent baselines.
arxiv-2602-16568:
Ziyun Chen, Jerry Li, Kevin Tian, and Yusong Zhu separate two models of sparse recovery. The task is finding the support of a sparse signal from few measurements. In the oblivious model, the guarantee need hold only for each fixed signal in turn. In the adaptive model, it must hold for all signals at once. The distinction matters for variable selection, where the goal is to name the right variables.

Under the oblivious model, the optimal error is reachable in near-linear time with a modest sample count. Under the adaptive model, far more samples are necessary for any algorithm to reach the same bound. That split contrasts with the standard squared-error setting. There, the smaller sample count suffices even adaptively. The paper also opens a partially adaptive model with nontrivial guarantees.
arxiv-2602-16868:
Joheen Chakraborty and co-authors present the first systematic study of minute-to-hours stochastic variability in the X-ray light of tidal disruption events, using XMM-Newton data and Fourier methods. They measure spectral traits, power spectral densities, fractional variability amplitudes, and energy dependence for eighteen events spanning fifty-four observations, split between thermal disk-dominated states and nonthermal hard X-ray corona states.

Events with coronae prove more variable with steeper power spectra, indicating longer correlation timescales. That state-transition behavior resembles X-ray binaries, which vary more in the hard state than the soft state. Yet newborn disruption coronae show flatter spectra and softer energy spectra than long-lived active galactic nucleus counterparts. Thermal event variability rises with photon energy, consistent with local temperature fluctuations boosted in the Wien tail, offering a probe of newborn accretion flow microphysics.
arxiv-2602-17068:
Xiaocai Zhang led a three-author team designing traffic signals for corridors used by many kinds of travelers, not just cars. Buses and trams deserve priority too, yet most signal control still scores vehicle flow alone. The paper presents STDSH-MARL, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework trained centrally and run locally, built around a dual-stage hypergraph attention mechanism that links signals across space and time.

A hybrid action space sets both the next signal phase and its green duration, so timing adapts to live conditions. Tests on a corridor network across five traffic scenarios cut tram waiting time substantially and consistently, while bus gains varied more by scenario. Against strong baselines the method won overall, and ablations singled out temporal hyperedges as the biggest contributor. The work maps the trade-off among network efficiency, tram priority, and bus service.
arxiv-2602-17268:
Weiyu Wu led a large team reporting sixteen early-phase type Ia supernovae from the pilot survey of the Wide Field Survey Telescope. The sample spans the survey's early months and includes three supernovae with early-excess emission features. Discovery magnitudes sat well below peak brightness, and color indices scattered widely in roughly the first ten days, signaling diverse early photometric behavior.

The early-excess objects showed relatively brighter peaks and longer rise times than their peers. The authors argue current theoretical models need further refinement to capture early photometric evolution fully. Drawing on high-cadence multi-band data, they stress that early near-ultraviolet observations are indispensable for pinning down explosion mechanisms and progenitor systems of type Ia supernovae.
arxiv-2602-17368:
Abhishek Padhy led a fourteen-author team programming polarization singularities in a photonic-crystal laser. Handling optical singularities in nanophotonic sources is usually limited by fixed resonator geometry. The team dodges that limit, showing all-optical control of such points in real space while keeping a momentum-space vortex from a symmetry-protected bound state in the continuum.

A shaped optical pump creates a smooth mesoscopic potential, changing slowly against the lattice period. That potential traps a Bloch band with negative mass into lasing states. Envelope functions, and thus far-field textures, follow the pump shape. Using a honeycomb crystal, the team gets room-temperature telecom-band lasing. The singularities sit pinned to key points of that envelope, changeable in number and place by pump shaping, while the intrinsic vortex stays fixed. Results agree in numbers with a math account joining Bloch modes with that theory.
arxiv-2602-17468:
T. C. Wilson led a four-author team on tolerances to driver-witness misalignment in a quasilinear plasma wakefield accelerator. Plasma machines can push particles to high energy with strong fields, and they can be staged or run over long distances. Proton drivers are prized because one stage alone may reach very high energy. In the quasilinear case, the plasma wake is only partly cleared out.

The team looks at what happens when driver and witness beams fail to line up. Their models track sideways motion of the witness bunch and link its spread to how well emittance survives. A single measure, based on witness density after phase mixing, sums up that survival. Tests with particle-in-cell runs set to AWAKE Run 2c values match the models closely. The result gives labs a way to set limits on alignment for AWAKE and similar schemes.
arxiv-2602-17568:
Sofiane Ennadir led a five-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper warning that time series preprocessing deserves more care. Normalization and scaling are basic steps in time series modeling, yet their effect on Transformer models lacked formal analysis. The paper gives the first formal account of how instance-based and global scaling affect Transformer expressivity for time series learning. A new framework measures how well a model separates similar from dissimilar inputs in representation space.

Using that framework, the authors derive theoretical bounds for Standard and Min-Max scaling. The normalization choice can strongly affect representational capacity, depending on task and data. Tests on classification and forecasting benchmarks with Transformer models confirm the theory. No single normalization method wins consistently, and in some cases skipping normalization entirely performs best. The findings call for principled normalization choices tailored to each task and data set, rather than habit.
arxiv-2602-17768:
Boda Lin and team introduce KPM-Bench, a benchmark for fine-grained motion-centric video understanding. Video captioning models still struggle to describe fine motion details and suffer severe hallucination, above all for motion-centric videos where limb dynamics matter yet get neglected. The team attacks both the data gap and the evaluation gap.

An automated pipeline joins kinematic-based motion computation with linguistic parsing to decompose and describe complex human motions in detail. The benchmark holds fine-grained video-caption pairs on limb-level dynamics, diverse question-answer pairs on motion understanding, and a curated set to assess hallucination in motion descriptions. A linguistically grounded extraction algorithm, MoPE, yields a precise hallucination metric independent of large vision-language models, and folding MoPE into GRPO post-training cuts hallucination markedly.
arxiv-2602-17868:
Vasilii Feofanov and team introduce MantisV2, closing the zero-shot gap in time series sorting with fake data and test-time tricks. Base models for time series sorting can serve as universal feature tools for varied later tasks, yet a large gap remained between frozen and fine-tuned nets in early models such as Mantis. The paper strengthens zero-shot feature extraction through three moves.

First, Mantis+, a version of Mantis pre-trained fully on fake time series, is introduced. Second, careful cut-out studies refine the design into MantisV2, an improved and light encoder. Third, an enhanced test-time method leverages mid-layer codes and refines output-token pooling, with self-mixing and cross-model vector fusion adding further gains. Tests on UCR, UEA, human activity recognition and EEG sets show MantisV2 and Mantis+ always beating prior time series base models, reaching state-of-the-art zero-shot scores.
arxiv-2602-17968:
Robert Parker and team propose a method for solving Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems that exploits block triangular submatrices. First, a Schur split isolates those submatrices; then a block backsolve factors only diag blocks of that form.

Standard factoring of symmetric-indefinite matrices with one-by-one or two-by-two pivots yields fill-in outside diag blocks. That differs from the proposed method. While exploiting a triangular submatrix limits fill-in, one-sided matrix factoring methods do not reveal inertia, which inner point methods need for nonconvex optimization. The team shows their target matrix has inertia known in advance, letting them compute KKT inertia by Sylvester's law. Finally, they show a speed edge on KKT systems from optimization problems with neural network stand-ins in constraints. It reaches up to fifteen times speedups over state-of-the-art symmetric indefinite methods MA57 and MA86 in a same-hardware test.
arxiv-2602-18068:
A Calabrò and colleagues investigate mergers in early-universe galaxy assembly. The team studies more than twelve hundred spectroscopic galaxies at redshifts five to fourteen in six JWST fields, finding mergers via Gini, M-20, and asymmetry measures.

The merger fraction barely changes from the present day to redshift eight. It averages about five percent for major mergers, thirteen percent with minor mergers included. After accounting for observability timescales, merger rates rise more than tenfold from redshift one to seven. Major mergers average about two per galaxy per billion years at redshifts five to ten, tripling with minor mergers included. Above redshift five, mergers boost star formation, though less than below redshift one. Over ten million years, their rates run about one point seven times higher than matched non-mergers, suggesting short bursty episodes. Mergers still contribute only five to ten percent of mass buildup.
arxiv-2602-18568:
Matthew Adiletta and two co-authors design a chip for reasoning models. Their 2026 paper notes large language model inference is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory wall: GPUs scale raw compute but struggle on memory-bandwidth-bound workloads. Reasoning applications worsen this with long outputs, low arithmetic intensity, and tight latency limits, dropping utilization and raising energy per inference.

The team presents the Reasoning Processing Unit, a chiplet-based architecture for scalable memory bandwidth. RPU introduces capacity-optimized high-bandwidth memory trading capacity for cheaper, lower-energy operation. A scalable chiplet architecture follows, with bandwidth-first power and area provisioning. A decoupled microarchitecture separates memory, compute, and communication pipelines, sustaining high bandwidth use. Simulations show up to forty-five point three times lower latency and eighteen point six times higher throughput over an H100 system at equal thermal design power on Llama3-405B.
arxiv-2602-18668:
Rooftop solar owners often make more power than they need, yet local wires still limit what they can share. Zeinab Salehi, with five co-authors, presents a 2026 market design that lets households trade both energy and reactive power with neighbours on the same distribution feeder.

Each household gets a dynamic operating envelope, a personal limit that keeps voltage and heat on the feeder within safe bounds. Trades settle at a competitive equilibrium, the market form of a Nash equilibrium in game terms, and the design is tested on the IEEE 13-node test feeder. The aim is wider use of solar and batteries without breaking the local grid.
arxiv-2602-18768:
Prime path coverage is a demanding test criterion, but listing every prime path in a program graph can explode in number. Jakub Zelek, with three co-authors, presents a 2026 method that generates prime paths without enumerating all simple paths first, by characterising them through strongly connected components.

That characterisation yields necessary conditions on valid endpoints and reduces the job to constrained cycle enumeration in an augmented graph. A streaming algorithm then outputs prime paths incrementally, using a Johnson-style traversal in a much smaller search space and pruning partial paths the moment they prove backward extendable. On real control-flow graphs from open-source C++ and Python projects, the method consistently beats existing approaches with stable delays between outputs.
arxiv-2602-18868:
Open-weight models can be fine-tuned for harmful uses after release, and no training resistance method yet offers theoretical guarantees. Domenic Rosati, with six co-authors, treats such interventions in 2026 as convergence-rate control problems. That framing links optimisation speed with the spectral structure of model weights.

From that insight, the authors develop spectral reparameterisation and derive SpecDef, an algorithm that provably and empirically slows first- and second-order optimisation in non-adversarial settings. In adversarial settings, they prove a fundamental limit for a broad class of such methods, including their own. An attacker with enough knowledge can bring back fast convergence, at the cost of a linearly larger model. Future work must therefore look beyond convergence-rate control alone.
arxiv-2602-18968:
When an agent uses many tools, trouble usually comes from how the tools fit together, not from one bad call. Tao Zhe, with eight co-authors, revisits tool invocation as orchestration in 2026. The core claim is that precise dependency graphs and fine-grained planning are not needed at all.

A coarse-grained layer structure gives enough global guidance, while mistakes at run time get fixed where they happen. The design learns a layered run structure from high-level tool links, then lets context constraints drive execution layer by layer. A schema-aware reflective correction mechanism spots and repairs errors locally, so faults stay with single calls instead of forcing a fresh plan for the whole path. The result is a light, reusable orchestration part, and tests show steady tool use with less complexity and overhead.
arxiv-2602-19268:
Edge devices for the internet of things need to run AI fast while sipping power, and vector engines are a key part of that hardware. Sonu Kumar and three colleagues present CORVET, a vector engine built around an iterative CORDIC unit for multiply-accumulate work. That classic trick computes with shifts and adds instead of costly multipliers. The design can switch at run time between approximate and accurate modes.

That flexibility lets the same chip trade a little accuracy for speed when a task allows it. Through vectorized, time-shared work and adjustable precision, it reaches up to four times the throughput on the same hardware. A shared block for activation functions plus a light pooling and normalization unit rounds out the design. The engine thus supports a wide range of edge jobs without a large resource bill.
arxiv-2602-19368:
Data cleaning is often treated as a routine chore, yet in practice it leans heavily on human judgment. Hazim AbdElazim and two co-authors report a careful survey study in which volunteers spotted errors, fixed data, imputed values, and matched entities in census-like scenarios with known validity. The study finds steady evidence for several cognitive bias patterns in these daily tasks.

Framing effects appear when surface formatting changes raise false-positive error flags despite the same meaning. Expert cues shift choices through anchoring, atypical but valid combos get flagged as odd ones out, and surface likeness drives confident false positives in entity matching. People also prefer leaving values missing over filling in plausible ones, an omission bias, while bowing to automation stays limited.
arxiv-2602-19768:
Vision-language models usually grasp a whole image at once, but people look around: their gaze traces a path, linking words to regions. A 2026 arXiv paper by Fan Yang and eight co-authors presents TraceVision, a model that builds path-aware spatial understanding into vision and language together.

A dedicated perception module fuses visual features with path information in both directions, while a simplification step extracts key points from raw gaze paths. A three-stage training pipeline lets gaze paths guide both description writing and region finding. The model extends to path-guided segmentation and video understanding, and the authors build a new reasoning-based narrative data set to strengthen it. Tests across captioning, prediction, region tasks, and segmentation show leading results.
arxiv-2602-19868:
Verified compilers must guarantee that compiling preserves what a program observably does. Loop optimizations strain the usual proof frameworks. A 2026 arXiv paper by David Knothe and Oliver Bringmann combines small-step and big-step semantics to verify such optimizations.

Small-step semantics suit local changes but sit awkwardly with structural ones. The authors therefore use big-step rules for structural changes, with an abstract behavioural layer as a shared interface. Coinductive big-step rules are extended to handle divergence with finite and infinite traces. That matches small-step expressiveness. That lets big-step changes sit inside an existing small-step pipeline without breaking top-level soundness theorems. The approach is shown in CompCert with checked loop unswitching and full loop unrolling.
arxiv-2602-20168:
Triage nurses decide fast with little information. Yet most models that predict deterioration are tested on signals unavailable at first assessment. A 2026 arXiv paper by KMA Solaiman and two co-authors benchmarks early deterioration forecasts honestly, under the time limits and sensing limits of real triage.

The cohort comes from MIMIC-IV-ED, with repeat patients removed. Two settings are compared: full triage and a vitals-only bare-bones setting. Both use only data from the first hour after arrival. Across methods, scores fall only slightly on vitals alone, showing early body signals carry strong clinical signal. Removing inputs one group at a time, and probing what models rely on, points to breathing and oxygen measures as the strongest early risk signals. Models degrade smoothly and stably as sensing shrinks.
arxiv-2602-20468:
Spotting anomalies in multivariate time series matters for industrial control, telemetry, and service monitoring, but shifting relations between variables and ever-present noise make it hard. Zhongpeng Qi and three co-authors propose CGSTA, a method with two innovations. Dynamic layered graph construction builds local, regional, and global views of variable relations per sliding window. Under this contrastive step, graphs from one viewpoint are set against each other, while matching time slices are brought into correspondence between viewpoints.

Stability-aware alignment then holds a per-scale stable reference learned from normal data, guiding fast-changing graphs toward it to suppress noise. Fused multi-scale and temporal features feed a conditional density estimator that scores each time step for anomaly. Across four benchmarks, CGSTA performs best on PSM and WADI and matches baselines on SWaT and SMAP.
arxiv-2602-20968:
Symmetries in quantum mechanics can break in fine ways when a system is nudged, yielding anomalies. Maxim Gritskov, Andrey Losev, and Saveliy Timchenko study those small-nudge anomalies with cohomology in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their start point is a Hamiltonian plus a symmetry maker, which form a unitary picture of a two-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra on a Hilbert space.

In that setup, nudges of the system match the first Chevalley-Eilenberg cohomology group, while anomalies of the symmetry match the second. The cohomology frame turns a physics question about broken symmetry into an algebra sorting problem. Readers get a tight math lens for telling when a nudge keeps a symmetry and when it spoils it.
arxiv-2602-21368:
Charafeddine Mouzouni alone authors a 2026 arXiv paper asking a plain question. At what confidence level can a user trust the output of a black-box AI system on a given task? The answer offered is a reliability level, one number per system-task pair. It is built from self-consistency sampling plus conformal calibration.

Self-consistency sampling cuts uncertainty fast. Conformal calibration gives exact, finite-sample guarantees that hold whatever the system's errors. Harder questions show up as larger answer sets. Weaker models earn lower levels. The full model scores about 95 percent on GSM8K and about 97 percent on TruthfulQA. The nano model scores about 90 percent on GSM8K and about 67 percent on MMLU. Tests span five benchmarks and five models, and sequential stopping cuts API costs by about half.
arxiv-2602-21568:
Yuvraj Agrawal and one co-author report moving developer output metrics from ad-hoc scripts to a managed ELT pipeline. Developer output dashboards show DevOps metrics such as Deployment Frequency and Change Failure Rate. But data trust issues often hurt their platform's dashboards.

Early intake scripts run as Cron jobs caused silent failures, with data gaps unseen for days, eroding team trust. The team moved to a robust Extract-Load-Transform pipeline using Directed Acyclic Graph control and Medallion Architecture. The paper details splitting data pulling from rework, keeping fixed raw history for changing metric meanings, and state-based link handling. Treating the metrics pipeline as a production-grade spread-out system emerges as a must for lasting engineering stats.
arxiv-2602-21668:
Junmyeong Lee and two co-authors present Motion Group-aware Gaussian Forecasting, or MoGaF, for space-time forecasting of dynamic scenes. Forecasting dynamic scenes stays a core challenge in computer vision, since limited observations make matching object-level motion and long-term temporal change hard to capture.

MoGaF builds long-term scene extrapolation on the 4D Gaussian Splatting model. Motion-aware Gaussian grouping plus group-wise tuning enforce physically consistent motion across rigid and non-rigid regions, yielding spatially matching dynamic models. Leveraging that structured space-time model, a lightweight future module predicts future motion, enabling realistic, temporally stable scene change. Tests on synthetic and real-world datasets show MoGaF consistently beating existing baselines in rendering quality, motion plausibility, and long-term stability.
arxiv-2602-21768:
Omayra Yago and one co-author present a learning-based tracking control design for joint transport of a rigid payload by multiple aerial lifters under rigid grasp constraints. A unified shape model yields a coupled agent-payload mixed system holding contact wrenches, payload motion, and internal force overlap. A leader-and-rest setup has one leader set a desired payload wrench from shape tracking errors, while the rest realize that wrench through constraint-fit force sharing.

Unknown shocks and model gaps are handled with Gaussian process fitting. Likely bounds on learning error feed into the control design, pairing Gaussian process advance fix with shape feedback. Lyapunov analysis proves uniform final bounds of payload tracking errors with high odds, with a final bound that scales with Gaussian process forecast doubt.
arxiv-2602-22368:
Code summaries help developers understand software, and language models now write them well, but human reading expertise might push them further. Jiahao Zhang and three co-authors propose EyeLayer, a lightweight module that feeds human eye-gaze patterns into code summarization as a proxy for expertise. It models where developers look, and how intensely, through a multimodal Gaussian mixture over token embeddings.

The module redistributes token embeddings from learned attention priors, teaching models generalizable focus patterns from eye-tracking data without disturbing existing representations. The team evaluates the approach across several model families, including LLaMA, Qwen, and CodeBERT variants. If gaze patterns transfer, human attention becomes a cheap, general guide for machine code understanding.
arxiv-2602-22468:
Brown dwarfs and exoplanets wear hydrogen-rich air whose spectra encode clouds, chemistry, and heat flow. James Mang and ten co-authors present PICASO 4.0, a major update to the open-source atmospheric model package. It builds on a radiative-convective equilibrium setup with new capabilities spurred by JWST observations of out-of-balance reactions and clouds.

Key new parts include a Virga link-up for self-steady cloud model work, flexible rainout and cold-trapping treatments for gases, light-driven reaction support, and a tunable energy-input scheme for extra heating. The team benchmarks the new parts against printed grids and model groups. Modelers gain an updated, open toolkit for the JWST era's cloudy, reaction-rich worlds.
arxiv-2602-22568:
Peihan Wu and four co-authors improve multi-view clustering, the job of grouping data seen from several angles, when noise varies in strength. Most robust methods assume data is either clean or ruined, but real contamination runs on a sliding scale, and that simplification lets noise leak through. Their framework, QARMVC, rates each item instead.

An information bottleneck pulls out core meaning for view reconstruction, and gaps between rebuilt and original views reveal how badly each item is contaminated, yielding per-item quality scores. Those scores then weight contrastive learning at the feature level and build a high-quality consensus for aligning views at the fusion level. On five benchmark sets QARMVC beat leading baselines, with its clearest wins where noise strength varied most.
arxiv-2602-22668:
Mingyu Ryu and one co-author report rare radio cores in spiral galaxies with double-lobed jets. Powerful jets were long tied to elliptical hosts, so spiral-hosted double-lobed radio-loud active galaxies, called spiral DRAGNs, break the usual story. Using public VLBI archives, the team found compact cores in four such galaxies and resolved parsec-scale jets in two.

The cores shine cool, near a billion kelvin, with jet-to-counterjet ratios implying only mildly relativistic speeds, below six tenths of light speed. Very low radio-to-Eddington ratios back the picture of weakly powered outflows. Three objects sit on the black-hole activity fundamental plane, and the mix of weak small jets with huge lobes points to recurrent or long-duty-cycle jet episodes.
arxiv-2602-22868:
Yushi Ye and six co-authors fix a quality-speed trade-off in diffusion language models. Side-by-side reading promises fast non-autoregressive guessing, but suffers a combo clash: tokens made jointly can form mixes that clash in meaning. Smooth codes, which preserve rich links between spots, offer a way out.

ReMix inserts a smooth mixing state between the initial masked state and the final decoded token state. Each token's code refines step by step in smooth space, settling conflicts with other tokens before folding into a discrete sample. A refusal rule sends shaky codes back to the masked state for rework, blocking error spread. As a training-free method, ReMix gains two- to eightfold speed with no quality loss.
arxiv-2602-22968:
Alaa Anani and four co-authors put circuit discovery on firmer ground with Certified Circuits. Mechanistic interpretability hunts for minimal subnetworks behind a behaviour, but existing discovery methods are brittle. Circuits shift with the chosen concept dataset and often fail out of distribution, raising doubts about what they really capture.

The framework wraps any black-box discovery algorithm with randomized data subsampling, certifying that inclusion decisions over neurons or edges stay invariant under bounded edit-distance changes to the concept dataset. Unstable parts are left out, yielding circuits that are more compact and more accurate. Across ResNet, ViT, and GPT-2, certified circuits gain up to fifty-six percent accuracy with up to eighty percent fewer components.
arxiv-2602-23168:
Nicolien Janssens and one co-author take a first principled look at how online deliberation platforms order policy proposals. Citizens post, comment on, and vote for proposals on these platforms, which aim to widen democratic participation. But the order in which proposals appear shapes what gets seen, and that choice is rarely justified in any systematic way.

The authors offer a framework that sorts sorting methods by their purpose and by the factors they weigh, so different methods can be compared on equal terms. They note that the choice of method is often ad hoc. They then criticize the common practice of ranking by raw approval counts, or likes. Approvals should enter the ranking only alongside other factors, they argue, and even then, better ways exist to honor approval counts than a plain like-based order.
arxiv-2602-23368:
Shreyas Subramanian and six co-authors ask how much vector stores and meaning-based search really add to retrieval-augmented generation over simple agentic keyword search. RAG grounds language model answers in existing knowledge bases, but it brings search quality needs, integration tangles, and cost. Agentic search and tool-using language model designs offer an other path.

The team systematically compares retrieval-augmented systems with tool-augmented agents whose only retrieval tool is basic keyword search in documents. Tool-based keyword search inside an agentic framework reaches over 90 percent of standard RAG scores, without any standing vector store. The approach is simple to implement and cost-effective, and it suits settings where knowledge bases change often, since keyword indexes update far more easily than vector stores.
arxiv-2602-23968:
David Fox and five co-authors propose a variational inference framework for learning generation orders in masked discrete diffusion models. The 2026 paper addresses a central tension in such models. Parallel token generation promises speed, but the order in which masked tokens are filled shapes sample quality. Current methods rely on fixed heuristics.

The authors parameterize the approximate posterior over generation orders in a way that supports parallelism and efficient sampling during training. Early tests on a math reasoning dataset show competitive performance against heuristic sampling in the highly parallel regime, reaching notably higher accuracy than standard rivals in only a handful of generation steps. The work opens a principled route to learned, parallel-friendly generation orders, with further experiments needed to map its full gains.
arxiv-2602-24168:
R. Leal Martir and five co-authors show how silver nanoparticles tune the memristive response of tantalum oxide devices. The 2026 paper treats defect engineering as a key lever for resistive switching, where oxygen vacancy dynamics govern how conductive filaments form and break in oxide memristors.

Devices without nanoparticles show two hysteresis switching loops of opposite chirality. Embedding silver nanoparticles in the top electrode lowers overall resistance and selectively suppresses one loop, leaving a single well-defined switching mode. Nanoparticle devices also show markedly lower cycle-to-cycle variability in the high-resistance state. Modeling attributes this to local metallization of the top interface, which partly blocks vacancy transport and confines switching to the bottom interface. In short, one loop now stands alone. The loop is clean. That loop is the win. The win helps memory last.
arxiv-2602-24268:
Alexandre Anahory Simoes and three co-authors propose a control framework on the rigid-body motion group, letting quadrotors run pointing-driven missions without a full attitude reference. The 2026 paper encodes the mission through virtual constraints that define a task manifold and its velocities.

Invariance of the task manifold is achieved by a feedback law obtained from a linear system in inputs. The invariance-enforcing input is defined under a transversality condition on the actuation distribution. The authors also derive a local off-manifold stabilization extension. In one test, they lock a body axis. The axis points along a prescribed line-of-sight direction, showing pointing missions can be enforced without over-specifying attitude.
arxiv-2603-00468: Wang and six colleagues benchmark agentic root cause analysis in cloud systems, where static tests lack live interaction and live testbeds vary too much for fair comparison. Cloud-OpsBench replays 754 verified fault cases across 57 fault types on two microservice workloads, tagging each with outcome labels and evidence graphs for matched comparison. Across ten agents the best final answer scores run high on both workloads, yet evidence closure lags far behind. Final answers alone thus flatter agents that cannot ground their diagnosis in evidence.
arxiv-2603-00568: Liu, Zhou, and Fan argue that atom centred molecule models miss bond level effects such as resonance and stereoselectivity, limiting prediction of subtle chemical behaviour. Their DeMol framework runs parallel atom centred and bond centred channels, fused by multi scale Double-Helix Blocks that learn atom atom, atom bond, and bond bond interactions. A covalent radii penalty keeps geometries chemically plausible. Across diverse benchmarks including PCQM4Mv2, OC20, QM9, and MoleculeNet, DeMol sets a new state of the art.
arxiv-2603-01168: Fu and ten colleagues build SphUnc, a joint model for calibrated prediction and clear uncertainty in multi-agent systems. It maps features onto sphere latents with von Mises-Fisher distributions, splitting uncertainty into knowledge gaps and data noise through information-geometric fusion. A causal model on those latents spots directed influence and supports intervention reasoning by simulation, with tests on social and affective sets showing better accuracy, calibration, and readable causal signals.
arxiv-2603-01368: Ai proves the inversion walk on labelled tournaments has a triangular cutoff threshold: inverting a vertex subset reverses its internal edges, and the walk repeatedly inverts a random subset. For each integer sequence, stationarity distance nears 1 when triangular number minus n grows without bound, and 0 when it falls without bound. So for fixed epsilon between 0 and 1, mixing time is n minus root 2n plus a constant. Ai maps the state space of the k-restricted inversion walk, where each step inverts a k-subset.
arxiv-2603-01568:
Leyla Roksan Caglar, Pedro Mediano, and Baihan Lin compare how people and AI vision systems handle new visual conditions. Their 2026 work uses rate-distortion theory, which studies how much detail a system keeps as inputs get harder. Standard scores show who is right more often, but not how grace under strain differs.

The team turns each system record of hits and misses into a curve of cost versus error. Two numbers sum up each curve: slope for the price of holding accuracy, and curve shape for how abrupt the drop is. People and eighteen deep models face the same controlled image changes. Both groups follow one broad compression rule, yet people trade off more smoothly. Deep models sit in steeper, more brittle zones, even when base accuracy matches.
arxiv-2603-01768:
Pratik Jawahar and Maurizio Pierini propose a new building block for learning over time in this 2026 work. Current units split into two flawed camps: discrete ones with unstable gradients, and smooth ones that leak information away. Both flaws hurt memory for long sequences and physical signals.

Their unit, CHLU, borrows its structure from relativistic Hamiltonian physics, the math of energy-based motion. A symplectic integrator, a stepwise solver that respects that structure, keeps phase-space volume strictly conserved. That conservation targets stability over endless horizons, with tunable filtering of noise as a bonus. As a proof of principle, the unit learns to generate handwritten digits from a classic data set. The authors present it as a physics-grounded primitive, not a full replacement for standard stacks.
arxiv-2603-01968:
Hyeonbin Hwang and Yeachan Park argue that task symmetry drives the sudden leap from memorization to generalization. Their 2026 work studies grokking, where a network first memorizes, then abruptly learns the real rule. Low-dimensional internal structure appears at that leap, but what organizes it was unclear.

They identify a three-stage dynamic that recurs across grokking cases in their tests. Memorization comes first, then symmetry acquisition, then geometric organization of the representation space. Generalization itself emerges during the symmetry stage, before the final tidy geometry settles in. Tests span algebraic, structural, and relational reasoning tasks with the same pattern. A symmetry-based diagnostic can flag the onset of generalization early, and the team proposes ways to speed that onset up.
arxiv-2603-02168:
Sergio Davis, Catalina Ruíz, Claudia Loyola, and colleagues extend a classic heat formula in this 2026 physics paper. The classic result links swings in motion energy to how much heat a closed system can hold. It was derived for one narrow case, the sealed system at fixed energy. Many real systems sit in broader settings, though, and need a wider rule.

Their new formula holds for any steady setting and any system size. It ties motion energy swings to total energy swings and to heat capacity. The old result falls out when total energy stops changing. Tests used computer sampling of vibrating springs and exact math for a flat energy case. The rule may help study small systems with odd heat behavior.
arxiv-2603-02268:
Jeet Bandhu Lahiri, Parshva Runwal, Arvasu Kulkarni, and colleagues test brain-wave models across hospitals in this 2026 study. Foundation models for EEG, the brain's electrical signals, often train on narrow hospital archives. Strong scores on like data may reflect the recording setup, not the brain. Their model, PRISM, varies training mix and tuning style while holding the rest fixed.

Narrow training won on matched tests, while diverse training adapted better to new data. On a hard new task, telling epilepsy apart from look-alike conditions, diverse training won by a wide margin. The diverse model also matched a far larger rival trained on many more hours. The team further shows that two benchmarks rank the same models very differently, and explains why.
arxiv-2603-02368:
Alexandra Diaconu, Mădălina Vînaga, and Bogdan Alexe release a Romanian speech benchmark in this 2026 paper. Speech recognition lags for languages with little training data. Romanian systems also face new domains that differ from their training speech. Their data set, RO-N3WS, aims to test and improve generalization across such shifts.

The set holds over one hundred twenty-six hours of transcribed audio. Sources range from broadcast news and audiobooks to film speech, children's stories, and podcasts. Leading systems were tested both as-is and after fine-tuning. Fake speech from expressive text-to-speech models was also compared. Even small fine-tuning on real RO-N3WS speech cut errors sharply versus zero-shot use. All models, scripts, and splits will be released for repeatable work.
arxiv-2603-02468:
Moeen Ul Islam, Cheng Ouyang, Xinda Qi, and colleagues build a modular soft robotic arm in this 2026 paper. Rigid robots can be unsafe around people and clumsy in messy settings. Soft arms bend safely, but single-piece designs limit reach and repair. Their arm stacks cable-driven segments that each move independently.

The body is molded silicone with tendon channels built inside. A dual-helical tendon layout protects the cables during bending. Stacking three segments grew the flat workspace roughly thirteenfold over one segment. Workspace volume grew far more, by nearly forty times. Silicone stiffness trades bend against strength: softer bends better, stiffer bears load better. Tuning that stiffness lets designers balance softness and power for each task.
arxiv-2603-02568:
Sugana Chawla, Si Chen, Julia Qian, and colleagues frame a workshop on responsible AI for STEM careers in this 2026 paper. AI now shapes feedback, advising, and access to career information for students. That makes AI part of the infrastructure forming career identity and readiness. How such tools should be designed and governed at scale remains unsettled.

The half-day workshop gathers researchers, educators, practitioners, and policymakers. Four themes structure the talks and group activities. They cover readiness definitions, AI's proper role in career choices, developmental fit across school levels, and equity risks. Lightning talks and cross-sector dialogue surface design tensions and governance principles. The goal is shared language and workable frameworks for developmentally grounded, responsible career AI.
arxiv-2603-02668:
Austin Letson, Leopoldo Sarra, Auguste Poiroux, and colleagues built SorryDB, a 2026 benchmark of real unfinished proofs. The tasks come from seventy-eight live Lean formalization projects on GitHub, where a sorry marks a step still to prove. Unlike fixed contest sets, this list keeps updating as projects change.

Because the tasks track real community needs, tools that climb this benchmark should help working mathematicians directly. The team tested language models, agent systems, and dedicated provers on a snapshot of one thousand tasks. An agent built on Gemini Flash scored best overall, yet no approach won everywhere. Older provers and even a fixed tactic list each beat the leaders on some tasks.
arxiv-2603-02768:
Bin Qiu, Wenchi Cheng, and Hongxiang He secure a wireless link by flying one antenna through a planned path. Their 2026 paper builds a virtual multi-antenna channel from a single-antenna autonomous aerial vehicle. The moving craft creates a synthetic aperture, focusing signal strength toward a chosen direction and away from others.

The team jointly designs the flight node placement, the symbol plan, and the sending and receiving beam patterns. Their goals are higher channel capacity for the base station, tight limits on what eavesdroppers can pick up, and low transmit power per node. A receiver design based on constrained variance filtering suppresses jamming. Simulations show the combined method lifts capacity over prior approaches while holding the security constraints.
arxiv-2603-03268:
Yushi Hamaguchi studies the long-run behavior of stochastic Volterra equations, used for processes whose future depends on their whole past. Because such equations are not Markovian, their present state alone does not summarize them, which blocks standard tools. His 2026 paper lifts each one into a larger Markovian system, an evolution law on a rich function space, where those tools apply again.

Hamaguchi proves the lifted system is exponentially ergodic, settling toward a single steady behavior, using a general version of Harris's theorem. The proof builds a custom coupling and distance that exploit the equations' nonlocal structure despite heavy degeneracy. He also shows finite-dimensional equations can approximate the stationary law closely. The result both analyzes the original ones and justifies the embedding trick that statistical physicists already use.
arxiv-2603-03468:
Olga Avsajanishvili confronts a universe whose vacuum energy might change with time. The standard cosmology treats that energy, the cosmological constant, as fixed forever. Her 2026 paper tests the alternative, a time-varying vacuum model, in both flat and curved space. The evidence combines the newest baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from the DESI survey with cosmic chronometer data that track the expansion rate directly.

A full statistical sampling analysis quantifies how vacuum dynamics would alter the expansion history, the effective behavior of the cosmic fluid, and the universe's deceleration. A formal model comparison then judges the varying model against the standard one. The data push hard toward the standard picture: the vacuum dynamics parameter is driven close to zero. Even so, the varying model reduces parameter degeneracies and eases the Hubble tension, the persistent mismatch in expansion-rate measurements.
arxiv-2603-03568:
Matías Leizerovich and four colleagues confront a new entropy-based cosmology with real sky data for the first time. The Luciano-Saridakis entropy generalizes textbook entropy with two extra exponents. Fed through the gravity-thermodynamics link, it modifies cosmic dynamics so an effective dark energy appears from entropy itself, while the standard model returns as a limiting case. Their 2026 paper tests that entropic cosmology at the background level.

Four datasets constrain it jointly: cosmic chronometers, the Pantheon-plus supernova sample tied to local distance measurements, new DESI baryon oscillation data, and compressed early-universe information. The model fits the combination robustly and satisfies all anchors at once, something the standard model cannot do here. Its parameters stay near standard values, yet the standard limit itself is excluded at modest significance in the space studied, hinting at relief for the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2603-03668:
Weizhi Feng and five colleagues recruit language models to help theorem provers with their hardest bottleneck. Constraints involving inductive definitions, recursive data types and functions, resist today's best solvers, which offer only limited support for them. Proofs stall for want of auxiliary lemmas, the small helper claims human experts invent. Their 2026 approach uses structured prompts to make a language model propose exactly those lemmas.

The full method is neuro-symbolic. The model iteratively conjectures lemmas, and a constraint solver checks each one for validity and usefulness toward the goal, so bad guesses die fast. Benchmarks span algebraic data types and recurrence relations. The hybrid improves on state-of-the-art SMT and CHC solvers, solving about a quarter more proof tasks involving inductive definitions than the solvers manage alone.
arxiv-2603-04268: For the Gaussian case, Hagen and colleagues identify which points of the L1 unit ball are extreme and which are exposed. The hyperbolic secant case, a quasi shift invariant space, receives the same treatment. Both settings are thus fully characterized, with the Gaussian and hyperbolic secant spaces treated side by side. The results settle the boundary points of each ball.
arxiv-2603-04468: Raya and colleagues recap MexNICA, Mexico's team in the MPD-NICA experiment. Founded in 2016, it joins five Mexican groups at the Nuclotron Ion Collider Facility in Dubna. Members span detector work plus phenomenological and theoretical studies with Monte Carlo modeling. Achievements include the miniBeBe trigger detector and studies of the baryon rich QCD region at NICA energies. Theory work uses lattice QCD and effective models. The team thus covers build, study, and theory. Mexican science thus gains a strong voice abroad.
arxiv-2603-04568: Mas and colleagues handle missing data in state space vision models with Partial Vision Mamba. Depth completion and similar tasks face arbitrarily shaped invalid regions. Convolutional partial convolutions solved this by mask aware re-normalization over valid pixels only. State space models like Mamba offer high performance at linear complexity, yet lack an invalid data mechanism at inference. Partial Vision Mamba ports partial operation principles to the Mamba backbone, with design rules for architectures using it. Tests on classification with invalid data, inpainting, and depth completion show efficacy and generalizability.
arxiv-2603-04768: Usama and Chang propose spread reward learning for cautious DRAM tuning. Tuning matters for signal health at multi-gigabit rates, yet current methods cost much and lack uncertainty gauges. Their framework joins squeeze latent codes with CVaR tuning. Rate-squeeze optimal packing speeds signal checks 51 times over eye plots while gauging doubt via Monte Carlo dropout. Tail fits enable worst-case tuning, with PAC-Bayes rules proving spread bounds. Tests on 2.4 million waves show mean gains for 4-tap tuners, with worst-case floors.
arxiv-2603-04868: Mingxuan Mu and team present K-Gen, a driving-simulation method that turns rasterized bird's-eye-view maps and written scene accounts into vehicle paths. Instead of forecasting whole paths at once, it first predicts clear keypoints expressing nearby agents' aims, then refines them into full paths, aided by a path-aware reinforcement method called T-DAPO. On the WOMD and nuPlan benchmarks it beats prior older models. which the authors read as evidence for mixing mixed reasoning with keypoint guidance.
arxiv-2603-04968: Amirabbas Afzali and team ask whether a weak language model can serve as a strong annotator for preference alignment, avoiding costly human labels or large API models. Selecting only the weak model's highly confident samples does better than using full human annotations. They build on this with Confidence-Weighted Preference Tuning, which re-weights samples by weak-model confidence across preference objectives. Notably, CW-PO trained on just 20% of human annotations outperforms standard DPO trained on 100%, suggesting confidence weighting can cut alignment cost while beating fully human-labeled training.
arxiv-2603-05168: Di Zhang and team show that 1.58-bit BitNet models tolerate semi-ordered thinness better than full-precision models. Their Sparse-BitNet method applies low-bit quantization and dynamic N:M sparsification as one while keeping training stable for the first time. Across model sizes and training schedules, the low-bit models lose less accuracy at equal thinness and survive higher ordered thinness before collapsing. A custom sparse tensor core turns the mix into large training and inference speedups, pointing to a hopeful route for lean language models.
arxiv-2603-05268: Saray Bakker and team present CDSM, a real-time method building dynamical systems on Riemannian manifolds and Lie groups for shape-respecting robot actions. It builds a nominal curve on the manifold, mixing tangential motion along the curve with normal attraction toward it. Balance analysis follows, with an S2 benchmark beating leading methods on path accuracy, path drift, and making and query times. Manipulator tests adapting SE(3) poses and damping matrices online, plus a mobile manipulator, show real use.
arxiv-2603-05468: Singh and Bhatia take on the feedback-control job of getting back conditional quantum states from continuous measurement streams in real time. Standard stochastic master equation solvers need exact models and known values, while unconstrained neural models can break positivity or trace rules. Their Kraus-structured output layer maps the hidden representation of a backbone onto a completely positive trace preserving operation, so each update stays true to physics. For each backbone tested, Kraus-LSTM does best, beating its unconstrained version on state estimation by 7%.
arxiv-2603-05768: Chaves and team look into merging fine-tuned models from distinct domains. Merging joins task models. Recent research improved in-spread or multi-task merging, but spread stays little studied. Looking at setting competition via singular value decomposition, they show shifts induce stronger subspace conflicts. These conflicts exceed multi-task settings. To ease this, they propose SCORE, easing subspace conflicts. SCORE finds a shared right-angle basis from main parts. It projects task tables into the basis, pruning off-line entries. SCORE beats current methods in domain spread across designs.
arxiv-2603-05868: Heo and colleagues propose zero-shot camera adaptation for viewpoint-robust vision-language-action models, needing no demonstrations, fine-tuning, or architectural changes. Fine-tuned manipulation models prove sensitive to viewpoint changes common in unstructured environments. The key idea adjusts test-time observations to match training camera configuration in real time via feed-forward novel view synthesis. This plug-and-play approach preserves pretrained capabilities for any RGB policy. On LIBERO, the method beats augmentation and 3D-aware baselines, and real-world tests confirm stronger robustness across varying cameras.
arxiv-2603-06068: Visser takes up a Bezboruah-Shepherdson gap result. This result tells us that weak PA-minus proves no theory's soundness, under certain guesses. Kreisel dismissed such a result as empty. The author takes up Kreisel's complaint and rejects it. The paper compares Pudlák's Second gap spread with the Bezboruah-Shepherdson Theorem. Finally, the author proves again the Bezboruah-Shepherdson Theorem using Nielsen-Markov sequence coding insight.
arxiv-2603-06368: Chen and colleagues describe large deviations above typical maximal energy of a spin glass with plus minus 1 spins. From an explicit rate function description, they show near minimum behavior is asymptotically quadratic exactly when an external magnetic field exists. The proof uses a Parisi type formula for fractional partition function moments, leveraged to obtain the Laplace transform limit of the maximum energy. Convex duality arguments rewrite this transform as a supremum over martingales, yielding an explicit rate function for the large deviation principle.
arxiv-2603-06568: Li and team build on the PEACOCK radiative transfer tool to study cool-to-warm galactic wind structure in nearby star-forming galaxies, using joint line tracing. Choppy speeds often match or exceed steady bulk outflow velocity, turbulent pressure rules tiny and ram pressure. Chop emerges as a kinetic energy budget part for the circumgalactic wind. Stellar mass and star formation rate scale metal mass outflow rates, wind kinematics, and ionic column counts, showing strong coupling between stellar feedback and halo shape.
arxiv-2603-06768: Muneeb and colleagues benchmark genotype-to-phenotype prediction across many curated binary phenotypes from openSNP. They compare three workflow families end to end: machine learning, deep learning, and polygenic scores. No workflow family dominates across the board. Polygenic scores lead on most phenotypes, while machine or deep learning lead on the rest, yet many wins are modest practical ties. Performance varies sharply by phenotype and by modeling and preprocessing choices, with distinct failure modes per workflow and higher peaks concentrated in smaller phenotypes.
arxiv-2603-06968: Li and colleagues present pqRPKI, an RPKI architecture for the post-quantum era. RPKI secures routing by binding prefixes to systems, yet its RSA base is vulnerable to quantum foes. A swap to post-quantum signatures fits poorly, since relying parties fetch and validate the repository, inflating CPU cost in transition. pqRPKI pairs a Merkle Tree Ladder with RPKI objects, moving verification material from certificates into the Manifest. It redesigns the manifest and delegation chain, with ladder-guided sync and bulk verification localizing diffs downward and rebuilding trees bottom-up.
arxiv-2603-07268: Duval and Echahed present databases as sketches, a categorical frame that treats each database style as a finite-limit sketch and each database as a model of it. Graph styles such as quivers, triple stores and property graphs all fit the same frame, with labels, types and paths handled by one set of constructions. Paths get special care, with inference rules that compute useful paths only when needed. A looser sketch variant then supports modular growth of large models.
arxiv-2603-07568: Wang and colleagues build a generative neural solver for vehicle routing that learns constraints explicitly. Attention-based solvers degrade when node representations look alike or horizons run long, and their gains stay confined to fixed-distribution benchmarks. The new framework diffuses a discrete noise graph to learn a constraint assignment matrix, then feeds it into an autoregressive solver as a structural mask. The fusion captures global and local structure together, reaching state-of-the-art results across benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-07668: Nguyen and colleagues test how code obfuscation affects human program reading through output guessing. They build levels from plain code to name renaming, misleading names, flow changes and combinations, applied to Python and JavaScript functions. Scrambling generally slows reasoning and lowers accuracy, but not in a straight line. JavaScript follows the usual pattern, while Python renaming sometimes matches or beats plain code, and moderate deliberation helps most.
arxiv-2603-07968: Chun and colleagues develop a framework for reading low-surface-brightness features, the faint traces that reveal how galaxies and clusters form. The K-DRIFT telescope will hunt such diffuse targets through deep, wide-field optical imaging reaching about 30 magnitudes per square arcsecond. To interpret its data, the authors built the Galaxy Replacement Technique, an N-body framework that swaps high-resolution galaxy models into low-resolution halos of a base cosmological run. That swap buys high resolution at lower compute cost than full hydrodynamic simulations, suiting faint-structure studies.
arxiv-2603-08068: Ye and colleagues tackle tool use in large language models, whose grasp of complex tasks is limited by what they hold internally. Tools such as Python interpreters for calculation and search engines for facts offer a way past that limit, yet getting models to use them well remains hard. Existing methods typically start with supervised fine-tuning and then add reinforcement learning, a cold-start pipeline with heavy data demands. The authors instead develop in-context reinforcement learning, letting models learn effective tool use from context during the task itself.
arxiv-2603-08368: Nowicki-Koth improves the threshold for local well-posedness of the quartic Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation. Using a bilinear smoothing estimate recently developed elsewhere, plus several linear Strichartz-type estimates from that work, the author proves local well-posedness in H^s on R times T. This holds for all s greater than one half. The result lowers the regularity threshold previously required, showing solutions exist locally for rougher initial data than earlier work allowed.
arxiv-2603-08568: Jaume de Haro rebuilds gravity from proper time, treating the invariant interval as a clock reading with real physical weight. Free fall becomes the path that stretches proper time most, and the universality of free fall plus Lorentz symmetry yields the static-field form. In the weak-field limit the result matches General Relativity, and any sound strong-field extension must bring in the Ricci tensor.
arxiv-2603-08868: Matthew Siebert and colleagues recalibrate pre-Servicing Mission 4 STIS echelle throughputs with a simple scaling. New stellar models shift far- and near-ultraviolet continua by a few percent against older models. Scaling old throughputs by the new-to-old continuum ratio updates eight echelle modes, improving fluxes by roughly half a percent to a few percent across both bands.
arxiv-2603-09068: Kayla Smith and Mark Marley track how clouds and deuterium burning shape brown dwarf habitable zones. Using modern evolution tracks with deuterium burning, cloud formation and dissipation, and recent air opacities, they replace analytic scaling relations. Clouds slow cooling, letting planets stay habitable far longer, and deuterium burning creates sweet spots where planets around different-mass dwarfs at the same orbit stay habitable equally long.
arxiv-2603-09168: David P. Woodruff and Samson Zhou study the distributed experts problem, where experts sit across servers and each expert's loss mixes per-server losses over time. The aim is low regret against the best expert while sending as few bits as possible. They give a protocol whose regret shrinks with the horizon up to log factors. Its communication cost improves on earlier work, scaling with the number of experts and servers divided by the squared target regret.
arxiv-2603-09368: Fabian Wiesner and Anna Pappa ask whether delegated quantum computation can be verified efficiently using only the cut-and-choose technique. In that method a weak client spends most rounds testing an untrusted quantum server's honesty and keeps the rest for real work. Adding tools like quantum error correction could crush cheating odds but at heavy overhead. They prove protocols relying solely on cut-and-choose cannot be both secure and efficient at once, so new techniques are required.
arxiv-2603-09868: Aleksei Rozanov and coauthors launch CarbonBench, a global test for models that scale up land carbon flux estimates. Flux towers are sparse, so models must work in places and climates they never trained on. The bench holds daily records from hundreds of towers across two decades, with shared weather and remote sensing features. Split rules test transfer to unseen plant types and climates, against several baselines.
arxiv-2603-09968: Freeman Cheng and coauthors present ReCoSplat, an online system that rebuilds a scene from a stream of views using Gaussian splatting. The model must stay renderable at every moment and work with posed or unposed inputs. A render and compare module renders the built scene from each new viewpoint and contrasts it with the real image, steadying training. A cache compression scheme also keeps long streams practical.
arxiv-2603-10168: Chiesa, Pawlowski and Reichert work out two to two scalar scattering in asymptotically safe quantum gravity. With the functional renormalisation group, they get the full slope of the scalar graviton vertex for spacelike momenta. A careful shift to the Minkowski branch then rebuilds the timelike vertex. That gives the amplitude and the cross section for the process. At low energies the result matches general relativity. Unitarity also holds in the ultraviolet, as the team shows in the paper.
arxiv-2603-10668: R Anand, V K Chandrasekar, and R Suresh study how phase lag and adaptive learning rules shape states in a network of pendulum oscillators. Coupling strengths evolve under two biologically inspired rules: Hebbian adaptation and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The Hebbian case yields cluster, solitary, and chimera states, while STDP gives splay and splay-cluster forms. The solitary state arises with no delays, nonlocal coupling, or outside kicks, driven purely by the phase-lag value. Phase diagrams from two incoherence measures map the transitions, with multistable regions confirmed by analysis.
arxiv-2603-10968: Quinn Campbell and coauthors search for a reliable first-principles test. The test asks which substrate-film pairs suit remote epitaxy. In this method, films grow over an inserted two-dimensional layer. The mechanism behind the technique is still unsettled. Older metrics such as electrostatic potential fail to explain which pairs work. The sliding barrier of islands on the surface proves the most rigorous criterion. It is computed with atoms free to relax. It points to island migration kinetics as the heart of the effect.
arxiv-2603-11068: Iman Peivaste and Salim Belouettar present a reasoning-and-acting language model agent. It does inverse design of high-entropy alloys. It proposes compositions meant to form a phase. It refines them in a loop. The agent checks its proposals against a calibrated XGBoost surrogate. That surrogate was trained on 4,753 experimental records spanning four phase outcomes. Against Bayesian optimization and random search, it rediscovers known phases more often. It lands far closer to experimental compositions. Domain priors push it toward exploring underrepresented composition space.
arxiv-2603-11168: Charles Wang and coauthors run a study of automatic speech recognition for Huntington's disease, whose uneven timing, unstable voicing, and unclear speech defeat standard models. They use a speech corpus never before used for end-to-end training, and compare model kinds under one test setup. They track substitution, deletion, and insertion patterns. Parakeet-TDT leads the baselines, and disease-specific adaptation cuts the word error rate. Biomarker-based supervision reshapes errors in ways that shift with severity, rather than simply lowering the rate.
arxiv-2603-11268: Matthew Albert and coauthors compute the linear response of films of the magnetic Chern insulator MnBi2Te4 to finite-frequency electric fields. The response splits into a Kubo contribution and a topological Hall term, absent for trivial insulators. Combining density functional theory with Wannier functions, they obtain optical conductivity and susceptibility for one, four, five, and eleven septuple layers. The eleven-layer film carries the same Chern number as the five-layer one, against reports of a higher-Chern phase. Spin-orbit-driven band inversions mark the topological phases.
arxiv-2603-11568: Raghoonanan and Byrnes blend quantum error correction with error mitigation in a hybrid scheme, PQES. Correction removes errors from a state; mitigation cleans noisy measurement data instead. PQES runs SWAP tests on many noisy copies to purify the state. The full outcome record combines all branches, with no postselection. Purification can also sit between unitary blocks, shrinking errors mid-computation. For local depolarizing noise, the error threshold sits at 3/4 for any register size. Local dephasing gives a 1/2 threshold, and Clifford twirling can lift it back up.
arxiv-2603-11668: Broadley, Lind, and King present a compact scheme that gives meshless PDE methods spectral-like resolving power. Meshless methods suit hard geometries and free surfaces, yet their operator accuracy can lag. The scheme builds on LABFM, which fits spatial operators to any polynomial order. It borrows the compact finite-difference trick: implicit stencils tuned to sharpen each operator's resolving power. The global system stays sparse and diagonally dominant at the same time. Tests on canonical PDEs show large accuracy gains, most for high wavenumber content.
arxiv-2603-11868: Hu and Guarnieri report early work on running SPHinXsys, an open-source multi-physics library, across mixed hardware through the SYCL standard. Particle methods like Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics are heavy to compute. Vendor-specific code paths for each chip family make such libraries hard to maintain. One SYCL build runs the same code on varied hardware, with clear speedups over the multi-core CPU version. The paper covers data layouts for parallel access, data sorting, and GPU benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-12168: Sardana, Goncharov, and Tremblay use targeted pulsar timing searches to turn black hole binaries into standard sirens. Blind all-sky searches locate such binaries too loosely for precision cosmology, a long-standing block. Targeted searches for supermassive black hole binaries sidestep that loose sky map. Simulated data based on current arrays show the Chinese Pulsar Timing Array alone could pin the Hubble constant tightly. That sharp, independent measure could help settle the Hubble tension. The method also handles several binaries at once and resists host galaxy confusion.
arxiv-2603-12368: Dong, Tang, and de Rijke add multi-step reasoning to generative retrieval for numeric documents. Such models store a corpus in their parameters and emit document IDs for a query. Complex financial queries expose weak reasoning in these models today. ReasonGR pairs task instructions with stepwise reasoning guidance in its prompts. A focused adaptation module sharpens the parameters tied to that skill. On the FinQA dataset of finance queries, accuracy and consistency both improve in their tests.
arxiv-2603-12468: Guichemerre and co-authors adapt weakly supervised localization under domain shift by forgetting dominant predictions. Such models often collapse under strong shift, sending most target samples to a few classes. Pseudo-labels then carry that bias into source-free adaptation and spoil the results. Their method flags prediction-dominant classes from the model's own target calls. Uncertain samples near the boundary form a forget set, while firm ones anchor a retain set. A new objective cuts the dominant class scores so other assignments can emerge and boundaries can move.
arxiv-2603-12568: Adriana Errico and co-authors ask how often hot Jupiter systems also hide a cold Jupiter far out beyond the snow line. They merged all public radial velocity data for 28 host stars with synthetic data. The tests varied cadence, time span, and precision to find detection limits. Current data proved poor at spotting such pairs. Campaign length mattered most, while precision mattered little. Small telescopes with modest precision thus suit this search well.
arxiv-2603-12968: Alzubair Hassan and co-authors propose a framework for engineering adaptive authentication systems. In settings like connected vehicles and health care, risk shifts with user, place, and device. Fixed methods cannot track that change well. Their frame uses a contextual goal model for requirements and risk links. An extended feature model lists candidate methods and their effects. At runtime, a fuzzy causal network solved with Z3 picks a fitting method. Tests cover vehicle and health scenarios.
arxiv-2603-13768: Wei-Chih Chen, Chien-yu Huang, and Hung-yi Lee use causal tracing to study audio-text fusion in large audio language models. How and where these models integrate acoustic features with textual context was unclear. They adapt causal tracing with layer-wise and token-wise analyses across DeSTA, Qwen, and Voxtral models. Layer-wise results show varied fusion strategies, from progressive integration to abrupt late-stage fusion. Token-wise results show the final sequence token acts as an informational bottleneck for audio retrieval.
arxiv-2603-13868: Müller and co-authors report precise mass measurements of zinc-75 in its ground and first isomeric states. The work used the ISOLTRAP Penning trap at CERN, with the isomer made by in-trap decay of copper-75. The isomer sits at an excitation energy of 123.7 keV, which matches decay spectroscopy within uncertainty. The ground-state mass excess is revised to -62681.0 keV, which corrects an earlier misassignment. Theory checks support a spin-1/2 ground state, as shell-model predictions suggest.
arxiv-2603-13968: Braides, Pinamonti, and Solci study how fractional Sobolev seminorms behave on thin film domains. The film shrinks in one direction, and the authors track the first energy scales that survive. The first scale captures vertical fractional oscillations along one-dimensional sections. A second scale gives dimension reduction, with a sharp change at the critical exponent one half. Below it, the limit stays fractional with a gain in smoothness. Above it, the limit turns local, of Dirichlet type.
arxiv-2603-14368: Esmer and co-authors compute light hybrid mesons made of a quark, an antiquark, and two gluons, using QCD sum rules. States with eight spin-parity-charge sets are covered, from 0++ to 1--. Currents built from light quark and gluon fields probe three flavor mixes, with strange quarks swapped in step by step. Quark and gluon condensates enter up to dimension twelve, which sharpens the mass and coupling estimates. Results can guide lab searches for these hybrid states and later decay work.
arxiv-2603-14768: Burfitt, Brodzki and Dłotko measure neural network decision boundaries by local surface volume. Boundary shape drives both accuracy and robustness in classification. A tube formula by Weyl inspires the new gauge. Local surface volumes sum into a practical complexity score. Smaller volume should mean simpler models that generalize better. Image tasks with convolutional nets confirm the inverse link to accuracy. Fully connected nets show a less stable pattern across tasks. For matched architectures, smoother boundaries track better scores, they find.
arxiv-2603-14868: Pilipovsky builds sequential convex programming for covariance steering with a free final time. The systems have fixed noise and noise that scales with state. Time is scaled, and each step can stretch or shrink. The mesh adapts, and time and control tune at once. He keeps first-order noise terms and their link to step size in the model. Each subproblem is solved with conic relaxations, end moment rules, and chance limits. He reports tests on a double integrator with drag show more exact covariance than frozen noise plans.
arxiv-2603-14968: Wang and co-authors check text watermarks from the outside with TTP-Detect, a black-box frame. Secret-key schemes tie checking to the provider's own tools. Outside auditors then cannot test provenance claims alone. TTP-Detect splits checking from marking entirely. Each check becomes a relative test on the query text. A proxy model boosts the mark-linked signals. Several relative scores judge the match. Tests across schemes and models show strong results, they report.
arxiv-2603-15268: Kalita and co-authors model a quantum battery that copies the light-harvesting units of bacteria, but lets charge flow one way only. Bright and dark collective states take set roles, and a single-mode cavity helps storage. Rates from a tailored Hamiltonian feed a master equation for the time path. They track stored energy, leakage, ergotropy, flux, and power. Each ring size peaks at a different job. Strong coupling boosts storage but cuts power output.
arxiv-2603-15368: Wilczynski and co-authors present IRIS, a framework for editable three-dimensional scenes that renders in real time. Neural radiance fields look sharp but train and render slowly, while Gaussian splatting is fast but less flexible. IRIS uses Gaussians as proxies to guide a neural field. An analytic sampling step finds the exact points where rays meet scene parts, which skips empty space. A feature blending rule along each ray replaces costly neighbor searches. The result keeps detail high, renders fast, and allows direct shape edits.
arxiv-2603-15568: Shoaib and co-authors estimate staged tree models by hierarchical clustering on the probability simplex. Staged trees extend Bayesian networks with context-specific dependence. Their study tests four divergence measures, from total variation to Fisher, crossed with four linkage rules. Simulations scored fit by relative BIC and structure by Hamming distance. Total variation with the Ward.D2 linkage won on fit, recovery, and cost. Backward hill climbing matched on quality but ran far slower, which favors the clustering route for large or urgent jobs.
arxiv-2603-16068: Zhang and co-authors survey attacks that make language models burn excess compute. Wasteful generation cuts service capacity and raises user costs. Such resource threats now span a full attack pipeline. The survey maps the field from induction to mitigation. Threat entry points and trigger styles get a unified scope. Mechanism studies explain how overlong outputs get provoked. Defense lines close the loop from detection to control. The review aims to firm up a young research area.
arxiv-2603-16568: Cheret and co-authors regularize autoencoders by matching distances, not coordinates. Their Manifold-Matching scheme aligns latent pairwise distances with input ones. Training minimizes the mean squared error between the two sets. Distance alignment also allows a lower-dimensional latent space. That freedom adds room to adapt. Tests beat rival schemes on neighbor-distance preservation. Other shape-based measures agreed. It further gives a scalable stand-in for multidimensional scaling.
arxiv-2603-16868: Ansari and co-authors tackle object-level 3D reconstruction of cluttered real scenes from images. Splitting a scene into single objects is hard due to varied shapes, occlusion, and contact. Robotics also needs reconstructions that respect physics, with no interpenetration. They release MessyKitchens, a dataset of messy kitchen scenes with precise object shapes, poses, and contacts as ground truth. They also extend SAM 3D with a Multi-Object Decoder for joint reconstruction. On three datasets, the authors report steady gains over prior state of the art.
arxiv-2603-17368: Chen and co-authors aim to make large reasoning models safer without losing skill. Safety drops only once chain-of-thought turns on, they find, not when it stays off. So they teach models to settle safety choices before reasoning starts. A small classifier pulls safety signals from a safe model as extra training cues. Safety rose a lot in their tests, while general reasoning skill held steady.
arxiv-2603-17468: Ma, Pu, Ai, and Wang present GuidedSAC, a reinforcement learning method with language-model guidance. A large language model reads recent trajectories and visual replays as a supervisor. It then suggests action-level fixes that steer exploration in wide state-action spaces. Theory shows the method keeps Soft Actor-Critic's convergence guarantees while learning faster, they report. Tests on text tasks and MuJoCo beat plain SAC and known exploration add-ons.
arxiv-2603-17668: Chunduri and co-authors present Halo, a long-context question answering system that uses domain knowledge as code. Whole-document calls degrade as text grows, and chunk retrieval still costs many passes. Halo extracts user hints about where to look, what to skip, and how to check answers. Each hint runs as an operator at the pipeline stage where it helps most. A fallback shuts off bad operators at run time. Accuracy rose up to 13 percent.
arxiv-2603-18068: Ali derives when real observers can resolve the imaginary phase problem of de Sitter space. The Euclidean path integral phase blocks a plain state-counting read of Gibbons-Hawking entropy. He splits observers into gravitational observers and topological spectators. At quadratic order, any sector with a metric-free infrared action factors out, so the phase stays. Only observers whose fluctuations share the conformal factor's negative modes can remove it, he shows.
arxiv-2603-18268: Grundbacher and Kobos determine exact Banach-Mazur distances for certain l_p sums and cones. A recent result on optimal position against the Euclidean ball drives the work. They give a closed formula for the distance of an l_p direct sum to Euclidean space. For p equal to 1, sums with l_1 keep the distance of the base space when it is at most 3. Cone versions swap in the simplex, with equalities for symmetric bases in dimension 3.
arxiv-2603-18568: Bajalan, Boyvalenkov, and Özbudak prove three structural results about mixed orthogonal arrays. These arrays let each column use a different alphabet size. First comes a Singleton type bound, with a description of MDS and almost-MDS arrays. Next, a trace duality links linear mixed arrays to error-block codes. That link reads the array strength off the dual code distance. Last, they study irredundant arrays, which help build maximally entangled quantum states. Extremal linear cases match error-block MDS codes exactly.
