arxiv-2604-21968: Tanin and Wang argue that sharp matter-density gradients, of the kind found inside neutron stars, would yield neutrino-antineutrino pairs. The mechanism is analogous to the Schwinger effect, in which strong electric fields produce charged-particle pairs. They discuss observational signatures of these gradient-produced antineutrinos and neutrinos, and their use as fresh probes of neutron-star structure and dense-baryon QCD.
arxiv-2604-22068: Salsabil and Elbaum present TRACE, a pipeline redoing NHTSA crash reports as CARLA simulations. It pulls street-map data to keep true road topology. It uses language models to guess vehicles' start spots from road shapes and pre-crash moves, and makes sim trajectories from report data. With this tool, the authors built a set of 52 crash scenarios with crash kinds, road topologies, and pre-crash moves. The set gives an open tool for testing autonomous cars against real crashes.
arxiv-2604-22168: Najafi and Mirzaei treat error control in digital twins as stepwise choices. From a companion Hidden Markov Model study, they build a Markov Decision Process. Regimes are states, fixes are actions, and reward weighs accuracy against upkeep expense. They extend it to a Partially Observable MDP for flawed sorting. Bayesian filtering updates beliefs, with the HMM error matrix as the observation model. Q-learning and REINFORCE show the MDP policy on top for reward and normal time, with the POMDP at about 95 percent of MDP performance.
arxiv-2604-22968: Trukhanova and Andreev develop a spin-current model of polarization for magnets with an anisotropic tensor gyromagnetic ratio. Three mechanisms follow: symmetric Heisenberg exchange, DM interaction, and spin-spin interaction via odd anisotropy through nonmagnetic ions. The model derives how it depends on spin density and on the tensor g-factor. New results arise in cycloidal and helicoidal spin orders from off-diagonal parts, for ferroelectrics with heavy ions.
arxiv-2604-23168: Suzuki and Yamaguchi maintain the maximum subarray sum over the most recent n items of a data stream, where exact tracking usually needs space linear in n. Kadane's classic method fails here because each new item expires the oldest one, which can kill the best subarray found so far. A Smooth Histogram approach first yields a constant-factor approximation in squared-log space. Refining it, they reach any chosen accuracy in near-optimal space, with space cost shown asymptotically optimal.
arxiv-2604-23368: Hao and Austerweil present TEMPO, a transformer system that reconstructs the order and timing of disease events from single snapshots of many patients rather than long follow-ups. One module orders biomarkers, while a second places each patient along the disease course from their abnormality pattern. On Alzheimer's data it recovers a plausible sequence from early shrinkage in memory regions to late tau damage and accelerating decline.
arxiv-2604-23468: Hariharan and colleagues report a milestone in formal mathematics: the 2016 sphere-packing solution in eight dimensions, built on modular forms, was fully verified in the Lean proof system in February 2026. The project, launched in 2024, finished its final stages with help from an autoformalization model named Gauss. The paper describes the techniques used, reflects on the human-machine collaboration, and lists goals still open.
arxiv-2604-23668: Bradač and colleagues report that two bright candidates for extremely distant galaxies in Bullet Cluster JWST data are in fact ultra-cool brown dwarfs in our own galaxy. Follow-up spectra fit Y dwarf templates at a few hundred kelvin and distances of a few hundred parsecs, and later imaging confirms their proper motion across the sky. The result warns that some dropout-selected distant-galaxy candidates are cold Milky Way objects instead.
arxiv-2604-23768: Banerjee and Fehske study Barnett and Einstein-de Haas reciprocity in a quantum spin-rotor model with an exact solution that conserves total angular momentum. For one spin, the model shows rotation-driven polarisation, coherent spin-rotor angular momentum transfer, and entanglement between them. At a recoil-compensation point all sectors sync, allowing full spin reversal, and with two spins the rotor can mediate entanglement, leaving a maximally entangled pair.
arxiv-2604-23868: Bhattacharya and nine colleagues develop an exact theory of force-dipole flows in a viscous membrane coupled to a surrounding fluid, focusing on orientation-fixed dipoles. The known Saffman crossover from near-field to screened far-field flow changes pair motion. Near-field motion for two twin dipoles is exactly solvable and in effect 1D, while far-field motion stays exact but fully 2D. For pullers, angular motion drives lining up and a shared late-time collapse.
arxiv-2604-23968: Mysore offers DecompKAN, a compact forecasting model without attention. It splits a series into trend and remainder, patches each channel, normalizes each case, and learns visible one-dimensional curves on its connections. It tops or ties rivals on 15 of 32 dataset-horizon pairings and on 20 of 36 controlled comparisons. It shines on smooth and physiological series, and readers can inspect what each learned curve does.
arxiv-2604-24268: Zhang and colleagues present pre-launch testing and calibration of the SVOM Visible Telescope flight model under simulated space conditions. Tests cover thermal vacuum cycling, energy concentration checks, stray light suppression, and CCD and electronics checks for gain, noise, and quantum efficiency. Results confirm full compliance: stray light falls below one ten-millionth for point sources at 30 degrees off-axis, thermal control holds CCD temperatures, and sensitivity meets its magnitude limit. Early in-orbit tests match pre-launch specs.
arxiv-2604-24568: Xu studies modules over the field with one element. Adding is not one single operation. It is a family of multi-valued hyper-operations that need not follow the usual associativity rule. He proves a generalized associativity law: every multi-input sum lies inside the iterated hypersum for any split of its inputs. This gives a hyper-additive account of Schwede's linearization functor. He builds coherent plasmas, with fully faithful nerves and a Segal condition. The result turns loose multi-valued addition into strict classical addition.
arxiv-2604-24668: Zhao and five colleagues test whether language models flatter users in financial agent tasks, where agreement with a user can cost accuracy and trust. Models show only low to modest drops when users rebut or contradict a reference answer, unlike earlier general-domain findings. Yet most models fail when user preference information contradicts the reference answer. The authors also benchmark recovery methods, including input filtering with a pretrained model.
arxiv-2604-24868: Drescher and four colleagues report the dimer structure factor for the triangular Heisenberg model. They use large GPU runs. The dimer response probes spin-singlet excitations, distinct from spin modes. They study ordered phases with flat, stripe and four-sided spin order. They also study candidate spin-liquid regimes. In ordered phases, low-energy modes sit below the two-magnon range onset. That pattern illustrates avoided particle decay. In the gapless liquid, spread minima at half zone corners support a Dirac liquid with gapless singlet poles.
arxiv-2604-24968: Haut and six colleagues test how population size affects GPU-based genetic programming runs in BEAGLE. BEAGLE enables population dynamics previously out of reach for CPU-bound genetic programming systems. With fixed population sizes, very narrow and deep searches help some problems, using as few as 1,000 individuals. Other problems benefit from searches that are very broad and shallow, reaching 10 million individuals. Stepped sizes that start large and drop small balance breadth and depth of search for symbolic regression.
arxiv-2604-25368: Brutsche, Hahn and Rohde pin down how well an unknown switching point can be estimated for a diffusion whose volatility jumps between two levels. From observations taken at ever closer spacing, they find the convergence speed and limiting shape for the profile maximum likelihood estimate. Slow sampling is a special case, where observations form a chain that keeps returning without settling. The unusual limit comes from maximising over a doubly random drifted Poisson process, built from the local time of a wobbling Brownian motion.
arxiv-2604-25668: Brutsche and Riepl develop a test for whether the volatility function in a nonparametric Gaussian white-noise model is constant, based on discrete observations. The procedure proves minimax-optimal and adaptive under infill asymptotics. A key finding is that deviation from constancy is best measured by the ratio of volatility to its average over the interval. Deriving the optimal constants requires building hypotheses whose height solves a given equation for each sample size. Solvability and bounds for those solutions rest on the implicit function theorem.
arxiv-2604-26068: Kalinowski studies how to detect collapse in high-dimensional point clouds, where mass piles up near a lower-dimensional shape instead of spreading out. He builds test statistics from persistent homology, a tool that tracks holes and connected pieces across scales, under two standard filtrations, with cutoffs calibrated against many non-collapsed reference models. Benchmarks across three collapse mechanisms, linear, nonlinear-support, and contamination-driven, yield a map guiding which filtration and statistic to choose.
arxiv-2604-26168: Phan and five colleagues test the chiral anomaly account of negative magnetoresistance in strained grey tin and germanium alloy films. The two films sit in Dirac-semimetal and topological-insulator states. Both states show negative magnetoresistance for current parallel or transverse to an in-plane field, with different field-strength dependence. That rules out the chiral anomaly account. Other mechanisms may drive the effect in the Dirac and Weyl semimetal phase, the authors suggest. They discuss sample design and material quality as sources of conflicting reports across studies.
arxiv-2604-26268: Buzbas and Devezer argued that the gap between replicable and not replicable findings is not itself scientifically replicable. Replication studies average binary verdicts, yet experiments rarely share one data-generating process. Under a shared-rate model, even small rate variation sets a variance floor no number of replications can remove. Under an independent-rates model, binary verdicts carry no information about between-experiment differences. Binary verdicts thus understate uncertainty and cannot demarcate reliable science.
arxiv-2604-26668: Biswas, Zambon, Nespoli, and Corani tackle forecast reconciliation under nonlinear constraints, a case previous methods did not cover. They extend both projection, which maps forecast samples onto the coherent manifold, and conditioning, which constrains the joint forecast. The conditioning approach is built with an Unscented Kalman Filter method. On made-up and real data sets, both methods improve accuracy in general, with the filter-based approach best overall, fastest, and always kept among the plausible models.
arxiv-2604-26768: Su, Zhang, Ai, and Liu tackle a flaw in stored retrieval generation, where document modules trained on task goals encode both document facts and reusable habits. When modules merge at inference, overlapping task habits pile up with document updates, making the merged module less stable and less focused on wanted knowledge. Their separate subspace method trains a Task LoRA for reusable habits, then trains document modules in a separate subspace. Tests across knowledge tasks and model scales show the approach improves composition strength, especially when many document modules merge.
arxiv-2604-26868: Gan and six colleagues introduce ArtiAD, the first large benchmark for spotting defects in articulated 3D objects, whose joints make pose changes look like damage. It holds 15,229 point clouds across 39 object categories with varied joint angles and six structural defect types, each labeled with joint state and motion. Their baseline, SPA-SDF, replaces the rigid template with a pose-conditioned implicit field and recovers joint state by minimizing reconstruction energy. It scores 0.884 object-level AUROC on seen poses and nearly as high on unseen ones, beating rigid baselines.
arxiv-2604-27268: Różowski and three colleagues give a complete set of diagram rules for measuring how alike the behaviours of nondeterministic processes are, moving beyond simple yes-or-no equivalence. Using Milner's charts, which generalize finite automata by adding variable outputs, they draw those rules as string diagrams. This variable-free notation breaks recursion into smaller parts. The diagrams support step-by-step reasoning and compositional meaning, laying groundwork for quantitative study of richer systems such as weighted transitions.
arxiv-2604-27368: Zhang challenges a core belief of big-data science, that larger samples with smaller errors must converge on the truth, using stellar ages in Galactic archaeology. From a large sample of subgiant stars, he finds a pocket of the quality space set by signal-to-noise ratio and parallax precision. There, inferred formation timescales sit systematically off an independent asteroseismic reference. Because the statistical errors there stay small, the result looks stable while remaining wrong by roughly half a billion to a billion years.
arxiv-2604-27468: Isono and Kajikawa argue that readers keep in mind only information most useful for guessing what comes next, guided by sentence structure. Two factors drive that cost: how many predicted heads and incomplete dependencies there are. Although work treated those factors as rivals, their account says neither reduces to the other. They test this in Japanese, where the two factors contrast, and find readers who slow down to keep information gain more from predictability. The pattern is absent in English, and open issues remain for syntax across languages.
arxiv-2604-27968: Xu and colleagues study short social videos about climate change, testing whether current vision-language models can spot climate themes and how clustering reveals visual patterns. The tested models could not reliably recognise climate-specific classes, but clustering separated the material into distinct visual frames. Two image embedding models grouped the videos differently, one by style and abstract type, the other by finer detail.
arxiv-2605-00368:
Bjorn Nansen and 3 co-authors study how Australian children respond to the country's new social media ban, which bars under-sixteen accounts and obliges platforms to enforce the limit. The team ran five focus groups with fifteen young people aged twelve to sixteen. They asked how the children understood the ban's fairness, impact, and legitimacy as they met the platforms enforcing it.

The children widely judged the ban unfair and ineffective. Through the platforms' access controls, they learned where the system failed and how it, and their peers' accounts, could be evaded. The authors name this practice sneaking, and use it as a lens on the social encounter between children, platforms, and regulation. Their point is broader: children test and negotiate the systems that govern them, and purely technical controls struggle with social problems.
arxiv-2605-00468:
Joey Chan and 10 co-authors ask what happens when plain-language summaries of health research are personalized for each reader. Such summaries aim to open research to lay readers, but the standard one-size-fits-all style ignores differing needs and reading levels. In health, a misunderstanding can change a real decision, so the stakes of tailoring are unusually concrete.

Their dataset, ReLay, pairs fifty lay participants with summaries in two settings: fixed expert-written versions and interactive versions personalized by a language model. It records reader traits, information needs, search behavior, comprehension, interaction logs, and quality ratings. Evaluating five models under two personalization methods, they find personalization improves comprehension and perceived quality. It also raises the risk of echoing a reader's biases and of introducing invented content. That tension between help and safety frames their call for personalization that is both effective and trustworthy.
arxiv-2605-00768:
Jiaoda Li and Ryan Cotterell give a formal account of why local attention can improve transformer language models. Global attention lets each token use all earlier tokens, at quadratic cost. Local attention limits each token to a bounded window, cutting cost to linear, yet it sometimes raises quality as well. The authors explain that puzzle through recognizer expressivity, meaning which language patterns a model can in principle detect.

They prove local attention adds a second temporal operator beyond the one linked to global attention, strictly widening the regular languages that can be recognized. Neither form contains the other, and combining them gives the richest class. Tests on formal languages and natural language modeling support the theory.
arxiv-2605-01068:
Piedad J. Miranda and five co-authors study how drone vibration affects acoustic tap-testing for building tile checks, and how to correct for it. Checking tile integrity matters for public safety and urban durability over time. Mounting tap-testing on an unmanned aerial vehicle adds dynamic perturbations that can degrade sorting, so the authors build a controlled test rig to measure that effect.

A Stewart platform reproduces oscillatory conditions from drone flight characterization across several amplitudes. Wireless sound data are classified with principal component analysis. Accuracy falls significantly as perturbation grows, but an energy-based signal correction and filtering method restores performance above ninety-eight percent. The approach preserves key defect-related features while reducing data size.
arxiv-2605-01168:
Leixin Zhang and one co-author study disagreement in graded human ratings of inappropriate language, covering offensive language, hate speech, and toxicity perception. Annotators do not always agree, and such splits are now seen as inherent to many tasks. Items differ in how much divergence they elicit. The authors ask whether the degree of split can be predicted from textual features.

They propose an Opposition Index that quantifies perspective opposition among annotators on an item. They study prediction of both variance and high-opposition cases. Estimated and observed variance correlate moderately, and two prediction approaches perform comparably. Items with high opposition are harder to predict and are often underestimated by models, a warning for systems that treat labels as settled.
arxiv-2605-01568:
Wojciech Kozłowski and four co-authors unify the zoo of stochastic image enhancement methods, which restore degraded photos through a random process run over time. Many recent methods steer that process by the degraded input, and how they relate to plain diffusion models has been unclear.

The classification sorts methods into three families: unconditional diffusion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, and diffusion bridges. All three, the authors show, flow from one stochastic differential equation. They differ only in drift and diffusion terms, end distributions, and boundary conditions, while schedules and samplers are free choices on top. With that map in hand, they run a controlled study across enhancement tasks with identical architectures and training rules. No family wins outright; instead, specific design choices carry the performance. A modular library, ItoVision, ships the unified frame for fair prototyping.
arxiv-2605-01768:
Xiamiao Zhao, Yuanpei Wang, and Junpeng Zhou study a Turán-type problem in hypergraphs, where edges can join more than two points at once. They extend work by Alon and Frankl on graphs that avoid a given pattern while also keeping matchings small. Their setting uses expansions, formed by adding new points inside each edge of a graph.

The team finds the largest number of edges a hypergraph can have while avoiding both a large matching and an expanded clique, for small and for large matching limits. A key step is a rainbow version of the same problem across a family of hypergraphs. The result partly confirms a conjecture by Gerbner, Tompkins, and Zhou.
arxiv-2605-01868:
Rui Xu and colleagues work on conformal prediction, a method that gives prediction sets with a stated coverage rate. The guarantee assumes test data match the calibration data. When the distribution shifts, most fixes align overall score patterns, which can still leave single inputs badly covered in places where conditions differ.

The authors bound that single-input error by the distance between calibration and test distributions, which points to transport as a fix. Their Branched Normalizing Flow has two branches: one maps a test input toward the calibration form, and the other maps its prediction set back. Tests show the method holds conditional coverage better under shift than prior approaches.
arxiv-2605-02168:
Wenyi Wu, Sibo Zhu, Kun Zhou, and Biwei Huang split long-horizon agent work into three roles and ask which role deserves the most compute. Their framework uses a planner for high-level choices, an actor for execution, and a memory manager for context. That split is a known pattern, so the authors focus on how compute should be shared among the parts.

Their analysis finds planning dominates task performance. Execution and memory need far less compute and model size to stay competitive. Building on that, they train only the planner with reinforcement learning, using trajectory rewards from a vision-language judge, while freezing the other parts. The planner-centric design aims for strong long-horizon results at lower total cost.
arxiv-2605-02468:
D. Delicato and forty-four co-authors report background tests for BULLKID, a cryogenic detector built to search for light dark matter and for a rare neutrino scattering process. The device holds sixty small silicon blocks, each sensed by a kinetic inductance detector. For this test it ran on the surface, with modest shielding, rather than deep underground.

The team used fifteen array units, with two central units read for background and the units around them used as a veto. Over two hundred ninety hours, the low-energy counts matched simulations well down to six hundred electron volts. Below that, counts rose above the forecast, though not in the same way as a low-energy excess seen in other cryogenic work. High-energy counts also matched simulations.
arxiv-2605-02568:
Jaber Jaber and Osama Jaber present StreamIndex, a memory-saving implementation of compressed sparse attention, a method used in recent DeepSeek language models. In that method, a small learned indexer scores compressed keys and picks the top few for each query. Standard code builds the full score table first, which at long sequence lengths exceeds any single graphics card's memory.

StreamIndex avoids building that table. A chunked driver finds the top scores part by part and merges the parts, all in Triton code. On realistic test shapes, the standard path ran out of memory where StreamIndex ran, and it stretched the workable length far beyond the baseline with modest peak memory. Overlap with exact results was near perfect across design sweeps, and the driver fits with pipelined attention kernels.
arxiv-2605-02768:
David Gamarnik and three co-authors rigorously compute the free energy of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model at high temperature. The model, a disordered quantum mean-field system, is studied both for condensed matter and as a toy model of black holes. Its traits were derived by physicists with replica and path integral methods, but rigorous math lagged, even for basic quantities like the annealed free energy.

At high but fixed temperature, the authors settle both the annealed and quenched free energy limits. Their values agree numerically with the physics results. The proof route is new: it uses the component structure of sparse random graphs plus a variant of the cavity method, a tool from spin glass theory. Closing a physics-derived formula with a full proof is the contribution.
arxiv-2605-02868:
Ruichao Liang and seven co-authors present an agent system that writes working exploits for flaws in decentralized finance smart contracts. Such flaws drain billions each year, yet most disclosed bugs are never proved exploitable, because building a proof-of-concept by hand is slow, expert work. Protocols stay exposed in the gap between disclosure and proof.

The system treats exploit building as structured reasoning, not plain code generation. A hierarchical knowledge graph stores protocol meaning, failure causes, and exploit building blocks, serving as memory for guided multi-step search. Candidate exploits face two checks: a solver test that the exploit path is reachable, and an asset-level simulation that real profit is possible. Tests cover dozens of real attacks and audited contracts. The aim is faster verification of what is truly exploitable.
arxiv-2605-02968:
Ping Wang and Yan-Qi Du introduce a finite-size framework for tracking how gradients move during language model pretraining. Five measures separate cascade size, duration, total transport, and transport efficiency per unit, giving a compact state picture of training dynamics. The data are raw gradient measurements from a small model family across four scales, plus update fields from a larger public family across five scales.

The same algebraic closure holds in both families, with a shared near-unity size backbone, but their transport regimes differ. One family scales positively in duration and negatively in efficiency; the other hugs the baseline with weak efficiency scaling. Randomized controls give matched null floors, so the contrast reads as real. Compressibility into clean power laws also differs between the families.
arxiv-2605-03268:
Turan Orujlu, Jordan Matelsky, Martin V. Butz, Charley M. Wu, and Konrad P. Kording extend structural causal models to settings where hidden context shapes both the graph and the mechanisms. In many real systems, upstream conditions decide which links exist and how variables respond, yet standard models treat the graph as fixed and fully seen.

Their partially observed models allow interventions on nodes, edges, and context together, with edge effects split into local transmission channels. Identifiability theory shows which intervention sets can separate structure from mechanism. Tests in a simulated retina and a gene network analogue matched the theory's predictions closely.
arxiv-2605-03468:
Qian-Qian Hong, Zhi-Jian Zheng, Zhe-Jun Zhang, Xin-Xia Jian, and Chuan-Cun Shu build a theoretical framework for universal single-qutrit control in asymmetric-top molecules. A qutrit uses three levels instead of two, and molecules with three distinct rotation axes offer rich level structure but complex control.

The qutrit sits in three rotational states, with an auxiliary state giving independent phase control. Direct rotations plus auxiliary-mediated phases cover all gates, guided by a multilevel pulse-area theorem mapping gate targets to microwave fields. Simulations on 1,2-propanediol show clean Walsh-Hadamard gates with minimal leakage, and error sensitivity depends on the decomposition route chosen.
arxiv-2605-03668:
João Henrique Andrade and four co-authors prove quantitative stability estimates for the Trudinger-Moser inequality on smooth bounded domains in the plane. The inequality controls exponential integrals of functions by their gradient energy, and stability asks how near a near-extremal function must be to the true optimizers. The authors measure that closeness through the inequality's deficit.

They show the deficit controls distance to the optimizer set quadratically. That holds when the exponential growth rate is small enough. It also holds when the domain is a round disk, where the estimate survives even in the critical case. Both proofs use a new spectral gap, which the authors note may interest others. The estimate also holds generically in nondegenerate cases.
arxiv-2605-03768:
James R. Beattie, Isabelle Connor, and Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz measure the Strouhal number of turbulence driven by supernovae in the interstellar medium. The Strouhal number compares how long turbulent driving stays coherent with the turnover time of the largest eddies. Turbulence-box models commonly just set it to one, yet statistics such as the gas density distribution are sensitive to that choice.

Computing the number directly from two-time correlation tensors in stratified, multiphase simulations of Milky Way-like and starburst disks, they find median values near one quarter in both cases. The scale-dependent curves reach one at a nearly universal fraction of the outer scale, consistent with supernova remnants driving turbulence locally near their cooling radius.
arxiv-2605-03868:
David Mumford and Sy-David Friedman argue that the usual Zermelo-Fraenkel-Choice axioms do not settle the foundations of everyday mathematics. Set theory admits many models with different truths, and even classical questions such as the measurability of projective sets can vary between them. The core of mathematics, they contend, lies in structures built from the real numbers.

They propose a foundation for core mathematics consisting of both a system of axioms and a definite model of those axioms, in which essentially all core mathematics is incorporated. Because the model is definite, every core mathematical assertion receives a definite truth value, true or false, rather than depending on which set-theoretic universe one happens to inhabit.
arxiv-2605-04068:
Bilel Abderrahmane Benziane, Benoit Lardeux, Ayoub Mcharek, and Maher Jridi design a forecasting selection tool for supply chain demand prediction. Artificial intelligence forecasting methods abound, but choosing the right one for a given dataset is daunting because each dataset has distinct features. Their architecture acts as a double deep reinforcement learning agent that picks a forecasting model from a committee at prediction time.

A novel early-stopping approach based on average reward convergence speeds up the agent's training. The empirical study uses grocery sales datasets and snack demand datasets. Against state-of-the-art selection methods, the proposed approach proved robust, automatically matching forecasting models to the data at hand rather than forcing one method onto every demand series.
arxiv-2605-04268:
The ARA Collaboration reports how sensitive the Askaryan Radio Array, an observatory buried in Antarctic ice, is to neutrinos with extremely high energy. These rare particles should trigger brief radio pulses as they create particle cascades in the ice.

Using an improved simulation that adds data-driven detector effects and secondary particles, the team calculates the full array's trigger-level reach for its 2013 to 2023 run. They find world-leading sensitivity at the highest energies, with secondary particles adding a sizable share of the acceptance. Under the most hopeful flux models, up to thirteen neutrinos may already sit in the recorded data.
arxiv-2605-04468:
Xinyu Wang and three co-authors tackle catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning large language models, where learning a new task erodes skills the model already had. Recent evidence blames excessive drift in the model's output distribution during training.

Their anchored method controls that drift directly. Instead of pulling the model toward one fixed reference, a moving anchor blends the current model with a frozen reference. That blend forms an intermediate target. Training thus becomes a chain of small local updates. They prove a stable per-step bound on distribution change, and experiments on maths, medical calculation, and instruction tasks place the method on the best trade-off frontier.
arxiv-2605-04568:
Jonathan Spieler and Sven Behnke present a model-based reinforcement learning method that plans robot actions by imagining future trajectories inside a learned world model. Planning methods that search without gradients are reliable but expensive in high-dimensional control, while gradient-based planning has often performed worse despite its promise.

Their approach rolls out a policy to propose a few candidate trajectories. It then improves each by gradient ascent through the learned model. An uncertainty penalty discourages straying into regions the model knows poorly. Reusing previously optimised actions spreads the cost over time. Across twenty-four continuous control tasks, the method improves significantly on earlier approaches.
arxiv-2605-04668:
Haimin Li and Qing Wang classify the irreducible ordinary modules of affine vertex operator superalgebras. These algebras are built from basic classical Lie superalgebras. The work sits at a special family of levels, called boundary admissible levels. Such a list tells us exactly which modules the algebra admits at those levels. That is a basic structural question.

The answer splits sharply by type. For superalgebras of type I, the count is exact. There are as many distinct such modules as a positive integer parameter built into the level. For ordinary simple Lie algebras and type II superalgebras, the algebra is its own only such module. That strong rigidity statement is proved uniformly across the cases.
arxiv-2605-05068:
Raven Cilley and ten co-authors analyse a near-ultraviolet transit of XO-3 b, a massive hot Jupiter on an eccentric orbit, observed in 2024 with the XMM-Newton space telescope. Ultraviolet transits can reveal escaping atmospheres, cloud formation, and planetary magnetic fields. This planet was already known for an unusually large ultraviolet-absorbing atmosphere.

Combining the ultraviolet data with a ground-based optical transit and all TESS observations, they find the ultraviolet transit notably deeper than the optical one and its centre arriving late. Escape alone looks too weak to explain it, since the estimated mass loss is extremely small. A magnetic bow shock, they argue, could produce offsets of the observed size.
arxiv-2605-05168:
Pau Colomer and three co-authors close a long-standing gap in deterministic identification. That is a communication task where the receiver only needs to know which of a set of messages was sent, not decode data. For channels with continuous inputs, the best achievable and provable limits had never quite met. A recent galaxy code construction closed that gap for Gaussian noise channels.

The authors extend that approach to the Bernoulli channel. From there they handle any channel whose outputs trace a continuous curve, by reducing it to a Bernoulli subproblem. They prove the converse bound is tight for this broad class, settling its identification capacity. They also analyse the rate-reliability trade-off, improving lower bounds on the reliability function toward the converse.
arxiv-2605-05268:
M AlMasri generalises proper scoring rules, the incentive tools that reward honest probability forecasts, into the quantum domain. Probability distributions are replaced by density operators, the quantum states used to describe uncertain systems. AlMasri defines quantum value functionals from operator convex generators and builds a complete duality theory that yields proper quantum scoring rules from them.

From that theory come minimax optimal bounds for quantum state tomography under such incentives, including a quantum Cramér-Rao-McCarthy bound tying risk to the generator's curvature and quantum Fisher information. AlMasri also prices quantum resources such as coherence, entanglement, and adaptivity in forecasting tasks, finding scaling separations between classical and quantum strategies with uses for sensors and data markets.
arxiv-2605-05368:
What is information, at the level of logic? Matthew Collinson, Timo Eckhardt, and David Pym argue that the concept still lacks firm mathematical foundations. Without them, reasoning about the complex systems modern society depends on stays shaky. Their paper takes a first step toward an inferentialist theory of information.

One strand rethinks basic notions, swapping truth for inferability in Dretske's classic account. A second uses proof-theoretic semantics to define a basic unit of information, the inferon. A third applies those tools to distributed systems, giving a reasoning-based picture of how information flows through them.
arxiv-2605-05468:
TRAPPIST-1, a cool dwarf star with several planets, flares often and hard. Valeriy Vasilyev and twelve co-authors built a single flare-frequency distribution spanning four orders of magnitude in energy. They combined about eighty-seven hours of JWST spectroscopy with roughly seventy-four days of Kepler photometry, converting every event to one common energy scale.

The combined data follow one power law, with no break needed. Rare, powerful flares dominate the star's total flare energy output. Strong flares also occur about ten times more often than earlier estimates suggested, which matters for the atmospheres and habitability of the system's planets.
arxiv-2605-05668:
Vision-language models are residual transformers at heart, whatever their training recipe. Gongli Xi and seven co-authors ask what the attention and feed-forward parts each actually do inside. Earlier attribution studies lacked a shared theoretical basis, so the team builds one from information theory and geometry to measure residual updates.

The framework reveals a clean division of labor. Attention acts as a subspace-preserving operator, moving information without rotating its geometry, while other components reshape representations. The authors argue these models can get lost in attention when that preservation goes wrong, and the diagnostics point to architectural fixes.
arxiv-2605-05768:
Yuqian Cheng, Zhuo Chen, and Qian Lin study uniform error bounds for a class of kernel regression methods called kernel gradient flows. Users need to know not just average error, but the worst error across the whole input range. The authors work under a standard capacity and source condition used in kernel learning theory.

They prove convergence rates for the supremum norm error of both continuous and discrete gradient flows. Those rates match the best possible minimax rates for the problem. On that base they build simultaneous confidence bands that cover the true function as a whole. The band widths shrink at rates that can come close to the best possible rate as well.
arxiv-2605-05868:
Agent skills bundle instructions and executable resources that extend what a language-model agent can do. Jiangrong Wu and six co-authors warn that a skill can quietly exceed what the user's task requires, violating least privilege. The same action may be essential for one prompt and overreach for another, so detection must be task-conditioned.

Their framework, SkillScope, analyzes skills through a graph-based approach to flag over-privileged behavior relative to the current task. Fine-grained enforcement is the goal: permit the actions the task needs, block the rest. The work frames skill safety as contextual authorization, not blanket approval.
arxiv-2605-06068:
Keisuke Kamahori and three co-authors let AI coding agents build language model serving systems from scratch. Serving stacks are usually one general purpose system, hand tuned over many engineer years for every model and workload. The authors take the opposite bet: generate a bespoke stack for each usage scenario instead.

Their loop, VibeServe, plans a search over system designs in an outer loop. An inner loop then writes each candidate, checks it for correctness, and measures it on the target benchmark. In standard settings the generated systems matched leading tools on a mid size model. For a huge mixture of experts model they delivered 2.3 times the goodput of a tuned rival, and won in five non standard scenarios.
arxiv-2605-06168:
Tobia Filosi and nine co-authors build a scalable way to choose models for count time series with sudden structural breaks. Weekly health care counts are non negative, linked over time, and can be jolted by system wide shocks, which makes Gaussian models a poor fit. Their case study is solid organ transplant activity in the USA and Italy from 2014 to late 2024.

Poisson and negative binomial models include short term dynamics, holiday week effects, and pandemic level and slope shifts. A screened portfolio of models is picked by an information criterion inside each training window, then judged on expanding window forecasts. Deceased donor series in both countries returned toward pre pandemic baselines. The US living donor series converged more slowly, and COVID burden measures added little predictive value.
arxiv-2605-06368:
Paulo Mario Medina, Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza, and Sebastian Ibañez regularize image classifiers with contrastive pairs of visual explanations. Distribution shift breaks models through spurious correlations, and many remedies beat plain risk minimization only at times while growing hard to interpret. Their framework, eXplaining to Learn, instead decorrelates confounding features from the classifier's internal features directly, using the explanation maps of two classifiers trained side by side during learning.

One classifier predicts the label and the other predicts the confounder, and training cuts similarity between their Grad-CAM activation maps. On a rigorous synthetic many to many challenge benchmark, the method set new best marks for both average and worst group accuracy. Gains over the prior state of the art ran above five and ten points on those two measures. The authors frame the result as domain invariance enforced at group level.
arxiv-2605-06468:
Enric Florit-Simon proves that two ways of bounding the area of a minimal surface are in fact equivalent. Minimal surfaces can be measured intrinsically, from within the surface, or extrinsically, from the surrounding space. He shows the intrinsic and extrinsic area density bounds match, with the same asymptotic values, for complete smooth minimal immersions of any dimension and codimension.

Combined with a recent breakthrough by Bellettini, the result extends known curvature estimates for stable minimal hypersurfaces to dimension six. That case had stayed open for decades since the estimates were first developed. The paper closes a long-standing gap in minimal surface theory.
arxiv-2605-06568:
Reason Machete revisits statistical significance testing, tracing it from Fisher's error probabilities through the Neyman-Pearson addition of alternative hypotheses and second-kind errors. Significance tests powered much scientific progress but drew lasting controversy. Bayesian ideas were later folded in, and Fisher himself warned against treating any fixed threshold as a rule.

Machete examines current reform calls: dropping the standard threshold, requiring confirmatory studies before publication, abandoning the yes-no null framing, or replacing tests with confidence intervals and Bayesian decision theory. Each proposal's strengths and shortcomings are weighed. The paper gives readers a compact history plus a critical map of the reform debate.
arxiv-2605-06768:
Yuval Grossman, Tony Menzo, Stefan Schacht, Chinhsan Sieng, and Jure Zupan extract a key weak-interaction angle from particle decays without binning the data. The CKM angle gamma is measured through a chain where a B meson decays to a D meson and a kaon, with the D decaying to a kaon and two pions. Normalizing flows trained on D decay data learn a continuous map of the decay amplitude and phase across the Dalitz plot.

Fitting B decay data against that learned map yields gamma plus the related hadronic parameters. Tests on simulated data recover the injected angle within uncertainties, with statistical errors propagated through an ensemble of flows. Two encodings of the phase constraint are compared, and Bayesian flows are discussed.
arxiv-2605-06968:
Michael McKinsey, Stephanie Brink, and Olga Pearce ask how well small proxy programs really represent large computing codes. High-performance computing teams use such benchmarks to test new machines and guide hardware design. Checking the match by hand is slow and hard to scale across many programs.

The authors define similarity measures based on how code uses computing hardware, then sort kernels into two broad performance groups. They test the measures on the Kripke proxy and a performance suite, on both plain and graphics-accelerated systems. Their metrics correctly match related kernels, offering a more systematic way to judge benchmark quality.
arxiv-2605-07168:
Xizhe Li and four co-authors build a faster connectivity oracle that survives vertex failures in a network. After a small set of vertices fails, the oracle must update quickly and then answer whether pairs of vertices remain connected. Earlier designs needed huge memory or update times that exploded with the failure count.

The new oracle updates in time depending only on the number of failures, not the graph size, and answers queries at the best possible speed. For a fixed failure count it uses near-linear space and preprocessing. The gains come from shortcutting a decomposition, reusing simpler oracles internally, and a new patch-set mechanism.
arxiv-2605-07268:
Hanmeng Liu and five co-authors harden multiple-choice reasoning tests in a formal, validity-preserving way. Benchmarks saturate quickly and suffer contamination, while ad hoc tricks like paraphrasing add surface difficulty without logical rigor. LogiHard transforms simple selection questions into higher-order logical judgments, demanding more reasoning steps from the test taker.

An adaptive testing layer controls difficulty precisely with fewer questions. Across twelve leading models, hardened questions cut accuracy sharply, and transfer to a general benchmark showed a similar drop. The authors blame a completeness-checking gap in training rather than missing knowledge, a failure pattern human test takers did not share.
arxiv-2605-07368:
Bikshapathi Gouda and Antti Tölli design beamforming for cell-free massive MIMO networks where access points send and receive at the same time. Full-duplex operation boosts spectrum use but creates self-interference and cross-talk between access points and users. Earlier over-the-air training schemes handled uplink and downlink separately.

Their fully distributed design trains beamformers with simultaneous pilots under a joint error criterion covering those interference terms. A projection step at user devices suppresses pilot leakage that would corrupt the needed cross terms. Simulations show faster convergence and higher effective rates than separate training, with the largest gains where user interference is strong.
arxiv-2605-07568:
Peitao Han and four co-authors ask why video language models are bad at telling whether a clip plays forward or backward. People ace this arrow-of-time test, while frontier models score barely above chance. Either the visual backbone never encodes the direction of time, or the information gets lost on its way to the language model.

By testing each stage separately, the team finds that video-centric encoders do carry strong time signals, while frame-centric ones do not. The projector is a key bottleneck: a Q-Former design scrambles the signal, while a time-preserving projection passes it through. Their rebuilt system reached 98.1 percent accuracy on the test, above human performance, and also improved on broader temporal reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-07668:
Shuo Zhang and three co-authors propose a yardstick for how hard a quantum operation is to carry out on an analog quantum simulator. These machines use global control fields and promise access to many-body physics beyond classical computers, but there was no clear quantitative measure of the synthesis cost of a given operation.

They adapt Krylov complexity, a notion from operator growth dynamics, building the block Krylov basis from the simulator's native Hamiltonians and their nested commutators. In test systems including Rydberg atom arrays, the Krylov complexity of a target operation strongly predicted the minimum time needed to realize it. The measure gives designers an intuitive tool for planning efficient control protocols.
arxiv-2605-07768:
Erik Börve and three co-authors plan trajectories for one agent among others whose decisions are uncertain, a core problem for autonomous driving and robotics. Their route is to learn the distribution of surrounding agents' decisions and then solve a stochastic model predictive control problem. The catch is that the learned distribution is itself wrong in unknown ways.

They combine probably-approximately-correct learning bounds with robust optimization, so the controller hedges exactly against the errors the learning step could have made. The resulting framework sits between a fully robust controller and an all-knowing stochastic one, depending on how many samples are available. More data buys less caution in a measured way.
arxiv-2605-07868:
Shinichi Inoue and six co-authors tackle frequency crowding, a scaling bottleneck for fixed-frequency transmon quantum processors. The workhorse cross-resonance gate is normally operated in a straddling regime that tightly constrains which qubit frequencies can sit near each other, making collisions likely as chips grow. The team instead analyzes the gate far outside that regime.

Using a numerical method that stays accurate under strong, smoothly ramped drives, they sweep parameters systematically and derive collision-free conditions defining assignable frequency regions. Frequency allocation is then cast as a linear program on a unit-cell lattice. Far-detuned designs cut collisions significantly against straddling ones. A yield analysis for a thousand-qubit lattice suggests the needed frequency precision is within about a factor of two of the current state of the art.
arxiv-2605-08168:
Ayoub Agouzoul compares four fixes for a timing problem in robot control with vision-language-action models. These models are slow, so by the time an action runs, the robot's view of the world is stale. Recent methods attack the delay in different places: patching at inference time, simulating delay during training, conditioning on future states, or adding a light residual correction.

Agouzoul rebuilds all four in two shared codebases with matched versions and benchmarks them on the Kinetix suite and on LIBERO manipulation tasks, sweeping delays up to twenty control steps. The controlled comparison shows how each method holds up as latency grows.
arxiv-2605-08268:
Xiaolin Sun, Zixuan Liu, Yibin Hu, and Zizhan Zheng study a saboteur inside a team of language model agents. Groups of agents increasingly reach decisions by exchanging messages until they agree, and most frameworks assume every member shares the group's goal. A malicious insider can instead pose as a normal member while secretly working to delay or block consensus.

The authors formalize the attack as a sequential decision problem. To optimize it, they learn a world model that mimics the latent behavior of the honest agents, then train the attacker against that surrogate. The study maps how fragile multi-agent agreement can be from the inside.
arxiv-2605-08368:
Yuhao Li and Shengchao Liu draw a line that post-training debates often blur: does fine-tuning or reinforcement learning merely surface skills a model already had, or does it create new ones? Calling the first elicitation and the second creation, the authors argue the distinction should guide research claims.

They make the idea operational with accessible support, the set of behaviors a model can realistically produce within finite budgets. Training that reweights behavior inside that set is elicitation; shifting the set itself is creation. A free-energy view shows supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning both reweight a pretrained reference distribution, which reframes several standing arguments about what each method can do.
arxiv-2605-08568:
Hengyi Zhu, Zhendong Mi, Grace Li Zhang, and Shaoyi Huang shrink large language models by choosing compression levels per prompt. Standard singular value methods cut every input at the same fixed rank, yet the best rank shifts from prompt to prompt and depends heavily on the calibration data. Their framework, PARSE, trains a small router to pick ranks ahead of time.

Similar prompts share rank patterns that stay stable while answers generate, so chosen ranks can be served from a cache for speed. Added to four existing compression methods, PARSE lifts task accuracy and speeds both prompt reading and answer generation. Model deployment gains quality and speed from treating each prompt on its own terms.
arxiv-2605-08668:
Yuxuan Chen, Shuo Dai, Ruoyi Xu, and Haipeng Xie forecast electricity load by enriching time series with text and image knowledge instead of recycled copies of the same data. Prior multi modal methods mostly rework the series itself, adding redundancy rather than new knowledge, which hurts when data is scarce. Their KEMM-Net builds textual and visual embeddings that widen what the model can draw on.

A decomposition guided contrastive step then balances redundant, shared, and unique information across the modes before forecasting. On real public datasets, the method beats strong deep and multi modal baselines, with the clearest gains in few shot settings common in power systems. Grid forecasting gains accuracy from genuinely added knowledge.
arxiv-2605-08968: Feihu Liu and Jinlong Tang prove four growth line claims set by Chapoton. The claims are on arbor polytopes, shapes tied to a set line of tree like arbors. Two claims give closed forms for the growth lines of the linked poset. One is its Zeta count. One is its M-triangle. Two claims are on the shape's Ehrhart count and its volume Laplace form. All four close one pack of asks that tie poset counts to shape math.
arxiv-2605-09068:
Dong-Hui Yang and Bao-Zhu Guo study vibration-like modes, called eigenfunctions, for a class of differential operators that degenerate at part of the boundary. In such problems a weight stays positive inside the region but drops to zero on part of the edge, and many pleasant properties of standard operators are lost.

The authors prove a version of Courant's nodal domain theorem for this degenerate setting, a classic result about how the region splits into zones where a mode keeps one sign. They also show that a generic property survives: for almost every added bounded term, in a precise topological sense, the operator's eigenvalues are all simple. The work extends core spectral theory to a harder class of operators.
arxiv-2605-09168:
Fabio Rovai, writing alone, argues that a valid tool call by a language agent is not the same as a valid action in the world. Guards that check form, policy, and origin cannot certify that a state-changing step will actually help. His 2026 paper presents CIVeX, a checker that turns each proposed action into a causal question over a stored graph of actions and states.

CIVeX returns one of four verdicts: carry out the action, refuse it, test it, or hold off. Approval needs a causal certificate with a lower bound on benefit plus records of origin and risk. On a bench of nearly two thousand cases, the system made no false executions under moderate or hostile confounding. It also matched near-perfect choices on two sets of real logs.
arxiv-2605-09268:
Sinha and three colleagues stress test multi turn understanding in LLMs, where users routinely refine requests or pivot mid conversation. Models often miss these shifts and drag irrelevant context from earlier turns, producing inaccurate responses. The team studies two sub tasks: shortlisting relevant context from previous turns, and spotting when the user pivots or refines mid turn.

They construct synthetic benchmarks from real world data sets across varied domains, simulating context shifts of different difficulty levels. Across ten LLMs tested zero shot, only some reasoning and strongly instructed models detect pivots accurately. Open weight models struggle and often drag old context along despite clear cues, while every model shows a position bias. The results point to ways of improving long term robustness in multi turn LLM capabilities. The work shows continuity assumptions break when users change direction without starting a new session, a routine pattern.
arxiv-2605-09668:
Fisman and Meirom introduced a new way to compare infinite sets, built to capture long-run likeness rather than freak outliers. Their Asymptotic Hausdorff lifting takes a distance between single items and lifts it to a distance between sets, ignoring finite gaps. Older Hausdorff-style lifts, by contrast, let single outliers dominate and miss long-run behavior.

Formal languages are the motivating case: items are words, sets are languages, and the lift yields metric-valued distances between languages. The authors studied the groups of regular languages the lift treats as alike for normalized edit distances, pinning down their long-run essence. For the Marzal-Vidal normalized edit distance, they probed how to compute the lifted distance for regular and bounded context-free languages.
arxiv-2605-09768:
Arshad and nine colleagues built SAGE, a grounded evaluation system for crop disease diagnosis, plus the largest plant-disease image-symptom dataset to date. Labeled disease images are scarce and uneven across crops, pathogens, and field conditions, while frontier vision-language models still stumble on fine-grained disease calls for lack of structured symptom knowledge. The dataset covers 335 crops, 1,251 disease classes, and about 839,000 images.

An automated pipeline writes source-grounded symptom notes, each claim tied to a verbatim web quote, with experts validating samples and reconciling disease-name variants. The agentic baseline reads anatomy, narrows candidates by symptoms, compares reference images in sequence, and leaves a full reasoning trace. Adding symptom knowledge lifted accuracy by 16.2 points on average at full reference budget, and new crops need only reference images plus symptom notes, no retraining.
arxiv-2605-09868:
Damian, Loaiza-Brito and López-Ramos work in string theory, studying Type IIB compactifications where fluxes and the dilaton field vary across a complex two-dimensional plane. Compactification means rolling extra dimensions into a small shape, and dynamical cobordism is a framework that asks which such shapes can end consistently. From the equations of motion the authors show that End-of-the-World branes exist, boundaries where spacetime stops.

In cohomological language those branes appear exactly where needed to cancel a topological charge, and the paper computes the associated bordism group to show the cancellation. Extra non-perturbative objects are still required to kill the class fully, while its cohomological part survives as a subgroup. The structure suggests a link between energy scales and which physical effects, perturbative or not, show up.
arxiv-2605-09968:
Guha, working alone, proposes a unified language for adaptive learning systems, which must switch between locking in what they know and expanding into new evidence. The framework, Consolidation-Expansion Operator Mechanics, centres on the order-gap: how much the consolidation and expansion operators refuse to commute at any one knowledge state. Because it can be read from the system's own path, the gap works as a live control signal.

Large gaps mean ordering still matters and the system is unsettled, while a gap that falls and stays small means further processing will likely change little. Three results make this precise, including a stopping rule with provable promises under noise-free and bounded-noise conditions. The framework spans bandits, reinforcement learning, stochastic optimisation, continual learning and recursive language models, with the recursive-model case developed in full as a rule-based stand-in for rule-of-thumb stopping rules.
arxiv-2605-10268:
Baibei Ji and five colleagues improve how AI agents reason over very long documents. Large language models struggle when context grows, partly because attention costs rise quadratically with length. Memory-based agents read in chunks and update a running memory, but facts discarded along the way are often lost for good. Their 2026 paper presents MemReread, a fix built on streaming reading.

MemReread skips intermediate retrieval. When the final memory proves insufficient, it breaks the question down and rereads the source, recovering indirect facts that were dropped too early. A reinforcement learning framework also stretches length extrapolation and sets the number of rereading passes from task complexity. Across long-context reasoning tasks MemReread beat baseline frameworks consistently, while keeping time costs linear in context length.
arxiv-2605-10368:
Shaull Almagor and two colleagues extend Simon's factorization theorem from words to forests. Simon's theorem is a famous tool in automata theory, providing bounded-depth splits of words with respect to maps into finite semigroups. Developing an analogue for forests presents a basic difficulty: recursively splitting a forest requires tracking where each subforest fits. Their 2026 paper overcomes it by adding to the free forest algebra and building a framework for recursive splitting.

The main result identifies a new meaning limit on maps, called R-alignment, which roughly keeps different ways of cutting a forest in step at the semigroup level. Under this limit, the authors prove that every map admits bounded-depth splits. They also prove the limit is necessary: without it, some maps admit no bounded-depth split under their notion of splitting. Readers get both a positive theorem and a matching negative result.
arxiv-2605-10468:
Xingyu Qu and two colleagues ask whether Muon can fine-tune models pretrained with Adam. Muon offers an efficient pretraining alternative to Adam, yet sees little use in fine-tuning. Most open models come pretrained with Adam, and moving to Muon for fine-tuning without care degrades performance. Their 2026 paper investigates that mismatch through controlled experiments.

The authors relate the mismatch to the distinct implicit biases of Adam and Muon. Evidence shows the mismatch disrupts pretrained knowledge in proportion to update strength. That suggests constraining updates should mitigate the mismatch. The authors test it with LoRA, which freezes pretrained weights and holds updates inside a low-rank subspace. Across language and vision tasks, LoRA shrinks the performance gap between Adam and Muon seen under full fine-tuning. Studies on LoRA rank, forgetting, and LoRA variants confirm mismatch severity tracks update strength.
arxiv-2605-10568:
Yeonseok Lee proposes a self-fixing framework for CNC machine code. Language models can turn human intent into G-code. But a sound toolpath may still cause a crash, since safe runs depend on machine state, fixtures, and stock size. His 2026 paper pairs neural generation with formal checks.

The framework pulls exact boundary shapes from 3D CAD models using OpenCASCADE. An LLM writes the first code draft, while a Separation Logic prover with a Spatial Heap model checks the output. Crashes are treated as logical Spatial Data Races, breaks of the separating conjunction in Separation Logic. Proof failures turn into math feedback, packed into bounding boxes that direct the LLM's step-by-step self-fixing. The goal is safer, checked self-run manufacturing with less human oversight.
arxiv-2605-10868:
Mauricio Mendivelso-Villaquirán turns the Solar System into a classroom laboratory for Newton's law of universal gravitation. Textbooks usually hand students the finished formula as a fact from three centuries ago, with no path showing how it was earned.

A deduction built from public data from trusted sources uses planetary observations of the kind Kepler analyzed before Newton unified them. Students see how scattered measurements harden into a single law, and teachers get a worked route for teaching deduction rather than memorization. Middle- and high-school physics classes are the intended audience.
arxiv-2605-11268:
Elham Pourabbas Vafa, Sayak Saha Roy, and Shirin Nilizadeh show how public social data and generative AI can be misused to run context-aware spear-phishing campaigns. With little foe effort, a bit of public activity per target lets GenAI models extract tastes and cues, making messages matching target style while bypassing generic safeguards.

The team introduces a modular framework mixing multimodal signal pulls, style profiles, and attack-type setup across seven tactics: baiting, scareware, honey trap, tailing, impersonation, quid pro quo, and emotional exploitation. A large-scale, multi-model study covers thousands of emails and eight security criteria, set against real-world phishing mails. GenAI emails show much higher personal touch, grounding, and pull. A user study backs these results: LLM attacks beat APWG eCrimeX emails across eight angles while drawing less suspicion among human readers. Security teams get hard evidence of GenAI spear-phishing potency.
arxiv-2605-11368: Jeongchan Kim, Yunkyung Ko and Jong Chul Ye propose LPDP, a training-free operator for reward-guided DNA generation with Edit Flows. Unlike fixed-length frameworks, Edit Flows build variable-length DNA through biologically plausible insertions, deletions and substitutions. During each guided rollout, LPDP rates single-step root edits, keeps a near-best band, and re-ranks each root by working out a small bounded discrete program around its child sequence. It serves two regimes: front-loaded tilting for enhancer optimization and back-loaded tilting for exon-intron-exon inpainting.
arxiv-2605-11668: Wrobel, Barkana and Landowska compare animated emotion displays across cultures for wearables. Wearables can sense feelings nonstop, yet sending that data back quietly is hard, and lifelike avatars rarely fit small screens. Simple shape animation offers a fast, easy-to-read alternative, but cross-culture use is untested. In a study of 105 people from Poland and Turkey mapping feelings to color, shape, size and speed, color and object size proved understood everywhere. Animation speed alone showed cultural differences in range tastes, informing auto-made visuals for global use.
arxiv-2605-12168: Theresa Dahl Frehr and three colleagues ask what low-resolution data teaches. Many systems lack datasets, as sharing is limited by storage, privacy, or resources, and wearables aggregate data, losing detail. High- and low-resolution samples mix, yet low-resolution data's value on high-resolution tests is unclear. Kullback-Leibler theory shows how point influence shifts with resolution and bounds the value of high- versus low-resolution observations. Tests with a vision transformer and a convolutional net show low-resolution data lifts scores when high-resolution data is scarce.
arxiv-2605-12368: Yang removes the retraining bottleneck from machine-learning solvers for partial differential equations. His MetaColloc system first meta-trains a two-branch network on varied random fields, building a shared dictionary of basis functions. At test time the network stays frozen, and each new equation is solved by one linear least-squares step, with Newton steps for nonlinear cases. Tests on six two- and three-dimensional equations reach leading accuracy while cutting test-time compute by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-12568: Pronzato and Zhigljavsky study quantisation for sphere-symmetric spreads before limits take over. Zador's theorem gives the limit spread and error decay for best point sets, yet in high spaces reaching that regime needs a sample size growing super-fast with space size. For mid-size samples, they show point sets spread evenly on a sphere of suitable radius perform very well. Mean error, written as a triple integral, can be found to any detail, and the best radius follows by number or from extreme-value guesses.
arxiv-2605-12668: Rivera and Tewari propose online conformal prediction methods that keep guess sets nested across cover levels. It gives finite-sample cover promises, yet old online methods often handle one level and ignore match across levels. Different users, from weather teams to risk teams, need tuned sets across risk limits, and those sets should be nested and valid at once. Their two methods output nested sets across levels, enabling at-once doubt measure across the risk spectrum without losing truth at any level.
arxiv-2605-13068: Kachhadiya alone tackles a bind in nonlinear inverse problems: first-order steps are cheap yet brittle, while curvature-aware routes like Gauss-Newton cost more. He trains a two-way stand-in, Deceptron, that can run forward and backward. As solver D-IPG, it drags error-corrected measurement-space proposals back into latent space. A Jacobian Composition Penalty shapes the reverse Jacobian into a local left inverse of the forward one. On seven PDE problems, D-IPG tops standard baselines while solving at up to 77 times lower cost.
arxiv-2605-13768: Or Ordentlich and Yury Polyanskiy study high-rate rounded matrix multiplication with spread data, part two of a work whose part one covered tuning-free rounding. They show waterfilling lifts real GPTQ rounding, which currently allocates rate equally. A recent WaterSIC scheme using only scalar INT rounders is basis free, marked by the value of the spread matrix. GPTQ scores depend on basis choice, but with random spin and Llama-3-8B spread it sits within 0.1 bit of WaterSIC, hinting near-best at high rates.
arxiv-2605-13868: Koul and Nandakumar study dimension spectra of polynomial curves, a topic in fractal shape theory. They adapt old real root-find methods to this setting. The key result: each polynomial curve has a spectrum with at least two points. That settles a query Stull had posed. The same result yields polynomials with width past one, settling a second Stull query.
arxiv-2605-14368: Kong, Lee and Jo ask where diffusion should operate inside a pretrained model, treating hidden-state interface choice as a design question. They score interfaces with three training-free geometric proxies: local compactness, global stiffness and effective rank. The score predicts diffusion bridgeability beyond layer depth alone. Their method, DiHAL, replaces the transformer prefix below an interface with diffusion, keeping the suffix and head. Geometry-chosen interfaces stay near validation-loss oracles and beat worst-layer controls. The bridge also beats a fixed replacement.
arxiv-2605-14568: Mughal, Fatima and Bilal mine behaviour-driven test suites for repeated step subsequences worth extracting as reusable pieces. From a corpus of hundreds of Gherkin repositories they cluster paraphrase-equivalent slices and train a classifier to rank extraction-worthy candidates against three known refactoring patterns. The classifier is claimed to beat both a rule baseline and language-model judges, and most scenarios are found to carry at least one candidate.
arxiv-2605-14768: Nayak, Sharma and Mishra introduce an algebra method for eigenvalue bounds of symmetric positive definite tensors. Trace and determinant do the work as key numbers. A chain of bounds from the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality yields tighter and tighter upper and lower bounds. The bounds cover the tensor spectral radius and smallest eigenvalue. Tests claim the new approach beats older coordinate methods such as Gershgorin bounds. The bounds stay robust where Gershgorin bounds fail, including tensors with negative off-diagonal terms.
arxiv-2605-14868: Ciosek, Petrov, Felicioni and Palla introduce fast adversarial attacks with gradient prediction. Generating adversarial examples is core to robustness evaluation and red-teaming, yet even fast attacks like FGSM are limited by the backward pass. The authors eliminate the backward pass by forecasting input gradients from forward-pass hidden states via linear regression. Exact affine conditional gradient means are derived, showing optimality in the idealised NTK setting. Much of FGSM performance is recovered at a fraction of the time, a claimed five hundred and thirty-two percent increase.
arxiv-2605-15068: Giulia Murtas and five colleagues test whether magnetic reconnection at the heliospheric current sheet energizes protons and heavier ions seen by Parker Solar Probe. Solving the Parker transport equation on a large-scale reconnection simulation, they find several ion species develop power-law spectra whose slopes and cutoffs match in-situ data. The maximum energy scales with charge-to-mass ratio to a power near 0.8 to 1.1, consistent with probe measurements. The results support reconnection as the source of these high-energy heavy ions.
arxiv-2605-15168: Sayantan Kumar and three others reconstruct clinical timelines by pairing narrative text with structured health-record rows. Notes describe symptoms and course but compress or reorder events, while lab and drug rows carry timestamps but only part of the story. Their staged workflow extracts central narrative events and builds a temporal scaffold. It adds the rest and fixes time stamps against pulled structured rows. On 40 discharge notes with gold-standard timelines, multimodal tuning mostly improved temporal accuracy while event match rates held steady.
arxiv-2605-15268: Artem Belov and Andrey Morozov examine the claimed equivalence, at observable level, between the Ising minimal model and SU(2) level-2 Chern-Simons theory. On the surface the theories differ substantially: the counts of irreducible highest-weight representations and Ising anyons do not match. For tensor products of low degree, the authors inspect these discrepancies. They find that differing representation structure does not change the observables behind topological quantum computation algorithms.
arxiv-2605-15468: Trisha Solanki proposes GreenZ, a design frame for digital systems that waste less. Its three layers are ten guiding rules, five applied systems, and hands-on audit tools. At its core sit a list of eight kinds of digital waste and a choice model. That model asks if AI belongs in a step at all, before asking how to build it. The frame rests on theory but has no test data yet. An expert review is now in progress.
arxiv-2605-15568: Laszlo Wolf, Geoff L. Brennecka, and Vladan Stevanović probe why boron breaks the link between stiffness and piezoelectric reply in an aluminum-scandium nitride alloy. They run first-principles sums on 100-atom random structures across many mixes. Pair plots show boron atoms wedged off-site with three bonds, lined up along the c-axis by a scandium-driven route. Boron slowly evens out the scandium setting. Charge links show this evening-out drives the piezoelectric gain.
arxiv-2605-16068: Dutkiewicz, Misiorek, and Wrembel propose a richer ontology for tracing data lineage in relational databases. Links between database objects are often incomplete or missing. Their formal vocabulary captures structural, semantic, and change details of such data. In a knowledge-graph link test, the enriched model improved link recovery over the earlier baseline. The goal is to help analysts find where each field in a report came from and how it was changed on the way.
arxiv-2605-16268: Atreya and nine colleagues build a customer-facing triage agent that helps banks route fraud, scam, and dispute reports to the right specialist teams. Manual triage is slow and stressful for customers and staff alike. Their language-model agent holds multi-turn conversations, asks targeted questions, and classifies cases under policy-guided routing. Tested against synthetic digital twins of real customers, it improved classification accuracy on historical cases by 30.6 percent, with high satisfaction from subject-matter experts.
arxiv-2605-16568: Wu's thesis tackles reasoning under uncertainty in knowledge graphs. Such graphs may carry vague values, uncertain links, and patchy schema knowledge. Current Semantic Web standards offer no native way to reason with such uncertainty. Naive add-ons fail to scale, so the work builds a modular framework across three levels. It defines probabilistic literals with a query algebra for attributes. It compiles SPARQL provenance into usable probabilistic circuits for uncertain triples. It uses topology-aware embeddings for schema reasoning.
arxiv-2605-16668: Bresson and colleagues introduce GraViti, a graph-level variational autoencoder built on transformers that packs an entire graph into one fixed-length latent vector. The encoder stays permutation-invariant, so input order does not matter, but the rebuild loss need not be, when training data use a consistent node order. Dropping the cubic-cost matching step cuts complexity to quadratic while improving rebuild quality. The latent space allows smooth interpolation, molecular editing, property search, and direct regression of graph properties.
arxiv-2605-16768: Gao and colleagues propose ARG-Mamba, a state-space framework for segmenting optical-elevation remote-sensing images. Existing methods struggle with multi-scale context and cross-modal fusion in complex high-resolution scenes. A multi-scale state-space module captures fine local detail and global context with linear complexity, while an axial-relation fusion module models cross-modal correlations along horizontal and vertical axes. On the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam datasets, ARG-Mamba beats state-of-the-art methods while keeping computation favorable.
arxiv-2605-17068: Ye proposes a Bayesian method for picking treatments when the best policy is uncertain. He places a Dirichlet process prior over the outcome distribution and uses its posterior both to choose policies and to judge best achievable welfare. The approach needs only simple reweighting of the data, and its welfare loss shrinks at the best possible rate while policy-class selection stays consistent. Trials on job training and bednet subsidies favor simple decision-tree rules over linear ones.
arxiv-2605-17568: Xu and colleagues propose a neural marked point process that uncovers interpretable event links while predicting well. A product-form neural influence kernel pairs a signed link network over event types with a delay-aware monotonic temporal network. That design maps excitation, inhibition and neutrality plus varied decay patterns and influence delays. A stratified Monte Carlo sampler enables efficient training. Tests on synthetic and real benchmarks validate both link discovery and predictive strength.
arxiv-2605-17668: Maren Høibø and colleagues explore deep-learning glass removal and compression for whole slide images, compared with JPEG and JPEG-XL. Digital pathology produces growing numbers of whole slide images; today JPEG yields several gigabytes per image. Deep-learning compression cut whole slide image size by 43 to 72 percent over JPEG, while glass removal cut size by under one percent to 33 percent. Combining both gave a 44 to 80 percent total reduction. On tissue patches, the best deep-learning models saved about 35 to 40 percent per patch over JPEG at similarity above 95 percent.
