The problem, eliciting latent knowledge, asks for an agent that truthfully states its beliefs about variables humans cannot observe. A tempting failure mode is goal misgeneralization: the agent learns to give answers humans would rate as true, which is not the same as its honest beliefs. The team formalizes this with causal influence diagrams, charts of how training, beliefs, and answers connect.

Their impossibility theorem is stark. No training strategy based only on the agent's behavior can, with certainty, produce an honest agent. This holds even when every piece of training feedback is correct. The gap is fundamental: behavior under feedback cannot distinguish an honest generalizer from one mimicking what raters reward. Under some conditions honest answers can be encouraged, and the paper maps where incentives help.
arxiv-2606-12668:
Shehata and colleagues study how quasar X-ray spectra relate to how fast their black holes are feeding, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A quasar is a bright galactic core powered by matter falling onto a supermassive black hole. The photon index measures the slope of the X-ray spectrum, while the Eddington ratio compares brightness with the theoretical maximum for its mass, a normalised feeding rate.

The team cross-matches catalogues from the XMM-Newton telescope and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, yielding 642 quasars. Of these, 561 are radio-quiet, meaning they lack powerful radio jets, and the rest are radio-loud. Radio-quiet quasars show higher feeding rates and softer spectra, with photon index near two. A clear positive correlation links the two quantities, supporting models where the accretion disc and its hot corona feed each other.
arxiv-2606-12968:
Ivanov and colleagues present Apollo, a room-temperature neuromorphic processor built from probabilistic qubits, or p-qubits, aimed at optimisation workloads, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A p-qubit is a bistable stochastic unit whose state fluctuations are driven by quantum entropy units feeding in non-deterministic quantum-derived randomness. The authors describe a 10,000-node processor built in 16-nanometre CMOS, running at room temperature with a power budget of about half a watt.

They report state-transition rates of 12.5 picoseconds per p-qubit at an energy cost of at most 10 femtojoules per transition. Through the Suzuki-Trotter isomorphism, the network's statistics are claimed to match those of a transverse-field quantum annealer in 1 fewer dimension. On the 3-dimensional spin-glass benchmark used to claim advantage for superconducting annealers, the authors use 300 disorder realisations. They report residual-energy scaling paths matching the hardware results and distinct from simulated annealing baselines.
arxiv-2606-13068:
Oddi and colleagues study how the predictive neighbourhood horizon shapes coordination in self-running railway traffic management, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a self-run system, trains predict their neighbourhood, propose traffic plans, and reach consensus with neighbours on a future plan, with no central dispatcher.

Through a closed-loop simulation, the study tests how varying the horizon affects the decentralised coordination process, from conflict detection to distributed schedule consensus. The design trade-off is between local tractability and computational responsiveness on 1 side, and global schedule fit and feasibility in a safety-critical environment on the other. Contrary to intuition, the empirical results show that short time horizons suffice. Long horizon values compromise local tractability and computational responsiveness with no gain in global schedule optimality. Larger negotiation zones make each local sub-problem harder and slow the consensus dynamics, with no gain for the final plan.
arxiv-2606-13468:
Abujadallah, Arabat, and Sayagh study why human reviewers reject fixes proposed by coding agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents such as Copilot, Devin, Cursor, and Claude now open pull requests proposing code fixes in projects. Mining the AIDev dataset, the authors find that over 46 percent of those agent fixes are rejected. Each rejection wastes effort on review, verification, and test runs for changes that are discarded. Understanding the failure modes is crucial for integrating agents as teammates rather than noisy contributors.

The paper analyses the rejected pull requests to characterise why they fail, distinguishing problems in the code from problems in how the change fits the project. The insights aim at agent builders, who can target the failure modes, and at maintainers, who can triage agent contributions more cheaply. As agent-generated code grows in volume, modest improvements in acceptance rates would save reviewer time.
arxiv-2606-13668:
Kachler, Sileo, and Denis make data attribution fast enough for large model datasets in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data attribution estimates how training examples shape a model toward particular outputs, for instance which samples might source toxic behaviour after training. Influence functions are the classic tool, but they are too slow and storage-hungry to run on dataset scales. The authors propose Influcoder: an encoder model distilled to imitate the influence rankings that gradient-based methods compute for decoder models.

Distillation transfers the expensive method's judgements into a compact model that scores new examples quickly. Curating training data by filtering harmful or useless samples is a pressing industrial need, and attribution is its scientific basis. If an encoder can reproduce influence rankings, dataset curation can run at inference speed rather than gradient computations. The work targets the bottleneck that has kept influence methods as research tools rather than production infrastructure.
arxiv-2606-13768:
Girish and colleagues present CineOrchestra in this 2026 arXiv paper, a video generation model with cinematic control. Cinematic video shows subjects acting at set moments, captured with camera movement and joined by shot cuts. Text-to-video models control those axes separately: multi-subject tailoring, temporal control, multi-shot synthesis, and camera control each have methods, and none integrates all four. The authors' diffusion model controls subjects, events, cameras, and transitions at once. Their insight is structural: these mixed elements share one form, each being an entity acting over a temporal interval.

All can be expressed through entity-centric primitives, with reference images for entities. One language replaces four mechanisms. The formulation reduces the architecture's complexity while expanding its range. For generated media, the gap between a clip and a film is this integration: a director's instructions are useless if the system can honour only one at a time.
arxiv-2606-13968:
Nassar and colleagues unify three ways of running large language models into one system with fast replies everywhere. Local models are free and private but limited by hardware. University computing centers offer free power yet sit behind firewalls built for batch jobs. Cloud APIs are strong but costly, with vendor data policies. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents STREAM, middleware routing queries among the tiers via a small model acting as judge.

A dual-channel design streams cluster answers through firewalls without rule changes. Control travels by Globus Compute, tokens by an encrypted WebSocket relay. Median time to first token on the cluster fell to zero point five four seconds, twenty-one point one times faster than batch mode. Encryption keeps tokens unreadable to the relay operator. On twelve hundred queries across ten domains, the small local model kept eighty-five point one percent on the free tier.
arxiv-2606-14068:
Si's team tests whether language models judge identical misconduct differently when the wrongdoer is a man or a woman. Prior bias studies mostly probe stereotypes or jobs. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds GAMA-Bench, a gender-mirrored benchmark of one thousand two hundred ninety-eight cases spanning intimate and public conflicts. Gender-neutral templates become paired first-person prompts differing only in actor gender. A structured protocol scores how responses allocate punishment, empathy, and blame.

Ten models showed a consistent male-disadvantaging gap. Male actors drew more punitive, escalatory, blame-centered framing for the same behavior. Female actors drew more therapy-like, empathy-oriented framing. The pattern persisted across families, scenario tracks, scale, and reasoning styles. Fairness testing must look past final verdicts: even when models reject the misconduct in both versions, blame assignment and risk escalation can diverge. Limits include binary mirroring and evaluator-extracted metrics, checked against human validation.
arxiv-2606-14168:
Xu and colleagues turn 3D scene editing into a checklist a team of agents works through, not whole-scene regeneration per request. Text-driven generators make plausible rooms but cannot refine them locally; small failures force full regeneration. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents MUSE, framing authoring as incremental requirement satisfaction. An Architect compiles instructions into structured requirements. A Sculptor executes local operations; an Inspector verifies each step, updating Working, Scene, and Skill Memory.

AuthorBench holds 145 construction cases, 1,584 editing cases. On construction, MUSE raised All-Goal success from thirty-seven point nine to eighty point seven over the strongest baseline. Surface-constraint fulfillment rose from thirty-five point zero to ninety-two point six. On a 240-case editing split it reached forty-nine point six All-Goal success, a ninety-nine point nine preservation rate, and only zero point six unintended change rate. Limits: indoor scenes and single-instruction edits only.
arxiv-2606-14568:
Marini, Grassucci, and Comminiello fuse three kinds of patient data to predict glioma outcomes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gliomas are brain tumors whose grading and survival forecasts need tissue images, gene activity, and brain scans together. Earlier models usually combined only two of these sources and aligned them pairwise.

Their framework, GLORIA, encodes whole-slide tissue regions, gene-expression profiles, and three-dimensional MRI volumes through separate encoders, then projects them into one shared space. A Gramian contrastive loss aligns all three at once by measuring the volume their embeddings span. A cross-modal gating module fuses the aligned features for three-class grading and survival prediction. On a matched cohort of one hundred thirty-two patients with complete data, GLORIA beat the two-modality baseline on every metric on the shared test set.
arxiv-2606-14668:
Zhang and Huang study when a language model should apply a stored fact edit in a 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge editing inserts corrected facts into a model. A good editor must also know when to suppress an edit. Nearby, unrelated behavior should stay intact. Their setting retrieves an edit memory at inference time. A small adapter then shifts the model's answer preference.

Their system, RRDA, uses two route-specialized adapters. A relevance router first decides whether a prompt deserves the edit memory. Routed prompts use an edit adapter trained to prefer the new object. Unrouted prompts use a locality adapter that preserves the original answer. Tests covered three benchmarks with one thousand cases each. Two base models were used. RRDA achieved the best overall preference accuracy on every benchmark. Ablations showed the memory supplied most of the gain. Routing balanced reliability against locality.
arxiv-2606-14768:
Gustavo Castillo and Nicolás Mujica review clumping through the lens of granular physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clumping drives systems from aerosol growth and cloud forming to dust piling in young planet disks. The classic account is Smoluchowski's equation. It gives an average-field view of growth through pairwise hits, assuming well-mixed grains.

Granular physics adds more effects. It adds energy-losing hits, patchy layouts, and force paths through contact nets. These expose the average-field picture's limits. The review shows clumping is a multi-scale process. It is shaped by contacts, structure, and group motion together. Sorting, jamming, and clogging show how contact limits redirect or halt growth. The authors blend granular physics, aerosol science, and astrophysics. They sketch one shared view of clumping in driven grain systems.
arxiv-2606-15068:
Gliksberg and coauthors build a low-cost spin coater that measures soft film thickness while coating in a 2026 study. Spin coating makes thin polymer films, but soft elastomers deform under contact gauges. Optical tools avoid contact yet cost too much for many labs. Thickness control matters because device performance, as in dielectric elastomer actuators, scales with it.

The benchtop system is mostly 3D-printed and targets films from fifty to three hundred microns thick. A laser reflects off the film onto a quadrant photodetector, and beam displacement gives thickness without touching the sample. Finite element checks support the printed structure's stiffness. Tests with calibrated metal shims show resolution near four microns. Silicone films land within about nine microns of their target thickness. The authors present the platform as proof that accessible optical metrology can join fabrication in one cheap device.
arxiv-2606-15268:
Pethick asks which Schatten-p norm an optimizer should use, and when, in a 2026 machine learning theory paper. Schatten norms measure matrices through their singular values, generalizing vector p-norms. Optimizers like Muon use the extreme Schatten-infinity geometry, with puzzlingly mixed evidence. Sometimes Muon shines, especially with large batches and short runs. Elsewhere methods match or beat it at scale. Pethick shows the verdict depends on the training regime. The choice interacts with gradient noise tails and problem geometry.

His analysis extends an accelerated optimizer framework to all p-norm geometries. It yields noise-robust acceleration rates for p. In low-dimensional regimes, smaller p can be optimal even under infinity-norm smoothness. That regime includes Chinchilla-style scaling, where models train on tokens. The theory explains why Muon needs no warmup and favors large batches. It also gives a batch-size scaling rule for each choice of p.
arxiv-2606-15668:
Majdoub extends the critical Hardy-Rellich inequalities in 2026, sharpening recent work by Castro on how gradients and Laplacians control each other under power weights. Hardy-type inequalities bound a weighted average of a function by its derivatives, and the critical exponent case is where they usually break. In Emden-Fowler variables, the question reduces to the classical one-dimensional weighted Hardy inequality.

The weighted inequality holds exactly when the weight exponent differs from the dimension, the unique critical value. Explicit constants come out for every dimension at least two, and the constant in dimension one is sharp. He extends the Laplacian form across the full Muckenhoupt range of weights, again excluding only the critical value. Together these results give a partial solution to an open problem posed by Castro. Sharp constants matter here because they mark the exact border between inequalities that hold and counterexamples that bite.
arxiv-2606-15868:
Weytjens and Weber benchmark next-activity prediction in business process monitoring in 2026, pitting a counting baseline against the field's escalating models. The task is to predict what happens next in a process case, from its event history. The field marched through LSTMs and Transformers to large language models, never jointly benchmarking them against a simple baseline.

The baseline, argmax, predicts the most frequent successor of the last activity, nothing more. Across seven event logs, it matches or approaches fine-tuned language models up to eight orders of magnitude larger, seeing only the last activity while they see the whole prefix. Pretraining confers no advantage over training from scratch, and model size matters little. Small Transformers from scratch often beat both, justifying their complexity on only two datasets. The message: do not bring a giant to a fight where a sling will do; benchmark against simple baselines.
arxiv-2606-15968:
Phukan and colleagues introduce SEA-CF in 2026, the first benchmark for detecting codec-synthesised speech deepfakes in South-East Asian languages. Codecfakes come from audio language models built on neural audio codecs; their signature differs from older vocoder fakes, so detectors trained on vocoder data generalise poorly. Existing benchmarks cover English and some Chinese, leaving the region's tonal, prosody-rich languages unexplored.

Built from public real-speech corpora across many speakers and codecs, SEA-CF shows top detectors trained on English-centric data failing on South-East Asian speech. Fine-tuning large audio language models helps, but their scale is impractical for low-resource, latency-sensitive deployment. Their proposed GARUDA, a small model tailored to the task, outperforms strong end-to-end and large-model baselines with far fewer parameters and lower latency. Benchmark and detector together give low-resource communities a practical defence.
arxiv-2606-16268:
Mészáros derives in 2026 a new way for two fluids to interact, based on how their volume elements move relative to each other. Most fluid models measure each fluid's particle density in its own rest frames. Mészáros instead defines the density of one fluid through the geometry seen by the other fluid's elements. The stress-energy tensor then depends directly on the scalar product of the two fluids' four-velocities.

That product can be rewritten through the relative physical speed of the volume elements, so the coupling strength tracks how fast the fluids stream past each other. The paper works out the resulting stress-energy tensor in full. As a first application, it studies Bianchi type-I spacetimes, the simplest anisotropic cosmologies, under small anisotropy. The interaction changes how such universes evolve compared with non-interacting mixtures.
arxiv-2606-16368:
Li and co-authors evaluate in 2026 whether language models truly personalize their answers, using logic checks instead of costly model judges. Current scoring relies on brittle surface matching or on large models grading outputs, which is expensive and hard to interpret. Their framework, NLICV, maps sentence meanings to truth-condition sets and verifies personalization constraints with a natural language inference model. It checks meaning, not wording.

Beyond a single score, NLICV sorts model behavior into four modes: personalization, generalization, sycophancy, and failure. That split exposes flattering agreement as its own failure mode, distinct from honest personalization. The framework aligns closely with human annotations while running up to 2,100 times faster than model judges, per the report. An ablation procedure pinpoints the sentences driving each verdict, giving faithful evidence a human can inspect. Personalization is a selling point of modern assistants, so a cheap, semantic, explainable test has immediate industrial use.
arxiv-2606-16668:
Yang and colleagues introduce CraBERT in a 2026 paper on text-to-speech, the technology that turns written text into spoken audio. A phoneme encoder reads the sound units of a sentence and helps speech sound natural. Training such encoders from scratch is slow, because they must learn word and sentence meaning as well as sound.

CraBERT borrows that knowledge from a pretrained subword BERT model, which reads word pieces rather than sounds. A cascade fusion design and an alignment algorithm merge the subword representations into a phoneme-level encoder. In listening tests, CraBERT after about one training epoch matched rival encoders trained for about ten epochs. Measured speedups over two named baselines were large, using one tenth as many training steps on the same hardware. Cheaper encoder training could make high-quality speech synthesis faster to build and update.
arxiv-2606-16868:
Bujotzek leads a team benchmarking federated medical image segmentation under label noise in a 2026 paper. Hospitals can train shared segmentation models without moving patient scans, thanks to federated learning. Real annotations differ by site, though: contours disagree, structures go missing or extra, and labels get confused.

Methods that learn despite noisy labels exist, but most evidence comes from synthetic noise in simplified setups. The new benchmark suite combines curated real-world noisy datasets with client-noise scenarios that mimic deployment, plus evaluation aimed at the noise itself. Analysis shows real label noise appears both alone and in mixed combinations of types. Comparing representative methods, from noise-aware aggregation to label correction, one approach called FedSelect performs strongest overall. The plain FedAvg baseline remains surprisingly competitive, and gains depend on dataset, noise type and scenario. A decision guide in the suite helps practitioners pick a method for their own noise profile.
arxiv-2606-17968:
Morfe and Wagner study when rare patches of a random material can cheat an interface out of its expected energy, in a 2026 analysis paper. The setting is the Allen-Cahn functional with random coefficients that vary on a microscopic scale far below the width of the interface itself. A companion paper showed that when that scale gap closes fast enough, the functionals settle to an effective surface energy set by homogenization.

Here the authors prove the opposite regime exists. If the gap closes too slowly, lucky rare configurations lower the limit below the homogenized value. For the one-dimensional random checkerboard they give a complete large-deviations description, where the limit turns on a precise combination of the two scales. They also build examples in any dimension, including almost periodic media, where rare events matter at algebraic scales.
arxiv-2606-18168:
Banik and colleagues audit whether the tests AI coding agents write actually check anything, in a 2026 empirical study. Agents now author pull requests by the hundreds of thousands, and their patches often include test files. A test with no assertions, though, runs code without verifying behavior, so counting test files overstates how checked the change really is. The authors call the verification content an oracle signal.

Mining over eighty-six thousand test-file patches from five agents, including Codex, Copilot, and Claude Code, they built a taxonomy of eight oracle signal types from close reading, then applied it at scale. Four fifths of the patches held weak or no explicit oracle signals, though rates varied widely by agent. After adjusting for patch size and review load, strong-oracle pull requests proved more likely to merge, giving reviewers a usable quality cue.
arxiv-2606-18668:
Xie and colleagues address a reliability failure in large enterprise multi-agent systems: small specialized sub-agents that answer requests they should have declined, in a 2026 paper on AI system design. In centralized architectures a coordinator routes work to cheaper domain sub-agents. Those agents, often built on small fine-tuned models, over-answer ambiguous, underspecified, or misrouted requests and hallucinate instead of reporting that something is wrong.

Their framework EARS reframes abstention as communication: a sub-agent returns not just a refusal but a structured, explained failure state that lets the coordinator clarify, reroute, or fall back. Training data come from interaction logs labeled by an ensemble of calibrated judge models under a taxonomy of failure modes, then fine-tuned into the sub-agents. Deployed in a production e-commerce assistant, EARS raised the response pass rate from roughly sixty-nine to seventy-nine percent.
arxiv-2606-18968: This paper explores audio-to-audio translation via diffusion warm initialization. The warm start gives the diffusion model a head start on the target audio. Their approach preserves content while transforming style. The audio-to-audio framing opens creative applications. It is voice conversion with diffusion power. The warm initialization is the key trick.
arxiv-2606-19168:
Li and colleagues propose Safety Reflection Pretraining in 2026, a pretraining-stage method for deeper safety alignment of language models. Recent work pushes safety earlier by filtering unsafe data or rewriting it. The authors argue that is not enough. Models can compose seemingly benign knowledge into unsafe behavior, so clean data alone does not guarantee safe conduct once the model generalizes beyond what it was shown in training.

Their method regularly inserts short safety reflections into pretraining corpora. Self-monitoring is thus woven into language modeling itself, building a base capability that later post-training can reinforce. Tests on models of about two billion parameters trained on FineWeb-Edu show better safety classification. Attack success at inference and after fine-tuning drops substantially too. A controlled synthetic world, MedSafetyWorld, isolates the effect. There, reflection pretraining clearly beats data-only approaches at stopping unsafe behavior generalized from safe data.
arxiv-2606-19268:
Hadfield defines the Patnaik-Pearson intrinsic dimension in 2026 and applies it to internal representations of neural networks. Intrinsic dimension measures the true degrees of freedom of a data manifold, which can be far lower than its ambient size. The new measure draws on heavy-tail spectral work by Martin, Mahoney, and Hinrichs, and on the TwoNN estimator of Facco and colleagues, combining their strengths into one tool for network analysis.

The author proves key properties of the estimator. For weight matrices whose spectral density follows a power law, the new dimension links directly to the heavy-tail analysis, with critical tail values matching. Theory and numerics then track how the dimension behaves under transformations typical of neural networks. Applications cover a BERT model and a distilled reasoning model. The study follows token embeddings from their initial manifold through the layers, showing how dimension evolves as representations deepen.
arxiv-2606-19468:
Johnson and colleagues characterize narrative content in web-scale pretraining data in 2026, in the first study of its kind. Narrative is a basic mode of human communication. Yet the narrative mix of the huge corpora used to train language models stays largely unexplored. The team studies Dolma, a three-trillion-token corpus. A framework from narrative theory spans agency, setting, and events, split into eleven interpretable dimensions.

After sampling and annotating hundreds of passages, the team fine-tunes NarraBERT, a narrative prediction model. Applying it to millions of passages yields NarraDolma, a new released dataset. Three findings stand out. Narrative structure is measurable at scale across mixed data. A continuous, multi-dimensional narrative structure underlies web text. And narrative qualities are spread unevenly across sources and topics, in ways current curation neither measures nor tracks. The work shows what kinds of stories models actually train on.
arxiv-2606-19568:
Acoustic gunshot classification sorts firearm sounds from recordings, a task with uses in public safety, military work, and wildlife protection. Commercial systems perform unevenly, and past studies rarely test how sound features should be extracted. A 2026 study tackles that gap head-on with a large, varied recording set.

The dataset holds 23,000 gunshot recordings across 85 firearms and 21 calibres. Three feature extraction techniques face off under twelve parameter settings in total. A ResNet-18 network classifies the extracted features in every run. Picking the right extraction method lifts top-one accuracy by up to 20 percent. Tuning the parameters of a chosen method adds up to 4.7 percent more. Feature choices, often treated as a minor detail, thus drive much of the system's skill. The results argue for care with features when detectors must generalise to new guns and settings.
arxiv-2606-20068:
Minsu Kim and Se-Young Yun show how a proof assistant can coach a language model while it learns to prove theorems, instead of only grading the final answer. Their 2026 paper works with Lean, where each proof step is a tactic checked against strict type rules. Standard training with verifiable rewards gives one binary signal per attempt, win or lose. That wastes the rich detail Lean reports about where a proof first breaks down.

Kim and Yun parse each attempt into its tactic sequence, and Lean marks every locally sound step plus the earliest failing one, producing dense, trustworthy credit signals for a GRPO-style learning objective. Tested with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover systems on MiniF2F and ProofNet, tactic-level supervision beats outcome-only training in most settings. Proof assistants, the authors argue, can act as reward oracles during training, not just judges at test time.
arxiv-2606-20668:
Leonhard Waibl, Felix Michalak, and Hadrien Mariaccia present BELLS-O in 2026, an operational benchmark for language model supervision systems. Such systems filter inputs and outputs and detect jailbreak attempts. They are a main safeguard against misuse. Yet older benchmarks often favor vendors. They also omit cost and latency. Few compare dedicated guardrails with general models reused as supervisors. BELLS-O is described as the first independent test of that kind.

The benchmark covers 28 systems from 17 providers. It includes guardrails such as LlamaGuard and ShieldGemma, plus frontier general models. Each system is scored jointly on detection rate, false positives, latency, and money cost. Tasks span eleven harm categories and thirteen jailbreak methods. Datasets mix handcrafted prompts, expert samples, and checked synthetic cases. Joint scoring matters because a safe filter that is slow or costly may never be deployed as designed.
arxiv-2606-20868:
Fathima Mashood and Mohamed Nabeel test in 2026 whether large language models can judge who owns a web domain that resembles a brand. A look-alike domain may be a phishing site built by attackers. It may also be a domain the brand itself registered, for defense or a new product. Flagging a brand-owned domain as malicious harms users and reputation. Resolving that question at scale needs brand intelligence.

Three tasks are evaluated: listing a brand's domains, open-ended attribution, and binary ownership classification. Four models from Google and Anthropic families are tested. The study is described as the first systematic evaluation of model brand intelligence. Zero-configuration use is attractive because no custom training is needed. Reliability is the open issue. Security teams need to know where model knowledge of brand and domain links can be trusted before using it in live defense.
arxiv-2606-20968:
Jeremie Pope and Swaroop Ghosh profile circuit replication in 2026 as a simple way to mitigate errors on current quantum computers. Noise from the environment limits practical use. Error mitigation and correction help, but they carry large costs in time and resources. Replication means running copies of a circuit and combining results. It is a naive method, long ignored because hardware was scarce.

Its simplicity is now attractive as a supplement to modern methods. The study tests replication under real-world noise profiles. The test case is a quantum optimization algorithm applied to the Max-Cut problem. Small cases show where the method helps and where it stops helping. Knowing effective limits matters for practice: a cheap supplement that works only at small scale should be used with clear eyes, not discarded for being simple or oversold as a general fix.
arxiv-2606-21168:
Yaling Shen and six colleagues propose Dementia-Agents in 2026, a multi-agent system for dementia staging and phenotyping from multimodal clinical data. Diagnosis joins assessments from many informants and clinicians. Data are often incomplete and mixed in form. Most AI work centers on Alzheimer's disease alone, as binary detection or three-stage progression. Real dementia spans many stages, phenotypes, and causes.

Their framework runs in three steps. A data agent turns structured records into faithful text that preserves missing-data signals. It routes cases to domain-aligned experts. Five fine-tuned expert agents give domain-level predictions. A coordinator agent aggregates them probabilistically into final staging and phenotyping decisions. Evaluation uses real-world clinical data. Syndrome-level staging could support clinicians facing the mixed presentations that single-disease models handle poorly.
arxiv-2606-22168:
Pham and colleagues compare, in 2026, five U-Net variants for medical image segmentation, tracing the shift from convolution to transformer designs. U-Net networks outline structures such as tumors and blood vessels, but convolution-based versions may miss long-range context. The study covers U-Net 3D, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin UNETR.

All five are evaluated on two benchmarks: BraTS 2023 for brain tumor segmentation in MRI volumes, and DRIVE for retinal vessel segmentation. Swin UNETR achieves the best overall performance. It scores a Dice of 0.8965 on BraTS 2023 and 0.8078 on DRIVE, where Dice measures overlap with expert outlines. The authors conclude transformer variants excel where global context matters. Residual learning still helps with fine structure segmentation, giving practical guidance for model choice.
arxiv-2606-22768:
Chamin Hewa Koneputugodage and nine colleagues work on training large language models outside big datacenters in this 2026 paper, published at ICML. DiLoCo trains workers separately and syncs them rarely, but each sync moves a large volume of data and blocks progress. One slow or failing worker can stall everyone else.

Their fix relaxes exact synchronization into approximate mixing, in the spirit of gossip protocols where neighbors average their states. Synchronization splits into a non-blocking mixing step that overlaps with computation and a blocking step that tightens agreement between workers. That split trades a little optimization stability for much better use of compute. On models up to a billion parameters in low-bandwidth settings, the framework improved compute utilization substantially over DiLoCo. Training progress ranged from comparable to closely matching the original, and the system proved more robust when workers failed or lagged.
arxiv-2606-23068:
Mikael Tacu argues that cold matter in spherical systems needs kinetic theory, not just fluid equations, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Cold collisionless matter, like dark matter or cold stars, is usually modeled as a pressureless fluid. Tacu shows the two views agree on how the system evolves over time in a spherical setup. Looked at as a spectrum of vibration patterns, though, they part ways. The kinetic system admits one extra discrete mode that the fluid equations miss.

Tacu identifies that mode's frequency as twice the central orbital frequency of the sphere. The effect is specific to three dimensions, since thin disks reduce cleanly to the fluid picture. Nonlinear simulations confirm the mode survives when small velocity spreads are added. Near the Milky Way's central black hole, the mode would sit at the inner edge of the stellar cusp.
arxiv-2606-23268:
Dragomir Grozev and Nikolai Nikolov revisit Ulam's segment motion problem in a 2026 geometry paper. The problem concerns moving a unit segment rigidly between two prescribed positions in space. Among all continuous motions, one can ask which minimizes the total path length traced by the two endpoints. Ulam posed the question, and earlier authors solved the minimization itself. Two natural lower bounds exist: the sum of the endpoint displacements, and the angle between the starting and ending directions. When is either bound actually attained?

Grozev and Nikolov characterize every pair of segment positions for which each bound is attained. Their characterizations hold in arbitrary dimension, for any space of dimension at least two. Both bounds, the endpoint-displacement one and the angular one, receive complete equality cases. The results finish the picture around the classical solution.
arxiv-2606-23368:
Zhirui Tang, Niels Horsten, and Giovanni Samaey speed up neutral particle transport simulation in a 2026 paper. Neutral particles in a plasma edge are modeled by kinetic equations, tracking full distributions rather than averages. Monte Carlo solutions are accurate but get very costly in reactor-relevant regimes. Fluid approximations run cheaply yet lose accuracy near boundaries or where collisions are rare. Hybrid methods try to combine both. The team builds a hybrid at the particle level, decomposing the distribution itself rather than splitting the domain.

Tang and colleagues derive a Navier-Stokes-type fluid system tailored to their scheme. The hybrid needs no iterative coupling between its fluid and kinetic parts and preserves asymptotic behavior. In one-dimensional tests, its fluid system matched a leading reference model's accuracy with far fewer nonlinear iterations. A tunable reflective boundary condition is also introduced.
arxiv-2606-23568:
Safari and Hutter shrink large language models by repairing what a standard compression method throws away, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Singular value decomposition, or SVD, rewrites each weight matrix as layered patterns ranked by importance. Dropping the weakest patterns compresses the model, but plain truncation wastes accuracy. Prior methods mostly argue about which patterns to keep and how to form them, not how to fix the survivors.

Their method, SVD-Surgeon, borrows the Optimal Brain Surgeon idea from classic pruning research. Treating each singular value as a tunable parameter, it computes a closed-form correction for the kept values. The correction cancels the loss caused by removed values, to second order. The same math yields a saliency score for choosing which values to cut. Layered onto the SVD-LLM compressor, it improves the perplexity versus compression trade-off on OPT models and LLaMA 2, with no retraining.
arxiv-2606-23768:
Gabbay proposes attaching cryptographic proofs of policy compliance to the actions of AI agents, in a 2026 paper on trustworthy AI. AI agents increasingly act in the world: booking flights, approving invoices, deploying code. Signatures can prove who sent a message, and logs can reconstruct what happened, but neither proves in advance that an action satisfies agreed safety or compliance rules. Trust currently rests on origin, not on evidence about the action itself.

The proposal writes the policy condition as a formal logical predicate. It compiles the predicate into a witness checking problem over polynomial constraints. A succinct proof system then certifies the result, optionally with zero knowledge. The agent's action travels with its certificate, and anyone can verify compliance without trusting the agent or rerunning its work. The paper sketches the mathematics and the open questions in specification, auditing, and deployment.
arxiv-2606-24068:
Lee and colleagues give exploring robots a memory organised like the places they move through. A robot in an unfamiliar building must notice what a task needs, spot what it has not seen yet, and go looking for the missing pieces. Their 2026 system, ObsGraph, stores observations in a three-layer graph: rooms as broad anchors, views capturing which objects appear together, and objects holding fine detail.

Retrieval runs coarse to fine under a fixed budget, starting at room level and narrowing only where evidence is thin. Crucially, what retrieval fails to find steers the next exploration step, choosing between searching a new room, refining a view, or heading to an unexplored frontier. Tests on embodied reasoning and exploration benchmarks show better success and efficiency than less structured approaches. Lee's team credits the tight loop between remembering, retrieving, and deliberately gathering the information still missing.
arxiv-2606-24268:
Askitas shows that a single conjectured unknotting move is at least strong enough to erase a classic knot invariant. The 4-move twists a knot's diagram in a specific four-strand pattern, and since Nakanishi's 1979 conjecture, nobody has settled whether repeated 4-moves can untie every knot. The Alexander polynomial, a venerable algebraic fingerprint of a knot, would obstruct unknotting if it survived the move unchanged.

It does not survive. Askitas proves every knot can be reduced, through a sequence of 4-moves and ordinary diagram isotopies, to a knot whose Alexander polynomial is trivial. The result, drafted during the 2020 lockdown and completed in 2025, falls short of the full unknotting conjecture, since a trivial Alexander polynomial does not make a knot the unknot. But it removes one natural place a counterexample could hide. Askitas's 2026 paper also recounts how the conjecture resisted attacks through knots of twelve crossings and famous candidate counterexamples.
arxiv-2606-24468:
Fabbrichesi, Floreanini, and Marzola propose testing quantum inseparability in its original form, with positions and momenta, at a particle collider. Entanglement tests usually use spin states. Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen framed their paradox with positions and momenta, though. The team first studies phase space non separability through EPR-like correlations in that original setting. It then shows how to measure momentum entanglement for particle pairs, by mapping continuous variables onto hemispheres. The variables reduce to a two qubit system.

Tau leptons made at an electron collider provide the worked example. Tau momenta must be recovered from their decays into pions and neutrinos. The authors handle that indirect measurement head on. A Monte Carlo run shows that phase space entanglement can be assessed with such data. The 2026 proposal extends collider quantum studies back to the variables where the EPR argument began.
arxiv-2606-24568:
Andersen and colleagues read the temperature of an ultracold atom cloud from the colours it scatters. Bose-Einstein condensates, matter waves formed when atoms crowd into one quantum state, coexist with a thermal component at finite temperature. Telling the two apart in place has been difficult. Their 2026 measurements use optical spectroscopy on rubidium-87 gases, with a dark field setup sensitive to single photons and a frequency agile laser sweeping the spectrum.

Distinct spectral features from the thermal and condensed components appear directly in the frequency domain. A model of light travel through the uneven cloud interprets the spectra. Temperature and atom number are extracted, benchmarked against standard time of flight absorption imaging. The spectral parameters prove sensitive to small thermal fractions in nearly pure condensates, exactly where imaging struggles. Dark field operation beats bright field clearly. Andersen's team establishes the method as a mapping tool for ultracold systems.
arxiv-2606-25368:
Factory inspection must flag products that look fine piece by piece but are assembled wrong, like a breakfast box holding the wrong count of items. Weizhi Nie, Zibo Xu, Weijie Wang, and Yuting Su propose a detector in 2026 that learns only from normal images. Frozen features from a vision model are distilled into patch, relation, and hypergraph statistics, where hyperedges link groups of patches that belong together. A combined score then weighs local, relational, and group evidence separately.

On validation data for a breakfast box task, the full model lifted logical anomaly detection well above a nearest neighbour baseline using the same features. Removing the hypergraph parts dropped the score partway back. The detector also held up with very few normal training images, and scrambling the relations raised its alarm sharply, showing the score tracks real structure.
arxiv-2606-25468:
Jacobi polynomials are a classical family weighted differently at the two ends of an interval, and their shape obeys tight inequalities. Geno Nikolov proves a new one in 2026 that reads like a sharpened mean value statement: the drop of the polynomial from its endpoint value bounds its slope times the remaining distance. The result holds on the right half of the interval for two ranges of the weight parameters, including an endpoint case tied to Chebyshev polynomials.

The inequality complements an earlier finite increment theorem for the same family rather than restating it. Nikolov's route builds on nonnegative expansions developed in prior work on trigonometric inequalities by Robertson and by Askey and Gasper. Special cases recover statements about Chebyshev polynomials of both kinds, which sit inside the Jacobi family at particular parameter choices.
arxiv-2606-25668:
Risk scores and prediction tools now shape bail, triage, and student support decisions, yet better predictions strangely often fail to produce better outcomes. Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Lydia Liu, and Angela Zhou argue in this 2026 perspective that the field grades the wrong thing. A prediction dropped into an organisation rewires workflows, judgements, and incentives around it, so accuracy alone cannot predict downstream effects. Their framework reorients the study of automated decision systems from forecasting individuals toward designing interventions in social systems.

Case evidence runs through the argument: a celebrated sepsis model with strong test scores missed most real cases in outside hospitals while over alerting on the healthy, breeding distrust. Pretrial and education tools show similarly mixed records. The authors propose that evaluation should start from the decision and its setting, treating the prediction as one moving part inside an intervention.
arxiv-2606-25768:
Interferometers built from many bosonic modes, light or atoms in Gaussian states, can measure phases beyond classical precision limits. Chenwei Lv and Ren-Bao Liu supply the missing general theory in 2026, built on the symplectic symmetry that governs all such devices with quadratic Hamiltonians. Two design questions get clean answers. For the best sensitivity, squeezing and displacement must be aligned in the same direction. A many mode echo scheme generalises the known two mode interferometer. It returns the system on itself. The measurement then reaches the precision set by the quantum Fisher information, the ultimate bound.

A geometric method for reversing many body dynamics comes with the framework, demonstrated on the bosonic Kitaev chain. The schemes fit optical, atomic, and mechanical platforms already in laboratories. Generic multimode Gaussian interferometry, the authors show, has a single symmetry language for both sensing and control.
arxiv-2606-25868:
G. Principe leads a very large collaboration reporting on 3C 279, a famous blazar whose relativistic jet points almost straight at Earth and flares across the whole electromagnetic spectrum. The Event Horizon Telescope observed the source in April 2017 at a sharpness near twenty microarcseconds. Partner observatories ran a vast simultaneous campaign at the same time. Coverage stretched from radio waves to very high-energy gamma rays.

Flux in the innermost core rose clearly between April 5 and April 11 of that year. Longer-wavelength radio monitoring showed matching brightening and polarization changes around mid-April, coinciding with a newly ejected knot racing outward at an apparent speed near twenty-five times the speed of light. A combined spectral energy distribution was built from the data. Turbulent multi-zone modelling then constrained how the jet forms, narrows, and speeds up its particles.
arxiv-2606-26468:
Nika Mansouri Ghiasi and ten colleagues present GRAINS, a system for analysing genome graphs inside a storage drive. Genome graphs represent many genomes as one branching structure. They beat single linear sequences for accuracy at population scale. But analysing huge graphs means moving vast data from storage to processors. Most of that data is used once, so the movement wastes time and energy.

Computing inside the storage device would keep data in place. Existing genome tools cannot run there, because drives have weak internal hardware. Earlier in-storage systems targeted linear genomes or ordinary graphs, not genome graphs. GRAINS is the first system built for this job. It redesigns algorithms and hardware together around storage limits. The design handles the special data structures and access patterns of genome graphs. The goal is fast, low-cost analysis for public health, precision medicine, and agriculture.
arxiv-2606-26568:
Yiwei Bao and Can Cui model the rings seen in young planetary systems. Telescopes such as ALMA reveal concentric rings in protoplanetary disks, the gas and dust disks where planets form. Why the rings appear is still debated. Many explanations invoke planets already present. Bao and Cui build a local model that needs no planets.

Their starting transport model moves material by drift and diffusion. By itself, that smooth process cannot make a repeating ring train. They add a fourth-order radial feedback, a term where the ring pattern reinforces itself. For a steady localised source, the response then oscillates while fading with distance. That oscillation sets a natural spacing. Under a scaling matched to observations, the spacing comes out at roughly a dozen astronomical units. One astronomical unit is Earth's distance from the Sun. Vertical diffusion shapes the background but does not cause the oscillation.
arxiv-2606-26768:
Ondrej Alexaj, Vojtěch Havlena, Ondřej Lengál, Yong Li, and Nicolas Mazzocchi extend a useful class of automata for checking tasks. Büchi automata accept endless runs and underpin automatic checking of system designs. Elevator automata are a well-behaved subclass found in most practical cases. Their components are each either either fixed-rule or weak. That structure yields faster complement and determinisation algorithms.

Emerson-Lei automata allow richer rules than Büchi automata. The authors define their elevator subclass and give a flipping algorithm for it. Complementation builds an automaton accepting exactly the rejected runs. Its long-run cost beats the best known algorithm for full Emerson-Lei automata by a wide margin. Experiments against the leading Spot tool confirmed the practical gains.
arxiv-2606-26968:
Beatrice Savoldi, Sara Papi, Wafa Aissa, Matteo Negri, and Luisa Bentivogli expose safety gaps in speech models outside English. Voice-enabled models now serve real users in many languages. Their makers rarely test safety beyond English, the authors find: only a small share of releases document any multilingual safety analysis. Their benchmark, RedVox, fills the gap with real voices.

RedVox covers unsafe and stereotyped requests in five languages. Eight leading models were evaluated. Weaknesses appeared even without adversarial tricks. They worsened in non-English languages and grew again when requests were spoken rather than typed. The team also surveyed the volunteers who recorded voices. Their answers document privacy and personal burdens unique to collecting speech data for safety research.
arxiv-2606-27068:
Todorov, ten Napel, and Müller extend open-source game theory, where players can inspect each other's decision rules before acting. Classic versions treat those rules as discrete programs or symbols. Their parametric version instead lets each player choose a vector of numbers, a smooth dial setting. A semantics map then turns the whole profile of dial settings into mixed actions in a small underlying game. The framework covers existence of stable outcomes, called equilibria, in this theory study of 2026.

In symmetric two-by-two games, the authors derive an exact coupling threshold where selfish gradient climbing flips from defection toward cooperation. A neural version follows, where each rule is a small network. There, cooperation hinges on how strongly one player's dials sway the other, relative to self-effects. Strong enough open-source coupling can thus steer purely selfish tuning toward joint cooperation.
arxiv-2606-27168:
Skákala, Higgs, and Moffat train deep learning stand-ins for a complex ocean ecosystem model. The target is ERSEM, a detailed marine biogeochemistry simulator of plankton, nutrients, and carbon in seawater. Full simulators cost heavily, limiting forecasts from days to decades. A simplified one-dimensional water column couples ocean physics to the full ecosystem model as training ground. In their 2026 forecasting study, two emulator designs are explored, both fed by the physics simulator's inputs.

Memory-based LSTM networks mimic a chosen subset of variables at daily steps. Physics-informed convolutional networks mimic the whole open-water system through the full water column. Both stay stable over multi-decade runs and reproduce the simulator skilfully. Spring bloom timing is predicted years ahead, and ten-day forecasts also score well. Trained on reanalysis data, the emulators beat the original model's forecast skill for key plankton variables by wide margins.
arxiv-2606-27368:
Roy proposes a new species of Dirac fermion whose order hides from ordinary probes. Standard Dirac materials pair a kinetic term with one masslike operator that anticommutes with it. Adding a second, independent anticommuting masslike operator yields what he calls hidden-ordered Dirac fermions. The spectrum stays linear in any spatial dimension, with a renormalised Fermi velocity. In the theory paper of 2026, phase diagrams change because the hidden order commutes differently with candidate insulating orders.

Insulating transitions get pushed to stronger coupling than in ordinary Dirac systems. Whether the hidden-ordered phase survives near criticality depends on the algebra between its order parameter and the insulating one. Concrete lattice models realise the construction, giving simulators a target. The proposal enlarges the known taxonomy of Dirac matter. Hidden order becomes a tunable axis rather than a curiosity. Experimental signatures are left as a challenge for lattice realisations.
arxiv-2606-27768:
Rapidly rotating Bose–Einstein condensates can host quantum Hall droplets. These droplets show robust stability. Xinyi Liu and seven colleagues study what happens when such droplets collide in 2026. The work uses the Gross–Pitaevskii framework. Two-droplet collisions and overlapping stationary droplets are both examined.

Collisions have two possible outcomes. The droplets merge, or they separate again. The initial relative velocity decides which occurs. The critical velocity follows a universal scaling law. It grows as the fourth root of the product of interaction strength and particle number. A simplified model explains the law through collision time. Droplet shapes can change greatly in a collision. Their centre-of-mass paths barely change, thanks to angular momentum conservation. Overlapping stationary droplets behave differently. Kelvin–Helmholtz instability can produce vortex arrays there. Extended states cannot be built from many overlapping droplets, the authors find.
arxiv-2606-28468:
Farokhnaz Hosseinifar, writing alone, studies the thermodynamics of an exotic black hole family. These are charged anti-de Sitter black holes in ModMax nonlinear electrodynamics, a theory that tweaks how electric fields behave. They are coupled to massive gravity, with entropy corrected in the Sharma-Mittal scheme.

Hosseinifar maps the thermodynamic geometry using the Weinhold metric over horizon radius and charge. Its curvature scalar reveals the effective microscopic interactions, and curvature singularities mark extremal limits where the metric degenerates. A rectangular heat engine built in the extended phase space gets an exact efficiency formula. It shows how the ModMax parameter and gravity couplings steer heat-to-work conversion. The entropy corrections shift the Carnot bound through the temperature. A final analysis of the corrected temperature and free energy then reveals known and novel critical points.
arxiv-2606-28768:
Konstantis, Sabatini and Zoller prove finiteness results for a family of geometric spaces that generalise the smooth toric varieties used across geometry. Their spaces are compact symplectic manifolds, meaning shapes equipped with a geometric structure that measures area-like pairings, carrying special group actions called GKM 3 actions. Positive monotonicity, a balance condition between two key geometric quantities, is assumed throughout the results.

Three theorems anchor the work. For fixed dimension and Euler characteristic, a count summing up the shape's topology, only finitely many cobordism classes can occur. The moment map image, a projection used to study the action, fits inside a box of bounded size, up to lattice changes. All Chern numbers, standard numeric invariants, obey bounds as well. A bound on the volume follows, mirroring a famous finiteness pattern for Fano varieties.
arxiv-2606-28968:
Deng and colleagues study how safety evolves over time for people who use role-play AI companions, apps offering emotionally responsive characters. The film Her imagined such bonds; the authors note that future has quietly arrived, blurring tool use and friendship. Safety implications remain poorly understood, because risks can grow gradually through emotional and behaviour dynamics.

Interviews with sixteen users identified three shaping factors: users' internalising problems, the personality the companion adopts, and risky interaction patterns. A second study then followed 102 users for fourteen days with ecological momentary assessment, brief repeated check-ins in daily life. Users with more such problems formed distinct profiles. Companions brought short-term relief while masking longer-term decline, the team found. Vulnerable users showed more unstable risk patterns over time. That makes risk harder to predict and poorly served by static safeguards. The authors propose three layers of adaptive design responses.
arxiv-2606-29068:
Ciani, Schweiger, Parada-Cabaleiro and Schedl probe how much emotion theory lives inside the representations of modern text encoders. Encoders compress text into dense vectors that keep meaning, and they are widely used for sentiment and emotion tasks. Whether those vectors capture well-defined psychological theories of emotion, rather than vague positivity, was unclear.

The team tested twelve recently released encoders. Their embeddings fed regression and classification tasks built on three established emotion frameworks, at both word and sentence level. A semantic leakage-prevention technique guarded the word-level tests against inflated scores. At word level, the newest instruction-aware open-weight encoders held as much or more affective information than proprietary rivals. At sentence level, task-tuned and proprietary encoders scored highest on emotion classification. A qualitative look at the latent spaces rounds out the comparison, showing which affective cues each family of encoders encodes and which it misses.
arxiv-2606-30068:
Ayan Pendharkar, in a solo study, shows a blind spot in how predictive world models learn. Such models predict future internal states rather than raw inputs. Features an agent cannot control may still decide its reward. If those features are hard to predict, the training objective drops them. Pendharkar isolates this failure in a tightly controlled experiment.

The design varies controllability and relevance independently, in a two by two grid. A predictability knob separates how foreseeable a feature is from its importance. Six objectives are compared, from reconstruction to several predictive variants. Every reward-free predictive objective leaves the key feature near chance accuracy. A reward-grounded variant keeps it, and keeps it selectively. As little as two percent reward-labeled data restores the feature. That pattern holds across two environments and many latent sizes.
arxiv-2606-30168:
Kai Jiang, Ruishu Zhu, Siqi Huang, Hongyuan Zhang, and Xuelong Li clean up the visual evidence that multimodal models reason over. Such models turn images into long token sequences. Question-relevant cues often drown in dense, redundant visual tokens. Their framework, Lens, purifies that evidence inside the latent space. It works without changing the model's backbone or token order.

A single learnable Lens Evidence Token scores each visual token. Scores say how strongly a token supports the current question. Guided by those scores, Lens injects adaptive noise into weak tokens. Low-relevance tokens are softly suppressed rather than deleted outright. Only one temporary control token and a small noise generator are added. Gains reach several points on most visual question answering datasets. Grounding tasks, which locate the referred object, improve similarly. Cleaner evidence helps more than longer reasoning traces.
arxiv-2606-30368:
Maximilian Haensch asks whether exact results in a flagship gauge theory stay positive in a strong sense. The theory is planar maximally supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory. Its results can be computed exactly at any coupling strength. The question concerns their behavior as functions of that coupling. A Stieltjes property would give each observable a dispersion form. That form integrates it over a positive spectral measure.

Haensch proves it for a broad class of observables. Integral representations settle several famous cases analytically. They include the octagon anomalous dimension and the circular Wilson loop. The Bremsstrahlung function and certain BMN-limit cases also qualify. Numerical evidence covers the cusp anomalous dimensions. Some quantities provably fail it, and he identifies them. It turns perturbative data into rigorous non-perturbative bounds. It also lets one bootstrap further coefficients.
arxiv-2606-30468:
Philip Held and six co-authors show a form of quantum entanglement that survives renaming the parties. Entanglement normally depends on how a system is split into parts. Change the mode basis and a state can lose its entanglement. The mode-independent kind persists under any such change of basis. That toughness suits quantum links over untrusted channels. No experiment had shown it before this 2026 work.

A flexible interferometer generates the states. Measurement-induced nonlinearities help produce heralded two-photon states. The states are entangled in two modes for every orthonormal basis choice. Tailored tomography certifies the claim in the lab. The measured fidelities validate its presence. The correlation is both resilient and operationally useful, they argue. It safeguards such protocols against basis changes. Noise and hostile parties in real networks motivate the pursuit.
arxiv-2606-30668:
Simon Jones and Sabine Hauert ask what culture emerges when language-model agents are given almost nothing. Inspired by swarm engineering, they built collectives of three agents with no memory between turns and minimal prompting. The agents can message each other and edit a shared text store that actively decays, so anything not maintained fades away. That decay creates evolutionary pressure to keep records alive.

Left alone, the agents spontaneously cooperated. They developed storage management strategies and produced complex, evolving cultural artefacts, with no top-down design. Jones and Hauert analysed the behaviour with dynamical-systems tools. They found structured coherence stretching far beyond the store's own memory horizon. The pattern matches emergent culture in the Sperberian sense, where shared meanings survive only by being continually recreated. The authors link the effect to stigmergy, coordination through traces left in a shared environment.
arxiv-2606-30968:
Koorosh Roohi, Javad Rajabi, Andrew Fleet and Babak Taati generate photomosaics, pictures made of many small pictures, at any resolution without training a new model. Diffusion generators struggle with the two scales at once. Direct high-resolution output is costly and tends to melt into one smooth image. Patch-by-patch tiling keeps local detail but loses the global scene. PhotoQuilt uses a bootstrapped tiled denoising procedure. A global composition is first produced at low resolution to fix the layout. It is then upscaled in latent space and partly re-noised, restoring the model's freedom to invent detail.

Denoising then proceeds inside fixed tiles, so each tile becomes a convincing image of its own while the shared layout holds the whole together. Because tiles are handled separately, the method grows to large canvases without quadratic attention cost. In experiments it beat current baselines for global structure and for local realism.
arxiv-2606-31068:
Patel builds a fast stand-in for finite element simulation, the standard but slow method engineers use to compute stress and strain inside materials. The target is two-phase composite microstructures, tiny geometric patterns of stiff and soft regions arranged as square, hexagonal, or triangular tessellations. A single finite element run can take minutes to days, which blocks large design searches.

Patel's hybrid UNet-Transformer model reads a microstructure image and predicts ten stress and strain field types in under a second. On periodic tessellations it reaches near-perfect scores, and most test sets keep very low error. Attention maps show the model focuses on physically sensible spots, such as phase boundaries and contact zones. It struggles mainly on irregular square grids with sparse soft inclusions, where sharp stress jumps are hard to reproduce.
arxiv-2606-31168:
Fan and two colleagues audit how tests for memorization in language models can disagree. They use a fixed probe that averages negative log-likelihood, a measure of surprise, over the first twenty tokens of a secret canary text. Their testbed is a Qwen2.5-VL-7B model tuned with LoRA, a light update method, on text-heavy data.

Fan reports three cases where that short-window probe clashes with full-span scores or exact recall checks. One miss hides damage outside the window, one false alarm sits almost fully on non-secret opening text, and one drop reflects a weak baseline. The authors urge reporting full-span scores, span breakdowns, exact recall, and decoy probes before claiming a secret was memorized.
arxiv-2606-31768:
Shetgaonkar and Sharma model a vector-borne disease where protection choices and mosquito feeding habits reshape each other. Insecticide-treated nets work well, but people adopt them based on perceived cost and infection risk. In a multi-host setting, vectors can also shift their feeding toward whichever host is less protected.

Thresholds R0 and Rc govern whether disease-free and endemic states exist and stay stable in their analysis. Bifurcation analysis finds saddle-node and Hopf points, marking shifts from steady endemic states to sustained oscillations. One counterintuitive result stands out: full net adoption by the primary host can raise prevalence in the secondary host. Diverted vectors feed more there, spreading infection instead.
arxiv-2606-31868:
Ciardelli and Conti supply a proof system for inquisitive first-order modal logic, a logic built to reason about modal dependence. The logic can express relations such as global supervenience, where the extensions of predicates depend, as a function, on one another across possibilities. Until now it had a semantics but no calculus to derive its validities from.

Their labelled sequent calculus extends one developed by Litak and Sano for a weaker inquisitive first-order logic. Labels track the information states that inquisitive semantics tests formulas against. The authors prove strong completeness for the calculus. It also enjoys prized structural properties: every rule is invertible, and cut is admissible, meaning lemmas added mid-proof can always be removed without loss.
arxiv-2608-00068:
Cui and co-authors introduce SafeBuild-Bench for construction safety testing. Safety models must spot real deployment risks, not just common objects. A worker near a scaffold edge with no guardrails is one example. Real inspection archives are redundant and long-tailed. They also span changing sites and months.

The benchmark is mined from over 100,000 industrial image-text records. It holds 3,314 tasks from over 3,000 expert-checked images. Tasks cover hazard choice questions and free-form hazard descriptions. A graph-enhanced selection pipeline, GEMS, made expert checking scalable. It mixes model confusion signals with graph diversity. Current models score near 60 at best, far from reliable safety sense, they report. Benchmark, scripts, and code are released.
brasseur-quatre-lettres-mexique-1868:
Charles-Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg spent years in Mexico and Central America copying old books and ruins. Quatre lettres sur le Mexique, printed in French in 1868, states his bold link between the Maya and Atlantis. Brasseur was the great Mayanist of his century, finder of lost texts.

In four letters he reads Maya myth, script, and ruin as signs of an Atlantic mother land. The letters show a pioneer scholar thinking aloud, half in proof and half in dream. Later writers on Maya and Atlantis all had to pass his work. The book is the founding statement of the Maya-Atlantis tie.
brinton-myths-of-new-world-1868:
Daniel Brinton, an American student of Native peoples, answered the lost-land school head-on in 1868. The Myths of the New World argues that like myths grow on their own in far lands. Brinton was a trained doctor turned scholar of tongues and lore.

He reads the myths of the Americas as the work of minds much like our own, facing the same sky and fears. No sunken land, he holds, is needed to explain why tales rhyme across oceans. Atlantis writers after him had to deal with his case or look weak. The book is the great skeptical counterweight of its age.
broca-eyzies-1868:
Paul Broca, a French surgeon and sage of the brain, wrote this memoir on the Eyzies finds in 1868. The text here is the English version of his report. Work men in the Perigord had found five frames in a rock shelter that year.

The frames were the first Cro-Magnon men known to science, tall and fine boned. Broca set out their skulls and bones with care and told how they stand to living races. The paper is the first learned word on the Cro-Magnon folk, our own kind in the ice age.
cia-0000007468:
Volume 6, number 2 of Studies in Intelligence appeared in spring 1962, inside the CIA's own publishing program. Studies was the agency's in-house journal, written by officers for officers about their craft. The issue's heading names a piece on Die Piratenchronik, a chronicle tied to pirates.

Because the journal was meant for internal readers, its pages speak more plainly than public statements do. Articles in the series weigh sources, methods, and past operations for lessons. Historians now use these issues to trace how American intelligence thought during the Cold War. The declassified copy comes through the CIA reading room mirror.
cia-0000009668:
The location of an American prisoner of war camp in Bac Thai province, current as of November, is fixed in a February 1970 item. Bac Thai, north of Hanoi, held camps close to the capital's prison system. A dated location mattered because camps moved and reports aged fast.

Pinpointing a camp served several needs: rescue planning, bombing safety, and the prisoner accounting itself. Analysts had to state how fresh the fix was, hence the November dating. Stale locations could mislead as badly as none. This short item shows the care taken to keep the prison map current month by month.
cia-0000009968:
France's current situation, including its strategic importance, fills a CIA paper dated November 1947. France was then governed by shifting coalitions, with the largest communist party in Western Europe newly expelled from government. Strikes shook the country that same autumn.

The paper reads France as a Cold War hinge: lose France, and Western Europe's defense crumbled. That reading drove aid, diplomacy, and quiet political support for the center. Coming months after the CIA's founding, the file shows the agency thinking continent-wide from birth. It also preserves French weakness, before recovery, as Washington plainly saw it.
cia-0000010668:
Six years after Japan's defeat, CIA analysts asked a hard question in March 1951: could Japan rebuild armed forces while working with the United States? Japan was still under American occupation, and its new constitution barred it from keeping an army. The Korean War, raging next door, made the question urgent for planners in Washington.

The study weighs what rearmament would take in men, money, and public support. It also considers how Japan's neighbors would react to a rearmed former enemy. The paper came months before the peace treaty was signed, and it foreshadows the Self-Defense Forces Japan created soon after.
cia-0000012268:
A letter meant for the appropriate authorities of the United States sits in the CIA files from June 1960. The document's spare title hides its errand: it is part of the routing around the Penkovsky operation. Oleg Penkovsky, a Soviet intelligence colonel, was reaching toward the West with offers of secrets that summer.

The file preserves how his mail was handled once it entered American hands. Cover sheets, routing marks, and careful logging guarded each step of the journey. For readers, it is postal history from the Cold War's greatest espionage case, plain on its face and grave in its stakes.
cia-0000013868: How American prisoners of war were treated is the subject of a CIA report dated July 4, 1967. Treatment covered food, care, housing, and the rules guards were told to follow. Reports like this reached officials who had to judge camp life in North Vietnam and the south. They also shaped what the public was told about the prisoners.
cia-0000014668: An admitted Soviet agent gave testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, in a CIA file dated February 1, 1966. The agent's name is left blank in the title line. Such testimony fueled public spy scares through the 1950s and beyond. The file keeps the hearing in the agency's long watch on Soviet work in America.
cia-0000014768: Birthday greetings for Togliatti sit beside Rosenberg clemency in a CIA file dated February 5, 1953. Palmiro Togliatti led Italy's huge Communist Party. Trieste's Communists looked to Rome as much as to Moscow. Pairing a party feast day with the mercy campaign shows the human weave of these small party reports. This party file is kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015268: An unexplained bright light traveled across the sky, in a CIA file dated September 1, 1958. The title gives no place, only the moving light itself. Traveling lights were the most common of all strange sky reports. With no place named, this one rests on the witness's word alone, plain and bare.
cia-0000015368: Comments on a sighting report fill a CIA file dated May 1, 1954. The report is coded OO-B-90229, a sighting of unconventional aircraft. The source date is marked unknown in the title. Comment files were where doubts and checks were voiced in writing. This one holds the office talk over a single coded case.
cia-0000015468: Above a Norwegian town, an unidentified object was seen, and a CIA record dated in 1952 kept the report. The title names neither the town nor the witness, so no detail is added here. Small place sightings formed the bulk of the saucer file in every country. Each one was minor alone, yet together they built the pile officials felt bound to track.
cia-0000022168: Israel's situation after its war with the Arab states is discussed in a CIA record dated in 1968. The war meant is the June 1967 war, which redrew the map of the region. A year on, officials were still taking stock of borders, armies, and talks. The clipped title frames the item as Israel discussing its own state, a view worth keeping.
cia-0000022368: Finns demanded to know why Powers had orders to land on a Finnish airfield, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. Emergency landing orders in his papers named fields in neutral Finland. That detail pulled a careful neutral country into a spy scandal. The demand shows small states guarding their good name when great powers fly secret missions overhead.
cia-0000042668:
A CIA Latin America brief for November 21, 1989 is dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog record. Parts of the brief are blanked out in the released copy. Its El Salvador item says the country faced human rights concerns.

Inside, the brief gives the region's news in short, ranked form. El Salvador's rights record was then under sharp attack at home and abroad. Congress in Washington weighed the charges each time new military aid came up for a vote. The file shows a daily brief doing its plain work. It placed one country's troubles on the morning page, where officials in Washington began their reading of the region each day.
cia-0000046768: CIA analysts looked ahead at Eastern Germany's likely course through 1952 in an estimate dated January 2, 1952. East Germany was then a new state, built in the Soviet zone of the defeated country. Forecast papers like this one show planners trying to read a satellite's politics month by month. Most such guesses were soon tested by events.
cia-0000049168: An update on progress in the Jesuit murder case is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Updates like this one were the case's pulse, taken for readers in San Salvador and Washington. Each reported a step, a stall, or a name, in a case that took years to reach a courtroom.
cia-0000049268: The 1990 certification of El Salvador fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Certification was the recurring act by which Washington declared the country fit, on human rights grounds, to keep receiving aid. Each round forced the war's record into a yes-or-no shape, and this file holds one round's paper.
cia-0000075168: Briefing of General Maxwell Taylor on redacted material is recorded in declassified CIA document 0000075168, dated June 6, 1961. The general is named while the briefing's substance stays blank in the heading. Readers get a short declassified briefing note whose interest lies in that contrast, a named senior officer and a subject the released record withholds.
cia-0000098268: China's Cultural Revolution in 1968 is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098268, dated November 5, 1968. The heading ties the movement to a single year. Readers find a short declassified paper taking that year as its frame. It is a year-specific companion to narrower China reports. Those reports covered provinces, factions, and daily disruption.
cia-0000100168: Biological Warfare USSR: Additional Rumors of an Accident at the Biological Weapons facility, in cut-short heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000100168, dated September 1, 1979. The word additional shows the rumors were not the first. Readers get the cluster's earliest rumor record, dated within the year of the suspected accident itself.
cia-0000102968:
