Gut microbes shape body weight and blood sugar, but which members drive disease, rather than merely mark it, is hard to prove. The pair isolated candidates from the faeces of hyperglycemic obese mice.

One isolate, a Lachnospiraceae strain catalogued as AJ110941, was seeded alone into germ-free ob/ob mice, which are genetically prone to obesity. Colonized mice developed higher fasting blood glucose, heavier livers and belly fat, and lower insulin with weaker beta-cell function readings than germ-free controls. A single ordinary gut resident, in other words, measurably worsened the metabolic picture in a susceptible host. The authors call for work on how the bacterium exerts that effect.
europmc-pmc4364968:
David Ebert and co-authors pooled trials of computer-based therapy for young people, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Anxiety and depression in children and teens often go untreated, and programs delivered by computer or internet could widen access. The team searched major databases up to December 2013 for randomized trials in people up to age 25. Thirteen trials with 796 young people met the rules, covering anxiety, depression, or both.

Across trials, computer-based cognitive behavioral therapy beat control conditions by a clear margin on symptoms after treatment. Gains held for programs aimed at anxiety alone and for those aimed at depression alone. Differences between studies were low, which strengthens the pooled verdict. The authors present such programs as a workable option where face-to-face care is scarce, while the trials base remains modest in size.
europmc-pmc4389268:
Jeremiah Cohen, Mackenzie Amoroso, and Naoshige Uchida recorded serotonin neurons in mice. Their study ran in eLife in 2015. Serotonin is a brain signal chemical. Its exact job has long been debated. One barrier was watching the right neurons during behavior. The team tagged serotonin neurons with a light-sensitive protein. Light pulses could then identify those cells. They recorded from the dorsal raphe area of the brain. The mice worked through blocks of trials. Rewards and punishments varied from block to block.

Many serotonin neurons shifted their steady firing over minutes. Their rate tracked whether the block was good or bad. Most also fired sharply at punishments. A subset fired at cues that predicted reward. Dopamine neurons showed no such slow shift. Serotonin thus reports good and bad outcomes at once. It does so on timescales from seconds to minutes.
europmc-pmc4392068:
Caroline Wright and a large Deciphering Developmental Disorders team reported scalable genetic diagnosis for children, in The Lancet in 2015. Genome reading was entering clinics for rare diseases, but labs needed robust pipelines to find causal variants and decide what to return to families. The British study recruited children with undiagnosed developmental disorders through all 24 regional genetics services, testing each child and their parents with microarrays and exome sequencing.

Each child carried about 80,000 variants, of which roughly 400 were rare and predicted to alter proteins. Focusing on new or inherited variants in known disorder genes gave a diagnosis for 27 percent of 1,133 children who had already been investigated without answers. Results went back to families through their local genetics teams. The yield shows genome-wide testing earns its place in routine rare-disease care.
europmc-pmc4507468:
Rommy von Bernhardi, Laura Eugenín-von Bernhardi, and Jaime Eugenín review how microglia go wrong in the aging brain, in a 2015 Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience paper. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. Aging is the chief risk factor for diseases that kill brain cells, and aged microglia shift into an active state that can feed harmful inflammation.

In old mice, microglia make more inflammatory signals and react more harshly to threats. Their power units, the mitochondria, gather oxidative damage, and the stress turns on pathways that raise output of IL-1β, a key inflammatory messenger. A calming signal, TGFβ1, also rises with age, yet the authors report its control path weakens after stimulation. The result is a lasting inflamed setting tied to memory loss.
europmc-pmc4516868:
Frank J. Kelly and Julia C. Fussell review air pollution and health in Environmental Geochemistry and Health in 2015. City air has improved over past decades, yet large shares of urban people still breathe air that fails European standards and the stricter World Health Organization guidelines.

Work over the past ten years ties fine particles in air to more harm, across a wider range of diseases, than once thought. The effects show no clear safe floor within studied levels and rise in a mostly straight line with dose, reaching close to background levels. Kelly and Fussell survey efforts to pin down which parts of the particle mix do the damage and how they injure the body. Better monitoring and public reporting form the last piece.
europmc-pmc4524368:
Henry Rosenberg and four co-authors review malignant hyperthermia, a rare but lethal reaction to anesthesia, in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases in 2015. In people with the inherited fault, common anesthetic gases or the relaxant succinylcholine can trigger runaway muscle metabolism. Heat, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, and acid buildup follow. Untreated attacks are likely to kill.

Reactions occur in roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 250,000 anesthetics. Yet the gene faults may sit in as many as one in 400 people. The review explains the calcium fault inside muscle cells that drives the crisis. It also shows how a rise in exhaled carbon dioxide gives an early clue. Families inherit the risk in a dominant pattern. Pigs, dogs, and horses can carry the same disorder.
europmc-pmc4552468:
Zachary A. King leads a seven-author team presenting a web app for drawing pathway maps, in PLoS Computational Biology in 2015. Biologists study metabolism through pathway diagrams, charts of the reactions that build and burn molecules. Old tools made such maps slowly and shared them poorly, so data often never reached a chart at all.

Their app, Escher, lets users draft new maps fast, with suggestions drawn from their own data and genome-scale models. Gene, protein, and metabolite data can be painted onto the reactions, so trends across data types show at a glance. Built on open web technology, maps can be tweaked, extended, shared, and embedded in pages. Example builds demonstrate each feature.
europmc-pmc4557968:
Bart Klijs and six co-authors check whether a giant Dutch health cohort mirrors its population, in PLoS ONE in 2015. LifeLines follows three generations in the north of the Netherlands, recruited through family doctors, then family members, then online self-sign-up between 2006 and 2013. A cohort that skews from its source population can distort later findings.

Against the national register, LifeLines adults were more often female, middle-aged, married, semi-urban, and native Dutch. After adjusting for that mix, participants also differed somewhat in income level, lifestyle, chronic disease, and general health from a regional living-conditions survey of 6,093 people. Recruitment route mattered too. The audit tells future users exactly where the cohort leans.
europmc-pmc4564568:
L. D. Selemon and N. Zecevic frame schizophrenia as a disorder of two growth windows, in Translational Psychiatry in 2015. Schizophrenia is now read as a brain development disease. Its risk rises with disturbances before birth and with social stress and drug use in adolescence, two oddly distant periods. The authors focus on the prefrontal cortex, the brain region most tied to the illness.

In the first trimester, prefrontal cells multiply and early populations form; animal work shows that curbing that growth yields schizophrenia-like brain changes and behavior. In adolescence, the same region prunes excess connections. Stress then raises dopamine drive, which may push pruning too far. The review ties both windows into one developmental account.
europmc-pmc4613668:
A team led by Yuan-Yuan Zhou published a 2015 review proposing that MAPK/JNK signalling helps control autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup system. Autophagy delivers worn-out parts and large molecules to lysosomes for breakdown. Cells rely on it during starvation and stress. The review appeared in Bioscience Reports.

The authors trace how the JNK branch of the MAPK signal family can switch autophagy on or adjust its level. They weigh both gene-based control and faster routes that do not need new gene activity. Autophagy normally acts as a housekeeper, clearing damaged parts before they turn toxic. Framing JNK signalling as a regulator gives researchers testable routes for diseases where cleanup fails, from cancer to nerve degeneration.
europmc-pmc4630968:
Emma Pierson and Christopher Yau presented a 2015 method called ZIFA for shrinking single-cell gene expression data down to a viewable form. Single-cell RNA sequencing measures thousands of genes per cell, but many readings drop out and appear as zeros. Standard reduction methods ignore that flaw. The paper appeared in Genome Biology.

ZIFA builds the dropout behaviour directly into its statistical model of the data. On simulated and real datasets it recovered the underlying structure more accurately than standard tools. Clearer low-dimensional maps help researchers spot cell subgroups and disease-related patterns. The method is aimed at the growing number of labs profiling gene activity one cell at a time.
europmc-pmc4663368:
Zoe Cesarz and Kenji Tamama published a 2016 review of growing mesenchymal stem cells as three-dimensional spheroids. Cells grown as balls behave more like tissue than flat layers do. Stem cells cultured this way show stronger anti-inflammatory and repair effects. The review appeared in Stem Cells International.

Spheroid stem cells survive transplantation better and show enhanced ability to form several tissue types. They switch on pluripotency marker genes, age more slowly in culture, and reorganize their internal skeletons, changing their physical properties. Gene activity profiles shift dramatically compared with flat culture. Yet the molecular triggers behind these changes are largely unknown. The authors map what is established and where the mechanism gaps lie for tissue engineering.
europmc-pmc4699268:
C. Humpel reviewed organotypic brain slice cultures in Neuroscience in 2015. Standard cell cultures grow one cell type alone, stripped of its neighbors. Brain slices grown as cultures keep the tissue's layered architecture, so cells interact much as they do in a living brain. The review traces how the method developed, with special weight on the membrane techniques that made it practical.

Practical guidance covers donor age, culture media, and handling. Two disease models get close looks: slices whose cholinergic neurons mimic Alzheimer's disease, and slices whose dopamine pathway mimics Parkinson's disease. Growing blood vessels in slices is also covered, including work toward an artificial blood-brain barrier. Humpel closes with the model's limits and likely future uses. For brain researchers, the review is a handbook for a method that bridges dishes and animals.
europmc-pmc4702768:
Sarah E. Calvo, Karl R. Clauser, and Vamsi K. Mootha presented MitoCarta2.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Mitochondria run energy production and many other core pathways, but science needs an exact list of their protein parts to study them well. The team built the first MitoCarta in 2008 by combining protein measurements from fourteen mouse organs with tagging studies and statistics. The update rebuilds the list separately for humans and mice with better data.

Each inventory now holds 1,158 genes. The human list keeps most original entries and adds 240 new ones; the mouse list adds 191. Improvements came from better gene models, fresh literature, and sharper matching between species. The free inventory gives researchers a shared framework for studying mitochondrial disease and aging. It turns a scattered literature into one checkable parts list.
europmc-pmc4714968:
Isabelle Cleynen, Gabrielle Boucher, Luke Jostins, and a huge international consortium studied the genetics of bowel disease subtypes, in The Lancet in 2016. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the two main forms of inflammatory bowel disease, and care still follows that split. The team genotyped 34,819 patients from forty-nine centers in sixteen countries and sorted them by the standard scheme of disease location and behavior.

Three gene regions stood out, tied mainly to where disease sits in the gut, a feature that stays fixed over a patient's life. Disease behavior, which changes over time, showed little genetic grip once location was counted. A combined risk score separated colonic from ileal Crohn's strongly, and flagged a few patients whose genetics suggested their diagnosis should be revised. The work supports sorting bowel disease by biology, especially location, rather than by the old two labels alone.
europmc-pmc4717368:
Venediktos V. Kapetanakis, Michelle P. Y. Chan, Paul J. Foster, and three colleagues charted world glaucoma patterns in the British Journal of Ophthalmology in 2016. Primary open angle glaucoma is the commonest form of a disease that blinds irreversibly. Its frequency by age, sex, region, and ancestry was uncertain. The team gathered eighty-one population surveys from thirty-seven countries, covering 216,214 people and 5,266 cases, and modeled prevalence with study design taken into account.

Black populations carried the highest rates, about five percent at age sixty and twelve percent at eighty. Prevalence climbed fastest per decade among Hispanic and White groups, slowest among East and South Asian groups. Men were more likely affected than women. Globally, the team counted 57.5 million cases in 2015, heading for 65.5 million by 2020. Surveys that skipped full visual field testing found fewer cases, a warning for planners who rely on them.
europmc-pmc4739768:
Economo, Clack, Lavis, and five colleagues build a platform for tracing single neurons across a whole mouse brain. The task is defeated by axons as thin as 100 nanometres that branch over many millimetres. Their system couples a high-speed two-photon microscope with an automated tissue slicer and software for stitching and reconstructing enormous image volumes.

They demonstrate it by rebuilding the full branching patterns of several motor cortex neurons within one brain, showing where each cell's axon actually goes. Because bulk tracer studies mix many cell types together, single-cell maps like these can define neuron types and reveal how signals are routed between regions.
europmc-pmc4749968:
Zhao and nine colleagues mimic the cell's habit of boxing enzymes into compartments, this time using self-assembled DNA nanocages. The cages hold enzymes at controlled numbers and positions. This lets the team test how enclosure and the cage's charged surfaces affect common metabolic enzymes, in bulk and one molecule at a time.

Encapsulated enzymes turn over substrate faster than free ones. Oddly, smaller proteins gain more than larger ones, which the authors attribute to the cage's water layer stabilising active shapes. The cages also shield their cargo from protein-chewing enzymes, a practical virtue for biotechnology and functional biomaterials.
europmc-pmc4823868:
Qiupeng Zheng leads a team of many co-authors in Nature Communications in 2016 profiling circular RNAs in human tissue. Circular RNAs are loops of RNA with no ends, long dismissed as splicing errors. Reading six healthy tissues and seven cancers with ribosome-free sequencing, the team found at least twenty-seven thousand candidate loops, many differing between healthy and cancer tissue.

They then dissected one abundant loop from the HIPK3 gene. Silencing the loop, but not the gene's straight message, slowed cell growth sharply. The loop proved a sponge for nine small regulatory RNAs at once, holding eighteen docking sites. One target, miR-124, is a known growth brake, and the loop's grip measurably weakened it. The work makes the case that loops are working regulators, not noise.
europmc-pmc4829868:
Narendrakumar M. Chaudhari, Vinod Kumar Gupta, and Chitra Dutta present a pan-genome pipeline in Scientific Reports in 2016. A species' pan genome has three parts. Core genes are shared by all strains. Accessory genes are carried by some. Unique genes belong to single strains. That map exposes diversity and evolution. Older software was slow, fussy to install, or thin in features.

Their tool, BPGA, runs the standard analysis at high speed. It adds seven modules. These build family trees from the core or the whole set. They check for genes special to chosen strains. They run subset analysis and base-composition checks. They map each gene class to its functions. The tool asks little of the computer. It offers a plain command line and clean graphics. A test on 28 strains of a strep species shows it off.
europmc-pmc4858568:
Ian Gibbs-Seymour and co-authors identified a protein, HPF1, in 2016 that steers a DNA repair worker called PARP-1. When DNA breaks, PARP-1 tags proteins with a chemical chain to rally repair. HPF1 binds PARP-1 firmly and rushes to damage sites with it, even before tagging starts. Tests showed HPF1 pushes tagging onto histones, the DNA spools, and curbs PARP-1 tagging itself.

Cells lacking HPF1 grew sensitive to DNA-harming drugs and to PARP blockers used in cancer care. HPF1 thus sits at a crossroads of the damage response, balancing repair signals. Its level might shape how well PARP blocker drugs work, a lead for tailoring cancer treatment.
europmc-pmc4906968:
Val J. Lowe and co-authors tested the tau scan tracer AV-1451 against autopsy tissue in 2016. Brain scans for tau, a tangle protein in Alzheimer's disease, need proof that the tracer sticks to tau and not to look-alike deposits. Brain sections from 38 confirmed cases across dementia types were stained for tau and two other problem proteins and matched to tracer binding on twin sections.

The tracer homed to neurofibrillary tangles, with less grip on younger, less mature tau. It favored the mixed 3R plus 4R tau of Alzheimer's over other forms and barely bound TDP-43 areas. Scan reads can thus be trusted as tau maps in living patients, with known limits.
europmc-pmc4937268:
Bert Vandenberk and seven co-authors ask which formula best corrects the QT interval on a heart tracing. Their study appeared in the Journal of the American Heart Association in 2016. The QT interval must be adjusted for heart rate before doctors can judge drug risk. Many formulas exist, and hospitals need one for automatic monitoring in electronic records. The team tested five formulas on tracings from 6,609 patients at a hospital in Leuven, Belgium.

Fridericia and Framingham corrected best, while Bazett, the most used formula, performed worst. In healthy patients its upper normal limits sat above current clinical standards. In survival models, the Framingham version flagged risk of death most strongly. The authors question whether Bazett should stay the clinical default. They argue switching the standard formula would sharpen risk checks for patients on drugs that stretch the QT interval.
europmc-pmc4937568:
David R. Kelley, Jasper Snoek, and John L. Rinn present Basset, a deep learning tool that reads the control code of open DNA. Their paper appeared in Genome Research in 2016. Most disease linked DNA variants sit outside genes, in regions that control gene use, and their effects are unknown. Basset applies convolutional neural networks, a form of deep learning, to learn which DNA patterns make a region open and active in a cell.

The tool trained on open sites mapped in 164 cell types. It predicted activity more accurately than earlier methods. Its scores separated likely causal disease variants from nearby harmless ones. A lab can sequence open DNA in its own cell type, then use Basset to score every variant in the genome for that cell. The authors release the package as open source software for genome interpretation.
europmc-pmc4994968:
Claire L. Brockett and Graham J. Chapman introduce the biomechanics of the ankle for clinicians. Their review appeared in Orthopaedics and Trauma in 2016. The ankle complex joins leg to foot and takes high compression and shear forces with each step. Despite that load it resists degeneration far better than hip or knee, unless injury intervenes. The paper lays out the bony anatomy that shapes ankle motion and sorts out which joints produce which movements.

Ligaments critical to stability and function get detailed treatment. The authors then walk through the movements of a normal gait cycle. They close with how surgery changes the picture, comparing total joint replacement with fusion. Replacement preserves some motion; fusion removes it and shifts stress elsewhere. The review aims to ground surgical choices in the mechanics they alter.
europmc-pmc5021368:
Waseem K. Raja and seven co-authors grow human neural tissue that mimics Alzheimer's disease, in PLoS ONE in 2016. Drug trials for Alzheimer's fail at a dismal rate, in part because flat cell cultures cannot show the clumping that marks the disease. The team used induced pluripotent stem cells, reprogrammed from patients with inherited Alzheimer's, and let them self-organize into three-dimensional brain-like tissue.

The grown tissues showed the disease's hallmarks as they aged: amyloid deposits outside cells, tau protein loaded with extra phosphate marks, and swollen endosomes. Tissue from healthy donors did not. Several patient lines, carrying different gene faults, behaved the same way. Drugs that block two enzymes cutting the amyloid source protein lowered both amyloid and tau problems in the tissue. The model offers a human test bed for screening Alzheimer's drugs before costly trials.
europmc-pmc5048068:
James R. Staley and eleven co-authors present PhenoScanner in Bioinformatics in 2016. Genome-wide association studies have tied thousands of genetic variants to diseases and traits, but checking one variant against every trait meant hunting through scattered papers. PhenoScanner gathers the published results into one curated database built for phenome scans, the cross-checking of a variant against many traits at once.

The database holds over 350 million association results covering more than ten million distinct variants, and unlike older catalogs it keeps all results rather than only the strongest hits. The companion web tool aligns each query variant's effects on a consistent basis and can add close proxy variants drawn from reference populations. Uses range from causal inference studies, where a variant stands in for a changeable risk factor, to mapping the wide consequences of disturbing one biological pathway. The tool is free online.
europmc-pmc5107568:
Larisa V. Kovtonyuk, Kristin Fritsch, Xiaomin Feng, Markus G. Manz, and Hitoshi Takizawa reviewed aging of the blood-forming system in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. All blood and immune cells arise from stem cells in the bone marrow, which mostly rest quietly yet can surge into action after blood loss or infection.

Aging brings a slow, low-grade inflammation, and the review gathers evidence that this simmering state reshapes blood formation over time. Stem cells, their supporting marrow niche, and immune defenses all shift in linked ways, a pattern the authors call inflamm-aging. They compare the changes seen in aging with those driven by open inflammation and ask how inflammatory signals may push stem cells toward worn-out, skewed output in old age.
europmc-pmc5115868:
Ray Yu-Ruei Wang and co-authors, including Axel T. Brunger as named in the text's byline, presented an automated refinement tool in eLife in 2016. Cryo-electron microscopy can now map huge molecular assemblies at near-atomic detail, but placing every atom correctly in such maps is slow, error-prone hand work over thousands of building blocks.

Their method plugs the Rosetta modeling software into the map-fitting process, improving the model's geometry while keeping its fit to the measured density. On three recent cryo-EM structures, it found and fixed backbone placement errors on its own and converged from poor starting points. The tool handled symmetric, very large, and RNA-containing assemblies, plus bound small molecules, and the authors offer it to streamline structure solving.
europmc-pmc5123068:
Carolina Villarroya-Beltri and nine co-authors found a switch controlling exosome release, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Villarroya-Beltri leads with her first surname, as the byline prints it hyphenated. Exosomes are vesicles cells send out for communication, formed inside compartments called multivesicular bodies that can either release them or dump them for destruction.

The team showed that a tag called ISGylation, added during antiviral defense, pushes those compartments toward destruction. Switching the tag on lowered compartment counts and cut exosome release in cells and mice. The tag marks compartment proteins, including TSG101, for clumping and breakdown in lysosomes; blocking that breakdown restored release. The finding adds a new control point over how much exosome traffic a cell produces.
europmc-pmc5176668:
A meeting report in The Indian Medical Gazette records a paper read to the Burma Assistant Surgeons' Association. Its subject was morphia injector's septicaemia. The disease was first described in Rangoon and is also called Whitmore's disease. The speaker, C. S. Krishnaswami of the Rangoon General Hospital, reviews six years of work on the illness.

Krishnaswami recalls taking over the pathological and post-mortem work in April 1910 under Captain A. Whitmore, with whom he published the first account in July 1912, covering about forty cases; Major Knapp added a few cases in 1915. His review now spans over two hundred cases from the hospital wards and mortuary and the Rangoon jail. He traces the early confusion with glanders: similar lung lesions appeared in people with no horse contact, and the glanders germ could not be grown from them.
europmc-pmc5178868:
Stephen M. Fleming and Nathaniel D. Daw presented a framework for self-evaluation in Psychological Review, with the hosted text dated 2017, and Keith J. Holyoak also named in the text's byline. People can report confidence in their choices and often notice their own mistakes, even without feedback, but no single computational account covered both abilities.

Their Bayesian model treats self-evaluation as second-order inference: a separate reading of one's own decision system, much like judging another actor's performance. When the machinery of deciding and the machinery of judging sit apart in space or time, this second reading arises. Simulations show the model unifies confidence and error detection, predicts new effects of one's own actions on self-judgment, and explains why self-knowledge can run ahead of, or behind, actual performance.
europmc-pmc5201668:
Leonard Rogers tests a safer antimony salt against kala-azar in this 1918 article. The standard drug, tartar emetic, worked but was dangerous. Two debilitated patients had died in collapse after full intravenous doses, which Rogers reported earlier. An accident sharpened the question: in a Calcutta hospital, three children collapsed after a dose from a solution that had precipitated, and one emaciated four-year-old died. Rogers turned to sodium antimonyl tartrate, already used in trypanosomiasis.

In May 1917 he compared the two salts in pigeons and rabbits. The sodium salt's minimal lethal dose was slightly lower, meaning it was marginally more toxic by that measure, contrary to hope. Still, isolated kala-azar cases at the Campbell Hospital had done well on it. Rogers set out a prolonged trial under matched conditions to settle the relative value of the two drugs fairly.
europmc-pmc5297868:
S. Vienberg, J. Geiger, S. Madsen, and L. T. Dalgaard reviewed microRNAs in metabolism in Acta Physiologica. MicroRNAs, short RNA strands of about 22 building blocks, fine-tune which proteins cells make. Within a decade they emerged as key regulators of the body's energy balance. The review walks through each major metabolic tissue in turn.

In the pancreas, microRNA families govern the balance between beta-cell growth and mature function, with miR-7, miR-375, and miR-335 controlling insulin release. MiR-33a and miR-33b steer cholesterol and fat handling, while miR-103 and miR-107 tune the liver's insulin sensitivity. In muscle, miR-1, miR-133, and miR-206 direct fiber type and formation; in fat, others drive white-to-brown conversion. MicroRNAs also ride in blood inside exosomes, acting as signals and candidate disease markers. Their disruption in obesity, type 2 diabetes, and artery disease makes them attractive drug targets, though large studies are still needed.
europmc-pmc5353968:
Robert Middleton and co-authors built a tool to study kept introns in gene messages, in Genome Biology in 2017. When a gene is read, spacer chunks called introns are cut from the draft message. At times a spacer stays in the final message, a quirk called intron retention. It is the least studied form of message editing, since kept spacers are hard to gauge with trust.

Their program, IRFinder, spots kept introns in reading data with care. Run on more than two thousand and five hundred samples, it found the quirk in all tissues tested, touching most coding genes. Kept spacers cluster in the same genes and carry set binding sites for RNA guide proteins. The quirk tracks cell maturing and the cell cycle. Messages that keep a spacer tend to make less protein, and those that dodge the cell's waste watch still sit idle, untranslated.
europmc-pmc5368368:
Chencheng Feng and co-authors reviewed harsh oxygen waste in worn spinal discs, in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2017. The discs between spine bones wear down with age and strain, a top cause of back pain. In worn discs, output of reactive oxygen species, the cell's harsh oxygen waste, runs high. The review asks how that waste drives the wear.

The waste sits mid-web in disc cell signaling. It tips the balance of disc web building toward breakdown, fans swelling, and pushes cells toward death, self-eating, and worn-out states. It also scars the disc web proteins themselves, which weakens the disc's spring. Guard compounds that mop up the waste help disc cells in dishes, raising web building and sparing cells. But proof in living bodies and patients is still thin, a gap the authors flag.
europmc-pmc5379068:
David S. Liu and co-authors found a weak point in mutant-p53 cancers in Nature Communications in 2017. The guard gene TP53 is flawed in more than half of all cancers. The flawed protein piles up in the tumor and marks a poor outlook. Drugs that hit such cancers in a set way are sorely needed. The team traced how the piled protein bends the cell's guard against oxygen harm.

Piled mutant p53 muzzles a gene that builds part of a cystine import pump. With less raw stuff in, the cell makes less glutathione, its main shield against harsh oxygen. Pump-blocking drugs then kill such cells by choice, while sparing sound ones. The muzzled gene's level also flags tumors that will answer a mutant-p53 waking drug. Pairing the two drug types killed the tumors far harder than either alone.
europmc-pmc5408368:
Asad U. Khan, Lubna Maryam, and Raffaele Zarrilli review a drug-resistance enzyme that threatens public health, in a 2017 paper in BMC Microbiology. The enzyme, called NDM, lets bacteria break down a wide range of penicillin-like drugs. That includes the carbapenems, often the last drugs left for hard infections. Since it appeared, forms of the enzyme have spread across many countries and many bacterial species.

The review covers the gene's variants, each differing by one or two building blocks, and tracks which species carry them and where. Common carriers include gut and hospital germs that already resist other drugs. Knowing how each variant is built should help explain how the enzyme cuts drugs apart. The authors say that grasp is needed to design blockers that restore drug power.
europmc-pmc5413968:
Pearce and co-authors present PanDDA, a method for finding hidden states in protein crystals. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Crystallographers often hunt small changes, such as a drug binding to a protein. The changed state may fill only part of the crystal. Its signal then drowns in weak, noisy electron density. Reading such maps by eye is slow and subjective. PanDDA tackles the problem with many data sets at once.

The method first builds a picture of the unchanged ground state. It does so from many ground-state crystals. It then subtracts part of that picture from a test data set. What remains shows the changed state far more clearly. A statistical check flags real changes without guesswork. The authors argue the approach should become routine practice. It also shows that single data sets cannot fully describe a crystal.
europmc-pmc5458068:
Nizard and co-authors show that tissue-resident memory T cells make cancer vaccines work better. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Resident memory cells settle in tissue for good. They never recirculate through blood. Their role in cancer surveillance was unknown. The team used a head and neck cancer model. Intranasal vaccination delivered a mucosal vector. The vector was the B subunit of Shiga toxin. Vaccinated mice grew local resident memory cells. Tumors grew more slowly.

Parabiosis experiments proved the cells were crucial. Shared circulation could not substitute for them. Blocking TGF-beta cut their induction. Vaccine efficacy dropped in step. Human data supported the mouse story. Lung cancer patients held more resident memory cells in tumors. Those patients survived better overall. The link held in multivariate analysis. The authors propose these cells as a biomarker. Vaccine design should aim to elicit them deliberately.
europmc-pmc545968:
Hall and co-authors share a free spreadsheet tool that scores other illnesses in cancer patients. Their article appeared in BMC Cancer. Doctors use the Charlson index to weigh a patient's other health problems. The score helps judge who can handle strong treatment. Yet hand scoring is slow, so the index sees little use.

The tool is a macro built into a Microsoft Excel file. A user enters a patient's conditions and gets the score at once. Age can be added in or left out. The authors also review proof that the index holds up across major cancers. They aim the tool at wider use in trials and care for older patients.
europmc-pmc5472168:
Peng and co-authors introduce BaSiC, a software tool for fixing microscopy images, in Nature Communications. Uneven light can shade the edges of an image and skew measured values. Time-lapse films also drift as background fades. Such flaws can distort counts of cells and tissue traits. The team built a method that needs no manual settings.

BaSiC splits each image set into a smooth background part and a sparse detail part. From that split it estimates the shading pattern and the camera offset. It then corrects both, plus drift over time. The authors report high accuracy with fewer input images than rival tools. BaSiC is free as a Fiji/ImageJ plugin.
europmc-pmc549068:
Smith, Goldsmith, and Eppig present a resource paper in Genome Biology. It introduces the Mammalian Phenotype Ontology, a structured word list for traits. Mouse studies produce huge amounts of trait data on mutations and strains. Free-text notes make those data hard to search or compare. A shared vocabulary with clear definitions was needed.

The ontology gives each trait a standard term and definition. Curators at the Mouse Genome Database use it to tag records. Tagged data can then be searched and compared by computer. The authors show how text searches miss records that tagged searches catch. The tool supports mice as models of human disease.
europmc-pmc5562268:
Astuti and co-authors pool the evidence on smoking and telomere length in Environmental Research. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes. They shorten with each cell division. Their length marks how fast cells age. Smoking speeds many age-linked diseases, so a link was plausible.

The review gathered 84 studies in all. Thirty of them entered the meta-analysis. Ever smokers had shorter telomeres than never smokers. The summary difference was small but consistent. Current smokers also measured shorter than former smokers. A dose-response pattern appeared as well. More pack-years meant shorter telomeres. Some analyses varied more than others. Bias checks found little sign of small-study distortion. Readers get a measured verdict: smoke exposure tracks with faster cellular aging.
europmc-pmc5589068:
Fazel, Yoon, and Hayes update a review in Addiction. They ask how common alcohol and drug use disorders are among people just entering prison. Firm numbers help plan treatment inside prisons. Only studies with clinical interviews or tested tools counted.

The search found 24 studies with 18,388 prisoners in ten countries. About a quarter of new prisoners had an alcohol use disorder. Drug use disorders pooled at 30 percent in men. In women the figure reached 51 percent. Rates varied widely between studies. Drug disorder rates rose in recent decades. Women showed higher rates than men. Readers get current estimates plus a clear view of what drives the spread.
europmc-pmc5653668:
Labidi-Galy and co-authors test whether high-grade serous ovarian cancer starts in the fallopian tube. This cancer is the most common type of ovarian cancer, and its outlook is poor. The team studied tube lesions, ovarian cancers, and spread sites from nine patients. They used whole-exome sequencing and copy number analysis.

Most changes found in the ovarian cancers were already present in the tube lesions. Those lesions include p53 signatures and early tube cancers called STICs. The shared changes hit genes such as TP53, BRCA1, BRCA2, and PTEN. Family-tree analysis put about seven years between a STIC and the ovarian cancer. Spread to other sites followed fast after that.
europmc-pmc5706368:
Puspita and co-authors review the role of oxidative stress in Parkinson's disease. Their review covers the slow death of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. Why those neurons die is still unclear. Clues point to mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum, alpha-synuclein, and dopamine itself.

Each factor can raise oxidative stress inside the cell. Past work treated these paths one by one. The authors stress that the paths interact with each other. Cell death looks like the joint product of many linked events. Oxidative stress acts as the shared thread among them. Grasping those links is key to better treatment plans, they argue.
europmc-pmc5788068:
Chen and co-authors present SOAPnuke, a tool that cleans high throughput sequencing data. Quality checks and preprocessing guard every later analysis step. Older tools split these jobs and scale poorly. SOAPnuke joins them in one program with a set workflow.

Four modules serve genome, small RNA, expression, and metagenome data. A MapReduce frame spreads work across a whole compute cluster. In tests on a standard human dataset, the single machine run balanced speed and resource use. Across sixteen nodes it ran far faster than rival tools. The authors offer it for large sequencing centers.
europmc-pmc5800968:
Chou and co-authors study TDP-43 clumps in ALS and frontotemporal dementia. TDP-43 is a protein that should stay in the cell nucleus. In these diseases it gathers in the wrong place. The team asks what else gets trapped with it.

Using a tagging method called BioID, they map proteins near the clumps. Pore and transport proteins of the nucleus stand out. Mutant TDP-43 pulls those parts out of place and blocks traffic in and out. Brain tissue from patients shows the same pore damage. Readers see a shared failure behind both diseases.
europmc-pmc5819568:
Gupta and co-authors argue for splitting the Mycobacterium genus into five. The genus holds 188 species, including the tuberculosis germ. Family ties among them were murky. The team runs genome-wide comparisons on 150 species.

Trees built from 1,941 core proteins agree on five deep groups. The groups bear names like Tuberculosis-Simiae and Abscessus-Chelonae. A set of 172 shared molecular signatures backs each split. The authors propose one kept genus plus four new ones. That naming would sharpen diagnosis and research. Readers get a data-rich case for redrawing a famous bacterial family.
europmc-pmc5835768:
Porporato and co-authors restore mitochondria to the center of cancer biology. Their review appeared in Cell Research. The old Warburg picture cast tumor cells as glycolysis-only. Mitochondria were treated as broken bystanders.

The authors show the organelles working at every stage of cancer. They supply energy and building blocks for new tumor mass. They balance redox and calcium signals. They also govern whether a stressed cell dies. Mutant enzymes fill them with oncometabolites that reprogram genes. Immune cells depend on the same machinery, so the review weighs cancer drugs that strike mitochondrial metabolism.
europmc-pmc5847168:
Böttcher and co-authors show that natural killer cells call in the dendritic cells tumors fear most. Their study appeared in Cell. Type 1 conventional dendritic cells spark antitumor immunity. Their numbers inside tumors predict rejection and therapy success.

In mouse tumors, those dendritic cells arrive only when NK cells beckon. The NK cells release two attractants, CCL5 and XCL1. Human cancers rich in both signals hold more of the pair and fare better. Tumors fight back with prostaglandin E2. It saps NK cells and blinds the dendritic cells to the call. Blocking that sabotage could aid immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc5854668:
Ribli and co-authors present a deep learning system for mammogram reading. Their article appeared in Scientific Reports. The system finds lesions in breast X-rays and labels them benign or malignant. It needs no human input once an image is loaded. The team built it on the Faster R-CNN object detection framework. Older computer aids gave mixed gains for radiologists, they note.

The authors report top results on the public INbreast database. Their system scored an AUC of 0.95 there. It also took second place in the Digital Mammography DREAM Challenge. As a detector, it missed few cancers and raised few false marks. Code, the trained model, and a viewer plugin are shared online.
europmc-pmc5875768:
Micha and co-authors review school food policies and children's diets. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE. The team searched for trials of school food environment policies. They kept 91 interventions from over 6,600 abstracts. Most ran in North America, Europe, or New Zealand. Policies fell into three types: direct food provision, competitive food standards, and meal standards.

Giving healthy foods raised fruit intake by 0.27 servings a day. Standards for rival foods cut sugary drink intake. Meal standards raised fruit intake and cut fat and sodium. Total calorie intake barely changed under any policy. Effects on body weight were generally not found. The authors call for more work on weight and metabolic risk.
europmc-pmc5891568:
Prinsen and co-authors present a COSMIN guideline for reviews of outcome measures. Their article appeared in Quality of Life Research. Reviews of patient-reported measures are complex undertakings. Each measure needs a review for each property. No tailored guidance existed for that work. The guideline rests on literature and expert opinion. It agrees with broader review guidance where possible.

A ten-step procedure structures the whole review process. Early steps cover searching and selecting studies. Middle steps judge study quality and measure quality. Feasibility and interpretability get their own steps. Final steps shape recommendations and the report. Combining both quality layers supports clear conclusions. Suitable measures can then be chosen on evidence.
europmc-pmc5936168:
Morris seeks the cause of increased electrical excitability in tetany. His paper appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. In tetany, nerves and muscles react too strongly to stimuli. Doctors used that overreaction to judge the condition's severity. Erb's work in 1874 had set the measure in place. Morris asks where in the body the change sits.

He argues the cause acts on the peripheral apparatus, not the central nervous system. Earlier work had passed blood from a dog with tetany through a healthy leg. The leg's excitability rose sharply, even after its nerves were cut. Morris points to the receptive substance between nerve ending and muscle. Changes there, he suggests, drive the rise in excitability.
europmc-pmc5938868:
Andrew gives an address on Molière and the doctors of his time. He spoke to the Glasgow Southern Medical Society in October 1923. The address appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Andrew had long served the Victoria Infirmary in Glasgow. Lately he had turned to French literature of the seventeenth century. Molière's plays about doctors drew him to study their world.

He draws on Raynaud's book on doctors in Molière's era. The address describes medical knowledge in seventeenth-century France. It also covers doctors' education, manners, and customs of the day. Andrew passes on what the plays and records reveal. He frames it as a measure of how far medicine has advanced.
europmc-pmc5966768:
Lindsey and a large team of co-authors give guidelines for experimental models of myocardial ischemia and infarction. Their consensus statement appeared in the American Journal of Physiology, Heart and Circulatory Physiology. Heart attacks arise from ischemia, with or without reperfusion. Research must model that range of events well. Scenarios run from angina to permanent vessel blockage. Reperfusion saves tissue but also adds injury of its own.

The statement recommends best practice for animal models. It stresses rigor and reproducibility in study design. Models span cell work, isolated hearts, and whole animals. The goal is results that other labs can validate. Sound models should sharpen insight into heart injury.
europmc-pmc5966868:
Liu and co-authors review reactive oxygen species and nutritional antioxidants in human disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Too much reactive oxygen species is tied to many chronic diseases. These include cancer, lung disease, and neurodegenerative disorders. In healthy bodies, antioxidants keep such species in fine balance. Some antioxidants are made inside, others come from food.

Poor diet plus low antioxidants can raise oxidative stress, the authors note. Long inflammation can overwhelm defences in several diseases. Trials of supplements give mixed results so far. Some ease damage, others show no clear gain. The review maps these links and calls for more study.
europmc-pmc5991768:
Kasowitz and co-authors show that the nuclear m6A reader YTHDC1 controls RNA processing during mouse oocyte development. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics. YTHDC1 is vital for embryo survival and germline growth. In females it is needed for oocyte growth and maturation. Oocytes lacking it stall at the primary follicle stage. The team traced what goes wrong inside those cells.

Loss of YTHDC1 caused wide alternative polyadenylation, they report. Transcript tails changed length across many genes. Splicing defects were massive as well. Adding back normal YTHDC1 rescued most splicing faults. A version that cannot bind m6A did not rescue them.
europmc-pmc5994068:
Einarson and co-authors estimate how common cardiovascular disease is in type 2 diabetes worldwide. Their systematic literature review appeared in Cardiovascular Diabetology. They covered studies published from 2007 to March 2017. Medline, Embase, and meeting reports were searched. Fifty-seven articles held data on 4,549,481 people with diabetes. Two reviewers extracted the data and checked bias with a standard list.

Cardiovascular disease touched 32.2 percent of patients overall, they report. Coronary heart disease reached 21.2 percent. Heart failure and angina each sat near 15 percent. Such disease caused about half of all deaths in this group.
europmc-pmc5997668:
Ludtmann and co-authors show that alpha-synuclein oligomers attack ATP synthase and open a lethal pore in Parkinson's disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Single alpha-synuclein molecules normally help ATP synthase work well. When they clump into oligomers, the effect turns toxic. The clumps settle on mitochondria near ATP synthase. They impair respiration that depends on complex I. They also oxidise the synthase beta subunit selectively.

These changes raise the chance the permeability transition pore opens, they report. Mitochondria then swell and the cell dies. Blocking the oxidation prevented the pore opening. Neurons grown from patient stem cells showed the same chain.
europmc-pmc6037668:
Jackson and co-authors map gut microbes against diseases and medicines. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Gut microbe links to health are often studied one disease at a time. Results then vary across studies and methods. A single large cohort allows fairer comparisons.

Data came from over 2,700 TwinsUK members. The team tested 38 common diseases. They also tested 51 prescription medicines. Seventeen diseases showed clear microbe links. Some known links were confirmed in the data. Several new links also emerged for testing. Diversity measures showed the widest pattern of links. Readers get a reference chart of relative effects. It can guide future gut microbiome studies in human health.
europmc-pmc6060068:
Rivenson and co-authors use deep learning to rebuild holographic images. Their research article appeared in Light: Science and Applications. Camera sensors record only light intensity, not phase. Phase carries much of an object's fine detail. Classic recovery methods need extra measurements and heavy math.

A trained neural network does the job from one hologram. It restores both phase and amplitude images at once. Twin-image and interference artefacts vanish in the output. Reconstruction takes only a few seconds per field. The team tested blood and Pap smear samples. Thin human tissue sections also reconstructed cleanly. No explicit wave physics was built into the model. The network inferred the patterns from training images. Readers get a fast new route for holographic imaging.
europmc-pmc6060168:
Lipsman and co-authors report an early human test of ultrasound opening of the blood-brain barrier in Alzheimer's disease. Their phase I trial appeared in Nature Communications. The barrier blocks most drugs from reaching the brain. Focused ultrasound with injected microbubbles can open it briefly.

Five patients with early to moderate disease took part. In every patient the barrier opened safely within the target area. It closed again and could be reopened in later sessions. No serious clinical or scan side effects appeared. Thinking scores showed no clear worsening at three months. Amyloid levels showed no group change after treatment. Readers get safety evidence for a new drug delivery route.
europmc-pmc6070868:
Oechslin reviews how bacteria develop resistance during phage therapy. His review appeared in Viruses. Phages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria. Therapy uses them against hard-to-treat infections. Antibiotic resistance drives the renewed interest.

Resistant bacteria emerged in most gut studies reviewed. Half of sepsis model studies saw them too. Three of four human trials recorded resistance. Yet resistance often costs the bacterium fitness. Some mutants lose virulence factors in the trade. The review covers how resistance arises and spreads. It urges monitoring during treatment. Readers also get strategies that turn fitness costs against the pathogen.
europmc-pmc6167468:
Huws and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology on the rumen microbiome and global farm challenges. The rumen, the first stomach of cattle and sheep, holds bacteria, protozoa, fungi, archaea, and phages. Together they break down plant material humans cannot digest. The host gains energy, while archaea release methane.

World population may reach about 9.7 billion by 2050, raising demand for meat and milk. Land is limited and environmental impact must fall. The review traces past and present research on rumen microbes. It argues that understanding this ecosystem can raise production efficiency and cut methane. Future directions for the field are laid out for researchers and industry.
europmc-pmc6254168:
Jäger and co-authors screened plants for a group of potent compounds called pentacyclic triterpenes. Their study appeared in Molecules. These compounds occur in fruit peel, leaves, and stem bark. Three families are named for their ring shapes. Tests show wide effects on the body with low toxicity. That mix makes them strong leads for new multi target drugs.

The team screened thirty-nine plant materials for rich sources. Parts with high levels were turned into dry extracts. The extracts held fifty to ninety percent triterpenes. Birch bark gave betulin, while olive leaves gave oleanolic acid. Apple pomace gave ursolic acid, and rosemary gave a mix of three acids. Such defined extracts can feed new plant based drug products. The work gives makers a sourced and measured starting point.
europmc-pmc6271968:
Ge and co-authors tested whether tiny RNA cargo in blood survives storage. Their study appeared in Molecules. Exosomes are small bubbles cells release into blood. They carry proteins and small RNAs called microRNAs. Those RNAs could serve as disease markers. But samples often sit in storage before testing. No one knew if storage broke the signal.

Plasma samples were stored under varied conditions, then exosomes were isolated. RNA was pulled out and measured with sensitive PCR tests. Exosomal microRNAs held steady across the storage options. Plasma microRNAs also held up, except after short cold storage at four degrees. The result means stored samples can still serve for marker studies. Exosome packaging seems to guard the RNA inside. That stability matters for clinics that bank blood samples.
europmc-pmc6274468:
Calixto and co-authors review nano carriers that deliver light activated cancer drugs. Their review appeared in Molecules. The treatment is photodynamic therapy. A drug settles in the tumour, then light of the right colour activates it. The active drug harms the tumour and its blood supply. Many such drugs dissolve poorly in water, which limits their use.

Loading the drug into nano carriers can fix that flaw. Carriers range from polymer particles and fat based particles to gold particles and gels. They can also help drugs cross cell barriers. Two drugs can ride in one carrier for a joint attack. The review weighs each carrier type for strengths and limits. It maps a fast growing route to stronger cancer care.
europmc-pmc6367568:
Monaco and co-authors present a resource research article in Cell Reports. They profiled 29 immune cell types from healthy donors' blood using RNA sequencing and flow cytometry. Bulk blood data mixes signals from many cell types, which makes results hard to interpret.

The team identified gene sets that mark each cell type and measured how mRNA content differs between types. Normalizing signatures by mRNA abundance let them estimate absolute cell proportions from bulk data. They benchmarked methods and validated the approach in independent cohorts. A free Shiny app, ABIS, applies the method to new datasets. The resource aids research, clinical work, and diagnostics.
europmc-pmc6416168:
The GBD 2016 Epilepsy Collaborators quantify the world burden of epilepsy in The Lancet Neurology. Seizures cause early death and lasting disability. Fair counts of that loss are needed to plan care and spend fairly.

The team assessed 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2016. They measured deaths, cases, and disability-adjusted life-years by age, sex, and place. They also related burden to a development index built from income, schooling, and fertility. Burden fell with development in many places, they report. Gaps in treatment remain widest where burden is highest. Most cases start in childhood or old age.
europmc-pmc6421268:
Parada and co-authors review short-chain fatty acids in bowel disease, in Frontiers in Immunology. These acids form when gut bacteria ferment fiber. Patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis often have fewer of the bacteria that make them.

Acetate, propionate, and butyrate help keep the gut lining calm and sealed. Their levels in stool run low in bowel disease, studies show. The review explains how the acids guide gut and immune cells. It also weighs feeding fiber or acids as a treatment. The gut's Western lifestyle shift frames much of their account.
europmc-pmc6465568:
Dorrington and Fraser review NF-κB signaling in macrophages, the immune cells where this master inflammation pathway matters most and is least modeled. Nearly four decades of research mapped how NF-κB proteins shuttle between cytoplasm and nucleus to start transcription, but most dynamics work used fibroblasts and other non-immune cells. Macrophages may run the same circuit differently.

Cell-type differences in timing and oscillation shape which genes answer a stimulus, and cross-talk with interferon and inflammasome pathways tunes the outcome further. Signals found only in living bacteria, for instance, shift response thresholds. New measurement tools should finally let researchers watch the dynamics inside real immune cells with precision.
europmc-pmc6554968:
Bao and co-authors profile gene activity in breast cancer, writing in Cellular and Molecular Biology Letters. They sequenced the transcriptome of invasive ductal carcinoma and nearby healthy tissue taken from the same six patients. Matching tumor to its own neighbor strips out much of the noise between people.

The comparison found 937 genes with changed activity, 487 raised and 450 lowered. A stricter pass kept 252 genes that shifted the same way in every sample. Follow-up tests in eight more patients confirmed twelve leads, including raised CST2 and SCD and lowered CA4 and PIGR. The standout pathway linked the cell's outer matrix to its receptors, through collagen, fibronectin and the THBS family. Dozens of the genes had not been tied to breast cancer before.
europmc-pmc6600968:
Pina and co-authors survey scaffolding methods for tissue engineering. Their review appears in the journal Materials. Scaffolds are porous frames that guide new tissue as it grows. They can carry cells, genes, or active molecules into a defect. The goal is repair of tissues such as bone, cartilage, skin, and nerves.

The review compares natural polymers, synthetic polymers, and inorganic materials. It also covers hybrids and decellularized tissue. Processing routes range from freeze-drying and electrospinning to 3D printing. Each tissue makes its own demands on pore size and strength. The authors review preclinical trials now under way. They close with open challenges and prospects for regenerative medicine.
europmc-pmc6675068:
Dineen-Griffin and co-authors review self-management support in primary health care. Their systematic review appears in PLoS ONE. Primary care staff are well placed to coach self-care. The team searched three databases for randomised trials. Fifty-eight studies entered the final set. Good support needed a structured swap between patient and clinician. One-on-one meetings anchored that swap. Ongoing follow-up and self-help materials completed it. Plans were tailored to each patient's needs.

Mixed plans worked across many conditions. Building knowledge, tracking symptoms, and action plans featured. Coping skills and owning one's medication helped as well. Gains spanned health markers and quality of life. Confidence and disease control improved too. The authors built a model for practice design.
europmc-pmc6784868:
NCD Risk Factor Collaboration show that rising rural body-mass index drives the global obesity epidemic. Cities were long blamed for the world's weight gain. The team pooled 2,009 population studies with height and weight measures on more than 112 million adults. They tracked mean body-mass index from 1985 to 2017, split by rural and urban residence.

Over 55% of the global rise came from rural areas. In some low- and middle-income regions the share topped 80%. Rural BMI rose as fast as urban BMI, or faster, nearly everywhere. The urban-rural gap has closed or even reversed in poorer countries. Rich countries kept a higher rural BMI all along. Rural nutrition needs urgent attention.
europmc-pmc6851668:
Zimmet and co-authors argue for a new name for a familiar problem, in the Journal of Internal Medicine. The metabolic syndrome groups risk factors such as belly fat, high blood pressure, and raised blood sugar. Together they predict heart disease and type 2 diabetes. What binds the cluster together has long been debated.

The authors point to the body clock. The circadian system steers sleep, hormones, and metabolism across the day. Its disruption links not only to the syndrome's core parts but also to sleep problems and depression that travel with it. They propose renaming the condition the circadian syndrome. That framing, they argue, sharpens recognition and points at causes.
europmc-pmc7067168:
Wang and co-authors announce a new resistance gene in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic against carbapenem-resistant bacteria, and mobile resistance genes that travel on plasmids threaten that last line. The team found a novel gene, mcr-10, on a plasmid in a clinical strain of Enterobacter roggenkampii.

The gene's closest match is mcr-9, at 79.69 percent nucleotide identity, and its protein shares 82.93 percent of amino acids with MCR-9. Cloned into a susceptible strain, mcr-10 raised the colistin dose needed to stop growth fourfold, from 1 to 4 milligrams per litre. Screening GenBank found the gene in several Enterobacter species across four continents, so it has already spread widely. Neighbouring DNA hints it moves by site-specific recombination or as part of a composite transposon. The authors call for immediate monitoring of this new arrival.
europmc-pmc7078068:
Ahmed and co-authors describe an artificial intelligence platform for precision medicine in the journal Database. Precision medicine promises to replace symptom-driven care with earlier, personalised treatment built on deep patient data. Putting it into practice means analysing records with wider population data, and spotting signs that separate health from coming illness. Disease complexity at the single-patient level long blocked that ambition.

The authors argue that electronic health records, once their scattered sources are integrated, can power real-time decision support. Their platform is meant to find patient-specific patterns of disease progression across clinical, laboratory, and public health systems. The paper surveys the analytic tools, databases, and networking needed, plus ethical questions that come with algorithmic care. It also weighs algorithms honestly: some stay accurate with missing data but cost more computation and resist easy explanation. The goal is the base, not a single model.
europmc-pmc7082968:
Castro-Giner and Aceto review circulating tumor cells and their role in cancer spread, in Genome Medicine. These cells break away from a solid tumor and travel in the blood. Studying them offers a liquid biopsy: a blood draw that tracks cancer without cutting tissue.

Single-cell studies show the cells vary widely, and only a fraction can start new tumors. Cells boost their chances by clustering together or teaming up with immune and stromal cells. Counting and analysing them may guide personal treatment choices. Early cancer detection looks harder with these cells than with tumor DNA, a limit the authors state plainly.
europmc-pmc7104368:
de Wit and co-authors tested the antiviral drug remdesivir against MERS coronavirus in rhesus monkeys, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. MERS causes severe lung disease with a case fatality rate near 35%, and earlier candidate treatments had shown limited effect in animals. Remdesivir is a broad-acting antiviral.

Given before infection or after it, remdesivir lessened disease severity, cut virus replication, and reduced lung damage. The results made it a promising candidate for human trials against MERS. The authors also note it may help against related coronaviruses, including the new virus then emerging from Wuhan, China. Animal results of this strength are the usual gate before human testing.
europmc-pmc7170368:
Meng and co-authors report that common blood pressure drugs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, were linked to better outcomes in COVID-19 patients with hypertension, in Emerging Microbes and Infections. These drugs act on the renin-angiotensin system, which the virus's receptor belongs to, raising early fears they might worsen infection. The team compared patients on these drugs with those on other antihypertensives.

Patients on ACE inhibitors or ARBs had a lower rate of severe disease, 23.5% versus 48.0% in the comparison group, though the small sample made the gap statistically uncertain. Their IL-6 inflammation levels trended lower, T cell counts were higher, and peak viral loads lower. The authors read this as support for continuing these medicines.
europmc-pmc7251068:
Vogel and co-authors test whether harmful tau protein spreads through the brain along nerve connections in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Animal work had suggested that tau moves from cell to cell through linked neurons, helped by amyloid-beta. Whether the same happens in people was unproven.

The team ran an epidemic spreading model, which simulates an outbreak moving through a network, and compared its output with tau scan patterns in 312 individuals. The model explained up to 70% of the variance in where tau appeared. It worked whether or not amyloid was present, though areas with more amyloid held more tau than connectivity alone predicted. The results support spread through communication pathways, sped up by amyloid.
europmc-pmc7255168:
Marijon and co-authors examine out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in Paris during the first COVID-19 lockdown weeks. Their population study appeared in The Lancet Public Health. Cardiac arrest outside a hospital is often fatal, and the pandemic changed daily life, emergency care, and hospital routines all at once. The team used the Paris Fire Brigade database, kept since 2011.

Over a 6-week period from March 16 to April 26, 2020, 521 arrests were recorded. The peak weekly rate reached 26.64 per million inhabitants, roughly double the 13.42 seen in the same weeks of earlier years. More arrests happened at home, fewer bystanders gave resuscitation, and the share of patients admitted alive fell from 22.8% to 12.8%. Rates returned toward normal in the final weeks.
europmc-pmc7261168:
Cabello-Aguilar and co-authors present SingleCellSignalR, a tool that infers how cells signal to each other. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Single-cell RNA data can show which cells are present in a tissue. It does not by itself show which cells talk to which. Much of that talk uses secreted ligands binding to receptors on other cells.

The tool pairs gene data with a curated database of 3,251 ligand-receptor pairs. A new regularized score rates likely links while keeping false positives down. Results come as tables, graphs and a full network view. The package is free in R. A test on mouse skin found signals flowing from outer to basal layers.
europmc-pmc7306068:
Ogunrinola and co-authors review the human microbiome and its effects on health. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Microbiology. Bacteria, archaea, viruses, and other organisms live on and inside every body site, each community adapted to its niche. Oxygen-loving microbes dominate skin and airways, while the gut favors species that thrive without oxygen.

These residents help run metabolism and immunity, and long coexistence has tuned them to the immune system. When the community shifts out of balance, a state called dysbiosis, the host becomes more open to infection, with the damage depending on the site involved. Lifestyle and underlying disease drive many such shifts. Understanding each site's microbes and their activities, the authors argue, is basic to understanding health itself.
europmc-pmc7314768:
Kneller and co-authors solve the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease at room temperature, revealing how flexible its drug-binding pocket is. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The protease, called 3CL Mpro, cuts the virus's long polyproteins into working pieces, making it an attractive antiviral target. Most known structures were frozen at low temperature with drugs attached.

The new structure shows the empty active site as it sits near body temperature. Comparing it with cold and drug-bound versions shows the cavity changes shape more than expected, a property called structural plasticity. Drug hunters who dock candidate molecules into a rigid cold structure may be misled. A realistic warm template, the authors argue, gives more relevant guidance for designing inhibitors.
europmc-pmc7322868:
Liu and co-authors test whether exosomes from melatonin-treated stem cells heal diabetic wounds better than ordinary ones. Their study appeared in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. Wounds in diabetic patients stall in the inflammation stage and can end badly, with few effective treatments. Exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells were already known candidates for their anti-inflammatory cargo.

Pretreating the stem cells with melatonin strengthened the effect. In cell tests, the treated exosomes cut the inflammatory factors IL-1beta and TNF-alpha and raised the calming factor IL-10. They also shifted macrophages from their inflammatory M1 state toward the reparative M2 state, through the PTEN and AKT pathway. Animal studies, including a diabetic wound model, confirmed faster, better-organized healing with more collagen and new tissue markers.
europmc-pmc7503568:
Kantor, McClements, and MacLaren review CRISPR base-editing and prime-editing for DNA correction. Many genetic diseases stem from single base-pair changes. Base editors can install point changes without cutting both DNA strands.

Two editor classes exist so far: cytosine base editors and adenine base editors. Prime editing widens the range to all small swaps plus tiny insertions and deletions. Safe delivery to the right cells is the chief hurdle for therapy. Adeno-associated virus leads as a carrier, thanks to its broad reach and low immune profile. The review traces how each editor grew and where each falls short. It weighs their promise for treating hard genetic diseases. Precision without donor DNA is the shared gain.
europmc-pmc7593768:
Nguyen and co-authors review localized delivery of interleukin-12 for cancer immunotherapy. IL-12 is a strong pro-inflammatory cytokine signal. It showed striking anti-tumor effects in early lab models.

Human trials in the mid-1990s hit dose-limiting toxicity. Systemic delivery caused severe side effects in patients. Interest stayed high due to its many immune effects. It can also reverse tumor-driven immune suppression. Local delivery aims drug at the tumor site. That limits whole-body exposure and harm risk. Methods range from fusion proteins to nanoparticles. Several local approaches have now reached clinical testing. The review weighs gains and limits of each method.
europmc-pmc7603668:
Pearson and co-authors give guidance for feasibility and pilot studies before implementation trials. Such early studies can test and refine delivery plans. They help clear doubts about design and methods.

The guidance covers aims, methods and study design. It also covers measures, progress rules and reporting. The team reviewed current advice for pilot work. They used a hybrid trial framework for structure. Early work can gauge likely strategy effects in settings. It can also reveal how a strategy might work. Progression criteria help judge when to scale up. Reporting standards for these studies are set out. The paper serves teams planning larger implementation trials in health care.
europmc-pmc7676268:
Klein and co-authors image SARS-CoV-2 as it builds new copies inside cells. They used cryo-electron tomography, which gives 3D views of virus structures in place. The virus copies itself in sacs and assembles at inner membranes. Much of this process had not been seen direct.

The team saw RNA strands inside the double-membrane sacs where copying occurs. They report that spike clusters do not bend membranes alone. Instead, spikes shift sideways during assembly, and genome bundles gather at curved bud sites. The bundles form distinct rod-like units. The authors propose the genome packs around many such units for flex.
europmc-pmc7824368:
Linardatos and co-authors review methods that make machine learning models explainable. AI systems now beat humans at many tasks. Their growing complexity turned them into black boxes. Users cannot see how a decision is reached. That opacity blocks use in touchy fields like health care.

Explainable AI aims to open the box. The authors survey the interpretability methods on offer. They sort the methods into a clear taxonomy. Links to working code implementations are included. Fairness and sensitivity concerns get their own treatment. The survey is meant as a reference for builders and theorists alike. Trust in automated decisions is the end goal.
europmc-pmc7826868:
Syafrudin and co-authors review pesticides in drinking water and ways to remove them. Farm and city use washes pesticides into rivers and groundwater. Rain carries soluble forms down through soil. These chemicals build up in water life and sediments. Long exposure at low levels harms human health.

Standard treatment shifts pollutants from one phase to another. Such methods cost a lot to run. They can also leave sludge behind. Advanced oxidation processes offer a cleaner route. These methods break stubborn pollutants down in place. The authors weigh how well each approach works. Their aim is safer supplies of drinking water.
europmc-pmc7830668:
Apostolopoulos and co-authors give a global review of short peptides and their medical promise. Peptides are short protein fragments. They carry signals through all forms of life. They also block or mimic protein contacts. The review marks 100 years of peptide therapy since insulin began in the 1920s.

Writers came from every continent for this survey. Early peptide drugs only replaced missing hormones. Modern ones cross cell membranes and hit inside targets. The review weighs strengths and weak points of short peptides. It covers better synthesis methods and nano delivery tricks. Computer design and smart materials feature as well. Disease uses range widely across the sections. The authors map what blocks wider use and what may clear those blocks.
europmc-pmc7870668:
Ozono and co-authors show that the D614G spike change helps SARS-CoV-2 enter cells more easily. The virus keeps mutating as it spreads. Spike changes can alter entry through ACE2. Whether they did so was unknown. The team tested natural spike variants.

A test virus with the parent spike entered cells poorly. The D614G form entered best of all variants tried. Shape and binding tests explained the gain. The changed spike grips ACE2 more tightly. Patient sera still neutralized it just as well, though. Entry gain thus came without immune escape. The authors call for world tracking of such changes. Spread risk turns on traits like this one.
europmc-pmc7905668:
Kosiol and co-authors present a review of G-quadruplexes as a target for cancer therapy. DNA and RNA can fold into shapes beyond the classic helix. One shape, the G-quadruplex, forms in guanine-rich stretches. It appears in most human cancer gene promoters and at chromosome ends. Those sites make it a tempting drug target.

Forming these shapes can also destabilise the genome. It can drive mutations, deletions, and harmful reshuffling. In breast cancer samples, more shape formation tracked with more varied tumours. Drugs called G4 ligands aim to lock the shapes in place. That can shut down cancer gene activity or block chromosome-end growth. The authors compare the approach across pancreatic cancer, leukemia, and melanoma. They frame it as a route to treatment matched to each tumour.
europmc-pmc7946268:
Moodie presents a study of head tumours among pre-Columbian Peruvians, part of his paleopathology series. The paper first sets the age of the material. Human life in South America spans hundreds, or at most a few thousand, years. Against the deep ages of the Old Stone Age, these Peruvians are recent. Their record still offers rich evidence of disease in bone.

Tumours of the head form the core of the study. Moodie describes the lesions found in the ancient skulls. He weighs what kinds of growth they may represent. The setting matters too: the rise of Peruvian civilisations frames when these people lived. The paper shows how much a careful reading of bone can say. It adds a chapter to the long history of cancer in the Americas.
europmc-pmc8010168:
Huang and co-authors show that two coronaviruses sharing one cell receptor enter cells by different routes. Both SARS coronavirus and human coronavirus NL63 use the ACE2 receptor. The team asked whether lysosomal proteases also play a part. Such enzymes help some other viruses infect cells. The experiments used both live viruses and retroviruses carrying each spike protein.

The authors report that SARS-CoV needs the enzyme cathepsin L to infect ACE2-bearing cells. Drugs that block cathepsin L stopped SARS-CoV infection cold. Adding extra cathepsin L sharply boosted it. NL63 needed none of this help. A drug that blocks endosomal acidification also hit SARS-CoV far harder. One receptor, two distinct doors into the cell.
europmc-pmc8046668:
Platten and co-authors report a first-in-humans vaccine trial against mutant IDH1 in newly diagnosed glioma. The IDH1(R132H) mutation defines a distinct glioma subtype. It creates a shared neoantigen shown on immune display molecules. A peptide vaccine had already worked in humanized mice. The multicentre phase I trial enrolled 33 patients. All had grade 3 or 4 astrocytomas carrying the mutation.

The trial met its primary safety endpoint. Vaccine-related side effects stayed at grade 1. Immune responses appeared in 93.3% of patients, across many immune types. Three-year progression-free survival reached 0.63, and death-free survival 0.84. Patients who responded immunologically did better still. Two patients without a response progressed within two years. Swelling that mimicked tumor growth, called pseudoprogression, was common and signaled inflammation.
europmc-pmc8101968:
Musuuza and co-authors pool the evidence on extra infections riding along with COVID-19. Some patients catch a second pathogen at diagnosis, a co-infection.
