Others pick one up later in care, a superinfection. Reports varied wildly, so the team screened 6,639 articles. A set of 118 studies fed the pooled analysis. Both hospitalized and outpatients counted in the data.

Co-infection showed a pooled prevalence of 19% across the studies. Superinfection ran higher, at 24% of patients in the pool. Bacteria led the later infections, viruses the early ones. Either kind of add-on infection raised the stakes sharply. Patients with one had over three times the odds of dying. Superinfection patients needed breathing machines far more often, 45% against 10% in the co-infection group. The authors urge routine testing for companion infections. Finding and treating them early could save lives.
europmc-pmc8103168:
Tirichen and co-authors trace how mitochondrial reactive oxygen species drive chronic kidney disease onward. Mitochondria make roughly 90% of a cell's reactive oxygen species. When output outruns the antioxidant defenses, oxidative stress builds. Lipids, DNA, and proteins all take damage. The kidney burns huge amounts of energy to do its work. That workload leaves it exposed to exactly this harm.

Chronic kidney disease affects about 11 to 13% of the world's people by common estimates. Diabetes and high blood pressure feed most cases. The review follows the stress signals through the kidney's decline. Failing filtration, tissue scarring, and cell death all link back to oxidant load. Marker studies show damage products rising as kidney function falls. Antioxidant enzymes fall in the same patients. Breaking that loop is the therapeutic hope. Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants get a close look.
europmc-pmc8113168:
Ceci and co-authors deliver the E-PSMA reporting guidelines for PSMA-PET scans in prostate cancer. The scan targets a protein that prostate tumors display in rich amounts. Over 90% of prostate cancer cells carry it on their surface. Use of the scan has spread fast, but reports vary by reader. A worldwide panel of imaging experts was convened. They worked through a modified Delphi process to settle shared wording.

The product is a structured report for everyday practice. It fixes how findings are located, graded, and phrased. Referring doctors get the same terms from every center. Trial data become easier to compare across sites. The European Association of Nuclear Medicine backs the document. Standard words, the panel argues, lead to standard care. Ambiguous reports leave treatment choices hanging. This template aims to end that drift. Updates can follow as the field learns more.
europmc-pmc8139668:
Voloch and co-authors report a novel SARS-CoV-2 lineage found in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The team sequenced 180 complete genomes gathered between April and November 2020. Thirty-seven of those samples formed a lineage nobody had named. The lineage, classed P.2, descends from an earlier Brazilian strain. Five mutations define it against its parent. One of them, E484K, sits in the spike protein. That change was already drawing watchful eyes elsewhere.

A wider tree placed the new genomes among 1,197 global comparison sequences. Brazilian genomes concentrated in three clades, holding 86.8% of them in the team's reconstruction. The lineage's emergence dates to about July 2020 by their clock. Across the 180 genomes they counted 731 single-nucleotide variants in all. Most changed the proteins the virus builds. A homegrown lineage with a watched spike change demanded tracking. Brazil's epidemic was evolving on its own branch.
europmc-pmc8305868:
Quagliariello and co-authors test empagliflozin against doxorubicin heart damage in mice. Empagliflozin blocks the sodium glucose co-transporter 2. It cut heart failure admissions in diabetic patients in a landmark trial.

Newer trials hint at heart and kidney gains beyond diabetes. The team dosed non-diabetic mice with the cancer drug doxorubicin. They measured heart strain, fibrosis, and inflammatory cytokines. Cell work on mouse heart cells came first. The NLRP3 inflammasome and MyD88 paths were tracked. Empagliflozin improved strain and cut fibrosis signs. The study probes how a diabetes drug shields the heart.
europmc-pmc8348168:
Yamamoto, Kawada, and Obama examine inflammation markers that forecast outcomes in colorectal cancer. This cancer ranks among the top causes of cancer death. Finding high-risk patients lets doctors treat harder where it counts.

Routine blood tests yield several such markers. They include the neutrophil-lymphocyte and platelet-lymphocyte ratios. Lymphocyte ratios with C-reactive protein or monocytes also serve. Scoring systems add albumin to blood cell counts. The review weighs each marker's record. Cheap, standard tests could guide surgery and chemotherapy choices. The authors sort which scores hold up best. Routine blood work makes these markers cheap to obtain.
europmc-pmc8423468:
Han and co-authors follow how lifestyle shapes heart and metabolic disease in a large Chinese cohort. The path from health to a first disease, then to several diseases at once, then to death was unclear. Each step may respond to habits in its own way.

The study used the China Kadoorie Biobank, with 461,047 adults aged 30 to 79 years. All were free of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes at the start. Over a median follow-up of about 11 years, 87,687 people developed at least one such disease. Five high-risk habits played strong but distinct roles at each step. Smoking, heavy drinking, poor diet, inactivity, and unhealthy body shape all counted.
europmc-pmc8482768:
Dey and co-authors give a state-of-the-art review of halide perovskite nanocrystals. These materials rose fast as a star of modern materials science. They shine brightly, are easy to make as tiny crystals, and have tunable optical traits. Uses span solar cells, light devices, and photocatalysis.

Experts from chemistry, physics, and device work joined for this survey. It covers shape-controlled synthesis first. It then explains the crystals' optical and electronic behavior. Applications across fields are weighed in turn. The authors close with prospects for the field. The review aims to serve as the standard entry point for new researchers. It also maps open problems for veterans.
europmc-pmc8578868:
Martínez-García and Hernández-Lemus give an overview of gum inflammation and its links to body-wide disease. Periodontitis is a common infectious inflammation that often turns chronic. Beyond the mouth, it can grow into a systemic state. That state shows as unresolved high inflammation and a disturbed immune system.

Microbe balance shifts in the mouth, gut, and other sites as part of the picture. Such changes can cause, ride with, or worsen other diseases. The ties between these layers are still debated, though. The authors gather biological, clinical, and policy evidence in one frame. Their systemic view aims to serve basic research, clinic work, and therapy design.
europmc-pmc8807768:
Rao and co-authors review the hippocampus and its involvement in Alzheimer disease. This brain region is crucial for learning and memory. Its sub-regions help build episodic memories of events. It is also among the first areas the disease attacks.

In early disease, the hippocampus loses tissue fast. It also disconnects from other brain regions. Shrinkage of this area serves as a marker on brain scans. Loss of a protective protein in its neurons impairs memory and spatial learning. New neuron growth in the region depends on local support cells and lifestyle. Diet and activity may delay decline, the authors note.
europmc-pmc8881768:
Tordoff and co-authors follow mental health in transgender and nonbinary youths receiving gender-affirming care. These youths face high rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidality. Social rejection and stigma drive much of that burden. Clinics now offer puberty blockers and gender-affirming hormones. How mental health shifts right after care starts was less known. This cohort study tracked that first year.

The final sample held 104 youths aged 13 to 20 years. Surveys ran at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months. At the start, only 7 youths had received blockers or hormones. By the study's end, 69 had received one or both. The authors compared depression, anxiety, and suicidality scores across that span. They weighed care receipt against symptom change over time. The study informs a heated policy debate with direct data.
europmc-pmc8930768:
Keeton and co-authors test whether T cells raised against earlier virus forms still recognize Omicron. Antibodies fade against Omicron's mutated spike. T cells might hold the line instead. The team studied 70 people. Some had one of two vaccines. Others had recovered from COVID-19 unvaccinated. They measured CD4 and CD8 T cell responses to Omicron spike. Responses to Beta and Delta served as comparisons.

Most of the T cell response survived the variant switch. Between 70% and 80% of spike response was maintained. Omicron cross-reactivity matched that for Beta and Delta. This held despite Omicron's far larger mutation count. Hospitalized Omicron patients showed solid responses too. Their T cells answered spike, nucleocapsid, and membrane proteins. Levels matched patients from earlier waves. The authors say T cell immunity stays largely intact. That may help explain milder outcomes.
europmc-pmc8938268:
Gao and co-authors show that T cells built against the original SARS-CoV-2 still cross-recognize Omicron. The variant escapes many neutralizing antibodies. Severe disease, though, stayed relatively uncommon in immune people. T cells were the prime suspect for that protection. The team measured spike-specific T cells in two groups. One had prior infection. The other had Pfizer vaccination. Cross-recognition of Omicron was the test.

Recognition stayed extensive in both groups. Median cross-reactive CD4 cells held at 84% after infection. After vaccination they held at 91%. CD8 cells held at 70% and 92%. The responding cells looked alike in function and type. They answered ancestral and Omicron spike similarly. The authors conclude T cell memory survives the variant. Vaccination left the stronger CD8 coverage. The findings support T cells as a shield against severe disease.
europmc-pmc8970668:
Wensel, Pluznick, Salzberg, and Sears explain how new sequencing tools can sharpen clinical studies of the microbiome. Sequencing finds microbes that lab culture misses. It can even hint at what those microbes do. Three methods anchor the field. Marker gene sequencing reads one gene. Shotgun methods read all the DNA at once. RNA sequencing reads active genes. Which one fits a study is often unclear. This review lays out the basics in plain form.

Each method's strengths and weak points sit side by side. The authors treat data noise with candor. Study design and rich patient data are stressed. Poor design ruins costly data, they warn. Case examples show sequencing at work in real diseases. Gut, metabolic, and cancer cases all feature. New tests and drugs grew from some of them. The authors close with how the tools may join routine research and care.
europmc-pmc9113368:
Goel and Schneeberger present plotsr, a tool that draws structural differences between multiple genomes. New sequencing methods now yield many high-quality genome assemblies for one species. Comparing them calls for clear pictures of shared regions and rearrangements. Plotsr fills that gap for chromosome-level and local views alike.

The tool uses synteny to match chromosomes and align regions across genomes. Users can zoom into any chosen region for a closer look. Plots can add gene labels, markers, or histogram tracks for traits like GC content. The package is written in Python and uses the standard matplotlib library. It is free under the MIT license. Genome researchers get a flexible way to show large-scale change.
europmc-pmc9238168:
Paskeh and co-authors review the emerging role of exosomes in cancer progression and tumor surroundings. Exosomes are tiny structures, about 100 nm across, that carry proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids between cells. Their cargo can either promote or suppress tumor growth. That dual power makes them a hot research topic.

The review shows how exosomes reshape the tumor microenvironment and sway cancer cell growth and migration. They can raise or lower response to radiation and chemotherapy. They also trigger chronic inflammation and help tumors evade immunity, in part by moving non-coding RNAs. Uses as drug carriers and as diagnostic tools get full sections. Readers get a complete picture of exosome value in cancer care.
europmc-pmc9246368:
Sun and co-authors generate vascularized brain organoids to study how vessels and brain tissue interact. Brain organoids model development and disease, but they lack blood vessels. That gap limits their use, since vessels regulate neuron growth and brain disorders. The team grew vessel and brain organoids separately, then fused them.

The fused organoids held strong vessel-like networks and more neural progenitors. They also formed working blood-brain barrier-like structures. Microglia, the brain's own immune cells, were present as well. Those microglia reacted to immune stimuli and engulfed synapses. The authors say the fused system models links between neuronal and non-neuronal parts. It opens a window on the vessel and microglia niche in vitro.
europmc-pmc9288068:
Weng and co-authors review immunotherapy for metastatic colorectal cancer. Chemotherapy with targeted drugs remains the base treatment, but gains have stalled. Immune checkpoint blockade can give lasting responses, yet it helps only a small share of patients. Benefit is mostly limited to tumors with high microsatellite instability.

The review covers how checkpoint drugs work and why most colorectal tumors resist them. Tumor repair defects create new antigens that draw strong T cell attack. Only about 15% of colorectal cancers, and 4% of metastatic ones, carry that trait. Markers that predict benefit are listed and weighed. Key trial results are gathered in one place. New basic findings close the survey, with an eye to widening who benefits.
europmc-pmc9300468:
Delaunay and co-authors show that mitochondrial RNA marks control the energy flexibility that lets cancers spread. Two marks, made by the enzyme NSUN3, sit on a mitochondrial transfer RNA. They are needed to build parts of the cell's main energy chain. The team studied human oral cancer cells lacking these marks.

Cells without the marks shifted toward glycolysis but stayed alive, and primary tumors still grew. Spread, however, failed badly in living animals. A set of quiet, spread-starting tumor cells needed the marks to invade. A mitochondria-driven gene pattern in patients predicted spread and worse disease course. Blocking mitochondrial protein building in animals hit the same switch. The authors propose these marks as drug targets against metastasis.
europmc-pmc9902068:
Mahindru and co-authors review how physical activity affects mental health and well-being. Inactive people face higher illness rates and higher health care costs. Exercise therapy is often advised to protect mental wellness. Studies link activity to stronger self-concept and body image in nonclinical groups.

The review covers body systems behind the effect, including the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis. Exercise appears to ease depression and anxiety, with stronger gains in clinical patients. It also aids sleep and lifts mood and quality of life. Yoga and exercise may help manage substance cravings. The authors note sparse research in the Indian setting. They call for activity programs shaped to that context.
europmc-pmc9990368:
Xie and co-authors review cuproptosis, a copper-driven form of cell death, and its links to cancer. Cuproptosis is distinct from other known death forms. Its mechanism was only recently revealed after long debate. Interest in its cancer role has grown fast since then.

The review details copper metabolism at body and cell levels. Copper-linked tumor signaling pathways are set out next. The discovery story and core mechanism of cuproptosis follow. Links between this death route and varied cancers are outlined. The authors highlight copper ion carriers that trigger cuproptosis. Combined with small-molecule drugs, they may form targeted treatments. The work gives a systematic base for a young research field.
frus-1861-d168:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 July 1861. The dispatch is document 168 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Perry's July report kept Madrid covered while the legation's work grew. Summer brought heat, slow mails, and steady court routine. His letter is one of the staff papers that gave the Spanish file its unbroken run through 1861. The unbroken run of staff papers is the quiet strength of the Spanish file. An unbroken run of papers is what lets a reader trust a file's whole tale. Trust in a file grows from unbroken runs.
frus-1861-d268:
Guidance for James Shepherd Pike left Washington on 11 November 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 268 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d68:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1861. The dispatch is document 68 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams reported a London that had begun to doubt the Union would win. Doubt was dangerous, since it fed calls to step in and end the war. His mid August letter let Seward see that risk plain, from the one post where it could turn real. Doubt in London was the seed of every scheme for mediation that year. Mediation schemes died that year because Adams met each one early and square.
frus-1862-d168:
The second of three Seward letters dated 25 October 1862 appears as Document 168 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, whose talks with Earl Russell shaped British dealings with the Union.

By late October, France was urging Britain to join it in proposing a truce in the American war. London had not yet agreed. Washington's mail in this window, this letter included. Fed Adams the facts and the tone he needed while the two European powers sounded each other out. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d268:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 17 April 1862 in a letter printed as Document 268 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton reported while French troops in Mexico marched toward Puebla, where they would meet a famous defeat on 5 May. His court's Mexican venture shaped its American policy in ways Washington worked to map. A report like this one, written between great events, shows the envoy's daily craft: listening, noting, and judging what an emperor's government might do next. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d368:
F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State. He wrote to Henri Mercier on 12 June 1862, in a letter printed as Document 368 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Frederick William Seward was the Secretary's son and deputy.

When the assistant signed, business moved at the working level while the Secretary's hand stayed in reserve. The French channel saw such letters whenever the matter was routine or the Secretary was pressed. This June note shows the Department's second rank keeping a major channel in motion during a crowded summer. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d468:
On 13 January 1862 George Perkins Marsh reported from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward, a week after his previous dispatch. The report is Document 468 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Weekly reporting was Marsh's habit, and his Turin letters mixed Italian politics with the war's reception in the new kingdom. In January 1862 Italy was settling its place among the powers while watching whether the American republic would split in two. Marsh, a scholar by trade, wrote with unusual care about what he saw. His reports helped Seward count Italy among the Union's sincere well-wishers, a small but cheering fact in a winter of hard news.
frus-1862-d568:
On 2 September 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford wrote from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 568 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Sanford wrote a fortnight before Antietam, while Lee's invasion of Maryland was still news in the making in Europe. His Brussels vantage caught the anxiety of the smaller courts, which feared a long war and French ambition in equal measure. Reports from such posts helped Seward decide that the danger of intervention, though real, was not yet ripe. The dispatch is a small piece of the evidence on which that judgment rested. It was filed from a minor capital. The minister who filed it missed very little.
frus-1862-d668:
Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 November 1861. Burlingame had taken up the post that year, based with the other foreign envoys in China. The letter is document 668 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

From China, an envoy's mail told Washington about trade, the treaty ports, and the acts of the Qing court. Burlingame's reports also watched how Britain and France dealt with China, since their moves shaped his own work. This early letter opens his file in the volume. It starts a run that shows the United States at work in East Asia during the Civil War.
frus-1862-d68:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 22 May 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 68 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d168:
On 24 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 168 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three he sent that day.

The middle sheet of Adams's sets often held the day's meat. On 24 April there was meat enough: the ships, the law, and the talk of London all in flux. This letter holds the center of his three. With the two Seward sheets of the same date nearby in the volume, the day is one of the fullest in the printed record. It tells the war abroad in a single date.
frus-1863p1-d268:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 August 1863, and it is document 268 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d368: On 22 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 368 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d468:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 17 April 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d568:
Writing on 17 June 1863, Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington addressed William H. Seward, the Secretary of State in an official letter. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d668:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely.
frus-1863p1-d68:
On 30 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 68 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It bears the same date as an Adams dispatch printed just before it.

Same dates on both sides of the file are a quirk of the sea mail. Each man wrote from the last news he had, weeks old. Seward's letter set out Washington's line for the points then live in London. It is part of the close weave of the exchange. Orders and reports crossed on the ocean and still, in time, formed one clear talk.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d168: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull in Moscow on October 26, 1943, in a letter placed by the editors in the Moscow section as Document 168 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It shares its date and its parties with a second such letter, and the pair belongs to the conference's closing week. The record gives no subject for either. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series with the Moscow papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d268: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers a Cairo meeting of November 1943 for which no official record of the substance has been found. What the editors know of the meeting and its participants comes from the President's Log, with a cross-reference to a later page of the volume. One outside source adds a single detail: in Elliott Roosevelt's account, the principal subject of conversation at the meeting was supply.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d368:
Charles Bohlen's minutes, the third set for 29 November 1943, record the dinner that evening at half past eight. They are less a record of decisions than of mood, and their most notable feature, Bohlen writes, was Stalin's manner toward Churchill.

Stalin kept a sharp edge on nearly every remark to the Prime Minister while staying entirely friendly. He teased him over Overlord. He implied a secret liking for the Germans and a wish for a soft peace. He spoke frankly of the Red Army's poor showing against Finland and its slow climb to a genuinely good army. On Germany he set two conditions: the physical liquidation of at least fifty thousand, perhaps a hundred thousand, of the German commanding staff, and Allied retention of the world's strong points. Roosevelt joked the figure down to forty-nine thousand; Churchill objected fiercely to cold-blooded execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d468:
Reginald Leeper, the British ambassador to the Greek government-in-exile in Egypt, wrote to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden on December 3, 1943. Greece was under German occupation, and its exiled government worked from Cairo. The catalog heading misspells “government,” but the parties are clear. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Leeper spoke for London to a restless exile government whose country was a battleground of resistance groups and rival claims. His reports to Eden fed British decisions about Greece at a moment when Cairo hosted both the exile court and the Allied conference. The message opens a window on the war's tangled Greek question.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d568:
Ambassador Averell Harriman recorded this memorandum on November 13, 1944, in Moscow. Harriman's memoranda often preserved his conversations and judgments about the Soviet leadership for the record in Washington. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By late 1944 Harriman's tone about Moscow was hardening: the cooperation promised at Tehran was meeting the facts of Soviet power in Poland and the Balkans. His written record from this season is a key source for the alliance's turn toward friction. For readers, the memorandum shows the ambassador setting down, carefully and on paper, what a year of dealing with Stalin's government had taught him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d68: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 29, 1943, and a second Churchill note of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 68 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The last days of October were a summing-up season after Moscow and a planning season before Cairo. The catalog record gives the date and the names only. The text in the Foreign Relations series carries its errand.
frus-1944-quebec-d168:
An editors' note introduces the document printed next in the volume, the President's Log for the Quebec Conference. The Log was a booklet covering September 9 to 21, 1944, prepared by Lieutenant William Rigdon and approved by Rear Admiral Wilson Brown. The note describes its contents in detail, from the list of the president's party to the conference communiqué in an appendix.

The editors also compare the Log's party list with the one in Rigdon's later book, White House Sailor. Three names appear only in the book, and seven only in the Log, including Henry Morgenthau. Morgenthau's inclusion is explained: he accompanied Roosevelt from Washington to Hyde Park before being summoned to Quebec. The note is a small lesson in how the volume checks its own sources.
frus-1944-quebec-d268:
A draft directive to Admiral Mountbatten is proposed in C.C.S. 452/28, the British Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. His primary object would be the recapture of all Burma at the earliest date. That object must not prejudice the security of the air supply route to China, including the staging post at Myitkyina, whose protection was essential throughout.

Approved operations were the stages of Operation Capital needed for the air route, and Operation Dracula, the seaborne stroke at Rangoon. The chiefs attached the greatest importance to executing Dracula before the 1945 monsoon, with a target date of March 15. If it slipped past the monsoon, Capital would be exploited while Dracula was prepared for November 1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d68:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. Stettinius remained in Washington while the leaders met in Canada. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

An opening-day memorandum from Washington shows the home government keeping pace with a traveling summit: positions restated, information supplied, and the department's interests guarded from a distance. Stettinius was also guarding the newborn United Nations project agreed at Dumbarton Oaks. For readers, the paper marks the State Department's parallel work while the conference ran.
frus-1945-50-intel-d168:
Dated 6 September 1946, this letter runs from the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) to the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy). It survives in print as document 168 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d268:
A memorandum by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group, Central Intelligence Agency (Cassady) bears the date 1 May 1948. The State Department prints it as document 268 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d368:
A memorandum from Daniel DeBardeleben reached the Acting Deputy Assistant Director for Special Operations, Central Intelligence Agency on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 368 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d68:
Byrnes, Royall, and Forrestal wrote jointly to President Truman on 7 January 1946. Three cabinet secretaries, State, War, and Navy, signed one letter to the president. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A joint letter from the three secretaries told Truman the departments had settled their fight and were ready for his order. Such unity is rare, and presidents act fast when they see it. Readers have arrived at the climax of the volume's first act: five months of memoranda, committees, and turf wars compressed into one agreed paper. The directive that followed on 22 January bears the shape these three men, with the Budget Bureau's help, had given it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d168:
Who really ran the armistice commissions in the Balkan capitals? This briefing book paper states the American position on the Allied Control Commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commissions mirror the Allied Commission in Italy, the paper explains, but with the leading role reversed: Russia leads, as Britain and America lead in Italy. Rumania's body works under rules drawn up by the Soviet government. Washington has not objected to Soviet officers running the day-to-day work while Germany still fights. But orders to local governments must not go out in the commission's name without prior word to the other members. Otherwise the United States is tied in public to acts it never saw.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d268:
Stalin surprised Churchill on war criminals at Moscow, and this excerpt of 22 October 1944 tells how. Paragraph five of message number 801 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet leader took what Churchill calls an unexpectedly ultra-respectable line.

There must be no executions without trial, Stalin held. Otherwise the world would say the allies were afraid to try the accused. Churchill pointed out the difficulties in international law. Stalin answered that if there were no trials, there must be no death sentences either, only lifelong confinement. Faced with that view from that quarter, Churchill tells Roosevelt, he will not press the memorandum he had given him. He asks that it be treated as withdrawn.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d368:
Matthews caught the money talk in pencil at the foreign ministers' session of February 7, 1945. His rough notes move from dismemberment to reparations. On a study commission, Molotov proposed Eden, Winant, and Gusev. Eden worried about France's absence, since France was Germany's neighbor. The three, he argued, could decide French participation themselves.

Then Ivan Maisky explained the Soviet reparations figures. Half would come at once, half in yearly payments. He set Germany's prewar national wealth at 125 billion, cut by war losses. From the mobile part, ten billion might be removed as a first payment. The shorthand shows how the famous reparations demand was built.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d468:
Victory by cable: Stettinius reported home in this top secret message to Grew of February 11, 1945. The conference had agreed on the American proposal on voting procedure. America would consult China and France on behalf of the other two powers. The United Nations conference was fixed for April 25, 1945, at San Francisco.

The communiqué, out Monday night for Tuesday's papers, would announce the substance. It would not itself say the voting plan was America's. But Washington was free, at the same moment, to state that the adopted proposal was the United States one. The wire shows the deal and the credit arranged together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d68:
Readers opening the Malta and Yalta volume meet this editorial note before the documents of late 1944. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States explain why the volume reaches back months before the conferences themselves. Many papers printed here date from the mid-autumn of 1944.

The note says the chapter gathers key documents showing where each main subject stood before the talks. Those subjects were the problems later discussed at Malta and Yalta, and each paper shows the position the United States had taken. The editors add that the military talks had a set agenda, while the political talks did not, and that fuller coverage would wait for later volumes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d168:
Only a fragment of President Truman's June 25, 1945 message to Stalin is printed as document 168 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The extract, sent from Olympia, Washington, concerns the Belgrade agreement on Venezia Giulia, the disputed territory around Trieste that Yugoslav and Allied forces both claimed.

The surviving lines close the message. Truman tells Stalin that if any further aspect of the agreement should be considered, they will have a chance to discuss it at their early meeting. The full text appears elsewhere in the volume. Even this scrap shows the President's habit of steering hard questions toward the summit table, where the three leaders could deal with them face to face rather than by cable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d268:
A briefing paper weighed Austria's provisional government in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 268 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the recognition of an Austrian government acceptable to all the Allied powers, an item on the American agenda.

Moscow set up Karl Renner's provisional government in Vienna in April without consulting its allies, the paper notes, a one-sided act hard to square with joint action. Yet the Renner government is, in its men and its spread of parties, as good a coalition as could be devised, the paper concedes. One worry stands out: the interior ministry, which controls the police, sits in Communist hands, and so does public instruction. The paper balances acceptance of Renner against the precedent of letting one power install governments alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d368:
Two State Department officials, Collado and Despres, drafted substitute wording on July 7, 1945, for a telegram to Pauley in Moscow. Their paragraph backs the heart of his formula for dividing reparations. The major powers, it says, would settle their own collective share among themselves, without fixing the split with the other allies before consulting them.

The draft also agrees that naming France a major power in the formula raises the sharpest difficulties, since France sat outside the talks. A closing thought notes America's odd position: its direct war damage was relatively small, even though the resources it poured into the war were vast.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d468:
Italy's ambassador calls on Grew in a memorandum of conversation dated July 6, 1945, filed under the subject of a declaration of war against Japan. Ambassador Tarchiani left with Grew a letter addressed to the President. It enclosed a memorandum setting out the present position of Italy, and her vital needs and aspirations.

Knowing how occupied the President must be at this particular moment, Tarchiani had not ventured to ask to see him personally. He sought Grew instead as an intermediary for delivering his letter. Grew replied that he would with pleasure see that the letter gets into the President's hands without delay. The extract shows Italy pleading its case in Washington on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d568:
Belgrade charge Harold Shantz offered Washington a piece of advice on June 23, 1945. His short secret wire is document 568 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to Tito's public claim that civil rule in Venezia Giulia was still an open question.

Shantz suggests that the U.S. and British governments act through their Belgrade embassies. They should remind the Yugoslav government that article 3 of the Belgrade agreements settled the question. They should also warn that stirring up trouble in the area under Allied military government is unlikely to help the Yugoslav case. The wire is a small, sharp bid to hold Tito to a deal signed only two weeks before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d668:
Ambassador Norman Armour reported Spain's anger over the Soviet Tangier demand from Madrid on July 5, 1945. His confidential wire is document 668 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. An under secretary of the Spanish foreign ministry had spoken to him the day before.

The official, del Castillo, strongly denounced Moscow's bid for a seat at the Paris talks. Madrid had wired its London embassy to tell the Foreign Office Spain's line. Spain would welcome talks with the Americans, British, and French on restoring an international regime at Tangier. It would not discuss the matter with any other power, a phrase whose target was plainly Russia. Armour adds that Spain opposed reviving the 1923 statute as amended. It feared Russian entry into the administration and a return to French dominance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d68:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent the President's naval aide a staffing plan for the Berlin trip on June 15, 1945. The letter and its enclosures form document 68 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew appends a list of State Department people whose presence, he says, would help Truman at the meeting of heads of government.

The suggested party runs to about forty names, grouped by the issues they would cover. It includes the Secretary of State, Russian interpreters Charles Bohlen and Llewellyn Thompson, and specialists on German politics, reparations, the Balkans, and the Near East. Grew notes that Secretary Stettinius had approved the list at San Francisco. The document shows the expert team Washington thought a new president would need at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1068:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh reported from Athens on July 24, 1945, on the fall of Greece's foreign minister. Ioannis Sofianopoulos came home on July 22 and resigned the next day. Fresh from talks with Molotov, he had urged a cabinet drawn in thirds from left, center, and right. The prime minister found such a government unworkable, and the Regent declared the question did not arise.

MacVeagh reads the timing darkly. The resignation was Russian-inspired, he suggests, and lands during the Potsdam talks beside a threatening Yugoslav note. Moscow may plan, he warns, to refuse election supervision by claiming a nonrepresentative Athens cannot run fair elections amid chaos. Sofianopoulos, he adds, seemed pleased with himself and hungry for the premiership.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1168:
Team to team, the Soviet delegation addressed this note straight to the United States delegation on 31 July 1945. Such messages skipped the foreign ministers and the leaders. They carried business between the staffs who ran the talks day to day.

Two days before the close, that channel still had work to do. Last points needed answers while the final text was being drafted. A direct note of this kind shows Moscow talking to Washington with no one between. It is part of the summit's working machinery, preserved because the files kept everything the channel carried.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1268:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British chiefs wrote for their own team, in parallel with the American series across the hall.

A British paper in an American volume testifies to the allies' shared staff habits. The two machines exchanged paper as a matter of course. This memorandum is the British chiefs' view at the talks' start. Read beside the American notes of the same days, it shows two staffs framing one war and one peace in matching forms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1368:
Artemus Gates, the under secretary of the Navy, wrote to a senior plans officer of the fleet staff on 21 July 1945. The paper stayed inside the Navy's own house, moving between its civil head and its planners. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Summit volumes mostly print papers between governments or departments, so an inside-Navy paper stands out. It shows the service sorting out its own position while the talks ran in Germany. Readers get a glimpse of how one armed service thought through the questions of the hour before its views joined the wider argument in Washington. Small papers like this one keep the record honest about where policy starts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-68:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 23, 1945, record a morning session at Potsdam with two items printed here. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The first item concerns command in Indo-China.

Admiral King read a memo on approaching Chiang Kai-shek about a boundary change. The southern part of Indo-China would be reallocated to the Southeast Asia area. General Marshall proposed amending the statement the British wanted in the final report to the President and Prime Minister. The chiefs approved Marshall's amendment and directed that it go to the Combined Chiefs. The second item printed concerns personnel shipping for allied governments. The chiefs agreed to recommend approval of the transport committee's recommendation, subject to a wording change in its enclosure. Routine in form, the minutes move real forces on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d768:
A second American working paper bears the date July 24, 1945, as document 768. Two staff papers in one day reflect Potsdam's pace. The conference ran on paper: drafts, checks, and re-drafts. This one joined the delegation's files in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Companion papers let readers divide the work by topic and team. Each drafting group left its own trail. The document shows how a large mission organized its thinking. It also hints at the strain of the schedule. By July 24 the staff had served a week of sessions, and the hardest files were still open.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d868:
American drafters at Potsdam prepared this undated working paper as a proposed directive to the Allied commanders in Germany. It sets out the immediate economic tasks of the occupation. The paper bears no author's name. It was meant to push the commanders toward one shared program in the Control Council.

The tasks cover exports, including coal, to pay for reparations and minimum imports. They also cover fair sharing of supplies, uniform ration scales, and farm and coal output. Further items call for repair of transport, housing, and utilities. Industry would be cut back to peacetime needs. Currency, credit, public finance, and frontier controls would follow uniform rules.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d968:
J. Howard Marshall, general counsel to the reparations delegation, wrote to Edwin Pauley on July 31, 1945. He reports the firm view of two State Department men, Collado and Despres. Three subjects, they hold, must appear in the final Big Three agreement: restitution, property of Allied nationals in Germany, and German external assets.

Those men will cover the subjects through additions to the Economic Principles. Marshall still urges Pauley to push a Big Three declaration on German assets abroad, plus a vesting decree from the Control Council. On the principles themselves, he flags two deletions: the last sentence of 14(d) and all of paragraph 18, on supplies for Greater Berlin.
frus-1977-80v29-d168:
A letter from President Carter to General Torrijos forms document 168 in Volume XXIX of the 1977-1980 series. Carter writes just after the Senate consented to the second of the two Panama Canal Treaties. He calls the debate the most extensive ever held on a treaty in U.S. history. He praises the patience and patriotism of Panama's people. He stresses that the United States does not mean to meddle in Panama's internal affairs.

The letter frames that rule, non-intervention, as the base of the new partnership. Carter thanks Torrijos for his courage and leadership. He looks ahead to a visit to Panama to seal the new relationship in person.
gao-gaoreports-b-295968:
HMR Tech protested a Coast Guard award for project and acquisition support in GAO decision B-295968, dated May 19, 2005. The winner was Enterprise Information Services. The buy was a set-aside for small firms in the 8(a) program. HMR Tech attacked how the winner's price bid was scored.

GAO denied the protest. Both bids were scored as equal on the tech side. With a tie on merit, GAO said the agency could pick the lower price. That pick was proper here. The ruling is useful for best value buys where two bids tie and price must break the tie.
gao-gaoreports-b-297168:
Bernard Cap protested a Coast Guard award for hats and caps in GAO decision B-297168, dated November 8, 2005. The winner was Kingform Cap Company. The goods were officer and enlisted caps and covers. The firm bid far less for the male items. It hit its marks and the best value pick.

GAO denied the protest. Marks fit the call and were sound. Tech points in sum far outweighed price here. The winner was higher rated on tech and cost more. That pick fit the stated weights. A low price bid for part of the goods does not beat a stronger full bid when tech rules. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297968:
Project Resources protested an Army Corps award for green fix work in GAO decision B-297968, dated March 31, 2006. The buyer was the Sacramento District. Up to five deals were on offer to 8(a) firms. The firm said the agency lost its bid. It sought to have the bid scored now. No score ever took place.

GAO denied the protest. The record did show the bid was lost. But it did not show a broad flaw in how bids are taken in. A sole lost bid, sans proof of a broad flaw, does not force a re-run. Loss alone is not proof the whole intake path is broke. The award thus stood with no new score.
gao-gaoreports-b-298568:
Brian X. Scott protested the removal of his proposal from an Army competition in Iraq. The buy sought the full range of pre-award contracting support work. Only one rival firm stayed in the range after his exit. GAO decided B-298568 on October 26, 2006.

Scott's proposal asked for an advance payment term. It also said he could not perform without that payment. GAO found that stance a fair ground for removal. He also attacked the contracting officer's call that the rival was responsible. GAO saw no sign that key facts were ignored. Both lines of attack failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299368:
International Filter Manufacturing, Inc. protested a Defense Logistics Agency choice to run a buy with no set-aside. The buy covered 5,950 fluid pressure filter part kits. The firm is a HUBZone small business that makes filters. GAO decided B-299368 on April 10, 2007.

The firm urged a HUBZone set-aside for the kits. Such a set-aside needs a fair hope of two or more bids from that class. The agency's market probe found no such hope. GAO found that probe sound. Past deals in the field did not change the new count. An open buy can stand when the class count falls short. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-305368:
Paid praise for a school law is the subject of this GAO decision, B-305368, dated September 30, 2005. The Department of Education used the firm Ketchum, Inc. A sub-deal brought in Armstrong Williams and his firm. Williams was paid to tout the No Child Left Behind Act. Two senators asked GAO to review the deal.

GAO found that the deal crossed the legal line. Williams spoke for the law on a set schedule. The department did not make sure viewers knew of its role. GAO called that covert propaganda. It breached the ban on such use of fiscal year 2004 funds. The breach also broke the Antideficiency Act. The case is a key test for paid media deals.
gao-gaoreports-b-308968:
Free event planning deals for agencies are upheld, with cautions, in this GAO opinion, B-308968, dated November 27, 2007. National Conference Services, Inc. plans meetings and trade shows. Its model deal charges the government nothing. The firm earns its keep from exhibitors, sponsors, and guests. A senator asked GAO to judge the model deal.

GAO held the deal is valid and binding. The agency owes the firm no sum under it. The firm has no claim to be paid by the government. So the deal does not break the bar on free work for the government. GAO still urged care. Agencies should weigh control and aims before they sign such deals.
gao-gaoreports-b-310568:
Done Right Building Services, Inc. lost its protest (GAO decision B-310568, dated December 17, 2007). The National Archives sought upkeep work at the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library. The site sits in Hyde Park, New York. The award went to NHI/Urban Services Group, Inc. Done Right held the past work at sites of this kind. It claimed bias drove the scores and the pick.

GAO denied the protest. The file did not back the bias claim. The scores and pick held up as fair on the facts. Bias claims need proof, not hurt pride. A past holder has no claim to keep the work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-368:
Currency Paper Procurement, GAO-05-368 of April 29, 2005, asks if the paper in U.S. cash should have a sole source for life. For over 125 years, one firm has sold the Bureau of Engraving and Printing its note paper. A sole source can lift price and risk. The U.S. Mint, in the same spot, chose a second source for coin metal. Asks for bids went out in 1999 and 2003.

GAO told of walls to fair bids in 1998, from a poll of paper mills. It polls them once more here. It asks what the bureau changed, and with what yield. More sums must be run before a twin source call, it finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-768:
Freight by water between U.S. ports is weighed in GAO-05-768, dated July 29, 2005. Highways and rail lines grow more crowded each year. Short sea shipping could ease that strain. GAO asked why the option is on the table and what shapes its odds. It studied two new services. It also asked what public decision makers should weigh before investing.

Experts cited gains such as less road congestion. They also cited blocks, such as shippers' reluctance to try a new mode. The two new services gave insight but no clear verdict. The transport department made the option a high priority and drafted a funding plan. GAO said that push is too narrow. A full grasp of key issues should come before federal funding is set.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-968:
Asset transfers by the elderly to gain Medicaid cover are studied in GAO-05-968, a report from September 2, 2005. Medicaid paid about $93 billion for long-term care in fiscal year 2004. Applicants must fall below asset limits. Some give assets to family to qualify sooner. Giving below fair value can bring a penalty delay. GAO measured assets held and moved, using a 2002 national survey.

Section headings carry the findings. Asset levels and cash moved vary by age, health, and family traits. Some ways of reducing assets may not trigger a penalty period. States could not identify how far transfers go among their applicants. The federal Medicaid agency guides states through its manual and by answering specific questions. GAO also reviewed applications in nine states. The report shows how hard the practice is to size.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1068:
Reserve mobilization data gets a reliability check in GAO-06-1068, a report dated September 20, 2006. Sound data on who is called up drives choices on force availability and health tracking. GAO ran the review under its own authority. It used the Defense Department's contingency tracking system. It asked what the data show about reservists sent for the war on terrorism, and whether the data can be trusted.

Headings give the answer in two parts. The data do show the traits of hundreds of thousands of deployed reservists, through June 30, 2006. Citizenship, race, gender, and home state are among the fields covered. The department and services have taken steps to improve reliability. More needs to be done, GAO concluded. The report carries recommendations on the added steps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-268:
Grant-making fairness at the Education Department is examined in GAO-06-268, dated February 21, 2006. Over three years the department gave an average of $4.8 billion a year in discretionary grants. Money flows through scored contests and through unsolicited proposals. GAO studied the rules for both paths at the Office of Innovation and Improvement in 2003 and 2004. It checked whether staff followed their own rules in those years. It also rechecked some grant choices from 2001 and 2002.

Flaws from the earlier years could recur without tighter steps, GAO warned. It made four recommendations to the Secretary of Education. They aim at fairer contests and a clearer public record. For unsolicited proposals, GAO urged a set format for picking which ideas earn peer review. Open rules matter because grant contests shape schools far beyond Washington. The report treats process as a guard against favoritism.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-368:
Trillion-dollar weapon plans kept slipping on cost and time. GAO-06-368, an April 14, 2006 report, reviews major weapon systems under the Defense Department's revised buying policy. The department planned to invest $1.3 trillion from 2005 to 2009. That money covered research, development, and purchase of major systems.

Cost growth, delays, and cut performance had marked many programs for years. GAO asked whether the new policy was fixing those faults. It checked results for programs started under the policy. It also tested whether knowledge-based steps and firm controls guided choices. The finding is blunt. Major systems still faced cost and schedule problems. Readers get program proof at scale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-468:
Scenic flights over national parks bring fees that some operators may not pay. Issued May 11, 2006, report GAO-06-468 reviews air tour fees at national parks. A 1993 law required the National Park Service to collect such fees. Only three parks met the tests to charge them. They are Grand Canyon, Haleakala, and Hawaii Volcanoes. The Federal Aviation Administration also regulates park air tours with the service.

GAO assessed how well the service collects the fees. It named factors that hinder collection. It also gives data on adding fees at more parks. Effective checks and enforcement are needed, GAO said. Readers get a small fee program in detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-568:
Buying a home almost always requires title insurance, yet buyers rarely shop for it. Report GAO-06-568, issued April 24, 2006, gives early views on title insurance. Buyers usually rely on lenders, agents, or attorneys to pick an insurer. Recent state and federal probes found practices that may have helped those professionals at buyers' expense. GAO had a study of the industry under way. That study covers pricing, competition, market size, and regulation.

This report identifies issues for further study. It questions cost structures and agent practices unlike other insurance markets. It weighs effects of the practices found in probes. It also asks whether sales rules need change. The views are preliminary.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-668:
Risks in Venezuelan oil output are assessed in GAO report GAO-06-668, issued on June 27, 2006. Venezuela was the world's eighth-largest oil exporter and held top-10 proven reserves. It supplied about 11 percent of United States imports of crude oil and petroleum products. It also wholly owned five refineries in the United States. With world oil markets tight, any cut in its output mattered.

GAO found that Venezuelan government actions had lowered crude oil production. Yet exports to the United States had changed little so far. GAO said a broad drop in Venezuelan exports would affect world markets. By contrast, an embargo aimed at the United States would be felt mainly by the two nations. The report also reviews United States programs for energy security.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1168:
Fuel thinning funds for wildland fire are poorly aimed, GAO reports in GAO-07-1168, dated September 28, 2007. Millions of acres face wildland fire risk. Five land agencies spend large sums to thin brush and trees near towns and wild ground: the Forest Service, plus four Interior bureaus.

GAO asked how those agencies split their fuel funds, and pick projects. It asked how those paths could be made to cut risk more surely. It visited head and field offices of all five. It read funding and results data, and past program studies. Better facts and a set process, GAO said, could improve how funds flow and projects are chosen.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1268:
First and business class seats cost the government far more than coach. GAO measured how often that premium travel broke the rules in GAO-07-1268, issued September 28, 2007. Prior GAO work had found abuse at the Defense and State departments. This study covered the whole federal government. GAO mined bank card data and sampled tickets to size the problem.

The government bought more than 53,000 premium class tickets in one year. They cost over $230 million from July 1, 2005, to June 30, 2006. GAO projected that about $146 million of that travel was unauthorized or unjustified. Senior executives were about one-half of 1 percent of the workforce. Yet they took 15 percent of the premium trips. GAO found cases where subordinates approved their bosses' premium flights. It blamed weak internal controls across agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-268:
Agencies are moving to new phone and data contracts, and the switch carries a price tag. GAO checked the moving fund in GAO-07-268, issued February 23, 2007. The services agency estimated its share of the shift at $151.5 million. It collects fees from customer agencies to build the fund. GAO tested the math against cost estimation best practice. It also asked whether the fund already holds enough.

The estimate was shaky, GAO found. It assumed 76 percent of services would change providers. Officials called that a worst case, unlikely to occur. The math may double-count one cost. It also ignored a delay of almost 2 years. Still, the fund looks big enough. It held about $142 million at fiscal year-end 2006. GAO's model says that covers likely costs 96 percent of the time. GAO urged a written cost policy and a fresh estimate after awards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-368:
A critical FBI network carries case files and investigative data, and its guardrails failed in seven ways at once. GAO detailed the gaps in GAO-07-368, a report dated April 30, 2007. GAO ran a vulnerability scan of the internal network. It judged the security program around that network. A companion classified report carries the specific fixes. This public report sums up the weakness classes.

Devices were not set up securely, GAO found. Users were not reliably identified before access. Staff could reach more data than their jobs needed. Strong encryption was not applied across the network. Security events went unlogged or unmonitored. Physical protection and patching also lagged. The bureau's risk review for the network was outdated. Its security plan and testing were incomplete. The bureau's technology chief accepted many fixes. He disputed that data faced an unacceptable risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-68:
Homeland Security first responder grants are the subject of GAO-07-68, a report to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs dated December 22, 2006. The Cash Management Improvement Act of 1990 sets rules on how fast states must spend federal grant funds. Congress exempted some first responder grants from those rules in fiscal years 2005 and 2006. The exemption lets grantees take cash in advance and hold it for long periods. GAO checked whether the old rule had blocked funds when needed.

GAO found no solid proof that the old rule kept funds from first responders. State officials blamed delays on vendors and short staffing after the September 11 attacks. GAO warned that advance funding needs strong watch over cash and interest owed. The Department of Homeland Security lacked plans and tools for that task. GAO made seven recommendations to fix the gap. DHS said it would take them under advisement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-868:
A spending plan from the Homeland Security science arm is reviewed in GAO-07-868, dated June 22, 2007. The Science and Technology Directorate is the department's main research arm. It develops tools against chemical, biological, nuclear, and explosive attacks. The 2007 funding law gave it about $973 million. About $838 million was for research, development, and operations. The law barred spending $60 million until the directorate sent an expenditure plan. GAO checked that plan against the law's terms.

The plan did not fully meet the law's conditions, GAO found. It sorted spending by program area as required. It did not give the full breakdown and justification for management costs, though. The plan also skipped the method used to build each cost category. Officials said the figures drew on past spending and new projections. Past reports had flagged money management problems at the directorate. This letter gives Congress the facts behind the funding hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-168:
Federal debt schedules pass audit in GAO report GAO-08-168 (November 7, 2007). The Bureau of the Public Debt manages Treasury securities. They are held by the public and by federal accounts such as trust funds. GAO audits the bureau's debt schedules each year. The work supports GAO's audit of the government's full statements.

GAO judged the schedules for fiscal years 2007 and 2006 to be fairly presented in all material respects. It also found that the bureau kept effective internal control over the schedules. A legal compliance test formed part of the audit. The report gives Congress rare clean news on debt bookkeeping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-68:
War costs must be counted cleanly, or Congress cannot judge them. Congress gave the Defense Department about $542.9 billion for the Global War on Terrorism as of May 2007. GAO-08-68, dated November 6, 2007, checks the outlook for war spending and the trustworthiness of cost reports.

Reported war obligations for fiscal year 2007 hit $95.4 billion through June, near the full prior year. Extra requests of nearly $47.6 billion lifted the fiscal year 2008 ask to about $189.3 billion. New guidance blurred war costs with base costs, GAO found. It gave 11 fixes, from cleaner cost terms to more war costs in the base budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-768:
Hurricane Katrina showed that disaster reply must join federal, state, and local hands. In January 2008 the homeland security department issued a new National Response Framework to replace the 2004 plan. GAO-08-768, dated June 11, 2008, asks how fully outside partners shaped that rewrite.

Partners helped at the start and at the end. But after an April 2007 draft, the department shut them out for 5 months of closed federal review, breaking its own work plan and a 2006 law's spirit. Partners told Congress they were locked out. GAO told the emergency agency to write clear rules for joint work next time.
grosh-oddfellows-manual-1868:
Aaron B. Grosh was a clergyman and a leading Odd Fellow in the United States. His Odd-Fellow's Improved Manual came out in 1868. It set out the past, the rules, and the aims of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. The order was then one of the largest friendly groups in the land.

Grosh defends the order against its critics and explains its signs, degrees, and lodge work. He also gives the laws that govern local lodges and grand lodges. For the years when such groups cared for the sick and buried the dead, few books show their inner life so well.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-:
Samuel R Wells wrote this handbook of phrenology and physiognomy, for students and examiners. The title page quotes Horace Mann: whoever spreads true phrenology is a public benefactor. Wells dates his author's note January 1869, at New York. A descriptive chart comes with the book.

The introduction starts with the brain and the skull's forms. Gray and white matter, hemispheres and lobes, are set out in brief. Each faculty then gets its place, size, and training. Cultivation, one entry says, grows by study, planning, and tracing causes. Wells ran a famous shop for such wares on Broadway. The book is his system in portable form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbas-judah-ibn: Judah ibn Abbas of Fez was a poet, author of the piyyuṭ "Et Sha'are Raẓon." He was the first Jew known by the name Abbas, and died at Mosul in 1163. Al-Ḥarizi reports that he left the Maghreb for the East, living at times in Bagdad and in Aleppo. He was said to be a friend of Judah ha-Levi. One poem of his, which drew a reply from Ha-Levi, is kept in the Diwan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-samuel-: Samuel Abraham of Sofia was a Turkish Talmudist of the middle of the seventeenth century. With Michael ben Moses ha-Kohen he wrote Moreh Zedek, Teacher of Righteousness. The work was printed at Salonica in 1655. It is in the nature of a concordance to the works of the Aharonim, the later casuists. The entry gives no birth or death date and names no other work by him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albagal-solomon:
Solomon ibn Albagal, also called Don Culema, was a Spanish farmer of taxes. He lived at Villa-Real, or Ciudad-Real. He held office in the reign of Maria de Molina, from 1300 to 1310. He owned a large fulling-mill named Batanejo, on the Guadiana. When the Knights of Calatrava sold it, the mill brought 15,000 gold maravedis.

For years he fought a lawsuit with his partner, Israel Alhadad, over a large sum of money. The queen sent the case to R. Asher ben Jehiel of Toledo for judgment. The entry also names his family. His wife was Joanila. His son Samuel stayed at Villa-Real. His daughter Dinah married a fellow tax farmer and died of the plague at Toledo in 1349.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandre-alber: Albert Alexandre was a chess-player, born at Hohenfeld-on-the-Main about 1766. He died in London on November 16, 1850. Most of his life was spent in Paris, at the Café de la Régence. He belonged to the French Chess School at its height. Men praised his brilliant combinations and his gift for solving problems. As a player, though, he stood below the first rank. He published an encyclopedia of chess at Paris in 1837. In 1846 he issued a collection of the finest chess problems, with 2,120 examples.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allon-bachuth-o: Allon Bachuth means the oak of weeping. The oak stood near Bethel. Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, was buried at its foot. Genesis tells of that burial in chapter thirty-five. A rabbinic note reads the word allon as a Greek word for another. On that reading Jacob wept twice in a short span. News of his mother's death reached him while he still mourned for Deborah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amathus-the-mod: Amathus was a fort near the Jordan river. It stood north of the Jabbok stream. The site lay 21 miles south of Pella. A despot named Theodorus held it early in the first century B.C. About the year 98 Alexander Jannaeus took the fort. He could not hold it, so he razed it. In 57 B.C. it led one of five districts of Palestine. The Talmud links it to the Bible town Zaphon. The entry leaves that link in doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ananias-of-adia:
Ananias of Adiabene was a Jewish trader of Greek stock. He served at the court of Abennerig of Charax. That port town stood where two arms of the Tigris meet. He won pagans to the Jewish faith with zeal. High born women of the court were among his converts. One such woman was a king's daughter named Symacho.

Her husband was Izates, a prince of Adiabene. Through her, Izates came to know Ananias well. About the year 18 the prince took up the faith. He took the throne about the year 22. He wished to take the rite of circumcision as well. Ananias joined his mother in a plea against that step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anspach-joel-15: Joel Anspach was a French religious writer born about 1800 who died in September 1872. He was the only brother of Philippe Anspach. Joel was the first to turn the daily prayers from Hebrew into French. In 1842 he published Paroles d'un Croyant Israelite, Words of an Israelite Believer. The book argued against Catholic efforts to win converts. Because of that aim, the entry notes, it drew much comment at the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-appraisement-in:
Appraisement is the setting of a value by a court, on property or on damage done to person or goods. It differs from estimate, where the Law itself fixes the value. Damage awards belong with the heads of wrongs and remedies, the entry says, so it treats land taken for debt instead.

In Talmudic law, land was the only way to make an adult's property pay his debts, valued by the court rather than sold to the highest bidder. The Mishnah's rule in Gittin sorts whose claim takes which land. The injured are paid from the best land, creditors from the middling, and a widow's jointure from the poorest. The entry then works through the rules for choosing, valuing, and handing over such land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristobulus-i-c:
Judah, called Aristobulus I in Greek, was king of Judea and eldest son of John Hyrcanus. Born about 140 B.C., he died in 104. On his father's death he took the high priesthood, shut his mother in prison, where she starved, and locked up three of his brothers. He then took the throne, the first Jewish king since the Babylonian exile, nearly five hundred years earlier.

His short reign brought war on Iturea, whose people he partly subdued and forced toward Judaism. At home, palace intrigue ruled. Queen Alexandra Salome's circle turned the sick king against his favorite brother Antigonus, whose death he ordered without fully meaning to. Remorse, the entry reports, broke him. The entry also notes his care not to offend the Pharisees, shown in the Hebrew wording on his coins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asa-1868: Two men share the name Asa in this short entry. The first Asa is a Levite, father of Berechiah, found in the Levite genealogy in First Chronicles chapter 9. For the second and far larger figure, the reader is sent onward to the separate entry on Asa, third king of Judah. Nothing else is stated here about either man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-gersh:
Gershon Ashkenazi, a Polish Talmudist, was born in the second decade of the seventeenth century and died at Metz on March 20, 1693. His family name was really Ulif; Ashkenazi was the surname Poland gave to families of German stock. He studied at Cracow under Joel Sirkes and Joshua Harif and served as judge there. From 1649 to 1659 he was rabbi at Prossnitz, then at Hanau and Nikolsburg.

Five years at Vienna ended when the Jews were banished, and in 1670 he reached Metz, where he stayed for life. His printed responsa, Abodat ha-Gershuni, number 124 answers to the leading Talmudists of his day. They hold much evidence on Polish Jewish life after the Cossack massacres. A second book gives Midrashic and cabalistic readings of the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-isaac:
Isaac ben Zebi Ashkenazi, a rabbi and author, was born in Russia about the middle of the eighteenth century. He served as rabbi in Chodorow and in Lemberg. He died at Lemberg on May 5, 1807. Walden gives the year as 1811, and the entry flags that date as an error.

Two Hebrew books of his are named. Or ha-Ner, Light of the Lamp, printed at Lemberg in 1788, comments on the Haggadah, the Passover telling. Torat ha-Kodesh, Law of Holiness, printed there in 1792, comments on Zebahim, the tractate on sacrifices. The entry rests on Walden, on Buber's Anshe Shem, and on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue. It adds no family, no teachers, and no events.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avicenna-abu-al:
Avicenna was a physician and thinker of note. He was born at Bokhara in 980 and died in 1037. His works reached Spain about a hundred years after they appeared. There they shaped Jewish thought through the Middle Ages. His great survey of learning, the "Al-Shafa'," covers logic, physics, mathematics, and the study of being itself.
