As a doctor he won the title Prince of Physicians. His "Canon" set out a full system of medicine in five books. For five centuries European universities used it as a guide. It stayed in use at Louvain and Montpellier until about 1650. Jewish scholars translated it into Hebrew, in 1279 and after, and wrote comments on it. Maimonides judged his philosophy sound but below al-Farabi. A smaller survey by Avicenna was turned into Hebrew at Rome in 1330.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baar-herman-226:
Herman Baar was an American educator. He was born in 1826 at Stadthagen, near Hanover, Germany. He studied at the gymnasium of Hanover, then read language study and theology at Göttingen. He taught eight years at the famed mixed school at Seesen. In 1857 he became minister of the Seel street synagogue in Liverpool, and he served there ten years.

Loss of voice ended Baar's pulpit work. Seeking a better climate, he moved to New Orleans and ran a school there. In 1876 he became superintendent of the Hebrew Orphan Asylum in New York city. He filled that post with great success until he resigned in 1899. His books include two volumes of sermons for children, on homely and religious topics. He also wrote a Bible history, whose first part appeared in 1901, and many magazine pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahya-ben-josep:
Baḥya ben Joseph ibn Paḳuda was a judge and thinker who lived at Saragossa, Spain, in the first half of the eleventh century. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his court title of dayyan. Near its close he wrote, in Arabic in 1040, the first Jewish system of ethics. Judah ibn Tibbon later turned it into Hebrew as "Ḥobot ha-Lebabot" (Duties of the Heart).

Baḥya held that most teachers stressed deeds of the body and slighted the duties of the heart behind the 613 laws. His ten "gates" move from the unity of God through reflection on creation, trust, and self-discipline, to the love of God. The entry works through each gate in detail. It praises his depth of feeling, his clear style, and his free use of non-Jewish moral writers. Parts of the book were read in the penitential days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-baruch-b:
Baruch b. Moses ibn Baruch was an Italian philosopher, Talmudist, and Bible commentator of the end of the sixteenth century. He belonged to the old Spanish family of Baruch, also called Bet Ya'aḳob. In 1598–99 he sat on the Venetian rabbinate and answered many legal questions there. He is also said to have proof-read Hebrew books. In 1602 he was at Constantinople, in scientific exchange with its scholars. Very little of his halakic writing survives.

His fame rests on a double commentary on Ecclesiastes: one rabbinic-exegetic, one philosophic. He reads the book as a dialogue in which Solomon sets Epicurean opinions beside those of the pious. The entry notes how near this comes to the modern gloss-hypothesis. His themes run from Creation and free will to Providence, retribution, and true felicity. Felicity, for him, is no passing joy but a continuous activity of the soul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bauer-bruno-266:
Bruno Bauer was a Christian theologian, philosopher, and historian born on Sept. 6, 1809, at Eisenburg. He died on April 13, 1882, at Rixdorf, near Berlin. The entry focuses on his stance toward Jews and their fight for equal rights.

In an 1842 article, later a book on the Jewish question, Bauer sided with the harshest foes of the Jews. He held their oppression to be just and denied that Judaism had added anything to civilization. The entry treats his case as a telling sign of German liberal thought at the time. A later piece from 1863 took up Judaism abroad in much the same harsh spirit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behar-moses-sha: Moses Shabbethai Behar was a rabbi and author who lived in Salonica at the start of the nineteenth century. The whole entry runs to two short lines. It names one Hebrew book by him, a collection of legal answers printed at Salonica in 1802. No dates for his birth or death are given, and no other work, post, or event of his life is recorded in this brief notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ben-jo: Benjamin ben Joab, called de Synagoga after Zunz, was a liturgical poet who lived at Montalcino in the fourteenth century. Two printed poems by him are named. One is a metrical opening to the Nishmat prayer for Passover, built in stanzas of ten lines with seven syllables each. The other is a penitential poem of five stanzas. Its refrain ends with the plea, Oh, give us prosperity. No further facts of his life are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berger-philippe: Philippe Berger was a Christian professor of Hebrew, born at Beaucourt in September 1846. A brother of Samuel Berger, he trained at Strasburg and settled in Paris. There he taught Hebrew in the Protestant faculty and served as a sub-librarian. A pupil and close friend of Renan, he followed his master into the study of Semitic inscriptions. He helped prepare the great corpus of those inscriptions for the academy. Two of his books treat the writing of Semitic inscriptions and the meaning of the names of the Hebrew patriarchs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bertensohn-vasi:
Vasili Alekseyevich Bertensohn, born in Odessa on September 12, 1860, was a Russian agriculturist who graduated from the Petrovsko-Razumovskoye Agricultural Academy in Moscow in 1884. He served the Department of State Domains across southern Russia, advising on the governments of Kherson and Bessarabia.

The entry follows his commissions on phylloxera and sericulture, his 1889 study trip to western Europe, and his rise by 1900 to chief expert on agriculture for Podolia and Volhynia. It also records his work for Odessa Jewish charities, his organization of the Hebrew Orphan Asylum farm, and his many articles in agricultural journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blessing-of-chi:
Blessing of Children treats the parental benediction. Respect between parents and children marked Hebrew homes. A father's words were held to carry real power. They could bring good or ill to a child. Genesis stories ground that belief. Noah blessed Shem and Japheth and cursed Ham. Rebekah schemed to win Isaac's blessing for Jacob. Esau cried for a blessing too.

The spoken blessing could never be recalled. Ecclesiasticus voices the same faith later. A father's blessing builds sons' houses, it says. The custom survives on Sabbath eve and holidays. Fathers still bless children before journeys. The entry prizes that continuity highly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bognar-frederik:
Frederike Bognar was a German actress born at Gotha on Feb. 16, 1840. Her father sang, and she first trained for music in Munich. Stage work in childhood parts at Budapest came before that training.

Bognar chose acting and made her debut at Zurich in 1856. She played at Hamburg and then at Vienna's Hofburgtheater till 1870. A long starring tour followed. She later joined theatres in Prague and Vienna. Her early roles included Gretchen, Ophelia, and Desdemona. Later she played Medea, Maria Stuart, and Judith. She trained for the stage under Denker and later under Laube. Music study under her aunt in Munich had come first, before acting won out.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borders-3568:
Borders are the ornamental designs that frame printed pages. The first ornaments for title pages were arabesque borders with white figures. They appear in books printed at Lisbon from 1489 to 1492.

Those plates later traveled to Salonica with a printer's types. Prague printers made borders of great beauty in prayer books and Pentateuchs. One Prague design shows Moses with the tablets and two lions. Portals were the most common frame, used by Bomberg at Venice. Printers also borrowed borders from non-Hebrew books at Frankfort. Eagles, angels, and Moses with Aaron all appear in later examples named here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breastplate-of-:
Breastplate of the high priest, called hoshen, was a pouch with precious stones. The high priest wore it on his breast in the Holy Place. Exodus gives full directions for its making in two chapters.

The piece was foursquare and doubled, a span in length and breadth. Twelve stones sat on its face in four rows. Each stone bore the name of one tribe of Israel, cut into it. Gold cords and a blue ribbon tied it fast to the ephod. Rabbinic notes say the stones called the patriarchs' piety to God's mind. No chisel was to touch the stones when the names were cut, tradition adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brunetti-angelo:
Angelo Brunetti, better known as Ciciruacchio, was a popular Roman leader who backed Jewish emancipation. Born in Rome in 1800, he drew his ideas from the patriot Mazzini. He worked both for his city's freedom and for the people of the Roman ghetto. His influence helped reconcile Jews and Christians there.

In July 1847 he won over the suburb of Regola, and a mass meeting for the Jews followed in the capital. That evening 6,000 Roman citizens entered the ghetto in friendship. When Pius IX ordered the ghetto walls torn down in 1848, Brunetti and his friends began the demolition. He and two sons were killed in a street riot in 1849. Rome's Jewish congregation set up a tablet to his memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canneh-3968: Canneh was a city named once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's list of places that fed the greatness of Tyre. The name occurs nowhere else, and its site is fought over. Cornill takes it for the Calneh of Amos. One manuscript supports that reading, though it might point to the Calneh of Genesis instead. Kiepert placed it on the Tigris. Another proposal rewrites the name as a far more common phrase. The entry quotes a critic who finds that fix hard to accept.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cemetery-4168:
Cemetery means a place for burial of the dead. The word comes from a Greek term for the place where the dead sleep. Hebrew names for it include house of eternity and house of the living. Polish-Russian Jews called it the pure place. Other names were garden of the Jews and Jewish hill.

Old law required a burial place to stand at least fifty ells from the nearest house. In Talmudic times tombs sat in caves or were cut from rock. A whitewashed stone marked the site, warning passersby of impurity. In the Middle Ages the Jewish cemetery usually stood at the far end of the ghetto. Hospital and other communal buildings often rose nearby. Crowded ground forced burials above older bodies, with six handbreadths of space between them. Some towns shared one cemetery, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chatzkin-isaac-: Isaac Andreyevich Chatzkin was a Russian physician born in 1832. He died at Odessa in June 1902. He settled in that city in 1869 and practiced there for more than thirty years. In 1870 he joined the Medical Society of Odessa and became a corresponding member at Kherson. Chatzkin wrote letters on physiology that appeared in a Russian journal in 1858. He also translated medical works into Russian. Among them were a professor's introduction to medical science and Virchow's Cellular Pathology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-edward-44:
Edward Cohen, an Australian statesman, was born in London in 1822 and died in March, 1877. Schooled in Australia, he joined his father's firm, then bought an auctioneer's business at Melbourne in 1846 and ran it until 1868. It grew into one of the city's leading concerns.

Charity and city work came early. He served twenty years as treasurer of the Melbourne Hospital and seven as president of the Melbourne Hebrew congregation. As alderman and, in 1872, mayor of Melbourne, he pushed a finance inquiry that reformed the city accounts. He sat in Parliament for East Melbourne from 1861 and once held office as commissioner of customs. Bank and railway directorships close the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coronation-chai:
Coronation Chair centers on the Stone of Destiny set in the coronation chair at Westminster Abbey. Tradition calls it the very stone on which Jacob rested his head at Bethel. Some linked it instead to the stone of Abraham's intended sacrifice of Isaac. A legend traced by the entry carries it from Palestine to Egypt, then to Spain, Ireland, and Scotland.

Kings of Ireland were anointed on it at Tara, and kings of Scotland at Scone. Edward I. removed it to Westminster, the entry says. Every English king from Edward III. to Edward VII. was crowned upon it. Londoners once blocked a plan to send it back to Scotland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crispin-isaac-i: Isaac ibn Crispin was a Spanish moralist and poet. He lived at the beginning of the twelfth century. Judah al-Ḥarizi praised him among the renowned poets of his age. The title The Great Prince set before his name hints at high office. His known work is an ethical book, Sefer ha-Musar, the Book of Instruction. Steinschneider held it to be one with a book of proverbs still kept in manuscript. That book may be an adaptation from the Arabic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dan-jaan-4868: Dan-jaan, if the reading is right, is a city named only once in the Bible. It stands in the route of Joab's census takers in Second Samuel. Their road crossed the Jordan, ran north, swung west to Sidon past Dan-jaan, then south to Beersheba. The natural guess links it with Dan, on Israel's northern border. Conder instead placed it near Achzib. Scholars have offered many fixes for the odd word Jaan. Gesenius read Dan of the wood. Others read Ijon, a city named next to Dan in Kings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delmedigo-josep:
Joseph Solomon Delmedigo was a philosopher and physician born at Candia on June 16, 1591, son of its rabbi Elijah. At Padua, which he entered at fifteen, he studied medicine, mathematics, and astronomy, the last under Galileo. His taste for secular study soon made life in Candia hard for him.

Delmedigo then wandered for years. He debated a Mohammedan professor on mathematics at Cairo and won. He studied Cabala at Constantinople, served as physician to Prince Radziwill near Wilna, and preached at Hamburg and Amsterdam. His answers to a Karaite scholar's science questions form his book "Elim." He settled at Prague about 1648 and died there on October 16, 1655.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dias-diaz-moses: Isaac's son Moses Dias was an author, publisher, and bookseller of Amsterdam. In 1695 he published Joseph Franco Serrano's Spanish translation of the Pentateuch. Between that year and 1715 he brought out a number of Hebrew books. His own work, printed at Amsterdam in 1697, reflects on the sacred history of Genesis. It builds on the comments of old and new interpreters. A second, enlarged edition came out at Amsterdam in 1705, dedicated to Selomo de Medina, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-domitian-titus-:
Domitian, in full Titus Flavius Domitianus, was Roman emperor from 81 to 96. Born in 51, he was assassinated in 96. In 69, when Vespasian was proclaimed emperor, Domitian led the Flavian party at Rome. He followed his brother Titus on the throne.

The entry paints a suspicious, despotic ruler who broke the Senate's power. He twice expelled philosophers from Rome, in 89 and 95. Converts to Judaism or Christianity faced death or loss of property. His cousin Flavius Clemens was killed for taking the Jewish faith. The Jew-tax, the entry adds, was gathered with great cruelty under him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-durkheim-emile-:
Emile Durkheim was a French writer born at Epinal, in the Vosges, on April 15, 1858. He was schooled in his home town, then at Paris. From 1882 to 1887 he taught philosophy in several lycées. In 1887 he took the sociology chair at Bordeaux.

Durkheim, the entry says, brought sociology into the French universities. In 1902 the Sorbonne called him to Paris. In 1897 he founded L'Année Sociologique, a yearly review of the field. His books include The Division of Social Labor in 1893 and The Rules of Sociological Method in 1895. His study Le Suicide followed in 1897. Many essays of his appeared in the Revue Philosophique and the Revue Bleue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eibenschutz-alb: Albert Eibenschütz was a German pianist born in Berlin on April 15, 1857. He studied piano under Reinecke at the Leipsic Conservatorium. Posts followed at Kharkof, Leipsic, and Cologne. In 1893 he took over the Cologne Liederkranz as its director. In 1896 he became first piano professor at Berlin's Stern Conservatorium. Two years later he owned and ran the Wiesbaden conservatory. Critics praised his brilliant technique, rich tone, and delicate, precise touch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elhanan-ben-iss: Elhanan ben Issachar Katz was a writer in Hebrew and in Judeo-German. He lived at Prossnitz in Moravia in the late seventeenth century. There he served as beadle, cantor, and scribe at once. His books mix verse, ethics, and prayer. One gives Judeo-German verses for the feast of Hanukkah. Another sets out moral sayings for the wall. He turned the penitential prayers into Judeo-German as well. He also brought out a book of prayers for success by an unnamed author.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-of-pesar: Elijah of Pesaro was an Italian Talmudist and thinker. He lived in the sixteenth century. After long years as a teacher at Venice, he set out east. His goal was a new life in Palestine in 1563. At Famagusta in Cyprus he heard bad news. Cholera was raging through the Holy Land at the time. He chose to go no farther on the road. His works rest in a library at Paris today. Among them is a letter home from Famagusta.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-engraving-and-e:
Engraving is the art of cutting signs into hard stuff. Stone, wood, and metal all take the cutter's marks. The high priest's gear in Exodus shows the art was old. Its stones and plates bear cut names and seals. The seal cutter's craft sets the mark for the work. A cut stone had to read clear, like a signet seal. Phoenicians had a wide name for skill in signet rings. Hebrews used such rings to sign bonds and deeds. A ring was part of the dress of a man of rank.

The entry tracks the Hebrew words for the art with care. One word names the skilled worker in the craft. Bezalel stands as the type of the God-gifted craftsman. God filled him with skill for the Tabernacle work. The entry weighs a word that may be a scribe's slip.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-estella-or-stel:
Estella, capital of a district in Navarre, had a Jewish community as old as those of Tudela and Pamplona. In 1144 King Garcia Ramirez gave its synagogue to the bishop, and it became a church. Twenty years later a charter fixed the Jews' legal status on fair terms. Under French kings they later suffered forced limits on their loans.

After King Charles I died on March 5, 1328, attackers stormed the Jewish quarter. The Jews defended themselves from its walls, but the quarter was burned and most residents killed. Menahem ben Zerah survived, though his family perished. The community had its own magistracy and worked mainly in trade and finance. In 1366 it numbered eighty-five families under heavy taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezra-book-of-59:
The Book of Ezra tells how the exiles returned from Babylon and rebuilt the Temple, and the entry first walks through it chapter by chapter. Cyrus lets the Israelites rebuild and hands back the gold vessels Nebuchadnezzar had seized. The returnees with Zerubbabel number 42,360, besides servants and singers. Foundations are laid in the second year, amid great joy.

Samaritan foes then stall the work until Darius finds Cyrus's decree and orders it finished. The Temple is dedicated in the sixth year of Darius. Ezra himself arrives with a royal commission and a list of family heads. The book closes with men who had married foreign wives sending them away, each bringing a sin offering. A critical view of the book's makeup follows the summary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franchetti-leop:
Leopoldo Franchetti, Baron, was an Italian deputy born at Florence in 1847. He studied law at Pisa. With Deputy Sidney Sonnino he traveled through Sicily to study its social, political, and economic state. Their findings were printed in two volumes. In 1878 the two men founded a weekly review.

It later became a daily paper at Rome, then died for lack of readers. In the last decade of the nineteenth century Franchetti governed the East African colony of Eritrea. In Parliament he gave his care chiefly to navy affairs. He published many reports for that body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedland-6368:
Friedland is a family that seems to come from Friedland in Mecklenburg or from the Bohemian town of that name. It settled at Prague. Nathan Friedland, head of the community and of the land of Bohemia, is the earliest known member of the Prague line. One branch sat at Zülz in Silesia toward the end of the seventeenth century. A member of it was a leading man at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1708. A note in a book printed there that year tells of him.

There was also a Friedland family in Russia. Its founders were likely kin to the Zülz branch. The best-known Russians of the name were the giver Meïr and his brother Moses Aryeh Löb. The earliest known Russian member was Abraham of Slutzk. One of the line settled at Dwinsk in 1846, but his sons moved on to St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galatia-6468:
Galatia was an inland district of Asia Minor that became a Roman province after 25 B.C. A Jewish settlement stood there, perhaps planted by Antiochus the Great. He sent many Jewish families to Asia Minor as colonists. Stone inscriptions found in Galatia name Jews. Rabbi Akiba is also said to speak of Galia, read as Galatia.

The chief proof of Jews there is Paul letter to the Galatians. Scholars dispute which part of Galatia held his readers. Older views point north. Newer scholars, Ramsay among them, point south. Growth of Christianity there may explain why Galatia Jews vanish from later records. The Galatians of Maccabees were in fact Gauls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gihon-6668:
Gihon is the second river of Eden in Genesis ii, said to circle the whole land of Cush. Scholars have long argued over which river it is. Josephus takes it as the Nile. Saadia and Rashi make Pison the Nile instead. Arab use of Jaihun for the Oxus points some critics east. Others pick the Orontes or the Ganges.

The entry also covers a fountain near Jerusalem of the same name. Solomon was anointed and proclaimed king there. Hezekiah is said to have stopped its upper watercourse. Robinson held it lay west of the city. Its waters, on his view, were led by hidden channels into town. The Targum and some versions read Shiloah for Gihon in First Kings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-greek-language-:
Greek language and the Jews is a study of Greek words in rabbinic books. The piece sets aside the Septuagint and New Testament by design. It treats the Talmud, Midrash, and Targum instead. Greek letters there are spelled by sound alone. That makes the spellings evidence for how Greek was pronounced. Surds and sonants stay apart, the entry shows.

Loanwords fill the second half. Greek words in rabbinic speech cover all of life. Politics and trade supply the most. Words for palace, colony, census, coin, and wagon all came from Greek or Latin through Greek. The entry warns, though, that some claimed borrowings in philosophy books are unproved. Krauss's study of loanwords closes the bibliography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gregory-bar-heb:
Gregory Bar Hebræus was a Jacobite Syrian writer. His full name was Abu al-Faraj ibn Harun. He was born at Malatia in 1226 and died at Maragha in 1286. His father Aaron was a Jewish doctor who became a Christian. Gregory studied medicine, theology, and philosophy. He rose to bishop of Aleppo in 1253. In 1264 he became primate of the eastern Jacobites.

He wrote thirty-one works in Syriac and Arabic. They cover history, grammar, medicine, and theology. His "Chronicle" and his Syriac grammar are the best known. The entry calls him the last great Syriac writer. It also says his work shows almost no trace of his Jewish birth. His Bible notes cite Jewish views mostly at second hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hakkafot-7068:
Haḳḳafot are processional circuits made by the congregation in the synagogue on the Feast of Tabernacles. The worshipers circle the almemar, in memory of Joshua vi and of Temple practice told in Sukkah 45a. The circuit is skipped on the Sabbath. On other days a scroll is brought from the Ark, and those holding lulab and etrog follow the officiant, who chants the Hosha'na refrain.

The word also names the sevenfold circuit of Rejoicing of the Law, when scrolls are carried seven times around the synagogue. Sephardim use the same word for circuits on Hosha'na Rabbah and at the cemetery, around a coffin about to be buried. The entry notes the chants used, the Seliḥot-like tones of Tabernacles, and the newer tunes of the Law feast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanan-7168: Hanan is a Bible name shared by nine men in this list entry. Two are Benjamites: a chief, and Azel's sixth son, of Saul's family. One, a son of Maachah, counts among David's mighty men. One founded a Nethinim family that came back with Zerubbabel. One was a son of Igdaliah, whose sons had a chamber in the house of the Lord. The rest tie to Ezra and Nehemiah: a Levite who helped read the Law, chiefs who sealed the covenant, and Zaccur's son over the tithe stores.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hannover-nathan:
Nathan (Nata) ben Moses Hannover was a Russian historian, Talmudist, and cabalist. His birthplace and death-place are both disputed. Zunz puts his death at Ungarisch-Brod, Moravia, on July 14, 1663. Jacob Aboab names Pieve di Sacco in Italy instead. Hannover fled Zaslav in Volhynia when the Cossacks attacked. He studied Cabala at Venice. Later he served as rabbi of Jassy in Moldavia.

His fame rests on "Yewen Mezulah" (Venice, 1653). It is a full history of the Chmielnicki persecutions of 1648 and 1649. It covers Russia and Poland, with a vivid picture of Polish Jewish life and its yeshibot. The entry ranks him among the best historians of the seventeenth century. His other works include "Safah Berurah," a four-language dictionary (1660). He also wrote the prayer collection "Sha'are Ziyyon" (1662).
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harris-david-72:
David Harris, born in London in 1852, was an English soldier and mine director in South Africa. He reached the Kimberley diamond fields about 1873 and grew rich dealing in diamonds and claims. At the same time he built a military career. He fought in the Kaffir war and the Griqualand West rising, and he was praised in official reports.

In 1897 Harris won the Kimberley seat in the Cape Assembly without a contest. When war with the Boers began in 1899, he helped defend Kimberley at the head of 2,000 men. By 1903 he acted for the firm of Barnato Brothers in Kimberley. He also served as head of the local synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hecht-7468:
Hecht is a family based at Boston, Massachusetts. Jacob H. Hecht was born in Germany in 1834 and came to America in 1848. After years in California he settled in Boston in 1869. There he led the United Hebrew Benevolent Association for over fifteen years. He also headed the Federation of Jewish Charities.

His wife Lina founded the Hebrew Industrial School in 1889, to Americanize and teach immigrant Jews. His brother Lewis served many charity boards and a railroad company. Another brother, Louis, led the Leopold Morse Home. The entry maps a family whose money and time ran much of Boston's Jewish welfare work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henriques-jacob: Jacob Quixano Henriques, born at Spanish Town, Jamaica, in 1811, was a West-Indian merchant and a son of Abraham Q. Henriques. In Jamaica he founded a Jewish school for boys and girls. After moving to London soon after 1840, he helped form the West London Synagogue. He served as its warden and later as council chairman. In business he retired in 1864 in favor of his son. He also chaired the London Chartered Bank of Australia. He died in London on Oct. 17, 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezekiah-hebr-m:
Hezekiah, king of Judah from 726 to 697 B.C., was son of Ahaz and rose to the throne at twenty-five. The entry calls him unlike his father and unmatched among Judah's kings. His first act was to repair the Temple, closed under Ahaz.

Hezekiah removed high places, broke the brazen serpent, and made the Temple the sole cult place. He beat the Philistines as far as Gaza and revolted against Assyria. When Sennacherib invaded, tribute failed to stop a siege of Jerusalem. The entry recounts prayer, Isaiah's prophecy, and the Assyrian army's destruction in one night. His illness and added fifteen years are also told.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirszenberg-sam:
Samuel Hirszenberg, born at Lodz in 1866, was a Polish painter. He studied at the Academy of Cracow from 1881 to 1885. He finished his studies at Munich from 1885 to 1889. Two early paintings won him a silver medal at the Paris Exposition of 1889.

In Paris Hirszenberg took in the French school, seen in a work on Esther and Haman. Back at Cracow in 1891, he painted a Jewish cemetery scene. From 1893 he lived at Lodz again. Later works won prizes at Berlin, Warsaw, and Cracow. His greatest work, on the Wandering Jew, drew warm praise at Paris in 1900, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-of-evreux: Isaac of Evreux was a French rabbinical scholar and Bible commentator of the thirteenth century. Mordecai invoked his authority, and Perez cited him in glosses on the Semak. The "Da'at Zekenim" mentions him as a Bible commentator, and the "Sha'are Dura" quotes his responsa. The "Kol Bo" records that he corresponded with R. Nathanael. Gross identified him with the tosafist Isaac ben Sheneor, who taught Isaac of Corbeil. The entry offers no firmer dates or places for his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-kingdom-:
The Kingdom of Israel article gives the fuller history of the northern kingdom, beyond the sketch in the People of Israel article. It divides that history into four periods. First came confusion and near-anarchy. Then came national consolidation and brave self-defense. A third period swung between deep misfortune and success. A fourth brought humiliation under Assyria and ended in national extinction.

The first period runs from Jeroboam I to Omri, 934 to 886 B.C. The land David and Solomon had ruled was no true federation, only districts loosely joined, and the north had never acted together except in revolt. Dynasties rose and fell fast: Nadab was slain by Baasha, Baasha's son Elah by a plot, and at last Omri took the throne. The survey then follows Jehu's coup, Hazael of Damascus, and Jeroboam II, kingship by kingship, toward the Assyrian end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jabesh-more-ful:
Jabesh-gilead was the chief city of Gilead, east of the Jordan. It first appears in the war against Benjamin. Its people had refused to march with the other tribes, so 12,000 Israelites were sent against them. All were slain except 400 virgins, spared as wives for the surviving Benjamites. Early in Saul's reign, Nahash of Ammon attacked the city, and Saul came to its rescue.

The people of Jabesh never forgot that debt. When Saul and his three sons fell to the Philistines at Mount Gilboa, men of Jabesh went by night to Beth-shan, took the bodies down from the wall, and brought them home. They burned them, buried the remains, and fasted seven days. Scripture later praised the deed. Josephus calls Jabesh the metropolis of the Gileadites. Robinson held the ruins of Al-Dair to be its site.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobi-abraham-:
Abraham Jacobi was an American physician born at Hartum, near Minden, on May 6, 1830. He studied at Greifswald, Göttingen, and Bonn, taking his medical degree in 1851. Caught up in Germany's revolutionary movement, he was jailed at Berlin and Cologne on a charge of high treason from 1851 to 1853. Freed, he emigrated to America and settled in New York. He soon stood among the city's leading practitioners.

His field was the diseases of children. He held the chair at the New York Medical College, then at the University of the City of New York, then at Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons, from 1870 to 1892. He presided over the New York Academy of Medicine from 1885 to 1889. His books include "Infant Diet" (1874), "Diphtheria" (1876), and "Therapeutics of Infancy and Childhood" (1878). In 1903 he chaired the American commission to the Madrid medical congress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehovah-8568:
Jehovah is a misreading of the Hebrew name of God, the four-letter name that Jews treat as too holy to say aloud. Readers in the synagogue say Adonay, the Lord, in its place. Later Christian writers took the vowels of Adonay and set them under the consonants of the holy name, and that mixed reading produced the form Jehovah, which grammar does not allow.

The entry traces the form through early Christian writers and names Peter Galatin, confessor to Pope Leo the Tenth, as its spreader from 1518. It also explains a second pointing that signals readers to say Elohim instead, and notes older Greek habits of writing the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-world-th: Jewish World, in Yiddish Die Yiddische Welt, was a Yiddish daily paper founded in New York on June 27, 1902. A Lebanon printing company issued it, with H. Masliansky as its president. Its stated aim was to push the American way of life among Russian newcomers. Each issue carried one page in English, edited in turn by Joseph Jacobs, J. de Haas, and others. D. M. Hermalin was general editor in 1904, and the Yiddish poet Morris Rosenfeld wrote for the paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-ben-el:
Jonathan ben Eleazar was a Palestinian scholar of the third century, a fellow of Hanina ben Hama and a pupil of Simon ben Jose. Born in Babylonia, he settled among the leading Babylonian newcomers to Palestine. One tale shows the pupil gently correcting his teacher on a hard ritual point, until Simon owned it was too deep and led him to another school for the answer.

Jonathan gave freely to charity. He loaded visiting officials with costly gifts, he said, to smooth the way when a widow or orphan might need their help one day. He also ruled that a son can be forced to support his father, and once made such a son do his duty. His teaching that one must look guiltless before men as well as before God closes the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-josel-be: Josel ben Moses of Frankfort was a dayyan, a judge on a rabbinic court, at Fürth in the first half of the eighteenth century. He was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main. His one named work is Torat Yosef, printed at Wilmersdorf in 1725. It is a study of the Masorah on the Pentateuch, with a commentary by the author. The entry gives nothing more: no birth or death dates, no family, and no other writings. Its whole notice rests on two catalogues of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-b-abun-in: Judah b. Abun, in Arabic Abu Zakariyya, was a Spanish poet who lived in Seville. He was probably the son of the Abun whom Moses ibn Ezra praised in poems and mourned in an elegy. Moses ibn Ezra counts Judah among the Spanish poets, and Judah ha-Levi praised his learning highly. Only one short poem of his survives. It was sent in friendship to Judah ha-Levi, who answered it with a poem of his own. He is not the Judah Samuel Abbas who wrote a noted akedah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kellner-leon-92: Leon Kellner was an Austrian scholar born at Tarnow in 1859. He read Bible and Talmud until he was eighteen. He then took school subjects at Breslau and Bielitz. At Vienna he studied Germanic language study, above all English. He took his doctorate in 1884. From 1890 he lectured on English at the University of Vienna. In 1904 he became assistant professor of English at Czernowitz. His works include a study of Shakespeare.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klausner-joseph:
Joseph Klausner was a Russian Hebrew writer. He was born at Olkeniki, in the government of Wilna, on Aug. 14, 1874. In 1885 he went to Odessa and studied at the yeshibah there. He pursued both Talmudic and secular subjects. From 1897 to 1902 he studied philosophy and Semitic languages at Heidelberg. Returning to Russia, he became editor of the Hebrew monthly "Ha-Shiloaḥ" in 1903. In 1904 he took charge of the Warsaw department of a Hebrew encyclopedia.

The entry calls Klausner versatile and prolific, and a sound critic. He contributed to nearly every Hebrew publication of his day. He championed the modernization of the Hebrew language and literature. His works include a pocket dictionary of modern Hebrew. He also wrote on anthropology and on spiritual Zionism. A German study of Messianic ideas in the age of the Tannaites appeared in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-korban-lit-an-o:
Ḳorban, literally an offering, means first a sacrifice of any kind, bloody or bloodless. Josephus also uses it for a vow offering or for goods devoted to God. A second sense is the sacred treasury that held gifts for the Temple, or the alms box for the poor.

Vow use brings the entry's main argument. A man could block others from his goods by calling them ḳorban, and rash vows of that kind drew strong rabbinic checks. The entry answers the New Testament charge of hypocrisy against the Pharisees on this point. It shows sages dissolving vows that harmed parents or broke basic duties to others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-laban-9568:
Laban, son of Bethuel, was the uncle and father-in-law of Jacob, with his home in Padan-aram. He is called the Aramean. The Bible account first shows him greeting Abraham's servant and leading the talks over his sister Rebekah's marriage. Fuller space goes to his dealings with Jacob in Genesis, from welcome to wage disputes and flight.

Rabbinic reading paints Laban far darker. The Rabbis link his name with glowing wickedness and call him a master of impostors. Tales say greed drove his warm welcome, since he hoped Jacob carried gems. The entry also retells the swapped bride plot, with pledges, wine, and a darkened feast room. A second, short Laban names a wilderness place in Deuteronomy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lauterbach-edwa: Edward Lauterbach, an American lawyer born in New York city on Aug. 13, 1844, graduated from the College of the City of New York in 1864. The bar took him two years later. He sat in the state Constitutional Convention and chaired its charities committee. From 1895 to 1898 he led the Republican County Committee. Railway, telegraph, and marine law are his specialty. He helped rebuild the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad. College and orphan asylum boards also claim his time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leon-thomas-coo: Thomas Cooper de Leon, a lecturer, journalist, author, and playwright, was born at Columbia, South Carolina, in 1839. He was a brother of Edwin de Leon. He served in the Confederate army from 1861 to 1865. After the Civil War he edited "The Mobile Register" in 1877, and "The Gossip" and the "Gulf Citizen," both Mobile papers, from 1873 to 1896. His books include "Creole and Puritan" from 1889, "The Puritan's Daughter," and "Four Years in Rebel Capitals" from 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liebermann-max-:
Max Liebermann, a German painter, was born at Berlin on July 29, 1849. He studied law at Berlin University for a year, then dropped it. In 1869 he took up painting at Weimar. He went to Paris in 1872, lived in Holland in 1876-77, and settled at last in Berlin.

His canvases show working people and plain scenes: goose pluckers, orphan girls in Amsterdam, women making preserves, and net menders. Galleries in Hamburg, Berlin, Munich, and Strasburg hold his work. At first he painted the darker side of life in a stark realist manner. His "Jesus im Tempel" showed at Munich in 1879. In later years he turned toward a freer naturalist style.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-of-shpola-1: Löb of Shpola was an early Hasidic rabbi who died at an old age on Oct. 4, 1810. He had been a poor teacher in his youth and never took a great teacher as master. A single visit to Israel Ba'al Shem-Tob was his main link to fame, yet two of that master's heirs opposed him fiercely. Known as the Shpoler Zeide, he was honored for deep piety. He lived simply, gave most gifts away, and left no writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublin-meir-ben:
Meïr ben Gedaliah Lublin (1558–1616), known as the Maharam, was a Polish rabbi born at Lublin. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn profiles him. From a family of rabbis, he learned chiefly from his father-in-law, the rabbi of Cracow. Before age thirty he was called to Cracow’s rabbinate.

Lublin later served at Lemberg until 1613, arguing sharply with Joshua Falk, then returned home as rabbi until his death. Wherever he settled he ran a yeshivah, drawing pupils such as Isaiah Horowitz. The article describes his printed notes on the Talmud, still included in major Talmud editions, and his 140 published legal replies. It also describes his bold method: he corrected texts, attacked famous rivals, and rejected parts of the Shulhan Aruk. Readers get a full picture of a forceful scholar whose opinions carried across Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheim-10368:
Mannheim, a town in the grand duchy of Baden, receives a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It held 141,131 people in 1900, including 5,478 Jews. No Jews are known there before the mid-seventeenth century. In 1660 thirteen families won leave from Elector Karl Ludwig to settle.

The article follows the young community through fire and rebuilding. A burial ground dates from 1656, and the first rabbi, Naphtali Herz, served from 1657. By an early date seventy-eight Jews lived in town, and officials asked for no more permits. French devastation of the Palatinate then drove nearly seventy families from their burned homes. Heidelberg sheltered them until Mannheim was rebuilt by 1691. A concession of 1698 raised the community to 150 families. In 1708 a wealthy founder's Klaus, with synagogue and study house, was dedicated. The entry traces a planned court city where Jews rebuilt alongside it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massarani-tullo:
Tullo Massarani, an Italian senator who was also an author and a painter, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar. Born at Mantua in 1826, he studied law at Pavia and threw himself into the Italian revolution of 1848. When it failed he fled abroad, lived at Paris and in Switzerland, and finally settled at Milan, sitting in Parliament from 1860 to 1867.

The entry balances his three careers. As a painter he is best known for "The Warm Baths of Alexandria" and presided over the art jury at the Paris Exposition of 1878. As a writer he made Heine popular in Italy through an 1857 essay and translations. A long list of his books on art, politics, and Italian public figures closes the sketch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-eleaza:
Meir ben Eleazar, called Meir Lombard the Preacher, was a French liturgical poet of the first half of the thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surviving work clusters around Passover. He wrote a series of poems for the seventh evening of the festival, some arranged in alphabetical order. He also wrote an alphabetical introduction, six strophes of four verses, to the Targum passage read on the seventh day.

He wrote a dirge for Zion that signs his name, “Meir Hazak,” in an acrostic at its end. The entry ends in a scholarly dispute. Landshuth credited Meir with the dirge “Ahbirah millin,” recited on the Ninth of Ab. Zunz reassigned that poem to the far more famous Meir of Rothenburg. The notice thus preserves both a small body of festival verse and the uncertainty hanging over part of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-catulle-:
Catulle Mendès was a French poet, dramatist, and critic of the Parnassian circle. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Bordeaux in 1841, he settled in Paris from 1859. In 1861 he founded the "Revue Fantaisiste." Three years later he founded the "Parnasse." From 1893 he collected his theatrical criticism for the "Journal." He gathered it in an annual volume, "L'Art au Théâtre."

The entry calls him a perfect stylist inclined to the sensual. The risk was real. His "Roman d'une Nuit" was condemned as immoral in 1867. It earned him a month's imprisonment and a fine of five hundred francs. Then comes the shelf: volumes of verse from "Philomène" to "Les Vains Amours." It holds novels of the Commune and of Parisian monsters. It holds dramas, "Gwendoline," "Isoline," and "Médée," all staged in Paris. The Legion of Honor followed in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meza-mesa-10768:
Meza, also spelled Mesa, was an Amsterdam family noted for how many of its members held rabbinic office. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling record the family in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry sketches four men of the Spanish-Portuguese community across the eighteenth century. Their surviving works are mostly sermons printed in Portuguese.

Abraham Ḥayyim preached a solemn sermon in 1747. His son David followed with sermons on liberty and sin in 1767 and 1786. David also made an edition of the Aramaic paraphrase of the Song of Songs. David de Jacob left responsa in a 1741 compilation. Solomon de Isaac was a physician and ḥakam. He co-signed the famous 1711 decision backing the Shabbethaian Nehemiah Ḥayyun, and he died in 1742.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirabeau-gabrie:
Gabriel Honoré Riqueti, Comte de Mirabeau, was a French revolutionary statesman born in 1749. He earns his Jewish Encyclopedia entry through one cause: Jewish emancipation. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote the article in 1906. A secret mission to Prussia had brought him into Berlin's Jewish circles. There he moved around Henriette Herz and the reform writer Dohm.

In London in 1787 Mirabeau published a book on Moses Mendelssohn and the political reform of the Jews. Entering the States General, he promised a Jewish friend, in the article's famous quote, I will make a human being of you. He kept the promise beside the Abbé Grégoire. He pleaded the Jewish cause in the Assembly through the debates of August 1789.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montoro-anton-d:
Anton de Montoro was born at Montoro in 1404. He was a Spanish poet who sold old clothes and wrote verses the great admired. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. El Ropero, the clothes-dealer, he called himself. Baptized in old age, he remained, the entry says plainly, a Jew at heart all his life.

His poems confess it. To a Cordova magistrate he lamented that hunger had driven him to break his ancestors' oath and buy pork. He pled with Henry IV after the Marrano houses of Carmona were plundered in 1474. At sixty-five he complained to Queen Isabella that he was still called the old, contemptible Jew. Santillana and Juan de Mena prized his verse. Poets of his own race scorned him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-botarel-f: Moses Botarel Farissol was an astronomer and mathematician of the second half of the fifteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a four-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote a work on the calendar called Meleket ha-Kebi'ah and compiled calendric tables under the title Nofet Zufim. Both works survive only in manuscript, kept in the royal library at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosessohn-aaron:
Aaron ben Moses Mosessohn was a German rabbi who died at Ansbach in 1780. Gotthard Deutsch and Louis Ginzberg wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He served first at Dessau and was elected rabbi of Berlin in 1763. His name is tied to Moses Mendelssohn, in whose circles he moved.

In 1763 Mosessohn preached a thanksgiving sermon for the Peace of Hubertsburg, and Mendelssohn put the rabbi's name on its title page. He edited the He-Aruk mi-ShaK, his great-grandfather Shabbethai Cohen's commentary on the Yoreh De'ah, adding notes of his own. About 1771 he became rabbi of Schwabach and chief rabbi of Ansbach. It was on his word that Berlin's congregation made Mendelssohn an honorary member.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagasaki-11268:
Nagasaki, a commercial seaport of Japan, had about one hundred Jews in 1904. Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the community. Most of its members had emigrated from Russia. In 1894 they founded the synagogue Beth Israel and bought a burial ground.

The article names the founders: Goldenberg, who married a Japanese widow who entered Judaism with her children, and Lessner. Lessner also started a benevolent society in 1901 for poor Jews at home and abroad. About 1902 the community formed a branch of the Anglo-Jewish Association. Two Christians of Nagasaki had lately embraced Judaism of their own accord.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-armin-1:
Armin Neumann was a Hungarian lawyer and deputy. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Grosswardein on Feb. 14, 1845. He first prepared for the rabbinate at Breslau. Then he turned to law at Berlin and Vienna.

He took his degree at Budapest in 1868. His law office at Papa opened the next year. Budapest made him a teacher of commercial law in 1887. That same year his district sent him to Parliament. His speeches on money and tax reform won attention. In 1898 he joined the commission codifying the laws. The emperor named him aulic councilor for his services. His books expound trade, insurance, and patent law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-offenbach-11668:
Offenbach is a town in Hesse, a state in Germany. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews cast out of Frankfurt came there in 1614. They came up the river with an armed guard. Crowds met them with hate at each bridge. Offenbach was the one place that fired on them.

The town is best known for Jacob Frank and his court. Frank bought its castle in the year 1786. He took the title Baron of Offenbach for himself. He held court there till his death in 1791. He was laid to rest with great pomp in the town. For sixteen years the town drew Polish Jews in throngs. Frank's kin sent out their famed red letters from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orlah-foreskin-:
Orlah is a tract on the fruit of young trees. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means the foreskin of the trees, in Hebrew. The law stands in the book of Leviticus. Fruit of a new tree is held as orlah for three years.

In those three years the fruit may not be eaten. The tract is the tenth in the order Zeraim. That order treats seeds and the fruits of the earth. It holds three chapters and thirty-five parts in all. The first part sets which trees fall under the law. It sets which parts of a tree count as fruit. Leaves, blooms, and sap do not count as fruit here. So they are not barred by the law of orlah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palestine-laws-:
The laws of Palestine are rules that hold in that land alone. The board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such laws bear a Hebrew name that means land-bound laws. The piece sorts those laws in a set of groups. Each group ties to a part of life in the land.

One group held in the days of the Temple at Jerusalem. It held the lamb of Passover and the first fruits. It held the three feasts of the year's great trek. One group dealt with rule, with kings, and with wars. One dealt with the fruits of the soil and fields. It held tithes, gifts to priests, and the poor man's rights. It held the year of rest for the land's soil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peacock-11968:
The peacock reached Israel by ship in Solomon's day. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word tukkiyyim is read as peacocks. They came among the goods from Tarshish. The entry is brief but draws on Talmud passages.

The bird is native to India, not to Palestine. Its name may echo a Tamil word for its tail. The Talmud knows the bird under a Greek name. It bars crossing the peacock with a hen. One passage shows the bird counted as clean food then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peter-12068:
Peter was a Jewish scholar of the twelfth century. The Executive Committee and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Samuel ben Meir and Jacob Tam. His notes survive inside the Tosafot on the Talmud. He belonged to the tosafist circle of France.

Peter died a martyr in the Second Crusade. He was walking with a funeral party for a community leader. Crusaders attacked the group and killed him on the road. Ephraim of Bonn recorded the killing for later readers. A later writer garbled the place and the facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinkes-from-a-b:
A pinkes is the register book of a Jewish community. The Executive Committee and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In it the community recorded its acts and affairs. The word first meant a simple writing tablet.

The Greek word pinax gives the term its root. The Mishnah knows three kinds of such tablets. One bore dust for quick sums in figures. One bore wax, cut by a sharp stylet. One was smooth and took ink directly. From tablets the word passed to bound books. The open pinkes became a byword for God's record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontremoli-benj: Benjamin Pontremoli was a Turkish writer on rabbinic law who lived at Smyrna. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the end of the eighteenth century. His one work is called Shebet Binyamin. It came out at Salonica in 1824. The book treats the drawing up of trade papers. He had two sons, Hayyim Isaiah and Hiyya. Both sons became writers on Jewish law as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-printers-marks-:
Printers' marks are signs or pictures printed in a book by its maker. Joseph Jacobs and A. Freimann wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such a mark may be a seal or a coat of arms. It stood at the end of a book at first. Later it moved to the title page. Its use began soon after printing itself began.

A mark often plays on the printer's own name. A deer, for instance, stands for the name Zebi. Town arms and printers' seals were used as well. The first known marks come from Spain and Portugal. A lion on a black shield marks one book of 1485. A lion on a red shield marks a book of 1487. The article shows how Hebrew printers used the custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raba-properly-r:
Raba, more rightly Rabba ben Ulla, was a Babylonian teacher of the third set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The time at which he lived is not fixed with care. He was a friend of Ulla, the pupil of Johanan. His words are named before those of younger men.

Rabba was a teller of tales and wise sayings as well. Some of his maxims have come down to us in the Talmud. His words stand in the tractate Shabbat in two places at least. The article picks out those sayings for the reader. It weighs where his name stands in the chains of teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-porto-mena:
Menahem Abraham Rapa was an Italian rabbi who died on December 30, 1596. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Porto and later at Cremona. From his new home he took the name Rapoport.

The article says he studied Hebrew, medicine, and Talmud at Venice. He also proofread Hebrew books printed there. In 1553 he saw the Talmud burned by papal order. He kept that date as a fast for life. In 1574 he became rabbi of Cremona. His works include a study of secret writing and a Pentateuch commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reitlinger-fred:
Frederick Reitlinger was a French jurist born on June 18, 1836. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ichenhausen in Bavaria. He attended Saint Anna College at Augsburg.

The article says he studied Talmud under Abraham Geiger at Breslau. He then read law at Munich and Heidelberg. His criminal pleading won him fame across Germany. In 1866 Napoleon III asked him to write on cooperative societies. That book won him full French naturalization after one year. He practiced law in Paris from 1867. During the siege he escaped Paris by balloon on a mission. He later wrote a lively book about that voyage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rintel-moses-12:
Moses Rintel was an Australian rabbi born in Edinburgh in 1823. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Melbourne in 1880. His father Myer was a Hebraist and Talmud scholar.

The article says he served as reader at Brighton synagogue. In 1844 he went to Sydney in Australia. In 1849 Melbourne's East congregation elected him minister. At Sydney he founded a Hebrew academy. He also helped form a proper bet din there. In 1857 he resigned and a new synagogue formed. Mikveh Israel opened in 1860 with him officiating freely. Chief Rabbi Adler named him head of the bet din. His two printed sermons rank among Australia's earliest Jewish publications.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-isido:
Isidor Rosenthal was a German physiologist born at Labischin, near Bromberg, on July 16, 1836. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1859.

Rosenthal rose at Berlin, then became professor of physiology at Erlangen in 1872. His books study breathing and its link to the vagus nerve. Others treat electricity in medicine and heat control in warm-blooded animals. His general work on muscles and nerves reached a second edition in 1898. He also edited the Biologisches Centralblatt, a biology journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbionetta-129:
Sabbionetta is an Italian town remembered here for one Hebrew printer's career. Joseph Jacobs wrote its short entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. From 1551 to 1559 Tobias ben Eliezer Foa printed Hebrew books there.

Foa's Sabbionetta output opened with Joseph Shalit's Merkabat ha-Mishnah in 1551. It closed with the Hoshen Mishpat of the Tur in 1559. He began a prayer book there and finished it after moving to Cremona. His career was ended by force over certain anti-Christian books. A Christian printer, Vicenzo Conte, then took up his work and type.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanchez-sanches:
Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Antonio Ribeiro Sanchez. He was a Russian court physician, born in 1699. He died in Paris in 1783. Sanchez came from a Marano family of Penamacor, in Portugal. He fled Portuguese persecution and settled in Holland. There he studied medicine at the University of Leyden.

At Leyden, Sanchez won the friendship of the great physician Herman Boerhaave. In 1731 the Empress Anna of Russia asked Boerhaave for a learned doctor. He sent Sanchez. Sanchez rose fast at the Russian court. He joined the Imperial Academy of Science. He treated the young Princess Sophia Augusta, the future Catherine II. In 1744 he saved her from a dangerous illness. Three years later he was suddenly dismissed. He sold his property and moved to Paris. The reason for his fall was never made clear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiff-josef-13:
Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Josef Schiff. He was an Austrian stenographer, an expert in shorthand. Schiff was born on February 25, 1848, at Ragendorf, in Hungary. In 1874 he became teacher of stenography at the Vienna Academy of Agriculture. In 1898 he lectured on Gabelsberger's system at the University of Vienna.

In 1883 Schiff founded the Centralverein for Gabelsberger business shorthand. The Emperor of Austria later gave him the title of professor. His books teach the Gabelsberger system step by step. They include a course text, an exercise book, and a reader for trade schools. He also made shorthand dictionaries with the Vienna and Dresden styles. His dictation book served writers of all German systems. The Austrian Ministry of Instruction approved several of his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sebastus-13368:
Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sebastus. Sebastus was the harbor of Cæsarea on the Mediterranean. Herod made Cæsarea a great seaport. He named the city for Julius Cæsar. He named the harbor Sebastus to honor Augustus, called Sebastos in Greek. Coins of Nero read Cæsarea at the Port of Sebastus.

The article corrects a reading by the historian Grätz. Josephus speaks of Cæsareans and Sebasteni together. Grätz took them as citizens of two towns. The authors argue otherwise. Sebastus was never an independent city. The Sebasteni were the military troops stationed at Cæsarea. The other term covers the civil population. A single Greek phrase, they show, splits one city's people into soldiers and civilians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-nahamu-:
Shabbat Nahamu is the first Sabbath after the Ninth of Ab fast. Cyrus Adler and Wolf Willner wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name comes from its prophetic reading, which opens, Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Those words stand in Isaiah chapter forty.

The reading belongs to a set series of special lessons. Three Sabbaths before the fast use warnings from the prophets. Seven after it use words of comfort. Old sources list the same order used today. Groups differ slightly on the weeks before, but all agree on this one. The entry shows how the calendar turns grief into comfort, week by week.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheshet-13568:
Sheshet was a Babylonian amora of the third generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He often argued points of religious law with Nahman bar Jacob. He sat in on Huna's lectures as a young scholar.

Sheshet spoke sharply about sayings of Rab that displeased him. Rab must have said that while asleep, he would remark. He studied first at Nehardea, then moved to Mahuza. Later he founded an academy of his own at Shilhe. Though blind and frail in body, he had an iron will. The entry draws a vivid portrait of a blind sage whose memory and energy outmatched his peers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-samuel-da:
Samuel da Silva was a Portuguese-born physician living at Amsterdam in the early seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He is known chiefly for his fight against Uriel da Costa. Costa questioned Pharisaic tradition in a bold new book.

Before Costa's book even appeared in print, Silva acted. He had read part of it in manuscript form. In 1623 he published a Portuguese booklet against its author. Leading members of Amsterdam's young Portuguese community directed that attack. Its title proclaims a treatise on the soul's immortality. The book ably defends that doctrine against Costa's denial. Silva mocks Costa as blind and incapable Uriel. The entry recalls a fierce print duel over the soul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sindbad-13768:
Sindbad is a set of tales about the wiles of women. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A stepmother seeks the death of an Indian prince. His seven masters delay his execution by telling tales. Each tale warns against the tricks of women. The frame works much like the Arabian Nights.

Benfey held that the book began as an Indian story book. It likely passed from India westward in stages. It was rendered into Zend, then Syriac or Arabic, then European tongues. The Hebrew version is called Mishle Sindabar. It holds four tales found in no other version. The entry follows the book across all these forms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jud:
Solomon ben Judah ha-Babli was a liturgist of the tenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Despite his name, he was likely not from a Muslim land. Rapoport held that ancient rabbis counted Rome as Babylon. Solomon may thus have been a native of Rome itself.

He taught Meshullam ben Kalonymus, a major figure of the age. He wrote many piyyutim and selihot for the prayer book. One yozer of his begins Or yesha, light of salvation. Rashi and Jacob Tam both mention that poem with respect. His selihot use four-line strophes without a Bible verse. Scholars must take care not to confuse him with Ibn Gabirol.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spiro-joseph-mo:
Joseph Moses Spiro was an Austrian rabbi and Talmudic author of note. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Trietsch, Moravia, about 1770. His father Abraham, rabbi in Trietsch, educated him at home. Though a sickly child, he became a fine Talmudist early.

He served as rabbi at Schafa, Habern, and finally Kanitz. He held the Kanitz post from 1824 until his death in 1830. He urged systematic instruction in religious literature for children. He condemned the pilpul method of study very severely. He edited the Sefer ha-Hinnuk at Brünn in 1799. His Mesillah le-Elohenu treated the evils of unsystematic child training.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-syria-14168:
Syria is a country of western Asia under Turkish rule. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The name Syria never appears in Hebrew scripture. It enters usage only in the Greek period. Scholars usually derive it by shortening Assyria.

Herodotus treated Syria and Assyria as one name in two tongues. Winckler instead traced Syria to a Babylonian word for the West. The Septuagint uses Syria to render the Hebrew Aram. In politics the name meant the Seleucid empire. Its capital moved from Babylon to Antioch on the Orontes. The realm shrank until Pompey made it Roman in 65 B.C.E. Strabo and Pliny fix its borders at Taurus and desert. The entry disentangles one name's shifting map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taussig-edward-:
Edward David Taussig was an American naval officer born in 1847. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at St. Louis on November 20. He entered the Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1863. He graduated in 1867 and stayed in active service.

Taussig climbed the officer ranks over three decades. He served on Pacific and European stations for years. In 1898 he took command of the Bennington. He claimed Wake Island for the United States. When Spain ceded Guam in 1899, he took charge there. The Philippines and China saw his service next. By 1903 he commanded the Pensacola navy-yard. Though of Jewish descent, he was raised Unitarian. The entry traces a sailor who raised flags for America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thessaly-14368:
Thessaly, a province of northern Greece on the Aegean Sea, held old Jewish communities. Isidore Singer and M. Caimi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews had lived there since very early times. Those present in 1905 spoke Spanish and claimed Spanish descent.

Communities stood at Larissa, Trikala, and Volo. None had a rabbi, and Hebrew study had decayed. Jewish schools at Larissa and Trikala taught religion with state support. Larissa once grew rich and earned the name Tree of Gold. A riot of poor Jews against the rich drove many away. The Greco-Turkish war of 1897 hurt the town further. Its fine synagogue still recalled better days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trabot-trabotti:
Trabot, or Trabotti, was a family of Italian scholars from France. Schulim Ochser and Isaac Broydé wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Members bore the extra name Zarfati, meaning the Frenchman. They flourished from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century.

Several Azriels served as rabbis at Rome, Florence, and Ascoli. One list of rabbis by an Azriel runs from Rabina to his own day. Jehiel Trabot held posts at Pesaro and Ferrara. His responsa survive only in manuscript copies. Levi Trabot left France for Italy, then Jerusalem. Nathaneel of Modena ranked among Italy's most respected rabbis. The entry follows the family town by town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ventura-14668:
Ventura was a family of rabbis and scholars in Italy and Greece. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Members of the family were active for three centuries. They served towns across Italy and the Levant.

The entry sketches several of them. Eliezer ben Samuel was rabbi of Ferrara, where he died in 1534. Elijah ben Abraham wrote comments on Talmud sayings and on Elijah Mizrahi. His three part work appeared at Salonica in 1799. Isaac Hananiah and Isaac ben Moses served at Pesaro and Ancona. Their legal answers survive inside other printed collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wertheimer-sams:
Samson Wertheimer was an Austrian court Jew, financier, and rabbi. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms on January 17, 1658. He died at Vienna on August 6, 1724. He studied at the yeshibot of Worms and Frankfort. In 1684 he moved to Vienna.

Wertheimer joined Samuel Oppenheimer in serving the emperor. He won Emperor Leopold's personal trust and gifts. During the Spanish succession war he raised army funds. After Oppenheimer's fall in 1703, he kept state credit alive. In 1703 the emperor named him court factor. His privileges ran for twenty years. Joseph I confirmed them all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wogue-lazare-el:
Lazare Eliezer Wogue (1817-1897) was a French rabbi and a top teacher of Jewish study. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Fontainebleau, he trained at the rabbinical school at Metz. He took his rabbi diploma in 1843 and went back to Paris.

In Paris he preached beside the chief rabbi of the city. In 1851 he won a chair of Jewish theology at Metz. He kept that chair until he retired in 1894. When the school moved to Paris, his load grew. He taught Hebrew grammar, Bible study, and German there. For sixteen years he also ran the paper Univers Israelite. France gave him the Legion of Honor in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zappert-bruno-1:
Bruno Zappert (1845-1892) was an Austrian playwright and news writer of Vienna. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His kin came from Bohemia and spread to two lands. His sire was a maker of goods in that realm.

He schooled at the town gym school in his youth. He wished to read at a great school of the land. In 1862 he joined a trade school to aid his sire. The death of his sire changed his plans in full. He went into the book trade at Vienna in time. In 1869 he took sole charge of a known book house. He ran that house for eight years of his life. He then turned to the stage and wrote for two houses.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume nine of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter sixty one. An event from the prior July is set in its place here. The King travels to Fontainebleau and stays till mid September.

The Duchesse de Berry, with child for the first time, falls ill. Her doctor, Fagon, begs that she put off the trip a day or two. The King grows angry and grants a boat in place of a coach. No one may go out, not even to the opera next door. Madame de Saint-Simon was ordered to watch that she obeyed. Court care here shows as strict watch over a sick lady.
nilsson-primitive-inhabitants-scandinavi:
Sven Nilsson, a Swedish sage of beasts and old times, wrote this classic on the first folk of Scandinavia. John Lubbock turned it into English in 1868. Nilsson had long taught that the north had its own stone age, rich with finds.

He sets out the stone tools, shell heaps, and graves of the first north men. He matches them with the ways of wild folk of his own day to guess their life. The book is the north's match to the French case for deep age man, and a classic of its kind.
npt-1968:
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signing in 1968, after years of fear that atomic weapons would spread to many nations. It rests on a bargain between the states that already had nuclear arms and those that did not. Nearly every country in the world has since joined, making it the widest arms control agreement in force.

States without nuclear weapons promise never to build or receive them, and they accept inspections of their atomic programs. The nuclear powers promise to work toward disarmament and to share peaceful nuclear technology. The bargain has kept the circle of nuclear-armed states small for over fifty years, even as disputes over disarmament and enforcement continue to test it.
nsa-ufo-hypothesis-1968:
Analysts at the National Security Agency weighed what UFOs might mean for human survival in 1968. UFO Hypothesis and Survival Questions sets out five hypotheses for the things seen in the sky. The paper is laid to Lambros Callimahos, a famed code man of the agency.

Each hypothesis is tried for what it would ask of mankind if it proved true. The close is a fable, the Tale of the Rattler, on how pride can blind a mind to a new fact. The monograph is philosophy from inside the most sealed of agencies. It shows cleared men wondering aloud at their own desks.
nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-1868:
Henry Callaway published Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus in 1868. Callaway, an English missionary and later bishop in Natal, took the tales down in the Zulus' own words. He prints the Zulu text with English translation and notes, so readers meet the storytellers' phrasing, not a summary.

Tricksters, ogres, and clever children fill the nursery tales, while the traditions recount chiefs and migrations. The histories preserve how Zulu elders of that generation told their own past. Callaway's method was new: record first, interpret with care, and credit the speakers. His volume became the founding English collection of Zulu oral literature. Folklorists still build on the texts he saved from vanishing.
openalex-w1979540468:
Nicolas Moiroux, Cédric Pennetier, and co-authors studied mosquito biting. The catalog record gives no author or year; the sample names them. They worked in Benin, France, Thailand, and Tanzania. Anopheles funestus is a major malaria vector in Africa. Its biting had shifted toward early morning hours.

The shift followed distribution of long-lasting insecticidal nets. Two villages in south Benin showed the change clearly. The team measured human exposure with behavior surveys and models. Net protection stayed high overall, they found. Yet much remaining exposure happened outdoors or near dawn. New control tools must target those gaps, they argue.
openalex-w2059124668:
Mark Costello, Marta Coll, Roberto Danovaro and colleagues summed up world knowledge of marine biodiversity. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. It drew on the Census of Marine Life. That programme ran for a decade worldwide. It was the largest study of ocean life ever.

The paper merged reviews from all major ocean regions. It counted species richness by region. It also counted endemic and alien species. Gaps in knowledge were mapped alongside the counts. Many regions remain sparsely and unevenly sampled. Numbers of experts and guides varied greatly too. The authors list future challenges for ocean science. Protecting marine life needs better basic knowledge first.
openalex-w2118672468:
Ary Teixeira de Oliveira-Filho and James Alexander Ratter traced the origins of central Brazilian forests. Their paper appeared in Edinburgh Journal of Botany in 1995. Central Brazil mixes savanna with several forest types. Where those forest plants came from was unclear. Distribution patterns can reveal ancient links.

The authors analysed over a hundred floristic checklists. They also mapped fifty-five woody species in detail. Two main distribution patterns emerged clearly. Dry forest species followed fertile soil patches southwestward. Gallery forest species followed moist river corridors. Those corridors link Amazon and Atlantic rainforests. Western galleries tied more strongly to Amazonia. Southern galleries tied more to Atlantic forests.
openalex-w2134712068:
Naoko Kozuki, Anne Lee, Mariângela Silveira, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in BMC Public Health in 2013. They asked how a mother's age and number of prior births relate to risks for her baby. Outcomes included babies born too small or too early, and deaths in the first month and first year.

The team combined fourteen cohort studies from low- and middle-income countries. First-time mothers under eighteen had the highest odds of every bad outcome studied. Risks were also raised for women with three or more prior births, including those over thirty-five. The authors urge renewed effort to delay first births and care that spans a woman's whole reproductive life.
openalex-w2229420368:
Alejandra Escobar-Zepeda, Arturo Vera-Ponce de León, and Alejandro Sánchez-Flores published this review in Frontiers in Genetics in 2015. They trace the road to metagenomics, the study of whole microbial communities through their DNA. Microbes fill every corner of the planet, yet most resist growing in a lab, which long hid them from science.

The review walks the timeline from Leeuwenhoek's first microbes and Koch's cultures to high-speed DNA sequencing. That leap remade both microbiology and computing, since community DNA data are huge and tangled. New software keeps arising to gather, clean, and mine such data. The authors stress that good experiment design, backed by real bioinformatics understanding, unlocks what a metagenome holds.
openalex-w2788640168:
Lorenzo Galluzzi, Ilio Vitale, and Stuart A. Aaronson lead the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death's 2018 recommendations in Cell Death and Differentiation. For a decade the committee has standardized how cell death is defined and described. The field keeps expanding, with new mechanisms blurring old categories. This update revises the classification around mechanism rather than appearance.

The authors give exact definitions for a dozen-plus forms of cell death. The list runs from intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis through necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis. It also covers rarer forms like entotic and lysosome-dependent death, plus senescence and mitotic catastrophe. They discuss when specialized new terms help and when they confuse. A widely accepted word set keeps talk clear across labs. The paper is the reference point for naming how cells die, as of 2018.
openalex-w2797697368:
Marianna Arvanitakis, Jean-Marc Dumonceau, and Jörg Albert lead these 2018 guidelines in Endoscopy, from the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. They cover care by endoscope for acute necrotizing pancreatitis, where part of the pancreas dies. Most cases of pancreatitis clear up quickly, but this severe form strikes up to a fifth of patients. It brings organ failure, procedures, and death at high rates.

The guideline weighs radiology, endoscopy, and surgery inside step-up treatment plans, drawing on many fields. It advises acting when infected tissue death is suspected or proven.
