Spatial features describe what a leaf looks like in one image; sequential features add how signs unfold across views or time. Better detection lets growers treat sick plants earlier and spray less widely. Agricultural imaging researchers and growers of this regional crop are the audience for a model tuned to its diseases.
plos-pone-0359068: Al-Halaseh and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a wild herb and its power against cancer cells. The plant is Artemisia herba-alba, used in folk medicine. The team tested a crude extract and its key plant compounds in lab dishes. Computer docking added hints about how the compounds might act. Early lab results like these guide which plant chemicals merit deeper study.
pmc-10655068:
Ying Gao led a team that made, in two thousand twenty-three, a film that can hide gear from scans. Scans read the light a thing sends back at many hues. A fake that looks green can stand out. The film must match how leaves send back light.

The film is polyvinyl alcohol with lithium chloride, chlorophyll, and titanium dioxide grains. The dye gives the leaf-like curve, and the grains scatter light. With ray tracing and a Kubelka-Munk model, the team worked back from tests of light sent through and off the film to the traits of each part. From those traits, they could tell how shifts in the mix change the curve. At grain, dye, and water shares of 0.7, 5, and 50 per cent, a film 0.3 mm thick met a US force rule. Its curve matched a sweet olive leaf, score 0.976.
pmc-10655468:
Amber Bidner, Eva Bezak, and Nayana Parange survey rural Australian clinicians about pregnancy ultrasound access. Their needs analysis from twenty twenty-three targets remote practice realities. Ultrasound catches high-risk pregnancies early enough to act. Rural women and babies face worse outcomes and thinner services.

An anonymous online questionnaire reached doctors, nurses, midwives, and managers. It probed service availability, actual use, and training access. Clinicians reported interest in more ultrasound training. Limited resources shape daily practice in these regions. Recommendations aim to raise service quality and access together. Training pathways for rural generalists are a key lever. The findings speak for remote regions worldwide too.
pmc-10656568:
Monika Ettinger leads a team on Th17 signals in Darier disease skin. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with a rare inherited disorder. Gene faults drive sore, infected skin in this disease.

Treatment options are few and weak for long term care. Skin samples from patients went to gene and protein profiling. Single cell sequencing mapped the immune cell mix. Th17 related genes and signals were raised in lesions. More Th17 cells were present in the skin. Antibody drugs against that axis helped a small case set. Gains were marked in those treated patients.
pmc-10669368:
Te-An Chen and colleagues test two soap-based ways to strip cells from a heart scaffold while keeping its frame, in this study from twenty twenty-three. The frame, called extracellular matrix, is the mesh that holds tissue together and cues cells how to grow. Their mesh came from heart fibroblasts grown in aligned sheets from human stem cells. It mimics the weave of real heart wall.

One wash paired EDTA with SDS. The other paired a bile salt with an enzyme that chews DNA. Both washes cleared cells to the accepted limit and kept most mesh proteins and growth factors. The EDTA and SDS wash did the job faster, so the team picked it. Heart muscle cells grown on the cleaned frame lined up along its grain and switched on mature heart proteins. The result is a recipe for heart-like lab-grown scaffolds.
pmc-10673368:
Ah-Hyun Park, Tae-Hoon Seo, and two colleagues grow light-emitting layers on an unusual base in this two thousand twenty-three materials paper. Gallium nitride makes near-ultraviolet LEDs, but it is normally grown on sapphire. The team tried growing it on hexagonal boron nitride, a flat, sheet-like material, and on graphene, to see if the nitride layer would form well. On boron nitride the layer grew with a smooth surface.

Checks with light emission and X-rays showed the crystal quality was worse than standard-grown gallium nitride. Still, the team built a near-ultraviolet LED stack on the boron nitride base. The device worked well in tests. The result shows boron nitride can serve as a base for growth of gallium nitride. It is a step toward LEDs built on layered materials that might one day peel free of their wafers.
pmc-10693568:
Zehua Du and colleagues improve appliance identification from household electricity signals. Their methods paper from twenty twenty-three targets non-intrusive load monitoring. Smart grids need to know which devices draw power, without extra meters. Voltage-current shapes carry clues, but classic mapping methods extract them poorly.

The new structured mapping rethinks how those shapes are drawn. A lightweight neural network, based on a known design, reads the maps. Tests used a standard load monitoring dataset for comparison. Accuracy rose clearly over earlier trajectory mapping methods. The design keeps computing demands modest for practical deployment. Utilities could spot appliance use patterns more reliably with such tools.
pmc-10701968:
Alice Malpass and co-authors report a project that used art to build research partnerships in this 2023 paper. Creative methods may help researchers and community members meet on equal ground. Artist partners designed four online workshops, each on a set topic. Topics were school mental health, Somali community wellbeing, air pollution, and health data.

Each workshop was observed, and chat logs were saved. Interviews with 21 participants added personal views. The team compared what worked across the four very different sessions. Good ideas could win seed funding to continue after the workshop. The evaluation asks whether shared creative work can start lasting, fair collaborations rather than one off consultations.
pmc-10706868:
Fuhang Liu, Dan Ma, Jinyu Yu, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It shows that boosting a rice gene, OsNAC016, makes the plant tougher against aluminum, a metal that poisons roots in acidic soils.

Rice already tolerates aluminum better than most crops, thanks largely to a master switch gene called ART1. The team found OsNAC016 by screening for partners of ART1, and confirmed it works in root cell nuclei. Deleting the gene changed nothing, a puzzle at first. But plants making extra OsNAC016 gathered less aluminum in their roots and grew better in its presence. Gene readouts showed cell wall and transport genes shifting in the boosted plants. The authors conclude the gene teams up with ART1 to run part of the tolerance program, a lead for breeding hardier rice.
pmc-10707768:
Mervat Youssef and co-authors test ways to strengthen armor steel in a 2026 paper. They added tiny amounts of niobium and applied repeated heat-and-quench cycles to refine the grain. The goal is lighter armor with a high strength-to-weight ratio.

Two lab-made steels were heated to two peak temperatures and quenched three times in a row. Microscopy showed mostly martensite of several forms, plus a small share of carbides. Software modeled how the phases transform during the cycle. Wear was measured with a pin-on-disc tribometer. The authors weigh how niobium and grain refining change wear behavior.
pmc-10715968:
Shapero and co-authors present a pregnancy case managed with lipid apheresis, a blood-filtering treatment for severe lipid disease. Familial hypercholesterolemia is an inherited disorder that causes very high cholesterol and early heart disease. Many of its drugs lack safety data in pregnancy, which limits care for expectant mothers.

Their patient carried the disorder through pregnancy and was treated safely with a combination approach. Lipid apheresis, which pulls lipids from the blood outside the body, formed a novel part of that plan. The case offers guidance for heart and pregnancy teams facing the same hard balance.
pmc-10716268:
Van Nguyen and co-authors follow eye degeneration in rabbits bred to model a human blindness-and-deafness syndrome, in a 2023 study. Usher syndrome type 2A erodes the retina over years. Twelve rabbits, half with the gene knocked out, were imaged repeatedly for a year with five non-invasive techniques. Sound-based, light-based, and dye-based scans each revealed different layers of the damage.

A key light-sensing band began breaking down at four months and kept worsening. Dye images showed the supporting pigment layer decaying as well. The sound-based scans mapped the optic nerve and tiny vessels in three dimensions. Numbers drawn from the images tracked the decline precisely. The authors say combined imaging gives drug trials a rich, needle-free scorecard.
pmc-10727668:
Yu Li, Le Fei, and Jiandang Shi ask whether infected spinal bone must be cleaned out in this two thousand twenty-three study. Brucellosis can infect the lumbar spine, and surgery typically includes cleaning the infected tissue. The authors compared sixty-three patients with single-segment lumbar Brucella spondylitis treated by rear fixation and bone graft fusion: thirty-four without cleaning, twenty-nine with. All were followed at least a year.

Skipping cleaning shortened operations, reduced blood loss, and shortened hospital stays, all clearly. Everything else matched: infection markers, pain scores, functional improvement, spinal alignment, and fusion rates, about ninety-two versus ninety-six percent, showed no clear differences. The authors conclude early single-segment lumbar brucellosis spondylitis can be cured by rear fixation and grafting alone. Avoiding cleaning offers less trauma and faster recovery without sacrificing cure.
pmc-10729168:
Iffat Zafar Aga and five co-authors used telepsychiatry to gauge mental health needs in a low-resource part of Pakistan, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Care was given through nurse-aided online clinics run by Sehat Kahani for low-income areas. Two short forms, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, were used to screen for low mood and anxiety. The study covered two thousand six hundred sixty people seen from October to December twenty twenty-two.

Nearly all who took part were women. About seventeen percent had moderate low mood and about twenty-one percent had severe low mood. People who were widowed or divorced were more prone to low mood than those who were single. The authors say women in Pakistan bear a heavy share of these ills, and that care by screen can reach them where clinics are scarce.
pmc-10731168:
Ting-Yu Jin leads a team with a case of double antibody nerve disease. Their case from twenty twenty-three deals with a woman of nineteen. Her illness is in the neuromyelitis optica spectrum group.

She had a year of dizzy spells, nausea, and vomiting at first. Blurred sight, slurred speech, and drooped lids came later. Weak arms and legs then set in ten days before admission. Spine fluid held two antibody types at her relapse. Scans showed bright spots in her brain on set views. Roles of the second antibody stay unclear.
pmc-10732368:
Orschiedt and Franklin study how learning context shapes control of the two hands. Two-handed moves underpin daily actions, yet how the brain joins learning across hands is unclear. Past work showed that arm motion context helps form internal models of new forces.

The open question is how the control system ties a learned memory to the states felt during two-handed moves. The team tested whether context changes the strategy people use and how well learning spreads to new situations. Results clarify how the brain stores bimanual skills, with lessons for training and rehabilitation after injury.
pmc-10735868:
Yanping Jiang, Fengyan Tang, and Bei Wu read how fitting in to a new culture shapes health in old Chinese migrants to the United States. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, deals with acculturation: the shift from Asian to Western values and ways. Past work on its health mark was mixed and most of it cut one time slice. Near three thousand elders in Chicago, age sixty to one hundred four, were tracked in a set cohort.

A twelve item scale read their fit by tongue use, friend ties, and media. Mood, body, and mind health were set next to that score across time. Readers in migrant health get a long view where most had a snap shot.
pmc-10736968:
Shelia Cotten and Amy Schuster challenge the assumption that constant digital connection equals digital inclusion, focusing on older adults. Most people now communicate and exchange social support through devices many times a day. Older adults, though, have adopted these technologies more slowly, and their patterns differ from younger groups.

Drawing on national data and life course theory, the authors argue that constant connection may be normative for the young without being right for older adults. Perhaps it should not be the goal at all. They close by examining how digital inclusion is socially constructed and how widely its meaning varies. The presentation asks researchers to rethink what inclusion should mean in later life.
pmc-10738568:
Varun Saraswathula and five co-authors compared belly pain care in the emergency room across age groups in a study from twenty twenty-three. A surgeon reviewed more than a thousand visits at one community hospital in the United States. The review covered tests, scans, diagnoses, and what happened to each patient.

Older adults got scans more often than younger adults, and their scans more often found urgent problems. The range of likely causes was also wider in older patients, which made their cases harder to sort out. Still, the authors judge that younger adults may be scanned too much. Older adults, in turn, may not be tested enough given their higher risk.
pmc-10738668:
Murad Taani, Yura Lee, Julie Ellis, Chi Cho, and Ammar Hammouri linked social isolation to thinking skills in older adults, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Isolation was scored across partnership, family and friends, worship, and club life. Data came from a national aging survey at two points, four years apart.

More isolated adults scored lower on a combined test of memory, orientation, and executive skill. Scores also fell over time for the group as a whole. White adults scored highest on average, with other groups ordered below. Race and ethnicity, though, did not change the strength of the isolation link itself. The authors call for programs that draw older adults into community activity to guard thinking.
pmc-10740668:
Ignacio Martin-Loeches and seven co-authors set out a many-center watch study of heart harm in grave lung fever caught out of hospital. Their study is from two thousand twenty-three.

The fever is the top cause of dire breath fail in deep care. Past watches tie it to heart ills in the ill folk. The risk of sharp heart harm is at its peak in the first month of the stay. The team took, in a row, deep-care patients with germ-proved cases. Fine heart scans and blood marks sought hid harm to the heart's frame. Patients were split by the germ at fault, to read how harm sorts by cause.
pmc-10742568:
Lara Girelli and co-authors published this study in 2023. It reviews join complications after bronchoplasty, a lung-sparing operation that rejoins the airway after removing a tumor section. A referral cancer center analyzed 280 such operations. Nine in ten were for lung cancer. Complications at the join occurred in about six percent of patients. Late narrowing was the most common, then a leak between airway and chest space.

Survival did not differ clearly between patients with and without join problems. But deaths within thirty days ran higher when complications struck. Spread to lymph nodes stood out as a risk factor, likely marking more radical surgery. For treatment, the center favors surgery for dangerous leaks. Benign narrowings get a balloon stretch through a scope instead.
pmc-10745068:
Tong and four co-authors test rutting in asphalt mixes rich in reclaimed pavement under full-scale loaded tracks, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Balanced mix design frees engineers from strict volume rules to design better roads. Virginia's new rules allow very high shares of recycled asphalt. The team asks whether those mixes rut more under heavy loads.

They test surface mixes with forty-five and sixty percent recycled content. All balanced high-recycle mixes rut deeper than the control mix. Extra binder added for crack resistance likely explains the gap. Lab rut tests track the full-scale results closely. The team suggests lowering the lab rut limit to screen out weak mixes. Findings rest on stated assumptions and limits.
pmc-10747168:
Taejin Kim, Hyojin Kim, and Qian Chen review bone loss in critically ill patients. Their review from twenty twenty-three explains causes and management options. Intensive care patients lose bone density at alarming speed. Fragility fractures then threaten recovery long after discharge.

Immobility, inflammation, hormone stress, and poor nutrition all contribute. Several common intensive care drugs also weaken bone. The authors count bone loss as part of post-intensive care syndrome. Nutrition and protein support help protect the gut and bones. Anti-resorptive drugs and physical therapy are under study. Recognising bone risk early could prevent later fractures. The review argues bone care belongs in critical care planning.
pmc-10750068:
Di Tang and five co-authors ask what esports is, in a systematic scoping review from twenty twenty-three. Definitions of esports and its related concepts crowd the literature. They disagree in ways that confuse research subjects and terms. The team gathered definitions and coded their characteristics thematically.

The coding brought out the disagreements and issues between rival definitions. The authors joined those results with facts about the current esports industry. Theories from similar fields also shaped the reconstruction. They propose a structured definition of esports. They also map how it links to neighboring concepts. These criteria aim to standardize terminology in esports research. Clearer definitions, they argue, will prevent misunderstandings in future studies of the field.
pmc-10752268:
Lv and six co-authors checked in twenty twenty-three if a blood mark from bile tracks kidney disease in folks with diabetes in the United States. In Asian groups that mark had looked like a guard. They used a large state health survey that ran for more than a decade.

More than five thousand folks with diabetes were in the check, and near three in ten had kidney disease. In the whole set the bile mark showed no firm link to that disease. In men, high marks went with near a third less risk than low marks. In folks past sixty-five, mid marks went with near a fourth less risk.
pmc-10752568:
Anna Jon-And and co-authors ask whether representing sequences could be an early step in the evolution of language. Language is compositional, open-ended, and sequential, yet the path from no language to language stays hard to trace. Decoding order is required for language, so a general ability to represent sequences is a candidate foundation. Using formal evolutionary analysis, the authors weigh the costs and benefits of that ability.

They find sequence representation is exceedingly costly. The memory systems seen in today's animals may block the abilities language needs. For the trait to evolve, minds must be able to ignore irrelevant information flexibly. Two further conditions help: plenty of useful sequential information in the environment and long learning opportunities. Both likely held early in human evolution. The authors propose this as a plausible route to human cognition and culture.
pmc-10753468:
Amanda Vivo and six co-authors review antibiotic outcomes in veterans in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Their patients had bloodstream infections with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter, a hard-to-treat bacterium. The team asked which regimens were used at Veterans Affairs hospitals and whether any tied to survival.

The cohort held one hundred eighty-four patients treated from two thousand twelve to two thousand eighteen. Most infections were one species, Acinetobacter baumannii. Two drug classes dominated prescribing. Early analysis hinted at lower thirty-day deaths for some regimens, but the links vanished after adjustment. Combination therapy did no better than single-drug therapy on any mortality window. The authors found no regimen with a clear survival edge.
pmc-10758668: Hatice Türe and Haluk Gümüş trace the first century of anaesthesiology and reanimation as a scientific field in the Republic of Turkey, in a historical paper from twenty twenty-three. The field began with easing pain during surgery. Over the century it has grown into a specialty covering far more complex techniques and areas of care. The authors review the path the field has covered in Turkey since the republic was proclaimed. They frame that record as groundwork for the next hundred years of the discipline.
pmc-10800168:
Shunsuke Tanoue and four colleagues assess wrist-artery access for brain vessel procedures, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The transradial route promises fewer puncture complications than the groin route. Real-world difficulties, especially seating the guide catheter, were understudied. Records covered procedures at one institution over about two and a half years.

Of three hundred ten patients, two hundred twenty-two were selected for the wrist route. Success reached ninety-five percent; five percent switched to the groin. Challenges arose in about a fifth of cases. Left-sided front-circulation targets caused most trouble. A sharply curved aortic arch type and age over eighty predicted difficulty. Severe puncture complications were the safety yardstick. The authors map where the wrist route works and where it strains.
pmc-10834868:
The authors report five cases of a rare type of multiple myeloma treated with CAR T-cell therapy, in work published in 2023. The paper is written in Chinese and covers the IgD subtype of the blood cancer, which strikes younger patients, carries a heavy tumour load, and has a poor outlook. Relapsed cases are harder still.

The therapy retools a patient's own T cells to target a marker called BCMA on the cancer cells. The five patients were drawn from a registered trial and had already failed many lines of treatment. The report details each case, the responses reached, side effects such as cytokine release syndrome, and survival follow-up. One patient reached a deep complete response that held for years. The series adds rare evidence for cell therapy in this subtype.
pmc-10845068:
Ayushi Gupta and Suresh Nair probe epigenetic diversity in brown planthopper populations, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The planthopper is a sap-sucking rice pest blamed for massive yield losses. Even populations that are genetically uniform show wide variation in their traits. Differences of this epigenetic kind are one candidate source of that spread.

Field populations were gathered across rice-growing seasons over two years in a row. A methylation-sensitive restriction assay gauged site-specific methylation in five stress-responsive genes. The protocol proved cheap to run and rapid. Populations that look the same to the eye turned out to be distinct in their epigenetic marks. Epigenetic polymorphisms not seen before showed up in the field samples. The authors present the markers as a platform for studying how such marks shape this pest's power to adapt.
pmc-11535068:
Five researchers report lab work from two thousand twenty-four on new drug leads for lung cancer. They focus on cancers that resist drugs aimed at a growth signal called EGFR. The team designed six new compounds that join three chemical parts: a chalcone, a triazole ring, and an isoquinoline unit.

The six compounds were tested on five human cancer cell lines and on one healthy lung cell line. Two of them stood out, killing lung cancer cells at low doses while doing little harm to the healthy cells. Computer studies helped explain the shape of the compounds. Tests also showed the two leads block the EGFR signal strongly.
pmc-11547368:
Mawuse Amedzo-Adore, Jeong In Han, and Teng Zhai dope a layered iron vanadate with shift metals to lift its charge store worth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The base stuff can host many charge acts, but its store score in use runs low. A cold gel route was used to add cobalt, manganese, nickel, or zinc in its place.

Doped forms with wider layer gaps beat the plain form on store tests. The manganese form scored best, with a high store mark and near nine in ten held after long use. The plain form held just past half. The team backs doped layered forms for store tools.
pmc-11588768:
Wang leads a large team reviewing a peony extract for kidney disease in children, in work from twenty twenty-four. The disease is IgA vasculitis nephritis, where immune deposits harm the kidney filters. It is most common in children.

Standard care uses steroids and immune suppressing drugs, which carry many side effects. Total glucosides of paeony are a natural plant extract with a good safety record and low cost. Past work shows it acts on many pathways and targets in this disease. The review sums up progress and future prospects, making the case for careful trials of a gentler option for young patients.
pmc-11590268:
Tatsuhito Ikezaki and co-authors study hip replacement after an earlier bone shelf operation in a 2024 paper. The shelf procedure adds bone coverage for hips with dysplasia. Whether it leaves enough bone for a later total hip replacement was unclear.

The team matched 46 conversion replacements after shelf surgery to 46 standard replacements for mild dysplasia. Before surgery, the shelf group had worse scores and stiffer hips. After replacement, scores and motion nearly matched between groups. All cups sat at the true hip center, though cup coverage was lower after shelf surgery. Bone grafting rates were similar.
pmc-11590368:
Rachel Jaber Chehayeb and colleagues followed cancer patients on immune therapy in 2024. Some older adults carry blood cell gene changes called CHIP. Those changes raise death and heart muscle disease risks. They also stir immune cell activation in heart failure. Whether they raise heart inflammation risk from immune drugs was unknown. The team enrolled solid tumor patients in a forward-looking study. Blood sequencing set each patient's CHIP status at entry. Heart inflammation events were tracked for years.

Half of the eighty-eight treated patients carried CHIP changes. Heart inflammation struck far more often in that half. Death also ran higher among CHIP carriers. Adjusted models doubled the risk from CHIP status alone. That matched the risk from using two immune drugs at once. Coronary calcium was the only uneven health trait. The authors urge CHIP checks before immune therapy starts. Closer heart monitoring may suit carriers, they say.
pmc-11595268:
Biyang Zhu and co-authors break seaweed sugars with light and peroxide to make better calcium haul chelates. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Calcium-bound sugars are a ripe path for calcium aids. Cut size split the yield: small cuts bound calcium more, thanks to more acid groups freed by the cut.

Cut chains ran short and soft against the stiff rods of the whole sugar. Bind to calcium was free and charge-driven on heat reads. Small chelates crossed gut cell sheets well and sped calcium in-flow. They also shield sheet walls from harm to tight joint parts. The team backs the cut route for aid design.
pmc-11603068:
Rosa Katia Bellomo and John P A Ioannidis offer a two thousand twenty-four appraisal of umbrella reviews in vaccine research. Umbrella reviews gather all systematic reviews on one question. They promise a top-level view, but only if done rigorously.

Vaccine literature is vast, with hundreds of thousands of papers and thousands of reviews. The authors examine how well umbrella reviews in this area report and conduct their work. Strengths and limits of the format are laid out through these examples. They close with improvements that could make such syntheses more trustworthy for public health decisions.
pmc-11605068:
Changwei Yang and co-authors simulate how vibratory rollers pack down highway roadbeds, in a 2024 study. Builders compact the soil layers under a road with heavy vibrating rollers, and settings decide the quality of the result. The team built a finite element model of roller and roadbed in the ABAQUS program and checked it against field tests. A signal method split the field vibrations by frequency band.

Each frequency band in the spectrum reflected how well a different zone of fill was packed. Peak shaking fell with distance from the roller, sideways and downward, but rose again at the edge of the vibration field. Some mix of force, frequency, and layer thickness worked best. The waves spread through the ground in an ellipsoid shape, weakening as they went.
pmc-11605868:
Taco van Welzenis and nine co-authors report quality-of-life results from the international IMPACT survey of adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, in a two thousand twenty-four rare disease paper. The condition, brittle bone disease, is usually tracked through fractures; its human cost is broader.

Fourteen hundred forty adults answered the online survey in eight languages. Depending on the life area, between forty-nine and eighty-four percent said the condition affected their quality of life: eighty-four percent for leisure activities and seventy-four percent for jobs. Worry about mobility loss, future fractures, and aging ran as high as ninety-seven percent on some items. Severity and fracture frequency consistently drove the burden.
pmc-11607868:
Yao and co-authors catalog the TALE gene family across the sorghum genome in this 2024 study. TALE transcription factors steer plant growth, development, and stress responses in many species. Sorghum had never had a systematic survey of them.

The team found 23 TALE genes on ten chromosomes, split between the KNOX and BEL1-like families. One tandem duplicate pair and seven segmental duplicate pairs turned up. Family members share conserved motifs and structures, and sorghum's set aligns most closely with maize. Most genes expressed most strongly in stems, while two favored leaves. Expression dipped late in grain development. The catalog gives breeders named targets for sorghum improvement.
pmc-11608168:
Alexey Surov and a large team test a simple score that predicts survival in liver cancer patients treated with a vessel-blocking therapy. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The score blends a blood protein, albumin, with the density of skeletal muscle read from scans.

The team looked back at seven hundred and eighty-four patients treated for the first time at six major centers between twenty ten and twenty twenty. Fat inside muscle and low muscle density mark poor muscle quality, a known risk in cancer. The combined score was checked against survival with standard methods. It sorted patients by outlook more usefully than muscle measures alone. Such a score, built from routine data, could help doctors judge who will do well on this treatment.
pmc-11608468:
Burton and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-four on an online singing program for mothers with postnatal depression. Lockdowns had cut in-person support for new mothers. A group singing program moved online and lifted symptoms in earlier checks. Interviews with twenty-four mothers explore how it helped. Two theory frames sort the program's active parts and change paths. Design, content, and group makeup match the in-person version. Social and setting parts differ in the online form.

Mothers report stronger confidence and brighter moods. Loneliness shrinks as bonds with family grow. New routines restore a sense of time. The authors distill design lessons for remote creative health work.
pmc-11610168:
Shinya Miura and co-authors studied early predictors of poor outcomes in children with acute respiratory failure in two thousand twenty-four. Breathing failure is a leading cause of critical illness in children. The team used a national inpatient database in Japan covering two thousand ten to two thousand twenty-two.

They included twenty-nine thousand three hundred sixty-two children who got ventilatory support in the first three days. Most received invasive ventilation, and pneumonia was the top diagnosis. About nine percent died in hospital or left with new health problems. Older age, underlying conditions, pneumonia, and treatment at a low-volume hospital each predicted worse outcomes. The authors say these early signs can guide risk sorting and care planning.
pmc-11610368:
Davide Antonio Mei and colleagues merge two large patient registries to study narrowed leg arteries in people with a racing, uneven heartbeat, in this analysis from twenty twenty-four. The heartbeat problem is atrial fibrillation, and the leg problem is peripheral artery disease. Both raise the risk of clots and death, but how they interact across regions was unclear.

The pool held more than fifteen thousand patients in Europe and Asia. About six in a hundred had the leg artery disease, and it was far more common in Europe than in Asia. Patients with the leg disease were less likely to get blood thinners, the standard guard against stroke in this group. They also died more often and had more major heart events, and the extra risk hit younger patients hardest. The authors urge doctors to spot the leg disease early in these patients and not hold back proven treatment.
pmc-11611968:
Tchaikovski and co-authors test blood serum from 31 patients with full blocks in heart vessels. In full blocks, side vessels grow to route blood past the clog. Beast tests show growth cues drive this, but human data stay thin. The team drew blood past the block and from the aorta root. They fed serum to vein cells in a dish and tracked cell growth. Serum from blocks aged one to three months drove the most growth.

Serum from blocks that were newer or older drove less cell growth. No trait of age, sex, or health state tracked the growth score. The peak lines up with the span when side vessels grow most in beast tests. The authors mark that span as the best time to try to boost growth.
pmc-11612168:
French and a large team report how open gene data across one children's hospital sped up rare disease care, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Rare diseases in youth are hard to diagnose without gene tests. The hospital built a shared program that offers high-grade gene reads to research studies. Results flow back to care teams and to shared research banks.

Since launch, sixty-six leads from twenty-six units have joined the program. They enrolled over four thousand families in forty-five disease groups. About a third of cases gained a firm or likely gene finding. The shared bank now holds data for over thirteen thousand patients and families. The program sparked new studies, more diagnoses, and faster research overall.
pmc-11612668: Ahmed Abdelkader and colleagues reported an adult bowel telescoping case in two thousand twenty-four. One bowel segment slid inside the next segment. Such events are uncommon in adults. A large growth in the small bowel caused this case. The growth acted as a lead point for sliding. The affected section was the jejunum.
pmc-11613368:
Yongcai Weng and co-authors compared two operations for children with fluid trapped behind the eardrum. One group of seventy-one children had only their adenoids removed; another group of seventy-four had adenoid removal plus a tiny ventilation tube placed in the eardrum. Records came from one hospital's cases between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three.

Three months after surgery, the combined operation worked better. Children recovered hearing sooner, ringing stopped earlier, the eardrum healed faster, and the fluid cleared more quickly. Their blood also showed lower levels of inflammatory markers, and fewer cases came back. Complication rates were the same in both groups. The authors conclude the combined approach is equally safe and more effective for this condition.
pmc-11614568:
Seven authors report a case in two thousand twenty-four of removing an early growth from the voice box area with an endoscope. The patient was a man of sixty whose stomach exam found a flat lesion, about one and a half by two centimeters, on the flap above the windpipe. Tests showed early abnormal growth, with no spread.

The team cut the lesion out from below the surface lining, working with the patient under water immersion. A thin tube placed through the nose kept his airway open during the work. The report walks through the imaging, the biopsy results, and each step of the procedure in this tight, hard-to-reach space.
pmc-11619468:
Laverde-Sudupe and co-authors report a complex HIV case in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A woman aged fifty-five from Cuba, living with HIV and taking her treatment, was admitted in Miami with painful swallowing and swollen neck glands. Tests showed a fungal infection, histoplasmosis, spread through her body.

Brain scans then raised concern for toxoplasmosis, a parasite infection of the brain, and blood tests supported that view. Her worsening may have been driven by immune recovery itself, a known problem when treatment restarts the immune system. She improved on drugs for both infections and left the hospital with follow-up planned. The authors stress wide thinking and close watching in such patients.
pmc-11620468:
Rana Abutaima and colleagues survey knowledge, attitudes, and practices around GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among the general public in Jordan. Their 2024 cross-sectional study uses a validated online questionnaire.

Three hundred eighty-nine responses were analysed, with women forming about two-thirds of participants. Over half were married, and most lived in central Jordan. Fifty-seven percent believed diabetes medicines could be used for weight loss. Recognition varied by brand, with one diabetes drug recognised by over two-thirds for weight use. Only about twelve percent had actually used medication to lose weight. Attitudes overall were neutral, and regression explored links with knowledge and attitude scores.
pmc-11627368:
Yuen, Lemaire, and Wilson review what is actually known about placental DNA floating in a pregnant person's blood in this 2024 article. This cell-free placental DNA already powers noninvasive prenatal testing in clinics worldwide. It also promises a window on the placenta's genome without invasive sampling.

The review covers where the DNA comes from and what its molecular traits are. Despite wide clinical use, the basic biology behind the fragments stays poorly understood. That gap limits both research designs and new clinical uses. The authors map the open questions and suggest directions for future work. The piece serves readers who use these tests and want their foundations made clear.
pmc-11629668:
Xinqia Huang and colleagues load bone-building instructions into vesicles from embryonic stem cells, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The exosomes were fed to umbilical cord stem cells in dishes, and packed into scaffolds placed in bone defects of rats whose ovaries had been removed, a stand-in for postmenopausal bone loss.

The vesicles pushed the cord cells toward bone: mineral staining rose, and master bone genes switched on. Profiling the cargo fingered one microRNA, miR-21-5p, which suppresses a brake protein called YAP1 and thereby wakes the Wnt growth pathway. In the rats, treated defects rebuilt denser, better-organized bone than controls. The authors propose embryonic exosomes as a cell-free bone therapy, with the microRNA axis as its engine, a strategy aimed squarely at osteoporotic repair.
pmc-11632468:
Mark LaGreca, Arash Badragheh, Nathan Jones, Thomas Falconiero, and Brian Danshaw review cases of a rare back compartment syndrome treated with no surgery. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. In limb cases, a tight fascial space is cut open at once. For the back form, some doctors had tried rest and care alone, with no review of those cases till now.

They gather all such reports in print. Weight lifting is the top cause, then hard sport and surgery. All patients are men, with sharp back pain, stiff muscles, and odd skin sense. Half get back to normal life, while half keep some signs. Late arrival is the top reason surgery was skipped.
pmc-11639868:
Jeremy Hengst and colleagues studied how a synthetic cannabinoid kills colorectal cancer cells in 2024. A special form of cell death can alert the immune system, and the team's earlier work linked fat-like signalling molecules called sphingolipids to that process. The compound studied raised levels of one such molecule, ceramide, in cancer cells.

Experiments traced the effect to a cannabinoid receptor and to fresh ceramide production inside the cell. Lowering a natural brake on that production pathway mattered, and one ceramide type made mainly by a specific enzyme proved key to the immune-alerting death. The authors conclude the receptor shifts ceramide production toward the forms that drive this death.
pmc-11640168:
Andreea-Mariana Negrescu, Leonardo Zampieri, Emilio Martines, and Anisoara Cimpean wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests a jet of cold plasma, a stream of energized gas, as a possible treatment for gingivitis, the early stage of gum disease.

Cold plasma can kill germs, calm inflammation, and help tissue heal, which makes it attractive for dentistry. The team aimed a homemade plasma jet at two cell types involved in gum disease: gum fibroblasts and macrophages, the immune cells that clear debris. They measured whether the cells lived and grew, how their shapes changed, and what signals they released. The tests map safe and useful treatment settings cell by cell. The authors present the work as a first step toward plasma tools for gum care.
pmc-11640968:
Tahrima Kayes and Vincent Ho review liver failure from a death cap mushroom. Their review from twenty twenty-four deals with Amanita phalloides. It is one of the most toxic mushrooms known to man.

Signs start late as gut ills that mimic stomach flu. Grave liver harm then hits, and many organs can fail. The poison blocks a key enzyme, which kills liver cells. Care runs from fluids and charcoal to blood clean methods. Drugs like silibinin and others are part of care. Liver transplant is needed in the worst cases.
pmc-11641368:
Yuanhua Gu and co-authors published a 2024 study on a tiny ring of RNA in goat muscle. Rings of RNA, called circular RNAs, are a newer focus of genetics. One ring stood out in the back muscle of goats, but its job was unknown. Muscle growth depends on satellite cells, spare cells that can multiply and turn into new muscle fibers.

The team first confirmed the ring is real and mapped where it comes from. It is built from parts of three genes that make muscle motor proteins, plus stretches between them. Most of the ring sits in the cell nucleus, with the rest in the surrounding fluid. It was most abundant in three working muscles. The team then tested what the ring does to satellite cells in the lab, covering how it affects cell growth and change into muscle. Such knowledge may help breeding goats for meat production.
pmc-11642968:
Nazila Ameli and co-authors build a decision support tool that reads dental notes to stage gum disease. Their study appeared in 2024. Periodontitis, a deep gum infection, needs staging and grading to plan care. Those facts sit inside free-text charts and notes. The team trained a language model, BERT, on 309 anonymized patient charts from a university clinic.

The model learned to assign stage and grade from the notes alone. On 32 unseen patients it scored 77 percent for stage and 75 percent for grade. A hand-built feature model served as the comparison. The authors say note-reading tools could speed diagnosis and make staging more consistent. The study is a step toward decision support that works from records clinics already keep.
pmc-11643868:
Cristina Mihaela Ormindean and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, how a high-fat diet in pregnant rats affects their pups, and whether plant compounds help or harm. Obesity is a rising health problem tied to a cluster of risks called metabolic syndrome. Fat tissue acts as a hormone organ, sending signals that shape many body tasks. The team used five groups of seven female rats. One group ate a low-fat diet. Four groups ate a high-fat diet.

Of the high-fat groups, one got no supplement. The other three got known drug or nutrient mixes with antioxidant plant compounds. The team tracked mothers and pups at set points in pregnancy and after birth. They weighed body changes in both.
pmc-11644268:
Bin Xue, Jun Li, Qu Yang, and a wider team wrote this engineering paper, published in 2024. It studies a tri-screw extruder, a machine that melts and mixes plastics with three interlocking screws instead of the usual one or two.

Standard extruders often mix high-grade plastic blends poorly. The team built math and motion models of the three-screw system, with a shaking force applied along the middle screw. Their analysis shows the tri-screw setup stretches and shears the plastic more than a twin-screw machine, which evens out the mix. The added shaking changed the strain rates further and improved how the melt flows and processes. The work gives designers a base for building better extruders for hard-to-mix materials.
pmc-11644668:
Seonghark Jeong and co-authors improve LiDAR mapping for self-driving cars by removing moving objects with a camera-based detector. Their 2024 paper starts from a weakness of GPS in cities, where signals are blocked. LiDAR maps offer a backup, but passing vehicles smear into them as false structure.

Their system pairs the YOLO vision detector with LiDAR, deleting vehicles and other dynamic objects while keeping buildings and other static features. Earlier LiDAR-only removal missed objects and flagged false ones. Tests used a mid-size SUV carrying both sensors. Map matching and localization errors fell in both open and urban areas, with the larger gain in the city. Cleaner maps help a car know where it is in dense traffic.
pmc-11646268:
Shan Su and Limin Tian link dietary tryptophan to bone strength in older adults, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Their data came from a national survey of 12,003 people aged fifty and up. Bone density and food intake were both on record.

People with low bone mass ate less tryptophan than those with normal mass. Each near-tripling of intake tied to about a fifth lower risk of low density. The top two intake quarters showed clearly lower risk after full adjustment. The link bent rather than running straight, and it held across subgroups.
pmc-11646868:
Jerry Fan and five co-authors report the preemptive use of a small heart pump in a woman with peripartum cardiomyopathy and cardiogenic shock during delivery, in a two thousand twenty-four case report. Managing heart failure around childbirth is a high-stakes multidisciplinary challenge.

Rather than relying on catecholamine drugs, the team placed an Impella CP microaxial flow pump early to unload the left ventricle and support circulation through delivery and recovery. The case illustrates how temporary mechanical support can be planned into delivery care at specialized centers. Anesthesia, maternal-fetal medicine, and cardiac intensive care coordination frame the report's practical lessons.
pmc-11648868:
Pornpun Laovachirasuwan and three colleagues published a 2024 study on a plant-based tablet meant to guard eye health. Two plant extracts go into the tablet. Lutein comes from marigold flowers, and naringin comes from the fruit membrane of the pomelo, a large citrus fruit.

Both compounds are linked to eye protection. The team used a special column method to pull lutein and naringin out more fully. Their best recipe mixed 350 mg of marigold extract with 300 mg of pomelo membrane extract. Lab checks then graded the tablet's quality and strength. A steady, well-made tablet matters if the supplement is to reach users with the dose the label claims.
pmc-11653768:
Tahereh Fathi Najafi, Sareh Dashti, Ali Naghsh, and Maryam Saboor Parsa examine why mothers died in Iran's Razavi Khorasan province. Their records study was published in twenty twenty-four. Maternal death is a core health measure, and knowing causes is the first step to prevention.

Forensic files held two hundred and fifty deaths across eight years up to twenty twenty-two. The team compared the earlier and later halves of the period on background, pregnancy care, delivery, and confirmed cause of death. Deaths from indirect and unrelated causes grew significantly in the later period. That shift suggests prevention must look beyond delivery care itself toward chronic illness and wider system gaps.
pmc-11654368:
Shen and Ding write a letter in twenty twenty-four on breathlessness in patients whose lungs fail to take in enough oxygen. They discuss a study of three hundred such patients in intensive care. In that study, stronger breathlessness meant a higher chance of needing a breathing tube, but not a higher chance of death.

The pair note a puzzle in the data. Patients who felt more breathless often had better oxygen scores, not worse ones. So breathlessness must reflect more than oxygen alone, such as harder breathing work or distress. They ask whether patients with strong breathlessness but fair oxygen scores always need early tube placement. Gentler support, like high-flow oxygen, might serve some of them instead.
pmc-11655568:
Elodie Rey leads a seventeen-author team assembling genomes for a diverse panel of quinoa plants, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Quinoa is prized as a future food security crop. Breeding better varieties requires deep knowledge of the species' genetic diversity.

Eight accessions, spanning lowland and highland types, received chromosome-scale assemblies. Long-read sequencing combined with optical mapping produced them. Each assembly runs about 1.28 billion bases, with tens of thousands of predicted genes. Roughly two-thirds of each genome is repetitive sequence. Aligning the eight genomes exposed their structural differences. The resource supports agronomic improvement as quinoa cultivation expands worldwide. Diversity panels like this one anchor modern crop genomics.
pmc-11655768:
Ho and co-authors test if older adults can use phone and tablet health surveys with ease. Such surveys, called ePROMs, collect patient reports in trials. Some fear that age or poor health may block their use in real studies.

The team ran 60-minute in-person interviews in the United States and France. The group included older people with and without bullous pemphigoid, a rare skin disorder. Staff watched each person do tasks on a tablet and a smartphone. They scored how easy each task felt and where users got stuck or needed help.
pmc-11655868:
Yang and co-authors uncover how a DNA-building protein helps cancer cells repair damage and resist treatment. RRM1 is the catalytic part of ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme that makes DNA building blocks. High RRM1 levels appear in many cancers and track with worse prognosis for patients.

The team found RRM1 boosts homologous recombination, a precise DNA repair route. It does so by raising RAD51AP1 transcription through USP11 and the E2F1 factor. Stronger repair makes tumor cells less sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy. The chain of links names new points where drugs might break that resistance.
pmc-11656368:
Basharat, Hussain, Arif, and Miran build in twenty twenty-four a sensor that detects dopamine, a brain signal chemical, without using enzymes. Tracking dopamine helps doctors spot diseases such as Parkinson's, but tests must be cheap, fast, and sharp. Their sensor coats a carbon probe with a mixed layer of copper framework, zinc oxide, and a conducting polymer, topped with a natural amino acid.

The team checked the layer with X-ray, light, and microscope methods, then tested it with three electric methods. The sensor picked out dopamine even when other body chemicals were present. It reached a very low detection limit and strong response per unit. The authors credit the mix of porous framework and fine particles for the gain.
pmc-11656968: Jacob Vine and co-authors reply to a letter about their trials of thiamine, vitamin B1, for septic shock, debating who the vitamin might help. The exchange appeared in 2024. Another group re-analyzed its trial for kidney outcomes and found no clear thiamine benefit in patients not yet on dialysis. Vine's team notes the endpoint differs from theirs, that death competes with dialysis and can hide benefit, and that the other thiamine arm began with worse kidney numbers. They keep the search for the right target population open.
pmc-11657568:
Junmin Dong and Xiaohua Hao benchmark, in twenty twenty-four, docking tools for finding inhibitors of BRD4, a protein that reads gene marks and drives some cancers. Virtual screening docks many candidate molecules into the protein's binding site on a computer. Accuracy depends on the docking protocol and the scoring function used to rank poses. They selected seventy-three crystal structures of the protein's first domain bound to ligands. Two docking methods were compared by how close their poses came to the crystal poses.

One protocol reached about eighty-six percent docking accuracy. Among seven scoring functions, PMF correlated best with measured inhibition strength, while Ludi3 was worst. Heavy atom count also correlated strongly with potency. The authors name PMF the best scoring tool for this target.
pmc-11658368:
Fang Chen and colleagues examine how bullying connects to suicidal thoughts in college students. Their survey study from twenty twenty-four covers online and traditional bullying. Emotional problems may carry bullying effects toward suicidal ideation. Two major suicide theories frame the analysis here.

Nearly three thousand students in South China completed the survey. Correlation checks mapped links between all key variables. Mediation models tested which feelings carry the effect. Hopelessness joins emotional distress in the proposed pathway. Specific affective problems were tested separately for their roles. Both bullying forms connected to higher suicidal thinking. Campus support should screen bullied students for those key feelings.
pmc-11663668:
Xuefeng Tan and co-authors mapped where sports tourism resources sit across the Sichuan-Chongqing city cluster in China, and what drives the pattern. Using geographic information systems and a tool called GeoDetector, they measured how concentrated the resources are. They also measured which geographic and economic factors explain the spread between the twin hubs of Chengdu and Chongqing and their neighbors.

Terrain shaped development differently around the two cities. Population density correlated strongly with resource density, which the authors note cuts both ways: crowds attract facilities, but chasing density alone deepens inequality between places. They present the analysis as a planning roadmap for spreading sports tourism more evenly and sustainably across the region's varied landscapes.
pmc-11664268:
Haque and five co-authors built and tested Dristi, a Bengali-adapted phone app for eye screening, in twenty twenty-four. Poor vision goes undetected in low-resource settings like Bangladesh, where clinic access is thin. A phone test in the local language could catch problems early.

The Android app checks far and near vision using adapted Bengali letters, modeled on the Snellen chart, plus color blindness tests and eye health lessons. Validation ran from June to September twenty twenty-two across hospitals, a school, and a clinic. Accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity looked promising for both distance and near tests, though results varied by site. Many participants also had diabetes or hypertension, common eye health risks. The authors see the app as a step toward wider mHealth eye care.
pmc-11667968:
Ko-Wang Yen and four co-authors report a new way to build fused ring compounds found in many useful chemicals, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Their method uses palladium, a metal catalyst, to join parts of a starting material together in one step.

The starting materials are ring-shaped esters tied to an oxygen-linked aromatic ring. Under palladium, the ring closes by forming a new bond at a carbon that loses hydrogen, giving benzofuran-fused products. Tests with heavy hydrogen suggested that breaking the aromatic carbon-hydrogen bond may be the slow step of the whole change. The work adds a direct route to these fused rings, which chemists can use as building blocks for more complex compounds.
pmc-11668668:
Zongyuan Xie, Liangjie Lin, Changjun Ma, and Ailian Liu published a 2024 study on reading a tumor trait from MRI scans. The cancer is endometrial carcinoma, which grows in the lining of the womb. Tumors that make a lot of a protein called HIF-1α, a response to low oxygen, tend to behave worse. Checking the protein now requires tissue testing after surgery.

The team looked back at 122 patients whose tumors were tested. Sixty-five showed high levels of the protein and fifty-seven low levels. All had two kinds of MRI before surgery. One kind highlights blood vessels and water movement; the other tracks how a contrast agent flows through tissue. Measured values from both scans were compared between the groups. The authors test whether scan numbers can stand in for the tissue test. Such a shortcut could guide care before any operation takes place.
pmc-11669668:
Sibo Meng and three co-authors map a research field with bibliometric tools in a 2024 paper. Their topic is the link between RNA methylation, a chemical tagging of RNA, and immune cells inside tumors. They searched a major citation database for a decade of articles and reviews, then charted the field with three analysis programs.

Thousands of papers qualified, and output has grown steadily. Chinese authors and institutions lead in volume and influence growth, with one university on top for paper count. One specialty journal carried the most papers, while a general journal's papers proved most influential. Hot topics now include a specific tag type, immunotherapy, and the tumor immune environment.
pmc-11669868:
Zhuan Zou, Bin Chen, and seven co-authors pool evidence on machine learning for spotting seizures in children. Their systematic review and meta-analysis, from twenty twenty-four, searches four major databases. Studies up to late August twenty twenty-three qualify. Quick, reliable seizure detection remains hard in pediatric wards.

Each study's bias risk is graded with a standard tool. A combined model pools accuracy across the studies. Results also break down by data type and algorithm. The synthesis gives builders of smart monitors a firmer base. Gaps in the primary studies stand out for future work. The authors aim to guide safer, better detection tools for children.
pmc-11673568:
Zhaojun Li and co-authors lift both light output and charge flow in atom-thin tungsten disulfide, in work published in 2024. Such thin sheets hold promise for future electronics, but flaws in the sheet hold their performance far below what theory predicts. Past attempts to mend the flaws gave uneven gains, because the surface chemistry at work was not well understood.

The team traced that chemistry and built a treatment in two steps. A sulfur-bearing molecule goes on first, and a lithium salt follows. Together they heal both neutral and charged sulfur gaps, the main flaws in the sheet. Light output and charge flow each rose about a hundredfold, in step. Fast light tests, deep X-ray probing, and theory-based sums back the claimed process. The authors present the result as a new quality mark for this class of material.
pmc-11673968:
Dai and seven co-authors measured shrimp feed genetics in this study from twenty twenty-four. Fishmeal is scarce, so farms want shrimp that thrive on plant-based feed. The team compared a fishmeal-free diet against a quarter-fishmeal diet in Pacific whiteleg shrimp. They tracked leftover feed, daily growth, and daily intake.

On plant feed, shrimp left more feed uneaten and grew far slower. The traits proved strongly heritable under both diets. Yet the genetic rankings shifted between diets, especially for growth. That genotype-by-diet effect was strongest for daily gain. The authors conclude breeding must target the plant diet itself, not assume fishmeal winners will transfer.
pmc-11674468:
Bahi and Dreyer test whether boosting a brain enzyme, uPA, eases stress-driven anxiety and low mood in rats. Early proof hints this enzyme shapes mood and thinking, partly through a growth factor called BDNF. Its role in set brain areas under stress was not yet clear.

Virus carriers raised enzyme levels in the hippocampus of rats after social defeat stress. Treated rats showed less anxiety in marble burying, open field, and maze tests. Normal movement did not change. Mood tests, such as the sucrose splash test, also improved. Higher BDNF levels are the proposed path behind these gains.
pmc-11675068:
Yunrui Lu led a large team mapping cell diversity in clogged arteries in a 2024 study. Fat-filled immune cells are a hallmark of the disease, but their variety inside human plaques was unknown. The team merged data from eight earlier studies, covering gene activity, tissue position, and gene control in single cells.

They sorted the fat-filled cells into five subsets with distinct jobs. Some drive more fat uptake, some clear dead cells, some move fat out, and some head toward death or a building role. A branching path links the early form to two late forms. Tests on tissue confirmed the subsets exist, and the work names genes that may steer the harmful path.
pmc-11675568:
Marta Pena and three co-authors examine how managing workplace relationships warmly supports employee well-being. Their study came out in 2024. They use a scale they validated in several hundred Spanish workers, measuring how people draw on relational resources to adapt at work.

The scale held up as reliable, with a confirmed three-part structure, though it behaved slightly differently for men and women. In their model, good relational management predicted life satisfaction mainly through one route: flourishing, a state of thriving and purpose. A second proposed route, through extra-role helpful behaviors toward colleagues, could not be confirmed in combination. The authors conclude that how people relate at work feeds their broader sense of a life going well. They highlight relationships as a practical lever for occupational health.
pmc-11676168:
Parvulescu and a large team make in twenty twenty-four tiny porous particles that carry two metals and can speed chemical change with light or without it. The base material is a well-known sponge-like silica with ordered pores. They built versions pairing one metal with one of four partners, then checked each with X-ray, gas, and light methods.

Adding the second metal changed the pore structure and the light traits, most when the partner came from a different metal family. The new particles drove oxidation of ring-shaped compounds better than the single-metal version. Slow feeding of the oxidant improved both selectivity and stability. Two versions also broke down dyes and phenol in water under light most strongly.
pmc-11676268:
Kamil Candan and colleagues described skink embryo development stage by stage in 2024. Lizard embryology has a long history. Skinks remain poorly studied despite that. Two Heremites species were compared here. Cleared and stained embryos showed bones. Skull bone timing was the focus.

One species ossified its skull later. Pigment and scales appeared earlier there, though. Timing shifts mark a heterochronic pattern. Scale cover completed by a set stage. Ossification started late versus other skinks. It also finished earlier than relatives. Developmental timing evolves independently by trait. Comparative embryology gains two new references.
pmc-11676968:
Hayera Lee and a team including Sang-Ho Baik study packets released by a gut bacterium and their effects on gut and skin. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The bacterium, a lactic acid type, is known to calm gut inflammation, but how it talks to host cells was unclear.

Using a gut-on-a-chip and cell models, the team triggered inflammation and added the bacterial packets. The packets repaired cell shape, sealed the gut barrier, and lowered inflammatory signals through a known control pathway. Gene reads flagged skin-linked proteins that fell after treatment. That led the team to test skin cells as well, probing the gut-skin axis of the title. The findings frame bacterial packets as messengers that may serve both gut and skin health.
pmc-11677668:
Mora-Ortiz and co-authors study how fat in the diet shapes blood chemistry after meals in people with metabolic syndrome. Most of the day is spent in the after-meal state, yet research on it is thin. The study drew 75 patients from a Spanish cohort. For 12 weeks, patients followed one of four diets with equal calories. The diets differed in how much fat they held and what kind.

After a high-fat test meal, the team profiled compounds in the blood. Profiles were taken both fasting and after eating. The aim was to see how long-term diet patterns steer the response to a fatty meal. Results could guide diet advice for people with the syndrome.
pmc-11679268:
Karina Piatek and eleven co-authors test blocking a calcium sensor to prevent gut inflammation in mice in a 2024 paper. The sensor sits on many cells and was proposed as a drug target for inflammatory bowel disease. Earlier, blocking it mildly eased very severe mouse colitis, leaving open whether severity had masked a real benefit.

Female mice received the blocker or a dummy treatment before a chemical triggered medium grade colitis. Symptom scores did not improve, but treated colons were significantly longer and had less ulceration. Two inflammation related genes quieted in different colon regions, and lymph node cell growth fell. The authors read the mixed picture as partial protection worth further study.
pmc-11688868:
Martina Brandt, Michal Levinsky, and Melanie Wagner build a comparative index of social integration for older adults across European welfare states. Social ties matter for health and survival in old age, yet no instrument allowed fair comparison between countries. The study adapts an index first set out by Berkman and colleagues. Data come from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe, and the analysis tests how gender and welfare regime interact.

Women prove less socially integrated than men. Older adults in more family-centered regimes also score lower on integration. Care arrangements shape the gender gap: in family-oriented systems, women act as primary caregivers, which limits their social life outside the home. The authors argue policy should actively support integration, above all for women, and should fit each welfare system.
pmc-11690168:
Eight authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on partnering with nursing home companies in practical clinical trials. Trials embedded in real nursing homes need the operators on board to start and to last. The authors share two ongoing examples where that partnership worked.

One trial, on improving sleep for residents, runs across three large nursing home corporations. A pilot phase trained staff and, at the same time, trained a corporate coach who now trains others. The other example, funded by the veterans' system, works on preventing falls. Engaging corporate partners early taught researchers the culture of the homes while coaches learned the intervention.
pmc-11690768:
Sarah Campbell and six co-authors describe a course that helps front-line nursing aides speak well with patients and with the care team. Their report, from two thousand twenty-four, comes from work in two large counties in the west.

Aides give much bedside care but are often left out of training. The team built a four-part course on falls, hard behavior, mental health, talk skills, and self-care. It used games, stories, rest, and writing to keep learners drawn in. More than six hundred aides, nurses, and others took part over three years, in live web, in-person, and self-paced forms. Learners said they gained skill in spotting change and in guarding their own health.
pmc-11692568:
Joonsik Yoon interviews ten Korean American adults about caring for aging parents who still live in South Korea, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Duty to parents runs deep in Korean culture, yet distance makes daily care hard. Long open talks traced what the adult children hope for and what blocks them.

Most held fast to a classic ideal of duty, even voicing a wish to live with their parents again. That wish clashes with modern life in both countries, where shared homes have faded fast. Big blocks stood between the ideal and real care across the ocean. Readers see a paradox of prized values that distance makes near impossible to live out.
pmc-11692768:
Hanzhang Xu and co-authors report a telehealth program that cut avoidable emergency visits by nursing home residents in Singapore, in work from twenty twenty-four. Nursing home residents visit emergency rooms often, and near half of those visits may be avoidable. Singapore's aging population makes the load grow fast.

A public hospital teamed with nursing homes to give video consultations for sick residents on site. Seven of thirty-five homes in the area joined, and more than eleven hundred calls ran over three years. The share of emergency visits from partner homes fell firmly after launch and stayed lower. Effects varied by home, tied to resident mix and staff experience. The authors back telehealth care coordination for older adults.
pmc-11693068:
Katie Zeitler reports a 2024 account of bringing the Dementia Friends program to Washington State. Dementia Friends is a worldwide movement that fights the stigma around dementia through short community information sessions. Trained volunteers, called Champions, lead the sessions and teach five key messages plus communication tips.

A pilot in 2018 and 2019 showed that attitude scores improved after a session and stayed better a month later. That evidence won state funding in 2022, and regional partner groups spread the train-the-trainer model across the state. Participation grew from 214 people in 3 counties in 2019 to 2,170 people in 24 counties in 2024. Reaching rural and underserved communities remains the main challenge ahead.
pmc-11700368:
Sai Upadhyayula and co-authors published this diabetes study in 2024 from Bengaluru, India. Type 2 diabetes can quietly harm eyes and nerves, and early warning is gold. The team tested two cheap blood and urine marks in 130 patients: a white-cell ratio from a blood count, and a urine protein ratio that flags kidney strain. They asked how well each foretold eye and nerve damage.

The urine mark won clearly, with accuracy near ninety-one percent for eye harm and strong scores for nerve harm. The blood ratio scored lower and lost its punch once other traits were weighed. Diabetes span, blood sugar control, and the urine mark stood as the true foretellers. The authors back the urine test as a routine early screen, while urging care in reading the blood ratio.
pmc-11709368:
Alyssa De Vito and ten co-authors published a 2025 study tracking daily function and thinking in older adults over time. Clinic visits every few months can miss small changes that matter in early Alzheimer’s disease. The team instead used frequent digital tests and home sensors that quietly record daily activities such as taking pills.

The study followed 59 people with normal cognition and 45 with mild cognitive impairment. Standard group comparisons found differences in a trail-making test and in how pillbox reports matched sensor records. A second method, comparing each person against their own usual range, found extra differences the standard method missed. Personal baselines may catch early decline sooner than group averages.
pmc-11728168:
Chi-Syuan Pan leads a team that compares poison care units for kidney harm. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with poisoned folks with acute kidney injury. Such folks face high rates of harm and death in hospital care.

The team looked back at cases at a large hospital over two years. Folks were split by where they got their care. Death rates and stay length did not differ by unit type. Yet kidney harm folks died more than poisoned folks sans harm. The group was small, so more work is needed.
pmc-11736368:
Vandana Blossom and co-authors worked out how long a bacterial toxin must be given to rats to model inflammation-driven brain degeneration. The toxin, called LPS, triggers body-wide inflammation that reaches the brain, mimicking aspects of diseases such as Alzheimer's. Picking the right dose schedule matters for every study that uses the model. The team gave six groups of rats weekly low doses for four to eight weeks and tracked memory, neuron counts, and immune cell activity in the brain.

Damage became clear at five weeks, with fewer neurons, more glial cells, and worse memory, then grew gradually until seven weeks. An eighth week added nothing significant. The authors recommend five to seven weekly doses as the working window for this chronic inflammation model.
pmc-11747668:
Montorsi and co-authors review surgery options for painful chronic pancreatitis with a widened main duct. Standard care links the pancreas duct to the small bowel in an open operation. A keyhole version aims for the same relief with smaller cuts.

The review gathered studies from 2000 to late 2023 and found nineteen, all looking back at past cases. Illness rates ranged from zero to 57 percent for keyhole surgery, versus 4 to 68 percent for open. Hospital stays were five to seven days for keyhole care, versus six to sixteen. Pain relief reached a median of 82.5 percent for keyhole surgery.
pmc-11814468:
Shen and co-authors probe how a gene part drives iron death in breast growth cells. The part, NCAPD3, is a pack part that can drive growth birth. Its role in breast growth had stayed dim in past work. Iron death, called ferroptosis, can curb breast growth in tests. A plant part, THSG, curbed kin cell growth in past work by the team. Full gene reads now hunt how the gene and part meet.

Join reads split shifts in gene outs and splice forms. Shared genes twixt those sets form the first pick pool. Bench tests then checked splice forms in the cell runs. Hub genes came from code reads plus two bench checks. Cell rounds and iron death got scored by flow and blot reads. The work ties the gene to iron death in T47D cells.
pmc-11831968:
Nishith Reddy and a large team engineer, in twenty twenty-four, suppressor T cells that calm immune attack only where it is needed. Immune health needs balance between attack and suppression. They fitted normal helper T cells with synthetic Notch receptors, switches that sense a chosen antigen. On sensing it, the cells produce anti-inflammatory payloads. Screening a library of suppression programs, the strongest effect came from combining calming factors with a sink that soaks up a growth signal for attacker cells.

The engineered cells protected tissues from attack without body-wide suppression. They shielded transplanted insulin-producing cell clusters from killer T cells. They also guarded specific tissues against off-target attack by cancer-hunting CAR T cells. The platform could serve autoimmune disease, transplant rejection, and cell therapy side effects.
pmc-12490468:
Romana Marusic, Tajana Turk, and Tatjana Bacun sift how to test, find, and treat pheochromocytoma, a rare adrenal growth. Their 2024 piece takes in growths that pour out too much stress drug from gland cells.

Signs take in head pain, a fast or hard heart beat, and sweat, but the wide range of ways it can show makes them hard to find. They can show up alone or as part of gene-linked ill sets passed down in a clan. A find is made firm by tests of break-down goods in blood and in pee kept for twenty-four hours. Scans that trace work in the body find where it is. Care is by knife work and needs a set prep step first, to stop sharp blood force spikes and heart beat flaws. Checks must go on since it can come back, and a missed growth can kill.
pmc-12660768:
C. G. Balaji and colleagues propose a combined design for future sixth generation wireless networks that leans heavily on artificial intelligence. Their framework, published in twenty twenty-five, joins several parts. Very high frequency terahertz links, smart reflecting surfaces that bounce signals toward users, quantum key methods for security, and learning shared across edge devices without moving private data. Predictive filtering estimates changing channel conditions so beams can be aimed well, and smart error correction supports the quantum security layer.

The team tested the design in network simulations run many times across several deployment setups. Compared with conventional approaches, they report lower delay, higher efficiency in spectrum use, better energy efficiency, and more reliable packet delivery. The authors present the unified framework as a base for robust and self-managing wireless networks, while the evidence rests on simulation rather than field trials.
pmc-12660868:
Jun Huang, Yuwei Sun, and seven co-authors improve shape tracking for composite panels using fiber optic sensors. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, targets wings, cars, and other light strong structures. Thin fiber sensors measure strain along the surface. Math must then turn strain into the full bent shape.

Two classic methods get upgrades. Angle averaging refines one; cross-validation tunes the other. A carbon fiber plate tests both in simulation and in the lab. Fiber Bragg sensors feed the strain data. Accuracy rises by about two percent for the first method. The second gains about one percent. Better shape reads support real-time health monitoring.
pmc-12662768:
Fabio Capilli and co-authors share early results from 2025 with a new stent used to treat aneurysms inside the skull. An aneurysm is a weak bulge in a brain artery. Doctors can block it with tiny coils, and a stent helps hold those coils in place. The device tested here is the ACCERO heal stent.

The team looked back at thirty-two patients treated at two German centers between 2021 and 2023. They recorded patient traits, aneurysm features, how the procedure went, and any problems. A standard scale graded how fully each aneurysm was closed, and scans checked how well the stent hugged the artery wall. In every case the stent sat well against the wall. Follow-up scans were checked for reopening and for narrowing inside the stent.
pmc-12691868:
Hung-Jen Tu and Jia-Lien Hsu enhance medical diagnosis document analysis with layout-aware multitask models. Their 2025 study builds a system that extracts key information from documents with diverse layouts while protecting patient privacy.
