Optical character recognition first converts document images into machine-readable text. A document-understanding model then identifies and extracts the important fields. A mutual learning approach improves the system's adaptability and accuracy across formats. Because real medical documents contain sensitive data, training data was generated synthetically to comply with privacy regulations while keeping dataset quality. The system performed strongly across many document layouts, extracting critical information while meeting privacy requirements throughout.
pmc-12695968:
Giulia Moro and a large team present a new single-cell sequencing workflow in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Single-cell methods read the active genes of thousands of cells one by one. They often miss key transcripts or the exact regions that matter most. The workflow, called RoCK and ROI, has two parts. One part captures chosen transcripts to enrich them. The other steers some sequencing reads to regions of interest.

Together, the parts raise the odds of spotting rare but vital signals. That helps identify cell types and complex states that plain sequencing overlooks. The team built the method for studies of development, health, and disease. Labs that profile single cells can add it to standard pipelines. The paper adds a sharper lens to a fast-growing field.
pmc-12701868:
Muhammad Mahmoud Abaza, Tarek Abdel Hamid Harhash, and Ahmed Abbas Zaky compare ways to remove the smear layer from root canals, a cleaning step that decides endodontic success. The in vitro study used 160 single-rooted premolars. They were instrumented and divided among four rinse methods: two laser systems, passive ultrasonic irrigation, and conventional syringe-needle irrigation. Each method was subdivided by rinse solution. The solutions included sodium hypochlorite with EDTA, each agent alone, and saline.

Rinses ran in repeated short cycles. Blinded graders scored smear layer from electron microscope images across the canal's thirds. The erbium laser achieved the best cleaning across all thirds, outperforming the diode laser, ultrasonics, and syringe rinse. The combined hypochlorite-EDTA solution was the most effective irrigant. Remarkably, saline activated by the erbium laser beat hypochlorite alone, evidence that the laser's physical effects dominate. Apical thirds were hardest to clean in case after case.
pmc-12704868:
Alessandra Meireles and a large team of co-authors report a household survey on food insecurity in Complexo de Manguinhos, a group of low-income areas in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The work appeared in 2025 and draws on the Comvida-1 survey, run from September 2020 to February 2021. Households were scored with a Brazilian food insecurity scale.

Among 3,864 households, about one in seven faced moderate or severe food insecurity. Rates ranged from 4 to 28 percent across the sixteen areas. Two sets of causes stood out. One was long-term poverty, marked by welfare payments and many children at home. The other was sudden pandemic loss, such as lost jobs, shorter hours, and lower income. Each set roughly tripled the odds of serious hunger. The authors say aid must cover both deep poverty and sudden shocks.
pmc-12706068:
Gad, Sami Soliman, and Emad Helal blend machine learning with engine tests to squeeze the best from biodiesel made of waste cooking oil. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Turning fryer waste into fuel cuts both waste and diesel use.

The team made biodiesel from waste oil and blended it with diesel at four levels. Pure biodiesel cut carbon monoxide, unburned fuel, and smoke at full load, but raised nitrogen oxides and fuel use. Three learning models were stacked so their predictions fed a final learner, which forecast performance and emissions with very low error. A swarm search then found the best engine settings. The hybrid gives engineers a fast way to tune engines for waste-based fuels.
pmc-12716468:
Zejing Lin leads a team on a blood mark for bleeding after stroke. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with acute ischemic stroke. The mark is the NLRP3 inflammasome in serum.

A second mark, occludin, was measured next to it. Stroke folks and matched controls joined over some months. Both marks were far higher in stroke folks than controls. Levels tied to infarct size and stroke severity scores. Folks who bled after stroke had much higher marks. Stats models and curves tested guess strength for outcomes.  Bleeding types also split by mark level in tests.
pmc-12717068:
Karla Kerlikowske and five co-authors asked what happens when race and ethnicity are dropped from a breast cancer risk model, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The model gauges a woman's six-year risk of advanced breast cancer and guides how often she is screened and whether extra imaging is offered. Leaving out race has been put forward as a way to cut bias in such tools.

When race and ethnicity were removed, the model overstated risk in Asian women and understated it in Black women. Far fewer Black women with advanced breast cancer were classed as medium or high risk, while more Asian women were. The authors warn that the blunter model could lead to screening plans that fit women poorly, and could leave more advanced cancers to be found late in Black women.
pmc-12720968:
Klára Boruzs, Viktor Dombrádi, and Klára Bíró survey what makes Hungarian adults stick with their antidepressants. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Depression burdens Hungary heavily, and skipped doses blunt treatment.

Two hundred thirteen patients on doctor-prescribed antidepressants answered an online survey in spring twenty twenty-five. Smokers adhered less. Patients happy with their family doctor adhered more. Collecting prescriptions monthly beat every longer interval by a wide margin. Beliefs mattered too: seeing the drugs as necessary raised adherence, while seeing them as harmful or overused cut it. Anxiety and background traits were modeled beside the beliefs. The authors urge doctors to discuss beliefs, not just doses.
pmc-12729068:
Joseph Ripberger and co-authors study how experts talk about combined risks, and how the public hears them, in a 2025 study. Risk assessors now weigh how many stressors act together on health, but little was known about how such combined risk gets explained. The team interviewed 15 federal risk communicators and surveyed a national sample of adults, testing combined-risk messages against single-risk ones.

Most officials said combined risk matters but admitted they rarely explain it, blaming time pressure, office silos, and doubts about the audience. The public side contradicted those doubts: most people preferred messages that covered several linked risks. Comprehension and intent to act were just as strong for combined messages. The authors call for tools and backing that help officials close this gap.
pmc-12729168:
Iron deficiency anemia drains the health of many women in Bangladesh. Md Nawal Sarwer, Md Riaj Uddin Reza, Faisal Mohammad Ahamed, Md Fazle Rabby, and Laila Begum study how much poor urban women know about fighting it with food. They surveyed one hundred and forty-nine women of childbearing age in Dhaka City. The survey asked what the women knew about the condition and how much iron-rich food they ate each day. It also asked how schooling and income shaped both.

The team links the condition to poor diet, low awareness, and tight budgets, and argues that teaching plus better food access are key to prevention. Their design weighs knowledge and daily habits side by side, so programs can target the gaps that matter most for this group.
pmc-12732068:
Gaetana Porto and a large team of co-authors test a protective oral gel for transplant patients battered by mouth sores, in a two thousand twenty-five supportive care study. Oral mucositis is a significant complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

Eighty-two patients were followed; thirty-nine used the polyvinylpyrrolidone, zinc gluconate, and taurine gel thrice daily during conditioning, and forty-three formed a historical control group. Severe mucositis rates were similar between groups. But sores resolved markedly faster with the gel, an eighty-four percent resolution rate per hundred person-weeks against sixty-two. Adjusted analysis gave a sixty-eight percent higher likelihood of earlier resolution. The authors recommend the gel as supportive care.
pmc-12733068:
Sara Raposo and colleagues review how specialised competencies and artificial intelligence meet in perioperative care, the high-stakes span around surgery. Surgical care grows more complex, and demands on staff rise. The review weaves in empirical studies, policy documents, and expert analyses from the last decade.

The team finds that AI can support clinical choices and streamline workflows. It can also help spot complications sooner, in all perioperative phases. These tools enhance the roles of nurses, anesthetists, and surgeons. They do not replace them. Good use rests on digital literacy, work across fields, and ethical care. Data privacy, bias in algorithms, and unequal access to technology all need thought, and plans must be inclusive. Human judgment and AI tools join in ways that uphold safety, equity, and person-centred values.
pmc-12733868:
Stefanos Balaskas, Ioanna Yfantidou, and Dimitra Skandali use eye tracking to study how women look at breast cancer screening advertisements, in work published in 2025. Good communication turns screening availability into actual uptake. Thirty screening-eligible women viewed six static public service ads while their gaze was recorded.

The team marked zones on each ad: text, images, symbols, logos, calls to action, and source labels. They measured time to first look, look counts, and look durations. Differences across ad categories were small. Story-like text and dense callouts held attention longer, while logos and abstract symbols got brief glances unless paired with action prompts. Small labels and sources were often scanned first. The authors derive design lessons for screening campaigns.
pmc-12735468:
Wagdy Eldehna and a large team of chemists present new drug candidates against cancer in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their plan is to block two proteins at once, VEGFR-2 and c-Met. Both help tumors grow new blood vessels, spread, and thrive. The team designed and built a fresh set of compounds based on a benzoxazole core with a piperidine ring.

They checked how well the compounds block each protein, using two known drugs as yardsticks. They also tested killing power on breast, prostate, and lung cancer cells grown in the lab. Further tests looked at cell cycle shifts, cell death, and gene changes tied to death pathways. Computer docking showed how the best compounds sit in the protein pockets. The study offers leads for dual-action cancer drugs.
pmc-12736468:
Zhe Guo and his team build a brain-like net that spots micro-moves of the face, the brief face moves that leak true feels. Their 2025 study aims at grasp of heart states, at talk twixt folk and screens, and at watch work for safe sites.

Ways in use find it hard to catch fine move flow through space and time with scant data and scant screen force. Their mixed net first makes move form strong. It joins flow gauge with a zone mix plan that spreads move forms out. A light step code for long chains then models long-span time in a swift way. A zone join step makes face traits in small zones sharp. Through more than one yard-stick set, the kit hit top right scores. It held up well on new data and cost scant screen force. That fit suits small real-time sense tools.
pmc-12737568:
Carla de Sanctis Pecora and three co-authors explain why, when, and how to treat forehead lines with botulinum toxin. Their guidance appeared in twenty twenty-five, drawn from an expert panel of dermatologists. Forehead lines form as the brow muscle works, and results hinge on fine detail.

The forehead muscle lifts the brow while partner muscles pull it down, so dose and placement must respect that balance. The panel weighs brow shape and position, the aging process, and each person's muscle pattern. They cover dose per point, depth, and where the points should sit. The aim may be to soften muscle pull or to improve skin quality with shallow doses. The paper turns recent anatomy findings into practical steps.
pmc-12737868:
So Youn Moon, Marcelo Lamers, and Adam Engler report cancer research from two thousand twenty-five on mouth cancer and the signals that push it to spread. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, some surface cells lose their form and turn invasive, a change called EMT. The team asked whether signals from already-changed neighbors drive that shift in fresh cells.

Fluid from mesenchymal tumor cells made naive cells migrate more and switch on EMT markers. Stiffness-shaped cells had their own signal mix. Matching signals to gene changes pointed to a handful of cytokines as drivers, and removing or adding them proved they matter. Two kinase pathways carried the effect, and blocking them cut migration. The authors say such cooperative spread may need both signals.
pmc-12738068:
Oscar Torres Gutierrez, Xiaoliang Liu, and Xuecai Ge published a lab protocol in two thousand twenty-five. It shows how to image tiny cell antennas in developing mouse brains. These primary cilia act as signaling hubs. Brain progenitor cells extend them into fluid spaces. Thin slicing disrupts their delicate shape. Whole-mount preparation keeps the surface intact.

The protocol adapts an adult method for embryos. Steps cover mounting and staining delicate cortices. Ages range from mid-gestation to newborn pups. Direct viewing reveals cilia shape at the surface. Researchers can survey many progenitors at once. Brain development studies gain a reliable technique. Signaling defects may become easier to spot.
pmc-12739168:
Hiisivuori and co-authors test how well men read zoo beast moods from short clips. Right reads of beast moods sit at the core of beast care. Yet what sways those reads had stayed dim in past work. Clips showed three kinds: apes, tigers, and markhor goats. All clips had cues and scene facts stripped out cold. Zoo guests at Korkeasaari scored mood tint and mood pitch per clip.

Pitch reads beat tint reads in the guest scores. Low pitch beat high pitch on the same count scale. Bad tint beat good tint in the clip scores. Scores split by kind as much as by mood type. Ape tint reads led the pack in the guest set. Goat pitch reads led, while tiger reads trailed both counts. The team holds that drill in reads could lift care.
pmc-12743568:
Jiaan Wang and others checked swelling markers in tiny newborns in 2025. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia scars growing lungs badly. Very small babies face highest risk. Two blood markers were tracked from records. Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein were measured. Disease presence and how bad it got were the end points.

Higher marker levels tracked worse disease. Both markers rose with how bad it got. Several risk factors acted on their own too. Womb illness was one such factor. Being early in pregnancy also counted a lot. Tracking markers may flag at-risk babies. Closer watching could follow early warnings. Stopping it early remains better than late rescue.
pmc-12745268:
Zhiming Zhao and six co-authors test a migraine diet that bans foods flagged by each patient's own antibody tests, in a two thousand twenty-five randomized trial. Food-specific IgG antibodies are proposed markers of inflammatory food triggers.

Ninety-eight migraine patients with at least one positive food IgG were split between true elimination and a sham diet excluding antibody-negative foods instead. After twelve weeks the true group improved more on migraine, gut symptoms, and sleep questionnaires, and their positive IgG counts fell. Inflammatory messengers interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the pain peptide CGRP also dropped. Adjusting for the cytokines shrank the migraine benefit, implicating inflammation as the mechanism.
pmc-12749868:
Hung Manh Pham and five co-authors build a deep learn fix for wrist light pulse reads spoiled by poor skin touch. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Wrist pulse reads track heart and breath on home and clinic tools. Loose touch, more than move, warps the wave and drops key traits in still folks.

Their frame, CP-PPG, reshapes warped waves to a clean form with a bred model and a pulse-fit loss. Tests spanned wave truth, health reads on past sets, and wild use. Wave error fell by near half, and heart, breath, and press reads all rose. Code is shared in full for wide use.
pmc-12750668:
Hadi Zare-Zardini and eleven co-authors review protein nanoparticles as a gentler way to deliver chemotherapy in children whose lungs are at risk. Chemotherapy's lung complications are a serious burden in pediatric oncology. Protein carriers can aim drugs at tumors, release them slowly, and avoid the toxic peaks that damage healthy lung tissue.

The narrative review compares carrier proteins, from albumin with its clinical track record to silk fibroin, gelatin, casein, and plant proteins that cost less. Size must be tuned by age, since lungs develop from infancy through adolescence. Preclinical results show controlled release lowering inflammatory markers. Approval hurdles, manufacturing scale, and global availability remain open problems, though one albumin drug already proves the route is passable.
pmc-12753368:
Veronica Maria Tagi and ten co-authors wrote a review in 2025 on gland and hormone ills in young ones with inborn faults in body chem work. These rare faults, from weak enzymes, quite often hit more than one body part at once, and glands are hit a lot. Some pairs are well known; for some there is no guide at all.

The review sorts the ills by which gland set is hit and by how the fault works. It says to think of a chem fault when gland ills come with odd signs that lack a cause, or when more than one gland fails. It pulls in the watch rules that are out there and adds notes on care that fits each case. The aim is to help child docs spot and track these mixed ills at an early stage.
pmc-12754868:
Hesham Al-Sharani and colleagues systematically review when and how often to start brushing children's teeth to prevent early tooth decay. Their 2025 meta-analysis covers observational studies of children under six years old.

Thirty-two studies entered the review from nearly three thousand records, mostly cross-sectional. Starting brushing late showed a borderline effect overall, but removing one outlier study made late starting significantly raise decay odds substantially. Brushing less than twice daily more than doubled decay odds. Results varied considerably between studies, though no publication bias was detected. The findings support starting brushing early and brushing at least twice a day in preschool children.
pmc-12772968:
Hayashi and a large team ask if a clot busting drip helps before tube treatment for a kind of stroke in twenty twenty-five. The stroke type comes from a hardened artery blocking a large brain vessel. Patients in a Japanese registry got tube treatment to clear the block. Some also got the drip first, and the team split cases by where the block sat.

For blocks inside the skull, the drip gave no gain in recovery at ninety days. Bleeding in the brain and death were both higher with the drip in that group. For neck artery linked blocks, outcomes tied with or without the drip. The authors advise against the drip for in skull blocks.
pmc-12785468:
Coronel-León and six co-authors review how ferment steps can lift new protein foods in this twenty twenty-five paper. New proteins from plants, germs, and bugs cut the land cost of food, yet they can taste off and digest poorly. Some also hold anti-food parts that block nutrient uptake.

Inside, old-style ferments can break down those anti-food parts and free good traits in the food. Germ growth can also be run to grow protein mass from farm waste streams. Fine-tuned ferments go one step more and make set food parts to order. The review weighs taste, gut ease, and nutrient keep for each route. It frames germs as key tools for sound, green food shifts.
pmc-12796468:
Xiao Zheng and co-authors rebuild the core loop of life, DNA copying coupled to protein making, inside a test-tube system drawn from crude cell extract. Their study appeared in 2025. Earlier attempts relied on purified parts, which miss the mess of real cytoplasm. Their system, LoopReX, uses just two enzymes: one copies DNA, and one makes the RNA primers that start copying while also driving protein production. Machine learning tuned the recipe for efficiency.

The tuned system copied DNA and produced protein at high yield, round after round. Artificial cell-like compartments formed on their own, organizing the DNA and supporting several functions at once. The authors say a single scalable platform for the full genetic flow brings synthetic life a step closer.
pmc-12801468:
Wenbin Yu and five colleagues published a 2025 study of a protein that controls growth and drug production in Cordyceps militaris, a prized medicinal fungus. The fungus makes cordycepin, a compound valued in traditional medicine and drug research. The genes for making cordycepin are known, but the master switches that control them were not.

The team identified a Velvet family protein, CmVeA, as a key positive regulator. Raising its activity increased growth, spore production, and cordycepin output by 2.3 times. Deleting the gene caused severe growth defects and cut the yield by 60 percent. The protein thus coordinates the fungus's development with its chemistry, a finding that could help producers grow more cordycepin.
pmc-12812568:
Zheng, Ai, Liu, Xing, and Xu built this sleep analysis framework in twenty twenty-five. It aims to run personal sleep coaching on small edge devices. Two barriers stand in the way: scarce body-signal data and weak small models. Their answer starts with synthetic data guided by a large language model.

A statistical generator, tuned under body-based rules, fakes realistic sleep signals in bulk. A distillation step then trains compact models with the user's own profile in the loop. Tests on public and in-house data reached quality near that of large language models. The small models stayed within the memory and speed limits of edge hardware. The authors pitch the frame for real-time, on-device health help.
pmc-12812668:
Yuan Zhao leads a nine-author team pooling trials of interventions against muscle loss in cancer patients, in a review published in two thousand twenty-six. Cancer-related sarcopenia is driven by tumors, inflammation, and treatment together. It differs from ordinary aging muscle loss and needs its own evidence.

Seven databases were searched for randomized trials from two thousand ten onward. Interventions had to report muscle mass, strength, or physical performance. A standard Cochrane tool graded bias risk. Subgroup analyses explored which approaches work best. Exercise, nutrition, and combined programs are the usual candidates in such trials. The meta-analysis asks whether any of them reliably improve muscle health during cancer care, and for whom.
pmc-12813568: Kenji Takata and ten colleagues report a rare, severe side harm of portal vein stenting, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. A woman aged fifty-eight, who had surgery before for pancreatic head cancer, got a blocked mesenteric vein from lesions that came back. Stenting the portal vein instead blocked her main mesenteric artery. Large parts of her gut lost blood flow and died. The authors call the side harm unique. They stress thorough checks before surgery to avoid such ends.
pmc-12816668:
Tomoya Ishikawa and three colleagues test what the jelly around goosefish egg masses truly does for the embryos inside. Yellow goosefish spawn floating gelatinous ribbons near the sea surface, where conditions swing. Experiments exposed eggs and larvae, with and without their gelatinous envelopes, to diluted seawater, drying, and warmth.

Embryos kept in the jelly survived diluted salinity with normal growth. Stripped eggs fared significantly worse. The matrix also held moisture and protected larvae during drying, though it could not shield them from heat. The authors provide the first experimental evidence that these envelopes are protective adaptations for variable coastal habitats, not just packaging.
pmc-12817768:
Caixia Wu and co-authors test stem cells plus their released vesicles as a combined therapy for autism in mice, in work published in 2025. Autism involves social communication deficits and repetitive behaviour. Evidence links it to immune imbalance in the brain and disturbed gut microbes, yet few therapies target those routes.

The team used mice exposed before birth to a drug that induces autism-like traits. Groups received stem cells from human umbilical cords, their vesicles, both, or neither. Each single treatment helped some symptoms but left gaps. The combination gave the strongest gains in social behaviour and cut repetitive acts. It also calmed brain inflammation, repaired cell structures, and restored gut microbe balance. The authors present the dual approach as a candidate for further study.
pmc-12820168:
Vincent Chak and five co-authors study how nanoparticle surface chemistry shapes oral tolerance. The particles are designed to teach the immune system to accept a protein swallowed rather than injected. Their paper showed up in two thousand twenty-five. Unwanted antibody responses undermine many protein treatments.

The particles carry phosphatidylserine, a lipid that marks dying cells for quiet clearance. Variants differing in chain count, saturation, and length exposed varied amounts of the lipid on the particle surface. Using ovalbumin as a test antigen, greater surface exposure meant lower antibody titers and more tolerance-promoting Th3 cells. The structure-function rule supports rational design of oral tolerance treatments.
pmc-12824368:
Jorge Calderon-Quintal and colleagues ran in two thousand twenty-five the first randomized field trial of a healing vaccine for dogs naturally infected with the Chagas disease parasite. Dogs are a major home host of the parasite, which damages the heart over time. Owned dogs received three doses of a two-protein vaccine or salt water, then were followed for six months.

Vaccinated dogs carried fewer parasites, and heart tracing changes were prevented or halted, with no safety problems. Immune profiling showed calmer inflammation and shifted T cell patterns. Veterinarians and public health teams gain real-world proof that treating infected dogs could slow heart disease.
pmc-12827268:
Xiao-Zhou Lu and co-authors trained an artificial intelligence model to spot liver fibrosis from photographs of the tongue. Tongue inspection is a cheap, non-invasive tradition in medicine, but human judgment is subjective. Their model learned from over two thousand tongue images from sixteen hundred patients, detecting fibrosis while also naming seven tongue features.

The model beat five rival systems at finding fibrosis, and it read features such as cracks and greasy coating very well. One feature, small red spots called petechiae, linked strongly to fibrosis. The team wrapped the model in a phone mini-program and simulated remote screening, reaching about seventy-eight percent accuracy with high sensitivity. They see promise for early checks in places short on resources.
pmc-12830768:
Xuelin Zheng and co-authors test how freezing speed changes the strength of shale rock. Their 2025 study serves cryogenic fracturing, a technique that cracks rock with extreme cold to release oil and gas. Rock conducts heat poorly, so different layers freeze at different rates and may not behave alike.

Below a moderate freezing rate, the cold actually strengthened the shale in their tests. Past a faster threshold, strength and stiffness fell off, in a curved pattern the team fit. Damage came from micro-cracks driven by thermal stress and by ice expanding inside pores. The authors propose a measure of thermal damage capacity based on stress gradients. Field crews can use the rate limits to design freezes that crack rock where wanted.
pmc-12837668:
Delgado-Giugni and co-authors pool surveys on antibiotic overuse for pulpitis. Pulpitis requires operative dental treatment, and antibiotics are not indicated for it. Nevertheless, inappropriate prescribing persists worldwide despite clear guidance. The team gathered twelve cross-sectional surveys with 3,189 dentists in total. Studies ran from 2015 to 2025 across five major databases.

The pooled prescribing rate was 19 point 2 percent overall. General dental practitioners prescribed at 26 point 9 percent. Endodontists prescribed far less, at 5 point 1 percent. Spread between studies was very high in all pooled groups. Certainty of evidence was rated with the GRADE approach. The authors urge training aimed at general practice dentists.
pmc-12839268:
Elisa Gentilotti, Carolina Alvarez Garavito, Anna Górska, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It tests whether lingering low-grade inflammation in the blood marks post-COVID condition, the long tail of symptoms that follows some infections.

Patients from the multinational ORCHESTRA cohort were followed for eighteen months, with blood drawn during illness and at three later points. The team related lab abnormalities to four symptom patterns found earlier: respiratory, chronic pain, chronic fatigue, and neurosensory. They also asked whether acute-phase blood values predict who develops the condition, and whether a rougher initial illness leaves a stronger mark. Routine labs are cheap and universal, so a reliable signal would matter. The paper weighs how much these ordinary tests can really say about a still-mysterious syndrome.
pmc-12839668:
Ahmed K B Aljohani and co-authors test a sea urchin extract as a possible diabetes treatment. Their 2025 paper studies an urchin common in the Red Sea, formed into tiny suspended particles to help the body absorb it. Sea life is a rich source of active compounds, and diabetes care still needs options with fewer side effects.

The team profiled the extract's chemistry and tested it on two enzymes that break down starch and sugars. It blocked both enzymes strongly in the lab. They then gave the particle form to diabetic rats made ill with a standard toxin. The study joins chemical, lab, and animal evidence in one chain. Results at this stage support more study, not clinical use, but they mark the urchin as a candidate source.
pmc-12846468:
Sara Busechian and co-authors published a 2025 preliminary study of fitness measures in show-jumping horses after their stomach ulcers heal. Such ulcers are a worldwide disease of horses. Exercise is thought to feed them: stress, and the shift of the gut organs in fast gaits. They can dull the form of a horse, as racing work has shown.

Twenty-one trained jumping horses with ulcers took part. Four dropped out: ulcers not healed, or lost to follow-up. The rest healed in full. Fitness measures were taken in a ridden test, flat work and a small jump course, with a tracking device on each horse. Speed and stride length rose after the healing. Top heart rate in exercise, and heart rate in recovery, did not shift. The team ties the gain to the end of abdominal pain.
pmc-12847868:
Mengqi Guo and five colleagues recreated deep-Earth chemistry to explain inclusions trapped in superdeep diamonds. Carbonate minerals sink into the mantle on subducting slabs and join the deep carbon cycle. The team compressed a mix of calcium carbonate, iron, and silica in a laser-heated diamond anvil cell. Pressures reached twenty-five to fifty-three gigapascals, mimicking the deep mantle. X-ray diffraction watched the reactions in place.

Between fifteen hundred and two thousand kelvin, redox reactions produced calcium silicate, iron oxide, and an iron carbide. At higher temperatures a different iron oxide and carbide pair formed. That hotter assemblage matches inclusions actually found in superdeep diamonds. The twenty twenty-five experiments support subducted crust as the source of those inclusions, tying surface carbon to the deepest diamond record.
pmc-12849468:
YanFeng Yang, BingJie Rui, and Ji Hyang Kim review how tiny cell parcels called exosomes shape early ovarian failure tied to the ovary's local environment. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. The condition ends fertility early, and it still lacks good warning markers and treatments that change its course.

Exosomes ferry active cargo between cells in the ovary. Harmful ones spread injury through the tissue. Helpful ones, by contrast, can restore balance and protect egg cells. The review maps their roles across cell death, aging, inflammation, blood vessel growth, scarring, and energy stress. It weighs exosomes as blood markers for prediction. It also covers therapies built from stem cell exosomes, engineered parcels, and gel-like carriers.
pmc-12849668:
Wei Li and co-authors link heart strain measures to filling problems in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in this 2025 paper. In this disease the heart wall thickens and relaxes poorly. Longitudinal strain from ultrasound spots subtle contraction weakness. Its value for grading relaxation failure was unclear, though.

The cohort held 145 symptomatic patients with the obstructive form and preserved ejection fraction. Relaxation grades followed a standard algorithm, with most patients at grade two. Worse strain tracked with worse relaxation grade. Thicker walls and higher BNP levels also marked the worse group. Women formed a larger share of grade two cases. Strain imaging may grade diastolic trouble when classic measures leave doubt.
pmc-12859968:
Oluwakemi Akinpelu and five co-authors review current knowledge of Helicobacter pylori infection in this two thousand twenty-five paper. This bacterium lives in the stomach lining. It is a main cause of long-term stomach inflammation. From there it can lead to ulcers, stomach cancer, or a rare lymphoma. Most people catch it in childhood, and it stays for life if untreated.

Nearly half the world's people carry the bacterium. Rates vary with place and sanitation. The review explains how it survives in stomach acid and how it harms the host. It also covers how doctors find it, through scopes, stool, breath, or blood tests. Given its link to cancer, the authors stress screening and treatment. The paper gives students and clinicians a clear, current overview.
pmc-12974268:
Xu and colleagues build a mouse model that copies the step-by-step gene faults of human eye melanoma. The cancer starts in the uveal tract, the pigmented middle layer of the eye. About half of patients later grow spread tumors, most often in the liver.

The model switches on a faulty GNAQ gene, the usual first fault, at normal body levels. Mice first grew benign eye lumps like the moles seen in people. Adding loss of a second gene, BAP1, pushed some lumps toward true cancer. Tumors could shift cell type over time, as human tumors do. The immune system stays whole in these mice, so immune drugs can be tested.
pmc-13001768:
Zhou and a large team studied in twenty twenty-five kidney harm after repair of a torn main chest artery. Low blood pressure during the long surgery may add to that harm. They asked how deep and how long low pressure must be to raise the worst stage of harm.

They split three hundred thirty-six adults by how low their mean pressure fell in surgery. Two in three had some kidney harm, and near one in five had the worst stage. Past kidney strain, long surgery, and low urine flow each raised that risk on their own. Deeper and longer low pressure raised it more, and adding pressure facts sharpened their risk tools.
pmc-13094568:
Jang and five co-authors read in twenty twenty-six the toll of blood transfusion need in low-risk blood cancer in South Korea over twenty-eight years. The ill leaves too few red cells, so many folks need transfused blood. Records came from one big Seoul center for more than three hundred such folks.

Near three in ten grew tied to transfusions in that span. Tied folks used more care, cost more, and died sooner than the rest. A hormone drug helped few once the tie had set in. Low risk in name does not mean low burden in life, they stress.
pmc-13094768:
Rémi Esser and a team of co-authors described a nurse led care path for older heart failure patients. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, deals with heart failure in later life. This illness hits older adults most and pairs with frailty and many other ills. Hospital first models can wear such patients down and cause harm. The team built a path led by advanced practice nurses in a joined geriatric and heart service.

In this model, those nurses take wide clinical and planning roles. Care leans toward clinics and home, not the ward. The paper tells how the path was built and run in practice. Readers who plan elder care get a worked model for joined heart and aging care.
pmc-13118668:
Sultan Büyüker and co-authors review the chemistry and healing promise of a medicinal tree in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Elaeocarpus sylvestris is an evergreen from East and Southeast Asia, long used for inflammation, fever, and infection. Modern tests credit it with many effects.

Its extracts fight oxidation, calm inflammation, and show antiviral, anticancer, and blood-sugar effects. Key compounds include geraniin and other polyphenols. Extracts have hit herpesviruses, flu A, and SARS-CoV-2 in lab and early human tests. Skin care uses, from whitening to blue-light guarding, add reach. The authors flag gaps in mechanism and dosing work before firm clinical claims can stand.
pmc-13126568:
Mboineki and Chen explored this health topic in twenty twenty-five: cervical cancer screening in Tanzania. Screening can catch the disease early, yet only a small share of eligible women take part. The team interviewed women in a ward of Dar es Salaam, the country's largest city. They asked what women know and feel about screening and what keeps them away.

All twenty-six women had heard of cervical cancer and screening. Yet only two had ever been screened. Most knew little about causes, risk factors, or when to go. Lack of symptoms, cost fears, and long waits all held women back. Attitudes were positive, and women said they would go if services were near, cheap, and well explained. The authors urge stronger teaching and easier access.
pmc-13134268:
Omima Taha and five co-authors survey Egyptian doctors who deliver babies, in a study dated 2026. Their topic is instrumental delivery, the use of forceps or a vacuum cup to help a baby out. The method can cut the need for cesarean surgery, but its use has been fading.

The online survey ran in early 2025 and drew 139 replies. More than half of the doctors had never tried the method, and most would not urge it even when it fit the case. The top reasons were fear of legal claims, lost training chances, and weak senior support during hard cases. The authors say rebuilding skills and supervision could revive a method that helps mothers avoid surgery.
pmc-13139768:
Mert Kılıç, Eyyup Kara, and Alperen Kılıç compare hearing and thinking in adults who wear hearing aids, in this twenty twenty-six study. Thirty-two long-term aid users with hearing loss in both ears took a set of hearing and memory tests. A matched group of thirty-two with normal hearing took the same tests.

Aid users scored far worse on fine hearing tasks, such as picking speech from noise and spotting brief gaps in sound. Memory and learning gaps were less clear-cut overall. The study links aided hearing skill to thinking skill, which may guide rehab that trains both ear and brain.
pmc-13144468:
Reham Abdelkader, Doaa Hamed, and Hanan Abdel-Khalek report food safety research from two thousand twenty-six on pads that protect fish fillets. Absorbent pads in packaging can carry germ-killing agents. The team built pads from bacterial cellulose soaked with tangerine essential oil, then tested them alone and with mild gamma irradiation against bacteria placed on fish.

Four bacterial strains were seeded on fillets and stored cold for six days. Untreated counts climbed steeply. The oil pads cut counts far more than plain pads, and irradiation alone helped as well. The combined treatment gave the deepest cuts, lowering each strain by about five orders of magnitude. Lab spectra showed new bonds forming between the cellulose and oil under irradiation. The authors call the pairing a green decontamination route.
pmc-13144768:
Thomas Hoag and co-authors examine how much discrimination patients with head and neck cancer feel they face in medical care. These cancers make up about 5 percent of United States cases and cause roughly 14,400 deaths a year. Minority and low-income patients often fare worse, arriving at later stages and getting weaker treatment. Gaps persist even after accounting for income, insurance, and disease stage, which points to other forces. The authors test whether perceived discrimination is one of them.

The team recruits 72 patients treated within the past five years and scores them on a standard scale. Most patients were white and male, and the average score was low at 9.1 out of 35. Income mattered most: lower-income patients reported clearly higher scores. Cancer stage showed no link. Patient comments added depth, tying stronger feelings of bias to stigmatized histories such as substance use.
pmc-13148168:
Fidela Anne Badilles and Michael Villa describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of Horner syndrome after ethanol ablation for recurring thyroid cancer. Ethanol injection treats recurrences when surgery or radioactive iodine cannot. Nerve injury nearby is a known but rare hazard.

Their thirty-one-year-old patient had prior thyroid removal and iodine therapy. A stubborn recurrence in the thyroid bed received ethanol ablation by preference and size. Afterwards her left eyelid drooped, with a smaller pupil and reduced sweating on that side. Clinicians should warn patients and watch for this complication after neck ablation procedures.
pmc-13149568:
Four authors present a survey study dated two thousand twenty-six on newborn screening in Turkiye. The screening takes a few drops of blood from a baby's heel to catch hidden diseases early. Its success depends on parents knowing what it is for and agreeing to take part.

The team surveyed three hundred fifty mothers with a structured set of questions. They recorded family background and what each mother knew, thought, and did about the screening. Their main measure was whether a mother reported concern about the process. They then looked for which traits tracked with concern or refusal, using models that adjust for several factors at once.
pmc-13149768:
Kuo and a large team of co-authors linked COVID antivirals to eye inflammation in this study from twenty twenty-six. Uveitis is inflammation inside the eye that can follow infections. Using a large health database, the team matched treated and untreated COVID patients one to one. Each group held over four hundred thousand people.

Patients with diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart failure also gained. Among the drugs, Paxlovid carried the clear signal, while two others showed none. The benefit appeared regardless of vaccination status. The authors suggest antivirals may shield the eye as well.
pmc-13158768:
Khanh N C Duong and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six cost-effectiveness analysis of Utah's mobile COVID vaccine clinic program. Vans brought vaccines to underserved communities for a year. Whether the investment paid off in health and equity needed rigorous testing.

A combined epidemic and decision model simulated millions of state residents for that year. Scenarios with and without the mobile program were compared. Infections, hospital stays, deaths, and costs were tallied. Results were split between Hispanic and non-Hispanic residents. Returns were judged from health system and societal viewpoints, guiding future outreach spending.
pmc-13179468:
Dorota Klensporf-Pawlik and co-authors study young drinkers' taste for alcohol-free beer in 2026. The market for such beer is growing fast, and brands want to know what young buyers like. The team tested lager, IPA, and wheat styles with young Polish consumers.

Tasters liked the lagers best, favoring beers that felt fresh and clear with a good aroma. The team then checked how brand and label shape liking, by testing the beers blind and with labels shown. Some beers scored better once the brand was known. How pretty and clear the label looked also predicted whether people said they would buy the beer. The results give brewers clear cues for design and marketing.
pmc-13183368:
Nastacia Goodwin and seven co-authors study aggression in male mice in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Aggression can be reactive, a response to provocation, or appetitive, sought out as a reward. Their setup let mice press a lever to attack an intruder, or receive attacks on a non-contingent basis.

Machine-guided scoring showed attack sequences looked alike in both setups. Brain activity patterns, though, differed between the groups, pointing to distinct circuits. One brain region, the nucleus accumbens, was active in both. A protein there, neuroligin-2, tracked with attack counts: more attacks meant less of the protein. The authors conclude that outward behavior can hide distinct neural routes to aggression.
pmc-13193368:
André Chacon and six colleagues published a 2026 case report of pulsatile tinnitus caused by an arteriovenous fistula inside the skull. Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic whooshing sound, usually caused by turbulent blood flow near the ear. It can seriously compromise quality of life.

The patient was a 51-year-old woman with the sound in her right ear for eighteen months. Standard CT and MRI angiography showed nothing significant, partly because the venous phase of the imaging was not completed. A carotid Doppler ultrasound, however, revealed abnormal flow that indirectly pointed to the fistula. The case shows how a simple, cheap ultrasound can catch a vascular cause that expensive scans missed.
pmc-13193768:
Helen Lamesgin Endalew is first author on a 2026 multilevel analysis of depression and anxiety among women in Lesotho, a low-resource country in southern Africa. Women's mental health shapes families and national development, yet population evidence for women of reproductive age there was limited. Data came from the twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four national demographic and health survey.

A weighted sample of three thousand two hundred and sixty-five women aged fifteen to forty-nine was analyzed with models that account for community clustering. About one in ten reported diagnosed depression, about one in twenty had questionnaire-based depressive symptoms, and about one in eleven reported diagnosed anxiety. Chronic illness linked to all three outcomes, and money barriers linked to depression measures.
pmc-13197168:
Lawrence O Barros and colleagues published a 2026 study of egg follicle cycles in plains zebras. Follicles are the small sacs in the ovary where eggs mature. Breeding plans for this declining species need such detail, yet no ultrasound study had tracked zebra cycles day by day.

Staff scanned four mares daily through natural cycles with no added hormones. Cycles ran long, at about thirty-eight days between egg releases. Few follicles grew at once, growth was slow at about one millimeter a day, and no wave pattern appeared. Womb lining patterns matched those of horses near egg release. Two mares also responded well to drugs that sync cycles. The data can guide zebra breeding work.
pmc-13197368:
Mahdi Mazidi and colleagues introduce a 2026 task for measuring attention bias toward bad news. Theories link such bias to anxiety, yet older tasks lack steady scores and real-life feel. A group of 168 students took the task plus anxiety measures. The bias score proved highly steady across split checks, a rare strength in this field. Students with stronger bias toward negative content scored higher on lasting anxiety. Bias also carried the link between lasting anxiety and state anxiety spikes when facing emotional content. The task is free to use and may serve many study areas.
pmc-13197568:
Yao and coauthors find a gene that drives drug resistance in liver cancer. A targeted drug is now a cornerstone for advanced liver cancer. Resistance to it soon cuts its clinical benefit, though. The team screened for genes tied to that resistance.

One gene, called RPRD1A, stood out as a top candidate. Raising it made cancer cells far less sensitive to the drug. Cutting it restored drug response in those cells. The gene competes with a partner for binding in gene copying. That contest lifts a growth and adhesion signal axis. Blocking that axis may restore drug gains.
pmc-13199068:
Masaru Nemoto and colleagues review kidney injury from imaging dye in a 2026 article, translated from a 2024 Japanese journal paper. Iodinated contrast dye helps doctors see vessels and organs, but it can injure kidneys, above all in people with weak kidney function. Once injury sets in, no cure exists, so prevention is key.

The review covers how dye harms kidney tubes both directly and by cutting blood flow to inner kidney zones. Risk runs higher with chronic kidney disease, older age, and diabetes. Vein delivery carries less risk than artery delivery. Salt water or bicarbonate fluids before the scan can help guard the kidneys. Using the least dye that still gives clear images is also advised.
pmc-13199968:
CJ Morrow and eight co-authors report from a symposium on mycoplasma germs, drug use in laying hens, and drug resistance. Germs that no longer respond to drugs are a growing risk for human health. The piece came out in twenty twenty-six.

The authors argue that routine preventive drug use should be phased out, most of all in dense animal farming. In poultry, drugs given through the laying period can drive resistance in two mycoplasma types and in gut germs that can reach people. Farms free of mycoplasma, or live vaccines against it, can cut the need for drugs and should be the path ahead.
pmc-13201968:
When one vertebral artery closes, extra blood flow stress may endanger the other, and a 2026 illustrative case by Yohei Kitamura documents how fast that danger can appear. The article follows a 52-year-old man whose right vertebral artery dissecting aneurysm progressed to complete blockage of that vessel.

Imaging at first showed the left vertebral artery was normal, yet six weeks later a new dissecting aneurysm had formed there. Because a key branch sat beside the lesion and the opposite artery was already closed, doctors used stent-assisted coiling to preserve blood flow. He left the hospital without deficits, and one-year imaging showed the artery open with no recurrence.
pmc-13202568:
Mahmood Dashti and a team of co-authors pool studies on how well large language models answer dental exam questions, in a review dated twenty twenty-six. Such models are now used in health and dental teaching, but their skill on expert tests was unclear. The team searched four databases and gathered data on model versions and score rates. Thirty-nine studies were found in total.

Across studies, the models scored about sixty-four percent on average, with wide spread between them. ChatGPT-4 and one rival tool scored highest, near three quarters right. Newer versions beat older ones in direct matches. The authors say the tools are not fit to make care choices alone but may help in teaching when their limits are kept in view.
pmc-13204068:
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors vary from harmless to aggressive, and a 2026 study by Abdallah Attia tests whether routine scans can sort them before surgery. The research article builds risk patterns from CT radiomic traits in a two-center records-based cohort, since tumor grade is normally unknown until tissue is removed.

Forty-four patients contributed scans, and the team combined image traits with clinical measures, also matching each tumor against the patient's own healthy pancreas. One combined pattern tracked progression most reliably on testing across the cohort. A compact classifier using that family of patterns beat the clinical baseline for predicting progression, backing forward-looking testing of radiomics as a planning aid.
pmc-13207368:
Two giant robber flies that hunt farm pests may shift their ranges as China warms, and a 2026 modeling study by Zhuoman Zhang maps where they could live. The research article builds an optimized ensemble distribution model for Microstylum dux and Microstylum oberthurii, large predatory insects found across eastern and southern China.

Highly suitable habitat currently concentrates in the southeast for both species in the model's reconstruction. Total suitable area stays roughly stable in future scenarios, but the best habitat expands while mid-grade habitat shrinks considerably. Ranges drift westward or southwestward, and the two species' overlapping preferences change over time, which matters for using them in biological pest control.
pmc-13207868:
Dan Levy Faber, Juna Azizi, Ronen Galili, Sonia Schneer, and Abed Agbarya test whether skipping suction on chest drains after lung surgery helps patients recover faster. Their trial was published in twenty twenty-six. Drains clear air and fluid while the lung heals, and suction is often applied by routine.

Patients at one center were assigned at random to continuous suction or no suction, all with the same digital drain system. Of two hundred and eighty-six patients analyzed, the no-suction group had their tubes out about thirteen hours sooner on average. Hospital stay and lasting air leaks did not differ between the groups. The authors conclude that routine suction lengthens drain time without clear gain. Their result may simplify care after lung removal surgery.
pmc-13209968:
Jihyun Hwang and colleagues published a systematic review in 2026. They evaluated a classic herbal formula for cognitive impairment. The formula, Liuwei Dihuang, is widely used for decline. Study quality varied with unclear blinding and randomization. Bias risk was judged as some concerns overall. Benefits are promising but not firmly proven yet. Better trials are needed before strong recommendations.
pmc-13211868:
Generative artificial intelligence is entering medical school faster than wellbeing support is growing, and a 2026 scenario study authored by Nora Arvai maps four possible futures from that tension. The foresight analysis scans the literature for trends, then builds scenarios from two uncertainties: how deeply AI integrates into curricula, and how much mental health support institutions provide.

The four futures range from a low-tech but supported student life to a high-integration world where support lags badly behind. Each scenario carries distinct risks for digital readiness, psychological health, and professional growth in the authors' telling. Their core message is that technology and mental health support must evolve together, with ready faculty and ethical guardrails.
pmc-13213568:
Shi Feng, Jing Liu, Zhuxin Li, and Shengyang Tao apply in 2026 a self-learning optimisation method to spraying seaweed-derived alginate into uniform microspheres. Bead size matters for drug delivery and tissue scaffolds, yet spray settings interact in tangled ways that defeat hand tuning.

Their framework paired Bayesian optimisation, which learns from each trial, with a microfluidic spray rig, aiming to maximise beads in a narrow size band. Starting from ten prior trials, it settled in twelve rounds, a third cheaper than a smaller start. Predicted and measured yields matched closely. Analysis showed gas and liquid pressures dominate size, giving makers a low-cost recipe for custom polymer beads.
pmc-13214468:
Mareike Rutenkröger and a team of co-authors set out a plan to test a German quality of life index. Their protocol, from twenty twenty-six, deals with vestibular schwannoma, a benign tumor of the balance nerve. Such tumors oft cause nerve and function harm that cuts life quality. Care has long stressed hearing saved and tumor control. Patients stress other loads more: vertigo, pain, clouded thought, and how care feels.

The study will run at many centers to check the German form of a set index. It also probes patient centered care in this field, a gap in past work. Readers who treat this tumor get a checked tool to hear the patient's full load.
pmc-13214568:

Using monkey scans as a diagnostic testbed, the team found a bias in how fibre directions are estimated deep in white matter, exactly where these pathways run. Their fix reweights the estimates using each individual's variability. With the correction, diffusion imaging in humans recovered the full pathways between the anterior cingulate, the insula, and a lower frontal region. The result supports the anatomy behind a well-known brain network.
pmc-13215368:
Manuel Montero-Odasso, Linda Lee, and David B. Hogan argue in 2026 that new anti-amyloid drugs for Alzheimer's disease must not swallow the whole brain-health agenda in Canada. The injected drugs help modestly, suit few patients, and cost a great deal.

Keeping eyes on that main prize, the authors say, is how scarce money serves everyone with cognitive concerns.
pmc-13218168:

pmc-13221368:

pmc-13221468:

pmc-13222768:

pmc-13223868:

pmc-13224268:

pmc-13226968:

pmc-13229468:

pmc-13231468:
Dae Young Bae and colleagues report in 2026 palladium complexes that break carbon-hydrogen bonds using plain oxygen in water. pmc-13232068:
Kinfeosioluwa S Bankole and colleagues build in 2026 a way to match matching gene transcripts across fruit fly species. pmc-13232568:

pmc-13233568:

pmc-13233768:

pmc-13233968:

pmc-13237268:
Jing Chen reported in 2026 a rare case of tuberculosis inflaming the back of the eye in a healthy woman in her early twenties. pmc-13237368:
Hagag and colleagues survey behavioural addictions among medical students across Egypt, Sudan, and Libya. pmc-13239068:

pmc-13239368:

pmc-13239468:

pmc-13242468:

pmc-13245768:

pmc-13246368:

pmc-13246768:

pmc-13247168:

pmc-13247568:

pmc-13248268:

pmc-13249068:

pmc-13249768:

pmc-13250168:

pmc-13250468:

pmc-13250768:

pmc-13250868:

pmc-13251368:

pmc-13251468:

pmc-13251768:

pmc-13253068:

pmc-13253568:

pmc-13253668:

pmc-13255068:

pmc-13255468:

pmc-13255668:

pmc-13255968:
Adeolu Adekunle and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review mapping research on risk factors for bovine respiratory disease across beef production. Early-life practices such as vaccination timing drew more attention in studies of young calves. Most research, though, concentrates on feedlots, leaving the cow-calf and backgrounding stages understudied. The authors sort risk factors into animal, management, and environment domains. They call for balanced research across the whole production chain so prevention can start before cattle reach the feedlot.
pmc-13256368:

Four learning tools were trained to classify sex from the measurements. All were right in over nine of ten cases. The best tool was right in nearly all cases. pmc-13256468:

pmc-13256868:

pmc-13257068:

pmc-13258368:

pmc-13259668:

The authors warn that small samples can manufacture perfect looking scores by chance.
pmc-13259968:

pmc-13260168:

pmc-13261068:
Nobuyuki Shirai and colleagues offered in 2026 ten practical tips for preventing falls in people on dialysis. pmc-13261568:

pmc-13262568:

pmc-13262668:

The authors note worsening after surgery in some cases, and motor and thinking decline that older patients should be watched for.
pmc-13263168:

pmc-13263268:

pmc-13263568:

pmc-13263668:

pmc-13263768:

pmc-13263868:

pmc-13264768:

pmc-13264868:

pmc-13265668:

pmc-13266368:

pmc-13266568:

pmc-13266768:

pmc-13266868:

pmc-13267068:

pmc-13267568:

pmc-13269468:

pmc-13269568:

pmc-13270068:

pmc-13270768:

pmc-13270868:

pmc-13271068:

pmc-13271468:

pmc-13272168:

pmc-13272668:

pmc-13272868:

The authors note that self-reported data limit the work, and call for steps to improve air quality in Saudi homes.
pmc-13273668:

pmc-13273868:

The authors say therapy translation has lagged. They urge biomarker-guided trials and microvascular repair.
pmc-13274168:

Blood albumin, hemoglobin, white-cell counts, and age mattered most. Dropping lab data clearly weakened the model.
pmc-13274968:
Congcong Hou and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional survey study on video games, loneliness, and stoicism in adults. Loneliness is a recognized public health problem, and the team asked whether relaxed solo games might ease it by building a stoic mindset, calm acceptance of what cannot be controlled. Their convenience sample of 2,252 adults was recruited near a video game store.

Players of the open-world game Zelda: Breath of the Wild scored far higher on stoicism and lower on loneliness than non-players. Players of the gentle game Yoshi's Crafted World showed the same pattern, more weakly. Statistical mediation suggested gameplay connects to less loneliness partly through greater stoicism. Because the survey is a single snapshot, it shows association, not proof of cause.
pmc-13275268:
Carlos José Monroy-Barrero reviewed entrepreneurship in Latin America through a sociological lens in a 2026 systematic review. Business research usually reads starting a firm as economics, which misses the social strain involved. The review asks how people carry that strain under inequality and informal work.

Following standard review rules, it combined counts and close reading across seventy-four articles from 2020 to 2025. National literatures differed: Brazilian work criticized platform gig work, Mexican work stressed resilience, and Colombian work treated enterprise as subsistence. Across the region, entrepreneurship looked more like a collective survival strategy than lone innovation. Monroy-Barrero frames it as a social ordeal, unevenly spread by class, gender, and place, in which the language of freedom can hide self exploitation.
pmc-13275468:
Codina Movileanu writes a 2026 editorial on nanomaterials in physical therapy. Classic methods such as stretching, ultrasound, and electrical stimulation help many patients regain movement and ease pain. Ageing populations and chronic disease, the editorial argues, now demand more precise and personal care.

Materials built below 100 nanometres can carry drugs, sense strain, or turn light into targeted heat. Gold particles, carbon structures, and loaded scaffolds each suit different repair tasks. Wearable sensors could feed movement data to software that adjusts therapy during a session. The editorial frames careful design for safety and body compatibility as the step that decides whether these tools reach routine clinics.
pmc-13275668:
Fengshan Yue and colleagues map research on Tai Chi, brain activity, and mental outcomes in a 2026 scoping review. Tai Chi is widely practised for balance and calm, yet its brain effects are scattered across many methods. The review charted which groups, brain tools, and mental outcomes researchers have studied.

Twenty-two studies met the rules, drawn mostly from older adults and university students. Brain measures included EEG, functional MRI, and near-infrared spectroscopy. Favourable mental changes often appeared alongside brain changes, especially in MRI studies of depression and fatigue. Many studies, though, reported both kinds of result side by side without testing whether they were truly linked.
pmc-13275968:
Sung Eun Kim and co-authors present a 2026 validation study of a Korean questionnaire for people with hemophilia. Hemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder that damages joints and limits daily life. The Haemophilia Activities List asks patients how well they manage everyday tasks, but it needed a tested Korean version.

Translators converted the questionnaire into Korean and back again, following standard rules. Eighty-seven adults with hemophilia then completed it plus two other health surveys. Answers were highly consistent within the questionnaire and stable when patients retook it later. Scores also lined up strongly with the other surveys, as expected. The authors conclude the Korean version is reliable and fits Korean culture, ready for use in clinics and research.
pmc-13276468:
Lui Malcon and a large team present a 2026 trial protocol on extra exam time for students with ADHD. Extended time is one of the most common exam adjustments for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Solid evidence for its benefit in college-age students is still scarce.

Each participant will take three versions of a test modelled on Brazil's national high school exam. The versions differ only in time allowed: standard, a quarter extra, and half extra. Order is randomised, and every student tries all three conditions. The team had enrolled 103 participants by early 2026, with analysis just starting. Results should show whether extra time helps, and how much time is enough.
pmc-13276568:
Liony Fransisca and co-authors present a 2026 safety study on a bold malaria dosing plan in Papua New Guinea and Indonesia. Primaquine can fully cure vivax malaria by clearing dormant liver parasites, but it can also destroy red blood cells in people lacking a protective enzyme. Testing for that enzyme first may allow stronger, shorter treatment.

Eight hundred patients at four clinics were tested at the point of care. Their enzyme status set the regimen: a high seven-day course for normal levels, a gentler fourteen-day course for middling levels, or a weekly eight-week course for deficiency. Nearly everyone was checked on days three and seven. Blood-related warning events were uncommon and mostly mild drops in hemoglobin without symptoms. Serious events touched two percent, mostly stomach intolerance on the short course. The authors say test-guided treatment was feasible and acceptably safe.
pmc-13276768:
Zhaoyinling Wei and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how weight-loss surgery sharpened memory in Alzheimer's model mice, apparently through gut hormones. Sleeve gastrectomy removes much of the stomach. The team used it as a probe of the gut-brain axis in mice carrying three Alzheimer's-linked genes.

After surgery the mice handled glucose better and their insulin worked better, without lasting weight or appetite changes. Their thinking performance improved and anxious behavior eased. Damage and abnormal tau protein in a memory region of the brain both fell. Two gut hormones, GIP and GLP-1, rose in blood and brain, switching on a growth pathway tied to learning. Blocking GIP's receptor in brain cells worsened tau changes, while GLP-1 added support. The authors back dual gut-hormone targeting for Alzheimer's.
pmc-13277068:
Ebrahem M Eid leads a 2026 study of carbon stored in soils of salt marshes along Egypt's Nile Delta coast. Marsh plants trap carbon in wet soil, a form of storage called blue carbon. The team took 200 soil cores across sites ruled by three salt-tolerant plants, plus bare ground, and modeled carbon by depth.

Carbon levels fell as soil density rose, across all site types. Different math models fit different plants best, but all three models matched measured carbon stocks well when filling in depths within a core. Such models could help local planners estimate how much carbon these marshes hold. The authors note that wider testing across varied landscapes is still needed.
pmc-13277668:
Aliaa Sherif Karam leads a 2026 study on printing knee meniscus tissue with aligned fibers, using only cells and no scaffold. The meniscus is a fibrous cartilage pad that cushions the knee, and its aligned collagen gives it strength. The team first grew stem cells in narrow channels and found the confinement lined collagen up along the channel.

Printing cell-only inks into a support bath made filaments, and thinner filaments aligned better and built more matrix. Blocking two force-sensing pathways disturbed cell alignment but not the collagen pattern or stiffness readings. The method scaled to sheets and ring-shaped, meniscus-like forms. Shape alone may guide graft design, the authors conclude.
pmc-13277768:
M-Jaber Kojak leads a 2026 case report of Susac syndrome in a 14-year-old boy. Susac syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease of tiny blood vessels in the brain, retina, and inner ear, and it is uncommon in children. The boy arrived with reduced consciousness after eighteen days of sleepiness, vomiting, blurred vision, and unsteady walking.

Brain scans showed round snowball-like lesions in the corpus callosum, a hallmark clue. Eye imaging later confirmed blocked retinal arteries. Steroids helped at first, but seizures and relapses during dose tapering needed plasma exchange and stronger immune-suppressing drugs, which stabilized him. Early recognition of the scan pattern can prevent lasting damage, the authors stress.
pmc-13278368:
Benardine Phillip Mallilah leads a 2026 case report of a baby born with seven toes on one foot. Extra digits, called polydactyly, are common, but seven digits with extra toes on both the inner and outer sides of the same foot is exceedingly rare. The nine-month-old girl had a normal other foot, normal hands, and no family history of such anomalies.

X-rays confirmed full duplication of the inner and outer toe rays, with no central duplication or fused toes. Surgeons removed the outermost extra rays on each side, preserved nerves and vessels, and reshaped the foot for stable standing. Healing was smooth, appearance improved, and early use of the limb was symmetric. Careful imaging guided the plan.
pmc-13278868:
Büşra Alper and co-authors enrich yoghurt with protected olive leaf extract in a 2026 food study. Olive leaf compounds such as hydroxytyrosol offer antioxidant effects, yet unprotected they degrade and can spoil flavour. The extract was packed into proniosome capsules and added before or after fermentation.

Both timings behaved much the same in fermentation, and a half-gram capsule dose performed best overall. Capsules raised antioxidant activity while leaving basic properties and taste largely unchanged. Liquid separation from the yoghurt fell compared with free extract versions. After lab digestion, yoghurts dosed after fermentation kept stronger antioxidant activity than those dosed before. The authors propose the capsules as a yoghurt upgrade.
pmc-13279168:
Jiahua Wu and colleagues report a 2026 study that hunts gene signs for gum disease. The disease is periodontitis, a long term swelling of tissues that hold teeth in place. It affects near half of all people and can loosen teeth. The team focus on genes tied to mitochondria, the power parts of cells.

Gene data and cell reads yielded six marker genes for the disease. A six gene chart sorted patients with strong accuracy in their tests. Single cell reads pointed to T cells, a type of immune cell, as key drivers. Tests in patient samples and rats backed three of the markers. A drug screen also named a compound that bound one marker well, a lead for later work.
pmc-13279268:
Daisy Yi Ding and colleagues report a 2026 study that reads cell aging from blood proteins. Aging does not move at one pace in all cells or organs. The team asked if blood tests could date many cell types at once. They read more than seven thousand proteins in blood from more than sixty thousand people.

Machine learning, meaning computer pattern search, built age scores for more than forty cell types. About one fifth to one fourth of people showed fast aging in just one cell type. Those scores linked to disease now and forecast new disease and death over fifteen years. Gene type APOE shifted brain support cell and immune cell ages in split ways. Extreme brain cell aging sharply raised Alzheimer risk in high risk gene carriers.
pmc-13279768:
Zineb Mekkaoui and colleagues report a 2026 study of metformin in a rare, fierce blood cancer. The cancer, BPDCN, grows from a rare immune cell type and has few care options. Metformin, a common diabetes pill, has drawn cancer interest of late. Its effects in this cancer were unknown. Tests ran in two lab cell lines and in fresh patient cells.

Key growth paths fell as well, four named signal chains in all. In mice, the drug cut tumour spread to the spleen and tuned two signal chains. Yet its hold on overall disease pace stayed limited. Dual hits on fuel and survival mark it as a helper drug lead.
pmc-13279968:
Grace E. Patterson and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of fish oil in moderate acute malnutrition. Acute malnutrition, or wasting, is a world health problem in children. Standard rescue foods are dense pastes rich in omega six fats, which can fuel swelling, and low in omega three fats, which calm it. Relapse rates stay high on those foods. Gut germ mix shifted in a sound way as well. Body wide swelling fell versus the standard fat mix. The result hints that fat quality, not just calories, drives recovery in wasting.
pmc-13280068:
Wolf C. Bartholoma and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of MRI based liver function in a rare bile duct disease. Primary sclerosing cholangitis scars the bile ducts and liver, with a course that varies a lot by patient. Spotting who faces poor outcomes is hard. Usual MRI scores lean on operator calls or still measures. The team test a pharmacokinetic model, which tracks how a contrast dye moves through the liver over time.

Twenty six patients had up to five yearly MRI scans, with follow up to seven and a half years. Endpoints held liver transplant, decompensated cirrhosis, a failed scarred liver, and bile duct cancer. The model score linked with two standard risk scores, the MELD score and the Amsterdam Oxford Model. Links were moderate and ran in the expected direction. Time based dye curves may give a firmer risk gauge than still images.
pmc-13280268:
Che-Chia Hsu and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective study asking whether longer biologic treatment buys longer remission after the drug stops in moderate-to-severe psoriasis. In Taiwan, reimbursement capped biologics near two and a half years, while pivotal trials treated patients for at least four. The two-center study compared 113 shorter-course patients with 51 longer-course patients on three biologics. It tracked time until relapse after discontinuation.

Median drug-free remission lasted 211 days after long treatment against 111 days after short treatment. They label the findings preliminary, needing larger prospective confirmation before reimbursement policy leans on them.
pmc-13280468:
Bahaa Mohammed Badr and colleagues report a 2026 trial of gum fluid markers in obese patients with periodontitis. Periodontitis stages and grades sort gum disease by severity and pace. The trial asks if two fat related proteins in gingival crevicular fluid, adiponectin and resistin, track those stages. It also tests if phase one periodontal therapy shifts their levels. Sixty class three obese patients split equally in four stage and grade groups.

Body mass index and HbA1c, a blood sugar marker, were assessed with periodontal indices. Gum fluid was collected and analyzed before and three months after treatment. A positive correlation was observed between BMI and HbA1c and periodontal disease stages. After therapy, adiponectin and resistin levels were obviously affected. In the stage three group, resistin fell sharply. Fluid markers may aid staging and grading calls in obese patients.
pmc-13280568:
Mehran Rahimlou and colleagues report a 2026 cross sectional study of dietary glycemic index and load in metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome raises cardiovascular disease risk, and its diet links remain poorly understood. Glycemic index ranks how fast foods raise blood sugar, and glycemic load scales that by amount eaten. Blood markers held malondialdehyde, high sensitivity CRP, TNF alpha, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and E-selectin, all swelling or vessel harm signals. Higher glycemic index and load trended with elevated malondialdehyde, TNF alpha and VCAM-1 levels. Artery wall thickness also rose across higher tertile categories of both diet scores. Fast sugar diets align with vessel harm marks.
pmc-13281468:
Zhibin Zhao and co-authors build a finer brain-signal measure to tell two grades of minimal consciousness apart. Their study appeared in 2026. Patients in the plus grade show richer signs, such as following commands, and recover better. The team recorded resting brain waves from 45 patients across three states of impaired consciousness, plus 15 healthy controls. Their new measure tracks the order patterns inside brief stable scalp patterns called microstates, catching shifts that simpler complexity scores miss.

The measure separated the plus and minus grades where several standard features were compared head to head. The authors say microstate order holds clinical information that steady-state summaries throw away. If confirmed in larger samples, such a marker could sharpen prognosis and care planning for families facing these diagnoses.
pmc-13281868:
Yurong Tang and colleagues built a survey on what lung patients need to know in a 2026 study. The patients have COPD, a long-term lung disease that narrows airways. Rehab helps, but patients differ in what guidance they want. The team drafted questions from past studies and talks with twelve patients. Thirty-five experts refined the draft in rounds. After a small pilot, three hundred patients at five hospitals in Changsha, China, answered the survey in 2024.

The final scale holds thirty-nine items in six areas of need. Math checks split the answers into six clean factors. Expert judges rated the content as highly apt. Scores were steady across repeats of like items. A second math frame showed each item sorted patients sharply. Most patients were older men, with an average age near seventy-one. The authors offer the scale for clinics to tailor rehab teaching.
pmc-13282068:
Jennifer S Ferris and co-authors wrote a 2026 research letter on two tests often used to screen for ovarian cancer in older women. One is a blood test called CA 125, and the other is an ultrasound scan done through the vagina. Using large insurance claim databases, the team tracked women over fifty at routine gynaecologic exams from 2008 to 2019. None had cancer history or symptoms that would justify the tests. More than seven million women with private insurance and about two hundred thousand with Medicaid were included. CA 125 testing fell over time for all women. Ultrasound use fell only among women with Medicaid. The letter tracks whether low-value screening is slowly fading in routine care.
pmc-13282268:
Thein Myint Twin and co-authors report a 2026 survey of mental health burden in Eastern Shan State, Myanmar.
