Standard questionnaires screened for depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and probable post-traumatic stress disorder, a condition that can follow traumatic events.

Nearly half the adults showed depressive symptoms. About one in five showed anxiety symptoms, and about one in eleven met the probable stress disorder screen. Joblessness, money strain, food insecurity, forced displacement, and living apart from family all raised the odds. Weak support from a close special person was a strong factor for both depression and anxiety. The authors call for combined help that pairs mental health support with livelihood recovery and food aid.
pmc-13282468:
Dagmar Haase and Dara Gaeva wrote a 2026 exploratory study on plant diversity and ecosystem services in Berlin allotment gardens. Allotments are small rented garden plots common in German cities. Urbanisation and intensive farming have cut plant diversity and pollinators elsewhere. The authors surveyed ten plots in 2019, comparing management intensity and sorting plants into use groups such as edible, ornamental, and nectar plants.

They found three hundred seventy-six plant species, including seventeen recommended natives and fourteen invasive species. Over half the plants served several uses at once. Native and weedy species richness, and plants supporting regulation services, fell as management intensified. Lighter mowing and trimming let more diverse plants persist. pmc-13282868:

The cross-sectional study enrolled 100 patients at Ain Shams University Hospital. Half had kidney disease and half did not. Blood CXCL10 was higher in the kidney group. Levels also rose with protein in urine, kidney strain, and disease activity scores. Levels fell as kidney filtration and protective blood proteins rose. The authors present CXCL10 as a candidate marker needing more testing.
pmc-13283068:
Akash Devi and Chitra Khanwelkar screen a muscle relaxant drug for possible anti-cancer action in dish tests. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The drug, thiocolchicoside, is built much like colchicine, a known cell poison, which hints it might harm cancer cells too.

Two human cancer lines were used: a breast line and a stomach line. Cells were dosed across a range for one to two days, and survival was read with a standard color test. The drug killed cells in a dose-linked way, though it was weaker than the standard comparison drug. The authors say the result justifies deeper work on how it acts and tests in animals. The study is an early, cheap screen, not proof of patient benefit.
pmc-13283168:
Curcumin lit by blue light attacks Candida biofilms unevenly across species, Joao Salviano Simoes Chagas da Silva and partners report for 2026. Biofilms shield yeasts from drugs and help infections persist. The treatment uses curcumin with blue light to create reactive oxygen that harms cells.

Light treatment blocked new biofilm growth in all species by wide margins. Effects on mature biofilms were also tested with the same setup. Benefit varied by species, which supports use as a preventive step more than a cure.
pmc-13283468:

Diabetes is a known dementia risk, yet the roles of its small-vessel complications and of blood sugar control were less clear. The review searched three databases for studies through March 2026 and rated their quality with a standard scale.

Five studies covering about 1.7 million people qualified. The authors back tighter sugar control and regular complication checks.
pmc-13283568:
Madison Brenner and colleagues surveyed teen athletes in 2026 about burnout and past leg injuries. Burnout was measured with a fifteen-item questionnaire covering physical and emotional exhaustion, souring on sport, and a reduced sense of achievement. Parents and athletes aged thirteen to eighteen answered online, reporting organised sport in the past year and any sport-related lower limb injury in that span.

The analysis covered 697 athletes, average age about fifteen, and 45 percent reported a past-year leg injury. Overuse and sudden injuries were counted separately. Physical exhaustion scores tied clearly to sudden injuries, with higher exhaustion raising the odds, and the team tested the same links for overuse injuries while accounting for age and sex. The work adds injury history to the known harms of burnout in youth sport.
pmc-13284068:
Tongxin Yang and co-authors presented in 2026 a lean image processor for robots and small smart devices. Turning raw camera data into faithful colour images is heavy work, which strains edge hardware with tight memory and power. Their system, EQISP, pairs a compressed neural network with a pyramid method that blends exposures across scales, keeping broad lighting and fine detail together.

In comparison tests the system reached strong image quality scores while cutting computing cost more than fourfold against a standard baseline. Running on a Jetson TX2 board, a common robot computer, it held a 57-megabyte model, answered in under two hundred milliseconds, and peaked at 2.2 gigabytes of memory. The authors offer it as a practical front end for embodied perception.
pmc-13284268:

Seventeen patients at a large fertility center gave in-depth interviews for the study. Sessions ran between December 2025 and March 2026 with chosen sampling. Four themes with thirteen subthemes organized the material from those talks. Repeat failure, invasive steps, and doubt fed the stuck feeling most. Family and medical stress added weight to daily life and mood.
pmc-13284468:

Among patients aged 65 and older with chronic prescriptions, counts fell from 525 to 492 in the first year. With no control group, the authors urge care in claiming the program alone caused the change.
pmc-13284868:

The analysis covered 271 patients in Ontario with uncomplicated bloodstream infection. Outcome rankings at 180 days were alike between the two duration groups under all three scoring versions tested here. Resistant germ or C. difficile events were uncommon in both arms. The authors say adding resistance data is feasible and may better show trade-offs of shorter courses.
pmc-13284968:
Alanood Almeraisel and co-authors survey skin doctors on one-step melanoma surgery guided by ultrasound in a 2026 study. Fifty-three dermatologists in the Loire Valley in France answered case scenarios and rating questions. One-step surgery was chosen in just over a quarter of cases, rising when biopsy proof existed and falling without it. Most saw ultrasound as useful and felt patients would prefer one procedure. Top barriers were poor access to high-grade ultrasound, fear of overtreatment, and legal risk without prior lab proof.
pmc-13285968:
Salah N El-Tallawy leads a multicenter study of pain after surgery in children, published in 2026. The study followed 325 children aged three to twelve having planned operations, split into preschool and school-age groups. Children's pain is hard to judge because age changes how they feel and report it, and evidence on what predicts severe pain has been limited.

Pain peaked soon after surgery, then eased over the first day. Severe pain hit about a quarter of the children, with no clear gap between age groups. Early pain, anxiety before surgery, and needing extra pain medicine predicted worse pain. Local anesthetic placed before the cut, regional blocks, calming premedication, and preparation beforehand all lowered the odds. Satisfaction with pain care averaged high.
pmc-13286368:

Published in 2026, the work uses a dual-band lidar that watches flying insects over a field and records thousands per day. Raw signals form two-dimensional patterns over distance and time, too bulky for quick species or direction judgments.

The authors reduce those patterns step by step into time series and then single values that still carry clues about flight heading and body traits. A one-night dataset served as the test case. The reduced measures confirmed expected patterns in insect darkening and revealed insects with unusual spectral signatures. Such summaries could make real-time monitoring practical for conservation planning.
pmc-13286568:
Kenji J Nishimura and colleagues pinpoint a thalamus hub behind stress-heightened fear in a 2026 mouse study. pmc-13286968:
Rawan A. Obeidat and colleagues measure vitamin D in Jordanian mothers and their newborns at delivery. Deficiency in pregnancy has been tied to complications for both mother and baby.

Nearly every sample fell below the sufficiency line, with typical levels around a third of that threshold. Fewer than one woman in five reported taking supplements. Mother and cord levels moved together moderately. Summer births showed higher levels than winter births in both generations. Babies born small for their age had lower cord levels. Screening and supplementation strategies need evaluation, the authors conclude.
pmc-13287268:
Edinael Rodrigues de Almeida and co-authors fed supplements to 48 suckling Nellore calves on pasture in 2026 for 117 days. Calves received minerals only, or a protein concentrate in a creep feeder. The concentrate carried no dried distillers grains, about half grains, or almost all grains.

Adding more grains lowered digestion of dry matter, protein, and fast carbohydrates in a steady pattern. Blood glucose and growth signals rose with concentrate feeding. Final performance did not differ by grain level. The authors say the by-product can replace corn and soy in calf supplements.
pmc-13287368:
Harui Bamba and co-authors reported in 2026 a man aged 63 with well-controlled HIV who developed a rare blood problem while on high-dose steroids for a kidney condition. Tests fit cold agglutinin syndrome, where red cells are destroyed in the cold. Blood also showed a raised load of Epstein-Barr virus, pointing to reactivation under weakened immunity. Care focused on support and a faster steroid taper. The authors warn that steroid treatment in people with HIV can open the door to such virus-linked complications.
pmc-13287668:
Xianbang Huang, Ling Li, and Song Wang wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It untangles the two-way links over time between exercise, social anxiety, and internet addiction in teenagers.

The team surveyed 877 middle school students in Jiangxi Province, China, twice, sixteen weeks apart. Cross-lagged analysis tested which factor at the first wave predicted the others later. Exercise predicted itself strongly and predicted less internet addiction later. Social anxiety predicted more of itself and more addiction, and slightly less exercise. pmc-13287768:

Agreement across raters was substantial overall, with a reliability score near 0.71. Three types reached near-perfect agreement, while one type scored only moderate agreement. Raters struggled most to separate two similar types, so the authors suggest merging them in a revised system.
pmc-13287968:

The man needed a second operation after a join leaked. Both recovered with normal blood values. The authors stress fast scope checks when long diarrhoea pairs with salt loss.
pmc-13288268: Ye Jiang and co-authors issued this 2026 correction for their study of cardiovascular death trends linked to rheumatoid arthritis among United States adults from 1999 to 2023. The notice is a correction only, fixing the captions of three figures and adding no new data or analysis. The captions for figures 3, 4, and 5 had been rotated onto the wrong charts. In the corrected version, figure 3 breaks rates down by gender, figure 4 shows deaths by urbanization level, and figure 5 gives rates by race. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13289168:
Shuai Jiang and a team of co-authors design a vaccine that guards against three types of echovirus at once, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Echoviruses spread widely and can cause brain lining infection, heart swelling, and grave illness in newborns. Many types exist, which makes one vaccine hard to build. The team focused on three common types, numbered eleven, eighteen, and thirty.

They mapped the parts of a shell protein that antibodies target most. Then they grafted loops from two types onto the frame of the third, keeping the natural shape. Both a protein vaccine and an mRNA vaccine built from this design made mice produce antibodies that blocked all three types. The work backs shape-guided grafting as a route to broad vaccines.
pmc-13289368:
Maria Solovyeva and colleagues raise a 2026 dosing concern for aciclovir, an antiviral drug, in children with obesity. Standard rules dose by weight or body surface area, yet body makeup differs sharply in obesity and can push doses too high or too low. Safety reports for the drug in children exceed 100 since 2015 in United Kingdom data cited.

Guidance switches methods by age, and weight-based dosing uses ideal weight for very heavy children, while surface area dosing still uses total weight with no such cap. Since the drug spreads with body water more than fat, total-weight dosing can overshoot safe levels. A sudden drop also occurs when methods switch at age 12 in current rules. The authors propose smoother, body-aware dosing.
pmc-13289568:
Shuo Li and colleagues build interactive software that grades childhood pneumonia severity from lung ultrasound, in 2026. Judging severity guides treatment, yet bedside calls can be subjective. The team collected ultrasound images from 293 children, split between mild and severe pneumonia. Software extracted 104 numerical features from regions that clinicians outlined. Ten machine learning methods were trained and compared on those features.

A model called LightGBM performed best on held-out test images. It reached about 90 percent accuracy, catching most severe cases while rarely overcalling mild ones. Explanation tools ranked shape-based features as the strongest signals in its decisions. The model was wrapped into software that walks a user from image upload to a severity score. The authors say such a tool could standardize assessment at the point of care. It may help smaller clinics match specialist judgment.
pmc-13289868:
Raffaele Ferri and colleagues lay out a 2026 protocol for the DREAMER cohort on isolated REM sleep without muscle relaxation. Dream-enactment behavior in REM sleep strongly predicts later synuclein diseases such as Parkinson disease. An earlier sign, loss of muscle quieting in REM sleep without behavior symptoms, may mark risk sooner, but whether it is harmless or a warning is unknown.

Four Italian sleep centers will screen adults aged 40 or older having full-night video sleep studies with shared rules. People with prior dream-enactment disorder or poor quality REM data are excluded from enrollment. A standard REM Atonia Index threshold defines the isolated finding. Planned follow-up will track who develops behavior disorder or degeneration.
pmc-13290468:
Cutting farm ammonia and nitrous oxide together works better than feared in China, Fangming Jiang and a large team report in 2026. The two gases pull against climate and air-quality goals, and whether policies help both at once or trade one off against the other was unclear.

Pairing detailed emission inventories with policy-by-policy scenarios for 2000 to 2022, the team found that both gases peaked around 2015. They then fell, ammonia by 16% and nitrous oxide by 30% by 2022 in the team's estimates. Fertilizer-reduction policies delivered about 90% of the post-2015 gains, with their joint benefit rising sixfold. Manure and straw policies were weaker and sometimes traded off, though optimized livestock management could flip that sector to synergy. The authors map where policies reinforce each other so future rules can aim there.
pmc-13290568:
Health workers across the Americas hold mixed feelings about ChatGPT, Ivan Cherrez-Ojeda and colleagues found in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. Evidence from Latin American practice is thin, and regional gaps in digital access color how such tools land.

The online survey ran from May to September 2023 and drew 747 respondents, most of them practicing in Ecuador, with physicians and dentists the largest groups. Just over half had heard of ChatGPT and about a third had used it, mostly for study help and research writing. Among those who knew the tool, most called it useful, yet judgments on ethics split: many rated AI-written manuscript text unethical, and using it as a sole clinical source drew wider disapproval. The authors map where enthusiasm and caution sit so training can meet both.
pmc-13291268:
Hidden values in light resonators are hard to pin down. Song-Yi Liu leads a 2026 study mixing physics with deep learning. Classic fitting can give many answers for one system. That flaw has blocked study of coupled resonators for years.

Their network learns from both data and physics rules. It checks its answers against true system responses. That check cuts the many-answer trap. Tests in simulation and in lab gear both passed. Run time fell by a huge factor. Accuracy rose by a large margin as well. A sensing test showed the method holds under strain. It may reshape how resonant gear is designed.
pmc-13291568:
A new gene fault is tied to a rare brain and bone disease. Qian Liu leads a 2026 case study of a Chinese family. Nasu-Hakola disease brings early dementia and bone cysts. Faults in the TREM2 gene cause most cases.

Their patient was a middle-aged man with ankle pain. His thinking declined early and kept worsening. Scans showed a shrunken brain and cystic bone lesions. Gene tests found a double dose of a fresh deletion fault. Lab cells made the faulty message but little protein. Past cases numbered 54 in the review part. Wide symptom variety marks this disease. Early gene testing is urged for odd early dementia.
pmc-13292068:
Ernest Famada Arboix and colleagues report a 2026 European study of gram-negative infections across several centres in artificial hip and knee joints. Three referral hospitals in Italy, Spain, and Switzerland reviewed every culture-positive joint infection diagnosed from 2014 to 2018. The team recorded patient traits, germs found, which drugs still worked, operations used, and whether treatment succeeded.

Of 780 confirmed cases, 71, or 9.1 percent of the total, came from gram-negative germs. Mixed growth led at 29.6 percent, followed by Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa among single germs. Patients skewed elderly, female, and burdened by diabetes or excess weight. Overall success reached 89 percent of cases treated, with two-stage redo surgery best at 94.8 percent, ahead of one-stage exchange and a washout that kept the implant. Ciprofloxacin featured in 72 percent of treatments.
pmc-13292568:
Jiyeon Min, Bernard R Brooks, and Muhamed Amin build a 2026 resource called FeSseqdb for finding iron-sulfur proteins, the workhorses carrying metal clusters for electron transfer and catalysis. Existing annotations are patchy, so they mined the Protein Data Bank and verified each cluster-bearing chain against its atomic coordinates. Standardized ligand labels turned the haul into a clean sequence-level database.

On top of it sits a prediction framework using only simple sequence features: amino acid makeup, cysteine metrics, and length. A random forest trained with SVMSMOTE resampling performed best among the classifiers tried. Explainable AI pointed to cysteine frequency and placement plus proline content as the lead signals, matching cysteine's known job of gripping the clusters. Serine, glutamate, and arginine contributed secondarily. The authors pitch the pairing as discovery tool and hypothesis source in one.
pmc-13292668:
Mohammed M Qaid and co-authors feed a 2026 plant mixture to broiler chickens deliberately infected with Eimeria tenella, the gut parasite behind costly coccidiosis. The blend pairs cinnamon with Rumex nervosus, a phytobiotic alternative to the synthetic drugs that resistance keeps eroding. Outcomes covered growth, carcass traits, cecal wall structure, and how many parasite eggs the birds shed.

Infection alone wrecked growth and cecal health in the untreated challenged group. The plant mixture cut oocyst shedding by as much as 75.8 percent against that group in the highlights. Anticoccidial index scores of 162 to 168 rated the activity as marked. The high dose best repaired cecal shape and thinned the swollen wall, while the low dose paradoxically gave the best growth among supplemented groups. The authors back phytobiotics as a serious control option.
pmc-13293368:
Christopher Koch and co-authors interview, in a 2026 study, young doctors from a digital-focused university in Germany about spreading digital health at work. Witten/Herdecke University teaches digital topics, and its graduates work in clinics, firms, and start-ups.

Nineteen graduates from the past 15 years described how they gained digital skills, mostly through self-study and learning on the job. They saw strong promise in their own role, yet cited knowledge gaps, scarce resources, and tangled rules as blocks. Better access to learning, clearer workplace structures, and supportive policy were named as needs. Their views may guide schools training digital-ready doctors.
pmc-13293568:
Vanessa das Graças José Ventura leads a 2026 study warning that a popular model score can mislead when health outcomes are lopsided. The score, called AUROC, stays high even when a model misses many rare but vital cases.

Records covered 17,018 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, with models predicting kidney replacement therapy and death. Both outcomes were uncommon next to survivors, yet headline scores looked excellent. Closer checks showed weak precision and recall for the rarer outcome, based on values the authors report. Rebalancing training data lifted recall but cut precision, with little change in the headline score. Wider metrics are urged.
pmc-13293668:
Jessica L. Harding and Stephen O. Pastan weigh new ways of judging kidney transplant programs in the United States, in a 2026 editorial. More than ninety thousand people wait for a donor kidney there. For years, programs were graded almost wholly on how patients fared after surgery, with little regard for what happened during the long wait.

Two newer measures now track how often programs accept organ offers and how many listed patients die before a transplant. A study of 220 programs from 2015 to 2020 found that bigger waiting lists came with worse scores on both counts. The authors worry that large centers, which often carry the sickest patients, may be blamed for size rather than poor care. They offer the work as a yardstick for judging the new rules.
pmc-13294368:
Samodya K. Jayasinghe and coauthors time gene activity during potato infection in a 2026 transcript study. Powdery scab soil germ also carries Potato mop-top virus, and both spoil tubers. Three cultivars with differing toughness gave early infection RNA data, mined with differential expression and co-expression networks to find high-confidence defense genes.

Eighty candidates emerged, 52 tied to the soil germ and 28 to the virus in the reported split. Immune receptors, hormone genes, and defense enzymes like lipoxygenase and glutathione transferase featured heavily. Named targets give breeders molecular handles for building potatoes that resist both threats at once, a step beyond slow field screening.
pmc-13294568:
Eldisugi Hassan Mohammed Humida and Hussain Gadelkarim Ahmed analyse heart disease in Sudan from 1970 to 2025 in a 2026 article. Their work draws on published studies and public data gathered during a period when civil conflict has badly damaged health services. Cardiovascular conditions and their risk factors weigh heavily on the country.

Sources included major medical databases, World Health Organization reports, and other public collections that met set criteria. Geography, population movement, climate pressures, poverty, and weak services all shape the pattern described. Stronger health systems, better data collection, public awareness, research, supportive laws, community action, and wider technology access are presented as needs for better monitoring and control.
pmc-13295068:
Feng Liu and colleagues compare two painkillers for sickness after thyroid surgery in a 2026 randomised trial. Nausea and vomiting are common after this operation and are worsened by opioid drugs. Oliceridine, a newer opioid designed to spare some side effects, was tested against the standard drug sufentanil.

Altogether 232 patients were assigned to one drug or the other during surgery, with outcomes tracked for 48 hours. Sickness struck about 12 percent of the oliceridine group against about 28 percent of the comparison group. Pain relief, recovery quality, and rescue pain treatment stayed similar, while rescue anti-sickness doses were also fewer with oliceridine.
pmc-13295468:
Petra Dannapfel, Annie Axelsson, and Susanne M K Gustavsson study a failed health record rollout in Sweden in a 2026 article. A large system, Millennium, was stopped soon after launch, leaving staff who lived through it with strong lessons. Interviews with 73 clinicians and office staff explored readiness before, during, and after the change.

Staff described poor communication from management, thin training, and little grip on the coming change. Many felt deceived, disappointed, and stressed, wanting a voice in the process and a view of the whole picture. Missing dialogue fed anxiety and a sense of abandonment, underlining that such rollouts are social projects as much as technical ones.
pmc-13295568:
Jokin Zubizarreta Oteiza and colleagues print personalised skull and face implants at the hospital in a 2026 study. Plain PEEK plastic is weak in strength, invisible on scans, and biologically quiet for such implants. Three filled versions were matched to three jobs: jaw plates, eye socket floors, and chin pieces.

Carbon fibre, barium sulfate, and mineral filled plastics printed with near-perfect success across the set. Printed shapes stayed within a fraction of a millimetre of their designs, and sterilising barely moved them. Layers bonded fully with no cracking seen. The work shows bedside making of tuned implants is workable while keeping custom fit.
pmc-13295768:
Linlin Song and a large team build a light-triggered nanoplatform against stubborn breast cancer in a 2026 study. Triple-negative breast cancer resists many treatments and responds weakly to immune therapy. Their liposome system carries light-heating dots plus a gas-storing liquid that can release ozone on cue.

Under deep-penetrating infrared light, the platform heated tumours, gave imaging signals for tracking, and burst out ozone in place. Heat plus oxidative attack killed cancer cells in a fiery, immune-alerting way. In animals, pairing the treatment with a checkpoint drug shrank both treated and distant tumours, with no clear body-wide toxicity seen.
pmc-13296068:
Yajing Li, Hongru Deng, and Yongquan Gu build a machine learning model that flags who may develop buttock pain on walking after aneurysm repair, in a 2026 two-center study. The pain, called buttock claudication, follows stent repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm and drags on recovery. Records covered 272 patients from two hospitals, and seventy-one of them developed the pain.

Risk ran higher with aneurysms that reached the iliac arteries, male sex, blood fat trouble, and sealing of one or both inner iliac arteries, while keeping more small branches open guarded patients. Ten learning methods were tuned and checked on held-out data, and a neural network read the risk best. Built-in explanations show which facts drive each score, and a web calculator puts the tool at the bedside.
pmc-13296168:
Matija Švagan follows up, in 2026, children who had one severe middle-ear infection needing surgery, asking whether a single fierce episode can harm hearing like repeated infections do. Sixty-five patients were tested a median of over eleven years after surgery and compared with healthy volunteers.

Both operated groups, whether they had deeper ear surgery or drainage tubes alone, showed raised hearing thresholds at high pitches and weaker inner-ear responses. Balance reflexes stayed normal, and the deeper surgery added no extra harm. The author argues infection severity itself leaves a lasting mark and backs long-term hearing checks.
pmc-13296268:
Ayat Tassanov and co-authors make, in 2026, ten layered sulphur-family crystals combining an alkali metal, copper and hafnium, and map how their internal arrangement shapes light behaviour. Crystals were grown at high temperature and read by X-ray methods, with theory backing the measurements.

Two stacking patterns appeared, and they split neatly by optical character: one gave direct band gaps, the other indirect, across a useful energy range. Larger alkali ions with smaller partner atoms favoured the first pattern. A learning model trained on known compounds turned those trends into a predictive map for hunting new optical materials.
pmc-13296868:
Xiaozhe Liu and colleagues review palmitoylation, a reversible fat-based protein tag, as a switch controlling regulated cell death in a 2026 article. Adding this lipid anchor changes where proteins sit, how long they last, and which partners they gather. The review covers apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy-linked death.

Named examples show the tag steering death receptors, inflammatory sensors, and protective enzymes in each pathway. Faulty tagging contributes to cancer, brain degeneration, and inflammatory disease in the gathered evidence. Hard problems remain, including measuring tagging dynamics and separating causes from side effects. Enzymes that add or remove the tag are proposed as drug targets.
pmc-13297268:
Haosong Du and colleagues review ultraviolet sensing as the guide thread for medical systems in a 2026 article. Ultraviolet light acts strongly on DNA, proteins, and other tissue parts, giving rich signals with no added labels. Three paths shape the field: imaging weighted to surfaces, dose checks worn on the body, and therapy steered by sensor feedback.

Cases range from sound-based microscopy that images cell nuclei without labels to fast tissue readout with no slides, plus flexible dose patches worn on skin. Computer tools help with fake staining, image repair, and dose forecasts in the systems surveyed. Shared steps link the uses, from signal capture through checks to feedback-led choices. Shared standards and care with doubt in readings remain the main hurdles.
pmc-13297368:
Ewelina Młynarska and a large team review how layered molecular data, read by artificial intelligence, could sharpen heart medicine, in a 2026 article. Heart and vessel diseases remain the top global killer, yet standard markers often miss early stages and cannot chart one patient's course. Single-layer gene or protein studies abound, with no shared frame to join them.

The review joins evidence on small regulatory RNAs and cell parcels with a hard look at learning models, from basic to deep networks. It maps routes that turn signatures, such as the gut product TMAO and certain heart RNAs, into risk models for heart failure and life after heart attack. The true block, the authors argue, is not scarce data but unshared workflows and models doctors cannot read.
pmc-13297668:
Probability distributions can be compared as points on a curved surface, and Argelia Aguilar Garduño with co-authors extend that geometric view in a 2026 mathematics paper. Their route describes each distribution through the coefficients of a quadratic curve fitted to its mean square error.

Those coefficients span a manifold of their own, letting distributions from different families be compared by the arc length between their points. The authors work out the geometry of this error-based surface and set it beside the Fisher-Rao distance, the standard yardstick of information geometry. Their empirical tests suggest the error-based description can reveal relationships between distributions that conventional comparisons may miss.
pmc-13297968:
Children who brush less and carry more cavity-causing bacteria gain more new decay over two years, found a 2026 longitudinal study in Mexico City led by Leonor Sánchez-Pérez. The team followed 118 schoolchildren aged 7 to 10, recording brushing habits, sugar intake, saliva measures, and bacterial counts.

Children who started cavity-free added fewer lesions in permanent teeth than peers, at 0.2 on average. Across the group, low brushing frequency raised the odds of new caries nearly threefold (OR = 2.77), as did high counts of Streptococcus mutans (OR = 3.38) and Lactobacillus (OR = 2.91). The authors recommend prevention programs that push hygiene habits and bacterial control together.
pmc-13298568:
Yasuko Kawahata challenges the assumption that more data always means truer results, in a 2026 sociophysics study. Social systems add conformity pressure and systemic bias, which can change what huge samples actually show. Simulations based on an Ising-style opinion model ran to extremely large scales using macro-dynamic approximations.

Beyond a threshold the author calls a signal cliff, information diversity collapses and minority signals get discarded as noise. Entropy falls as the system shifts from a varied phase toward a fixed one, which the author frames as mathematical epistemic injustice. A proposed diagnostic test aims to separate healthy consensus from distorted convergence in digital public debate.
pmc-13299268:
A growth guide strand that sits in nets round brain cells may tune how well mice hold a learned blink. Geoffrey-Alexander Gimenez and his team test that thought in a 2026 brain study. The strand is Sema3A, a repellent that steers young nerve fibers and rests in the adult brain in tight nets round some cells.

The team blocked the strand's signs in two ways while mice learned to blink at a tone. A virus-borne decoy in one deep brain node cut scores early in the hold phase, though sore tissue at the site clouds that read. Mice born with weak Sema3A signs from birth did the flip: they held the blink a bit more well early on, with no clear change in cell links. The team read the gene result as a hint that life-long weak signs fine-tune this kind of memory.
pmc-13300368:
Ruotong Shen and co-authors report a 2026 study of how mild carbon dioxide levels affect the larger black flour beetle, a stored grain pest spreading worldwide. Grain bulks naturally reach carbon dioxide levels between a quarter and four percent, and such levels might support fumigation or controlled atmosphere treatments. Beetles were raised at five gas concentrations and two temperatures, then compared with controls breathing ordinary air on survival, development, egg laying, and life table measures.

Carbon dioxide in the tested range changed survival and development at both temperatures. Once levels passed a quarter or half percent, generation time, survival rate, egg laying, and population growth measures all shifted significantly. The authors argue these biological responses matter when setting exposure times for gas based pest control. Their results add a reference point for managing this beetle in modern monitored grain stores.
pmc-13301568:
Fish gelatin, a by-product turned printing ink, gets a cross-sector audit in a 2026 review by Beril Bayrak and colleagues. The survey follows marine gelatin into three-dimensional printing for medicine, food, and health products, where its body-friendly nature, low cost, and adjustable flow draw designers. Print quality hinges on concentration, temperature, gelling behavior, and machine settings.

Blending gelatin with other additives stiffens prints and sharpens accuracy, patching its natural weakness. The authors map uses from tissue scaffolds and drug carriers to personalized foods and biodegradable packaging. Fish sources also ease cultural objections and valorize seafood waste, though mammalian gelatin still dominates the market they describe.
pmc-13302468:
R Fonseca Oliveira Suruagy Motta and colleagues review, in a 2026 single-centre series, upgrades from ordinary two-chamber pacemakers to multisite pacing for stubborn heart failure. Years of pacing from the lower right chamber can itself weaken the heart by forcing uncoordinated contraction. Rewiring the system to pace several sites aims to restore coordination.

Seventy-one patients were upgraded among more than nine hundred multisite implants performed since 2006. Chagas disease was the commonest underlying cause, ahead of coronary and valve disease. The upgrade succeeded technically and clinically in about seventy-eight percent of cases, with no complications reported during or after the procedures. Most patients also received a defibrillator function, and pumping strength improved in fifty-two patients over the following year.
pmc-13302568:
Amato Serra and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, a simple liver-fibrosis score as a warning marker in heart failure. The FIB-4 index is calculated from routine blood values and age, and it may capture the liver congestion that a struggling right heart produces. Evidence was compared across heart failure types and against the standard hormone marker.

Raised scores tracked closely with venous congestion and right-sided dysfunction, and predicted bad outcomes most strongly when pumping strength was preserved. In weaker-heart forms, the score's value faded and was muddied by primary liver disease. During acute admissions, a falling score during treatment carried its own favourable signal. The authors want prospective work to fix cut-offs and test responses to newer drugs.
pmc-13302768:
N Varma and co-authors measure, in a 2026 study, how many alerts from modern implanted heart monitors turn out to be clinically pointless when judged by strict guideline rules. Clinics drown in device transmissions, and each brand pre-filters differently. An independent committee re-read episodes under one standard annotation scheme.

The dataset held 2,659 episodes from 1,710 patients carrying monitors from four major makers. Among devices without built-in artificial intelligence, about forty-five percent of episodes were non-actionable and a fifth were unreadable or uncertain. Artificial intelligence models did better on real events but left even more episodes in the uncertain bucket. Pause alerts misled most often, frequently caused by undersensing, and the authors demand better universal analysis tools.
pmc-13305268:
Marika Mortuladze leads a 2026 review of survival after living donor liver transplant in Georgia. Outcomes there lag rich-country results, so knowing which factors cut survival can target fixes.

Records covered 103 recipients transplanted between December 2014 and July 2024. Overall survival estimates fell most during the first year, then steadied across later years. Thirty-eight patients died during follow-up. Complications during or after surgery more than doubled death risk in adjusted models, and liver cancer as the transplant reason tripled it. Tackling changeable risks may lift Georgian results toward levels reported in high-income countries.
pmc-13305668:
Vahid Mohammadkarimi described a 2026 case where fluid built up in the abdomen soon after radiation for stomach cancer. The patient, a 51-year-old man, had received chemotherapy and surgery that cleared visible disease before adjuvant radiation began.

Drained fluid was rich in protein and lymphocytes, with no cancer cells found on testing. Imaging, repeat surgery with tissue samples, and lab checks ruled out recurrence plus heart, liver, infectious and other causes, leaving radiation injury as the likely explanation. One drainage cleared the fluid without return, and the authors urge vigilance and better ways to predict this rare problem.
pmc-13305768:
Georgina Hutchinson, Zara Tariq, and Sarah Denman report a 2026 pharmacy project in Leeds on penicillin allergy labels recorded during admission. Many labels describe side effects rather than true allergy, yet they stay on records and block first-line antibiotics. Pharmacy technicians checked histories against hospital guidance on an acute admissions ward.

A baseline audit found most reviewed patients might suit a penicillin challenge, and none had their allergy status checked during admission. In the follow-up audit, flagged patients were given a clinical note and a pharmacist alert. Two weeks later, no label had been removed by ward staff or general practitioners. The team calls for stronger multidisciplinary follow-through once suitable patients are spotted.
pmc-13305968:
Antonio Shegani introduces a 2026 special issue devoted to radioactive tracers and radiopharmaceuticals for cancer care. Tracers can reveal disease biology inside the body, guide treatment choices, and show whether a drug target is present across tumours. Paired diagnosis and therapy, known as theranostics, frames much of the collection.

Contributions span peptide probes for PET scanning, SPECT agents that profile receptors, and chemical tweaks that keep radioligands stable longer. One highlighted study labelled a peptide with gallium-68 to image blood-vessel receptors in breast cancer. Another measured HER2 levels with a technetium-labelled scaffold protein. Shegani presents the issue as a map of where tracer design, preclinical testing, and clinical translation currently stand.
pmc-13306168:
Ewelina Hallmann weighs pears grown under organic and standard orchard rules in a 2026 study of three types: Alexander Lucas, Conference, and Xenia. Organic rules ban man-made crop sprays and mineral feeds, so orchards rely on natural care and prevention. Fruit was tested for polyphenols, carotenoids, chlorophylls, and vitamin C.

Organic pears held clearly more vitamin C, total polyphenols, flavonoids, carotenoids, and chlorophyll than standard pears. Xenia stood out with the highest levels of several tested compounds. Growing season also shifted fruit makeup, so year-to-year weather counted next to farm system. The results feed a wider debate about whether organic fruit gives extra food value. The title's three-year framing sits beside season data centred on 2019 to 2020 in the summary.
pmc-13306268:
Chuzheng Zhang defined a dark plant state driven by anthocyanin pigments in a 2026 conceptual review. Intense colour arrives with wider cell and control changes, rather than pigment build-up alone, under stress from light, sugar signals, heat and hormones.

Control centres built around MYB, bHLH and WD40 proteins link pigment making with storage, transport and defence in the gathered evidence. Chemical marks on DNA and later gene editing steps further tune strength and staying power. Open puzzles include how stable the state stays, whether it stores stress memory, and how plants balance colour against growth costs.
pmc-13306368:
Donna Danijela Dragun spun polycaprolactone membranes with plant-derived solvents for organ-on-chip use in a 2026 study. The polymer suits medical work, yet standard spinning relies on hazardous solvents that greener labs want to avoid.

A mix of acetic and formic acids replaced the usual pair, and voltage, distance and flow settings were tuned through a planned design search. Resulting fibres were smooth and bead-free with mean width of 247 nm, about 37.3% finer than conventional mats in reported measures. Infrared checks confirmed full solvent loss, supporting safer membrane production.
pmc-13306568:
Lucia O. Pareja tracked a fast RNA-cutting response after leaf wounding in common bean in a 2026 plant study. Beans matter for protein and nitrogen fixing, yet tissue damage from pests and weather often cuts harvests.

Gel tests showed ribonuclease activity rising quickly while other nuclease activity stayed flat. Protein analysis named the main enzyme as PvRNS2, and its gene activity peaked at 2 hours with a 600-fold rise in reported figures. Damaged young roots showed a 55-fold rise as well, marking a broad wound signal. The fast reply hints at a role in priming the plant for more harm.
pmc-13307068:
Katy Sutcliffe set out a 2026 Cochrane protocol for a qualitative synthesis on weight care for groups often left out. The review asks what is known about behavioural weight programmes for people with mobility limits, intellectual disabilities or severe mental illness.

Five goals cover lived experience of weight and programmes, barriers and helpers for healthy weight, and how carers view support in the protocol plan. Access, communication, cost and programme fit receive close attention for each group. Findings will guide kinder, more reachable weight services. The team says the synthesis will shape how such reviews are run from now on.
pmc-13307168:
Huaqing Li separated slow drift from wear signals in turbine oil monitoring in a 2026 study. Multi-sensor oil streams drift with heat over time, hiding faint early damage traces inside noisy, uneven residuals.

The ResAD-Net design splits trend from residual, then models residuals with a diffusion method conditioned on the current trend. Dependency learning inside the residual stream exposes linked changes tied to early wear. The authors present the chain as a sharper early warning route for gas turbine maintenance decisions. The split of trend and wear trace is the core step that makes the warning work.
pmc-13309368:
M E Arnold and co-authors published a scoping review in 2026 about sex that college students later regret when drinking is involved. Earlier reports gave mixed claims about how common such regret is and whether men or women feel it more. The review gathers that scattered work into one clear summary.

Five databases were searched and 15 studies met the rules for inclusion. Lifetime rates ranged widely for both women and men, and most studies found no clear gap between the sexes. Only a few studies pointed in either direction. The authors argue that broad programs may work better than sex-specific ones and call for longer studies with more varied student groups.
pmc-13310768:
Xinzhu Sun and Nan Ge review a scope guided heat treatment for pancreas cysts in a 2026 paper. Some pancreas cysts can turn into cancer, yet surgery is major and watchful waiting can last for years. A needle based heat method offers a middle path for patients who cannot face surgery.

An ultrasound scope guides a thin probe into the cyst, and heat destroys the lining that makes fluid. Care teams weigh the method against fluid drainage with alcohol wash, by cyst type. Current proof shows high success with low harm in chosen cases. Gaps remain in proof quality and in shared steps, so stronger trials are needed.
pmc-13311068:
Yunbo Xie reports a 2026 case of ozone blood treatment as add on care for dermatomyositis. The autoimmune disease marks skin and inflames muscle, and steroid reliant patients face relapse and drug harm. A woman dependent on steroids added cycles of major ozone blood treatment without raising her steroid dose.

Care ran in 15 day treatment blocks split by 15 day rests over about 15 months in total. Blood muscle enzymes fell, shoulder skin ulcers healed, facial swelling eased, and skin looked normal again. Steroid side effects also lessened during the course. Solo case proof is weak, so controlled trials must test the add on.
pmc-13311168:
Oukhdouch Anass and colleagues map a plant compound against high grade glioma through network methods in a 2026 study. Glioblastoma is the most harsh adult brain tumor, and runaway cell cycling drives its growth. Hinokinin from a pepper plant shows anti cancer signs, yet its glioma targets were unknown.

Gene databases, target forecasts, and docking tools were joined in one pipeline. Thirty six shared genes emerged, rich in cycle control and kinase roles. Five hub genes stood out, all raised in tumors and tied to poor survival and p53 path faults. Docking and drug trait checks backed hinokinin fit. Lab tests must confirm the map.
pmc-13311368:
Gordon Manu Amponsah and co-authors analyze the 2026 twelve-year record review of heart rhythm problems in Ghanaian patients who came in with palpitations. A normal resting tracing can miss rhythm faults, so 24-hour monitoring was used.

The review covered 495 patients at a specialist heart clinic from 2010 to 2022 who wore a Holter monitor for a day. Clear rhythm trouble showed in 223 patients, or 45.1 percent of the group in this review. Extra beats were common, and rarer findings included atrial fibrillation and heart block. The results show how much a day-long tracing adds beyond a quick clinic check.
pmc-13311568:
Antoine Hennard and co-authors examine how well a Swiss health workforce cohort matches the wider workforce in a 2026 comparison study. The cohort recruited members indirectly, without a full national register to draw from.

The team set cohort profiles against 14 national data sources gathered from 2016 to 2023 across ten health professions. Sex balance matched outside sources well. Age mix, language mix, and some job details differed, reflecting both real diversity and gaps in the source data. The lessons apply to any country that must build workforce studies without a complete register.
pmc-13311968:
Joanne Hunt and Charlotte Blease write a 2024 article on how disabled scholars get shut out of health research, framed as a form of epistemic injustice. Disabled people face wide health gaps, and their insight could sharpen research.

The first author, largely home-confined by energy-limiting conditions, spent over three years seeking an accessible PhD program in the United Kingdom. The piece joins her account with published findings on barriers in academia. It frames the loss plainly: a mostly non-disabled research community overlooks problems and chances that lived experience would surface. Policy and academy habits both need change, the authors argue.
pmc-13312568:
Anne Rydland and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, whether the protein cargo of tiny cell-made particles in blood differs in people with ME/CFS. This exhausting chronic illness, marked by crashes after exertion, pain, and deep fatigue, still lacks a known mechanism. Extracellular vesicles, which ferry signals between cells, might carry a readable trace of it.

The team enriched vesicles from the plasma of 49 patients and 50 healthy controls and measured their proteins with high-resolution proteomics. Patients carried significantly higher vesicle concentrations. Of 424 proteins analyzed, 11 differed between groups, mostly tracing back to red blood cell, liver, and plasma B cell origins. None of the differences survived strict correction for multiple testing, though. As the largest such study so far, the authors present it as encouragement for deeper work on vesicles in this disease.
pmc-13312668:
Jordi A. Matias-Guiu and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a trial of Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 against the cognitive problems of post-COVID-19 syndrome. Brain fog is frequent after COVID, its mechanisms remain murky, and no proven treatment targets them, while the ginkgo extract fights neuroinflammation, aids microcirculation, and has shown benefit in other cognitive disorders.

The multicentre trial will randomize about 400 adults with confirmed or probable past infection, at least two months of cognitive symptoms, measurable impairment, and mild-to-moderate anxiety or depression. Participants take 240 milligrams of the extract or a matching placebo once daily for twelve weeks under triple-blind conditions. Outcomes span cognition, mood, sensory symptoms, and daily functioning. The authors hope to learn whether a plant extract with this profile can fill an empty treatment space.
pmc-13312768:
Nour El Kazwini and five co-authors improve estimates of where single cells are heading in development in a 2026 paper. RNA velocity infers a cell's near future from the balance of fresh and mature gene messages in its data, a prized tool in single cell studies. But tying those velocity arrows to the regulatory machinery behind them has proved hard.

Their model, CRAK-Velo, folds in chromatin accessibility, which shows which gene regions are open for use, through a semi mechanistic design. The added layer yields velocity estimates that stay consistent with biology and trace developmental flows more faithfully. It also separates mixed cell types accurately. Gene to chromatin region interactions become visible, shedding light on the regulation driving each cell's path.
pmc-13312968:
Wen Zhang and co-authors grade, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, the meniscus injury videos circulating on Douyin, the Chinese short-video platform. Patients increasingly learn about knee injuries from such clips, so the team asked how credible, educational, and professionally deep the supply really is.

Searching two Chinese keywords on July 31, 2025, the team sieved 300 collected clips down to 143 that truly addressed meniscal injury. Two trained raters scored each video on standard benchmarks for transparency and reliability. Overall quality, plus a meniscus-specific scale built from orthopedic academy guidance. Median scores sat low across the board, signaling thin sourcing and modest teaching value, though depth varied widely. Videos from physicians and rehabilitation therapists beat those from fitness enthusiasts and patients, and treatment pathway clips scored deepest while recovery clips most often skipped key points.
pmc-13313268:
Badypwyla Israël and colleagues report a 2026 survey of expert views on child vaccination in Lubumbashi, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The national vaccine program began in 1978 and leans on families to seek shots, yet coverage stays low, and the household factors behind that gap had not been mapped.

Experts in immunization were picked on purpose, from varied fields, with deep national and outside experience per the report. They were asked whether a study of what drives coverage in Lubumbashi, under the SCAVA and VACCIN+CONNECT-OS effort, is worth doing and how it should run. The paper grounds a planned project in that expert judgment. Its aim is to raise child coverage in a city where vaccine-preventable disease still takes a heavy toll on young lives.
pmc-13313868:
Trenton Oliver and four co-authors audit, in a 2024 study, bladder cancer care at one academic hospital in Johannesburg, South Africa. Data on this cancer in low- and middle-income countries are thin, from causes to outcomes. The team read the files of 115 patients treated in the radiation oncology unit from 2010 to 2020.

The mean age was near 61 years, and men made up about six in ten cases. Smoking, male sex, Black race, and older age were the top risk marks in the group. The common tissue type was the urothelial form, ahead of the squamous cell form. The two forms were compared for age, risk factors, traits, and outcomes. Patients with the urothelial form tended to be older. The authors aim to spot patterns that could reduce the toll of this cancer in their setting.
pmc-13314468:
Yan Wu and colleagues survey first-year medical students on a tutorial model that blends clinical and humanities teaching, in a study printed in 2026. Joining bedside skills with humanistic literacy early is a stated goal of modern medical schools, and Zhejiang University tried a new format for it.

The study ran in the Whole Life Cycle Health I course and drew 275 students, as counted in the report. A self-report survey asked about fit with the model, learning interest, gains in joining clinical and human sides, module worth, and self-rated skill growth. Most students fit the model well, at a share of 90.9 percent as given, and most said interest rose, at 88.0 percent in the report. Male students agreed more strongly on interest and on the joining effect. The results back early, guided blending of the two sides of medicine.
pmc-13314568:
Sanjiv Kandhari and fellow experts set out advice for using the drug abrocitinib in eczema care in India, in their 2026 paper. Atopic dermatitis is a long, flaring skin disease that ruins quality of life through itch, lost sleep, and repeat flares.

Older whole-body drugs such as cyclosporine and methotrexate often give weak itch control and wear poorly over time. Abrocitinib, a pill that blocks the JAK1 signal, cut itch fast and cleared skin in big trials with a fair balance of gain and risk, as the authors report. Yet real-world guidance for Indian patients was thin. Their advice covers who should get the drug, how to dose it, and how to chase lasting calm of the skin, tuned to local practice.
pmc-13315168:
Pak Thaichana and colleagues link seasonal smoky air to lung adenocarcinoma in northern Thailand, in a 2026 study. Fine dust known as PM2.5 has tied to lung cancer worldwide, yet proof for this subtype from real registry data in Southeast Asia was thin.

The team worked across eight upper northern provinces and 103 districts, as counted in the report. Daily PM2.5 readings were matched to cancer registry rates for the years 2013 to 2017 by each patient home district. Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer subtype, as the authors note. Models that handle clustered data weighed the dose link. In a region where seasonal burning spikes the air, hard numbers on cancer risk can push cleaner air policy.
pmc-13315368:
Barbara Seliger reports in 2026 on the nineteenth Tumor Immunology Meets Oncology meeting, held in May 2025 in Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany. The gathering covered basic and applied tumor immunology, with talks on how tumors differ, their surrounding tissue, and what that means for care.

Alongside the main symposium, junior scientists and clinicians presented short talks and posters, and a linked workshop covered cancer and inflammation. Sessions stressed how host and tumor cells interact, mapped with omics tools, as a base for new immune therapies and drug combinations. Biomarkers, immune escape, and anti-tumor responses ran through the program.
pmc-13315668:
Emre Demirel and colleagues report in 2026 on long-term swallowing after laser surgery that opens the airway in people whose two vocal folds are paralyzed. The operation cuts across the back of one vocal fold with a carbon dioxide laser, easing breathing, but its lasting effects on swallowing needed mapping.

Seventeen adults were checked once, well after surgery, between January and June 2025, using a flexible camera test with thin liquid, moderately thick yogurt, and a cracker. Standard scales graded airway entry, throat residue, and oral intake ability. Patient reports and functional scores were set beside the camera findings to guide follow-up care.
pmc-13315968:
Anna C Hornbach and co-authors report in 2026 a primary pelvic Ewing sarcoma growing outside bone in a young woman, paired with a review of gene-confirmed cases in female genital organs. Such tumors are extremely rare there, and firm diagnosis needs proof of the EWSR1 fusion gene that drives growth.

A healthy 21-year-old had two weeks of malaise and pelvic symptoms, and scans showed a 10 centimeter mixed cystic and solid mid-pelvis mass seeming to arise from the front of the uterus. Wide surgery removed the mass with clear margins, and gene testing confirmed the diagnosis. Care follows bone Ewing guidelines.
pmc-13316168:
Bercin Tarlan and Onur Konuk report in 2026 an eye socket case where spread of multiple myeloma looked like ordinary age-related eyelid fat bulging. A 57-year-old man whose myeloma was in remission had three months of growing fullness in the right lower eyelid.

Examination suggested slight upward eye shift and uneven fat herniation without inflammation. CT imaging instead showed a dense mass at the front lower orbit, distinct from fat. Removal and biopsy proved a plasmacytoma, positive for CD138 and kappa light chain, meaning metastatic myeloma. New eyelid fullness in such patients deserves imaging, the authors warn.
pmc-13316268:
Manana Jikurashvili and co-authors describe, in 2026, a man whose bowel cancers returned repeatedly over eighteen years before cancer reached his pancreas. The patient had a strong family history of colorectal cancer and features pointing to Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk. Spread of bowel cancer to the pancreas is rare and hard to recognise.

Now aged 58, the man developed a mass in the body and tail of the pancreas during routine surveillance. Tissue examination showed a high-grade cancer with solid and nested growth and extensive dead tissue. Staining favoured a bowel origin and showed loss of two mismatch repair proteins. The authors stress careful clinic and pathology correlation and long-term team surveillance.
pmc-13316368:
Lena Sophie Rudolf leads a 2026 study checking whether Germany's national learning catalogue for medical students, NKLM 2.0, teaches enough about food advice for children and teens. Good early nutrition guidance can prevent later disease, so gaps in training matter.

The team first built an evidence-based list of needed skills, then coded the catalogue against it, ending with 82 codes across 1,426 segments. Knowledge for prevention and communication skills took the largest shares, while five codes found no teaching content at all. Gaps included food for breastfeeding mothers, kitchen skills, eating behavior, gentle talk about body weight, and nudging methods. The authors suggest targeted courses and clearer rules on teaching formats and time.
pmc-13316668:
Naman Jain and co-authors describe, in 2026, a fatal clotting complication after severe head injury in a 35-year-old man with chronic substance use. He arrived after an unwitnessed fall. Clotting in surface veins of both arms is uncommon after trauma and usually signals body-wide inflammation rather than a local vein injury.

On day six, discolouration spread from the left hand to the right arm. Ultrasound confirmed clots in the cephalic and basilic veins without deep vein involvement. Platelet counts fell sharply, chest imaging showed extensive lung injury, and blood thinners could not be given because of bleeding inside the skull and very low platelets. He died on day eight from refractory breathing failure.
pmc-13316868:
Donato Decarolis and a large team show, in a 2026 catalysis study, how a sponge-like metal-organic framework can freeze palladium particles in their pure metal state. Palladium normally soaks up hydrogen and changes phase during reactions, muddying which form does the work.

Trapped inside the pores of NH2-UiO-66, clusters under one nanometer wide held only surface hydrogen under reaction conditions, never shifting phase. Live X-ray probing during the reaction plus simulations backed the claim. In a test reaction turning butadiene into butenes, the locked-metal catalyst stayed active, chose the wanted product more often, and overcooked less to butane than standard catalysts. Tiny size control, the team argues, can settle long phase debates.
pmc-13317568:
Pian Yu and a large team created, in a 2026 study, a dissolving microneedle patch that plants a radioactive immune trigger inside melanoma skin tumors. Melanoma often hides from immune therapy behind a suppressive local setting, so the team combined radiation with a STING alarm signal in one material.

The polymer self-assembles from lutetium-177 and nucleotide building blocks, mimicking the body's own STING activator. Pressed into skin, the patch stayed at the tumor, switched on STING, and burst tumor cells through a fiery death that drew immune attackers in. Mouse tumors shrank and survival stretched; adding a PD-L1 antibody deepened the effect and left lasting immune memory against distant tumors too.
pmc-13317768:
Xinru Yang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, the HER2 growth receptor as a target in cervical cancer, where patients with returning or resistant disease run out of options. HER2 drives breast and stomach cancers and is druggable there, but its cervical role is murkier.

Changes in HER2 are uncommon across cervical cancers overall, yet they cluster in glandular subtypes, including HPV-independent forms. The review covers the receptor's biology, how often it appears, what it predicts, and how testing should be standardized. Antibody-drug conjugates, above all trastuzumab deruxtecan, have revived interest by showing activity in HER2-carrying tumors. Careful biomarker selection, the authors argue, will decide which patients truly benefit.
pmc-13317968:
Charlie Pauvert, David Wylensek, Selina Nüchtern, and Thomas Clavel release maldipickr in a 2026 software paper. The open R tool sorts bacterial isolates by their protein fingerprints to cut duplicate work in big culturing projects. Growing microbes is back in fashion, but sequencing every colony is costly and slow.

MALDI-TOF machines already fingerprint isolates cheaply in minutes, yet standard use leans on closed commercial databases. Their package clusters fresh spectra without a reference library, grouping likely clones so teams keep one of each and drop the rest. The tool is light on computing power and fully documented on CRAN. Smarter triage lets culture collections capture more diversity per dollar.
pmc-13318568:
Yidi Zhu and co-workers report a 2026 imaging study of brain waste clearance. Their patients had a narrowed middle cerebral artery. Narrowing can weaken blood flow and vessel pulsing. The team used two related diffusion MRI measures, DTI-ALPS and a redirected version.

Scans and thinking tests covered 37 patients and 41 matched healthy controls. Both clearance measures came out clearly lower in patients. That pattern suggests waste removal around blood vessels is impaired. Each measure also fell as choroid plexus volume rose. Correlation values sat near −0.54 and −0.57 in the patient group examined. The authors propose the measures as imaging markers. They might help track how the disease progresses.
pmc-13318868:
Laya Krishnan and colleagues offer a 2026 scoping review of AI applied to gut microbes for spotting dementia. A gut-brain imbalance is linked to slow decline in thinking. AI tools now hunt gut markers that set apart dementia types and stages. No full review had gathered that work.

Searches of four databases through July 2025 found 896 papers. Screening narrowed them to 28 for close reading. Models such as random forests and neural networks came up often. Alzheimer's patients showed fewer butyrate-making gut species, including Faecalibacterium and Eubacterium. Other microbes linked to inflammation were raised. Even superagers showed distinct, perhaps protective microbe patterns. The authors argue gut signatures could back earlier, mixed test approaches.
pmc-13319368:
Rauf Khan and co-authors describe a 2026 study of thin films that clean oily water with help from data models. Two flat materials, graphene oxide and MXene, were layered on a nylon base. Four film mixes with varied amounts of one layer were made and tested for how well they held back oil.

Math models were trained to guess how well each film would work from mix and pressure settings. One model type gave the closest guesses and showed that film mix and pressure mattered most. Pairing new materials with such models could cut trial and error in filter design. Larger data sets are planned to make the guesses hold up more widely.
pmc-13319668:
Tuo Lan, Yikyung Park and Natasha Tasevska present, in 2026, a method for splitting protein intake into animal and plant sources within two common diet assessment tools. Interest in protein source is growing, yet standard recalls and food records report only total protein. A practical estimation protocol was missing.

Data came from 926 adults who completed repeated automated 24-hour recalls and two four-day food records over a year. Each reported food was linked to national nutrient databases to assign its protein to animal or plant origin. Summed estimates matched original totals almost exactly, and most foods fell within a tiny margin. Animal protein supplied well over half of intake, led by red meat, poultry and cheese, while bread led plant sources. The protocol supports future diet and health studies.
pmc-13320568:
Godknows Osarhiaekhimen, Ayomide Ayo-Salami and Adeolu Morawo describe, in 2026, a treatable inflammatory brain condition that caused two episodes of rapid dementia seven years apart. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy deposits a protein in small brain vessels. In a rare variant, the immune system attacks those vessels, producing fast cognitive decline that can be hard to diagnose.

Their patient was a 76-year-old man whose first episode, with weakness and seizures, was never definitively explained despite extensive testing. During the second episode, advanced imaging showed the characteristic one-sided white matter changes. Tissue examination then confirmed amyloid angiopathy with related inflammation. The authors stress matching clinical and imaging clues, and confirming with tissue where presentations are atypical or recurrent, because treatment can reverse decline.
pmc-13320668:
Melodie E. French, Jonathan R. Delph, and Cailey B. Condit explain in a 2026 article what limits the size of the largest earthquakes at subduction zones. Earth's biggest quakes grow along the megathrust fault where one plate dives under another, yet why growth stops at depth was unsettled. The authors link that limit to how rocks deform at each depth.

In shallow zones, all rocks break by friction, letting quakes grow large. Deeper down, sediment stops breaking and instead flows slowly, so quakes stay small and shrink with depth. Those small deep events may reflect the size of uneven patches in the fault. Modelling rock behaviour this way should sharpen hazard estimates.
pmc-13323068:
Yannik M Glauser leads a team presenting Fourier pixels for two-way light control, in a 2026 optics paper. Normal pixels only sense or emit light intensity, which wastes the phase and polarisation information carried by light waves.

Their elements use surface plasmon waves running across metal toward wavy microstructures shaped by Fourier analysis. Launched that way, the waves build clean optical wavefronts with chosen amplitude, phase and polarisation. Run in reverse, the same elements read incoming light fully on those three traits. Stacking several elements yields pixels that sense and shape light together. The authors extend the idea to waveguide modes and point to uses in displays, communication and quantum work.
pmc-13323368:
Xinyue Zheng and her team uncover, in 2026, a self-reinforcing loop that coronaviruses use to keep their copying factories running. Infected cells reshape internal membranes into double-walled vesicles where the viral genome is copied. What other cell structures play a part was unclear.

Forming those vesicles tears apart contact sites between two organelles, the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, and the mitochondria get damaged. A mitochondrial enzyme then leaks into the cell fluid and protects a key viral protein from being tagged for destruction. Shielded, that protein drives still more vesicle formation, closing the loop. Strengthening the organelle contacts or blocking the enzyme's grip on the viral protein suppressed replication in the team's tests, pointing to fresh antiviral targets.
pmc-13323568:
Yuezhong Huang and co-authors build a machine learning model for coronary artery disease risk from UK Biobank blood proteins, reported in 2026. Participants with protein and genetic data and no prior disease were split into training, internal validation and a Scotland and Wales external validation set.

A score built from 202 proteins tracked future disease in a dose-like pattern. Adding genetic scores and the protein score to standard factors lifted discrimination in both validation sets, and a compact nine-protein panel was picked for practical use. Follow-up came from linked health records. The authors argue that blood protein patterns can sharpen heart risk prediction beyond clinic measures alone.
pmc-13324668:
Najib Aziz and colleagues report an unusual HIV case in a 2026 case report. A man with high-risk sexual exposure stayed HIV negative from 1984 through May 2021, a span of about 35 years, without ever taking preventive PrEP drugs.

During those years he had several other infections, including gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis. In fall 2021 he tested positive, and a December test found 19,100 copies per mL of HIV-1 RNA. Genetic checks showed one copy of the CCR5 delta32 change plus HLA A*02 and HLA B*5701 types. The authors suggest layered genetic traits, not one factor, likely delayed infection and may shape outlook after it.
pmc-13325168:
Beth James and co-authors evaluate a ruthenium compound against drug-resistant urinary germs and their biofilms in a 2026 study. Catheter infections persist because biofilms shield bacteria from most antibiotics.

The compound, KLS-116, killed diverse resistant species at doses at or below 25 micromolar in lab tests. Mixed with standard antibiotics it never clashed, giving neutral or additive effects. In flow models of catheters it shrank mature biofilms, and in still models it cleared them fully at 16 times the base dose within a day. Over 42 days of exposure, bacteria barely shifted in sensitivity, unlike rapid ciprofloxacin resistance. Acid levels did sway its strength.
pmc-13325368:
Parimal C. Bhomick and co-authors extrude biodegradable films loaded with herbicide-carrying frameworks in a 2026 study. Slow, targeted weed killer release could cut the chemical load reaching soil and water.

Two metal-organic frameworks, UiO-66 and its amino version, were loaded with 2,4-D, MCPA, or glyphosate. The loaded powders were blended into polycaprolactone at 10, 20, and 30 percent by weight through twin-screw extrusion. Films grew stiffer as framework share rose, beating films with herbicide mixed in directly. Release tests showed a slow, sustained leak from the framework route. The solvent-light process scales well and suits farm delivery films.
pmc-13325668:
Takeru Ikenaga and colleagues report a rare racing heart circuit inside the superior vena cava in a 2026 case report. The big vein above the heart can spark atrial fibrillation, but a self-contained loop there is almost unheard of.

Their patient was an 83-year-old woman returning a year after a first ablation for repeat tachycardia. Mapping first showed a loop on the left atrial back wall, and pulsed-field ablation fixed the veins and wall. The rhythm then shifted to a new pattern traced wholly inside the vein sleeve. A ring-shaped pulsed-field catheter isolated the vein without harming the sinus node or the phrenic nerve. Tissue selectivity made the delicate site treatable.
pmc-13325868:
Jacqueline MacDonald Gibson argues in a 2026 perspective that official United States water figures hide wide insecurity. Headline statistics credit 97.6 percent of Americans with safely managed drinking water.

Her account shows the count leans on piped access and a narrow set of system violations, missing private wells, shutoffs, and missing plumbing. Adding those groups yields an estimated 37 to 55 million water-insecure residents, some 11 to 16 percent of the 2024 population. Private unregulated systems alone may leave 16 million people exposed. She calls on environmental engineers and scientists to close the gaps in measurement and service.
pmc-13326768:
Maxime Fieux, Philippe Gevaert, and Leigh J. Sowerby tested the infectious risk of biologics for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Their 2026 paper notes that biologic therapy transformed treatment of severe, resistant disease by targeting the type 2 inflammatory cascade, yet downstream immune effects remain possible. The focus is TSLP, an epithelial alarmin that drives type 2 inflammation but also supports antiviral CD8 T cell responses, so blocking it could theoretically impair local antiviral immunity.

Pooled data from the WAYPOINT trial showed an odds ratio of 2.76 for infectious adverse events, a pattern different from all other trials of biologics for this condition. Individual and serious infections did not rise significantly on their own, and exacerbations that could be inflammatory or infectious were excluded from the pooled analysis. The authors call for continued vigilance, long-term tracking, and vaccination guidance, particularly for patients with comorbidities or more immune risks.
pmc-13327668:
Soufia Charaf and team report a repeat pelvic lipoblastoma squeezing the sciatic nerve in a baby. Their 2026 case paper tells of a 17-month-old boy with a left pelvic lipoblastoma reaching into the buttock, who limped worse over six months with nerve harm in the left leg. Lipoblastoma is a rare kind tumor of baby fat, most often found before age three, and pelvic sites are rare, with squeeze harms hinging on size and spread.

MRI showed a big fatty tumor reaching past the pelvis and squeezing the sciatic nerve, and lab study of tissue confirmed lipoblastoma. Full surgery removal was done, but a local return five months later needed a second removal, with no further return during follow-up. The team stresses MRI's key role before surgery planning and after-surgery watch, tissue study for proof, and full removal as the mainstay of care for this rare growth.
pmc-13328168:
Hessah Ibrahim Al Suwaidan and co-authors build a national One Health plan for Saudi Arabia in a 2026 mixed-methods study. One Health joins human, animal, and environmental health against zoonoses, drug resistance, and ecological hazards, but Saudi policy links remain loose. A survey of 400 health professionals and students came first, then interviews on system barriers.

Awareness was low, with 81 percent reporting no prior knowledge of One Health, collaboration scored a mean of 0.51 on a zero-to-four range, and agreement on which body owns zoonotic disease roles was poor. Awareness predicted how much action respondents reported, and interviews blamed ministry silos and murky data routes. The authors propose a national structure to join the pieces.
pmc-13328568:
Ianire Astobiza and a large team report in 2026 that an enzyme in support cells around tumours can slow cancer growth signals. The enzyme, called aspartoacylase or ASPA, was often turned down in tumour stroma and in fibroblasts linked to cancer. The team studied how ASPA interacts with TGF beta signalling in these cells.

They found a two-way effect: TGF beta lowers ASPA, while ASPA limits the changes TGF beta drives in fibroblasts. Those changes include scar-like tissue building, new blood vessel growth, and immune cell states that help tumours. In human samples, low ASPA linked to worse outcomes across several tumour types. The work points to fibroblast ASPA as a brake on harmful tumour support.
pmc-13329668:
Saurav Sharma and co-authors report an exploratory Ayurvedic study in mild cognitive impairment in 2026. Mild impairment sits between normal ageing and dementia and can hinder complex daily tasks. Care ran in sequence: Trikatu powder for 7 days, then Brahmi ghee for 90 days, each taken twice daily after food.

Of 27 people enrolled, 24 finished the single-arm open study. Thinking was scored with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment before and after care. Scores improved with a large effect size in the reported results, and no adverse events were noted. The authors stress limits: no control group, no fixed lifestyle rules, and other medicines were not tracked. Controlled trials are needed before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13330468:
Xueli Quan and colleagues report a crisis from an adrenal tumour in a teenager in a 2026 case. The boy, aged 13 years and 8 months, had belly pain for three days and was first treated for gut infection.
