Oxygen cutting drives fuel cells and clean peroxide making, yet good catalysts usually rely on metals. Their materials are hyper-crosslinked polymers, knitted in solvent from simple building blocks.

Both test polymers sped the reaction along a clean two-step path. Oxygen gathered inside the catalyst film above the level in the surrounding fluid, which raised current. Meeting points of electrode, polymer, and watery film seem to be where the action happens. Computer checks found only weak oxygen grip, ideal for shuttling it through. Nitrogen-bearing units boosted the rate further.
pmc-13404568:
Gonzalo Ramírez-Guerrero, Thiago Reis and Claudio Ronco comment in 2026 on the CLEANSE trial of blood filtering in septic shock. The trial tested the HA-330 cartridge, which soaks up cytokines and similar molecules from blood. It stopped early, having enrolled 128 patients out of a planned 206.

Reported 28-day deaths were 44 percent with filtering and 58 percent without, a gap too small to rule out chance. The commentators argue that sample size assumptions, uneven timing between groups and endpoint choices leave the result hard to read either way. They praise the team for running a pragmatic randomised trial in a field full of small uncontrolled studies. Their warning is against citing the trial as proof for or against the treatment.
pmc-13404868:
Xindi Shen and team studied how AI-aided health management bears on self-rule among older adults. Their 2026 empirical ethics work surveys 312 community-dwelling older adults who use AI health tools, plus talks with 24 of them, probing privacy, algorithm reliance, and relational dynamics. Older adults face digital literacy blocks and lean on family and doctors, yet how those factors shape self-rule in practice had been little probed.

Privacy awareness and felt self-rule ran middling, while reliance on AI advice ran fairly high. Greater algorithm reliance tracked with lower felt self-rule, a link shaped by relational factors. Talks showed thin grasp of data practices led to box-ticking rather than real consent, and AI advice often felt commanding. Family and doctor backing could enable shared choices or prop up paternalism. The work urges self-rule-aware AI design.
pmc-13405068:
Jingjing Zuo and colleagues review surgery for a rare benign bone tumour in children's shoulders, reporting in 2026. Chondroblastoma at the top of the upper arm bone can damage the growing joint. The centre treated it by scooping out the tumour, burning the cavity and packing it with bone graft.

Seventeen patients treated between 2008 and 2018 were followed for at least seven years. Their average age was 10.9 years in the reported data, ranging from 8 to 14. Arms rested in splints for four weeks after surgery. Check-ups used symptoms and X-rays to hunt recurrence, while shoulder function was scored with MSTS and QuickDASH scales, and complications were recorded.
pmc-13405368:
Kunal Rajput and colleagues map machine learning tools built to defend health care from cyberattack, in a 2026 scoping review. Recent breaches halted pathology services for weeks and exposed millions of patient records. Conventional defences react slowly to new attack styles, while learning systems promise prediction in real time.

Searches of three databases in July 2025 gathered studies from 2019 to 2025 on organisational-level defence in health settings. Tools are charted against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, now in version 2.0 in the account given. Performance summaries sit beside gaps and practical barriers, so security teams can see where learning methods are proven and where evidence is thin.
pmc-13406768:
Hideaki Hasegawa and colleagues remove a stress kinase from mice to see how skin inflammation changes, in a 2026 study. The imiquimod cream model mimics psoriasis, and the kinase ASK1 sits above a known inflammation pathway. Its exact role in the skin disease was unclear.

Knockout mice developed worse lesions than normal mice, with thicker skin and higher inflammatory signals including IL-17 and TNF-alpha in the reported measures. A protective skin sensor, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, rose in the knockout lesions alongside its partner gene. Binding tests suggest ASK1 normally holds that receptor down. The authors read ASK1 as a brake on psoriasis development through that receptor.
pmc-13407568:
Josiel Ferreira and co-authors fed lambs, in a 2026 trial, a tropical shrub silage to see effects on body heat, methane output, and gut microbes. Twenty young crossbred lambs ate either sugarcane silage alone or a half-and-half mix with Tithonia diversifolia silage for the study period, under warm tropical conditions.

Lambs on sugarcane alone breathed faster and ran hotter on most body surfaces, while core rectal temperature stayed equal between groups. Methane production, a climate concern for livestock, did not differ between diets. One fibre-digesting gut microbe, Ruminococcus flavefaciens, grew more abundant in the mixed-diet lambs, while other measured populations held steady. The shrub improved comfort and fibre digestion support, the authors conclude, without cutting methane under these conditions.
pmc-13407968:
João Reboleira and team tested enzyme sugar-release to unlock edible seaweed Ulva as a fermentation base. Their 2026 work takes on a block: seaweed cell walls curb microbe growth, slowing novel food work despite seaweed's promise. Three enzyme plans were weighed: a fungal crude extract, a commercial cocktail, and their mix.

The mix freed the most fermentable sugars, with glucose and galacturonic acid leading, showing breaks in key structural polysaccharides. Later fermentations with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and Cyberlindnera jadinii grew two logs more than in untreated media, with greater acidification and nitrogen shifts apt for food work. Some cell wall sugars resisted breakdown, so further enzyme work is needed. The work positions sugar-release as a key enabling step.
pmc-13408068:
Olusanya J. Oluwole and co-authors survey, in 2026, smokers living with HIV in under-resourced communities about phones, apps, and quitting. Digital health could widen access to tobacco treatment. The study heard from 205 current smokers, mean age about 51. Most came from racial and ethnic minority groups with very low incomes, and they reported their habits, barriers, and technology.

Three quarters had tried to quit before. Cravings defeated 45.4 percent, treatment cost 28.8 percent, and limited care access 25.9 percent, while depression and risky drinking were common companions. Technology reach was high despite poverty: 91.7 percent owned a mobile phone and 63.9 percent had internet access. Plain phone calls were the most wanted digital format, ahead of texts and apps, and mindfulness and nicotine replacement were the most popular helps. Interest ran significantly higher among Black and non-heterosexual participants.
pmc-13408168:
Suzanna Powell and colleagues surveyed Montana school administrators in 2026 about student use of vaping devices. Schools sit on the front line for preventing, catching, and helping students quit nicotine vaping. The team wanted to know which prevention, discipline, and quitting strategies administrators actually use and judge effective.

Forty-two administrators answered the survey and eleven sat for interviews during 2025. Just over half had seen students vaping on school grounds that year. Education sessions, patrols, and telling parents about a first offence were rated most effective, while quitting support options were patchier and administrators wanted more of them. Interviews stressed teamwork with peers, parents, and school resource officers. Education sessions, signs, and posters, the cheapest measures, were also the most widely used.
pmc-13408668:
JiaQing He and co-authors unveil in 2026 a gel that grips, lets go, and reports its own grip strength wirelessly. Switchable adhesives serve climbing robots, smart grippers, and electronics handling, yet adapting to varied roughness while sensing the hold in real time has been elusive. Their material is a eutectogel whose adhesion switches with applied heat.

Mechanical tests and molecular characterisation explain how the phase transition flips the surface between sticky and release states. A machine-learning layer interprets sensor signals to estimate adhesion force on the spot, feeding robots awareness of their own attachment. Demonstrations covered adhesion-aware sensing, robotic grasping, and wall climbing, each relying on the grip-release cycle plus live feedback. The authors pitch the system as a step toward gripping surfaces that are adaptive and self-perceptive at once.
pmc-13408768: Ivo Verheijen, Gianpiero Di Maida, Gabriele Russo, and Thomas Terberger authored a 2026 Scientific Reports study of animal exploitation at the ancient elephant hunting site of Lehringen in Germany. The notice is a correction only. It fixes the first figure's legend, where Di Maida's first name was misspelled. It also aligns the legend's colour key with the map's dots for each chronological period. The site map and the article's findings are otherwise unchanged.
pmc-13409068:
Allison Valle-Bravo and co-authors test in 2026 whether thirty seconds in a kitchen blender changes what cactus mucilage can do to a real gold-mining waste liquid. The slimy extract of prickly pear pads can clump dissolved contaminants out of water. A cyanidation barren solution from actual mining, carrying lead, nickel, arsenic, cadmium, and zinc, supplied a harsh test bed for powders blended for zero, thirty, or sixty seconds.

Blending shrank the rehydrated particles, lowered water activity, and shifted surface charge, though not in proportion to blending time. Every version removed over ninety-eight percent of the lead, nickel, and arsenic across a range of doses. Cadmium removal depended on which powder was used, and zinc removal stayed lower and erratic. Microscopy found the captured metals inside the recovered flocs, confirming genuine transfer out of the liquid.
pmc-13413668:
Ahmed M. El-Sawah and Ghada G. Abdel-Fattah review in 2026 how helpful microbes might cut nitrous oxide gas escaping from farm soils. The gas warms Earth roughly three hundred times more strongly than carbon dioxide. Fertilized fields are its main human source. Bacteria and root fungi sold as inoculants can tighten how soil handles nitrogen. They help crops use nitrogen well. They crowd out the germs that leak the gas. They also switch on genes that turn it into harmless nitrogen gas.

Bacteria such as Bradyrhizobium, Paenibacillus, and Bacillus head the list of options. Two groups of root fungi join them. Salty soils get a close look, since salt shifts soil germs and can lift gas output. The authors build these threads into a plan for kinder farming that guards food output.
pmc-13415968:
Yuto Sasano and colleagues describe emergency airway rescue in a patient whose kidney cancer spread had narrowed and bloodied the main airway, in 2026. Metastatic lymph nodes in the chest squeezed the left main bronchus and caused coughing of blood. Doctors first embolized the bronchial artery, blocking the bleeding vessel through a catheter.

With bleeding risk lowered, the team placed an AERO hybrid stent to hold the airway open. Breathing improved rapidly afterward. Systemic cancer therapy could then start without delay. Pairing embolization with stenting served as a bridge strategy for a life threatening blockage, the authors conclude.
pmc-13417168:
Faris Alqurashi and Muhammed Anaz Khan build a screening framework for capsules that store heat in phase change materials, published in 2026. A polymer shell stops the core from leaking when it melts. Choosing shell and process means balancing stored heat, core share, capsule size, and melting point, yet studies rarely compare routes side by side.

Their dataset held 90 published capsule records across 11 routes and eight shell families. Machine learning models predicted stored heat only modestly, matching simple baselines, a result reported openly. An optimisation search ranked emulsion, sol gel silica, and in situ routes highest. The code and data are shared for reuse.
pmc-13417268:
Sandra Arroyo-Urea and co-authors design highly selective activators of the dopamine D3 receptor, in a 2026 drug discovery paper. D3 is close kin to D2, a receptor tied to movement, thinking, Parkinson disease, and addiction. The two share identical main binding pockets, so selective drugs seemed out of reach.

A ligand was found to tidy a flexible segment of D3 into a new pocket shape that D2 lacks. Building two part molecules that reach both pockets gave activators over 100,000 times more selective than older ligands, some at picomolar strength. The set offers sharp tools for probing D3 biology and may seed better brain medicines.
pmc-13417968:
Carmen Aranda and colleagues set blood value ranges for captive European mink in a 2026 study. The mink is one of the most at risk mammals in Europe. Sound ranges for blood cells and blood chemistry help vets judge health in breeding and release work. The team checked how sex, age, and body state shaped the values.

The values looked much like those of kin such as ferrets. Young mink stood out on values tied to growth and immune growth. Sex gaps showed on some values too. Body state moved just a few values, and only by a small amount. The ranges give breeding centres a firm base for health checks.
pmc-13418068:
Cui and colleagues present a 2026 computational hunt for unconventional antiferromagnets, materials whose magnetism cancels out overall yet splits electron spins in useful ways. Such materials promise fast, dense spin electronics, but known examples are few. The team screened a large materials database with physics-based filters, heavy exchange calculations, and symmetry analysis to find hidden candidates.

From over thirty-seven thousand magnets, the screen narrowed the field to 189 orderly antiferromagnets. Symmetry checks sorted out 36 altermagnets and 11 Luttinger-compensated ferrimagnets, most of them never reported before. The finds can support spin Hall effects without relativity and spin transport whose direction can be switched by doping. Turning a broad database into a short, classified list gives experimental teams concrete targets, instead of the case-by-case luck that has governed this field so far.
pmc-13419268:
Jose Raul Velasquez Vides and colleagues speed up a brain scan that maps three tissue values at once in people with multiple sclerosis. Those values help doctors tell healthy tissue from damaged areas, yet full scans run long. Their method pairs a two-part scan sequence with a model-based rebuild that works from thinned data.

Tests on phantoms and in patients showed the rebuilt maps matched the standard reference methods well. An earlier version lost sharpness at high speed gains and was thrown off by field quirks, flaws the new rebuild aims to fix. All three maps come from one run rather than separate passes. Shorter, combined scans could ease the load on patients who struggle to lie still and on busy scan schedules.
pmc-13419868:
Horacio Balam Alvarez Garcia and colleagues run a pilot trial of brief behavioral therapy for insomnia in people who had recovered from COVID-19 infection. Sleep loss, anxiety, and low mood all rose during the pandemic, and short drug-free therapy is a proven lever for sleep. The randomized trial compared treatment forms head to head, with no passive wait-list group.

Measures were taken before treatment, right after it, and again three months later. Sleep quality, anxiety, depression, and life quality were the tracked outcomes. Remote delivery held a special draw in the setting, since it cuts travel and reaches far towns at lower cost. Pilot results like these tell larger trials whether the brief format deserves a full test after illness.
pmc-13420068:
Esenia Bechir and colleagues describe an 85-year-old woman struck by toxic epidermal necrolysis, a rare drug reaction that strips skin and can kill. She arrived with spreading red eruptions over more than 60 percent of her body surface, in the measure given, plus raw denuded areas and sores in the mouth and other linings. The trigger was a common antibiotic pair she had taken on her own for a urinary infection.

A skin sample showed full-thickness death of the surface layer with little active inflammation beneath. Death rates for this emergency run from 30 to 50 percent in the ranges the authors cite, driven by infection and shock through the open skin. Fast recognition and immediate intensive care offer the only real chance. The case warns against self-treating infections with leftover antibiotics, above all in older patients.
pmc-13420268:
Alula surveyed in 2026 children in rural North Gondar, Ethiopia, about trachoma, an eye infection that can blind. Trachoma spreads where water, sanitation, and hygiene are poor. The study checked 456 children aged one to nine for active disease using the World Health Organization grading method.

About one in five children had active trachoma, a high share for a preventable disease. Risk was higher in homes using unimproved water sources and in homes without latrines. Children whose faces were washed poorly, meaning less than twice a day or with discharge present, also faced higher risk. Homes with many eye-seeking flies around the child's face showed higher risk as well. The author backs stronger water, sanitation, and face-cleanliness work under the WHO SAFE strategy.
pmc-13421068:
Octavian Augustin Mihalache and colleagues measure fungal toxins in the bodies of Italian adults and set the levels against what those adults eat. Diets are shifting plantward for health and climate reasons, which can change exposure to toxins that fungi leave on crops. Volunteers came from an acute feeding study, giving overnight fasting urine collected under standard conditions.

The group held 300 adults aged 19 to 73 years in the reported span, and 57 percent of the volunteers were women in the same account. Body measures sat near the lean end, with median weight of 66.5 kilograms across the group in the reported values. Linking measured toxin levels to diet records turns guesswork about exposure into numbers. Risk assessors can then judge whether greener diets carry a hidden chemical cost.
pmc-13421468:
Giardino and a large team present the first detailed immune profile of a patient with DEGCAGS syndrome, in this 2026 case report. The rare developmental disorder is caused by losing both copies of the ZNF699 gene. Their patient, a 20-year-old man, carried a novel missense variant in the gene and suffered recurrent infections with a combined immune defect: low T cells and almost absent circulating B cells.

Blood testing showed impaired production markers for new B cells. Antibody levels stayed surprisingly normal, though. A rectal biopsy then found B cells hiding in the gut lining despite their absence from blood. DNA methylation profiling, a chemical fingerprinting method, matched the patient's blood to the established DEGCAGS signature. It also separated him from a look-alike syndrome. That firmed up the diagnosis. The authors argue such methylation tests sharpen diagnosis in puzzling inborn immune errors.
pmc-13421668:
Yin and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study of the charged layer that forms where battery fluid meets an electrode in strong lithium salt solutions. This layer steers lithium ion flow, which sets battery speed and life. The team combined electrical tests, live laser surface readings, and computer simulations.

Screening of charge did not grow steadily with salt strength, as simple models suggest; it rose and fell in a nonmonotonic pattern. In the strongest solutions, lithium ions sat in anion-rich shells, and they swapped those anion partners faster than they swapped solvent molecules. Higher disorder in the shell favored this anion-rich setup. Ions that can reshuffle their shells quickly enter and leave electrodes more smoothly, which improves charge speed and reversibility. The findings give designers heat-and-motion rules for better electrolytes.
pmc-13421768:
Stefano V. Davila-Philipps leads a large team describing, in a 2026 study, leptospirosis in the Peruvian Amazon with a special eye on the youngest children. The waterborne bacterial disease is common in the tropics, yet its face in children under five — vague symptoms that primary care can miss — was poorly documented.

Records from four health centres in Belén, Loreto, covered 2022 to 2024. Of 2,325 suspected cases, 400 were laboratory-confirmed and analysed; 28 were under five. Malaise and fever dominated in the toddlers, half of whom lived in flood-prone areas, and nearly half arrived within three days of falling ill. Older patients more often reported headache and chills. The authors stress early suspicion in small children after flooding.
pmc-13422368:
Saroj Kumar Gupta and colleagues report a 2026 case of a hookworm found living in the bile duct, a site never before documented for this parasite. A 53-year-old woman endured eight months of worsening belly pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting, with gallstones and bile-duct stones on imaging.

During endoscopy doctors spotted a live worm in the bile tract, confirmed as a hookworm, and antiparasitic treatment plus supportive care brought marked improvement within a week. The case puts hookworm on the list for unexplained bile-duct disease in endemic settings where worms are common.
pmc-13423368:
Mauro Serapioni and four colleagues examine public participation inside hospitals of Portugal's National Health Service, asking how far advisory councils and other channels actually work. Their study pairs a review of participation schemes in several European hospitals with a survey sent to the heads of Portuguese hospital bodies.

Taking part, they found, mostly stops at giving information and asking patients for their views. Patients can state preferences, but they rarely share real decisions. Genuine involvement of patients and their voices in hospital decision-making remains rare and still weak, in Portugal and across Europe. The authors argue hospitals must move past asking views toward a real say in decisions, and they set out what that shift would require in practice.
pmc-13423968:
Hanxiao Chen and seven colleagues chart real-world later-line treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer carrying targetable gene changes, across six Chinese centres. Choices after first targeted therapy fails vary widely, and the RECAP study sorted regimens into six families, from targeted drugs alone or in combination to chemotherapy and vessel-blocking therapy.

The cohort held 658 patients, nine in ten with EGFR mutations. Targeted therapy use fell from 75.3% in first line to 49.3% in second, while combined vessel-blocking plus chemotherapy rose to 16.5%. Paths depended heavily on which first drug was used and whether the T790M resistance change appeared. By third line, chemotherapy-based mixes dominated the small group reaching it.
pmc-13424068:
Yuheng Jiang and nine colleagues 3D-print radar-absorbing structures loaded with an unusually high share of magnetic and dielectric filler, about 84% by weight, for shielding electronics from interference. Getting such heavy inks to flow and hold shape is the core problem, and the team mapped how composition sets thickness, flow, and print quality.

Their printed honeycomb absorber soaked up waves across an ultra-wide span, from 18 gigahertz into the terahertz range, with a deepest reflection loss of −84.30 decibels. Mounted on a terahertz reconfigurable surface, the absorber sharpened the main beam by just over 3 decibels. It also cut stray reflected beam width by roughly 58%. That shows device-level value beyond the material itself.
pmc-13424368:
Weiming Yu and three colleagues measure how artificial intelligence adoption pushes the green transition of cities in China's Yangtze River Delta, one of the world's largest urban clusters. Panel data from forty cities between 2012 and 2024 fed benchmark regressions, non-linear checks, and spatial models that account for influence between neighbouring cities.

Artificial intelligence clearly lifted green transition scores, working through production, consumption, and clustering channels. Green progress itself clustered strongly in space, while the AI effect stayed mostly local, with little spillover to neighbours. Benefits varied with a city's rank, location, resources, and market maturity, and were channelled through capital stock, industry upgrading, and consumption. Effects also faded past certain thresholds in related sectors.
pmc-13424568:
Parr and collaborators ran a randomized trial in Australia comparing time-restricted eating, confining all food to a self-chosen nine-hour window ending by 7 p.m., against individualized dietitian guidance in adults at risk of type 2 diabetes. The trial asked whether meal timing alone could match professional dietary advice for blood sugar control.

A total of 247 participants were randomized, 124 to time-restricted eating and 123 to dietitian guidance, each receiving five telehealth consultations. At four months the eating-window approach was non-inferior for HbA1c change, with a between-group difference of minus 0.02 percent that met the preset margin. By twelve months the difference had widened to 0.05 percent and non-inferiority could no longer be concluded from the data. Both groups started near an HbA1c of 5.8 percent, reflecting their at-risk rather than diabetic status.
pmc-13424668:
Andreas Göteson leads a twenty-author team measuring proteins of the synapse in spinal fluid across major mental illnesses, hunting a shared signature. The team used a targeted protein-measuring method in 672 people. Groups covered anorexia nervosa, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia-spectrum illness, plus healthy controls. The proteins measured are scarce but central to synapse function.

Schizophrenia-spectrum patients showed the deepest drops in these proteins, with bipolar disorder and ADHD in between. Modelling across diagnoses surfaced one pair: raised LAMP1, a marker of the cell's recycling sacs, alongside reduced NPTX2, a protein tied to synapse activity. Their ratio, combined with genetic risk scores, sharpened sorting of patients, and the pattern repeated in a separate first-episode psychosis cohort. Synapse failure, the authors argue, can be measured across diagnoses.
pmc-13424868:
Kazuma Ito and eleven colleagues report early experience with blood-based genomic profiling for metastatic colorectal cancer at their Japanese centre, using a commercial test that reads tumour DNA circulating in plasma. Nineteen patients were profiled between November 2023 and May 2025, many chosen for blood testing because tissue was scarce, old, or complicated by a second cancer.

Tumour DNA turned up in eighteen of nineteen patients, with results back in a median of eleven days. A median of five gene changes appeared per patient, and fifteen carried clearly harmful ones. Three patients labelled RAS-mutant by tissue testing proved wild-type in blood, received antibody therapy on that basis, and achieved shrinkage or stable disease. The authors call the findings exploratory.
pmc-13425768:
Wischmann and co-authors reanalyze a stroke trial in this 2026 post-hoc study, asking whether a worn-looking brain recovers language more slowly after stroke-related aphasia. The parent LEXI trial randomized patients with acute aphasia to tablet-assisted or standard speech therapy. This analysis scored each participant's baseline brain scan for frailty. The score, from 0 to 3, combined shrinkage, white matter damage, small scars, and old strokes.

Fifty-six patients, median age 75 years, entered the analysis, and 23.2 percent carried high frailty scores of 2 to 3 in the blinded ratings. Higher frailty independently predicted worse language scores at ninety days, with white matter damage doing most of the harm. More therapy hours helped regardless, and frailty did not measurably change therapy's benefit. The authors suggest routine white matter grading could sharpen prognosis and trial design.
pmc-13426068:
Payel Roy and coauthors report self-reactive CD8 T cells against apolipoprotein B in severe coronary artery disease in a 2026 immunology study. Atherosclerosis carries a strong autoimmune element, and plaques hold expanded clones of CD8 T cells, yet human CD8 responses to apolipoprotein B had not been described. Starting from computer prediction of HLA-A*02:01 restricted epitopes, the team screened the top 64 candidate peptides using blood cells from healthy carriers.

Finding which apolipoprotein fragments these killer T cells recognize opens a path to tracking disease-driving immunity in patients. Such cells could become biomarkers or targets for tolerizing therapies in coronary disease.
pmc-13426868:
Mitchell and Belay wrote a 2026 essay for the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases linking its cover artwork to the history of glassmaking and to pattern recognition in public health. The cover shows a 2022 glass composition by Belay, a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention official who works in glass as an artist. The piece opens with a quote from painter Piet Mondrian about stripping things down to their fundamental qualities.

Mitchell traces glassworking from core-formed vessels in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, through medieval cathedral windows and the workshops of Murano. The story ends with the twentieth-century studio glass movement, made possible by small affordable furnaces. Belay describes being drawn to glass for its merging of color with translucency after watching Murano artisans at work. The essay uses that craft history to frame how seeing patterns, in art and in disease data alike, is central to the journal's field.
pmc-13427068:
Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how wearable devices are used to watch over patients who live with both obstructive sleep apnea and high blood pressure. Each condition worsens the other, and care rarely tracks both at once. Wearables promise steady night-time data without a sleep lab, but the evidence for this combined group was scattered.

The search across four databases ended with thirteen studies from nine countries, covering about fifty-six hundred participants. Devices ranged from wrist bands and fingertip sensors to patches and portable multi-signal monitors. Uses centered on screening and risk sorting, watching night blood pressure swings, and long-term remote follow-up. The authors warn that devices differ in standards, thresholds, and proof, so wearables should support, not replace, formal sleep studies and standard blood pressure checks for now.
pmc-13427268:
Guerra and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what decades of research have taught about American tegumentary leishmaniasis in Brazil's Amazonas state, a skin and tissue disease spread by sandfly bites. The Amazon carries a heavy share of cases in the Americas. The review pulls together studies from 2011 to 2025 plus national notification records and state health reports.

One parasite species, Leishmania guyanensis, dominates locally, and case growth tracks deforestation and unplanned city spread that push people and flies together. Diagnosis has improved through wider molecular testing and a stronger front-line care network. Trials support several drugs, including pentamidine and miltefosine, for local treatment. The authors also gather work on social conditions, parasite genetics, and lab models. They call for telemedicine, joint research planning, and control policies shaped to Amazon life.
pmc-13427368:
Spasojevic and colleagues present in 2026 a hardware security method that uses voltage to move nitrogen ions inside tiny magnetic dots, building protection into the material itself. Software encryption is costly and increasingly strained. Their array uses dots of an iron-cobalt-nitrogen compound that is non-magnetic until voltage drives ions and creates magnetic layers thinner than fifteen nanometres.

The voltage can set each dot's magnetic state and tune the odds between two forms, a single uniform domain and a swirling vortex. Those states give each chip a magnetic fingerprint that cannot be cloned, the basis of a physical unclonable function used to prove identity. The random orientation and swirl direction can also generate true random numbers, and the states support probabilistic computing in memory. The authors claim tamper resistance, low power use, and easy scaling for next-generation secure hardware.
pmc-13427468:
Moumita Majumder and coauthors compared complement blockers at different pathway levels in a mouse model of ALS in a 2026 study. Complement activation contributes to motor neuron disease, yet failed human trials of C5 blockers such as ravulizumab and zilucoplan, plus systemic C3 blockade with pegcetacoplan, left the driving step unclear. Their targeted agent CR2Crry blocks C3 exactly where complement deposits, while BB5.1 blocks C5 like ravulizumab.

Treatment began at symptom onset in SOD1 mutant mice and ran to humane endpoint, with both drugs engaging targets across spinal cord and sciatic nerve. Site-targeted C3 inhibition, unlike C5 blockade, slowed neurodegeneration in their results, reframing why past trials failed.
pmc-13427568:
Ayako Kamiunten heads a 2026 study on a protein called MALT1 in adult T-cell leukemia and lymphoma. This fast-growing blood cancer follows infection with a virus named HTLV-1, sometimes decades later. Many of these cancers carry faults in the signaling chain that MALT1 helps run. The team built a new drug, coded CRD-1441551, that blocks MALT1's cutting action with precision.

They tested the drug on three cancer cell lines and five tumor models grown from patient tissue in mice. Two models shrank strongly, three responded modestly, and three did not respond. Models with MALT1 switched on and its downstream signals running hot did best. The results suggest a targeted option for a defined subgroup of a cancer that now has few good choices.
pmc-13427668:
Zorik Shamish and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, sensors that find traces of toxic heavy metals in water at extremely low levels. Cadmium, lead, and copper can harm health even at a few parts per billion. The team printed tiny clusters of bismuth or mercury onto a surface using dip-pen nanolithography, a method that draws with a nanoscale pen. Cluster size and spacing set how much surface each sensor exposes.

The bismuth sensor detected metals down to about a quarter of a part per billion, roughly twice as sharp as the mercury version. Computer modeling showed both metals grip the targets about equally, so geometry explained the gap. A bismuth device also avoids adding much mercury, itself a pollutant, to testing. Water utilities gain a route to sensitive checks with less hazardous material.
pmc-13428268:
Juan Kong and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, whether family doctors in southeast Henan, China, see ongoing training as necessary. Continuing medical education keeps general practitioners current, yet busy doctors do not always value it. An online questionnaire went to registered doctors in Zhoukou City in late summer 2024. Valid replies came back from 2,480 doctors, about 45 percent of those eligible.

Only about 36 percent called the training necessary, even though about 90 percent had taken part during the prior three years. Knowing that training credits link to career advancement showed the strongest tie to valuing it, nearly quadrupling the odds. Workplace support, strong self-directed learning, low anxiety, and long experience also helped. The authors suggest clearer policy, better backing from employers, and tiered courses matched to each doctor's level.
pmc-13429468:
Li and co-authors review the merger of two laboratory technologies reshaping preclinical research. Their 2026 paper covers organ-on-a-chip systems, which grow living tissue in engineered micro-devices, and organoids, miniature organ-like structures from stem cells. The timing is pointed. In April 2025 the United States Food and Drug Administration issued guidance to phase out animal trials in favour of such systems. The National Institutes of Health opened a dedicated office weeks later.

The review surveys single-organ and multi-organ chips, organoid-on-chip hybrids, and uses spanning disease modelling, host-microbe interactions, inter-organ networks, and prediction of drug handling and toxicity. It also analyses the obstacles to pharmaceutical and clinical adoption. The authors argue that combining materials engineering, biosensing, and artificial intelligence could make these systems act as patient surrogates, speeding precision medicine and rare disease work.
pmc-13430768:
Li and colleagues reported in 2026 a way to build silicon-centred chiral molecules that carry sulfur, a class prized in materials and drug chemistry. Their reaction adds a sulfur group to a distant carbon-hydrogen bond on a ring-shaped silicon compound, with the handedness of the product steered. The trick is a pair of catalysts working together: a chiral Lewis base built around a sulfur-bearing phosphoric triamide, plus a plain acid whose strength is tuned.

Li obtained the products in yields up to about ninety-four in a hundred and with handedness purity up to above ninety-nine in a hundred, across a wide set of starting materials. Control tests suggest the process runs in two stages, a symmetry-breaking step followed by a sorting step that enriches one hand. pmc-13436468:

pmc-13436668:

pmc-13441768:

pmc-13442368:

pmc-13447268:

pmc-13449668:

pmc-13454668:

pmc-13455368:

pmc-13462268:

pmc-13463068:

pmc-13474868:

pmc-13476768:

pmc-13478368:
John Robert Rilveria and seven colleagues tested in 2026 whether a mental health app called SAGIP improves wellbeing and distress over time in a university community. Members were randomised to the app or a waitlist and assessed monthly for three months.

App users improved wellbeing more and cut distress more than waitlist controls during the randomised phase. Distress fell fastest early, while wellbeing gains grew gradually and strengthened later. How often or long people used the app tracked their starting mental health but did not predict their trajectories. Gains largely held through month six, suggesting timing and quality of engagement matter more than quantity.
pmc-13478468:
Peijia Jiang and coauthors published a 2026 review of MLKL, a protein famous as an executioner of necroptotic cell death, and its lesser-known role in keeping cancer cells alive. MLKL punches pores in cell membranes to kill cells, yet in some settings it protects them instead. Blocking it slowed several tumor types in animals, while mice lacking it stayed healthy.

The review gathers the survival mechanisms proposed so far. MLKL can trigger autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and preserve mitochondrial function. Both actions may block a second death route called parthanatos, driven by overactive PARP1 chewing up DNA. The protein also helps tumor cells resist death-receptor signals and secrete growth-promoting cytokines. The authors argue this safety profile in normal animals makes MLKL an attractive drug target.
pmc-13479268:
Amber Boskma and coauthors published a 2025 inventory of staff well-being programs across the seven Dutch university medical centers. Stressed and dissatisfied health workers feed staff shortages and worse patient outcomes, so hospitals run many support programs with little shared oversight. The team interviewed 31 nurses, doctors, human resource staff, and occupational health staff by video call in 2021.

The centers reported 203 separate initiatives, spanning coaching, training courses, apps, and tools. Most targeted physical fitness, mental fitness, personal development, work-life balance, or team collaboration, and nearly all aimed at individual employees rather than teams or the organization itself. Almost none had been evaluated for whether they actually improve well-being. The authors call this individual focus and missing evaluation the field's main weaknesses.
pmc-13479568:
Jingru Chen and coauthors present a 2026 retrospective cohort study of remnant cholesterol and long-term outcomes after kidney transplantation. Abnormal blood fats are common after transplant and relate to graft survival, yet standard lipid measures predict inconsistently. Remnant cholesterol, the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich leftovers, may add information. The cohort held 1,943 living-donor transplant recipients.

Lipid exposure was averaged over the first year after surgery under a landmark design, so later events could be tied cleanly to earlier levels. Survival models compared remnant cholesterol against five conventional lipid measures, with curved dose-response checks and subgroup analyses. The study asks whether this single extra number sharpens prognosis enough to guide lipid management in transplant clinics.
pmc-13479868:
Panagiotis D. Velentzas, Fei Chai, and Eric H. Baehrecke published a 2026 study of hermes, a cell-surface pyruvate carrier, and its grip on autophagy, the cell's self-eating recycling system. The carrier normally supports a growth signal pathway and switches autophagy on during development. The team screened for genes whose change could rescue the carrier's mutant defects.

The brake on autophagy depended on pyruvate entering mitochondria and feeding the Krebs cycle. Losing the carrier raised reactive oxygen species, and merely dampening that rise restored autophagy and signaling. In adult animals, carrier loss shortened lifespan and broke autophagy in gut tissue. The work ties a membrane transport protein to mitochondrial chemistry, oxidative stress, and whole-animal health.
pmc-13480068:
Burcu Soy Telli and co-authors describe a 2026 effort to adapt a parent-report scale of early social skills for Turkish children. The scale covers joint attention, copying others, and grasp of what others think and feel. Four linked studies tested children aged 4 to 39 months, starting with 124 families and adding further groups for each check.

Unlike the English version with two parts, the Turkish form worked as a single scale. Two weak items were cut, leaving 19 items with strong internal consistency. Scores tracked closely with a known autism screening checklist, and repeat scores after one month held steady. A pooled check across 246 children showed the scale worked well across varied family backgrounds. Clinicians in Türkiye gain a tested tool for early social development research outside Western settings.
pmc-13480368:
Ugnė Žulpaitė and Vilma Petrikaitė build tiny hybrid particles that carry curcumin, the active part of turmeric, toward tissues starved of oxygen. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Curcumin can shield cells from harm, but it barely dissolves in water and the body takes up very little of it.

The pair blended fat-like and plastic-like parts to form the particles, then tuned the mix ratio. They measured particle size, charge, and stability, and how much curcumin each batch held. They also watched how fast curcumin leaked out at normal body acidity and at the sour level found in sick tissue. Last, they tested the particles on cells kept in normal air and in low-oxygen-like settings. The goal is a carrier that frees more of its load where tissue is acidic.
pmc-13480568:
Max Kadarauch and co-authors present a 2026 study on building handed ring molecules with help from electric attraction rather than bulk. Most handed catalysts steer reactions by blocking space, yet pull-based steering can speed reactions and widen scope. The team used a charged palladium ligand to join an aryl group and a nitrogen ring closure in one step, forming indolines, a ring pair found in many natural drugs.

Many pairings of the two partners gave products with high handed purity under gentle conditions. Trends linked the electronic pull of each partner to purity scores, which let the team retune the nitrogen shield group and rescue weaker pairings. The findings give makers a fresh dial for handed synthesis, since charge guidance can be tuned in ways that bulk alone cannot.
pmc-13481568:
Meng Zhang and eight co-authors test engineered immune cells against blood cancers carrying a certain marker, in a paper dated 2026. The therapy, CAR-T, retools a patient's own T cells to hunt cancer. It shines in lymphoid cancers but has disappointed in myeloid ones, the target here.

Fifteen patients with myeloid tumors received cells aimed at the CD123 marker. Results were weak: a few reached deep remission, most did not. The team then asked whether a cancer drug, venetoclax, could sharpen the cells. In dishes, modest doses left the CAR-T cells unharmed while stressing cancer cells, and pairing raised killing and signal output. Pre-treating the cells with the drug is explored as the next step. The paper is candid that this target needs help to work.
pmc-13482868:
Baran and team tested a light-based way to kill germs inside the belly after a burst appendix, using rabbits as stand-ins for patients. In their 2026 study, 19 rabbits developed a perforated appendix, a torn appendix leaking bacteria into the abdomen. Nine received methylene blue dye washed through the belly, followed by red laser light shone through a thin surgical scope. Ten got the dye wash without the light.

The light treatment proved workable and caused no clear harm to organs checked under the microscope afterward. Bacterial counts fell in only one treated rabbit, though, and rose in most animals in both groups. The gap between groups was not statistically clear, and Baran calculates the study had only modest power to spot a real effect. Larger trials would be needed before doctors could judge the approach.
pmc-13483668:
Abigail Helm explores how common lasting pain is among people in drug treatment courts who also have mental health conditions. Published in 2026, the secondary analysis covers participants from five courts, comparing 61 people with a chronic pain history against 109 without one. Intake data span pain, mental health, substance use, legal history, and quality of life.

Chronic pain history appeared in 36 percent of participants, a share the authors flag as high for this setting. That group reported stronger pain and more interference with enjoyment and daily tasks. Two thirds reported non-medical prescription opioid use, far above the share in the group without pain history, alongside more oxycodone misuse and overdoses yet fewer nights in jail. Mental health and quality of life scores did not differ. Courts are urged to screen for pain routinely.
pmc-13483868:
Koovekallu and co-authors examined how giant atmospheric waves traveling along the equator intensify extreme rain on India's west coast. These waves, coupled to storm clouds, circle the tropics and can pile moisture against the Western Ghats mountains. Their 2026 study compared extreme rainfall on wave-active days across all seasons, separating three wave families by their motion patterns.

Rossby waves, slow westward swirls, amplified land rainfall extremes the most among the wave types studied. Overall the waves boosted extreme rain over land by roughly 20 to 60 percent, and by over 150 percent over nearby ocean in the strongest cases. One wave family peaked sharply during the June to September monsoon, while others stayed active year-round. In winter the effect shrank to India's southern tip. Koovekallu says forecasters should track these waves when warning coastal districts.
pmc-13485668:
Bing Li reviews Piezo channels, the molecular pressure sensors that turn physical force into cell signals, as targets for physical therapies. Published in 2026, the synthesis starts from the channels' three-bladed propeller shape and tension-based opening mechanism. Roles across skeleton, heart and vessels, nerves, and immunity follow, together with disease links spanning genetic disorders, joint wear, and cancer.

Later sections survey hands-off control methods, including ultrasound and magnetic fields that nudge channel activity without contact. Piezoelectric materials that imitate the channels' trick are covered for tissue repair, nerve modulation, and drug delivery. Force-based medicine often lacked a molecular address; Piezo proteins supply one. Readers get both the mechanism grounding and the device frontier in a single map.
pmc-13486668:
Dai and colleagues used a national aging survey to test whether older Chinese adults who suffer headaches are more likely to lose hearing. Headaches rank among the world's top causes of disability, and hearing loss isolates older people, yet the pair are seldom studied together. Their 2026 analysis drew 3,872 adults aged 45 and older drawn from a national retirement survey, the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, excluding anyone already hearing-impaired at the start.

Headache sufferers showed about two thirds higher odds of later hearing impairment after the team adjusted for other health and social factors. The link ran stronger in men, whose odds were more than double in the subgroup analysis reported. The pattern persisted across the confounder adjustments the authors applied. Dai suggests treating headaches early might double as hearing protection, while calling for work on the biological pathway connecting the two conditions.
pmc-13487368:
Joseph Schulz and three co-authors build, in a 2026 paper, a planning method for prostate brachytherapy that holds up when catheters land off mark. In this treatment, thin tubes place a radioactive source inside the prostate for short dwell times. A slip of a few millimeters can thin the tumor dose and spill dose to the bladder and bowel. Past plans tune dwell times alone, for a fixed set of tubes.

Their method picks catheter positions and dwell times in one pass, with built-in uncertainty about each tube's landing spot. Extra candidate paths fan out from each tube, and a sparsity rule keeps the selection lean. A guard term caps dose at the surfaces of nearby organs. On 32 past cases, the method held tumor dose far better under simulated slips than clinical plans. The share of acceptable plans rose by a wide margin.
pmc-13487568:
Maria Zofia Lisiecka and Joanna Luczak give a short 2026 review of natural rubber latex allergy. It sets out causes, signs, and new test methods. The pair sift 67 papers from 2019 to 2024 across key databases. Fresh latex is 60 percent water, 35 percent polyisoprene, and 5 percent proteins and fats. Its Hev b proteins spark most of the risk.

Allergy rates run 5 to 17 percent in health staff. Plant and shop workers reach about 12 percent. Top risks are past allergy, cross-hits with tropical fruit, and many child surgeries. Skin tests, blood antibody tests, and challenge tests all scored well in the sifted work. Shared test rules and firm product rules are still weak points. Man-made swaps and faster tests can cut harm.
pmc-13487968:
Christopher A. Rock and a large imaging team present a finer way to map heart muscle structure in a 2026 methods study. Diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging tracks water movement to infer how heart cells are arranged, but standard scans give only a few measurement points across the wall. Their free-breathing method reaches submillimeter detail and groups each tiny volume by its diffusion traits and fiber angle patterns.

Healthy volunteers and patients with severe aortic valve narrowing, whose heart walls had thickened, both showed four recurring structural classes. Despite the thickening, cell organization stayed largely orderly in the patient group. Checks against tissue samples and lower-resolution scans supported the approach. The authors offer it for studying how heart muscle remodels in disease.
pmc-13488568:
Chibueze Anosike leads a large team surveying mental health among women petty traders in Nsukka, Nigeria, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Small-scale market trading brings heavy money stress, yet mental health in informal work is little studied. Structured interviews with 331 women at Ogige Market measured anxiety, depression, coping styles, and where women would turn for help, using standard screening and coping questionnaires.

Roughly a quarter of women screened in the moderate to severe range for anxiety, and a similar share for depression, in the reported figures. Emotion-focused coping was most common, while avoidant coping tracked with worse symptoms. Most women would seek help from partners, parents, or family, and most would avoid professionals or helplines. The authors call for trader-friendly community support.
pmc-13489768:
Matthew R. Wilson leads a very large international team testing preventive high-dose methotrexate in ultra high-risk large B-cell lymphoma in a 2026 combined analysis. The fear is relapse inside the brain and spinal cord, which standard treatment reaches poorly. Two earlier datasets were merged to give 1,923 patients classed as ultra high risk. Classing came from score or from spread to sites like testis, kidney, or breast. Patients were split by whether preventive drug was given.

Three-year brain relapse rates were close in both groups, at a level near nine percent without the drug against a level near eight percent with it in the raw figures. Adjusted models and a landmark check among early responders also found no clear benefit. Isolated brain relapse rates matched as well. The authors question routine use.
pmc-13490368:
Li and colleagues mapped the ancient rock layers hosting a giant gas field in China's Sichuan Basin, explaining why the reservoir performs brilliantly in some spots and poorly in others. The rocks are microbial dolomites from the Sinian period, built partly by ancient microbe mats after a global glaciation. Their 2026 study combined drill cores, microscope slides, rock physics measurements, and seismic surveys to reconstruct the original seafloor.

The seafloor formed a staircase of platforms, shaped by old north-south cliffs and east-west faults that moved while sediment settled. Three rock types arranged into three settings: microbial mounds, grain shoals, and the quieter seas between mounds. The lower part of the member stacks these settings in a distinct vertical order the team charts. Li says the step model predicts where porous, gas-friendly rock should hide.
pmc-13490468:
Xie and co-authors mined liver cancer data for genes tied to autophagy, the cell's self-recycling system, and built a four-gene risk model around them. Liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, behaves very differently between patients, and recycling pathways shape both growth and immunity. Their 2026 study clustered patients by 221 autophagy genes, trained the model on registry data, verified it on separate cohorts, and zoomed into single cells to locate the lead gene.

Two autophagy subtypes emerged with clearly different molecular profiles, immune landscapes, and survival outcomes. The four-gene model separated high-risk patients, whose tumors carried more mutations and more immune checkpoint genes, from low-risk ones across cohorts. Single-cell data showed the lead gene, ATIC, concentrated in tumor cells rather than surrounding tissue. Cell experiments supported ATIC actively promoting cancer progression. Xie offers the model for risk stratification and ATIC as a drug target.
pmc-13490968:
Choi and Kwak, food scientists in Korea, set out in 2026 to make rice snacks both healthier and still liked by buyers. Plain rice snacks are mostly refined starch, with little fiber. The pair added barley at six levels, from none up to the full mix, and then checked the snacks for plant compounds, antioxidant strength, and taste scores.

More barley raised total phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant scores on all four lab tests they ran. Ferulic acid was the main free phenolic found, and it grew as the barley share rose. Buyers liked the snacks most at the mid levels of barley, about two fifths to three fifths of the mix. Past that point, extra barley made the snacks harder and darker, and scores fell off.
pmc-13491668:
Martina Tosi leads a ten-author team describing in 2026 how routine colonoscopy preparation clashed with the strict diet of a woman who has phenylketonuria, an inherited disorder usually called PKU. Her body cannot handle phenylalanine, an amino acid in protein, so she lives on a tightly limited diet. Standard bowel preparation demanded low-fibre eating, then clear fluids, plus laxatives that can contain sweeteners.

The twenty-four-year-old British woman tolerated only 250 milligrams of phenylalanine daily and kept her blood levels well controlled. During preparation she dropped her amino acid supplement, then took a second laxative dose that unknowingly contained aspartame, a phenylalanine source. She became dizzy, exhausted, and confused, with a severe headache. The authors call for preparation plans and product warnings tailored to metabolic diets.
pmc-13491968:
Shiva Satija leads a twenty-two-author team unveiling in 2026 MutAIverse, an artificial intelligence platform that hunts for DNA adducts, the chemical scars that toxic substances leave on DNA before mutations form. Existing analysis tools rely on libraries of already proven adducts, missing novel ones. The platform instead simulates how the body activates toxins, building a library of chemically plausible adducts and tracing each back to its parent chemical.

Checked against experimental mass spectrometry datasets, the platform recovered known adducts and flagged new ones that older libraries missed. Applied to tissue from head and neck cancer patients who used smokeless tobacco, it found selective enrichment of several adducts, and a subset was confirmed by follow-up analysis. The authors offer the tool for toxicology and cancer exposure research.
pmc-13493868:
Li and Yu build a simple score from routine blood tests to capture oxidative stress, the imbalance where damaging oxygen by-products outpace the body's defences, and test whether it tracks inflammation. Using survey data from 6,044 Chinese adults collected in 2009, their 2026 score adds up six fasting measures. Four push oxidation up, including uric acid and ferritin, and two are protective. Scores ran from 6 to 30 points.

Each extra point came with a small but highly consistent rise in hs-CRP, a standard blood marker of body-wide inflammation, and the relationship stayed straight-line across the whole range. The score also cleanly separated groups already known to be at high risk. Stress tests that removed one component at a time barely moved the result, suggesting no single ingredient drives the link. The authors offer the score as a cheap way to flag the stress-inflammation pairing in large studies.
pmc-13493968:
Xingyu Liu and others study why farmers in Fars Province, Iran, join or avoid agricultural marketing networks such as cooperatives. In 2026, the mixed-methods study first talks thirty-two farmers to find barriers, then surveys 332 farmers and models intentions with structural equation model. Adoption remains low despite promotion of networks for market access and income.

Talks yield economic, institutional, social-informational, and mental barriers. In the model, attitude, perceived control, and social networks clearly predicted intention, while subjective norms and knowledge did not, and trust strongly shaped views. Perceived barriers slightly reduced intention. The authors recommend trust-based, socially embedded policies rather than information campaigns alone.
pmc-13494068:
Wenwen Zhao and co-authors test whether a muscle-and-fat condition links sitting time to diabetes in older adults, in a 2026 study. The condition, sarcopenic obesity, pairs low muscle mass with excess fat. The team enrolled 2,480 community-dwelling adults aged 35 and over who came for physical exams. Sitting time came from a standard questionnaire, and body makeup was measured with an impedance scanner.

Statistical mediation analysis found the condition carried about a fifth of the sitting-diabetes link overall. That share was larger in women, about 23 percent, than in men, near 9 percent. The pattern also shifted with age. Because the study is a snapshot in time, it shows correlation rather than cause. The authors suggest tackling muscle loss and fat together when fighting diabetes in aging communities.
pmc-13494168:
Mallinson and colleagues ask whether a single long overnight fast changes how muscle handles the next meal. Repeated long fasts seem to sharpen muscle's protein-building response, but one night might do nothing. In their 2026 crossover study, nine healthy young men each completed two mornings. Once they had fasted a normal ten hours overnight, and once sixteen hours. Each time they drank a labelled milk protein and sugar meal while the team tracked the label into muscle protein.

The longer fast did not change how much meal protein got built into muscle over three hours. Nor did it change how much amino acid or glucose the forearm took up. It did trim the insulin response after the meal and lowered a gut hormone signal. The authors read those changes as early steps toward better insulin handling rather than improved sensitivity itself.
pmc-13494568:
Santucci and colleagues tested a heat-killed version of an eight-strain probiotic mixture in mice with chemically induced colon inflammation, in a 2026 study. The study concerns postbiotics, preparations of dead microbes that may be safer than live probiotics for fragile patients. Colitis was triggered with dextran sulfate sodium in drinking water for seven days, mimicking ulcerative colitis, and the preparation was given during the second half of that week.

Santucci found treated mice recovering signs quickly, with better disease activity scores and less colon shortening than untreated colitic mice. Inside the colon wall, three inflammatory messenger molecules dropped, and production of occludin, a protein sealing the gut barrier, partly recovered. Yet two measures did not budge: an enzyme marking neutrophil infiltration stayed high, and tissue damage looked no better. The authors read the result as partial protection, supporting work on heat-stabilized postbiotics toward inflammatory bowel disease studies.
pmc-13495168:
Ebuderda Günay and colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, how to freeze Aseel rooster sperm so it survives thawing in good shape. Frozen semen guards rare poultry lines and aids breeding, yet glycerol, the usual freeze shield, can harm sperm and even act against fertility in the hen. The team tried adding iodixanol, a gentle medium, so glycerol doses could drop.

They pooled semen from ten roosters and froze it in mixes with two glycerol levels and three iodixanol levels. After thawing, lab tools graded movement, membrane health, energy organelles, and DNA state. The higher glycerol mix alone gave the strongest movement and membrane scores. In the low-glycerol mixes, iodixanol lifted movement clearly, and the equal low pairing of the two agents scored best overall. The authors say the pairing could let breeders cut glycerol while keeping frozen stock sound.
pmc-13495268:
Isaac Emmanuel Omara and a large team trace, in a 2026 genomic study, how Rift Valley fever virus has changed across African outbreaks in people and animals. The virus, spread by mosquitoes and farm animals, threatens health and livestock trade, yet the forces letting it persist and adapt stayed murky. The team gathered nearly six hundred genome segment sequences from thirteen countries, spanning 1944 to 2022.

Over seven thousand protein-changing mutations turned up, with the richest variety in South Africa, Kenya, and Madagascar. Non-human hosts carried the broader mix, and family trees showed human cases sprouting from livestock lines, which the team names as the main source of human outbreaks. Seven mutations recurred across the genome, several in the copying enzyme and surface proteins, with signs of active selection at those spots. The authors flag these sites as candidates shaping how well the virus copies itself and dodges immunity.
pmc-13498968:
Zhang and colleagues looked for early brain-network signs that spinal cord stimulation will produce recovery in patients with disorders of consciousness, such as unresponsive wakefulness and minimally conscious states. Their 2026 study followed thirty-one patients receiving cervical stimulation, recording brain waves before treatment and at one week and one month. They related network features to consciousness scores six months later.

Zhang found recovery accompanied strengthening of network energy in the faster alpha and beta rhythms across five brain networks. It peaked at one month, while slower rhythms changed weakly and inconsistently. Communication architecture consolidated most in the beta band, with broader cooperation within and between networks in recovered patients. Two features stood out as predictors: alpha energy in the frontoparietal network at one month and beta energy in the cingulo-opercular network at one week. The authors propose these as monitoring markers while stimulation therapy is young.
pmc-13499068:
Henry Bair writes in 2026 about a new Medicare model that brings computer-assisted review to traditional fee-for-service coverage in the United States. Under the model, companies will use artificial intelligence tools alongside licensed clinicians to check medical necessity for selected services prone to fraud, waste, and abuse. Pre-approval systems can curb low-value care, yet they can also delay treatment, burden clinicians, and hide unfair patterns.

Bair argues that judging the model by savings alone would miss what makes such review legitimate. He asks for proof on patient-relevant outcomes, on fairness that lets decisions be contested, and on equity across groups, all at national scale. Two design features draw his focus, namely computer-shaped workflow choices and review after care is delivered but before payment, which can stall reimbursement. He offers three practical additions to strengthen the programme.
pmc-13501568:
Guiqin Liu leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 study of how high-altitude low oxygen changes the way medicines reach the brain. The blood-brain barrier normally keeps most drugs out of the central nervous system, and altitude hypoxia alters its structure. Working with rats and a human brain vessel cell line called hCMEC/D3, the team measured barrier leakiness with dye staining and microscopy. They then profiled drug transporters and metabolizing enzymes with proteomics, gene expression tests, and protein blots.

Hypoxia increased barrier permeability while raising the efflux transporter Abcb1, which pumps drugs back out of cells, and lowering the enzyme CYP2B1, which breaks drugs down. Test drugs spread differently through the brain. Their half-life lengthened while total clearance fell, showing slower handling overall. The authors argue that low-altitude drug dosing may not transfer to people living on high plateaus.
pmc-13501968:
Geoffrey Akena and five co-authors measure anemia, a shortage of red blood cells, among pregnant women infected with intestinal worms in western Uganda. Their study came out in 2026. Anemia is common in pregnancy worldwide, and worm infections, especially hookworm, make it worse by causing blood loss.

About one in four of the women studied had anemia, split across mild, moderate, and severe cases. Risk rose step by step with hookworm intensity. Moderate infections nearly doubled the risk, and heavy infections raised it more. Deworming treatment at least three months earlier was protective, as was using borehole water. The authors call for timely deworming, safer water, and stronger antenatal care in areas where worms are common.
pmc-13503768:
Xuhui Feng leads a team that made a glass glowing in near-infrared light with near-perfect yield, in a 2026 study. Such emitters serve in imaging and night vision, yet bright molecular glows often die out when packed into a solid block. Clumping, shaking, and air all drain the stored light.

The team set tiny molybdenum clusters inside a hybrid glass based on cadmium chloride. Tests of three cluster salts showed that chloride tips gave the strongest glow. In the glass, the clusters spread out evenly and sat still, shielded from air. The best glass turned about 97 percent of absorbed light into glow inside, and about 91 percent escaped for use. The result suits small lamps for imaging work.
pmc-13503868:
Zhenfu Wen leads a team that found a brain pattern marking sleep loss, in a 2026 study. Lost sleep dulls thought and mood, yet brain scans have mostly been read one spot at a time. A whole-brain signature could track harm from poor sleep more reliably.

Using machine learning on large scan data sets, the team trained a pattern that split sleep-deprived brains from rested ones. It held up in fresh data sets from both lab studies and daily life. The pattern still showed traces of harm after a night of catch-up sleep, and it reacted to partial sleep loss as well. It also tracked how long people in the general public sleep. The authors map which brain links drive the signal and which recover fast.
pmc-13504968:
Colleen Cheek leads a team telling the stories of older adults with advanced chronic illness who land in emergency departments, in a 2026 study from Sydney. Such patients visit emergency care often, and demand is rising as populations age. Their own view of those visits is little known.

Twelve interviews covered older patients and family carers across three departments. Two built stories show patients growing passive as dependence deepens, yielding to a system felt as split, rigid, and process-bound rather than person-bound. A carer's story adds the pain of watching a loved one treated as a passive case and feeling unable to speak for them. The authors call for earlier illness planning and emergency care designed around older people's needs.
pmc-13505068:
Amir Hossein Barjasteh leads a team reporting a rare skin condition in an unusual place on a kidney transplant patient, in a 2026 case report. The condition leaves the skin open to wart viruses and usually shows as pale patches on sun-exposed skin. It arises in people whose immune defenses are suppressed.

The patient, a 38-year-old woman nine years past her transplant on three immune-suppressing drugs, developed pale patches confined to her genitals. The patches were first read as a fungal rash and treated as such without success. A skin biopsy showed the swollen, blue-gray cells that mark the condition. The authors stress biopsy for odd genital patches in transplant patients, plus watch for skin cancer over time.
pmc-13505168:
Maryam Gholam Tamimi and Mohammad Reza Daliri examined how brain networks reorganise while people process emotional faces. They used task-based brain scans from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project. Activity was summarised across 264 brain regions grouped into ten large networks, and connections between regions were mapped for face and shape viewing conditions.

Face viewing changed connection patterns at both region and network level compared with shapes. Higher thinking networks linked more positively with each other, while basic perceptual networks showed stronger opposing patterns. Overall measures suggested the brain's modules became more separate, a sign of greater specialisation. At the same time, key hub regions across attention, vision, movement, and deeper brain networks kept selective links, holding the system together. The results may help frame how these networks shift in mood and emotional disorders.
pmc-13505368:
Fasheng Wu leads a large team that re-examined radiation dosing for lung cancer that had spread to the brain. They reviewed 449 patients treated with focused CyberKnife radiation between 2006 and 2025. Two tools were combined: a dose-response model based on biologically effective dose, and an interpretable machine-learning method that explains which factors drive its forecasts.

Dose needs varied with tumour size, and tumours between two and three centimetres across required the highest dose for a fifty percent chance of control. The learning model predicted early decline in daily functioning well. Its explanations showed dose effects flipping with starting condition: lower doses raised decline risk in patients already weak, while higher doses protected those starting strong. Continuous targeted drug therapy paired with high dose gave the best tumour control. The authors offer the combined approach as a guide for tailoring dose to each patient.
pmc-13506668:
Gabriel C A Costa and colleagues report 2026 work on a protein from the cattle tick, a pest that drains farm output across warm regions. The protein, named RmTIL, comes from tick saliva glands and can block protein-cutting enzymes. The team made a lab copy of its active part and tested what it blocks.

The lab copy strongly blocked two human enzymes and a bacterial enzyme at very low doses. Silencing the RmTIL gene in female ticks lowered egg survival and raised bacterial levels in ovaries and eggs. Infection of ticks also raised RmTIL output. The protein seems to guard both feeding and microbe balance, making it a candidate target for tick control.
pmc-13507068:
P Bhuvaneshwari and colleagues propose, in 2026 work, a system that watches heart disease in real time by linking medical sensors, deep learning, and blockchain records. Wearable devices collect heart sound and electrical signals, which are cleaned, split into features, and sorted by a hybrid neural network. Blockchain methods guard the data against tampering.

Tests used public heart signal sets and a classic heart disease dataset. Reported scores reached about 99 percent for accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score, a combined precision and recall measure. The authors present the system as a secure and scalable option for near real-time heart checks outside hospitals. Independent clinical testing would still be needed.
pmc-13507268:
Gaurav Kumar Soni, Dinesh Yadav, Ashok Kumar, Swati Varun Yadav, and Manish Varun Yadav design, in 2026 work, a tiny flexible antenna for 5G wearables in the N77 and N78 bands. Wearable radios must bend with the body, stay light, and keep radiation exposure low. Their monopole design adds a symmetric multi-stub resonator on a thin flexible substrate.

Built and measured prototypes resonated near 3.5 gigahertz with about 1.3 gigahertz of usable bandwidth and modest peak gain. Tissue-model safety tests gave absorption values far below typical limits. On wrist, chest, and leg placements plus bending trials, performance held up well. Smart clothing and health monitors could adopt the compact, body-safe design.
pmc-13508168:
Brett Story leads a large team testing gene therapy for eye damage in sheep with Tay-Sachs disease, a fatal brain disorder, in 2026 work. Jacob sheep are the only large-animal model of this disease, yet their eye damage was poorly mapped. Groups included healthy sheep, untreated sick sheep, and sick sheep given a virus-based therapy by vein or into spinal fluid. The therapy carried working copies of two missing enzyme genes. Eye tissues were checked with microscopy, cell counts, and gene tests.

Untreated sheep showed swollen nerve cells in the retina, lost cells, and damaged optic nerve fibers. Vein delivery did not prevent that damage. Delivery into spinal fluid, though, preserved cell counts and nerve scores over the short term. It also cut the fatty storage buildup inside retinal cells. Little therapy virus reached the retina itself, a puzzle the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13508368:
Katarzyna Szczepanik, Paweł Kurowski, and Małgorzata Siekańska compare stress and coping in children who train in judo with peers who play no sport, in 2026 work. Ages ten to fifteen bring intense social and emotional change, yet sport-based comparisons of coping were lacking. The study covered 553 students, split almost evenly between regular judo trainees and non-training peers. A standardized coping questionnaire and a custom survey captured stress sources, symptoms, and responses.

Judo students reported far less school-related stress than their peers. Far more of them said they rarely or never feel stressed, and more felt always safe at school. Grades, teacher criticism, tests, and loneliness troubled the non-training group more often. Body stress symptoms, like poor focus, also split the groups. The authors suggest regular sport may build coping strength, and they offer the findings as targets for school prevention programs.
pmc-13508668:
Cheng and colleagues examine what happens when an American genetic screening playbook is applied in East Asia. The US CDC designates three hereditary conditions as Tier 1 for population screening because catching them early saves lives. Their 2026 study read whole genomes from nearly four thousand Taiwanese biobank participants and annotated variants in those Tier 1 genes. It added two genes tied to conditions commoner locally: a stroke-causing vessel disease and hereditary hearing loss.

Carriers of harmful variants in the Tier 1 genes made up roughly two percent of each cohort, higher than a comparable American project's rate. Inherited high cholesterol accounted for over three fifths of the findings. Soberingly, over two fifths of carriers did not know their cholesterol was high, exactly the gap screening exists to close. The authors argue screening panels must be re-derived, not just imported, for each population.
pmc-13508768:
Bishop and colleagues developed pHarmony, an algorithm that matches peaks between multidimensional NMR spectra, the magnetic resonance fingerprints used to map protein structures and screen drug fragments. Matching peaks across spectra is slow, especially where signals crowd together, and tools rarely say how confident a match is. Their 2026 method models how peak deviations arise from noise versus shifts.

Bishop used Bayesian inference to assign each match a reliability score. The method, a statistical framework that updates beliefs with evidence, considers all mappings together rather than one peak at a time. Tests included mapping between triple-resonance assignment spectra and between two- and three-dimensional spectra from a fragment-based drug discovery screen perturbed by ligand binding. The algorithm stayed accurate even when peaks vanished through exchange effects or picking errors, and it handles peak lists of any dimensionality, filling a gap left by picking-focused tools.
pmc-13509368:
İlgenli and co-authors ran a 2026 laboratory study on the safety of modified mineral trioxide aggregate, a calcium silicate material dentists use to repair teeth. Adding chitosan, a natural polymer, or an antiseptic called Octenisept might change how the material treats nearby cells. The test cells were fibroblasts from the ligament that holds teeth in place.

Extracts of five material versions were placed on the human cells at several strengths for one and three days. İlgenli measured survival with the MTT assay, counting anything under seventy percent survival as toxic by international standard. Direct exposure to the antiseptic solution was most damaging to the cells. Among material extracts, only the version with one percent chitosan stayed non-toxic at full strength after three days.
pmc-13509568:
