Hu and colleagues reported in 2026 that a purified polysaccharide from goji berries, called Lycii Fructus, extends healthy life in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Complex sugars from plants are a focus of ageing research. This fraction was tested for its effect on the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, a repair program that keeps the cell's energy factories healthy. Worms got the fraction across their lives while the team tracked lifespan, movement, and stress resistance.

Hu found treated worms lived longer, stayed healthier, and resisted heat, oxidation, and ultraviolet stress better than controls. Their mitochondria stayed more plentiful and better shaped, energy output rose, and harmful reactive oxygen fell. The lifespan gain vanished in worms lacking either of two genes, ATFS-1 or UBL-5, that drive the repair program. In human skin cells, the fraction also cut a marker of cell ageing and improved mitochondrial function.
pmc-13509668:
Johanna Müller-Diesing and eight co-authors revisit patients with long-lasting dizziness whose cause stayed unclear at first testing, in 2026 work. The group first saw these patients between 2009 and 2012, when each had felt dizzy for at least a year without a firm diagnosis. Fourteen to seventeen years later, the team reached 51 of them by phone and repeated a standard handicap score for dizziness.

Scores fell sharply over the long gap, with the median total dropping from the high range to the low range. Nearly every patient, 49 of 51, reported improvement, and the largest gain came in daily functioning rather than in body symptoms or mood. Gains appeared across sex, age, and later diagnostic groups alike. The authors say the long view is reassuring, though larger groups are needed before a general forecast can be trusted.
pmc-13510568:
Xiao-Xin Liang, Haochen Wu, and Yong Wang build an electronic tongue that reads tears for eye disease screening, in 2026 work. Tears carry clues about eye health, yet lab tests for them are slow and hard to carry into clinics. The device joins a tiny fluid chip with sensors that make their own power from droplet motion, working in three modes that read droplet behavior in different ways.

Tuned settings kept readings steady within a narrow error band across all three modes. Paired with a learning method, the system sorted artificial tears by acidity with accuracy above ninety-six percent. Disease-linked markers, including an enzyme, an inflammation signal, and a germ tied to eye infection, each gave distinct electrical patterns that allowed type and level checks. The authors present the self-powered mini system as a step toward quick tear testing at the point of care.
pmc-13510968:
Bovio and colleagues build a wearable that estimates blood pressure continuously without a cuff. Their 2026 paper pairs the SOUNDI device, a multimodal sensor platform, with a neural network mixing convolutional and memory layers to read physiological signals and predict systolic and diastolic pressure. Data came from twenty healthy volunteers measured against a validated ambulatory reference device.

Two evaluations were run. Testing on entirely unseen people, the honest test of generalisation, the best subject's average error was about five millimetres of mercury for systolic and under four for diastolic pressure. Under a personalised split, where the model sees part of each person's data, errors fell to about three millimetres for both values, with correlations near 0.95 for systolic pressure. The authors present the results as feasibility evidence for cuffless monitoring, while noting the gap between personalised and person-independent performance.
pmc-13511268:
Iulia Stratulat-Chiriac and nine co-authors examine deaths among children born with gut malformations at a Romanian surgical center from 2020 to 2024, in 2026 work. Such birth defects remain a major cause of child death, above all in the newborn period and in lower-resource settings. Records covered 231 children admitted over five years, including the pandemic period, and the team compared survivors with those who died.

About one child in nine died during the first admission. More than half of deaths came within thirty days of arrival, and most followed surgery. Death rates ran highest for a severe joined outlet malformation and for a blocked upper bowel present at birth, among other types detailed in the full report. Eastern European data of this kind are scarce, and the authors say naming the baseline traits tied to death can guide earlier referral and sharper newborn care.
pmc-13512668:
Xufeng Fu, Bipeng Lai, Rongling He, Xiuji Huang, Qin Jiang, and Hui Li present a two-stream graph neural network for sorting diseases from multi-omics data, in 2026 work. Layers such as genes, RNA, and methylation differ in scale and grain, which makes joining them hard. The design builds a mixed graph of samples and features, with fast mutual information setting the prior strength of dependency edges.

One stream, built on a transformer, reads feature interplay in vector form, while a graph attention stream models structure among samples and molecular features. An uncertainty-aware ensemble steadies answers when samples are few or noisy. Five public benchmarks tested the system, covering Alzheimer data, glioma, breast cancer, colon tumor staging, and a kidney set used as a ceiling check. Sorting held competitive, and explanation tools surfaced breast cancer marker genes. The authors stress readable biomarker ranking as the real prize.
pmc-13512968:
Margaret K. Corley and co-authors trace the origins and spread of the invasive Asian tiger mosquito across the Americas through population genetics, in 2026 work. The mosquito now thrives across the continent and can carry dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. Samples came from fifty sites in the invaded American range, fourteen in Europe, and twenty-eight in the native Asian range.

American populations descend from many separate introduction events drawing on several distinct native sources, not one founding wave. South American populations stood genetically apart from those in temperate North America and Europe. After arrival, American populations also mixed with each other, most likely through human transport moving eggs or adults along trade and travel routes. The authors say knowing invasion sources helps managers predict spread and target control of this disease carrier.
pmc-13514268:
Alexandru Mihai Micu and nine co-authors build a low-cost digital workflow for printing patient-specific practice teeth with layered enamel and built-in decay, in 2026 work. Standard plastic training teeth look idealized and feel uniform, while virtual simulators cost too much for large classes. Mouth scans and cone-beam images from one de-identified case were merged into a virtual patient, and a socket design lets each printed tooth be swapped by a screw through its root tip.

Two printing routes and a hybrid were compared on cost, time, and fidelity, and the hybrid pairing won for full two-jaw models. Fifty dental students handled one premium print and scored teaching value highest, with visual realism beating touch realism. Nearly all rated it at least equal to a natural extracted tooth, and most preferred it, though hardness felt off. Touch remains the priority for better materials.
pmc-13514868:
Park, Park, and Nam describe a new sample holder for X-ray crystal studies in twenty twenty-six. The method uses very short X-ray pulses to read crystal structure with little radiation damage. Samples sit on a fixed target that is scanned through the beam. The holder material can scatter X-rays and add noise to the data.

Their holder uses a thin film of PET, a common plastic. In tests, it gave low background scatter at the fine detail range that matters most. Its higher scatter at low detail did not harm data processing. Holes poked by hand in the film helped crystals settle in random orientations. The team read structures for a small chemical and for a protein at room temperature.
pmc-13515568:
Shiquan Su and five colleagues report a field experiment in a subtropical moso bamboo forest in China, published in 2026, on how drought and nitrogen shape soil life. The team cut the rain reaching some plots and added nitrogen to others, mimicking two global changes at once. They then measured how many soil jobs, from nutrient cycling to productivity support, the soil kept performing, and profiled its bacteria and fungi by gene sequencing.

Reduced rainfall clearly lowered the soil's combined performance, and added nitrogen made that loss worse. Surprisingly, the count of microbe species barely changed, and performance did not track diversity at all. What mattered was which microbes were present and how they linked together in networks. Rising shares of three groups, among them Acidobacteriota, went with stronger soil performance. Su's team concludes that global change rewires soil communities rather than emptying them, and the rewiring drives the function loss.
pmc-13515768:
Paul Grama and colleagues review whether scope-based weight-loss treatments suit patients who have both obesity and inflammatory bowel disease. The treatments, such as stomach balloons and sleeve reshaping, sit between drugs and full bariatric surgery in intensity.

Direct trials in bowel disease patients barely exist, so the review leans on general scope studies and surgery data. The best candidates, it argues, are patients in lasting remission with stable nutrition and uncomplicated disease. Active upper-gut Crohn's disease, narrowed or penetrating disease, recent surgery, and heavy steroid use should prompt caution or avoidance. Grama calls for registries and trials split by disease type before firm advice can be given.
pmc-13517168:
Jingmin Luan and eight colleagues build an image-analysis method that reads brain blood vessels more faithfully after stroke, in a 2026 study. OCTA scans can watch the brain's smallest vessels over time, but stroke weakens the signal and blurs vessel edges, corrupting measurements. Their structure-aware segmentation was tested in mice with a clot-based stroke model, scoring overlap, boundary accuracy, centreline continuity, and branch-point survival against hand-drawn references.

The method beat plain approaches on those structural scores and held up when images were deliberately degraded. Applied across time, its vessel masks showed less detectable perfusion coverage and shorter apparent vessel length after the stroke, while average vessel width barely moved. Luan's team frames the work as exploratory and preclinical. Its point is methodological: stroke studies need segmentation judged on network structure, not just pixel overlap, before derived numbers can be trusted.
pmc-13518768:
Chih-Hao Chiang and colleagues described a gentler way to attach metal contacts to ultra-thin semiconductors in 2026. Devices built from two-dimensional sheets can perform poorly because the usual process for depositing metal electrodes damages the sheet. The team instead transferred ready-made electrodes onto molybdenum disulfide sheets with help from a polycarbonate film.

Transferred contacts left the sheet structure and electronic behaviour largely intact. Test transistors switched stably, and devices still covered by the film performed better in open air, with higher electron mobility and steady switching ratios. The authors present the method as a route to stable performance that could scale to larger production.
pmc-13518868:
Ruohan Zhong and four colleagues propose in 2026 a poverty clue hidden in cooking energy: the share of a household's energy spent preparing food. Money-based measures miss families who farm for themselves or trade without cash. Engel's law says poorer households devote a larger share of resources to basic needs.

Using a nationwide Chinese household survey, the team built an Energy Engel Coefficient and checked it against regional patterns, subjective experience, and asset ownership. The new measure followed Engel's law more faithfully than the classic spending version. It flagged 13.9 percent of households as poor, and 85.8 percent of those were missed by the traditional coefficient, mostly small low-income rural homes.
pmc-13518968:
Deimler and co-authors trace a gene shift that bends a cap-wear ill in one kin line. Strand caps, called telomeres, guard the ends of straight strands. They are built of six-part codes run in long chains. A shift in the RNA mold swaps one code in the chain. The new chain reads GTTTAG in place of the stock code. Kin with the shift show the ill dyskeratosis congenita in most tales.

Lung scar is the lead sign in that kin line's ill hosts. The bent mold works at a slow pace in direct tests. Long-read scans track the bent codes down the kin line. Hosts who lack the mold shift still bear bent codes in spots. A spare shift, in RTEL1, joins the tale in two hosts. With both shifts, the ill strikes hard and young in them.
pmc-13519268:
Yichi Zhang and a large team dissect the vessel wall of narrowed dialysis fistulas in 2026 to learn why mature arteriovenous fistulas fail. Narrowing strikes 20 to 40 percent of mature fistulas, the go-to access for hemodialysis, yet the wall makeup of late failures was barely studied. Twenty-one removed specimens were checked with a custom machine-learning method.

Proteoglycans and collagen filled the wall more than muscle cells, with breaks along needle tracks. Narrowed segments showed compact collagen plus high levels of perlecan, versican, and its fragment versikine. Muscle cells there favored a quiet contractile state rather than growth. Zhang's team proposes the narrowing matures through phases, which may explain mixed responses to drug-coated devices.
pmc-13519768:
McDermott and co-authors issued a 2026 United Kingdom guideline on gene testing to prevent hearing loss from aminoglycoside antibiotics. These powerful drugs treat severe infections but can permanently damage hearing in people carrying certain mitochondrial variants. Three variants in the MT-RNR1 gene, found in about one in 330 people, carry that risk.

Carriers can lose hearing irreversibly after even a single dose at normal drug levels, the guideline stresses. McDermott recommends avoiding aminoglycosides at any detectable variant level and using alternatives where possible for carriers. Laboratory testing is nationally commissioned in England, while rapid bedside testing serves time critical cases such as newborn sepsis in some centres. Where results are unavailable and urgency is high, treatment should not be delayed. Early economic evidence suggests newborn bedside testing may save money.
pmc-13520168:
Shifang Tan leads a twelve-author study in 2026 testing Node-RADS, a standardized scoring system for judging lymph nodes on scans, in cervical cancer staging. Whether nodes harbor cancer decides treatment intensity, and ordinary MRI misses many deposits. Records covered 439 patients who had preoperative MRI plus node removal, with four readers of differing experience scoring preset nodes blindly.

Senior readers agreed almost perfectly and detected metastases with an area under the curve of 0.868. Junior readers agreed less and scored 0.758, needing consensus three times more often. Agreement between the senior and junior groups on node status was still substantial. Experience clearly shapes performance, the authors note.
pmc-13520268:
Donghoon Kang leads a six-author study in 2026 testing whether stomach microbes plus routine clinical facts can flag gastric growths, from precancerous adenoma to cancer. Samples from mouth, healthy stomach lining, and lesions were sequenced for 231 people: 129 with adenoma, 73 with cancer, and 29 healthy controls.

Microbial diversity thinned step by step toward cancer, and certain genera bloomed in cancer lesions while gut-friendly types faded. A combined prediction model using 33 microbial genera and six clinical variables reached a discrimination score of 0.830 at separating growths from healthy stomachs, beating microbe-only and clinical-only models. It also split adenoma from cancer well. Kang and colleagues propose the pairing as an endoscopy aid.
pmc-13520368:
Habib Daneshpajouh and colleagues present in 2026 a single map of gene control states built from 1,698 human tissue samples. A global group gathered the samples over many years. Older maps were made one cell type at a time. That method grows hard to run as cell types pile up.

The team used more than 9,500 signal tracks from the samples. Their model made 33 simple scores. The scores capture start sites, boost sites, active copying and silent zones. The scores also capture cell-specific patterns. Tests of gene activity matched or beat rival methods. A side score flags zones rich in disease-linked gene changes.
pmc-13520468:
Weikai Chen and colleagues present in 2026 a complete, gap-free genome assembly for common tobacco, a major crop formed by merging two wild species. Earlier assemblies left hundreds of gaps, especially in repetitive centre regions of chromosomes.

The new assembly spans 4.2 billion bases from end to end, with the two inherited subgenomes separated. Centre regions evolved unevenly after the merger, with frequent repositioning and distinct chemical marking patterns between subgenomes. One subgenome diverged faster in sequence. Plant scientists gain a reference for studying how merged genomes reorganise, plus a firmer base for tobacco breeding and gene work.
pmc-13521868:
Tong Zhang and co-authors report a rare kidney case in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Several tumors of different types grew in the same kidney at the same time. Such mixes are uncommon and can look like a spreading kidney cancer, which makes diagnosis hard.

The patient was a woman aged seventy-nine with a mass first seen on a scan a year earlier. Detailed imaging showed three lesions in different parts of the right kidney. Surgeons removed the kidney, and lab tests showed three distinct benign tumor types, one in each spot. A month later she was well, with no sign of return. The authors stress careful imaging and note that genetic advice may be wise in such cases.
pmc-13522268:
Yanwen Li and Yubin Li profile in 2026 a fat-handling gene called LCAT across three kidney cancer subtypes, where molecular programmes and immune surroundings differ enough to demand subtype-by-subtype judgement. Public cancer atlas data supplied gene, survival and immune measures.

Gene levels fell in chromophobe tumours yet rose in clear cell and papillary tumours versus normal kidney. Survival links flipped by subtype, harming outlook at opposite ends of expression in two subtypes while helping one outcome in the third. Immune scores and cell mixes shifted with gene level in every subtype. Copy number, methylation and RNA editing regulator links round out the portrait.
pmc-13522368:
Saha and colleagues report a 2026 study of mango ginger, a turmeric relative used in pickles and folk medicine, tested against chemical liver poisoning in mice.  Mice received the plant extract at two doses alongside the poison, and blood markers, tissue slices, and computer models of its compounds were examined.

The extract, which chemical analysis showed holds 62 probable compounds, clearly lowered the raised liver enzymes and bilirubin that signal liver damage. Kidney markers and blood fats also fell toward normal, and tissue slices showed the poison's damage reversed. Computer docking showed its compounds bind well to targets tied to inflammation and cell protection. The results support developing mango ginger compounds into liver and kidney protectors, though human proof is still far off.
pmc-13522468:
Kipyo Kim and colleagues propose a way to estimate a patient's usual kidney blood marker from a CT scan in a 2026 study of acute kidney injury. Diagnosis depends on comparing current creatinine, a waste product measured in blood, with a prior usual value that is often missing. Features drawn from segmented kidney images at two large hospitals were fed into machine learning models.

Using the imaging features, the models estimated the usual value more closely than the standard back-calculation method. Staging of the acute injury based on predicted values agreed far better with the true staging, and cases were much less often overstated. The externally tested approach could help clinicians judge acute kidney injury when no earlier blood result exists.
pmc-13523268:
Hosein Azizi, Elham Davtalab Esmaeili, and Ali Reza Shafiee-Kandjani relate social and economic status to quality of life in older adults in northwestern Iran in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Eight hundred six adults aged sixty or older were enrolled by stratified random sampling. Quality of life was measured with a standard World Health Organization questionnaire, and status was scored with a validated short instrument.

A clear gradient appeared: each step up in status tracked a higher quality of life score, with the highest group scoring about eight points above the lowest after adjustment. Younger seniors reported better quality of life than the oldest group, while widowhood tracked notably lower scores. Sex showed no independent link after adjustment. The authors recommend stronger financial support and social services focused on disadvantaged and widowed older adults.
pmc-13523368:
Eli M Soyfer and colleagues test whether the time of day of immunotherapy infusions affects cancer outcomes in a 2026 real-world study. Nearly one thousand patients receiving checkpoint inhibitor drugs for solid tumors at one health system between 2018 and 2022 were grouped by whether infusions started before or after noon. Disease control, meaning shrinkage or stability, was the main outcome.

Early infusion was linked to higher disease control, at just under half of patients versus two fifths for later infusion. The association survived adjustment for stage, age, and ethnicity, and held across sex, age, stage, and drug subgroups, as well as in matched and sensitivity analyses. Evidence in the Hispanic subgroup was inconclusive because of small numbers. The authors call for prospective trials of treatment timing.
pmc-13523468:
Cansu Özbaş and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study from Ankara, Türkiye, on what adults believe about thirdhand smoke and on voluntary smoking bans at home and in cars. Thirdhand smoke is the residue that lingers on surfaces after tobacco smoke clears. Adults attending a university hospital in June 2023 answered a 33-item questionnaire in face-to-face interviews.

Complete bans were reported by 57.4 percent of participants at home and 63.2 percent in cars. Stronger belief scores on a validated thirdhand smoke scale were linked with bans in both settings. Homes without a resident smoker were far more likely to enforce a ban, and nonsmokers banned smoking more often than smokers. Higher education raised the odds of a car ban. The authors argue that teaching about residue risks could widen smoke-free private spaces.
pmc-13524468:
Sachiko Nishina and others analyze, in a 2026 Japanese study across many centers, the genes and medical features behind two groups of eye disorders present from birth and affecting both eyes. One group covers the front of the eye, including aniridia, while the second group has abnormally small or absent eyes. Single gene causes were likely, and families needed clearer guidance.

A total of 111 patients and family members had targeted sequencing with panels covering eleven to twelve known genes per condition. Diagnoses were reached for half of the front-eye group and 37.5 percent of the small-eye group, including eleven new variants. Distinct genes led each condition, with some variants arising new and others inherited from parents with mild or distinct features. Glaucoma clustered with two genes, and systemic or neurologic problems grouped with others.
pmc-13525168:
Gestiada and Ladia surveyed older university employees in the Philippines in 2026 to learn what shapes their subjective well-being, meaning how good they feel their lives are. The study covered 69 randomly chosen staff aged 50 and over at the University of the Philippines, including faculty and administrative workers, using the WHO-5 well-being questionnaire.

Almost ninety percent of respondents reported better well-being. Yet none of the tested factors showed a statistically significant link with well-being scores. Perceived health, diagnosed conditions, and being a care recipient did not track with the scores, and neither did learning new skills, growth, work value, or work environment. The authors suggest larger and qualitative studies to explore cultural and workplace factors their survey could not capture.
pmc-13525968:
Jiaxi Hu and colleagues explore, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study, whether radiation dose calculations for a targeted prostate cancer therapy can be simplified without losing clinical meaning. Standard dosimetry uses scans at several time points, yet sampling limits and model assumptions introduce error. Their outcome-driven approach judged each method by how well doses predicted side effects and tumor marker response.

Data from fifty patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer treated with lutetium-177 PSMA therapy were analyzed. Single-time-point dose estimates for bone marrow, taken one, two, or three days after treatment, tracked anemia grading about as well as multi-time-point doses. Cumulative tumor dose from early single scans also predicted prostate marker response comparably. The authors conclude the optimal single time point chosen by outcomes matches the physics-based choice within two days.
pmc-13526368:
Yue Wu and colleagues tested a compound that may shield the heart during sepsis, when infection-driven organ failure raises death risk. Published in 2026, the study used animal and cell models of sepsis, treating with 4-phenylbutyric acid, a drug known to ease endoplasmic reticulum stress. Transcript data from septic patients had pointed to that stress pathway as central to sepsis-related heart dysfunction.

The compound markedly eased heart dysfunction by curbing the formation of junctions between endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria and restoring mitochondrial balance and function. It acted by binding two catalytic sites on an enzyme called HK2, cutting glycolysis and lactate buildup, which in turn reduced a protein modification that drives junction assembly. The authors propose a new treatment chain for septic heart injury. Readers get a mechanistic lead, still preclinical.
pmc-13527268:
Henric Rydén, Ola Norbeck, Sophie Schauman, Mikael Skorpil, and Adam van Niekerk present, in a 2026 MRI methods paper, vendor-independent recipes for ordering scan views. The recipes let any chosen echo land at the center of the data space. In multi-shot sequences the echo placed centrally sets image contrast, yet commercial systems tie that choice to other parameters.

The constructions assign echo and shot positions across a chosen set of phase-encoding steps while avoiding large jumps near the center. Implementations in two RARE variants and in MPRAGE were tested in phantoms and in people. Shifting the center echo moved contrast weighting exactly as theory and simulation predicted, and artifact patterns matched the symmetry of each ordering. An interactive dashboard lets others reproduce the schemes, which fit common acceleration strategies.
pmc-13527968:
Winnie Nambi and ten colleagues survey HIV self-testing among nursing and medical students in eastern Uganda for a 2026 study. They questioned 384 university students about testing habits and preferences. The median age was 24. Self-testing lets young people check their status privately, which may raise uptake where clinic testing lags.

Fifty-five percent had used a self-test. A similar share said they would prefer self-testing in future. Privacy, confidentiality, and convenience were the main reasons given. Students who preferred clinics cited counseling and trust in result accuracy. Self-testing was linked with fourth-year study and having multiple partners, among other factors. The authors suggest tackling accuracy worries and counseling gaps to widen use.
pmc-13528068:
Diane Geindreau and four colleagues map research on the Making Every Contact Count program in a 2026 scoping review. The program trains health staff to use every patient contact for brief healthy-living advice. Searches covered three databases for work from 2010 to early 2026. From 304 records, twenty-two articles passed. All came from the United Kingdom and Ireland.

Studies looked at training, delivery, and views of staff, patients, and students. Most outcomes were attitudes and barriers, not health results. Quality and reporting varied widely. Gaps included working conditions, how much advice is enough, and cost-effectiveness. The authors warn that evidence for a cousin approach, screening plus brief referral, cannot simply transfer. They call for stronger trials in varied settings before wide claims are made.
pmc-13528168:
Xue Zhou and seven colleagues build a timed, targeted drug system for a deadly ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. The cancer is high-grade serous carcinoma. The target is PLK1, a cell division switch. Its blocker, Bi2536, halts the cycle and triggers cell death in lab tests. The team noticed PLK1 levels rise and fall with the daily clock.

They wrapped the drug in a shell fused from ginger vesicles and tumor cell skins. The shell homes to the tumor and adds chemical attack of its own. In mouse grafts the system beat free drug clearly. Giving doses at the daily PLK1 peak helped even more. The authors unite three ideas: a strong target, a smart carrier, and clock timing. They pitch the mix for cancers where gene-based options run out.
pmc-13528768:
Hoang and co-authors pool research on heart failure in older adults who face homelessness. Knowing how common heart failure is in this group is key to fair care design. Older people without stable housing often miss routine heart checks and medication support that keep the condition stable.

The team ran a systematic search of databases including MEDLINE for past studies. Their meta-analysis combined prevalence and risk data across those studies. The pooled picture shows the burden of heart failure in homeless older adults. It also highlights gaps in care that housing and health services could jointly address.
pmc-13530368:
Feabie Mendiaz and colleagues test in 2026 a combined repair for torn shoulder labrum tissue in rats. Surgeons created a Bankart tear in the right shoulder of each of 50 rats, then groups received stitching alone, a growth factor, bone marrow stimulation, or both additions. Healing checks ran over eight weeks with weekly walking analysis.

Marrow stimulation alone drew almost no repair cells to the tear. Adding the growth factor multiplied cell arrival sevenfold and improved tissue building and sugar-rich matrix staining. Walking recovery was strongest in the combined group. The pairing offers a candidate upgrade for human labral repair.
pmc-13530868:
Caner Öksüz and colleagues test whether blood type shapes fate in Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The tick-borne virus kills a fraction of its victims, and host factors are poorly mapped. The team reviewed one thousand one hundred forty-three confirmed patients treated at one Turkish center over nine years.

Overall, eight point five percent died in hospital. Blood groups A, B, AB, and O, positive and negative alike, showed no meaningful differences in death, intensive care need, viral load, or tick exposure history. Two pancreatic enzymes differed slightly between groups, and nothing else did. In adjusted analysis, blood group still predicted nothing. The authors conclude ABO and Rh status are dead ends for prognosis in this disease, and multicenter prospective work should look elsewhere.
pmc-13531768:
Yan Feng and co-authors present a 2026 case of a rare bone-forming cancer growing under the skin of a Samoan man buttock. The 45-year-old noticed a painless lump growing for a year before care. Scans showed a large, well-bordered mass with no contact with bone, an unusual spot for this tumor type.

Surgery removed the mass, and microscopy found aggressive spindle cells making bone-like material, confirmed by marker staining. Cancer reached the deep cut edge, yet the patient declined further therapy and was lost to follow-up. The report stresses full testing even for harmless-looking surface lumps.
pmc-13532868:
Sophie A Rosser and colleagues tested whether parent and child reports of food allergy quality of life can swap for each other after oral immunotherapy. Published in 2026, the study pooled 86 parent-child pairs and 14 parent-teen pairs from three trials of peanut, egg, or milk immunotherapy, with scores taken twelve to twenty-four months after treatment. Questionnaires capture allergy life quality from parent, child, and teen viewpoints.

Parent and self reports correlated moderately, yet agreement stayed limited, with gaps beyond clinically acceptable thresholds. The instruments therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable, even as children age through follow-up. The authors urge trials to keep reporter types distinct when tracking life quality after immunotherapy. Readers get a methods warning: correlation alone does not license swapping scores.
pmc-13536768:
Maïva Faye-Ropaul and Carine Khalil interview French nursing home professionals about trusted persons in a 2026 study. French law lets adults name a trusted person to voice their care wishes if they become unable to speak for themselves. Fourteen directors, doctors, nurses, psychologists, and managers were interviewed between 2021 and 2022. Accounts were analyzed to build an explanatory model of daily collaboration.

Professionals described constant balancing among patient needs for safe and dignified care, family needs for support, and their own needs for legal safety and workable routines. Confusion about the system, impaired residents, and family strain at the end of life shaped that balance. Practices for informing families and involving trusted persons varied widely. The authors suggest teaching families early, before admission.
pmc-13536868:
Zhen Li and co-authors study quality of work life among bowel cancer survivors who returned to work in a 2026 survey at a Chinese hospital. A total of 290 survivors answered questionnaires between January and May 2023 covering work life quality, coping styles, and social support. Group comparisons and combined models searched for traits tied to better or worse work life after cancer treatment.

Average work life scores left clear room for gain. Higher family income, active coping, and fuller use of social support tracked with better scores, while avoidant coping tracked with worse scores. Survivors who paid costs directly, held basic resident insurance, or lived with a stoma also scored lower. The authors advise personal support that spots money strain, insurance type, and stoma needs early in return-to-work planning.
pmc-13538168:
Natalie Simon and co-authors published a 2026 study of who starts psychiatric drugs after a craniectomy, the removal of part of the skull, and how to flag the risk. Psychiatric illness after such surgery is underexplored in past work. Physical scores rule the follow-up, and no risk tool was available. The team reviewed the records of one center for five years.

Over a hundred cases of top-of-skull surgery were included. A third of all patients were on psychiatric drugs afterward. Of those with no past psychiatric diagnosis, over a sixth were started on new psychiatric drugs. No single factor stood firm in the joint analyses. A shrinkage-fit tool kept four soft marks: a higher consciousness score, fewer past illnesses, greater age, and a lower anesthesia grade. The tool was tuned with bootstrap checks inside the data set.
pmc-13538668:
Vijaya Bhaskar Sadu and colleagues design a deep learning model for outlining lower spine structures in MRI scans in a 2026 study. Accurate outlining of vertebrae and discs guides diagnosis and surgery, yet precision usually costs heavy computing. The network pairs multi-scale attention blocks with adaptive feature selection across pyramid levels and gated links between encoder and decoder. Training used 215 expert-labeled lumbar scan volumes.

Overlap scores beat three established rival models by clear margins, and boundary error measures improved by roughly a fifth to a quarter over the best baseline. Quality held steady across all spine levels and discs, with ablations crediting each new block. Training time and memory stayed manageable. The authors position the model for surgical planning and diagnostic support.
pmc-13539868:
Daniel Falkstedt and six co-authors ask whether easing physical workload mid-career lowers the risk of disability from muscle and joint disorders. Their register study was published in twenty twenty-six. Sweden's records allow whole-population tracking.

Over one point seven million workers were followed from twenty six to twenty nineteen. Workload in nineteen ninety and twenty five was scored from job matrices, and changes were classed by direction. About two in each hundred workers became disability cases. Any drop in workload, compared with staying high, came with lower risk. The finding supports moving strained workers to lighter duties before damage becomes permanent.
pmc-13540068:
Manoj P Shettigar and four colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether wavy undulations in the pigment layer at the back of the eye warn of a tear in that layer. Tears are a damaging complication of wet age-related macular degeneration, a common cause of sight loss in older adults.

Records covered 936 eyes with the disease, of which 79 had documented tears confirmed by photographs and autofluorescence imaging. The wavy sign, nicknamed the oscillatory sign, appeared in just under half the torn eyes, giving modest sensitivity. Its strength lay elsewhere: it was almost never seen in eyes without tears, and its absence predicted an intact layer with high reliability.
pmc-13540268:
Hironori Katsuki and colleagues describe the demographics and psychosocial backgrounds of patients overdosing on a common cough medicine in Japan. Their 2026 multicentre prospective study enrols patients across eight emergency departments.

Seventy-eight patients were included, with median age twenty and over four fifths female. Most were socially active, yet about two thirds said the overdose aimed at suicide or self-harm. Many learned about overdosing through social media or internet searches. Most bought the medicine at retail stores. About three fifths of screening respondents scored moderate or higher on a drug abuse test. The study compares younger teenagers with older patients to guide prevention.
pmc-13540868:
Yuejia Liu and seven colleagues catalogue, in a 2026 genome study, a family of gene switches in wild jujube, a hardy tree valued in dry regions of China. The R2R3-MYB family helps plants grow and answer environmental stress, yet its membership in this species was unmapped.

Ninety-one family genes were found scattered unevenly across twelve chromosomes, mostly switched on in leaves. Family growth came mainly from segmental duplication under conservative selection. Thirteen genes tied directly to water shortage responses and to the drought hormone abscisic acid. Four genes, ZjMYB5, ZjMYB53, ZjMYB57, and ZjMYB85, emerged as core drought responders with tissue- and time-specific patterns, offering breeding targets.
pmc-13541568:
Abhinav B Anand and Ketan Rajawat surveyed AI use in the heart-rhythm lab. Published in 2026, the review covers tools that read heart signals, images, and anatomy to guide rhythm spotting and treatment. In the electrophysiology lab, AI aims to cut reader-to-reader spread and sharpen the hunt for faulty heart tissue.

Pairing AI with heart CT and MRI scans gives tissue slices, wall measures, scar maps, and channel hunts for fast lower-chamber rhythms. AI-guided maps of spread-out signals and focal drivers in atrial fibrillation showed steadier sessions and hopeful early results. Each patient's digital twin lets teams test plans and ideas without putting patients at risk. The authors flag limits too: models can falter on new centers and patient mixes, so workflows still need human care.
pmc-13541768:
Tang and co-authors test whether antibodies that mimic the human ACE2 receptor can keep neutralising SARS-CoV-2 as the virus keeps mutating. Most antibodies fail when the spike's receptor-binding region changes shape. A receptor mimic, though, grips exactly the patch the virus cannot afford to change, since it must still latch onto ACE2 to infect cells. Their 2026 study challenged a panel of such antibodies against recent variants, measuring killing power, binding strength, and the physical interface in structural detail.

One antibody, VIR-7229, held up best, potently neutralising the original strain and three major variant waves while keeping considerable activity against the newest lineages tested, KP.3.1.1, XEC, and a descendant of XEC. Binding assays and structural analysis showed its grip on the spike essentially intact despite the accumulated mutations around it.
pmc-13542168:
Jin Shao and colleagues model river flows in a 2026 hydrology study. The project is a water diversion in China. It links the Yangtze River to the Han River. The lower Hanjiang also loses water to a national transfer project. Judging each project's true effect is hard. The projects overlap on the same river.

A watershed simulation combined all the pieces. It included the new link and the national project. It also included a side diversion and the dam chain. The team then reran the system without the new link. The incoming water failed to offset the national withdrawal. Most of it served the side diversion instead. Flow steadiness in the lower river did improve.
pmc-13542268:
Jun-Eul Hwang and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study identifying a circulating protein, LGALS3BP, as an active driver of liver injury during sepsis rather than a passive marker of illness. Sepsis is the body's damaging overreaction to infection, and it frequently harms the liver. Blood levels of the protein climbed in two mouse models of sepsis, and its production rose in several organs, most notably the liver itself.

Forcing liver cells to make extra LGALS3BP worsened injury, raised liver enzyme levels, and cut survival. The protein primed liver cells for pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death, by switching on a signalling chain that activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. An antibody that neutralised the secreted protein calmed that chain and protected the cells. Blocking this protein could therefore become a treatment strategy for sepsis-related liver failure.
pmc-13543468:
Huamei Tang and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a fetus found before birth to carry a newly described duplication of part of chromosome 6, spanning bands 6p25.2 to p22.3. Duplications of this arm are rare, and about a quarter of reported cases include heart defects. This fetus had a functional single ventricle together with persistent truncus arteriosus, a severe combination where the heart's outflow fails to divide. The authors say it is the first such pairing reported with a pure duplication of this region.

Testing showed the extra segment had been inserted within the chromosome and came from the mother. Comparing published cases, the authors point to the chromosome's tip, the last bands of the p25 region, as the likely critical zone for heart and lung-artery problems. Two duplicated genes, RIPK1 and FARS2, are proposed as possible modifiers of the heart defects and flagged for future research.
pmc-13543568:
Öykü Akkaş and colleagues published a 2026 survey of what final-year medical students in Izmir, Turkey, know and feel about autism spectrum disorder. Across four universities, 748 sixth-year students described their training, information sources, and confidence, and completed validated scales for autism knowledge and societal attitudes. Two thirds had attended at least one autism training session, and a quarter had joined follow-up of autistic patients.

Despite that exposure, about thirty-nine percent said they were not confident managing a suspected case, and over eighty percent wanted more clinical observation of autism built into the curriculum. Students who had examined patients, received extra training, or simply knew someone autistic scored significantly higher on both knowledge and attitude measures. Book learning alone, the authors argue, is not enough: direct contact with autistic people is what turns information into competence.
pmc-13543768: Yuru Sun and his team pull out two new gamma-lactone goods with acts that fight burn from a fungus that lives in mangrove trees. The goods, named alterlactones A and B, came from an Alternaria kind that lives in mangrove plants. One known kin good came. The team set their build with light tests. Those tests took in NMR, mass tests, and math on bent light. Both new goods showed strong acts that fight burn in lab strength tests. The first was a bit more strong than the next.
pmc-13544868:
Anjusha and colleagues examine an overlooked burden of Wilson's disease, the inherited copper overload disorder that damages liver and brain: sexual health. Their 2026 cross-sectional study assessed 87 patients, men and women split by whether disease was active or in maintenance, alongside 63 healthy controls. It used a standard sexual experience scale plus depression and anxiety questionnaires and a Wilson's disability rating.

Men's sexual scores did not differ significantly between disease phases or against healthy men, a null the authors report plainly. Women's story differed: those in the active phase scored markedly worse than women in maintenance and healthy women alike, with both gaps statistically significant. In both sexes, worse sexual function tracked with greater overall disease disability, but not with the amount of copper spilled in urine at diagnosis, the classic toxicity marker. The authors call for registries and newer copper biomarkers.
pmc-13547168:
Ishaan Dharia and co-authors asked in 2026 whether inflammation of the defunctioned rectum during staged colon surgery predicts later inflammation of the small cuff of tissue left at the pouch join. Their review covered 281 patients with ulcerative colitis who had a three-stage pouch operation at one hospital between 2008 and 2020, all with at least one later pouch examination.

About a quarter showed diversion proctitis, the inflammation in question, on the removed rectum specimen. Those patients needed rectal treatment between stages more often than others. Rates of later cuff inflammation, the main outcome, were statistically indistinguishable between the groups, at roughly 19 percent against 14 percent. The authors conclude the early inflammation signals treatment need but not later cuff trouble.
pmc-13548268:
Sanina and colleagues lay out a protocol for a cross-border chronic pain campaign. Their protocol paper from twenty twenty-six covers the Ems Dollart border region. Chronic pain affects roughly one in six adults there. Lower incomes and physical jobs raise the burden locally.

The campaign teaches modern pain science to the general public. It targets common myths about pain causes and management. A before-and-after design will judge campaign effects. Dutch and German communities both sit inside the study region. Health literacy gaps form part of the problem addressed. Large public campaigns are rarely evaluated this carefully. Results may guide pain education in other border regions.
pmc-13548668:
Elaheh Lael-monfared and colleagues analyze more than six thousand animal bite cases in Sarakhs County, Iran, in a 2026 cross-sectional study spanning 2017 to 2024. Bites threaten rabies and cluster where people live close to animals. Records from rabies prevention centers supplied the case census, and the team examined who was bitten, where, when, and by what.

The yearly rate approached eight hundred bites per hundred thousand residents. Nearly four in five victims were male, students were the largest occupational group, and most bites happened in villages during spring afternoons. Dogs caused nine in ten bites, almost all of them domestic animals, and legs took most injuries. Statistical links tied bite frequency to age, sex, job, season, time of day, animal type, and injury site. The authors target education at rural communities and schoolchildren.
pmc-13549168:
Benjamin Claytor and colleagues review the intertwined conditions of thymoma and myasthenia gravis, in a 2026 clinical article. The thymoma is a tumor of the gland behind the breastbone, the commonest in that chest compartment. Roughly a fifth to a third of patients with one develop myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune muscle weakness. Nearly all such patients carry antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, and their weakness tends to be widespread and stubborn.

Contrast CT scanning is the workhorse for finding and sizing the tumor. MRI and PET play supporting roles. Surgery is advised for every thymoma, since all are considered malignant. Keyhole approaches now match open surgery for early stages, with fewer complications. The review covers preparing stable patients, the small risk of new weakness after surgery, and added drug and radiation treatment for advanced tumors. Returning weakness, it notes, can signal recurrence.
pmc-13550268:
Yukihiko Nakajima and colleagues describe a corneal infection that hid behind the mask of a viral inflammation for months, in a 2026 case report. A forty-eight-year-old contact lens wearer arrived with a painful red eye, a cloudy swollen cornea, and inflammation inside the eye. Yet she showed none of the classic signs of Acanthamoeba keratitis, a parasitic infection of lens users. Virus tests on eye fluid were negative, so steroids were given for presumed viral endotheliitis.

Scrapings later found no microbes by microscope, culture, or genetic testing, and the cornea kept necrotizing despite revised anti-infective treatment. At thirty-four weeks, the dead corneal tissue sloughed off on its own. Under the microscope, that tissue held the double-walled cysts of Acanthamoeba, finally proving the diagnosis. The authors warn that this infection can mimic inner-eye inflammation and defeat standard sampling.
pmc-13550568:
Seyed Karim Irani Takleh and colleagues dose wheat with three organic compounds to find recipes that hold yield together under water stress, in a 2026 two-year field study. Fulvic acid, humic acid, and amino acids were combined at several rates in a split-factorial trial on the Taktaz cultivar, under both normal watering and drought. Nearly every measured trait responded to the three-way interaction of the ingredients.

Under normal irrigation, high humic acid alone or paired with a moderate amino acid rate stood out as stable winners. Under drought, the full trio at high rates, six liters of fulvic acid, three of amino acids, and twelve of humic acid per hectare, performed best. Correlation networks across both years repeatedly favored moderate fulvic acid with high humic acid. The authors say raising organic inputs helps wheat regulate its metabolism against drought.
pmc-13551868:
Jia Shi, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a rare metabolic disorder that impersonated viral brain inflammation in a young child. The six-year-old boy arrived with headache, vomiting, intermittent fever, and lethargy, and MRI showed swelling injury in white matter and the corpus callosum, the bridge between brain halves. Steroids helped briefly, yet imaging changes persisted, prompting metabolic and genetic workups.

Tests found markedly raised sarcosine levels and two different mutations in the SARDH gene, confirming hypersarcosinemia, an inherited disorder of amino acid breakdown. Folic acid and a vitamin B12 form were started, with partial imaging improvement the authors caution may not be caused by treatment. They present the case as a first report of this presentation pattern, needing confirmation.
pmc-13551968:
Emily R Edwards, leading fourteen colleagues, published a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of dialectical behavior therapy adapted for justice-involved veterans. Contact with the criminal legal system precedes a large share of suicide deaths in the United States, yet few treatments address legal involvement and suicide risk together. The adapted program, DBT-J, was built specifically for at-risk veterans facing both problems.

The multisite trial will compare treatment approaches, and the protocol was registered in July 2023 under the identifier printed in the article. Beyond the comparison, the paper details design choices around veteran culture, suicide risk assessment and management, and keeping participants engaged. The authors offer those lessons for anyone building programs for similarly at-risk groups, since the trial's results are not yet reported.
pmc-13552168:
Roua Faroun leads a team with a case of Askin tumor and Ewing sarcoma. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a girl of twelve. She had thigh pain and swelling for four months, with a limp.

Askin tumors are rare and grow from the chest wall zone. Ewing sarcoma is a top bone cancer in kids and teens. Sound scans of both thighs pointed to Ewing sarcoma at first. A CT scan was done at the same time for more detail. The gene swap that marks this cancer is set out. Such a first show in the femur is rare.
pmc-13553268:
Vanessa Neto and co-authors pool what marks a thyroid lump as cancer, in work published in 2026. Thyroid lumps are common, most of all in women and older adults, yet few are cancer. The team searched four data banks and kept near two hundred studies. About a quarter fed pooled math on traits named in at least five studies.

Male sex, a family past of thyroid cancer, and higher gland signal levels each raised cancer odds. Several scan traits did too, from dark, solid lumps to gritty spots and ragged edges. Older age and larger size cut odds instead. The authors urge joint use of these traits before needle tests.
pmc-13554268:
R Nareshkumar leads a five-author team designing energy-saving routes for wireless sensor networks in a 2026 study. Sensor nodes run on small batteries, and clumsy routing drains them fast. Their framework learns when nodes should sleep or wake, based on leftover energy and position. A hybrid search method, blending whale and wolf pack strategies, picks cluster leaders and stable multi-path routes.

Simulations showed about ninety-eight percent of data packets arriving safely. Total energy use stayed low while data flow at the base station held strong. Paths were judged by stability, leftover energy, and link quality before use. The authors argue the blend beats older routing rules on lifespan, delivery, and fairness across the network.
pmc-13555868:
Yao Huang leads a nine-author team automating measurement of leaf pores in melon plants in a 2026 study. These pores, called stomata, govern how plants breathe and lose water, yet counting them by hand is slow. The team built a melon image set with more than eight thousand labelled pictures. Their model pairs a vision transformer with attention heads that swap information flexibly, plus a module sharpening channel detail.

Detection precision ran high on the melon test set, topping ninety percent at loose overlap. Oval fitting then measured pore length, width, count, and area automatically. Those measures agreed closely with hand measurements by expert counters. The model also transferred fairly to cucumber, watermelon, pumpkin, and loofah, though each test set was small.
pmc-13556668:
Sajjad Hussain and co-authors make magnetic nanoparticles by a green combustion route and test them as a caffeine sensor. Their 2026 paper starts from a regulatory need: caffeine is common in food and drink, and high levels can harm health, so its level needs accurate checks. Standard sensors can lack sensitivity and stability in messy real samples.

The particles are a strontium-tin ferrite with a hexagonal crystal shape. X-ray tools confirmed the crystal phase and probed the local atomic layout, while microscopes mapped surface and size. Coated onto an electrode, the particles gave the sensor both magnetic and electrochemical traits. The authors present the platform as a more sensitive and selective way to measure caffeine in complex products like drinks and foods.
pmc-13557868:
Joyce W. Y. Chan and four colleagues reported in 2026 the first results for a robotic bronchoscopy system that confirms, live, whether its needle truly sits inside a lung nodule. Older navigation methods reach the target area yet can drift from the scan's map. The new system updates lesion position with digital tomosynthesis during the procedure. Data were collected prospectively on 27 nodules in 25 patients treated in a hybrid operating room between late 2023 and late 2024.

A cone-beam scan afterwards confirmed that the tool was inside or touching the lesion in nearly all nodules, with the needle centred in about six of ten. Diagnosis was secured in a strong majority of cases, and no complications occurred. The authors say real-time confirmation answers the main weakness of earlier robotic systems.
pmc-13558668:
Shanmei Li and four colleagues treated in 2026 a crumbly mixture of red clay and tungsten mine tailings with two plant gums to stop it falling apart in water. Such mixed soils erode fast, and pond covers built from them fail early. Specimens dosed with xanthan or guar gum at several levels were cured for up to twenty-eight days across three moisture contents. They were then tested for disintegration. Imaging tools probed pore water, chemistry, and fabric.

Both gums stretched the time to full disintegration sharply, and guar gum at modest doses kept samples from ever fully breaking down during testing. Wetter and longer-cured amended soils resisted even better, with cumulative breakdown falling to a few percent in the best cases. Microscopy showed hydrogel networks coating grains, bridging clumps, and shrinking pores. The authors offer the treatment for stabilising tailings in place.
pmc-13559568:
Tang and colleagues ask whether clearing circulating tumor DNA from the blood can serve as an early sign that a cancer treatment works, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Circulating tumor DNA, fragments shed by tumors into blood, falls when therapy succeeds. Drug developers hope trial-level clearance rates could replace waiting years on survival data. The review pooled trial results and stress-tested the link with cross-validation, checking predictions against held-out trials rather than the data that built them.

The cross-validated association was strongest for progression-free survival, at 0.41 on the reported scale. It was weaker for overall survival at 0.26, and negative for recurrence at minus 1.66. The survival signal came from just eight palliative or metastatic trials. Post-treatment DNA status still predicted individual outcomes across endpoints. Tang concludes clearance remains an exploratory signal, not a validated endpoint for approving treatments.
pmc-13561168:
Yu and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on methods in a meta-analysis of electrical acupoint stimulation for shivering after anaesthesia. The treatment, shortened to TEAS, sends mild current through acupuncture points on the skin. Miao and colleagues had pooled trials and found far less shivering, but Yu questions how firm that evidence is.

Yu notes the search combined stimulation terms with shivering terms only, so trials reporting nausea outcomes without stressing shivering could be missed. That gap makes the nausea findings look stronger than the search can support. Most pooled trials also hid how patients were assigned or who knew their group, which can inflate benefits. With only one trial clearly blinding both patients and assessors, Yu urges more cautious conclusions.
pmc-13562068:
Marta Ruiz-Solana and colleagues report a 72-year-old man whose right hilar lung lesion, spotted on CT during follow-up after coronary surgery, proved to be a pulmonary hamartoma. It was diagnosed by needle sampling through the airway. Their 2026 case report showcases endobronchial ultrasound-guided aspiration for a centrally placed benign tumor, a spot where hamartomas, usually peripheral, rarely sit.

The scan showed a partially calcified, fat-containing mass beside the right main bronchus. Bronchoscopy found no growth inside the airway, but ultrasound displayed a well-defined, mixed-echogenicity lesion with bright punctate spots and shadowing behind it. Needle aspiration proceeded without complications. Cytology and cell block analysis confirmed hamartoma, the commonest benign lung tumor. The authors argue the ultrasound-guided technique is a safe, effective way to settle the nature of central lesions and spare patients bigger surgery.
pmc-13562268:
Rachel Trotter and three colleagues test a standard enhanced recovery protocol for metabolic bariatric surgery at a Midwestern community hospital. Their 2026 pre-post quality study weighs patients treated before and after the set pathway replaced patchy local habits. The many-part protocol unified care across the whole surgical path, from prep through discharge.

Opioid use after surgery fell sharply once the protocol began: the median need dropped from eighty morphine milligram equivalents to twenty-two and a half in the comparison. Nausea and vomiting rates and length of stay, however, did not change clearly. Use of the protocol ran high, at 89.4 percent of planned elements in the audit. The authors conclude that unified care around surgery cut opioid needs safely in a community setting, and they back wider use of such pathways in bariatric programs.
pmc-13562368:
Autumn Bertch and two colleagues report their centre's results using covered stent grafts to repair arteries torn or pierced by injury. Working from the inside of the vessel avoids large open wounds in already damaged limbs. Their 2026 case series covers nine adults treated between 2014 and 2025 at one hospital. Most injuries came from penetrating trauma, and most involved leg arteries. Records supplied injury details, procedure notes, and later outcomes.

Every repair succeeded on the day, and eight of the nine patients kept the limb. Three patients needed a further procedure, and clotting blocked the graft in two. Nobody died, bled from the repair, or developed an infection there. Among patients who could be checked at a median of two years, six of seven grafts stayed open. The authors call the approach workable while noting that nine cases cannot settle long-term durability.
pmc-13563168:
Shauket, Safeer, Ali, Mahmood, Pervaiz, and Okon profile teenage lifestyles in Bahawalpur, Pakistan in twenty twenty-six. Habits formed in adolescence shape lifelong health. Data from rural Pakistani districts are scarce. The team surveyed students at four public schools in one subdistrict.

Three hundred nineteen adolescents aged eleven to nineteen took part. A nine item score summarised diet, activity, and screen habits. Most students landed in the middle range, and none reached the top band. Girls scored slightly higher than boys. Only school grade independently predicted a better score. Screen time was high, produce intake low, and vigorous activity limited. The authors recommend school programs targeting those habits.
pmc-13563768:
Pengli Yang and four colleagues measure a metabolic sensor protein in children sick with infectious mononucleosis, the glandular fever caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The illness throws the balance between two T-cell camps out of kilter: inflammatory Th17 cells and calming Treg cells. Their 2026 case-control study enrolled 40 child patients and 37 healthy children matched for age and sex. Blood tests for the sensor, HIF-1α, plus its partner signals and cell counts painted the picture.

Patients carried more HIF-1α and the inflammatory signal IL-17A. Their Th17 ranks swelled, their Treg ranks shrank, and the ratio between the camps jumped. The calming signal TGF-β1 fell in step. Every link in the correlation web pointed the same way: the higher the sensor, the hotter the immune tilt. The authors propose HIF-1α as a gauge of severity and a hint that metabolic pathways could be drugged to restore calm.
pmc-13563868:
Ifeoluwa Eunice Adewole and eleven colleagues ask what rural Nigerian schoolgirls know about the HPV vaccine while the national rollout is under way. Nigeria added the vaccine to routine immunisation in October 2023, delivering through schools and communities. Their 2026 survey covered 441 girls at twelve secondary schools across three rural areas of Oyo State in May and June 2024, during the rollout phase. Questionnaires measured knowledge, beliefs, and self-reported vaccination, and models hunted uptake predictors.

Awareness stayed low: under three in ten girls had heard of cervical cancer, the virus, or the vaccine, with schools the commonest source for those who had. Only 41 girls, 9.3 percent, reported being vaccinated. A favourable view of the vaccine dwarfed knowledge as a predictor of uptake and willingness. Among the unvaccinated, half lacked information; others felt at low risk or feared side effects. The authors press for school-based messaging built around trust, not facts alone.
pmc-13564068:
Kameda and five co-authors describe care for one man with a hard-to-treat blood infection, in a case report from twenty twenty-six. The germ resists most drugs, so choices are few. The man was in his forties, had a high body weight, and needed a blood-cleaning machine for his kidneys. The infection came after a mix of germs had spread in his blood, belly, and chest.

The team paired two drugs and tuned the dose step by step. They had to work around a short supply of one drug as well. They also drained the source of the germs. The blood cleared and the infection did not come back. The team warns that one case alone cannot set a rule for all care.
pmc-13564268:
Slavica Ranković and six co-authors study how diet shifts links among minerals, fatty acids, and cell stress in rat liver. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The liver runs fat use, fat build, and energy balance in the body. They feed rats one of three diets for a month: fish-based, milk-based, or standard.

Liver samples are read for mineral levels, fat profiles, and stress marks. The milk diet shows the fewest links, close to none. The standard diet shows the richest web of links, with the fish diet next. Two metals stand out as top drivers of a stress mark, one in the fish group and one in the standard group.
pmc-13565168:
Alexandra Morar and six colleagues published a 2026 veterinary study of primary pulmonary carcinoma, lung cancer arising in dogs. The team examined two DNA mismatch repair proteins, MSH2 and MSH6, as possible biomarkers. These proteins fix copying errors in DNA; their loss is a known cancer signal in human oncology but was uncharacterized in canine lung tumors.

The affected dogs had a median age of 10.6 years. Sixteen tumors were adenocarcinomas and one was adenosquamous carcinoma, with papillary architecture the most common pattern. Stains for general epithelial and lung markers were positive in all cases. The researchers then related the repair protein staining to the tumors' pathological features, a first step toward prognostic markers in canine lung cancer.
pmc-13567568:
Xiuqing Li and eight co-authors test how branched chain amino acids, a supplement, affect nursing mice and their pups under normal or low protein diets. These amino acids feed into sugar and fat use and energy balance. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Mothers were split by lot into four groups after birth, with varied protein and supplement mixes. The low protein diet cut mother weight, pup growth, and sugar test response, while liver fat and stress marks rose. The supplement raised pup growth on the normal diet but cut food intake and pup growth on the low diet. Its metabolic effects also split by diet.
pmc-13568768:
Jackson Rajendran and colleagues test whether blood count ratios predict kidney injury in cardiogenic shock. Their multicentre study from twenty twenty-six uses an intensive care database. Kidney injury is common when the heart fails to pump enough. Cheap inflammation ratios might flag high-risk patients early.

All ratios came from one admission blood sample set. Kidney injury was defined by standard creatinine criteria. Several popular ratios and combined inflammation indexes were tested. pmc-13570268:

pmc-13571268:

pmc-13571368:

pmc-13572368:

pmc-13572568:

pmc-13573468:

pmc-13575768:

pmc-13576168:

pmc-13576368:

pmc-13576568:

pmc-13579068:

pmc-13580168:

pmc-13581268:

pmc-13582668:

pmc-13582768:

pmc-13583868:

pmc-13584068:

pmc-13586868:

pmc-13587468:

pmc-13588268:

pmc-13589568:

pmc-13591668:

pmc-13594468:
