Isabel D. Hermsmeyer, Ziru Li, and Ormond A. MacDougald review in 2026 how glucocorticoids, steroid hormones used widely as medicines, cause bone loss and reshape the marrow inside bones. Extra hormone, whether from long treatment or from the body making too much, raises fracture risk. It acts on bone-building cells, bone-keeping cells, and bone-eating cells alike, and it also swells the fatty tissue in marrow.

One main route is the damping of a growth signal called Wnt, which cuts bone building and lets marrow fat grow. The review covers drugs and plant compounds that aim at these paths, plus tiny parcels called vesicles that marrow cells use to pass messages. The authors also warn that many lab studies fail to report basic details, making results hard to compare, and they urge tighter methods in bone research.
pmc-13614968:
Caloni and Hartung wrote a 2026 review on using AI against fungal toxins in food. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that creep into grain and other foods. Standard lab tests are accurate but slow, costly, and expert-hungry. The review covers AI tools for spotting, forecasting, and curbing these toxins.

Detection systems using AI topped 90 percent accuracy in lab settings. Forecasting models scored between 75 and 99 percent across studies reviewed. Early control strategies reached 80 to 86 percent success in trials. Pairing AI with gene-level data could sharpen risk calls further ahead. Shared standards and openness remain the hurdles the authors stress most. Fewer animal tests could follow if the models prove trustworthy.
pmc-13615268:
Matthias Voß, Rodrigo J. Velasco-Guillen, and Philipp Beckerle compare in 2026 three ways of turning muscle signals into torque for lower-leg prostheses, tested in a virtual balancing task. Sixteen volunteers used signals from opposing lower-leg muscles to steady a computer pendulum that was knocked off balance. Four controllers were tried in random order: a simple proportional map, a muscle-model controller, and two versions adding simulated stretch reflexes at different strengths.

Every participant managed all four controllers. The muscle-model version gave steadier control with less effort, because its paired virtual muscles mimic how real tissue builds force. Adding reflex feedback, which injects a quick velocity-based response like the body's own stretch reflex, was tested for further gains. For prosthesis designers chasing control that feels natural, the study ranks the options with user strain counted, not just accuracy.
pmc-13615468:
Abhishek Pratap and co-authors run a phase 3 trial of a phone-based digital therapeutic for the negative symptoms of schizophrenia. These symptoms, above all lost motivation and pleasure, drive poor outcomes. No drug is approved in the United States for them in specific. Talk-based care can help, but access is thin and keeping patients engaged is hard. The app, CT-155, packs evidence-based psychosocial strategies into a phone program used next to drug treatment.

The CONVOKE trial ran at 66 sites in the United States from March 2023 to June 2025. Adults with negative symptoms, on up to two antipsychotic drugs, were randomized evenly to the app or a control. The design was double-blind, the standard for drug trials, applied here to software. The trial marks a shift: a prescription app tested with the same rigor as a pill.
pmc-13615968:
David N. Buckley leads a team introducing in 2026 a blood test called MammaTrace that watches for breast cancer's return by reading chemical tags on free-floating DNA in plasma. After curative treatment, stray cancer cells can linger unseen, called minimal residual disease, and later seed incurable spread. Most current tests need a piece of the original tumour; this one does not.

The team found tag regions tied to spread and recurrence by scanning DNA from patients with advanced cancer, healthy controls, and early patients who did or did not relapse. Those regions fed a targeted panel and a classifier, then the test was checked in 107 early-stage patients followed over time with repeated blood draws. Catching a return signal from blood alone could let doctors act months before a scan shows anything.
pmc-13616268:
Miran Joo leads a team studying how the share of ruthenium in four-metal alloy films changes their power as catalysts for splitting water to make hydrogen. The films mix gold, palladium, platinum, and ruthenium in one random crystal, and such mixed surfaces can beat single metals. A sputtered library of films covered a wide range of mixes, screened quickly for structure and for how well each drove the hydrogen-making reaction.

Three blends, carrying 4, 26, and 52 percent ruthenium, got close study. All kept the same cubic crystal pattern while their lattice spacing and defect patterns shifted with the mix. Local strain and chemistry at the surface, not just the recipe, steered performance. The map helps engineers tune cheap, mixed-metal catalysts by composition rather than by trial and error alone.
pmc-13616668:
Yehong Fang and colleagues study whether a glioma brain tumour's molecular marks and its location jointly shape a patient's thinking and feelings before surgery. Modern tumour classification runs on molecular features, yet how much they explain mood and cognition, beyond where the tumour sits, was unknown. The team enrolled 101 newly diagnosed patients and 52 matched healthy controls, all given a full battery of thinking and emotion tests.

Analysis first split patients by tumour site, then tested molecular and clinical links within each site group, and finally modelled the interplay across everyone. Early results show no simple across-the-board molecular effect, pointing instead to effects that depend on anatomy. For care teams, the message is that a tumour's address in the brain frames what its genes do to the mind, so assessments should read the two together.
pmc-13617868:
Yusuff Adebayo Adebisi and three colleagues examine long COVID among adults in Scotland through the lens of disability, asking whether people whose daily activities are already limited report the condition more often. They pooled the nationally representative Scottish Health Surveys of 2023 and 2024, covering nine thousand three hundred twelve adults with complete data. Activity limitation was graded as none, a little, or a lot.

Overall long COVID prevalence was about seven and a half percent, climbing in steps from about five percent among people with no limitation. It rose to about nine percent among those limited a little and over fourteen percent among those limited a lot. Adjustment for age, sex, education, deprivation, and smoking barely dented the gradient, which amounted to roughly nine extra cases per hundred adults in the most limited group. The authors urge surveillance that keeps disability breakdowns and services that reach people with limitations.
pmc-13617968:
Areen Tawil and three colleagues survey radiation safety for medical students attending orthopaedic surgery, where live X-ray imaging exposes everyone in the theatre to ionizing radiation. Students from two United Kingdom medical schools in their clinical years answered a nine-item questionnaire over ten days in December 2023. Seventy students responded, reporting what teaching they had received, what protective gear they actually wore, and how safe they felt.

The gaps were wide. Only half wore a lead apron that fit properly, and about two in five said their apron fit badly. Consistent thyroid shield use was reported by about two in five, while nearly half never wore one. Just sixteen percent had received formal radiation safety teaching before attending theatre, and a third felt unsafe around the imaging equipment. The authors recommend structured teaching before theatre exposure and guaranteed access to correctly fitted protective equipment.
pmc-13618168:
Zijie Gao and twenty colleagues uncover a metabolic circuit that helps glioblastoma, the deadliest brain tumor, survive chemoradiation and recur. They found palmitic acid, a common fatty acid, pooling in the tumor's oxygen-starved zones, where it pushes cancer stem cells toward an aggressive mesenchymal state. It also recruits a suppressive immune cell population, together building a recurrence-friendly niche. A fat-tagging modification on a key glycolysis enzyme sits at the circuit's center.

An enzyme called ZDHHC12 attaches the fatty tag to lactate dehydrogenase A at one specific site, boosting its activity, rewiring sugar metabolism, and conferring treatment resistance. Tagged enzyme also ships out in tiny vesicles that reprogram incoming immune cells into suppressive partners. The team identified rutin, a plant flavonoid, as an inhibitor of this tagging step, and blocking it re-sensitized the tumors to chemoradiotherapy. They propose the circuit as a target against post-treatment recurrence.
pmc-13619068:
Mohammed Bendaoued and eight colleagues design a flower-shaped, four-port antenna for 5G millimeter-wave wireless, small enough for fixed access gear. Multi-antenna systems boost speed and uptime but suffer interference between elements packed closely. Their answer is a hybrid defected ground structure: a central round slot ringed by four trapezoidal cut-outs in the ground plane, beneath four matching elliptical radiating elements set for dual-band use.

The radiator measures twenty-one millimeters square and resonates near twenty-seven and thirty-eight gigahertz, covering slices of two standard 5G millimeter-wave bands. Gain reached seven and a half decibels at the upper band. Simulations in a standard tool predicted strong isolation and diversity. The team built a prototype whose tests confirmed the results. For engineers building compact 5G terminals, the work offers a tested recipe for keeping four antennas apart.
pmc-13619768:
Kenichi Nakajima led a 2026 imaging study that cleans up a measurement problem in dual-tracer heart scans for ischemic heart disease and cardiomyopathy. Scanning fatty-acid metabolism and blood flow at once with two tracers is valuable. Their energy signals bleed into each other, muddying the washout rate that tracks how fast the fatty-acid tracer leaves heart muscle. The team built a simple correction from fixed energy spill ratios measured in phantoms and patients.

Applied to 38 scans from 36 patients, the correction used a thallium spill ratio of 0.12 and tracked uncorrected washout rates very closely, with mean differences near one percent for both flat and tomographic images. Normal-versus-abnormal calls stayed the same in 92 percent of flat-image studies and 95 percent of tomographic studies. Nuclear cardiology readers get a practical, standardized fix: uncorrected values roughly suffice, but correction matters when numbers must be trusted across datasets.
pmc-13620868:
Tetsuro Ohba and six colleagues report a frightening bleed during spine surgery on a seventy-eight-year-old woman with degenerative scoliosis, a sideways curve that develops with age. She was having multilevel side-approach fusion from the second to the fifth lumbar level. While a trial implant was placed at one level, massive vein bleeding began, with blood loss nearing four liters.

Angiography found no arterial leak, pointing to a vein. The wound was packed and heavy resuscitation stabilized her. Three days later, surgeons working with a vascular specialist found the culprit. A small vein branch near the big body veins had been torn away, most likely pulled by the stretching of the correction itself. A sealant patch and steady pressure stopped it. Staged back fixation finished later without trouble, leaving good alignment and no nerve damage. The authors urge slow distraction and early vascular help.
pmc-13621268:
Paulo Simão and three co-authors report a case of new lupus with kidney and brain signs after a COVID-19 vaccine. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, deals with systemic lupus erythematosus. The mRNA vaccines have shown strong safety on the whole. Rare self immune events have been told of, among them new lupus and kidney flare. Their patient was a healthy adult with no past such illness.

Shortly after the shot, severe kidney lupus and brain linked lupus showed at once. No other trigger was found, and the timing hints at a vaccine sparked immune slip. Cause cannot be proved from one case. Readers learn to watch for this rare but grave pattern so care can start fast.
pmc-13623368:
Denise Saquetto leads a team translating and validating a questionnaire on genital self-image into Brazilian Portuguese. The Genital Self-Image Scale, in a twenty-item form, measures how women feel about their genitals, which shapes self-esteem, sexual confidence, and willingness to seek care. A translation must keep meaning, not just words, so the team followed a five-step adaptation method.

Two translators produced Portuguese versions, a merged draft was translated back into English by native speakers, and an expert panel checked wording and cultural fit. Fifteen women pre-tested the draft for clarity. The final version was given to 148 women in three groups, including women with severe pelvic organ prolapse and women who had never given birth. Scores separated the groups as expected, and repeat testing showed the scale was stable and consistent. The authors offer it as a tool for Brazilian clinics and research.
pmc-13626368:
Chunfeng Shi and colleagues cook soil's dark matter in a sterile flask to learn how clay steers its birth. Humic-like substances, the backbone of soil carbon, can form without life through the Maillard browning reaction, and the amino acid glycine drives it. The team varied glycine across five doses with glucose and catechol as partners, in the presence of two common clays, montmorillonite and kaolinite, whose crystal structures differ sharply.

More glycine pushed aromatic, complex fractions onto the clay surfaces, leaving simpler material in the water, and the effect ran stronger with kaolinite. Montmorillonite, by contrast, kept the reaction's turning point steadier across doses. A middle glycine dose best built up humic-like acid. Such mineral fingerprints may help predict which soils lock carbon away longest.
pmc-13626768:
Yang-Tai Lin and colleagues describe a 61-year-old man whose lung disease hid behind a misleading wash test. He had asthma, two months of growing breathlessness on effort, and a worsening wet cough, with blood eosinophils, an allergy-linked cell type, clearly raised. Scans showed the hazy patches at the lung edges that typify chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, a rare condition named for those very cells flooding lung tissue.

The wash from his airways, though, held mostly neutrophils and only six percent eosinophils, and antibiotics changed nothing. A surgical lung biopsy settled it: dense eosinophil invasion with an organizing pneumonia pattern, and steroid treatment worked well. Discordant wash results, the authors warn, should not overrule a strong clinical picture when biopsy can answer.
pmc-13627068:
Yuqing Wang and co-authors mapped how positive and negative feelings connect in women being treated for breast cancer. Patients often face anxiety and depression, yet many also report benefit finding and posttraumatic growth, a sense of positive change through hardship. Instead of scoring each feeling alone, the team surveyed 707 patients at five hospitals in northern China and built a network of how the dimensions of all four measures move together.

One dimension, personal growth within benefit finding, sat at the center of the network and also bridged the positive and distressed clusters. Relating to others and worldview were other key bridges, while anxiety and depression were tightly linked to each other. The authors suggest support care should strengthen these bridging resources.
pmc-13627668:
Marco Túlio Pacheco Coelho and José Alexandre Felizola Diniz-Filho argue in a 2026 essay that macroecology needs both theory-first and data-first reasoning, not a contest between them. Macroecology studies broad patterns of life across space and time, from local populations to global ranges, speciation, and extinction. One tradition derives models from general principles, while another builds models around data, and the authors place these on a continuum of formalization rather than opposite poles.

Their case is that the field grows stronger when theories and models swap roles, each constraining, synthesizing, and sparking the other. That exchange matters because patterns at large scales do not simply add up from local processes, and new regularities can emerge only at broad scales.
pmc-13628668:
Pazur wrote a solo bibliometric analysis of a Zagreb dental school, in work from twenty twenty-six. Bibliometrics counts and maps scientific output: papers, journals, languages, and topics over time. Such audits show how an institution research profile evolves.

The sample held more than fifteen hundred papers from the School of Dental Medicine, University of Zagreb, indexed in a major database from twenty oh six to twenty twenty-two. Productivity indicators covered document types, publication years, journals, and subject categories, plus open access status. The analysis gives school leaders a factual base for research strategy.
pmc-13629568:
Yue Lang and four colleagues ran a pilot study hunting for chemical clues to Parkinson's disease. They combined blood profiling with genetic causal analysis. The first phase was small: fifteen patients and ten healthy controls. It found hundreds of differing compounds among the thousands detected.

Machine learning and pathway analysis singled out one candidate compound. Caffeine handling emerged as the top pathway. Genetic analysis using large Finnish data then suggested a link. Higher predicted levels of the candidate tied to lower Parkinson's risk. A caffeine-linked compound showed the same tie. An inflammatory protein may carry part of the link. The authors stress the work is early and idea-forming. The tiny profiling sample demands care.
pmc-13631568:
Catarina Pedro and four colleagues investigated a protein called TTF2, which helps switch genes off while a cell divides. Gene activity stops during division and must restart at the right moment afterward. The team used polymerase-specific tools and labeling of new RNA to watch what TTF2 does across division. Their focus was whether one factor can control several kinds of RNA production at once.

Removing TTF2 left extra transcripts stuck to chromosomes during the middle of division, mostly from one polymerase. A surprise followed later in division, when a different polymerase restarted too early and began making ribosomal RNA ahead of schedule. Parts of the nucleolus, the cell structure that builds ribosomes, were also pulled in too soon. That loss of timing left nucleoli broken up in the next cell stage, showing how one control protein guards orderly restart.
pmc-13634168:
Denis George, Nicolas Van Rompaey, and Emmanuel Noel measure how differently anesthesiologists respond to the same blood pressure drops, in a cohort study published in two thousand twenty-six. Low blood pressure during surgery is linked to organ injury. Treatment thresholds are studied; individual habits are not.

Adults in elective non-heart surgery who recorded at least one very low pressure reading formed the cohort. Each hypotensive episode was the unit of analysis. The outcome was whether ephedrine or phenylephrine was documented for that episode. Adjusted models separated clinician variation from case mix and episode order. Wide unexplained variation would argue for protocols; narrow variation would vindicate professional judgment. Either way, quantifying the spread is the paper's contribution.
pmc-13635168:
Bastien Lechat and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study of a mattress-based monitor for sleep apnea used over many nights. Sleep apnea, where breathing repeatedly stalls in sleep, is usually judged from a single lab night. Severity swings between nights, so one night can mislabel patients. The team gave one hundred people with suspected apnea an under-mattress sensor that estimates breathing pauses at home for three months, alongside the standard lab test.

Ninety-two people supplied data. Nearly all reached fourteen valid nights in the first month, proving the zero-effort setup works. Against the lab test, the home device sorted moderate-to-severe disease with solid accuracy. People it flagged while the lab test did not tended to show wild night-to-night swings, short lab sleep, and little back-sleeping time in the lab. The authors say multi-night home monitoring can rescue missed diagnoses.
pmc-13635468:
Ruta Virsinskaite and ten colleagues built and validated a cheap exercise device that works inside an MRI scanner. Exercising during a heart scan reveals hidden weakness, yet commercial exercise machines for scanners are costly and rare. Their device is disarmingly simple: two half-pipes on a wooden base, with small weights tucked into knee socks. Patients alternate bending and straightening their legs to a beep that speeds up to raise the workload.

Twenty people, half healthy and half with pulmonary arterial hypertension, exercised on both the new device and a standard ergometer in random order. Peak measures on the two machines correlated well, from oxygen use to stroke volume, though the simple device reached lower peaks. Both machines cleanly separated patients from healthy volunteers on key measures. The authors present their build as an affordable, portable way to spread exercise heart scanning into more clinics and studies.
pmc-13644268:
Mary Ellen Mackesy-Amiti and three colleagues present a 2026 report on developing SRI-AVLOD, a training that fights drug use and HIV stigma among Tajik labor migrants in Moscow. Migrants who inject drugs face stigma inside their own diaspora on top of HIV risk.

Focus groups and interviews with sixty-five migrant workers and eighteen health workers shaped a four-session course for traditional community leaders, the avlod heads. Two groups of eight leaders piloted it in Tajikistan in September 2025 and rated it highly on acceptability and usefulness. Their stigmatizing attitudes fell after training, and early reports of spreading the message at home were favorable.
pmc-13649068:
Silvia de Andres Quevedo and three colleagues tell of a man in his sixties who sprang a rare leak of milky lymph into his belly days after a chest drain. The drain had been placed for pus round the lung. Scans then found liver cirrhosis that no one knew he had.

The lung pus grew two germs tied to tooth rot. The belly fluid was rich in fats, which proved the leak. Cirrhosis jacks up lymph pressure, so a small tear from the chest work could spill lymph into the belly. Low-fat food and plain support care dried the leak up for good. The authors urge teams to watch for this odd side effect in liver patients.
pmc-13649268:
Federico Cortese and five colleagues, in a 2026 review, pin down dyadic capability: how a stroke survivor and their carer, as a pair, turn facts and tools into real acts at home. Classes raise readiness, but home life is where care is won or lost.

The team searched seven databases to May 2025, screened over two thousand records, and kept 22 studies. They merged the yield with a formal concept study. Three marks define the concept: self-belief, bounce-back strength, and drive. Gains ran from more self-rule to less carer strain. No tested scale yet measures the pair trait, a gap the authors flag for nurse research.
pmc-13649468:
Hongqing Ma and six colleagues built a chart tool to predict survival for bowel cancer that has spread to both the liver and the lungs at the same time. Care choices for this group are hard, and few tools guide them. The team drew cases from a large United States registry and checked the tool on 65 patients at a Chinese hospital.

Nine facts, from age and tumour size to spread in bone and whether spread sites were cut out, fed the chart. It sorted risk well in all three groups and split patients into clear low- and high-risk bands. An early look hinted that cutting out the main tumour helped mainly the low-risk band. That hint needs proof in fresh studies.
pmc-13649568:
Joseph Hamley and a large team of colleagues present a method for mapping how single genetic variants affect gene regulation. Millions of variants are linked to disease, but most sit outside genes and their mechanisms stay hidden. The twenty twenty-six paper introduces a Micro Capture-C platform that reads chromatin structure one allele at a time. It can connect a variant in a regulatory element to the gene it controls.

The team applied the method to 405 regulatory elements tied to immune diseases in CD4 T cells. They uncovered a previously unknown gain-of-function mechanism: a variant creates a new CTCF binding motif. That motif blocks a super-enhancer from reaching the SESN3 gene, raising autoimmune risk. The platform can also test variant effects directly after genome editing.
pmc-13649968:
Feng Liu and seven colleagues built a deep learning tool that measures scarring and growth zones across whole liver tissue slides from rats dosed with a liver toxin. Hand scoring of such slides is slow and varies between experts. Their tool was trained to mark two targets: fibrous scar tissue and one pooled class of growth and tumour zones set by pathologists.

For each slide, the tool reports how much of the tissue each target fills and how many split zones it finds. A treated group dosed with the toxin plus hydrogen showed less of both lesion types than the toxin-only group. The authors are blunt about limits: training used a patch-level split with no clean audit trail, so outside proof is still owed before any care claims.
pmc-13650468:
Megan E Austin-Cherry and one colleague review fifteen years of group prenatal care around the world. In that model, eight to twelve pregnant people at similar stages meet together for health checks, interactive learning, and community building. They meet this way instead of attending brief one-to-one appointments.

Across diverse settings, women in group care consistently reported more empowerment, social support, better mental health, stronger health knowledge, and closer adherence to care, alongside lower rates of gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia. Babies gained indirectly through mothers' improved habits, including more breastfeeding and timely immunization. Providers described closer patient relationships, yet they also flagged the skill needed to run groups well, plus time and workload strains. The authors conclude that group care works broadly, provided programs fund training and resources, and they ask for long-term studies of children's health.
pmc-13650768:
David J Romano and fourteen colleagues demonstrate a method for recording X-ray scattering with energy resolution, something ordinary imaging detectors cannot do. Scattering maps how a molecule's electrons are arranged, and adding the energy each X-ray loses would merge scattering with spectroscopy, potentially filming a reaction's path through its electronic states.

Their filter is a thin zinc foil placed between the target and the detector. X-ray pulses from a free-electron laser fluctuate naturally from shot to shot, and a ghost-imaging algorithm exploits that randomness to reconstruct the full scattering pattern by energy and angle. Fluorescence from the foil itself must be corrected away. The team proved the method on a sulfur fluoride gas, whose large scattering signal suits the demanding technique. They argue that brighter future X-ray sources will widen the approach to smaller molecules and real reaction watching.
pmc-13650968:
Alexander Muacevic and six co-authors catalog the gene changes behind second-line drug resistance in tuberculosis isolates, knowledge that decides which backup drugs can still work. Fast change testing matters because multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is spreading. Its treatment hinges on fluoroquinolone antibiotics and older injectable drugs.

A commercial line-probe assay was run on 85 drug-resistant strains spanning several resistance classes. About a third carried fluoroquinolone resistance, and a smaller share shrugged off the injectables. The final sorting found a large pre-extensively drug-resistant group. Among fluoroquinolone-resistant strains, one change in the gyrA gene dominated, present in just over half, with two others trailing. Injectable resistance sat on the rrs gene. No resistance changes of the eis promoter type showed up alone. The authors argue such gene maps speed correct regimen choices.
pmc-13660868:
Ferreira and co-authors relate a soccer fitness test to endurance markers in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test is a standard shuttle test for team sport stamina. The team asks which lab measures best explain test distance in professional players, and whether acid handling in muscles plays a role.

Twenty-six professionals took the field test and a treadmill exercise test. Distance on the field test tracked most strongly with maximal aerobic speed and peak oxygen uptake. Two submaximal thresholds showed no link. Midfielders tolerated acid buildup better than defenders, a positional difference the authors flag. Buffering capacity itself did not separate positions.
pmc-13668468:
Nazila Ameli and six co-authors train a deep learning system to flag mispronounced sounds in children's speech recordings. Speech sound disorders are common and can affect school and social outcomes, but expert listening assessment is slow and varies between raters. Automated screening could triage children where specialists are scarce.

One hundred participants aged six to eighteen recorded eighteen hundred words under a protocol focused on fricative sounds. Two expert speech-language pathologists labeled each recording, with a third settling disagreements, and reliability was measured carefully. A pretrained transformer speech model was fine-tuned on the cleaned audio for present-or-absent classification. Imbalance tricks included augmentation, weighted sampling, and focal loss. Performance was judged on a held-out test set.
pmc-13688368:
Seung-hak Lee and four co-authors teach a computer to grade newborn lung disease in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Respiratory distress syndrome troubles premature babies, and its severity guides care. Doctors grade it from chest X-rays by eye, a slow and variable task. The team gathered over twenty-three thousand radiographs labeled by trained neonatologists. Images were split by patient into training, tuning, and outside test sets.

One network outlined the lungs; a second sorted severity into five grades. Most grades landed exact or one step off, and detection of the disease was strong. Heat maps showed the model watching the right lung zones. Such tools could support small hospitals at night. Neonatologists and medical AI teams are the readers.
pmc-2658868:
Excoffier, Laval, and Schneider present version three of Arlequin, a software package for the genetics of groups. The package joins basic and advanced methods for analysing genetic data from populations in one place. It computes standard measures of genetic diversity and estimates how common each gene variant and combination is.

The package also tests whether variants depart from expected patterns of independence. Such tests reveal migration, selection, and population history. By putting many analyses together in one shared design, the package became a workhorse for studies of human ancestry and species care.  Field teams use it to judge how cut off an at-risk group is.
pmc-3930868:
Abraham, Pedregosa, Eickenberg, and co-authors show how machine learning with scikit-learn can serve neuroimaging analysis. Brain imaging analysts increasingly turn to statistical machine learning methods. Their main virtue is handling high-dimensional datasets, such as brain activation images or time series recorded at rest.

Supervised learning is typically used to decode brain states or predict clinical traits from scans. The authors connect the general-purpose scikit-learn library to neuroimaging workflows. That bridge let neuroscientists use well-tested machine learning tools without building their own from scratch.  Decoding contests adopted the pipeline as a baseline for comparing new algorithms fairly.
pmc-4823868:
Zheng, Bao, Guo, and their team profiled circular RNAs in 2016. Circular RNAs are a widespread class of RNAs that form closed loops instead of straight chains. They may regulate gene expression in eukaryotes, but human circular RNAs were still largely unknown.

The team generated sequencing data from six normal tissues to build a profile of these molecules. They found one abundant circular RNA, circHIPK3, that regulates cell growth. It acts by sponging multiple microRNAs, soaking them up so they cannot silence their targets. The work showed circular RNAs are not rare oddities but active players in gene control.
pmc-5788068:
Yuxin Chen and colleagues introduced SOAPnuke, software for cleaning high-throughput sequencing data, in 2017. Raw reads from sequencers contain adapters and low-quality bases that must be removed first. Older tools often lacked key functions or ran too slowly on huge files.

SOAPnuke combines quality checks and filtering in one program and speeds the work with a map-reduce design. It can spread a job across machines when files get very large. Clean input data protect every later step from garbage results. Labs that sequence at scale use tools like this as their first gate.
pmc-5847168:
Jan Bottcher and colleagues reported in 2018 how natural killer cells help fight tumors. A dendritic cell type called cDC1 is vital for anti-tumor immunity. Tumors rich in these cells are more often rejected and respond better to therapy.

Working in mice, the team shows that natural killer cells release signals that draw cDC1 cells into tumors. Without those signals, the dendritic cells stay scarce and immunity weakens. The finding links two immune cell types in one chain of defense. It suggests that boosting killer cell signals could make cancer immunotherapy work for more patients.
pmc-5891568:
Cecilia Prinsen and colleagues wrote the COSMIN guideline for reviews of patient-reported outcome measures in 2018. Such reviews differ from reviews of treatments and can be very complex. Reviewing one questionnaire can mean separate reviews for each measurement trait.

The guideline walks authors through each stage, from searching for studies to rating the body of evidence. It pairs with the COSMIN checklists for bias and content validity. Clear steps help readers see how final grades were reached. Teams planning a measurement review can use it as a full roadmap, which raises the standard of published reviews.
pmc-5994068:
Thomas Einarson, Annabel Acs, Craig Ludwig, and coauthors reviewed heart disease in type 2 diabetes in 2018. Heart and vessel disease is a frequent companion of diabetes. Its share among patients had been growing over time.

Searching a decade of studies, the team estimates how common cardiovascular disease is in adults with type 2 diabetes. Roughly a third of patients in the pooled studies had such disease. Heart attacks and stroke dominate the totals. The figures remind clinicians that managing diabetes means managing heart risk at the same time, not after it in everyday practice.
pmc-6421268:
Daniela Parada Venegas, Marjorie De la Fuente, Glauben Landskron, and coauthors reviewed short-chain fatty acids and gut immunity in 2019. Inflammatory bowel diseases arise from tangled genetic, immune, microbial, and environmental causes. A disturbed gut community is now seen as a likely driver.

Gut microbes make short-chain fatty acids when they ferment fiber. These products feed gut lining cells and help keep immune responses calm. Too little of them may weaken the barrier and stir inflammation. The review links diet, microbes, and bowel disease through this chemistry, and weighs therapies that aim to restore it.
pmc-7619468:
Annelise Binois-Roman and three colleagues investigate a mass grave of sheep in Louvres, France, dating from the seventeenth to nineteenth century. Sudden livestock die-offs shaped food security in past communities, yet archaeology had never tied one burial ground to a named disease agent. The deposit held nine complete, joined skeletons of mostly older sheep, unbutchered but bearing marks of skinning, and the bones showed good health with no visible cause of death.

Ancient DNA work supplied the missing answer, with evidence pointing to sheeppox, supported by written history and veterinary reasoning. Settling a cause of death centuries later shows what combining genetics, animal bone study, documents, and animal medicine can recover from a silent pit of skeletons. The case also gives historians a dated, located outbreak to set against the paper record of epidemics.
pmc-7857468:
Mansi Joshi and two colleagues use a treadmill that jerks underfoot to study why stroke survivors fall. A sudden trip-like shift of the standing surface tests reactive balance, the emergency response that keeps a person upright. Fourteen stroke survivors who could walk in the community were compared with older adults of similar age and with young controls, each group facing the same unexpected perturbation.

Every group lost balance forward and took a first recovery step of similar length. By the time that step landed, stroke survivors held a less stable body position and bent their trunks further forward than the young group, with weaker support from the stepping limb. Pinpointing where the recovery breaks down, at landing rather than at step size, gives therapists a specific target: train the landing, not just the step.
pmc-9635468:
Tarfah Al-Warhi and co-authors test two new compounds against cancer cells and a growth receptor that tumors lean on, in work the text dates to 2023. The catalog lists 2022. From a family of pyridine and pyrimidine candidates, compounds 8 and 14 stood out across seven cancer lines. The pair were checked for antioxidant effects, cell death patterns, and cell cycle disruption in a liver cancer line.

Both compounds blocked the receptor's normal form and the drug-resistant mutant form credibly. Computer docking showed how they sit in the target, and absorption modeling rated their drug-like prospects. The authors present the pair as leads worth developing against resistant disease.
podcast-joerogan-WZ1Dm-dcl68:
Journalist Amber Lyon joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 470. Lyon reported for CNN before leaving with sharp claims about how stories get steered and killed. Her visit is an exposé of media manipulation from a person who worked inside a major newsroom.

She tells Rogan what she saw: sponsors shaping coverage, war stories softened, and her own reporting on protest movements spiked. Rogan asks why more reporters do not speak. The episode is a young show's early statement of a theme it never dropped, that the news is a product, told here by a defector from the factory floor.
poems-pg1568:
William Ernest Henley published his Poems in a first edition in January 1898. The David Nutt edition of 1907 proudly lists the impressions that followed: ten printings in under a decade. Henley dedicated the book to his wife. A bust portrait and a Shakespeare motto about the summer's flower front the volume. Fitting emblems for a poet who wrote his best work from a hospital bed and a shortened life.

Henley lost a leg to tuberculosis of the bone and wrote his famous hospital verses from an Edinburgh infirmary, turning pain into discipline. His best-known poem, Invictus, with its unconquerable soul, became a byword for defiance in the face of fate. The steady reprinting tells the story of his hold on readers: a disabled editor and fighter whose verse taught a generation to keep its head unbowed.
redi-generation-of-insects-1668:
Francesco Redi, doctor to the dukes of Tuscany, ran these famed trials on the birth of insects in 1668. The text here is the 1909 English version by Mab Bigelow. In Redi's day most men held that maggots were born from rot itself.

Redi set meat in jars, some open, some sealed, and some veiled with fine gauze. Flies laid eggs on the gauze, and no maggots grew in the sealed jars at all. The clean result struck the first strict blow at the claim that life springs from rot. His method of matched jars is still taught to young students.
skene-four-ancient-books-wales-vol-2-186:
William F. Skene was a Scots sage of the Celts and their past. His Four Ancient Books of Wales came out in two books in 1868. Book Two holds the texts and their English dress. The four books are old Welsh tomes with poems from the dark age of Britain.

Poems tied to Taliesin, Aneirin, and the bards of the old north fill the text. Gods, kings, and wars of the Britons crowd the wild verse. Skene prints the Welsh text with his dress at hand for the reader. The set is a chief source for the first verse of Wales.
skene-four-ancient-books-wales-vol1-1868:
William F. Skene published the first volume of The Four Ancient Books of Wales in 1868. The book gathers the oldest Welsh poems, the verse that stands behind much of British legend. Skene printed the Welsh texts with English renderings for scholars and general readers.

Taliesin sings praise songs for the princes who paid him. The Gododdin mourns a war band that rode south to its doom. Llywarch Hen, an old man, laments his lost sons and his own cold age. Together these poems open a window on heroic Wales, the bardic world from which the Arthur stories grew.
smyth-antiquity-intellectual-man-1868:
C. Piazzi Smyth argued that man is far more old than most held in On the Antiquity of Intellectual Man, out in 1868. Smyth was a star chief who read dates in stone and sky. He draws on ice ages, star shifts, and the dates writ in the Great Pyramid to push man's dawn far back in time.

His case lands in the midst of the row sparked by Darwin. Church and lab men both felt its force. Smyth holds faith and deep time can stand as one. The book shows his stone school at its most bold.
solomon-in-all-his-glory-1768:
Solomon in All His Glory, printed in London in 1768, carries the subtitle The Master-Mason. Its author claims to be Thomas Wilson, master of a lodge. The exposé centers on the third degree, the Master Mason's own, and it preserves key evidence for the Hiramic legend's ritual form in the 1760s.

The death and raising of Hiram, the master builder of Solomon's temple, form the degree's drama. Wilson's text tells that story in its full ritual shape. Exposés remain the chief printed witnesses to how the legend was worked before official rituals stabilized. For students of the master myth, this pamphlet is a prime source. Solomon's glory here belongs to the builders, and to their slain master.
sterne-sentimental-journey-1768:
Laurence Sterne published A Sentimental Journey, his tour of France and Italy, in 1768, his last work in print. The unfinished travel narrative named sensibility and founded sentimental travel literature in the English tradition of prose. Sterne died weeks after its first volumes charmed London readers with Yorick's gentle, wandering heart abroad.

Parson Yorick drifts from Calais to Paris, collecting small scenes of feeling over sights and facts. A monk refused alms, a caged starling, and a peasant's dead ass become tests of his heart. He flirts, weeps, and moralizes by turns, and the journey breaks off mid-sentence at his death. The book taught Europe to value the traveler's inner weather over maps, miles, and monuments en route. Its influence runs through travel writing and the novel of feeling for a hundred years.
stowe-men-of-our-times-1868:
Stowe gathered short lives of leading men in Men of Our Times, printed at Hartford in 1868. The title page lists Lincoln, Grant, Garrison, Sumner, Chase, and Greeley among its subjects. Eighteen steel portraits illustrate the book, which was sold by subscription only.

Generals, statesmen, and orators of the Civil War years fill the pages, from Farragut and Sherman to Douglass and Beecher. Stowe wrote for young readers and aimed to teach character as much as history. Each sketch asks what made its man great and what boys might learn from him. The volume shows Stowe the moral teacher at work.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Return to Naples, part of Adventures in the South in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, uses the 1894 London edition translated by Arthur Machen, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter Eight brings Casanova before Cardinal Passionei in Rome. The cardinal keeps him standing, since his vast hall holds only the chair he writes in. He warns that the Pope does not like him, and doubts the Pope esteems him either.

Passionei then calls the Pope a fool in plain Italian and names Cardinal Tamburini as the only man fit for the tiara. Casanova notes the morsel down at once, delighted to have heard a cardinal speak so freely. At dinner he asks Winckelmann who Tamburini is, and hears of a man respected for virtue and character. The chapter promises the Pope himself and arrival at Naples. Readers get Vatican politics at their most indiscreet, served as table talk.
tob-0168:
Snorri Sturluson, an Icelandic chieftain of the thirteenth century, wrote the Prose Edda to keep Norse myth alive for poets. Christian Iceland was forgetting the old stories, and skaldic verse needed them. Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur's translation is the classic English version.

A deluded king hears the gods' tales from three mysterious hosts: the making of the world from a giant's body, Thor's adventures, and the fires of Ragnarok. Later parts teach the kennings, the riddling phrases of Norse poetry. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, Brodeur's Snorri remains the handbook through which most readers meet the Norse gods.
tob-10468:
Part One of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica, the Prima Pars, asks the biggest questions first. Aquinas proceeds by questions: each topic opens with objections, states a contrary authority, gives a reasoned answer, and replies to the objections. The method is as famous as the conclusions.

Does God exist, and what is God like? How did creation unfold, including angels, the six days of Genesis, and the nature of human beings, body and soul? Aquinas argues each step from Scripture, earlier thinkers, and reason. Readers watch the most orderly mind in medieval thought at full stretch, building a system meant to hold together.
tob-4068:
Robert Ernest Hume, a Harvard Sanskritist, gathered the Thirteen Principal Upanishads into one English volume. Isa, Kena, Katha, and their companions appear with his notes and introductions. Generations of students learned Hindu philosophy from Hume's pages, and many still start there.

The Katha sends a boy to argue with Death about what survives the grave. The Chandogya teaches that the self and the world's ground are one: thou art that. Hume renders the Sanskrit with care for both sense and music. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the volume remains the classic school text of the Upanishads in English.
tob-4168:
Ernest Renan published Vie de Jésus in French in 1863, after traveling in the Holy Land, and scandalized Europe. His life treats Jesus as a historical figure, an incomparable Galilean moral teacher, rather than through the creed's claims. Written beautifully, in the landscapes where the story happened, the book sold hundreds of thousands of copies.

Renan's Jesus is a genius of religious feeling whose legend grew after his death, a portrait built from critical history and nineteenth-century sentiment alike. Churches condemned it; the reading public devoured it. By making the historical Jesus a public question for ordinary readers, Renan changed religious debate permanently, and the French original preserves his celebrated style unfiltered.
ufo-symposium-house-1968:
Scientists took the UFO question to a House panel in the summer of 1968. The Symposium on Unidentified Flying Objects, held July 29 by the Committee on Science and Astronautics, prints their talks in full. Allen Hynek, Carl Sagan, and James McDonald stood among the speakers.

The men split: some held the reports hid a true wonder worth a hunt, others saw error and noise. Leo Sprinkle and James Harder added their own cases and claims. The talks form the science counterpoint to the Condon study of the same year. The file shows the UFO fight argued at its highest level.
un-ga-res-a-69-68: Kathmandu hosts the UN office praised in Resolution A/69/68, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific was set up in 1987 and renamed a year later. From its Nepal base it gives staff support, on request, to peace and disarmament work agreed by states of the region. The text notes the centre's move into full work on the ground and the Secretary-General's report on it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/68 comes from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session in 2014. It concerns the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific, based in Kathmandu. It thanks Nepal for hosting and funding support. It lists the Centre's recent regional workshops and conferences. It appeals for voluntary contributions. Those are the Centre's only resources for carrying out its disarmament work across the region.
un-sc-res-1368: Catalogue data places Resolution 1368, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 2001. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1468: Security Council Resolution 1468 survives here as an official-record transcription prepared by English Wikisource. Resolutions are the Council's binding voice: fifteen members, five of them permanent, voting on a single agreed text. Readers get the decision exactly as issued, with its opening findings followed by the numbered paragraphs that carry its force in international law and practice.
un-sc-res-1568:
Cyprus's force was reshaped as it was renewed in October 2004. The Secretary-General had reviewed UNFICYP after the failed referendum. On 22 October 2004 the Council backed his plan to change its size and working methods. It then extended the mandate until 15 June 2005. Work on missing persons had just resumed after years of pause. The Council welcomed that step. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift all limits on the force. They also had to restore the military position at Strovilia as it stood before June 2000. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, led by 1251 of 1999. The leaner force that resulted still patrols the buffer zone.
un-sc-res-1668: Resolution 1668, a 2006 act of the Security Council, is kept in this collection in its official-record form. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Inside, the members speak first in the language of concern and recollection, then in the language of decision. That shift in register, preserved intact, is the signature of the genre.
un-sc-res-168: Filling the office of Secretary-General is the sole business of Resolution 168, adopted without dissent on 3 November 1961. The General Assembly had fixed a term for the office ending on 10 April 1963, and the post had fallen vacant partway through it. The Council recommends that the Assembly appoint U Thant as acting Secretary-General for the unexpired portion of that term. The record is three lines long.
un-sc-res-1768:
Congo sanctions were extended for only ten days by the Security Council on 31 July 2007. The Group of Experts had filed its final report under resolution 1698 (2006). A Council mission had visited Kinshasa on 20 June 2007. Armed groups and militias still plagued North and South Kivu and Ituri. Illegal weapons kept flowing into and within the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures of resolution 1493 (2003), as widened by resolution 1596 (2005), to 10 August 2007. The transport controls ran for the same short span. So did the money and travel measures against embargo breakers. The Group of Experts' mandate was extended over the same period. The ten-day bridge kept the regime in force without a gap while the Council finished work on the longer renewal that followed in resolution 1771 (2007).
un-sc-res-1868: Kept as Resolution 1868, a Security Council act survives in this collection through a transcription of the UN's official record. The document carries the standard signs of its kind: the Council acting under the Charter, prior texts recalled, steps decided in numbered order. The whole is preserved, so nothing depends on a secondhand account of it.
un-sc-res-2068:
Children in war zones are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2068, adopted on 19 September 2012. Some armed groups kept harming children year after year. They recruited child soldiers, killed and maimed children, and attacked schools and hospitals. Naming and shaming alone had not stopped them. Four Council members abstained, the first such split on this theme.

The Council says it stands ready to impose targeted sanctions on groups that keep abusing children. States should prosecute offenders in their own courts. The Council's working group on children and armed conflict must weigh, within one year, fresh ways to press repeat offenders. The text shows the Council shifting from warnings toward punishment for the worst abusers.
un-sc-res-268: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 268, entered in this catalog under the year 1969. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-368:
The United Nations Emergency Force in Sinai came up for a short renewal in 1975. On 17 April 1975 the Security Council kept the force for three more months. Its mandate now ran until 24 July 1975. The Secretary-General had reported on the force's work. The Council noted events in the Middle East with concern. Tension in the area, it said, remained high.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. That text demanded a ceasefire and a negotiated peace. The Secretary-General owed a report by the end of the term. It would cover events and the steps taken toward 338. The force stood between Egypt and Israel while diplomacy moved slowly.
un-sc-res-668:
Cambodia's long war moved toward a settlement in September 1990. The five permanent Council members had drafted a framework for peace. All Cambodian parties accepted it at Jakarta on 10 September. On 20 September 1990 the Security Council endorsed that framework. It praised the five powers for their work. The Paris Conference on Cambodia would turn the outline into a full settlement.

The Cambodian parties had agreed to form a Supreme National Council. That body would stand for Cambodia abroad during the transition. The Council welcomed its creation. The parties also pledged free and fair elections under United Nations supervision. The framework became the base of the 1991 Paris agreements. Those deals ended the war and set up a huge peace operation.
un-sc-res-68: Arms control led to a Council vote: Resolution 68, adopted on 10 February 1949 by nine votes to none, with two abstentions. The General Assembly had passed a text on conventional arms that November. It now needed study by the expert body built for that work. The Council sends Assembly Resolution 192 (III) to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. The commission is to act on it as its terms direct. The whole resolution is that single act of referral, a routine step in the early arms-control machinery.
un-sc-res-968:
Tajikistan gained a United Nations observer mission on 16 December 1994. The government and the opposition had stretched their Tehran ceasefire to 6 February 1995 at the Islamabad round of talks. A protocol set up a joint commission to watch the truce. The Secretary-General's report of 30 November set out a mission plan.

The Council established the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, UNMOT, on the Secretary-General's plan. It would serve for up to six months. Its life past 6 February 1995 depended on the ceasefire holding and both sides staying pledged to a settlement. The Secretary-General had to report on the mission's work and on the talks. His special envoy would keep pushing for national reconciliation. The parties had to work fully with the mission and guard its staff's safety and movement. Tajikistan had to conclude a status agreement with the United Nations quickly.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Within a day of the 11 September 2001 attacks, the Council answered. Terrorists had struck New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania, and the scale of the deaths was still becoming clear when members met on 12 September. The text is short and carries the shock of that moment.

The attacks are condemned in the strongest terms and named a threat to world peace and security. Sympathy goes to the victims, their families, and the people and government of the United States. All states are called on to work together to bring the planners, attackers, and sponsors to justice, and anyone who aided or sheltered them is warned they will be held to account.

Peace steps in Congo are welcomed on 20 March 2003, while atrocities in the east are condemned in the same text. Congolese parties had reached agreement in Pretoria on transitional arrangements. At the same time, a report on the Ituri region described grave abuses against civilians there.

Massacres and other systematic violations of human rights and aid law are condemned, including sexual violence used as a weapon of war. Abuses by the MLC, RCD-National, and UPC forces in Ituri are named, with a warning that there would be no impunity for those responsible. In filling key posts in the transitional government, the parties are also told to weigh each person's record and commitment to the peace deal.

Cyprus peacekeeping gets a careful review in Resolution 1568, adopted unanimously on 22 October 2004. The Council welcomed the resumption of work by the Committee on Missing Persons, which had restarted in August after years of inactivity. It also noted the Secretary-General's broader review of UNFICYP, the force present on the island since 1964.

Because conditions on the island still required it, and Cyprus agreed, the Council kept UNFICYP in place past December 2004, extending its mandate to June 2005. It took note of a calmer security picture and a judgment that fighting was increasingly unlikely to resume. Even so, the resolution treats the force as still necessary while a political settlement remains out of reach.

One judge of the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is allowed to finish a case he is already hearing, in this text of 10 April 2006. Responding to the Secretary-General's request, the Council confirmed that Judge Joaquín Canivell could keep sitting in the Krajišnik case beyond April 2006 until it ends. His total service would thereby pass the usual three-year limit for judges of his class, which the Council set aside for this case.

An acting Secretary-General for the United Nations is recommended on 3 November 1961. The office had fallen vacant, and the term fixed by the General Assembly ran until 10 April 1963. The Council recommended that the General Assembly appoint U Thant as acting Secretary-General for the unexpired portion of that term. Under the Charter, the Assembly appoints on the Council's recommendation, so this short text is the step that put him in the post.

Resolution 1768, adopted on 31 July 2007, extends Congo's arms embargo by just ten days. The experts monitoring the embargo had filed their final report, and the Council again condemned the illegal flow of guns into Congo and around its east. Militias in North and South Kivu and Ituri kept the whole region insecure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures, first imposed in 2003 and widened several times since, until 10 August 2007. A renewal this short is a scheduling device, not a policy shift: members needed the measures kept in force while they finished negotiating the regime's next, longer phase. The Council also noted its mission's June visit to Kinshasa.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended until 23 March 2010 on 23 March 2009. There is no purely military answer to Afghanistan's problems, it is stressed, and a broad approach is needed. A Council mission to the country in November 2008 informed the renewal, and elections were due later in 2009.

UNAMA's mandate is kept, and the mission and its head will keep leading world civilian efforts, under Afghan ownership. Priorities include support for elections, governance, aid coordination, counternarcotics, and regional cooperation. All Afghan and international actors are called on to work with the mission and to protect United Nations staff, whose freedom of movement is treated as essential.

Children in armed conflict are the focus of Resolution 2068, adopted on 19 September 2012. The Secretary-General's April 2012 report showed progress — thousands of children demobilized, action plans signed, some parties delisted. But in several conflicts parties kept recruiting and using children, killing and maiming them, and committing sexual violence, in open disregard of the Council.

The Council strongly condemns all such violations and demands an immediate end to them, including attacks on schools and hospitals and denial of humanitarian access. It tells states to bring perpetrators to justice at home or through international mechanisms. It repeats its readiness to adopt targeted, graduated measures against persistent offenders. Its Working Group on Children and Armed Conflict must, within one year, weigh a broad range of options for increasing pressure on those offenders. Annual reports continue, the next due by June 2013.

Portuguese forces bombed a village in Zambia in 1969, and the Council answered on 28 July that year. The village was Lote, in the Katete District of Zambia's Eastern Province. It stood near the border with Mozambique, which Portugal then ruled. Zambian civilians were killed in the attack, and property was destroyed.

The Council strongly censured the Portuguese attacks. Portugal was told to stop violating Zambia's territory and to end unprovoked raids at once. Zambian civilians kidnapped by Portuguese forces had to be released and returned. Those forces operated from Angola and Mozambique. Property taken from Zambian land also had to be given back. If Portugal failed to comply, the Council warned, it would meet again to consider further measures.

The Sinai buffer force gained just three months in the spring of 1975. On 17 April, the Council adopted Resolution 368. Thirteen members voted yes and none voted no. The force had been built by Resolution 340 in October 1973. It kept Egypt and Israel apart after the Yom Kippur War. Tension still hung over the area, the Council noted.

The text calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 at once. That 1973 order pairs a truce with peace talks. The mandate then runs to 24 July 1975. A report from the Secretary-General is due at the end. The short term fit the moment. Shuttle talks over a fresh pull-back in Sinai were then at their peak.

On 20 September 1990 the Security Council unanimously endorsed a framework meant to end the conflict in Cambodia. Five permanent members of the Council had drafted the plan after the 1989 Paris Conference stalled short of a full settlement. Cambodian parties accepted the framework at a meeting in Jakarta earlier that month.

Under the plan, a Supreme National Council would speak for Cambodia while the country moved toward free elections run by the United Nations. The resolution welcomed the parties' pledge to turn the framework into a complete political settlement through the Paris Conference. It gave UN backing to the blueprint that soon produced a transitional authority and Cambodia's first UN-run elections.

Arms control filled much of the UN's early agenda. Resolution 68, adopted on 10 February 1949, is a short housekeeping text on that effort. Nine members voted in favor. The Ukrainian and Soviet delegations abstained. The General Assembly had passed its own arms resolution the previous November.

The Council simply sent that Assembly text onward. Assembly Resolution 192 asked for work on conventional weapons. The file went to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. That body handled plans for limiting non-nuclear forces. The resolution shows how the two UN organs passed disarmament tasks between them in the Cold War's first years.

Civil war in Tajikistan is the setting for Resolution 968, adopted on 16 December 1994. The government and the Tajik opposition had signed a temporary ceasefire deal in Tehran that September and had just agreed in talks in Islamabad to extend it. A joint commission was set up to watch over the truce, and talks on settling the conflict were set to continue in Moscow.

The Council sets up the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan, called UNMOT, for up to six months. Its observers help the joint commission track the ceasefire, look into reported breaches, keep contact with both sides, and back wider peace work. The mission lasts past 6 February 1995 only if the truce is extended and both sides stay committed to peace talks.
vera-clavicola-1868:
La Vera Clavicola, the True Little Key, was printed at Milan in 1868. It is the Italian edition of the Grimorium Verum tradition, Italy's own true grimoire. Seventy-six sections set out its spirits and operations, rite by rite, for the magicians of the peninsula.

The Italian text follows its French sources while wearing a local cut. Conjurers get lists of spirits, their seals, and the hours and tools each rite requires. The Milan printing shows the grimoire trade alive in nineteenth-century Italy. Complete and unabridged, the Vera Clavicola served practitioners who wanted the Verum in their own tongue. It pairs naturally with the French True Grimoire.
welsh-triads-skene-1868:
Welsh lore was kept in threes: three names, three deeds, three fates bound in one short saying. Trioedd Ynys Prydein, the Welsh Triads, gathers hundreds of these brief groups. Two Victorian versions stand here, William Skene's of 1868 and the Rhys and Evans text of 1887.

The triads name heroes, battles, bards, and wonders of old Britain in terse, packed lines. Bards used them as hooks on which long tales and poems could hang in memory. Read in bulk, they map the whole world of Welsh legend. The paired translations let readers test one rendering against the other.
